16085-a-voyage-in-a-balloon-1852:
Jules Verne's short balloon piece first reached American readers in Sartain's Union Magazine in May 1852. It translates a French article from the Musee des Familles of August 1851. That piece was a family-magazine answer to a riddle. It differs from the later Hetzel version known as A Drama in the Air. The redactor's note carefully sorts out that publishing history.

The piece itself belongs to Verne's early science writing, when balloon flight still fired the public mind with wonder and argument. Readers meet a young Verne testing the mix of fact, fancy, and clear explanation that would make his name. The short text offers a charming first step into his world of voyages and machines.
16294-england-in-america-1580-1652:
Lyon Gardiner Tyler's England in America, 1580 to 1652, published by Harper in 1904, traces the first English colonies in North America. A portrait of Sir Walter Raleigh fronts the volume. Contents run from the genesis of colonization through the Gilbert and Raleigh colonies. The founding of Virginia, gloom and transition in Virginia, and social and economic conditions there follow. Maryland's founding and contentions follow.

Plymouth's founding and development, the genesis of Massachusetts, and its founding close the survey's early chapters. Tyler, a historian of Virginia, writes with scholarly clarity for general readers. Students of colonial America will find a solid, well-ordered introduction to England's American beginnings.
23280-the-shirley-letters-from-californi:
The Shirley Letters come from the California mines of 1851 and 1852. The text presented here sits within a larger historical volume, whose notes trace the first explorers' voyages along the coast. Those notes also cover the expeditions of Gálvez and Bucareli for settling California and founding its missions.

The volume adds a fresh index and a portrait, plus a Spanish map of the coast as known by 1791. Readers get gold-rush letters framed by deep Spanish colonial history. The mines are shown as only the newest chapter in a coast explored and claimed for centuries before.
31162-the-international-monthly-volume-5:
Volume five, number three of The International Magazine of Literature, Art, and Science, dated March 1, 1852, opens with a remarkable New York exhibition. At the Society Library, crowds gathered to see two small persons, aged about twelve or thirteen and eighteen, presented as Aztecs. Their elegant proportions and striking faces drew idlers, wonder-seekers, and serious students of human history alike.

The article sets the show against Mexico as a land still largely unknown, citing Kingsborough's collections, Prescott's history, and the travels of Stephens and Squier among ruined cities. As a magazine number, the issue captures mid-century America's fascination with ancient America, just as its ruins were first coming into view.
32945-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-febr:
The February 1852 number of Harper's New Monthly Magazine offers a broad cross-section of mid-century American reading. Jacob Abbott opens with the public life of Benjamin Franklin, and John S. C. Abbott follows with Napoleon Bonaparte, while other pieces cover the Syrian expedition, the Sublime Porte, and the Italian liberal Mazzini. Fiction, anecdote, and a child's history of King John's reign by Charles Dickens sit beside them.

A monthly record of current events from the United States, South America, and Europe closes the number, with an editor's table to round it off. Together the contents show a magazine trying to give its readers the world in one volume: history, travel, humor, and news, pitched to a general audience that wanted both instruction and entertainment.
4761-the-cossacks-a-tale-of-1852:
Leo Tolstoy wrote The Cossacks, A Tale of 1852, translated here by Louise and Aylmer Maude, in forty-two chapters. Chapter one finds Moscow hushed, with wheel noise rarely breaking the silence of a street deep in snow. Windows stay dark, the lamps stand unlit, and only church bells carried across town hint that morning is near.

The roads lie empty. Now and then a night driver's sled churns snow and grit toward a fresh corner, and there he dozes while awaiting a passenger. That still, wintry Moscow opening gives way to the Cossack country of the tale's title. Readers get Tolstoy's early novel of Moscow society left behind for the steppe, its horsemen, and a life governed by nature rather than drawing rooms.
a-voyage-in-a-balloon-1852: Jules Verne takes an early voyage in a balloon in this piece from Sartain's Union Magazine of May 1852, translated from the Musee des Familles of August 1851. The French original answered a July enigma, and the redactor notes that this version differs from Hetzel's later Un drame dans les airs of 1874. In this early work, with five illustrations by de Bar, the balloon becomes a vehicle for popular science in the family magazine.
arxiv-2412-00552:
Nascimento and co-authors extend a regular black hole solution in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The Hayward black hole avoids a central singularity by design. The team solves Einstein's equations with a nonlinear field, a cosmological constant, and a fluid of strings around the hole.

Whether the new solutions stay free of singularities hinges on a label value. The authors probe this with a curvature measure and by checking whether paths through spacetime can end abruptly. For one choice of the label, the regularity holds, and they work out its heat behavior: pressure, heat capacity, and critical points. Those traits shift with the charge and string settings, and phase changes are mapped through the equation of state.
arxiv-2412-01052:
Shi, Talak, Zhang, Jin, and Carlone present CRISP, a system that finds the pose and shape of an object from one color and depth image. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. CRISP does not need to know the object's class in advance. It pairs a shape model with a network that finds points in a fixed pose frame.

A second part fixes pose and shape errors that come from a gap in the data. A third part lets CRISP train itself at test time, using its own checked fixes as labels. Tests on three data sets show strong results. The self-training step can bridge a large gap, and CRISP can work on objects it has not seen.
arxiv-2412-01752:
Vedant Khandelwal, Vishal Pallagani, Biplav Srivastava, and Francesca Rossi combine fast intuition with slow logic to color graphs in a 2024 study. Graph coloring assigns labels so neighbors differ, a model for scheduling and allocation problems with strict constraints. Symbolic solvers are exact but slow, while language models alone fumble the precision such problems demand.

Building on an earlier architecture modeled on Kahneman's fast. Slow thinking, the new version adds refined metacognitive control that decides when to trust the quick neural guess and when to call the careful solver. Graph coloring serves as the test bed for the partnership.
arxiv-2412-02252:
Da Ma and co-authors present a memory saving method for large language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Long documents swell the key-value cache a model keeps while generating text. Older compression methods drop less relevant tokens outright, which can lose key facts and hurt quality.

Their method, called PoD, sorts tokens by importance and position. Tokens near the start and end of the context keep their full cache. Distant tokens instead share key states across nearby layers, since their attention patterns repeat. A light round of extra training adapts the model to the shared setup. Tests cut cache memory by up to thirty-five percent with no loss in quality.
arxiv-2412-02352:
Ethan Smith and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on fast personalization of text to image models. The common tool is LoRA, a small low rank patch trained per style or face. LoRA saves memory but not wall clock time: training still takes thousands of steps. Most user wants cover a small slice of what LoRA could learn.

Their route trains a hypernetwork that writes LoRA weights on demand. A prior over zones of interest shrinks the search space. The writer hits near instant setup for a new user input. Quality on set domains matches trained LoRA. The team frames priors as the missed lever in cheap tuning.
arxiv-2412-02752:
Aleksey Generozov and eleven co-authors explain a puzzling empty zone in the orbits of stars that circle our galaxy's central black hole. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. These S stars whip around the giant hole on tilted, stretched paths. Plotted by closest approach and stretch, they avoid one clear region.

The team models stars born as pairs far out that wander near the hole. The hole's tides rip most pairs apart, flinging one star and keeping the other. Slow nudges from the crowd of stars then reshape the kept star's orbit. Their simulations reproduce both the empty zone and the known spread of orbit shapes. Gaps remain in how many pairs start out, and in the nudging model. Still, the match shows S stars can read out the center's history.
arxiv-2412-02852:
Yang Zhang and seven co-authors slim down image-generating diffusion models without retraining. Their 2024 paper tackles the size of modern vision models. Bigger models cost more memory, money, and energy to run. Standard pruning usually demands costly retraining to heal the cuts.

The team learns a mask that marks which parts to drop, and the mask itself can be trained. A new goal scores pruning across the whole denoising path, not just one step. A checkpointing trick cuts memory during this training. On SDXL and FLUX models, up to twenty percent of weights were cut. Image quality barely changed to the eye. Cheap pruning could widen access to strong image models.
arxiv-2412-05652:
Ali Hasan Ali and Zsolt Páles bound the values of linear expressions by splitting them into factors. Linear functionals assign a number to a function based on its values or rates of change. Sharp bounds on them drive error checks for many numeric rules. The authors first prove a set of factorization results for such expressions.

From those results, they draw bounds through a broad form of Taylor's theorem. The theorem expands a function around a point to gauge the error of a shortcut rule. Two uses are worked out in detail, for the trapezoidal rule and for a Simpson-type rule. Both rules estimate areas under curves, and the new bounds state their error in clean form.
arxiv-2412-05852:
Dinesh Parthasarathy and co-authors evolve solver methods in a 2024 computing paper. Multigrid methods solve large equation systems fast, but their speed hinges on hand-picked parts and standard cycle shapes. The team instead bred new cycles with genetic programming guided by grammar rules.

Their flexible cycles choose smoothers and weights freely at each step. The evolved methods were built into a standard solver library and tuned for two jobs: a standalone solver for a lopsided three-dimensional problem, and a preconditioner inside a multiphysics code. The bred cycles beat the standard V, F, and W shapes on efficiency. The work shows that automated search can find solver designs humans would not try.
arxiv-2412-05952:
Juan Guillermo Garrido, Pedro Pérez-Aros, and Emilio Vilches present a 2024 mathematics paper on a Newton-like flow for optimization problems with kinks. Many real objectives are nonsmooth or nonconvex, so the classic Newton method stalls. The authors build a moving system whose paths slide downhill on such terrain, borrowing second-order news from a graphical derivative.

They prove the system's paths exist, are unique, and settle down in the long run. Two sets of conditions give convergence with explicit speed estimates. One rests on a regularity property of the problem's solution map. The other uses a classic inequality that controls how flat the valley can be. The theory extends a trusted method into territory where gradients break.
arxiv-2412-06952:
Michal Dory and Shaked Matar present a 2024 paper on fast methods for finding near-shortest paths in huge graphs when many machines work in parallel. The setting, called massively parallel computation, splits a graph across machines with limited memory each. The authors give randomized methods that finish in very few rounds of communication.

Their first result is a method that finds paths from one source to all other points with length close to optimal. Their second is a distance oracle, a compact structure built once that can then answer the distance between any two points, again close to optimal, in a single extra round. Both work on graphs with no edge weights and no direction. The results push down the cost of basic graph tasks at very large scale.
arxiv-2412-07752:
Korbinian Pöppel, Maximilian Beck, and Sepp Hochreiter speed up classic recurrent networks in a 2024 paper. Transformer models dominate sequence work but track state poorly, a skill that matters for time series and logic tasks. Recurrent networks track state well yet must process steps one by one, which looks slow. Their work shows how fast such networks can get on modern chips.

Their kernels tune the computation down to the register level on graphics processors. A variant also runs several smaller networks side by side, like heads in a transformer. Speed gains over a standard library version were dramatic, and much larger hidden sizes became possible. The code is released openly.
arxiv-2412-08452: Rainer Schicker reports on pion and kaon pair production in double gap events at ALICE in a 2024 conference paper for the collaboration. ALICE is a detector at the Large Hadron Collider. It received a major upgrade during a long shutdown. The upgrade allows much higher data rates in recent runs. The paper describes upgrades to systems used for double gap events. In such events, two empty regions flank the produced particles. It also presents the improved data taking capability for those events.
arxiv-2412-08852:
Hernandez-Marquez and Escamilla-Rivera bound a clump mark in a DGP brane frame. The frame sets our space as a sheet in a five-part flat space. Two arms of the frame get care: plain and self-speed arms. The mark, sigma-8, sizes how much mass clumps at a set scale. First, sky sets cap the frame marks for both arms. Pantheon+ lists and fake wave lists do that cap work.

A count solve then tracks mass sway growth in each arm. A scale fix for the chief form and a set p mark drive it. Growth in both arms strays from the stock dark frame tale. Sigma-8 lands at 0.774 for the plain arm in the runs. It lands at 0.913 for the self-speed arm in the runs.
arxiv-2412-09752:
Kyle Chickering, writing alone, speeds up hard derivative math for neural networks in a 2024 paper. Networks used to solve differential equations need derivatives of their own outputs, sometimes many layers deep. Standard autodifferentiation slows at an exponential rate as the order grows, which blocks that use. Chickering extends a classic method called TangentProp, which pushes derivatives through a network layer by layer.

The new method, n-TangentProp, computes the exact nth derivative in near-linear time instead. It suits dense feed-forward networks with smooth activation rules. Tests across depths, widths, and derivative counts backed the claim. In physics-informed networks, which bake equations into training, the method cut training time sharply. Gains grew with model size and with the number of derivatives the loss required. Code is released with the paper.
arxiv-2412-10052:
Alexandre Parriaux and co-authors showed a new way to lock the pulse rate of a quantum cascade laser comb in two thousand twenty-four. A frequency comb is a set of evenly spaced light lines. Locking its rate steadies it for spectroscopy and precise measurement.

Instead of electrical modulation, they shone modulated near-infrared light on the front face of the laser. That approach uses mature, high-bandwidth near-infrared gear and skips custom electronics for the laser. With only a few milliwatts of light, frequency noise fell sharply. Their checks show the locking range follows Adler's law, and the optical method beat the standard electrical one in their comparison.
arxiv-2412-11952:
Yuti Liu and colleagues trained a multimodal model to judge image beauty in depth in a 2024 paper. Aesthetic assessment should score a photo, explain its strengths, and suggest fixes, but models usually train for one such task on scarce labeled data. Their system learns from masses of unlabeled images instead, guided by text at several scales, from whole-image impressions down to local details.

A multi-scale alignment module ties image features to those layered descriptions during self-supervised pretraining. After extensive instruction tuning, the model set new state-of-the-art results on scoring, commenting, and personalized assessment benchmarks. Learning aesthetics without labels at scale may finally give photo tools a critic that explains itself.
arxiv-2412-12852:
Paheli Bhattacharya and Rishabh Gupta compare in 2024 methods for choosing few-shot examples to help language models explain code. Good examples boost explanation quality, but selection methods had been tested mainly on closed models. Syntax of the programming language was also often ignored in past work.

They benchmark open-source code models across two data sets. Their new method selects examples using named entity information from the code. Results show it beats leading token and embedding methods. The study claims to be the first systematic benchmark of open code models for this selection task.
arxiv-2412-12952: Slobodan Filipovski gives a partial proof of Brouwer's conjecture in two thousand twenty-four. The conjecture caps sums of top Laplacian eigenvalues of a graph. The cap blends edge count with a binomial term in the count taken. He proves the bound for two ranges of graphs and indices. One range ties edge and vertex counts by a square root law. The other sets the index in a band built from those counts. Both bands are wide but not the full claim.
arxiv-2412-13152:
Paolo Gabriel and co-authors present an artificial intelligence system that watches hospital patients by video in a 2024 paper. Falls harm many weak patients each year, and staff cannot watch every room at once. The system reads room video in real time and notes who is present, where beds and chairs sit, and when a patient is left alone. Results are stored in the cloud for later review.

Data came from eleven partner hospitals and covered more than three hundred high-risk patients. The system's object spotting and role sorting scored high on standard tests. A cleaned public subset of the data lets other teams check and improve the work. Steady passive watching could warn staff before a fall happens.
arxiv-2412-13952:
Eleni Sgouritsa and five co-authors teach language models causal reasoning in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Correlation alone does not prove causation, yet models are often asked to infer one from the other. Several large language models do poorly at that task. The authors offer a prompting strategy built on a formal algorithm.

Their method, PC-SubQ, splits the task into fixed subquestions. Each subquestion mirrors one step of the PC algorithm for causal discovery. The model answers one step at a time. Each new prompt carries the answers so far, so the chain stays grounded. They tested the approach on the Corr2Cause benchmark. Performance improved across the models they tried. Readers get a way to lend algorithmic discipline to a model's guesses.
arxiv-2412-14652:
Six researchers wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-four on condensates of magnons in antiferromagnetic insulators. A magnon is a ripple of magnetism in a material. In ferromagnets, magnons can settle into a Bose-Einstein condensate, a shared low-energy state; in antiferromagnets the idea is barely explored.

The authors study two systems, one with a single easy axis and one with two. Two-component condensation and interactions between magnons prove essential for a lasting state. In the one-axis system, the condensate stays stable only when its two populations balance. A sound-like collective mode also emerges in the two-component case.
arxiv-2412-14752:
Marco Drewes, Jan Heisig, and Valentin Weber report a 2024 search for heavy neutrinos made inside the Sun. Such particles, if they exist, would be born in nuclear reactions in the solar core and then decay into electrons and positrons. The team looked for that extra signal in space near the Sun.

They used electron counts in the MeV range from the Ulysses and SOHO satellites. No clear excess showed up, so they set the strongest direct limit yet on how much these heavy particles mix with electron neutrinos. The limit is held back mainly by how poorly we know how electrons drift through the inner solar system.
arxiv-2412-16352:
Christy and Kowalski present a paper from twenty twenty-four on learning more from a trial than its average effect. Their setup uses just a yes-no treatment and a yes-no outcome. From the trial's random design alone, they build odds for how the sample splits into four types. Those types cover people who always take, never take, follow, or defy the assigned arm. A chart they add shows when samples with defiers can explain the data in more ways. More ways to explain the data can mean a higher fit score for that sample.

The fit score can move within known bounds, unlike the standard score. Proof is weak, they stress, but it is real. They show the method on health cases with their own software pack.
arxiv-2412-16452:
Flora Shi, Stephen Bates, and Martin Wainwright study tests where the data providers act in their own interest. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, sets up a game-like form of hypothesis testing. A lead analyst wants a test with a known error rate. Each agent holds private data and can choose whether to join.

An agent joins only if the gain looks worth it. That choice leaks a hint about what the agent already believes. The authors use that hint to bound the false discovery rate. They prove the bound cannot be beaten in a strong sense. Their protocols also guard the privacy of each agent's data.
arxiv-2412-17052:
Shaina Raza, Caesar Saleh, and a large team present a benchmark and framework for spotting bias in news that mixes words and pictures in a 2024 study. A story's slant often lives in the pairing: a neutral caption under a loaded photo, or the reverse. Text-only classifiers miss that interplay entirely.

Their data set holds tens of thousands of text and image pairs from varied outlets. Each pair is labeled for bias with a short rationale, gathered through a two-stage process where a language model annotates first. A question-answering style framework then detects bias and reasons about it, giving editors an auditable second reader.
arxiv-2412-17452:
Rukmini Nazre and co-authors guard networks with a temporal convolutional model that reads traffic as sequences. Intrusions hide in the order and timing of packets, not just in single flows. Their network stacks dilated filters in residual blocks to span long spans stably. Parallel processing makes it faster than recurrent rivals on the same task.

Tests used the Edge-IIoTset data with normal traffic plus fourteen attack types. Accuracy hit 96.72 percent with a very low loss score. The model beat plain and hybrid convolutional-recurrent baselines across the board. Per-class scores held up for malware, injection, and flooding attacks alike. The authors pitch it for complex modern network defense.
arxiv-2412-18552:
Yice Zhang and seven co-authors transferred the sentiment skills of large language models into much smaller models, in a paper published in 2024. Fine-grained sentiment analysis extracts exact opinions from reviews, but large models cost too much to run at scale. In their approach, the large model reads reviews and writes out its interpretations. The small models then train on that generated text.

The team also built a broad benchmark for sentiment tasks and ran many models on it. Training on the large model's interpretations raised small model scores by six points on their main scale. One small model with 220 million parameters beat a far larger open model. On new tasks with no task-specific training, the small models even matched or beat their teachers. The authors release their code, data, and model weights, and present distillation as a low-cost path to strong sentiment tools.
arxiv-2412-18652:
Antinucci, Copetti, Galati, and Rizi set limits on defect dynamics in this physics paper from twenty twenty-four. Defects are extended objects, like lines or surfaces, living inside a quantum field theory. Their flows across energy scales are hard to track when coupling grows strong. The authors study how bulk symmetries behave near defects to find rules that hold regardless.

They define defect anomalies, traits that cannot change along the flow. Several known ideas, such as higher-form symmetries, turn out to be faces of this notion. They also define symmetry reflecting defects, which must stay coupled at low energy. Both ideas forbid lazy, trivial outcomes for defect flows. Worked examples in simpler theories confirm the constraints.
arxiv-2412-19052:
Zhong-Heng Tan and co-authors present, in a 2024 math paper, a method to flatten donut-shaped surfaces onto a flat sheet while keeping angles true and edges matched in a doubled periodic way. Such flattening serves texture mapping and medical imaging. Their method seeks the map that least distorts angles, under matched-edge rules.

The search reduces to a clean quadratic problem with a sparse linear system at its heart. The best boundary shape and shift vectors come out together with the map. No cut path needs to be chosen, so no seam distortion appears. One-to-one mapping is assured under a mild weight rule, with a fix for general meshes. Tests ran five times faster than the best rival.
arxiv-2412-19752: Nicolas Curien's lecture notes tour the meeting point of random walks and random graphs in a 2024 course text. The notes come from a master's course taught at Orsay between 2019 and 2024. Part one covers one-dimensional random walks, the cycle lemma, and family-tree processes. Part two turns to the classic random graph model and gives three proofs of how a giant component suddenly emerges. Part three treats random recursive trees, random permutations, and continuous-time embedding tricks. The set offers students several doors into one connected theory.
arxiv-2412-19952:
The CMS Collaboration reports in two thousand twenty-four the first evidence for a subtle matter-antimatter asymmetry in decays of Bs mesons. CP violation, a difference between matter and antimatter behavior, is a key test of the Standard Model. The target decay ends in a J/psi and a phi meson, which further split into muons and kaons.

A new machine-learning flavor tagger combined two tagging styles to label about twenty-seven thousand decays from proton collisions at thirteen teraelectronvolts. A time- and angle-based analysis measured the weak phase at about minus seventy-three milliradians. Combined with an earlier result, the value sits about three standard deviations from zero. All measured parameters matched Standard Model predictions where available.
arxiv-2412-20152:
Mohammed Abdellaoui, Nour-Eddine Abouelkhir, Abdallah Slaoui, and Rachid Ahl Laamara compare detection schemes for quantum phase estimation in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, in a two thousand twenty-four quantum optics paper. The quantum Cramér-Rao bound sets the best precision any unbiased estimator can reach.

The input state is a spin-coherent state from the SU(2) algebra. Three readouts are tested: single-mode intensity, difference intensity, and balanced homodyne detection with an external phase reference. The authors compute single- and two-parameter quantum Fisher information for each. All three schemes can saturate the Cramér-Rao bound for this input, and precision improves as the total angular momentum quantum number grows.
arxiv-2501-00452:
Pratik Nag explores, in 2024, adversarial networks as composers of new music. Sequence models dominate music generation, while the two-player setup of generative adversarial networks remains little tested there. Nag builds two systems on a creative variant of the framework.

One system learns a body of pieces without style labels. The other learns a composer's style and then deliberately deviates from it, chasing novelty. An unrolling trick is added to fight the collapse where generators repeat a few safe outputs. Both the plain and creative networks are compared for creativity and variety, extending the creative adversarial idea from images into music.
arxiv-2501-01152:
Jun Yan studies counting problems for lattice paths in a 2025 paper. Lattice paths are step-by-step routes on a grid, and each route can be weighted by the lengths of its upward runs. Recent work linked such counts to parking function problems that puzzled researchers.

Yan broadens those results to a large family of paths and weight rules. He solves the weighted counting problems for that whole family at once. The paper also draws links to other counting problems and to entries in a known integer sequence database. The unified view helps mathematicians see separate puzzles as cases of one general pattern.
arxiv-2501-01652:
Cai and seven co-authors introduced a testbed in twenty twenty-five for judging how well large language models handle complex social play. Their framework, called MIRAGE, drops models into murder mystery games, where they must act a part, hunt for clues, and decide whom to trust.

The setup uses eight written scripts with varied themes and styles. Four scores grade the play. One tracks trust and suspicion, one tracks clue hunting, one tracks how well a model stays in character, and one tracks how well it follows the script's rules. Even strong models such as GPT-4 struggled with the tangled social demands of the games. The authors share the scripts and code so others can run the same tests. The work offers a playful but sharp way to probe social skill in machines.
arxiv-2501-02452:
Zhongjian Cui and co-authors close a gap between speech cleaning and speech recognition, in a 2025 paper. Cleaning noisy audio helps human ears but can distort sounds that recognizers rely on. A known fix mixes some noise back in, guided by a bridging module that picks the mix level.

That module was trained only on fake noisy speech, which mismatches real recordings. The authors train it on real noise instead, using a quality score that needs no clean reference. Extra constraints harden the module against odd cases. Each test sentence is scored across many mix levels by the recognizer, and those error patterns teach the module in a multi-task setup. The result is cleaner handoffs from enhancement to recognition on real-world audio.
arxiv-2501-02652:
Shivaram Kalyanakrishnan, Sheel Shah, and Santhosh Guguloth connected two classic learning ideas in a 2025 theory paper. In reinforcement learning, an agent facing an unknown world often builds the most likely model of that world from what it has seen, then acts as if the model were true. That certainty-equivalence method is intuitive and known to need near-optimal amounts of data in some settings.

A seemingly unrelated planning trick, the trajectory tree method, was built for fast decisions in huge partially observed problems. The authors show the first method is really an instance of the second. The new view yields simpler proofs of its data needs, under a weaker assumption on rewards than earlier work required.
arxiv-2501-02852:
Shang Li and Jun-Qing Xia test general relativity on cosmic scales in a paper from 2025. They use a statistic that compares how matter clusters with how strongly it bends light, a direct probe of Einstein's theory. Data come from a large photometric galaxy survey and a cosmic microwave background lensing map, with neural networks rebuilding the growth rate of structure.

Measurements in four distance bins all matched the standard cosmology model within their error bars. Photometric distance errors are the main limit today. Forecasts for a future space telescope survey plus a next-generation ground survey suggest the test could soon reach about one percent precision.
arxiv-2501-03252:
Zhenwei Lyu and co-authors surveyed what science wet extreme mass-ratio inspirals could deliver in a 2024 paper. Such a system pairs a small black hole spiraling into a giant one inside the gas disk of an active galaxy. Space detectors like LISA will hear their gravitational waves for years as the small hole orbits.

Gas changes everything versus dry systems in quiet star clusters: the disk can drag, feed, and light up the pair. The authors catalog the tests these signals enable, from mapping the giant's gravity to probing the disk itself. Wet systems may be common among detections, so planning their science now shapes detector analysis pipelines for the next decade.
arxiv-2501-03552:
Yujie Wang and Xiangru Xu present a control method from two thousand twenty-five that aims to keep a system safe. Their plan joins two older lines of work. One uses barrier functions, which mark a safe zone and push the system to stay inside it. The other uses Lyapunov ideas to keep motion stable and on track.

The authors split the full system into two simpler parts. One part handles safety, and the other handles tracking of a set path. A new filter-based tool watches for outside forces that do not match the model. Tests with numbers show the plan works, and it needs a model of only the small proxy part.
arxiv-2501-03952:
Jurgita Kapociute-Dzikiene, Toms Bergmanis, and Marcis Pinnis test open-weight language models on the languages of the Baltic states. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with Lithuanian, Latvian, and Estonian. Privacy rules in Europe can bar the use of hosted commercial models in government and defense work, so local models matter.

The team tried size and precision variants of four model families on translation, quiz questions, and free writing. Gemma 2 came close to top commercial models on some tasks. Yet all open models made word-level errors often, with made-up words in at least one word in twenty. Translation scores looked strong, but the word errors show a real gap.
arxiv-2501-04252:
Qian Xu, Dong-Jie Liu, and Yuan-Chuan Zou estimate the width of gamma-ray burst jets from their fading glow. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses early X-ray afterglows caught by the Swift satellite. A burst's jet is a narrow beam, and its opening angle sets how much true energy the burst released.

Some afterglows show a steep drop after a phase of high-latitude emission, which marks the moment the jet's edge comes into view. The team fits a broken power law to such light curves and reads the break time. With an assumed emission radius, that time bounds the opening angle. The angles are sensitive to the radius, a caveat the authors note.
arxiv-2501-04752:
Nuno Crokidakis models bullying in schools with equations in a paper from 2025. Students are divided into four groups: susceptible, bullies, exposed, and violent. Rates between groups encode triggers like romantic rejection and conflicts with peers or teachers. Parents and administrators enter as forces that can damp the cycle. The model asks when bullying dies out and when it persists.

Strong school anti-bullying programs can control the problem, the analysis finds. Weaker efforts let bullying settle into a lasting state. Threshold conditions separate the two regimes. The author presents the work as a planning lens for schools. It turns a social problem into testable dynamics.
arxiv-2501-05752:
Lee and co-authors present SEAG, a method that helps language models solve hard problems with less wasted search. Tree search can explore many reasoning paths, but it burns compute and repeats itself. Easy tasks get needlessly deep searches. Paths that differ in wording but not meaning get explored again and again. SEAG adds a gate that judges the model's confidence in a quick first answer.

Only low-confidence cases trigger the fuller tree search. Inside the search, steps with the same meaning merge into one. That merge cuts repeated work across paths. The design targets both cost and redundancy at once. Tests weigh how much accuracy survives the trimming.
arxiv-2501-08952:
Henrique Legoinha writes lecture-style notes introducing the bosonic string, the entry point of string theory. For physicists, string theory is a sandbox where hard problems become tractable. For mathematicians, unusually, the flow of ideas runs from physics into new mathematics. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the notes develop the bosonic string action comprehensively. From the action they derive the equations of motion. The effective mass spectra of open strings, with endpoints, and closed strings, in loops, are worked out.

The review is pedagogical in intent, a single on-ramp to a famously technical subject. No new results are claimed. Its value is consolidation: the action, the dynamics, and the first physical consequences in one careful treatment for newcomers.
arxiv-2501-09352:
Xianghu Yue and co-authors present PAL, a learner that keeps adding classes across mixed data types even when one type goes missing, in a 2025 paper. Real feeds pair sound with image or text with image, and parts often drop out. Missing parts can deepen the forgetting that plagues step by step learning.

PAL fills gaps with prompts tuned to each data type, keeping a whole view of each case. It then turns the learning task into a least squares problem with a closed form path. That framing also cures a weak fit flaw in such learners. On food and news data sets PAL beat rivals and forgot less.
arxiv-2501-09552:
Tuan Truong and four co-authors design a system to find private health details burned into medical images in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Before images are shared, names and other identifiers printed on them must be caught. Few AI tools for this had been properly benchmarked.

Their pipeline has three stages: spot text, read it, then judge whether it is private. They tested a detector, an OCR engine, and a large language model across setups and two data sets. The best setup gave each stage its own specialist model, balancing accuracy, speed, and cost. Language models also improved the reading stage itself. The authors offer the study as a design guide for privacy pipelines in medical imaging.
arxiv-2501-10152:
Seung-Hyun Nam, Hyun-Young Park, Si-Hyeon Lee, and Joonwoo Bae ask whether quantum methods, in a 2025 preprint, can beat classical ones at private hypothesis testing. The task is to judge which of two distributions produced some data. Each data holder must keep their sample private, under a rule called local differential privacy. Privacy costs accuracy, and the trade-off can be scored by error exponents. The authors study both balanced and one-sided forms of the test.

They first bound how well any classical privacy mechanism can do for a family of smoothed point-mass distributions. In certain cases those bounds are exact. They then build a quantum mechanism that beats the bounds. It prepares special symmetric quantum states and passes them through a noise channel. The edge shows under strict privacy and small data alphabets. The paper claims a genuine quantum advantage in this private testing corner.
arxiv-2501-10952:
Jingyi Liao and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on squeezing tiny device messages into the spare signals of a phone network. New ambient internet-of-things devices must run on far less power than standard gear allows. One trick is backscatter: a device reflects existing radio waves and stamps its message on the reflection.

The team fit this trick into the sounding signals that phones send up to LTE base stations. The channel checks at the base station let it read the faint stamped message on top. The authors design the receiver, work out its error rates, and test it by simulation and with a real prototype. The link held a usable error rate within a few wavelengths of range, with almost no change to the LTE system.
arxiv-2501-11152:
Thomas Zacharias and co-authors demonstrate a low-energy way to measure ultra-short light pulses on a chip, in a 2025 paper. Fast photonic circuits need tools that can check pulses lasting only dozens of femtoseconds, but the standard bench method does not port well to chips. The team built a chip version based on a tiny amplifier that exploits a strong nonlinear effect in engineered waveguides.

Their device measured pulses shorter than 80 femtoseconds with very low pulse energy. The gate pulse that does the measuring used orders of magnitude less energy than bench tools need for similar pulses. The authors expect the method to grow toward checking single-photon-level pulses. That would give chip designers a practical meter for the weakest, fastest signals.
arxiv-2501-11452:
Andrey Chekhlov, Peter Danchev, and Patrick Keef work on abstract algebra in a 2025 paper. They study groups with a property called co-Hopfian, and define two broader versions of it. The goal is a full account of which groups fall in the new classes, much as earlier work did for related classes.

They describe the new classes for several kinds of groups, including those built from prime cycles and those without such cycles. Many cases split cleanly into sums of special pieces. One surprise is that the relative version, for prime-cycle groups, turns out to be exactly the original class. Rank-based descriptions settle the strongest versions at the end.
arxiv-2501-12352:
Ke Alexander Wang, Jiaxin Shi, and Emily Fox propose one framework to explain many designs for sequence models, the systems behind modern language AI. Models like Transformers and their recurrent rivals look unrelated at first glance. The authors argue that a single skill links them: associative recall, the ability to fetch earlier items that fit the current context.

Their framework splits recall into storing items and then retrieving them. Storing is cast as a regression problem, a classic task of fitting values from examples. Each model layer then does this regression at test time, while the input streams in. Famous designs, from linear attention to state-space models, emerge as special cases of three choices: how examples are weighted, what form the fit takes, and how it is computed. The view explains known strengths and flaws, and points to unused corners of the design space for building stronger attention.
arxiv-2501-12852:
Madhava Krishna Prasad, Jonathan Paul Goss, and Jonathan David Mar study quantum light emitters in layered materials in this two thousand twenty-five letter. Defect color centers in hexagonal boron nitride can act as single-photon emitters and spin qubits for quantum technologies. Putting them into electronic devices requires electrical control of their charge state. The authors examine stacks where boron nitride is encapsulated with graphene.

They show that electrostatic screening from the graphene changes the electrical levels inside the boron nitride, driving charge transfer onto the defects. Charged defects, in turn, face only low energy barriers to reorientation, barriers that moderate gate voltages can overcome. The practical message is that accurate modeling of a defect's charge state is essential before anyone can electrically control these emitters reliably. The work informs the design of quantum devices built on boron nitride.
arxiv-2501-13152:
Alessandro Savino and co-authors present a Hubble telescope survey of dwarf galaxies around Andromeda in a 2025 paper. Andromeda, called M31, is the nearest large galaxy to our own. Its small companion galaxies carry records of how they formed stars and when they stopped. The team gathered over a thousand orbits of telescope imaging to read those records evenly.

Color charts of single stars reach the oldest turning point of star life in thirty-six dwarf galaxies. From them, the team measured each galaxy's full history of star birth. Smaller and closer companions tend to be older and to have quit forming stars earlier. Distance and brightness predict the quitting time well. The survey gives a shared base for testing how big galaxies shape small ones.
arxiv-2501-13752:
Thanh Dat Hoang and colleagues map the warm envelopes feeding massive young stars in the inner galaxy. Ninety-nine dense clumps from a major survey were observed with a submillimeter telescope in a mid-level carbon monoxide line. These envelopes are the reservoirs that accretion draws on, and star formation's feedback reshapes them in return. Morphology and motion together tell the story.

The line was detected in about eighty-three percent of sources, across all evolutionary stages. Detection rate, line width, and peak strength all grow with evolution. Line brightness tracks the clump's total luminosity and mass tightly, tying excitation to star formation itself. Simple single-core sources show clean power-law radial profiles. Velocity centers are compared against small- and large-scale gas motions to trace where envelope movement originates. The survey links envelope structure to the clumps' life stories.
arxiv-2501-14752:
Yu-Bo Liu and co-authors explain a striped magnetic pattern in a nickel oxide that superconducts under pressure, in work the text dates to 2024. The catalog lists 2025. Squeezed hard, the compound La3Ni2O7 carries current without resistance near 80 kelvin. At normal pressure it instead shows a diagonal double-stripe spin wave, which experiments can actually reach. The team built an eight-band model from first-principles bands and ran a standard fluctuation analysis.

Their calculation produced a spin-density wave driven by nesting of the Fermi surface, with a wave vector close to the one experiments see. The pattern came out as two layers opposing each other, striped diagonally, matching soft X-ray results. For superconductivity, the same analysis gave a pairing state with a far lower transition temperature than under pressure. The authors say the magnetic order fits an itinerant electron picture.
arxiv-2501-15752:
Mojdeh Saleh, Abhishek Kumar, Dmitrii L. Maslov, and Saurabh Maiti study how electric fields and spin trade places in thin electron systems. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. One effect turns a current into a spin imbalance, and its twin does the reverse. Both rest on spin-orbit coupling in systems that lack a center of symmetry. The authors add the push and pull between electrons themselves.

They focus on chiral-spin modes, waves of spin that need no magnetic field. Both effects spike when driven at the modes' own frequencies, in the terahertz range. The paper works out how electron interaction shifts and shapes those spikes. It also covers spin pumping and charge-to-spin conversion from the same modes. The findings matter for fast, small spin-based devices.
arxiv-2501-16952:
Zheng Zheng, Xinyi Ni, and Pengyu Hong let a retrieval system fetch knowledge at several zoom levels at once. Standard retrieval-augmented generation pulls fixed-size chunks as references. Questions, though, arrive at different abstraction levels, and one chunk size serves them poorly. Too much retrieved text also triggers the lost-in-the-middle failure and busts token budgets.

Their approach indexes text at four levels: multi-sentence, paragraph, section, and whole document. The generator can then cite the granularity each question needs. A glycoscience testbed, an under-explored scientific domain, hosts the evaluation. Answer correctness judged by AI evaluators rose about twenty-six percent over single-level retrieval on glyco-related papers. The lesson generalizes beyond sugars: match the reference's scale to the question's scale. Abstraction, treated as an indexing choice, becomes a retrieval feature.
arxiv-2501-17452:
HyunSeok Daniel Jang and four co-authors compare three popular Bluetooth location trackers in real-world use. Apple AirTag, Samsung SmartTag, and Tile devices all depend on passing phones and tablets to report their position. Makers promise accurate tracking, but field performance was poorly documented.

The team ran controlled tests with a known spread of reporting devices, plus uncontrolled trials in the wild. Twenty-two volunteers carried tags across twenty-nine countries. AirTag reported its location much more often than in earlier studies. The strongest factor was simply how many companion devices were nearby, which mattered more than brand differences. Post-pandemic travel patterns also shaped the results.
arxiv-2501-17952:
Amorphous solids creep slowly under steady stress, and how they yield depends on how stable their glassy state is. The three authors simulate athermal creep across a wide stability range, using the imposed shear stress as the control knob. They track both the bulk strain over time and microscopic events inside the material.

The least stable samples show a strain rate that falls monotonically. More stable samples show an S-shaped curve with a sharp upturn, the signature of failure by shear banding. A fluidization timescale diverges near failure, and the team extracts its critical exponents. Comparisons with scaling theories for soft matter work for ductile samples, but the stable, brittle-like glasses challenge those theories. The study watches shear bands being born during creep in materials from soft matter to metallic and oxide glasses.
arxiv-2501-18452:
Xi Weng and co-authors study why self-supervised learning builds such well-clustered internal representations, and how to exploit that strength. Their paper appeared in 2025. These methods learn from unlabeled data by pulling related views together. The team measured clustering at several points inside the model and found the encoder's output clusters best and most steadily.

They built a method, called ReSA, that feeds this clustering strength back into training. The model assigns its own outputs to clusters and learns from those assignments, guiding itself. On standard benchmarks, models trained this way beat leading rivals by a clear margin. Analysis showed clustering improved at both fine and coarse levels. The authors argue that self-supervised models already know how to group; ReSA simply lets them teach themselves.
arxiv-2501-18752:
Rossella Anania and six co-authors present a 2025 method for estimating ultraviolet radiation at planet-forming discs. Massive stars bathe nearby discs in far ultraviolet light, which blows material away and starves planet building. Measuring that light is hard because distances to the stars are uncertain. The team infers true three-dimensional separations from the pattern of pairwise separations on the sky, assuming the clusters look the same from any angle.

Tests on synthetic clusters beat prior methods clearly. The team then published a catalog of ultraviolet fluxes for star-bearing discs in seven nearby regions, six Orion regions, and Serpens sub-regions. Discs near late B and early A stars reached levels that matter for disc evolution. Hints of a link between flux and dust mass emerged only when region ages were averaged.
arxiv-2502-00852:
Pochinda, Dhandha, Fialkov, and de Lera Acedo super-resolve the cosmic twenty-one centimeter signal with diffusion models, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The signal maps early universe hydrogen across gigaparsec scales. Simulations at full resolution are expensive to produce. Score-based diffusion models learn to upscale low-resolution runs.

One simulation suffices for the model to learn the task robustly. Best errors reach about zero point six millikelvin per pixel. Power spectrum residuals stay small across three volume sizes at redshift ten. The method unlocks all spatial scales the SKA-Low telescope covers. Early universe astrophysics constraints could follow from cheaper simulations.
arxiv-2502-00952:
Dora Zhao, Diyi Yang, and Michael Bernstein wrote this study in 2025 on silence in online groups. The spiral of silence theory holds that people who feel in the minority speak less, which makes their view look rarer still. The team tested that loop on political Reddit groups. They surveyed members of twelve such groups and got 439 replies on touchy topics.

About seventy-two percent of those who saw themselves in the minority stayed silent. They posted at half the rate of members who felt in the majority. Groups that felt more mixed showed less self-silencing. The authors warn that public posts are a warped lens on true opinion. They suggest fixes at the group level, such as rewarding brave posts and making moderation rules clearer, so quiet views can surface.
arxiv-2502-01652:
Soham Sane presents a reinforcement learning method that mixes group comparisons with a learned value guide, in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning trains software by reward and penalty. A recent popular method, GRPO, dropped the value guide and judged actions only by sampling many tries and ranking them. That keeps things simple but can make learning jumpy. Sane's hybrid keeps the sampling while restoring a steadier guide.

The hybrid scores each action by blending its sampled results with the guide's estimate of future reward. The paper sets out the maths side by side with two earlier methods, the long-standing PPO and plain GRPO. In a controlled test setting, the hybrid learned faster, updated more smoothly, and used samples better than both. The author also sketches add-ons that could carry the idea further.
arxiv-2502-02252:
Zahra Alizadeh and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a layered compound that was tipped to superconduct but does not. The compound, LiPdH, was thought to beat its kin PdH on electron and lattice coupling. Tests in the lab found no superconductivity at all. The team runs first principles sums on its ambient phase.

Both smooth and anharmonic lattice modes are checked. No superconducting act shows in any run. High pressure hunts find no shape change up to a huge load. More load thins the states at the Fermi level and weakens the coupling more. The sums say the tip was wrong from the start.
arxiv-2502-03552:
Haritha Ananthakrishnan and four colleagues report a surprising use for cross encoders in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Cross encoders judge whether two sentences are related, but they need both sentences at once. That limitation supposedly confines them to re-ranking search results.

Dual encoders, which embed sentences separately, fill the retrieval role instead. They need much more training data and still trail cross encoders in accuracy. The authors found that embeddings from earlier layers of a cross encoder work inside a retrieval pipeline. They show how to distill a lighter dual encoder from a cross encoder. The distilled model ran more than five times faster at inference. The finding blurs a standard architectural divide.
arxiv-2502-03852:
Yanbiao Ma, Wei Dai, and Jiayi Chen published this computer vision paper in 2025. Object detectors often do worse on some categories than others. The standard explanation blames uneven counts: categories with few training examples get neglected. Yet the authors note that bias appears even when counts are fairly balanced, so the count story cannot be the whole truth.

They propose a new measure, the category information amount, which gauges how much there is to learn about a category. It tracked accuracy far better than raw counts did. Building on it, their training loss widens or narrows each category's decision space in line with its information amount. The method improved results on long-tailed test sets and also helped rare categories in a balanced dataset. The authors offer the measure as a general tool for studying category bias.
arxiv-2502-04352:
Hoppe, Ilievski, and Kalo test how robust language model reasoning is when logic tasks are perturbed, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Models score well on clean logic tasks, but real inputs are messy. The team wants to know which design choices help models hold up. They sort reasoners by format, formal syntax, and error feedback style.

They build seven perturbed data sets with two attack types. One adds adversarial noise, and the other swaps in counterfactual claims. Noise mainly hurt methods that first translate tasks into formal code. Counterfactual claims hurt all methods. Rich feedback cut syntax errors but did not raise overall accuracy. Models still struggle to fix their own logic slips.
arxiv-2502-04852:
Sandhaus and Keller estimate a person's age from a face photo by refining a first guess against known faces. Most systems guess age outright, which misses fine age-linked detail. Their network compares the input face with reference faces of known age. It learns to predict the age gap between the pair. That gap then corrects the first estimate. An extra training trick models how the first guess errs and repeats the fix.

The method beat prior systems on the MORPH II and CACD photo sets. It reached the best reported accuracy on both. The team also probed biases in current age estimators. Relative judgment, they argue, suits the slow way faces change with age.
arxiv-2502-04952:
Yongchao Wang, Yuandao Cai, and Charles Zhang speed up path sensitive value flow analysis in a 2025 paper. The technique tracks how values move through a program to find bugs. High precision demands many function summaries, and computing them blindly wastes time and memory on summaries unrelated to the bug being checked.

Their approach identifies and removes redundant summaries without losing soundness. On large programs, time fell by nearly half and memory by about a quarter compared with a leading tool. The identifier found most redundant summaries with tiny overhead, saving hours on the largest database project tested.
arxiv-2502-05652:
Helena Montenegro, Maria Cardoso, and Jaime Cardoso use image filling to preview how breast surgery may change a patient's shape. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that breast cancer surgery often leaves scars or uneven shape. Patients need a clear view of likely outcomes to choose a treatment plan. The team edits pre-surgery photos to show such changes.

Their inpainting models shift breast shape and nipple position in the image. Some builds can work without hand-marked outlines or nipple points. They test several network designs on two breast image sets. The models made changes that looked real to the eye. Post-surgery unevenness from real cases could be matched in pre-surgery shots. The tool aims to support frank talks between patients and care teams.
arxiv-2502-06852:
To see how a language model thinks, labs trace its inner circuits, but the tracing tools can go numb. Lin Zhang and seven co-authors show in 2025 that scoring methods based on slopes can hit flat spots where scores stop tracking the input. Their fix walks a path from the input that bends with the gap between clean and spoiled runs, dodging the numb zones. Edge scores along that path grade each wire in the circuit.

Tests ran on three sizes of one known model family across six data sets. The new path beat past methods on how true the found circuits stayed, by up to a sixth. Against hand-drawn circuits it matched or beat the old tools on hits and misses alike. The team offer it as a steadier lens on model minds.
arxiv-2502-09252:
Andrew Draganov and six co-authors settle what the length of a learned embedding does in self-supervised learning. Most such methods grade embeddings by the cosine of their angle, which puts them on a ball and seems to bar length from play. Their 2025 work shows length is at work in two ways. It sets how fast training converges, and it codes the confidence of the network, with short embeddings for odd samples.

Proof, simulations, and bench runs all back the pair of roles. Push length by hand and convergence speed swings wide. Length is thus no scrap of the ball trick: it is a dial. Read it for confidence, tune it for speed, they say. Past readings that set length aside miss half the story of such learning.
arxiv-2502-11352:
Zikang Xiong, Joe Eappen, and Suresh Jagannathan taught self-driving planners to score their own option paths with learned logic rules in a 2025 paper. Planners typically put forth several trajectories, then a scorer picks one. Hand-written scoring rules are interpretable and can encode safety law, but tuning their tangled settings by hand misses patterns in real driving data. Training sets contain only successful driving, never labeled failures.

Their FLoRA setup learns scoring rules written in time-based logic, form and settings jointly, from demonstrations in a large public driving data set. The learned rules judge actions credibly despite seeing positive cases only. Interpretable learned scorers could win regulator trust that black-box selectors cannot.
arxiv-2502-11552:
Karoly and a large team chart in twenty twenty-five the magnetic field woven through the dense gas at the Milky Way's centre. Polarised dust glow picked up by a submillimetre telescope traces field direction across the central zone between two landmark clouds. Whether the field follows the gas orbiting the central black hole, or is scrambled by star birth, was open.

The field proved strikingly ordered and mostly parallel to the orbital gas flows, a pattern far from random. It matched models where field lines sit within a modest angle of the flow in three dimensions. Departures clustered where clouds were heavier, denser, and busier forming stars. The authors suggest flows drag the field until gravity and feedback locally stir it.
arxiv-2502-12652:
Jia-Wei Ying and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on quantum secure direct communication with a fully passive source. In this scheme, secret text rides on quantum states in direct form. Real gear can leak through side channels, above all where active parts shape the states. Their source shapes both the state and the decoy strength with no active parts.

A system model and dial tuning give the best secret rate at each loss level. Rates fall fast as loss grows, and the reach tops out short of the active form's reach. Still, the reach holds most of the active form's span. The trade buys strength against side channel attacks.
arxiv-2502-13252:
Jiayi Wang and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on training multilingual language models with machine-translated data. Large language models work best in English because high-quality training text is plentiful. Most other languages lack comparable corpora, so model quality lags badly behind.

The team translated a high-quality English educational web data set into nine languages, creating a corpus of 1.7 trillion tokens they call TransWebE. They find that translated text from one strong source language can significantly raise the pretraining quality of multilingual models. The result challenges the assumption that only naturally written text will do. If translation can close the data gap, strong models for hundreds of underserved languages become far cheaper to build.
arxiv-2502-14952:
Matteo Becchetti and five co-authors work out a loop-level correction for a rare collision that makes a top quark pair plus a W boson. Top quarks are the heaviest known bits of matter, and this trio is a key test of the strong force laws. Exact math for it is a step toward a twice-as-fine grade of predictions for collider data. Their 2025 paper gives the first loop sums at a deep order in the size rule.

The sums are split into shape parts, each written as a blend of a set base of clean math forms with neat weights. A plain form for the parts is given to the first orders, built from logarithms and double logarithms. The full set of forms is solved by a step-wise series method. The layout is meant as a frame the next, two-loop step can build on.
arxiv-2502-15552:
Ullah and six co-authors measured this satellite internet service in twenty twenty-five. Starlink sells a flat high-performance terminal built for vehicles, ships, and heavy home use. Few studies had tested that terminal, and even fewer in far northern regions. The team ran tests in Finland, both at fixed sites and while moving.

They tracked response time and upload and download speeds against six servers in different places. The service gave fast links with low delay while parked. Speeds swung up and down and dipped a bit in motion. The team also traced how traffic was routed across the network. They compared satellite response times with those of ground networks. The results give a clear picture of the service at high latitudes.
arxiv-2502-15852:
Li Yin and Jumei Zhang derived new formulas for a family of generalized gamma functions in a 2025 paper. The k-gamma and k-digamma functions extend Euler's classical gamma machinery by a parameter, and special functions built on them inherit rich identities waiting to be catalogued. Working from those two functions, the authors produce four series expansions for a Furdui-type integral that involves the Riemann zeta function and the hypergeometric function.

Further results give identities, series expansions, and inequalities for the Hadamard k-gamma function and the Nielsen k-beta function, two relatives in the same extended family. An open problem closes the paper, inviting the next contribution. Such catalogues of exact relations are the working tools of analysts who evaluate integrals and series in closed form.
arxiv-2502-15952:
Akshay Kumar and Jarvis Haupt study how neural networks train in their 2025 paper. They look at homogeneous networks, whose outputs scale in a clean way when their weights are scaled. Early in training, such weights stay tiny but line up in a set direction. The authors ask what happens next, once the weights escape that starting zone.

They trace the flow of weights under the training rule past the origin. Their math describes the first saddle point the flow meets, a spot where progress can stall. They also show that the sparse pattern the weights gain before the escape survives until that saddle point. The results help explain why networks settle where they do.
arxiv-2502-16052:
Keran Chen, Alex Clinton, and Kirthevasan Kandasamy design a data marketplace that pays people to gather honest data for estimating an average. Their paper appeared in 2025. A broker hires contributors to sample a hidden distribution, sells the pooled data to buyers, and passes the revenue back as pay. The hard part is incentives: contributors might shirk or fabricate. The team sets prices that reward reports agreeing with the crowd's pattern, making honesty the best strategy.

In the resulting equilibrium, the two cheapest contributors gather everything. Two impossibility results frame the design: no mechanism can make honesty a dominant strategy here, and none beats theirs under equilibrium play. The authors say the market can work, but only within those proven limits.
arxiv-2502-16152:
Kieu Thao Nguyen Pham and four co-authors present DUPRE, a faster way to price how much each data set helps a learning model. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Game-based pricing is fair but needs the model retrained on many data subsets, which costs a lot. Past speed-ups cut the count of subsets, not the cost of each test.

DUPRE flips the fix and cuts the cost of each test. From a few true scores, it fits a smooth model that guesses the score of each new subset. The guess uses a sliced gap gauge between data spreads, proven sound in the paper. Tests showed low guess error and real speed gains.
arxiv-2502-17052:
Jasper Postema and Servaas Kokkelmans determine what bivariate bicycle codes can and cannot achieve as quantum memories. These error-correcting codes recently drew attention for promising compact storage with low overhead. The open question was the exact trade-off among their length, dimension, and distance.

Exploiting the codes' ring structure, the authors predict their dimension and give conditions for a code with given parameters to exist at all. The sobering headline is asymptotic badness: as the codes grow, their rate or relative distance must vanish. That rules this subclass out of the hunt for truly good low-density parity-check codes. Moderate-length examples already known, however, remain useful and can still beat surface codes in experiments.
arxiv-2502-17152:
Cainã de Oliveira, James Matthews, and Vitor de Souza ask where the highest-energy gamma rays along a nearby galaxy's jet are made in a 2025 paper. Centaurus A, the closest active galactic nucleus, shines from radio to gamma rays. HESS telescope data show ultra-fast electrons along its jet, but what accelerates them is unknown.

The authors test the idea that knots in the jet do the accelerating. They model the knots as shocks where the jet rams the winds of powerful stars. Hydrodynamic simulations plus shock theory predict each knot's spectrum and maximum electron energy. Comparing those predictions with radio and X-ray data judges the idea knot by knot.
arxiv-2502-19052:
Thi Lan Dinh and four co-authors compare algorithms that dodge bad local minima in hard imaging problems. Their twenty twenty-five paper studies nonconvex feasibility, where a solution must meet many constraints that clash. A test case is orbital tomography from ARPES data, a way to image electron orbits in materials.

Three methods are run on fake and lab data: cyclic projections, a relaxed Douglas-Rachford method, and a product-space variant. The product-space method converges slowly but shakes loose bad minima that trap the others. Their advice flips standard practice: run cyclic projections first, then use the slow method to escape, and not the other way around.
arxiv-2502-19152:
Sunny Pradhan and co-authors wrote this physics paper in 2025 on the quantum six-vertex model, a lattice system tied to a spin chain. They study how entanglement, the deep linking of quantum parts, grows with system size. Their lens is a Shannon-Rényi entropy at infinite order, read from the ground state's weights. That lens also fixes the entanglement of a linked class of wave states.

A quirk showed up: when the chain holds an odd count of sites, an extra log term joins the scaling. The cause is frustration, as the ring's wrap forces clashing spin patterns on odd chains. The extra term's weight ties straight to a key trait of the low-energy theory. The authors say size parity, odd versus even, must enter any sharp account of entanglement here.
arxiv-2502-19252:
Graph neural networks learn from network-shaped data, but each new domain or task usually means retraining from scratch. Li Ju and co-authors present GraphBridge in this 2025 paper, a framework that lets a trained network carry its knowledge into very different graph tasks.

The design bolts new prediction heads and a small bridging network onto the old model, so outputs of any size are possible without touching the graph or the task setup. To avoid harmful carry-over, the source model is blended with a fresh one trained alongside. Across sixteen data sets and four transfer styles, the method held up well.
arxiv-2502-19352:
Johannes Gedeon, Izzatjon Allayarov, Emadeldeen Hassan, and Antonio Calà Lesina design a thin-film metasurface that absorbs light very well, using topology optimization, in a two thousand twenty-five light-science paper. The method works for any dispersive materials over any chosen spectral range.

Their figure of merit is the time-averaged power lost as heat inside one unit cell of a periodic array. A time-domain adjoint method inside the optimization loop shapes complex structures with broadband light uptake. Applied to a silicon-on-insulator film, the design process explores structural and excitation parameters across the visible and UV. Because the material model covers any linear medium, the approach transfers to dielectric, plasmonic, or hybrid metasurfaces.
arxiv-2502-19952:
Money laundering often hops between banks, yet banks cannot pool their records because of privacy and legal limits. Zhihua Tian and co-authors propose the first method in this 2025 paper that hunts laundering across institutions while keeping each bank's data private.

To test it, they built a huge real-world data set joining a major payment platform with a partner bank, covering hundreds of millions of accounts and transactions. The method found cross-bank laundering groups effectively. Tests on synthetic data also ran in minutes at million-transaction scale. The work points toward teamwork against laundering that respects the walls between institutions.
arxiv-2502-20052:
Tomas Dacik and Tomas Vojnar present a static analyzer that hunts data races in multithreaded C programs, built as a plugin for a established verification platform. Data races, two threads touching shared data without order, are among the nastiest bugs in concurrent code. Their tool is frankly heuristic. It analyzes each thread's sequential behavior with the platform's abstract interpreter, then generalizes the results with a mix of under- and over-approximation to reason about interleavings. No formal guarantees are promised.

The report was written for a software verification competition. In its category the analyzer placed second, with the most correct verdicts among non-meta tools and only a handful of false positives. The authors trade proof for pragmatism: a race detector that scales and mostly tells the truth.
arxiv-2502-20552:
Botond Barta, Endre Hamerlik, Milán Konor Nyist, and Judit Ács built HuAMR in twenty twenty-five, the first Abstract Meaning Representation resource for Hungarian. AMR graphs encode sentence meaning in a language-neutral form, but resources cluster on English. To create the data set, they generated draft annotations with a large language model, then refined them by hand.

On this foundation they trained parsers based on two architectures, a multilingual T5 and a small Llama, testing fine-tuning strategies. Adding machine-made silver data did not lift all scores, but it did improve parsing on Hungarian news text, the data set's home domain. Scores used the standard Smatch metric. The authors offer HuAMR as a base for semantic parsing research beyond English.
arxiv-2503-00552:
Zheng Zhao, Attaphon Kaewsnod, Kai Xu, Nattapat Tagsinsit, Xuyang Liu, Ayut Limphirat, and Yupeng Yan wrote a 2025 physics paper on exotic particles made of four quarks. The catalog title garbles the particles' spin label with stray code, but the head gives it cleanly. Normal matter uses two- or three-quark bundles, yet labs keep finding heavier states that may hold four quarks.

Using a standard quark model with settings fixed from known particles, the team computed the masses of a family of these four-quark states and how fast they should fall apart. The lightest should sit near a known energy. They suggest several puzzling states seen in labs, the so-called Y states, may be these four-quark bundles. Lab searches can test the assignments.
arxiv-2503-01052:
Yanzhou Pan and seven co-authors present ALinFiK, a method for pricing single training examples for large language models, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Good data drives model quality, and buyers with limited budgets need to know which samples earn their price. The authors define a score, the linearized future influence kernel, that estimates how much one sample will improve a model during training.

Computing that score directly is heavy, so ALinFiK learns to approximate it, making valuation fast enough for large collections. The pitch is a third-party service fair to both data sellers and model builders. In the team's tests, the method beat existing baselines on both accuracy of the ranking and speed, and its edge grew as the models got bigger.
arxiv-2503-01152:
Shilin Tong and co-authors present STGAN in a 2025 paper on predicting road surface damage over time. Cracked and worn pavement threatens safety and raises upkeep costs. Real damage records are collected irregularly, so data are uneven, out of sync, and sparse across places and times, which breaks standard models.

Their graph network folds time into the spatial graph. Each node pairs a place with a time, and edges link similar nodes. Prediction then becomes a step by step growth of the graph, adding future nodes in sequence. The design aims at accurate forecasts from messy real world records.
arxiv-2503-01952:
Morawetz and Polkovnikov design control protocols that steer quantum systems fast without leaving them excited, using only local time scales. Counterdiabatic driving normally needs full knowledge of the system's energy rules in advance. Their method works in Krylov space, built from how operators grow over time. It needs only traits like lattice vibration rates or qubit drive speeds. Those local scales set the protocol's shape. Surprisingly, success hinges on the far high-frequency tails of response curves.

That link joins slow, long-time behavior to fast, short-time operator growth. Krylov complexity sits at the center of the bridge. The result hints at a deep unity in how quantum systems respond. Practical control may need less prior knowledge than feared.
arxiv-2503-03352:
Nicolas Esser and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about whether tiny black holes could be part of dark matter. The black holes in question would have masses like asteroids. In faint dwarf galaxies, stars could capture such holes, and a captured hole would quickly destroy its host star.

The team used Hubble Space Telescope images of three very faint dwarf galaxies to study their star counts by mass. They found no clear sign that black holes had thinned out the stars. In one galaxy, Triangulum II, the results rule out some shares of dark matter in this form. The work narrows where this dark matter idea can still hold.
arxiv-2503-03552:
Abraham Loeb and Richard Cloete argue that a so-called dark comet may in fact be a lost Soviet spacecraft. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies object 2005 VL1, one of a new class of near-Earth bodies. These bodies speed up in ways gravity alone cannot explain, yet show no comet tail. Loeb and Cloete match the object against Venera 2, launched toward Venus in the mid-nineteen sixties.

The timing fits: the object passed near Earth the month Venera 2 launched. Its brightness suits a bright craft with broad solar panels. Its path took it close to Venus soon after, a rare fluke for a random body. Orbit values for both line up closely. The push from sunlight on a light, broad craft also matches the odd speedup. The authors make a case that the dark comet is human-made.
arxiv-2503-05552:
Perrier and four colleagues track how election talk synced across groups on Twitter in twenty twenty-five. Their case is the twenty twenty-two French presidential race. They grouped users by candidate support and by the media they followed. The goal was to spot, in real time, when groups lit up on the same topic at the same moment.

Two tools build shifting webs of linked words from the posts. One web grows over time and shows old topics flaring back to life. The other rolls over a short window and catches brief, sudden topics. Used together, the tools confirmed older hand done findings at far larger scale. The authors say the pair can help judge fair treatment of news.
arxiv-2503-06252:
