Kun Xiang and co-authors teach multimodal models to think in small, named steps in this 2025 paper. Models that see images and do math often ramble or overthink. The team's idea is that reasoning skill comes in levels, and a question should draw only the level it needs.

Their framework breaks each solution into minimal semantic steps and lets the model assemble its own chain from them. A data engine first manufactures clean step-by-step paths for training. Fine-tuning on those paths installs the habit, and a policy-guided loop runs it over several turns at test time. A new metric scores how well each single step gets used. On two visual math benchmarks the method lifted baseline accuracy by over ten points on average, used training data five times more efficiently than template rivals, and answered much faster.
arxiv-2503-07852:
Jongwon Park, Heesoo Jung, and Hogun Park hide graph parts by a rule of conditional independence, not by dice. Graph self-teaching hides traits or links to learn from the rest, yet random hides can cut the key facts or keep dross. Their 2025 method, CIMAGE, asks that the hidden and shown parts share the least while each holds the most for the task. That state needs task labels in the plain form.

A hidden-space split builds two views, with group labels from label-free clusters as stand-in labels. The task is to build the hidden view from the shown one alone. Proof says the learned marks split near-clean by class. On bench graphs the method tops rank means for node and link tasks.
arxiv-2503-08652:
Wei Chen and Qiang Qiu fight uneven data in federated learning by splitting each filter into parts. Their paper from twenty twenty-five addresses training shared across many devices. Each device holds unlike data, which skews the shared model and slows its settling. Their trick breaks a convolutional filter into a sum of shared atoms, each scaled by a weight.

Sharing then moves atoms and weights, not whole filters. Cross terms from the two sums act like many extra hidden clients. This spread cuts model variance, as both theory and tests show. Atoms and weights can train on split plans, which aids tailoring and trims message size. Benchmark tests show clear accuracy gains for federated methods. The change is simple, the authors stress, yet it buys extra clients at no cost.
arxiv-2503-08852:
Rohan Vernekar and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on flow in a gut like channel lined with tiny hairs, called villi. Wave like swings of the wall, named pendular waves, stir the small gut in life. The hairs sway in step with a lag to their neighbors. The team fakes the flow in two dimensions with a lattice method.

A mixing layer forms just above the hairs, full of half whirls that ride with the wave. In the main channel, a steady flow runs against the wave's path, the flip of the usual pump case. Trapped fluid paths that do not retrace explain the flip. A shape based law gives its size. Past a threshold, inertia caps the layer.
arxiv-2503-10952:
David d'Enterria and Karen Kang gauge how often protons and nuclei that collide should make exotic even-spin systems when their photons fuse, with no other products. They treat photon-fusion processes in ultraperipheral collisions at the RHIC, LHC, and future FCC colliders. They also treat proton-air collisions at the highest cosmic-ray energies. Cross sections use the equivalent photon approximation with realistic photon fluxes.

Four families of even-spin systems are covered. They are quarkonium bound states from the lightest pion up to toponium, plus exotic multiquark candidates. They also cover leptonium atoms such as positronium and dimuonium. They cover mesonium and baryonium atoms bound by quantum electrodynamics as well. Yields are given for about 50 such composite resonances that LHC tests could rebuild.
arxiv-2503-11452:
Reddi and Vinnicombe show deep aides in a dodge game act like hawks and doves. Two aides play a plain grid game where paths must cross. Each must reach its aim with no crash and no wrong exit. One net drives both aides in the game runs. That net is shared, so both aides learn from one brain. Best-play forms from the trained nets get read in the work.

Past full train, the net shows hawk-dove acts in the game. One aide takes a fierce path to its aim in the runs. The next aide learns to yield and dodge the fierce one. That split rose with no hand code for roles in the net. It came from the train path of the shared net lone.
arxiv-2503-11952:
Scott Carter, Seonmi Choi, and Byeorhi Kim study in 2025 how branched covers of the three-sphere can be folded. Note that the catalog title differs from the text's own title, and the text governs here. A branched cover wraps one space over another, with special behavior over a knot.

A folding maps the cover into a product space so that projection recovers the covering. Away from the branch set, the map is a smooth immersion. Cyclic and dihedral covers can both be folded. The paper gives a detailed folding for the dihedral cover branched over a torus knot, which is itself a three-sphere.
arxiv-2503-12752:
Sicheng Zhou and eight co-authors present a failure-handling system for parallel computing in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Task-based frameworks split big jobs into many small tasks across machines. Failures are common at that scale and can spoil results or waste hours. Older fixes retry every failure the same way, blind to its cause. The authors' system, WRATH, sorts failures by the layer of the framework where they arise.

Each layer gets its own response, matched to the failure type. A distributed monitor spots problems, and a resilience module acts on them. The design respects the mixed hardware and task-level faults of these systems. Tests show steadier completion of large workloads. The paper serves teams that run scientific computing at scale.
arxiv-2503-14452:
Louis and a large team of colleagues set out the sixth sky-glow file set from a Chile scope bank in this twenty twenty-five paper. The scope maps the faint glow left from the young hot globe. Those maps test the stock tale of how all space grew and spread.

Inside, glow strength charts span a wide band of fine sky scales. Fit packs let peers rerun the team's fits on the same files. Stock tale grades fall out of those charts with tight doubt bands. Team files pair the glow charts with cross-checks from kin scopes. The set is cast as a base file bank for world-build tests.
arxiv-2503-14752:
Máté Matolcsi, Ákos Matszangosz, Dániel Varga, and Mihály Weiner begin a systematic study of triplets of mutually unbiased bases in a 2025 paper. Such bases are sets of measurement directions in quantum theory that are maximally incompatible with each other. How many can coexist in a given dimension is a long-standing puzzle.

The authors show each triplet in dimension d is captured by a three-dimensional array they call a Hadamard cube. They describe the cubes' basic properties and how to rebuild a triplet from one. They also offer an algebraic identity guessed to hold for all triplets in dimension six. If true, it would settle Zauner's conjecture that three is the maximum there.
arxiv-2503-14952:
Mirosław Werwiński, Andrzej Szajek, Agnieszka Marczyńska, Lesław Smardz, Marek Nowak, and Mieczysław Jurczyk wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests what happens when some lanthanum in a lanthanum nickel alloy is swapped for magnesium, for use as a battery electrode material.

The team made a set of alloys by mechanical alloying, with four levels of magnesium. X-ray tests show the samples hold two main crystal forms side by side. Charge tests show the stored charge grows with magnesium, peaking at the mid level of the set. Computer models based on density functional theory back the lab work, match where magnesium sits in the crystal, and help read the measured photoelectron spectra.
arxiv-2503-17152:
Araujo-Pardo and Mendoza-Cadena wrote in twenty twenty-five a note on mixed cages, the smallest possible graphs with given degrees and girth. A mixed graph combines directed arcs with undirected edges at each vertex. Girth is the length of the shortest cycle in the graph. Cages are the record-holding smallest examples for their parameters. The note targets girth five, a classic hard case. It constructs a family of such graphs for prime power parameters.

The construction obeys a stated relation between directed degree and edge degree. Those graphs improve the best known upper bounds on cage size. Smaller constructions mean the true minima sit lower than previously shown. Cage problems guide the design of sparse, well-connected networks. Even incremental bound improvements matter in this record-chasing field. The note adds a flexible infinite family to the known examples.
arxiv-2503-18652:
Yaoyao Yun and Jianwen Xu improve face recognition for the hard cases: faces heavily covered or damaged. Sparse coding approaches work well on clean portraits but their accuracy drops sharply under occlusion. The authors build two related models to withstand those conditions.

Their wing-constrained sparse coding model, and a weighted version of it, combine wing loss with sparsity regularization. An alternating direction optimization method solves the resulting problems. Tests ran on four standard face databases, including ORL, Yale, AR, and FERET. The weighted model kept a very high recognition rate even with heavy occlusion or damage. Comparisons against published methods support the claimed robustness.
arxiv-2503-19752:
Lewis Newsham, Ryan Hyland, and Daniel Prince give fake computer users distinct personalities so they can lure attackers for longer, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The setting is cyber deception: honeypot systems that pretend to be real targets so defenders can watch attack behavior unfold.

Their architecture, SANDMAN, uses language model agents as decoys that chat and act like people. The trick under study is personality. A prompt schema based on the five-factor model of personality traits is used to steer each agent's style. The authors run experiments to measure whether these prompts truly produce distinct, stable personas. They find the induced personalities do generate varied, realistic agendas and behavior. Longer, more human-seeming engagement means more time to observe attackers. The work suggests persona-driven decoys can sharpen cyber deception strategies.
arxiv-2503-20952:
A research team published a research paper in 2025 on an attack that reconstructs private time series data from the updates shared in federated learning. Hospitals and utilities train forecasting models together without pooling raw data, but a curious server might invert the shared gradients to recover the inputs. Attacks were well studied for images, not for forecasting.

Their method, TS-Inverse, predicts quantiles of the hidden series and penalizes breaks in trend and seasonal rhythm. Across four forecasting models and four data sets it recovered series far more accurately than older attacks, improving the error score by two to ten times. The result warns that federated forecasting needs stronger privacy defenses.
arxiv-2503-21252:
Benedikt Klein and Mario Ohlberger build a layered trust region method that learns reduced models at many fidelity levels while solving optimization problems bound by parabolic equations. Classic model reduction splits work into offline and online stages. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Here the reduced models grow on the fly inside the outer search loop, by active learning. Three layers share the work: a full model, a reduced model, and a machine learning model. A strict after the fact error gauge guides updates inside an error aware trust region frame. Numeric tests show the approach runs with good efficiency, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-22552:
Sapna, Sushant Singh, and David Wagner model spin in the quark-gluon plasma in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In heavy-ion collisions, the plasma's spin can polarize the Lambda hyperons that fly out. Describing that spin flow needs hydrodynamics that include dissipation.

The team solves spin evolution equations drawn from quantum kinetic theory, under three interaction scenarios. They compute global and local polarization for gold-gold collisions at top collider energy. A spin potential that starts at zero relaxes toward the plasma's rotation, driving global polarization. The sign of the local, longitudinal polarization flips with the interaction type. The authors stress that dissipation must be handled with care to match experiments.
arxiv-2503-22652:
Nikhil Kodali, Kartick Ramakrishnan, and Phani Motamarri wrote a 2025 numerical methods paper on finding a few key eigenvalues of very large sparse matrices. A well-known filtering method handles this task, but it can falter when the matrix products it relies on are computed roughly rather than exactly.

The authors recast the method so it works with residuals, the gaps between current guesses and true answers. Their version keeps converging even with sloppy products. It can use cheap rough inverses, low-precision math, and compressed messages between processors. Tests on random dense matrices matched the new theory. The approach suits physics codes that must repeat this task many times inside larger solvers.
arxiv-2504-00252:
Giorgio Krstulovic and Vincent Labarre present a Julia software kit that solves wave kinetic equations, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such equations track how waves swap energy in wild systems, from sound in fluids to matter waves and ocean swells. Each system needs its own solver, a slow build from scratch.

Their kit, WavKinS, ships with solvers for many known wave systems built in. Its frame splits the work into shared parts, so a new solver for a fresh system can be put together from ready blocks. The kit runs fast and is free to use and change under an open license. The authors expect the shared frame to cut the time from a new wave model to a working code.
arxiv-2504-00352:
Kaier Liang, Guang Yang, Mingyu Cai, and Cristian-Ioan Vasile make robot navigation safer around moving obstacles in a 2025 paper. Nonlinear motion is hard to predict, and safety demands honest error bounds. Their framework learns a linear style model of the motion from data, using Koopman operator theory, then wraps its predictions with conformal prediction, a method that gives statistical error guarantees.

Those error bounds tighten the safety constraints inside a predictive controller, so plans keep a margin sized to real uncertainty. A reference generator supplies waypoints through a layered control design. Simulations validate the approach. The authors pitch the combination as principled safety for robots in dynamic surroundings.
arxiv-2504-01052:
Sherzer predicts queue behaviour with neural networks in twenty twenty-five. Queues with several servers are hard to analyse when arrival and service times are general. Exact stationary distributions are rarely available in closed form. He trains networks to predict how many customers occupy the system.

Two systems are covered: identical servers, and a pair of unlike servers. Inputs are just the first four moments of arrival and service times. Adding a fifth moment did not improve accuracy. Errors stayed under five percent in most tests. The identical server results match or beat the best existing methods. The mixed server case had no prior predictor at all. Inference is fast, with thousands of predictions in a fraction of a second.
arxiv-2504-02552:
Alberto Maione, Fabio Paronetto, and Simone Verzellesi study variational convergence when the anisotropy of a problem keeps moving, in a two thousand twenty-five analysis paper. Anisotropy means the energy of a summed functional depends on heading, not just place.

The authors set up the working setup for such problems. They prove uniform Meyers-Serrin type approximations, Poincaré inequalities, and compactness traits for the function spaces that matter. Several Gamma-convergence results follow, spelling out the limit conduct of sequences of functionals. The paper then applies those results to H-convergence of anisotropic linear differential operators, a question about how sets of equations settle to a limit.
arxiv-2504-02852:
Yike Qiao and five colleagues wrote a 2025 robotics paper on planning motion for nonholonomic robots, machines whose wheels or joints prevent them from moving sideways directly, like a car. Vector fields are a popular guide for such robots because they prescribe a desired heading at every point. The hard part is adding curvature limits, since a car-like robot cannot turn arbitrarily sharply.

The authors design the vector field and the tracking controller together rather than separately. Their framework uses a target limit set, a region the robot is guaranteed to reach or pass through. The robot follows a curvature-bounded path to its target configuration. The co-design avoids the mismatch that arises when a field demands turns the controller cannot execute.
arxiv-2504-03052:
Hyun-Ho Choi, Kangsoo Kim, Ki-Ho Lee, and Kisong Lee present a computing paper from 2025 on body pose from cameras. Phones and small devices must guess a person's three-dimensional pose in real time. The task is heavy, and small devices have weak chips and slow links.

Their method splits the work between the device and a nearby server. Each device runs a light model and keeps clear cases for itself. Only hard, unclear images go to the server, which runs a stronger model. The team works out the best cut-offs for sending and the best send times. Tests show a clear trade-off between pose error and delay. With the best settings, error fell a lot while delay stayed within the set limit.
arxiv-2504-03352:
Kaustubh Shejole and Pushpak Bhattacharyya tackle stereotype detection in AI in a 2025 paper. Stereotypes harm people, so spotting them matters, yet the field has often blurred stereotypes with the broader notion of bias. That confusion, the authors argue, has slowed real progress.

They offer exact definitions that separate stereotypes, anti-stereotypes, and two kinds of bias in a five-part scheme. On that base they built StereoDetect, a carefully curated benchmark data set aligned with the definitions. Tests show that even strong models like GPT-4o often misread anti-stereotypes and miss neutral overgeneralizations. The authors release the data and code to push detection research onto firmer ground.
arxiv-2504-05252:
Five physicists measure a special Hall effect in a magnetic material in a paper from 2025. The material, a compound of manganese and germanium, is a Weyl semimetal with magnetism built in. When current flows, sideways voltage appears from both the band structure and the spin arrangement. The team grew a single crystal and measured the effect along different planes.

The sideways response differed sharply by direction, matching band calculations that predict many special points. A second, topological part of the effect came from spins that twist out of plane. Two forces compete to set that twist, one favoring alignment and one from dipolar coupling. The authors say the second force may help form tiny spin swirls called skyrmions.
arxiv-2504-06452:
Xuesong Bai and Thomas G. Fai model how a growing cell keeps the size ratio between its nucleus and the rest of the cell nearly fixed, in a research paper from 2025. The ratio stays steady through the cell cycle, and past work ties it to how proteins split between the two zones. Transport through the nuclear skin sets that split.

Their model joins protein transport physics with simple cell growth. It shows the nuclear skin must grow leakier in step with the cell to hold the ratio. Transport and protein-making settings shift the ratio strongly. One carrier protein can cover for a missing partner, but only if its spent form crosses the skin alone.
arxiv-2504-06752:
Rishubh Parihar and co-authors give text-to-image models a compass in a 2025 paper. Current image generators follow text well but cannot set the exact facing direction of each object in a scene. A prompt can ask for a chair turned left, yet the model turns it as it pleases.

Their method, Compass Control, feeds the model a set of orientation cues, one per object. The generator then builds scenes where each object faces its assigned way. Tests cover crowded scenes with several objects under separate control. Precise facing matters for product mock-ups, storyboards, and training data for robots. The work adds a missing dial to image generation: not just what appears, but which way it looks.
arxiv-2504-07052:
Tian Qin, David Alvarez-Melis, Samy Jelassi, and Eran Malach wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It weighs two ways to spend extra compute at test time for language models: step-by-step search with backtracking, versus drawing many tries at once and picking the best.

On the CountDown task the step-by-step path lost, while on Sudoku it won, so backtracking is not a sure win. The authors blame two foes: training on fixed search traces can lock a model into poor routes, and worded chain-of-thought drills can crowd out silent thought. With reinforcement learning, models that can backtrack gained much, while those that cannot gained little. Task shape and training rule the outcome.
arxiv-2504-07152:
Matthew Roughan presents a 2025 method to breed random surreal numbers for use as test data. Surreal numbers are a vast number system that holds all real numbers and much more. They have stayed a mostly pure idea, in part since all but the smallest are hard to work with in practice.

Fast methods to handle them need good test sets, which did not exist. The method uses an evolution-style search that grows sets of surreal numbers with set traits. Users can steer and study the traits of the sets it makes, rather than take whatever chance gives. The process in fact builds networks with defined traits. The author expects the same tack to serve for other kinds of network test data.
arxiv-2504-07252:
Rajhans Singh, Rafael Bidese Puhl, Kshitiz Dhakal, and Sudhir Sornapudi adapt a vision model for farm tasks with very little labeled data. Their 2025 paper starts from Grounding DINO, a model that finds objects in images from text prompts. Farm uses need labeled images, and making those labels takes much time and work.

The team found that plain text prompts failed on hard targets such as single leaves. Their fix removes the text reading part and trains a fresh text code in its place. The adapted model beat fully trained rival models on plant, weed, insect, and fruit data sets. It also led on remote sensing tasks. The method offers a cheaper path to tools that count plants and spot pests.
arxiv-2504-07652:
Luan Vinícius Fiorio, Ivana Nikoloska, and Ronald Aarts cluster acoustic scenes categorically in two thousand twenty five. Urban sound data overlap heavily in time and frequency. Soft clustering blurs when points pile on top of each other. A categorical model enforces sharper cluster assignments instead here.

The Gumbel-Softmax distribution makes the categorical choice trainable by gradient methods. Backpropagation flows through the soft approximation during learning. Softmax temperature becomes the main tuning knob for sharpness. Results impress across all the datasets they tried. Strong overlap no longer defeats the clustering quality.
arxiv-2504-09552: Huai-Liang Chang, Sanghyeon Lee, and Jun Li wrote a math paper from 2025 on fields used to count curves on a special three-fold shape inside a product of two planes. They lay out the fixed parts of the space of these fields, sorted by graphs. Their main result is a vanishing rule: any term tied to a fixed part whose graph is irregular adds nothing to the count, unless the graph is a pure loop. The same rule holds for a wider version of the fields.
arxiv-2504-10152:
Ahmet Tekcan defines a new clan of integer sequences spun off from the balancing numbers, a family tied to Pell equations and triangular numbers. The new objects come in four kinds: neo balcobalancing numbers, their Lucas-style partners, and the balancers attached to each. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Tekcan derives general term formulas converting the new sequences into the classical balancing family and back again. Balancing, cobalancing, and both Lucas variants are all expressed through the new numbers.

The paper then works through the standard anatomy of such sequences. Closed forms, recurrence relations, and Cassini-style identities are established. Links to Pell and Pell-Lucas numbers, triangular and square triangular numbers, and Pythagorean triples are drawn. Sum formulas for the first many terms close the development.
arxiv-2504-11652:
Marvin Williams and Peter Sanders present a 2025 paper on faster priority queues for parallel programs. Priority queues drive scheduling, simulation, and greedy algorithms, but a single strict queue becomes a bottleneck when many threads push and pop. Relaxed queues trade a little ordering exactness for speed.

Their MultiQueue keeps several ordinary queues inside and spreads work across them. Buffering, batching, and cache-friendly access patterns lift throughput further. Two quality measures are studied: how far a removed item sits from the true minimum, and how many smaller items were skipped ahead of it. On benchmarks including shortest paths, the MultiQueue beat rivals and can be tuned to favor speed or precision. A wait-free locking trick in the design may serve other data structures too.
arxiv-2504-14152:
Hooper and co-authors propose in 2025 a fine grained mixed precision method to shrink large language models for fast hardware inference. Cutting numeric precision saves energy and memory, but crude cuts harm accuracy. Their method keeps most values at low precision and spares the blocks that matter most.

A policy weighs each block's disturbance by its effect on model loss to pick which blocks stay at high precision. A weighted clipping step helps blocks that do drop in precision keep accuracy. Hardware changes support the mixed scheme at block level. The co design aims to give hardware level speed gains without the usual accuracy loss.
arxiv-2504-14452:
Tong Chen and co-authors teach language models to paraphrase rather than repeat their training data, in work from 2025. Models can spit back memorized text word for word, which raises worries over rights, copying, and privacy. Their method, ParaPO, tunes a model to favor reworded takes on memorized spans over the raw spans.

A prompt-based variant still lets the model quote famed lines when asked with care. On a mid-size open model, the method cut repeat scores across all test sets. Older unlearning tools helped only inside their narrow target zone. On a tuned chat model, the prompt variant cut stray repeats while keeping famed quotes.
arxiv-2504-14552:
Combining p-values from many tests is a common way to judge an overall effect, and the Cauchy combination test is valued because it holds up when tests are not independent. Huda Alsulami and Silvia Liverani check how well this test behaves for count data, where the single p-values come from a normal approximation to the negative binomial distribution.

Using simulations, they vary the distribution's success parameter, the number of combined p-values, and the strength of correlation, modeling linked counts with copula methods. Both the success parameter and the count of p-values could disturb the false-positive rate when tests were independent or weakly linked. The choice of copula mattered a lot for both this test and a rival minimum-p method. With one common copula family, the Cauchy test kept better control as correlation grew. The findings guide analysts who combine count-based tests.
arxiv-2504-15252:
Tue Vo and seven co-authors build a data pipeline for water invertebrates in Vietnam in a 2025 arXiv paper. Small water creatures are fine gauges of river and lake health. Yet photo data for naming them in Vietnam is scarce, and hand labeling is slow.

Their pipeline, SuoiAI, covers the full path from field collection to a trained naming model. It leans on partial self teaching to cut the labeling load: a model trained on a small checked set helps tag the rest. Off the shelf tools spot each creature in a photo and sort it by kind. The team aims at hard cases too, such as telling near twin species apart and working in mixed field settings. The set is meant to back watch programs for Vietnam's waters.
arxiv-2504-15952:
Daichi Igarashi and five co-authors rebuild 3D fluid stress fields via photoelasticity in two thousand twenty-five. Stress maps matter in engineering, medicine, and bioengineering alike. Classic routes infer stress from velocity, but fail for complex fluids. Their constitutive laws are unknown in those hard cases.

Photoelastic reads show stress inside a flow without touch. A model named PICED learns to turn those reads into full fields. It joins a convolutional encoder decoder with physics informed learning. Tests on a rectangular channel flow hit high accuracy. Many interpolated points in the volume are predicted at once.
arxiv-2504-16252:
De Freitas, Sobrero, Macedo, and Svaiter study sound-like excitations in simple liquids under random disturbance, in a 2025 paper. They treat the liquid's flow fields as quantum fields. High-energy effects from outside those fields enter as a noise field. The noise is random at each point in space and time. The team builds a generating tool for the linked statistics of the system.

Averaging over all noise patterns uses a device borrowed from a zeta-function method. The result is a series that can be handled term by term. Each term describes free excitations in the liquid. Most follow the usual sound-like pattern. Extra terms show excitations with gaps in their momentum pattern. From the same frame the authors compute how heat capacity at fixed volume changes with temperature. They apply it to several simple liquids.
arxiv-2504-17152:
Sampaio, Rabelo-Soares, and Torrieri rebuild the theory of flowing matter from randomness up in a 2025 paper. Relativistic hydrodynamics usually starts as a smooth, averaged theory and expands in gentle gradients. These authors instead treat each fluid cell as a small statistical system with its own partition function. The flow then emerges from the statistics rather than being assumed.

Working with Gaussian fluctuations, they use gravity's Ward identities, rules linking averages and variances, to keep full general covariance: the theory stays valid in any coordinates. The flow field appears as an approximate symmetry direction of the geometry. Linear response formulas also come out covariant, provided the fluid's own symmetry is respected. The reframing changes what limits the theory's reach, no longer the usual gradient count.
arxiv-2504-18052: Jiang, Kang, and Lü develop in twenty twenty-five a theory of paired structures for a broadened kind of algebra. Their algebra loosens the usual rule for how products group, and sits among a small set of notable types. They define paired forms built from two matched halves, then prove those forms match a second, related notion. They also set out a key equation for this setting and a special class of paired forms. Last, they show how certain operators yield neat, balanced solutions to that equation.
arxiv-2504-18152:
Yi-Xing Peng and co-authors introduce ActionArt in this 2025 paper, a video data set for fine-grained understanding of human action. Smart systems that work with people must track small limb moves, not just broad activity labels. The data set holds thousands of videos of actions and object use, each labeled in detail down to every limb movement. The team built eight test tasks from it.

Current large multimodal models did well on broad tasks but fell short on the fine detail. Hand labeling such detail is costly and hard to scale. So the team designed proxy tasks fed by labels that models generate on their own. Those tasks sharpen both spatial and timing perception. Tests show they close much of the gap toward hand-labeled training.
arxiv-2504-18352: Timothy Chan and Isaac Hair give a faster algorithm for sliding one convex polygon to overlap another as much as possible in this 2025 paper. Both shapes have many edges, and only shifting, not turning, is allowed. Finding the shift with the largest shared area is a classic geometry problem. Their randomized method runs in time that grows just in step with the edge count. That beats a method from 1998 that held the record for over twenty-five years. Special-case methods from recent years are also surpassed.
arxiv-2504-19152:
Gabriel Bathie, Nathanaël Fijalkow, and Corto Mascle published a 2025 computer science paper classifying how hard it is to test regular languages. Property testing asks a cheap question: by sampling a few positions of a long word, can we tell whether it belongs to a language, or is far from any word that does? A 2001 paper opened this field for regular languages, those recognized by simple finite machines.

The authors prove the landscape splits into exactly three classes. Each class has its own best possible number of queries. Better, they characterize which languages fall where using a concrete combinatorial tool: minimal blocking sequences, patterns read straight off the machine. The analysis reasons directly about automata rather than through heavy machinery. The trichotomy settles the complexity map for a classic problem. It also feeds streaming algorithms, where the same sampling logic decides what a data stream contains.
arxiv-2504-21152:
Shayan Alahyari and Mike Domaratzki present SMOGAN, a 2025 method for teaching prediction models about rare values. In imbalanced regression the target crowds in one range, so models master the common values and flub the rare ones that often matter most.

Older fixes fake new minority examples by blending neighbors or adding noise, which misses curved real patterns. SMOGAN starts from such an oversampler, then refines its fakes with a distribution-aware adversarial network trained to match the true joint pattern of features and target. Across twenty-three skewed data sets, the refined examples improved predictions where data are sparse, without wrecking the dense regions.
arxiv-2504-21352:
Chaos is easy to spot and hard to grade. Marat Akhmet proposes an uncertainty principle for chaos built on two of its hallmarks: alpha unpredictability and Lorenz sensitivity. The principle sets a limit on how two infinite sequences behind those concepts can relate. It applies to both deterministic and stochastic dynamics, which the author frames as a step toward unifying the two fields.

Early progress came through work on Markov chains with alpha labeling. Akhmet also suggests how the principle could grade the degree of chaos in a given process. He closes by listing open questions about how the many types of chaos connect, including a modification of the recurrence theorem.
arxiv-2505-00452:
Gregory Schroeder, Mohamed Sabry, and Cristina Olaverri-Monreal present a small data set for camera calibration from straight lines in a 2025 paper. Cameras can be calibrated by how straight edges in the world bend in images, a well-founded method in computer vision. Outdoor scenes make it hard in practice, with clutter, broken line views, and changing light.

No dedicated data set existed to drive better detection methods. The authors describe how they built their data set, named ClearLines, and share lessons from the process. They offer it as a guide and testbed for building algorithms that find straight three-dimensional lines in real scenes.
arxiv-2505-01352:
Arghadeep Pal and seven co-authors blend two different light-bending effects, from two different materials, inside one tiny chip resonator. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Nonlinear optics on chips usually relies on a single material's effect. That limits what designers can combine.

Their resonators pair a silicon nitride core with a fused silica cladding. The cladding supplies Raman gain, an effect the core lacks on its own. The core supplies the Kerr effect that builds frequency combs. Together they produced Raman lasing at modest on-chip power, matching simulations. Shaping the waveguides then yielded a broad combined Raman-Kerr comb. The hybrid trick could pair other effect families too, like second and third order materials. Compact lasers and precision spectrometers stand to gain.
arxiv-2505-01452:
Franco Maria Nardini and colleagues remove the neural network from the query path of learned sparse search, replacing it with a table lookup. Learned sparse retrieval encodes text as weighted word bags and answers from inverted indexes. Training usually regularizes hard for sparsity, but newer engines changed the trade-off. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team first shows regularization can be relaxed, yielding stronger encoders. The bottleneck then moves: encoding each query with a network now dominates the cost. Their method learns a fixed score for every token at training time, so query encoding becomes a seamless lookup.

The result set state-of-the-art effectiveness in their tests, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Gains over a strong baseline appeared on two standard benchmarks. Speed and quality, usually traded against each other, improved together.
arxiv-2505-02452:
Anisha Banerjee, Roni Con, Antonia Wachter-Zeh, and Eitan Yaakobi decode messages damaged by insertions and deletions through a new reduction, in a 2025 paper. Such errors scramble stored data, notably in DNA storage. Most known decoders rely on synchronization strings. Those convert the problem into simpler error types. This work instead reduces decoding to list recovery. In list recovery, the decoder outputs a short candidate list.

The authors prove the bridge formally. Any suitably list-recoverable code becomes a list-decodable code for insertions and deletions. They apply the idea to Reed-Solomon codes. Those have fast list recovery up to a known bound. The result gives the first efficient decoder of this kind for most such codes. Random error channels get a better rate trade-off. A classic soft-decision algorithm is adapted to the channel too. The paper is theoretical computer science with storage uses.
arxiv-2505-03352:
Anton Sofronov, Dina Yakovleva, and Alexander Yakubovich speed up the automatic design of silicon light chips in a paper from 2025. The catalog title carries journal text, but the head title is clean, and the description follows the head. Inverse design shapes a device so light behaves as wanted. Their scheme describes shapes with smooth parameters that support gradient calculations. Most steps become special convolutions that run fast on graphics processors.

Paired with an open-source simulator and a custom optimizer, the tool produces layouts in minutes to hours instead of days. The optimizer also keeps final designs manufacturable. Results are not globally optimal, the authors note. They do reflect how fields naturally prefer to travel through the device.
arxiv-2505-04452:
Romano and co-authors report a long X-ray watch of a binary star system, in work from 2025. The system, called 4U 1909+07, pairs a neutron star with a huge blue companion whose wind feeds it. The team used the Swift telescope for one hundred thirty-seven looks, spanning many short orbital rounds and longer superorbital rounds.

Folded on the short round, the data confirmed swings in brightness and in gas blocking the view, as the star sweeps through the wind. Folded on the long round, no clear swing showed. Other data hint the long beat had faded at the time. The team weighs what that means for a wind-clash model.
arxiv-2505-04552:
Bo Yang and Naoki Negishi found a leaner way to fake quantum motion in a 2025 paper. Quantum computers can act out how a group of particles moves over time, a task too hard for normal machines at scale. The standard recipe chops time into small steps, but it needs many long-range gates, and today's noisy hardware garbles such deep circuits.

Their recipe leans on the mirror-like balance built into many particle setups. It cuts both the left-over error of the chopping and the gate count at once. The result is a circuit that stays closer to the true motion on real hardware. Such lean circuits help near-term machines do useful work.
arxiv-2505-04752:
Li, Zeng, Xue, and Feng model episodic memory by joining pretrained AI with brain like dynamics in twenty twenty-five. Episodic memory stores the events of a person's own life, and modelling it is a hard problem for both neuroscience and AI. Past models were either hard to interpret or hard to use. Their VLEM framework splits the job between two systems that work as one.

Pretrained vision language models turn sensory input into meaning rich codes, acting as neocortex. A hippocampus module stores and retrieves them through attractor dynamics. Working memory and a gateway region connect the two parts. A three dimensional simulation platform, EpiGibson, makes memory test data. Tests showed fast learning of high level time based representations. The authors stress robustness and interpretability for real world use.
arxiv-2505-07752:
José Mancias, Brent Vela, Juan Flórez-Coronel, and four colleagues map how metal microstructures form during rapid solidification in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The question matters for additive manufacturing, where molten alloy freezes quickly into cellular, dendritic, or planar patterns. Their phase-field model captures solute trapping, kinetic undercooling, and interface instabilities across wide ranges of growth velocity and thermal gradient. A binary iron-chromium alloy stands in for a common stainless steel.

Gaussian process based Bayesian active learning steered the expensive simulations, so the transition map across composition, velocity, and gradient was built efficiently. The classical KGT theory accurately predicted the gradient above which interfaces stay planar. Unstable intermediate microstructures appeared near the dendritic-planar border at low gradients. The authors offer the approach as a design tool for process parameters.
arxiv-2505-08252:
Yusuf Fayziev and Shakhnoza Jumaeva study a fractional equation in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their equation blends two layers of fractional change over time. It also includes an operator that can grow without bound. Such equations model memory effects in complex materials and systems.

The pair take up the starting value problem for this equation. Under set conditions, they prove a solution exists and is the only one. They build the solution from the operator's own modes, summed in a series. Each term of the series respects the fractional rules of the equation. The paper adds to the theory of Langevin type models with memory. It is aimed at readers in analysis and mathematical physics.
arxiv-2505-08752:
Jeffrey Boland and Lane Hughston draw a geometric picture of the tone network used in music theory in a 2025 paper. The tonnetz arranges tones in a triangular lattice and links major and minor triads. The authors recast it as a graph with twelve points for major triads and twelve for minor triads.

They show this graph can be drawn as twelve points and twelve lines in the plane, with exactly three points on each line and three lines through each point. That pattern is a known configuration type from geometry. The paper develops generalizations of the tonnetz configuration and proposes them as a fresh basis for composing and analyzing music.
arxiv-2505-09152:
Nour Elhouda Guesmia, Abdelhakim Necir, and Djamel Meraghni build a new gauge for the tail weight of data that is cut off on the right. Such data arise in loss claims that are not yet full. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Their gauge rests on a classic step gauge of the chance law for cut-off data, smoothed with a kernel. Under plain terms, they prove the gauge settles on the truth and takes a known bell shape for large sets. A small set of fake runs shows it has less bias and more steadiness than past gauges, at a slight rise in mean squared error. They show its use on real insurance loss data.
arxiv-2505-09852:
Apollinaire Poli Nemkova and co-authors present a 2025 study on whether language models can forecast violent conflict. Such forecasts serve early warning and aid planning. A model may hold useful facts in its trained weights, or it may need fresh data fed at query time. The team tests both modes across the Horn of Africa and the Middle East for the years 2020 to 2024.

In the first mode, models predict trend labels and death counts from memory alone. In the second, they read fresh event data and news through a retrieval setup. Calls are scored against the true record. The results map where baked-in knowledge holds and where fresh context is a must. The work gives policy teams a sober view of model use in war watching.
arxiv-2505-10552:
Barhydt and colleagues present in twenty twenty-five a new class of robot grasping that changes shape topology to grip well. A gripper must first form a grasp, then hold it. Single-shape designs trade off strength, gentleness, and range. Their design starts as an open loop, so the tip moves freely to wrap varied objects, then closes the loop to hold.

Closed, the loop holds strongly yet bends with near endless softness, which keeps fragile items safe. The team formalises the two shapes and builds a version from soft growing tubes, winches, and clamps. Tests gripped objects and settings that had long challenged robot hands. The authors frame the shape shift as the key advance.
arxiv-2505-12452:
Siyang Wu, Honglin Bao, and colleagues ask whether language models lack knowledge or merely fail to use it, using patents as the test bed in a 2025 study. Models recall facts superbly, yet stumble on technology judgment tasks such as classifying patents, where deep conceptual understanding separates inventions that sound alike. The authors frame two hypotheses: the knowledge is missing, or it is present but unused.

Their patent experiments are designed to tell those apart, since the remedies differ entirely, more training data versus better elicitation. The missing-versus-unused question decides where research money should go for professional AI tools.
arxiv-2505-13152:
Jonas Brenig and Radu Timofte fix a weakness of diffusion-based image compression: pretty results that drift too far from the original picture. Generative compressors win on how natural their images look but lose on fidelity measures like PSNR. The authors' hybrid first runs a decoder trained for low distortion, producing a faithful draft. A diffusion model then polishes only the leftover difference, guided by the compressed code, to restore natural texture.

On standard test sets the scheme gained up to 2 decibels of PSNR over the CDC diffusion compressor while keeping perceptual scores about level. The same design extends to video, with similar gains. The authors frame the split of labour, fidelity first, realism second, as a practical way to have both virtues in one codec.
arxiv-2505-13252:
Rikhil Amonkar and co-authors give language models a reality check as translators of word problems into solver-ready code. Their paper appeared in 2025. The fashionable pipeline has the model write a formal program, then lets an exact solver finish the job. Across four real-life constraint benchmarks, six models, and two formal languages, that pipeline lost to simply letting the model solve directly in fifteen of twenty-four combinations, despite its checkable outputs.

Worse, formalizing degraded with problem complexity just as fast as direct solving. The team caught models burning tokens on solver-like reasoning and sometimes hard-coding answers. The authors say formalization is no free lunch: the translation step itself is where capability leaks, and future work must shore it up.
arxiv-2505-13352:
Prakash Timsina and co-authors simulate frustrated pyrochlore magnets and find hidden high entropy phases between the known ones, in work from twenty twenty-five. These crystal magnets cannot settle all their spins at once, which breeds exotic states. Three stable phases were already mapped for two iridate compounds.

Monte Carlo runs charted the full heat phase map. Between the stable phases, two extra metastable phases appeared at mild temperatures. They show strong magnetic response and high entropy with no long range order. Entropy wins there because rival orders nearly tie in energy near the borders. The authors frame frustration plus heat as a design tool for building highly responsive, disordered states on purpose.
arxiv-2505-13652:
Karina Zainullina and co-authors improve how AI agents search for solutions when the workbench cannot be rewound, in a 2025 paper. Coding agents work inside containers whose state cannot be saved and restored cheaply. That blocks classic tree search, which needs to revisit earlier states.

The team tests two guided strategies that fit such settings: peeking one step ahead, and picking the best full attempt after several tries. Both lean on a learned value estimator that grades partial work. On a verified benchmark of real software tasks, the strategies doubled the average success rate of a fine-tuned large model, reaching about forty-one percent. The results give agent builders search tools that respect the limits of real sandboxes.
arxiv-2505-13752:
Oliveira, Zesta, and Garcia-Sage track falling Starlink satellites in this 2025 study. Low-orbit satellites face drag from the thin upper atmosphere, which shortens their lives. Storms in Earth's magnetic field make that drag worse.

The team used public tracking data for 523 Starlink satellites that reentered between 2020 and 2024. That window covers the rising phase of solar cycle 25, which proved stronger than the cycle before. Satellites clearly fell faster when geomagnetic activity was high, because decay rates rose with drag. Forecast errors also grew during active periods. The findings matter for collision warnings and for predicting where debris risk falls.
arxiv-2505-14152:
Salcedo develops a linearized take on renormalization, the cleanup that removes infinite terms from quantum field theory, in work from twenty twenty-five. Start from an action already cleaned so its predictions stay finite. Then ask how the action must shift when the cleanup conditions shift a little.

That small shift view yields the induced change in the theory's correlation functions directly. For simpler super renormalizable theories, the program gives explicit formulas built from full propagators and vertices in a handful of graphs. The fully renormalizable case stays finite but needs a regulator in the formulas. A projective scheme keeps the conditions intact. Extensions reach composite operators and the Schwinger-Dyson equations.
arxiv-2505-14352:
Bartosz Cywiński, Emil Ryd, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, and Neel Nanda probe whether language models can keep secrets, in a 2025 paper. As models grow stronger, operators worry that a model might hide what it knows. The team built a test model trained to describe a secret word without ever saying it.

The secret word never appears in the model's training data or its prompts. The researchers then tried two ways to extract it. Plain questioning and probing worked to a degree. Tools that read the model's inner workings, such as lenses on its layers and sparse feature maps, also pulled the secret out. Both routes succeeded in this simple setup. The authors present the testbed as a first step toward auditing hidden knowledge in bigger models.
arxiv-2505-14452:
Lance Wilhelm and four co-authors ask managers how they would use an AI partner to practice hard talks at work. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Good talk skills make or break a manager, yet few get steady, personal training. AI role-play could fill that gap at scale.

The team built a practice tool, CommCoach, and used it as a probe in talks with managers. Managers liked low-risk drills that adapt to them for tough scenes like reviews or conflict. They also wanted clear, context-aware feedback and more say over the AI's role personas. They saw value in teaming with human coaches too. The study flags real tensions: feedback must be both flexible and steady, and scenes both true to life and free of bias. The findings guide how such training tools should be built.
arxiv-2505-15252:
Zhengyi Li and co-authors speed up private GPT use by letting a public model do the drafting, in a 2025 paper. Running a language model under cryptography protects both client and server, but secure decoding is slow. Their key observation: checking tokens costs about the same whether one or many are checked at once. So the client drafts a batch with a public model, and the private model verifies the batch securely.

Accepted tokens stand; rejected ones are replaced under the same privacy rules. Two tricks raise the acceptance rate: a sampling step tuned for cryptographic work, and distilling the private model's habits into the drafting process. Across three model pairs and varied networks, the scheme ran two to six times faster than standard secure decoding. Quality and privacy stayed level with the slow route.
arxiv-2505-17452:
Zhang and a large team present a transformer method to separate overlapping galaxies in twenty twenty-five. Deep sky surveys inevitably capture galaxies that overlap on the sky. Blending is a major source of error for future surveys. Older tools fit fixed profiles to each galaxy, which can be rigid and imprecise.

Their network, built on a U-net transformer design, learns from both colour and multi band images. It needs only the rough centre of each target galaxy as input. Deblended colour images kept a high signal to noise ratio and close likeness to truth. Flux recovery error was about one percent for four way blends, far below a standard tool. The team deblended hundreds of known overlaps and tens of thousands of survey images.
arxiv-2505-17852:
Francois Chaubard and Mykel Kochenderfer show how to train very large recurrent networks without the usual back-propagation method, in this 2025 paper. Recurrent networks read long texts cheaply because they compress history into a fixed memory. Training them the standard way, though, eats memory that grows with text length.

Their replacement, zero-order optimization, guesses gradients from random probes instead of stored activations. It matched or beat the standard method across three test settings and used far less memory. One variant also smoothed the training target, which aided generalization. The work scales recurrent models to a billion parameters, reviving an old design for long texts.
arxiv-2505-17952:
Che Liu and eight co-authors ask whether a medical language model can learn to reason without copying worked examples from a closed model. In a 2025 paper they present AlphaMed, a model trained with reinforcement learning alone, guided by simple rule-based rewards on public multiple-choice medical questions.

AlphaMed topped six medical question benchmarks, beating models trained with the usual mix of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. On the hardest test set it even passed much larger closed models. The team also studied what drives the gains and found that how much a data set teaches matters most. They close by calling for harder medical benchmarks that test reasoning more directly.
arxiv-2505-18052:
Liu and six co-authors present BOTM, a method to outline heart chambers in ultrasound movies with stable anatomy, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Heart ultrasound frames vary in shape and can be noisy or partial. Standard outlining often invents broken structures in hard frames. BOTM matches image tokens between frame pairs to enforce sound anatomy.

Matching runs both ways, forming a cross-transport attention step. That step ties frames across the heartbeat cycle so shapes stay consistent. Tests on standard heart data sets show more stable and accurate outlines. Gains include a better boundary score and a higher overlap score. The matches also explain which regions correspond across frames. That clarity may help clinicians trust the outlines.
arxiv-2505-19052:
Seokcheon Lee argues in two thousand twenty-five that pinning down the matter density is the key to probing dark energy with the DESI survey. Dark energy may change over cosmic time, and surveys aim to catch that change. How strongly each observable responds to each unknown decides what can be learned.

Lee shows standard observables respond far more to today's matter density than to dark energy parameters. At mid-range redshifts the gap is more than tenfold. The choice of formula for dark energy also matters: one common form hides change, another reveals it. DESI data alone so far give only upper limits on change. Lee urges better matter density precision and smarter formulas before claiming a detection.
arxiv-2505-19152:
Zhenyu Li, Özlem Tuğfe Demir, Emil Björnson, and Cicek Cavdar present a 2025 study of backup links for cell-free wireless nets. In such nets, many access points serve users as one team, fed by fronthaul links to a central unit. If a main link dies, service dies with it. The team add smart wall panels that can bend radio beams, giving a wireless backup path with a clear line of sight.

A sharing scheme also borrows spare cable room from neighbor access points. The pair of tricks is tuned as one math problem, mixing a beam design method with slope steps on the panel settings. In tests, the panels cut the spare capacity needed for 99 percent survival by about two thirds. Gains peaked when the main link failed fully. Cheap panels may guard future nets.
arxiv-2505-19552:
Minkyu Kim and co-authors make, in a 2025 paper, diffusion samplers scale by pairing them with the classical sampler they were meant to replace. A diffusion sampler learns to draw samples from an energy landscape given only the energy formula, no examples. In high dimensions with costly energies it starves: it rarely wanders into modes it has not already found, so it never learns them.

Their framework sends a Markov chain sampler out as a searcher, steered by a novelty bonus toward under-visited ground, and feeds its off-policy finds into the diffusion model's training. A second diagnosis names primacy bias, the model's overweighting of its earliest experiences, as the engine of mode collapse, and cures it by periodic re-initialization. Across standard benchmarks, higher-dimensional tests, and real molecular shapes, the hybrid trained faster and covered more. The moral is cooperation, not replacement.
arxiv-2505-19752:
Hengli Li and co-authors proposed a new frame for learning from discrete data in a 2025 paper. Discrete data, such as words or codes, are modeled well by diffusion-style methods that add noise step by step. Past forms fix the noise schedule in advance, which caps how rich the learned codes can be and narrows the design space.

Their frame, called Discrete Markov Bridge, learns the step matrix itself as part of training. A second part learns a score that guides the steps back toward real data. The authors prove set pledges for the matrix part and show the whole frame settles as it should. The design opens more room for models of word-like data.
arxiv-2505-19852:
Aryasetiawan lays out a reformulation, in a 2025 preprint, of how theorists compute the behavior of electrons in materials. The standard tool is the one-particle Green function, which tracks how an electron moves through a crowd of others. Custom puts the key physics in a quantity called the self-energy. The newer formalism swaps that for a dynamical exchange-correlation field. This field acts on the Green function at each point in space and time.

At its heart sits a hole-like quantity that pictures the dip in electron density around an added charge. Its electric potential is the new field, and the hole obeys sum rules shared with the static hole of density-functional theory. The scheme has been tried on several model systems, from chain-like magnets to the uniform electron gas. The author hopes simple approximations for the field could dodge costly self-energy calculations.
arxiv-2505-20452:
Hao Zhao and Rong Pan published this study in 2025. It detects change points, the moments a time series shifts its pattern, in restless real-world data. Finding several shifts at once is hard because patterns vary so much. Their method pairs deep Gaussian processes, flexible models that stack uncertainty layers, with active learning. Active learning picks the most useful new samples instead of checking everywhere. A spectral scan first flags candidate change zones.

The hybrid adapts to many kinds of spectral change and pinpoints multiple shifts. Tests on simulated and real data beat existing methods on both accuracy and sampling thrift. That thrift matters when labels or measurements are costly. The authors aim the method at monitoring jobs like sensor streams and process control, where the ground keeps shifting.
arxiv-2505-21052:
Liu, Zhou, Xu, Xiao, and Hao design in twenty twenty-five a search method for picking profitable node sets in huge networks under edge penalties. The problem generalises the classic independent set problem and appears in forestry, facility siting, and social network work. Large real networks make it hard to solve well.

They first craft fourteen reduction rules that shrink a graph while guaranteeing the best answer survives. Their search then weaves those rules through setup, starting solutions, and local improvement. On several hundred graphs from varied fields, the method beat known solvers on most cases. It even solved graphs with hundreds of millions of edges, where every rival failed. Analysis credits the reductions for much of the edge.
arxiv-2505-21252:
Aalok Gangopadhyay, Prajwal Singh, Ashish Tiwari, and Shanmuganathan Raman compute hand poses that cast chosen shadows in a 2025 graphics paper. Shadowgraphy, shaping figures with hands against a light, is an old stage art. The authors recast it as an optimization problem: deform a digital hand model until its rendered shadow matches a target picture under a set light. Differentiable rendering supplies the gradients that guide the shaping.

They show pairs of hands forming target shadows and smooth pose blends between two shadow images. What puppeteers learn by feel becomes a solvable inverse problem. The tool could help animators and performers design new shadow figures before ever raising a hand to the lamp.
arxiv-2505-22052:
Keno Hassler, Philipp Görz, and Stephan Lipp pit two bug-hunting crafts against each other in a 2025 security paper. Memory safety flaws cause over seventy percent of serious software vulnerabilities. Fuzzers hunt them by flooding programs with random inputs at run time, while static analyzers reason over source code without running it. The team ran five analyzers and thirteen fuzzers over more than one hundred known flaws in C and C++ programs.

Fuzzers found a strikingly similar set of bugs to one another, while analyzers reported more varied catches. Best of all, the two crafts barely overlapped, so together they found far more than either alone. The manual checking of which reports mapped to which flaws grounds the comparison.
arxiv-2505-22252:
Magdalena Proszewska, Tomasz Danel, and Dawid Rymarczyk build a test set in a 2025 paper on explaining AI for chemistry. Graph-based models predict traits of molecules, and chemists need to know why a model made its call. Past tests of explanation tools used fake data or simple tasks, so they missed real-world strain.

Their benchmark, B-XAIC, is built from real molecule data with tasks whose true reasons are known. That design lets each explanation be checked against the actual basis for a label. A broad run of current tools on the set exposed clear limits in the molecule domain. The authors offer the set as a shared yardstick. Better scores on it should mean explanations chemists can trust.
arxiv-2505-23852:
Reproducing a published study by hand is slow, so Nic Dobbins and co-authors hired a simulated research team of AI agents to try. Given five Alzheimer's studies, the dataset they used, and only each paper's abstract, methods, and data dictionary, the agents wrote and ran their own analysis code.

Across thirty-five headline findings, the agents approximately reproduced about half per study. Exact numbers and ranges often drifted. The agents also chose different statistical settings than the originals, though trends and significance sometimes matched. Failures traced to coding flaws and missing method details. The authors call the system a promising, scalable rigor check, not yet a replacement for human reproduction.
arxiv-2505-24152:
Anirban Polley simulates how alcohols of varied chain length sink into a cell membrane. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such alcohols are known to dull feeling and to pass into membranes, but how they act is still not clear. He runs atom-level simulations with a model membrane made of a common lipid.

Longer chains sink deeper, and they make the lipid tails more ordered. A cut-off length shows up: past it, the alcohol takes longer to cross and forms clusters in the membrane. Below it, the alcohol spreads evenly and crosses fast. The split may help explain odd traits in how these drugs split into membranes.
arxiv-2505-24452:
Anda Tang and co-authors propose, in a 2025 machine learning paper, a single learning rate plan that works across networks and tasks when training time is fixed in advance. How fast a model learns at each step governs its final quality, yet plan design has rested on trial and error. Budgets make that waste costly.

Their plan, called UBA, comes from a new framework that weighs how sharply the error surface curves in each region. One knob trades flexibility against simplicity, and theory links that knob to a known trait of the problem. Tests across vision and other tasks showed the plan beat common schedules under varied budgets, with proofs of convergence for each knob setting.
arxiv-2505-24752: Gregor Kemper, Christian Liedtke, and Christiane Ott extend a classic degree bound from invariant theory to group schemes, in a 2025 paper. Noether's bound caps the degrees needed to generate a finite group's invariants by the group's size. The authors prove the same cap for finite group schemes that are linearly reductive, a broader setting. They also generalize Molien's counting formula to that setting. On the other side, they build infinitesimal group schemes where the needed degrees run without bound, showing the result cannot stretch to cover every case.
arxiv-2506-00552:
Pingping Zeng, Gongqiu Zhang, and Weinan Zhang work out fall risk in twenty twenty-five. A drawdown shows how far a fund drops from its top point. It is a core gauge in risk work for funds, but it leans on the full path. That path link makes its key counts hard to work out in broad model forms.

The team builds one plan for five drawdown counts from past work. Sets of straight line laws and fast solve steps first treat chains that jump in time steps. Proof then shows the counts tend to the right marks for broad Markov forms. Most steps cost no more than path free tasks: cubic in state count in broad cases, straight line cost for spread type forms. Mild terms are all the proofs need. Broad tests back up both the truth and the speed of the steps.
arxiv-2506-00952: Alexander Skutin, in a 2025 math paper, takes up the class-breadth conjecture for groups built from a prime power. The conjecture caps a group's nilpotency class by its breadth plus one. Counterexamples are known when the prime is two, but the case of odd primes stays open. Skutin's article is devoted to that general odd-prime case, which makes it a focused attack on one of group theory's standing questions.
arxiv-2506-01152:
Alejandra Aguirre-Santaella, Miguel Sanchez-Conde, and Go Ogiya simulate how the Milky Way's gravity shreds dark matter clumps, challenging the belief that cuspy ones always survive. Many studies claim subhalos with a dense inner cusp endure any tidal battering. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team ran a subhalo around a realistic galaxy model, complete with disk, bulge, and a potential that evolves over time, using an improved simulation code. They varied the subhalo's starting concentration, orbit, and inner profile, comparing sharp prompt cusps against the standard profile.

Tracking the structure at both the far and near points of the orbit mattered: the inner size shrank faster than the peak rotation speed. Concentration climbed steadily, roughly a hundredfold by today in velocity terms. Prompt cusps behaved noticeably differently at the far point. The refined tidal tracks feed predictions for dark matter searches that look for these surviving clumps.
arxiv-2506-01252:
Traditional Chinese medicine speaks its own diagnostic language, and general AI benchmarks barely test whether models can use it safely. Shufeng Kong and co-authors built a benchmark with certified practitioners. Twelve datasets cover five arenas: factual knowledge, language understanding, diagnostic reasoning, prescription writing, and safety.

Sources include real case records, national licensing exams, and classical texts. Early results draw a clear line. Today's models handle foundational knowledge respectably. They stumble on clinical reasoning, on composing prescriptions, and on safety compliance, exactly where errors hurt patients. The authors release everything publicly and argue domain benchmarks like this one are prerequisites for trustworthy medical AI.
arxiv-2506-01552:
Roman Plaud and colleagues ask how a classifier that outputs probabilities over a hierarchy should turn those probabilities into a final answer. Hierarchies matter when mistakes differ in severity, as when confusing a pedestrian with a tree is far worse than confusing two plants. Decoding rules in practice are often rules of thumb that may not match the score a task is graded on. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team derives, for a given target metric, the decision rule that is provably best after training, without retraining the model.

They give universal algorithms when the answer must be a single node, and tailored rules for a family of hierarchical scores when the answer can be a set of nodes. Wide experiments show the optimal rules beat standard practice, most clearly when data underdetermine the answer. Code is released with the paper.
arxiv-2506-01752:
Guilherme Santos and colleagues build a fast evolutionary method for finding communities in huge networks. Classic tools optimize one score and run fast, but they blur small groups and hide rival splits. Evolutionary methods juggle several scores at once, at heavy cost. Their method, HP-MOCD, aims to keep the quality and drop the cost.

It grows from a well-known genetic algorithm, with operators shaped by the network's own links. Full parallel running and bit-level tricks add speed. On test networks it handled over a million nodes and ran hundreds of times faster than rival evolutionary methods. Across fourteen real networks, it alone finished the six largest in good time. Its output is a front of trade-off splits, not one answer. Decision makers can pick the split that fits their goal.
arxiv-2506-02752:
A team of co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on setting up solvers for hard planning problems. Such solvers, for mixed-integer programming, have huge numbers of settings, and the right settings change from problem to problem. Claims about learned settings have often rested on uneven tests and leaked data.

Their benchmark, BenLOC, offers a shared, open pipeline for learning settings problem by problem. It fixes how data sets are picked, how training and test data are split, and which baselines count. Using it, the team compared classic learning models with hand-built features against deep learning methods on five known data sets.
arxiv-2506-02852:
Yun Kuen Cheung, Richard Cole, and Yixin Tao generalize a simple market rule, proportional response, so it settles markets with a broad class of tastes. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In proportional response, buyers shift spending toward goods in proportion to the pleasure they give. The rule is known to reach fair market equilibria for several taste families.

The new version covers gross substitutes utilities, where raising one price pushes buyers toward the other goods. The authors prove it converges to a competitive equilibrium in Fisher markets, a first for this taste class. Prices approach their targets at a clean inverse-time rate in experiments. A lazy variant also settles the richer Arrow-Debreu market, where buyers bring goods to sell. The work widens the reach of a beautifully simple dynamic.
arxiv-2506-03152:
Robert Bayer and co-authors make image work on tiny satellites both flexible and sturdy, in work from 2025. CubeSats are cheap space platforms, but their lean hardware and remote perch cramp how photo pipelines can change after launch. The team built two systems to fix that.

One, DIPP, splits pipelines into swap-ready modules that can update with slim data cost and shrug off bad uploads. The other, DISH, is a small language and runner that schedules photo jobs on weak chips. Tests showed the split design adds near no overhead. DISH matched a known scripting tongue in range while using less memory.
arxiv-2506-03452:
Timothy Mahoney and four co-authors test sub-scalp EEG for brain computer interfaces in two thousand twenty-five. Brain interfaces let people with severe disability act on the world. Current systems need skull surgery or vessel implants, both risky. Electrodes under the scalp promise a lower risk path.

The team logged signals at varied depths in a sheep model. Peg electrodes in the sub-scalp space neared the quality of surface brain reads. Vessel arrays matched reads from the bone surface instead. High gamma brain waves were caught, with range set by depth. A compute model probes what drives those gaps. Human trials are the next step.
arxiv-2506-03952:
Qin and Wang wrote a mathematics paper in twenty twenty-five on how several advanced algebra structures arise from Rota-Baxter structures. Algebras are systems of symbols with rules for combining them. A homotopy version loosens those rules in a controlled way used in modern geometry and physics.

The authors define a cyclic form of these structures, with added symmetry, and give a way to build it called cyclic completion. They then study pairs of algebras that act on each other in matching ways. They prove that when the acting algebra carries the right structure, the base algebra gains a pre-Calabi-Yau structure. Using a known link, they describe the matching Poisson-type structure as well.
arxiv-2506-04352:
Ethem Alpaydın wrote a paper from 2025 on a leaner kind of hidden unit for neural networks. A normal hidden unit trains every weight that feeds it, so wide inputs mean many trained numbers. His half unit splits the job into two stages. First it sums its inputs with fixed random weights that never change. Then it scales and shifts that sum with just two trained weights before the usual bend.

Each half unit thus trains only two numbers, no matter how many inputs feed it. Half layers can sit first in a network or deeper in, even after image-scanning layers. Tests on two standard image sets, handwritten digits and clothing items, gave sound accuracy with far fewer trained numbers. The fixed random links act as a brake on overfitting. Alpaydın offers half layers as a way to shrink models where size and training cost matter.
arxiv-2506-05052:
Yi Liao, Xiao-Dong Ma, and Hao-Lin Wang build the theoretical machinery for proton decay into a vector meson, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Baryon-number-violating decays would reveal physics beyond the standard model. Experiments have searched hard for two-body decays into vector mesons, yet no consistent calculation framework existed.

The authors match all triple-quark baryon-number-violating interactions onto hadronic interactions among vector mesons, baryons, and pseudoscalars, extending earlier work that covered only pseudoscalars. The matching opens the door to a complete study of these decays. As a demo, they show how combining limits from vector-meson and pseudoscalar-meson decay searches can break degeneracies among the underlying couplings.
arxiv-2506-06352:
Christian Tarsney asks whether advanced artificial agents should be expected to seek power over people by default. A common worry in AI safety holds that power is useful for almost any final goal. A capable agent will chase it as a stepping stone, whatever its goal happens to be. Skeptics have pushed back on that claim. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Tarsney builds a decision-theory framework to state the claim precisely. It defines what it means for a goal to be instrumentally convergent and for an option to count as more powerful than another.

His verdict is mixed. The claim holds at least partly, yet it may predict little in practice, because options cannot be ranked by power without knowing the agent goal in detail. The argument gains force for agents within reach of total or near-total power. The paper gives safety debates a sharper shared language.
arxiv-2506-06752:
Anna Jakobsen, Anders Clausen, Jaco van de Pol, and Irfansha Shaik wrote this computer science paper, published in 2025. It recasts the task of fitting a quantum circuit onto limited hardware as a logic puzzle, solved in a way that guarantees the shallowest possible layout.

Quantum chips only let certain qubit pairs interact, so circuits must be rewritten before they run, and noisy two-qubit gates make depth costly. Earlier logic-based methods chased gate counts instead. The new encoding targets total depth or two-qubit depth directly, using stepwise solving and parallel plans for speed. It ran ten to a hundred times faster than the previous depth-guaranteeing tool. Noise simulations added a twist: cutting gate count cut noise more than cutting depth alone. Doing both gave the best results, a nuance the authors flag for compiler builders.
arxiv-2506-07452:
Yuxin Xiao, Sana Tonekaboni, Walter Gerych, Vinith Suriyakumar, and Marzyeh Ghassemi studied how writing style can break language model safety in two thousand twenty-five. A request can be phrased in a set style, like a list, even when its intent is harmful. That style alone may raise the chance a model complies.

Across thirty-six models and seven benchmarks, nearly all showed higher attack success when style was added. Models that attended more to style were hit harder. Fine-tuning on a style also made models weaker against attacks in that same style. Their defense, SafeStyle, adds a small set of safety examples matched to the training styles and beat other defenses.
arxiv-2506-07952:
Orfanides, Hoheisel, and El Halabi study how to minimize the gap between two submodular functions. Such functions, defined on sets or on smooth domains, show up across machine learning and sensing. Earlier work covered mainly the set case.

The team shows that on discrete domains every function, and on smooth domains every smooth function, can be written as such a difference. The discrete problem then matches a known form, the difference of two convex functions. Their new variant of the standard algorithm for that form carries matching theory.
