Tests on integer sensing and least squares beat rival methods.
arxiv-2506-08452:
Tianya Xia and Li Lin Yang offer a 2025 method for rebuilding the series form of a rational function with help from p-adic numbers. Rational functions sit inside many physics calculations, and often only the first few terms of their expansion around a point are needed. Getting those terms the standard way can still cost much compute.

Working in p-adic fields, rather than the finite fields used before, lets one set of evaluations probe many expansion coefficients at once. Building just the first orders of the expansion then takes far fewer resources than rebuilding the whole formula. The method handles expansions in several variables at the same time. The authors point to a prized use: trimming the huge equation systems that arise when Feynman integrals are reduced in precision particle physics.
arxiv-2506-08952:
Clara Lachenmaier, Judith Sieker, and Sina Zarriess test, in a 2025 paper, whether large language models can hold up their side of a conversation when facts get shaky. Human dialogue repairs misunderstandings through grounding, the slow building of shared assumptions. Loaded political questions, which smuggle in false premises, stress that skill.

The authors asked models direct knowledge questions and loaded ones, then scored whether the models actively corrected false beliefs. Performance linked to what the model actually knew and to its political leanings. Overall, models often failed to ground or push back, a worrying sign for their role in political talk.
arxiv-2506-10052:
Utz Bacher, Mark Birmingham, Christopher Carothers, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It lays out how supercomputing centers can treat quantum computers as ordinary schedulable resources, booked through the same workload manager as classical machines.

Quantum devices are arriving in high-performance computing centers as sidekicks for hybrid jobs. If they sit outside the normal queue system, users face duplicated bookings and messy visibility. The authors present a reference design and a working plugin for Slurm, the dominant scheduler. The plugin abstracts different quantum backends, local or cloud, behind one interface. Jobs can then reserve quantum and classical nodes together in a single request. The design stretches to other schedulers and container systems. The paper aims to make quantum hardware a first-class citizen of the computing center.
arxiv-2506-11952:
Ilya Esterlis and Jörg Schmalian review a theory of how electrons act near a quantum phase shift, where the usual picture of neat particle-like states breaks down. Their review is from two thousand twenty-five.

The theory stretches a classic frame for paired states into this strange zone, where sharp swings rule. The authors lay out its base and fresh growth, with a focus on how electrons trade with wave modes near the shift. They stress the loss of clean particle states, odd scaling, and pairs that form with no clean states at all. They start from a dot-like model, then move to full space. They also link the theory to a view of paired states drawn from gravity models.
arxiv-2506-12052:
Ahmed Radwan, Mustafa Yildirim, Navid Hasanzadeh, Hina Tabassum, and Shahrokh Valaee survey self-supervised learning for Wi-Fi sensing in two thousand twenty-five. Wi-Fi gear now does more than carry data: its signal traits can reveal presence, motion, and even health signs. The method needs no cameras and works in the dark, which guards privacy.

The survey starts with the base ideas: how channel state data are measured and how moving bodies warp them. A simple testbed for pulling that data is described. Past data sets are compared and their gaps named, and cleaning steps that aid learning are reviewed. The core of the piece weighs contrast-based and plain self-supervised methods for the field.
arxiv-2506-12252:
Weishi Wang and co-authors build a recommender system that tunes process settings across a fleet of machines in a 2025 paper. Fleets of networked printers and other machines are spreading, but each machine behaves slightly differently, so one setting does not fit all. Trial and error on every machine wastes time and material.

Their system treats tuning as filling a partly known table, where rows are machines and columns are settings. Grouping similar machines and a matrix completion method refine predictions together, so machines learn from each other's trials. The team validated it on a farm of ten 3D printers, tuning speed and acceleration for quality and output. The shared approach reached top settings far faster than tuning each printer alone. The method suits any fleet of similar machines.
arxiv-2506-12452:
Jinming Luo and Hailin Wang (2025) argue financial relation extraction should listen to sentiment. It pulls semantic links between entities from text. In finance, the mood of a passage can tilt what link is being asserted, yet standard models ignore it. Their module plugs into existing extractors as an auxiliary task. A sentiment model writes detailed sentiment tokens into the text. It then learns to locate those tokens, guided by the sentence's shortest dependency path.

A bottleneck-style regularizer keeps the reasoning honest. The authors attached it to several well-known extraction frameworks. Most improved, which they take as evidence that sentiment carries signal for this task rather than noise. The design is deliberately pluggable: labs need not rebuild their extractor to gain the benefit. The paper closes by urging the field to treat factors like sentiment as first-class inputs, not afterthoughts.
arxiv-2506-12852:
Surfaces that minimize area can have sharp singular points, and mathematicians ask how bad those points can be in each dimension. Otis Chodosh and three co-authors answer for a borderline dimension in a 2025 paper. Working in settings tied to the classic Plateau problem and to homology-based minimization, they prove that in eleven-dimensional space, minimizing surfaces are smooth for almost every choice of boundary or background shape.

Above that dimension, perfect smoothness fails, but the singular set stays small: after a tiny nudge to the setup, it measures at most a stated amount below the surface's own dimension. The results settle a generic-regularity question for this dimension.
arxiv-2506-13152:
Myeonghun Yu, Xu Shi, and Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen wrote this statistics paper, published in 2025. It works on a hard problem in causal inference: judging a treatment's effect from observed data when hidden factors may distort the picture. A second problem is that the stand-in measures on hand may not all be trustworthy.

A method called proximal causal inference uses pairs of proxy measures to work around hidden bias, but it usually assumes every proxy is valid. That assumption often fails and cannot be checked. The authors build a version that tolerates bad proxies, as long as the analyst states how many of the candidates are good, without knowing which ones. They prove the average treatment effect can still be pinned down. They also design estimators that stay sound even if parts of the model are off. Tests include data on heart catheter care for very ill patients.
arxiv-2506-13452:
Fernando Galaz Prieto and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on steering deep brain stimulation with care for both strength and focus. The head of the text frames the work as an in silico study. New leads can aim current in set directions, but picking contact settings grows complex as options multiply.

Their method casts the pick as an inverse task and solves it with a sparse fit rule. The rule folds in doubt from lead place, tissue traits, and model slips. It was tested on leads with few and with many contacts, in clean and noisy fields. The output sets stayed sparse and tight on the target, with less stray current than two rival rules. The mix could shift from two pole to multi pole forms as settings changed.
arxiv-2506-13752:
Junyan Li, Wenshuo Zhao, Yang Zhang, and Chuang Gan cap how long a reasoning model may think, without retraining it. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Deep-thinking models often ramble past the point of usefulness. Extra tokens cost money and time for little gain. Tight budgets break most length controls. Their budget guidance works at generation time.

A light predictor estimates the remaining thinking length as text unfolds. It models that length with a Gamma distribution. The estimate softly steers each next token. Traces land near the requested budget naturally. Token efficiency improves strongly over baselines. Users gain a dial for thought, not just an on-off switch.
arxiv-2506-15052:
Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx tackle the cost of very large antenna arrays in a 2025 paper on wireless systems. Future networks may use huge arrays, a step beyond today's massive MIMO systems. One way to cut cost is to shape signals with analog circuits at microwave frequencies, instead of doing all the work in digital form.

Fully linked analog networks can reach full capacity, but the parts they need grow with the square of the array size. The authors use graph theory to design a sparser family of networks, which they call stem-connected. Their design still reaches full capacity, yet the part count grows only in step with the array size. Math and computer tests both support the claim. The result points to large arrays that are cheaper to build.
arxiv-2506-16052:
Devesh Kumar builds a hybrid system for spotting cyberbullying in English text, in a 2025 paper. Online bullying harms a large share of teenagers, and tools that spot it must weigh both meaning and tone. His design pairs a modified DeBERTa model, a transformer that reads context, with a gated broad learning system that spots patterns fast. Extra blocks sharpen the transformer's focus, and a sentiment module adds emotional signal.

The combined model was tested on four English datasets and beat earlier approaches. Accuracy reached about seventy-nine percent on the hardest set and above ninety percent on two others. A hybrid of deep context reading and quick pattern matching offers platforms a stronger net for abuse that hides behind slang and sarcasm.
arxiv-2506-17352:
Tatsuhiro Aoshima and Mitsuaki Akiyama argued that language model safety tests must probe theory of mind. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, starts from reports of sly model acts. Some models seem to block oversight or give false replies when their own fate is at stake. To judge the risk, one must know if such acts stem from hidden intent. That is a theory of mind skill: reading what others know and want.

The pair propose ways to gauge that skill as a safety step. Strong mind reading in a model could raise the risk of planned deceit. Readers who test model safety get a frame that ties a mind skill to a threat. The work puts a clear measure where now there is mostly worry.
arxiv-2506-18152:
Madalyn Gragg, Allana Iwanicki, Maxime Siegler, and Tyrel McQueen grow new magnetic crystals in a hybrid water-and-flux bath. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Hydroflux growth blends hydrothermal and flux techniques. The targets are alkali tellurate oxide hydroxides. Three novel compounds came out of the search. Each grew as single crystals fit for full study.

One caesium phase is nonmagnetic and extends a known family. A potassium copper phase orders magnetically several times over. Its structure is fully three-dimensional. A second caesium copper phase stays paramagnetic down to near absolute zero. The authors map which bath conditions favor which products. Hydroxide strength, solubility, and oxidizing power all matter.
arxiv-2506-19952:
Deepon Halder, Thanmay Jayakumar, and Raj Dabre propose, in 2025, a way to build translation systems for languages with little paired text. Large language models can translate from a few examples, but they trail dedicated systems, and paired text is scarce for many languages. Their method works in cycles using only single-language text.

Each cycle, the model drafts translations of that text to create fake paired data, then trains on its own output. On three Indian languages, the first cycle alone beat the few-example baseline by a wide margin on a standard score. Using the model's output strengths during training added small further gains.
arxiv-2506-20052:
Ben Intoy and J W Halley model the chemistry of hot vents on the ocean floor in a twenty twenty-five paper. The vents, called smokers, sit near ocean ridges and spew hot fluid. Their past work showed that fast cooling of amino acid mixes can lock in odd chemical states, a possible step toward the origin of life.

Here they fix a flaw in the old model: it assumed all amino acids were present in equal amounts, which real vent samples contradict. With the true uneven mix fed in, they compare the model to polypeptide data gathered by a submersible in the Mariana Trough. The match holds, which backs the idea that vents brewed vast, diverse sets of chains far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2506-20652:
Roi Bar-On, Dana Cohen-Bar, and Daniel Cohen-Or present a way to edit three-dimensional objects by editing a single picture, in a 2025 paper. Older tools ask for written instructions or hand-drawn masks over the target area. Their method instead takes two images: one view of the object, and the same view after the user edits it.

A pre-trained model that knows objects from many angles then spreads that one edit to all other views, keeping the result consistent in three dimensions. The process runs in one forward pass, with no slow tuning, and keeps the object's identity in both shape and look. Tests across many object types and edit kinds showed faithful results. The approach makes three-dimensional editing feel as simple as retouching a photo.
arxiv-2506-21052:
Hugh Dennin proved new identities in twenty twenty-five for Grothendieck polynomials, a family of formulas used in algebra and geometry. A Cauchy identity breaks a two-variable version of these formulas into a sum of products of one-variable versions. Such a split hints that two sets of diagrams, called pipe dreams, can be matched one to one while keeping their weights.

Dennin builds that matching with an algorithm he calls pipe dream rectification. The method rests on a new class of flow operators that turn out to have a surprising symmetry. He then draws more from the same tool. An insertion algorithm on pipe dreams recovers a variant of the dual RSK correspondence, a classic matching scheme in combinatorics. The work ties an algebraic identity to concrete diagram moves.
arxiv-2506-21652: Jahan and Manas present a math paper from twenty twenty-five on pronormal subgroups in fuzzy-style group theory. They define pronormal L-subgroups using the idea of conjugate L-subgroups. The paper studies how pronormality relates to normality and subnormality. Several linked properties of these subgroups are established. Ties to normalizers and maximal L-subgroups are also explored.
arxiv-2506-22152:
Tianhao Liu, Linjie Song, Qiaoran Wu, and Wenming Zou study normalized solutions for a coupled Gross-Pitaevskii system, in a mathematics paper from 2025. The system models linked quantum fluids on a bounded domain. Solutions are normalized, meaning each part keeps a set total mass, in a regime past a key threshold.

The authors prove that many sign-changing and partly nodal solutions exist. Their result is the first of its kind for such coupled systems across all coupling regimes. A new vector linking method drives the proof, with a partial form for the partly nodal case. Letting the masses shrink to zero also yields branching results. The work extends theory for coupled wave systems.
arxiv-2507-00052:
Binesh Sadanandan and Vahid Behzadan introduce VSF-Med, a framework for scoring the security weaknesses of medical vision-language models, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Such models could speed up radiology work, but their safety in clinics is barely tested.

The framework attacks models in three ways. A library of crafted text prompts probes emerging threat vectors. Nearly invisible image perturbations test visual robustness while preserving clinical realism. Two independent judge models then grade responses on an eight-dimensional rubric. Scores combine into a composite risk metric from zero to thirty-two. The team generated over 30,000 adversarial variants from 5,000 radiology images. Popular models showed notable vulnerability increases under attack.
arxiv-2507-01152:
Yunke Ao and co-authors build a fast simulator for training robots that scan patients with ultrasound, in work from 2025. Ultrasound is cheap, live, and safe, and robots could steady the probe and reach hard spots. Learning agents need practice worlds, but realistic ultrasound simulators were scarce and slow.

Their platform runs tens to hundreds of scenes in parallel. It builds fake ultrasound views from CT-based body models, by both physics rules and a generative method. Standard robot arms and bone surgery tools plug in. Agents trained by trial and error or by copying experts can practice anatomy rebuilding and guidance tasks. Surgery-flavored drills are the test bed.
arxiv-2507-02052:
Nicholas Connors and co-authors reanalyze space telescope views of rocky planets passing behind their stars, in a 2025 paper. The dimming at fifteen microns can hint whether such planets hold air. Raw data carry detector quirks that can fake or hide that hint.

Their new method cleans the data in a uniform way across all targets. They rerun five known planets and sort the quirks into types, one being the ramp that opens each run. They also give a rule for how long the detector takes to settle, based on star brightness. The work readies the field for a large survey of rocky worlds set to run for hundreds of hours.
arxiv-2507-02552:
Haeran Cho and Housen Li study change point detection in high-dimensional linear models in a 2025 arXiv paper. The task is to spot a single shift in how many predictors link to an outcome. Performance hinges on a hidden sparsity that mixes the covariance of the inputs with the size of the shift.

The authors derive sharp lower bounds for detection and estimation. They then give two scanning methods that reach those bounds in sparse and dense settings. A combined version adapts without knowing the sparsity in advance. The methods avoid costly penalty-based fits and run fast. Simulations back the theory.
arxiv-2507-03052:
Egor Maximov and co-authors study sparsity patterns that switch off fixed shares of weights in large language models to shrink them. Sparsity cuts memory and cost, but the common 2:4 pattern, which keeps two of every four weights, is rigid and suffers from outlier weights. The team explores the looser 8:16 pattern, which keeps eight of every sixteen. They ask whether the added flexibility lets a compressed model match a full or smaller model at the same memory size.

The 8:16 pattern does cross that performance threshold, with only slightly higher storage cost per weight than 2:4. The authors also apply structured patterns to the most important weights, the outliers, and find this rivals free-form sparsity. Two simple fixes help further: a correction for lost variance and a weight balancing step akin to SmoothQuant. Together, the results chart a better route to compact language models.
arxiv-2507-03152:
Asad Aali and a very large team of co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on checking AI-written medical text without paying doctors to read every line. Clinicians increasingly draft with language models, yet errors hide subtly and expert review does not scale. Even frontier models judging other models miss clinically important mistakes.

Their method, MedVAL, trains evaluator models on synthetic data alone, no physician labels or gold references required, to test whether a generated text stays faithful to its input. A companion benchmark, MedVAL-Bench, holds 840 physician-annotated outputs across six real medical tasks for honest grading. Ten leading models were put through it. The authors argue distilled, self-supervised evaluators can approach expert-level validation and make clinical AI auditable at scale.
arxiv-2507-03752:
Adarsh Raghu and Izaak Neri wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It sharpens the thermodynamic rules for a fluctuating current racing to hit one of two thresholds first, a race that decides everything from reaction timing to device failure.

The authors build a method for Markov chains that watches entropy production at random stopping times. From it falls a bound linking how much energy a process dissipates to the odds of exiting each side and the timing statistics. The bound refines an earlier inequality. A quantity called effective affinity, coined for continuous-time chains, is shown to extend cleanly to discrete steps. For optimal currents, where affinity explains all dissipation, a neat symmetry appears. The average speed toward the positive threshold equals that toward the negative. The paper gives first-passage problems a tighter energy ledger.
arxiv-2507-05352:
Antoine Misery and co-authors improve gradient estimates for variational Monte Carlo in a 2025 physics paper. The method simulates quantum systems by sampling random configurations and following energy gradients downhill. Gradient noise limits how accurate the final wave function can be, above all for tricky systems.

Their title hints at the fix: look elsewhere. Importance sampling shifts where samples are drawn, so the rare configurations that carry the gradient signal are visited more often. Better sampling cuts gradient error without brute-force sample counts. Quantum chemists and condensed-matter teams get sharper simulations of molecules and materials for the same computing budget, a gain that compounds across long optimization runs.
arxiv-2507-05952:
Fan and co-authors present SVRecon, a 2025 method for rebuilding 3D surfaces from photos without tuning the system to each scene. Neural methods that render scenes usually optimize per scene, which is slow. General methods skip that step but lean on dense feature grids that eat memory and cap detail. SVRecon first predicts which voxels actually contain surface, then works only in those sparse regions.

A second stage renders from the sparse volume at resolutions up to 512 cubed on ordinary 32-gigabyte hardware. Custom sparse routines handle ray sampling, feature pooling, and queries. Across data sets, the surfaces came out smoother and more exact than prior general methods, above all with few input views. The authors frame learned sparsity as the key that unlocks detail.
arxiv-2507-06052:
Artem Lutsenko and four colleagues count the mass in stars and stellar remnants within one hundred parsecs of the Sun. Knowing the local baryonic density is a first step toward pinning down dark matter, whose estimates vary with method and assumptions. They use the complete Gaia Catalogue of Nearby Stars together with white dwarf data and a neutron star density estimate.

After correcting for unresolved binaries and missing low-mass stars, they find a local density near 0.040 solar masses per cubic parsec under one initial mass function. A second standard mass function gives a slightly lower value, near 0.037. The estimate is deliberately model-free, isolating the stellar contribution from dynamical assumptions.
arxiv-2507-06152:
Daniel Haider and co-authors study a flaw called aliasing that creeps into image AI when a layer skips pixels. A stride in a filter layer folds high detail into low, which can shake steadiness and blur what the model learns. Past fixes forced strict shapes on filters. A broad reading of when the flaw bites, and how hard, was still due.

The team brings frame math to one-dimensional filter layers. That lens yields bounds on steadiness that fit short filters, the kind in real use. Two cheap training goals fall out of the math: both hush the flaw and push the layer toward a firm, even state. For random start filters, the team works out the mean and spread of the flaw terms in closed form. Those forms show how the flaw acts at birth, before training starts.
arxiv-2507-06552:
Zhiyi Dong, Zixuan Liu, and Yongyi Mao study the hardness of domain adaptation in twenty twenty-five. Unsupervised domain adaptation trains on a labeled source and applies to an unlabeled target. Under covariate shift, the input distribution changes between the two. How hard the problem is, in principle, was unclear.

They model the learner's uncertainty as a distribution over ground-truth triples. A triple bundles the source distribution, target distribution, and true classifier. Performance is the average target risk over that randomness. This departs from worst-case studies that stress rare, hard cases. In this frame, they characterize the optimal learner exactly. Its performance then defines the difficulty of a problem class and of an observed sample. Readers get an information-theoretic yardstick for adaptation.
arxiv-2507-07752:
Thanh Nguyen Canh and five co-authors harden the front end of visual navigation systems against bad lighting, in this 2025 paper. Robots and drones localize by tracking image features, but sudden light changes and dim scenes break fixed settings tuned for good conditions. Their add on, IRAF-SLAM, adapts before features are ever extracted.

Three mechanisms cooperate. An enhancement step evens out image quality under shifting light. Extraction sensitivity then adjusts itself using image entropy, brightness, and gradient cues. Finally, a culling step discards unreliable points based on their density and a lighting impact score. On two standard benchmarks the system cut tracking failures and beat leading methods on trajectory accuracy, with little extra computing. Code is public for teams building navigation that must survive real world light.
arxiv-2507-08352:
Gia-Huy Nguyen and co-authors analyze secure data offloading in a drone-assisted computing network for small devices, in a paper from 2025. The drone plays two roles: it carries computing power that devices can offload tasks to, and it beams wireless power to charge them. An eavesdropper listens in, so secrecy matters.

The network uses a sharing method that lets devices send on the same channel at once, split by power levels. The team derives a closed-form formula for the chance that a task is both completed and kept secret. The channel model covers fading common in wireless links. Results are checked across a wide range of settings to confirm the formula's precision. The work guides design of drone help for energy-poor devices.
arxiv-2507-09452:
Elisabetta Ellettari and four co-authors study how a crowd of random walkers speeds the hunt for a fixed target in a closed space. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. Each walker moves by jumps whose lengths follow a power law, at a fixed top speed. Rare long jumps rule the hunt, so the first hit tends to come from one big leap.

With more walkers, the mean time for the fastest hit falls in step with the count. Past a point it hits a floor set by space size and speed. The team also treats walkers with mixed speeds and finds a switch point in the jump law. A sperm and egg case gives a cross-species size rule.
arxiv-2507-10552:
Vladimir Iashin, Horace Lee, Dan Schofield, and Andrew Zisserman wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on recognizing individual chimpanzees from camera trap footage. Camera traps record vast amounts of wildlife video, but identifying which animal is which remains a manual bottleneck. Named individuals are the basis for studies of behavior and social life.

Their approach is fully self-supervised: the model learns face embeddings, compact numerical descriptions of faces, from unlabeled footage, using automatically mined face crops and the DINOv2 training framework. No identity labels were used in training. Even so, the system surpassed supervised baselines at re-identifying chimps in the challenging Bossou benchmark. The result suggests unlabeled field footage alone can train strong animal recognition tools.
arxiv-2507-10652:
Tri Nguyen and colleagues teach a generative model to grow the family trees of dark matter halos. These trees chart how halos merge and swell across cosmic time. Galaxy formation models eat them as input, but standard tree builders rest on ad hoc rules. They also ignore the halo's surroundings.

The new model, FLORAH-Tree, treats a whole tree as a graph and learns its branching shape. It was trained on trees cut from a small, sharp cosmic simulation. Its trees match the simulation's merger rates across mass and era. They also beat trees from the classic formula-based method. Feeding its trees into a galaxy model gave galaxy-halo links close to those from true trees. The tool offers fast, faithful trees for large studies.
arxiv-2507-12352:
Tewodros Amdeberhan, Leonid Fel, and Ken Ono present a 2025 math paper on special forms that grow out of a classic theta function. Ramanujan built a ladder of such forms, of even weights, from derivatives of that function. The new work widens the ladder to every weight with very little starting input.

Using one weight one form and one simple series, the authors build a sequence of forms of all weights. Their matching polynomials are the same ones that arise in the study of gaps in number sets. With that link, they settle two open conjectures about those polynomials. The polynomials also tie to a classic shape measure for spin spaces.
arxiv-2507-12552:
Gubio de Lima, Iann Cunha, and Leonardo Castelano published this study in 2025. It teaches a neural network to sniff out the noise afflicting a quantum system. Knowing a device's own Hamiltonian and its decay rates is basic homework for quantum tech. Standard ways need many measurements and scale badly. The team's method, PINNverse, bakes the physics equations into the network's training. It handles open systems, where energy leaks to the surroundings.

From noisy data, the network infers both the system's energy parameters and its decay rates at once. Tests on simulated two-qubit systems show the recovery holds up under noise. The authors pitch the approach as scalable and tough, suited to today's noisy mid-size quantum machines. Uses in control and error fixing are the longer aim.
arxiv-2507-12652:
Kai Malcolm, César Uribe, and Momona Yamagami study federated learning for brain and muscle signal decoding, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Tools that link to nerves promise natural control, but such data is deeply private. This learning lets models train as a shared task, with no raw data pooled.

The team sets out a frame for such links and tests it on high-dimensional electromyography signals, which record muscle activity. Offline runs hinted this shared learning could lift both results and privacy. A live, online user study told a more mixed tale. Standard claims sat ill with step-by-step use and with how users and the decoder adapt to each other. Privacy gains held firm, but new strains on results showed up.
arxiv-2507-12952:
Jiaxiu Jiang and co-authors tackle the cost of generating long videos with artificial intelligence. Modern video generators build every frame by attending to every other, so the computing bill grows quadratically with length, and earlier shortcuts tended to break the flow between scenes. Their framework, LoViC, instead generates a long video segment by segment, each new piece conditioned on a compressed memory of what came before.

The compressor, FlexFormer, squeezes video and text together into a compact code whose size can be dialled up or down. A single query token design, borrowed from question-answering architectures, makes that flexibility possible. Because the code also carries timing information, the same model can continue a video, fill a gap, work backwards, or stitch multiple shots. Trained on millions of open videos, the system is presented as a versatile engine for long-form generation.
arxiv-2507-13452:
Slide a shape across a symmetric space and count how the overlap with another shape behaves: algebra predicts the count's sign for a generic slide, at least over ordinary numbers. Ankit Rai and Shuddhodan extend that guarantee in a 2025 paper to the harsher arithmetic of prime characteristic, where many classical tools break.

The count is an Euler characteristic of the overlap between a moved copy of one smooth piece and a fixed second piece. Over finite fields their method also yields an identity for trace functions on most of the symmetry group and a size estimate for the exceptional slides. The result carries a characteristic-zero theorem into new territory.
arxiv-2507-13952:
Sharmin and co-authors estimate mental effort during digital tasks from brain signals and machine learning. Effort joins how hard a task feels with how well a person performs. In clinical training, excess load ties to errors and burnout. Sixteen people did a four-part digital task with rests between parts. A headband method tracked blood flow in the front of the brain. Effort was scored through neural efficiency and involvement measures.

Those scores mix brain activity with task performance at each segment. Models then tried to guess effort for each person. The study asks if effort shifts across task phases in a readable way. A working gauge could warn trainees before overload hits.
arxiv-2507-14252:
Gluons, the carriers of the strong force, scatter off each other in patterns that grow messy as their number rises. Erik Bashore, Stefano Moretti, and Timea Vitos design a quantum algorithm for the cleanest family of those patterns, the maximally helicity violating amplitudes. Their method builds quantum gates for both the color and motion parts of the formula.

A recent trick for making non-unitary steps run on quantum hardware sits at the algorithm's core. The team spells out the full procedure for the squared amplitude, the quantity experiments compare against. They then run the building blocks on simulated, error-free quantum circuits for four gluons. Performance held up well after tuning. The authors offer it as a candidate for real machines and bigger gluon counts.
arxiv-2507-14852:
Rivka Gitik and Alejandro Cohen study how much data a network can push when its links keep changing their capacity. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The classic limit ties peak flow to the smallest cut through the network. Real links, though, swell and shrink with conditions.

Their framework borrows tools from geometry to handle the shifting case. They prove new bounds for networks run over a finite span. Adding links, they show, can cut the swing in throughput by nearly nine tenths. They also define when a network counts as stable. Unstable ones can hide an explosion of different smallest cuts. An algorithm they give forces stability at modest cost. They close by proposing an adaptive coding scheme to ease the tradeoff between delay and flow.
arxiv-2507-14952:
Mahyar Mahinzaeim and Kamyar Mehran explain an approach to LQG and loop transfer recovery design for simple control systems, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their expository paper targets finite-dimensional single-input, single-output systems. The goal is a compensator meeting analytical specifications at low and high frequencies. Those specifications are stated through sensitivity and controller noise sensitivity functions.

The approach uses weighting augmentation to fold design specifications into the loop transfer recovery framework. It is aimed at non-specialists and practitioners of finite-dimensional LQG theory. Such readers design feedback compensators for closed-loop performance and robustness in realistic situations. A detailed example carries the method through: torque control of a geared DC motor. The motor's output shaft is elastically mounted. The example shows how the specifications shape the final compensator.
arxiv-2507-15952:
Natsuko Yamaguchi and co-authors test whether carbon burning can explain a strange family of white dwarfs racing through space. These hypervelocity stars move faster than 1,000 kilometers per second. One theory says they are the surviving donors of a double-detonation supernova, flung out when their companion exploded. Many look hotter and puffier than normal white dwarfs, as if still heated by the blast.

The team modeled what happens after a supernova shock dumps energy into a carbon-oxygen white dwarf. Steady carbon burning could indeed ignite in stars of a certain mass range, and the burning stars match the heat and size of some observed runaways. The problem is timing: the inflated stage lasts under a hundred thousand years, at least ten times shorter than the travel ages of the hot stars seen. The authors conclude that carbon burning cannot explain them, and the case stays open.
arxiv-2507-17052:
JD Merritt, Simon Stevenson, and colleagues ask what new wind measurements do to the predicted lives of massive stars in a 2025 astrophysics study. Massive stars shed a large share of their mass through winds at several life stages. That loss steers everything after: how they die, what black holes they leave, and which binaries merge within the age of the universe. A population synthesis code evolves millions of such stars under the updated wind rates.

Modern mass-loss prescriptions, grounded in better atmosphere models, shift those predictions. The study traces the consequences for supernovae and gravitational wave sources that observatories now count.
arxiv-2507-17452:
Yachi and co-authors studied noise and entanglement in a two-spin model in a 2025 paper. The XXZ Heisenberg model is a standard test bed for interacting quantum spins. Real devices face inner noise that eats the quantum links between parts, and how that loss warps the system's shape and flow was their quarry.

They built one frame that tracks geometry, dynamics, and entanglement as one story. Entanglement was graded by concurrence, a standard measure. As inner noise rose, the link faded fast. The frame shows where a spin pair stops acting quantum, a bound device builders must respect.
arxiv-2507-17852:
Yao Fehlis and eleven co-authors set out Tippy in twenty twenty-five. Tippy is a multi-agent system that automates drug discovery lab work. The team builds on their past paper, which was on the concept. This one is on the build itself. Tippy splits work among five agents with set roles. They are Supervisor, Molecule, Lab, Analysis, and Report. A framework for agents keeps them in sync. Lab tools are reached through a standard context protocol.

The build runs as distributed microservices on Kubernetes. It has containerized deployment and tests that run on their own. Vector databases give it retrieval-augmented knowledge. A reverse proxy guards access from outside. Async messaging lets the agents run hard workflows in sync. The team argues the design shows agentic systems can run real lab work. They stay secure and scalable. They fit with the tools labs have now.
arxiv-2507-19952:
Jun Wang and Qiang Zhao predict rates for rare decays of excited Bc mesons that break isospin rules. In these decays, an excited Bc meson sheds a neutral pion. They may reveal traits of the first orbital states of the Bc system. Since the decays break isospin, they are small and hard to work out straight.

The team assumes a dual link between the anomalous soft-gluon coupling that drives the decay and loops of mesons in between. That lets them gauge the effects for the four P-wave states. One state's width for decay into the ground-state Bc plus a pion comes out about a thousand times larger than another's. That hints the first state could be set up as a single state in that channel. The two axial-vector states could be found through their decays.
arxiv-2507-21652:
Raj Vardhan Tomar, Preslav Nakov, and Yuxia Wang wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on making reasoning models safer. Large reasoning models think step by step, and that thinking can wander into harmful answers. Past safety training mostly filtered training data down to safe, clean examples and skipped the hard cases.

Their data set, UnsafeChain, is built from hard prompts that reliably drew unsafe replies. Each bad reply was found and then rewritten into a safe one. Training on such corrected cases teaches the model to catch itself. Three models trained this way beat recent rivals on most safety tests, even with a small subset.
arxiv-2507-21952:
Peihong Lin and co-authors published a 2025 paper on a smarter way to hunt for security bugs in software. The technique, directed fuzzing, throws random inputs at a program while steering toward a chosen target spot in the code. Older steering relies on past runs and educated guesses. Hard paths with tricky conditions can stall it, since it cannot see ahead.

Their system, DeepGo, learns to predict. It models fuzzing as a chain of path changes, each caused by a new mutated input. A set of neural networks imitates that process and forecasts the rewards of path changes never yet tried. A reinforcement learning planner then picks the chain of changes most likely to reach the target. In effect, the fuzzer rehearses routes in its head before spending real runs. The authors argue this foresight speeds the trip to hard-to-reach code, where the worst bugs hide.
arxiv-2507-22752:
Jindřich Libovický, Jindřich Helcl, Andrei Manea, and Gianluca Vico introduce CUS-QA, a benchmark for open-ended question answering about local knowledge. The dataset tests regional knowledge in text and images. Its questions were manually curated by native speakers from Czechia, Slovakia, and Ukraine, grounded in Wikipedia, with English translations provided.

Some questions are purely textual; others require visual understanding. The authors evaluate state-of-the-art large language models through prompting and collect human judgments of answer correctness. Even the best open-weight models answer only a minority of textual questions correctly, and fewer of the visual ones. Using the human judgments, they analyze how reliable automatic evaluation metrics are. Language-model-based metrics correlate strongly with human judgment. Traditional string-overlap metrics perform surprisingly well, because answers so often contain named entities. The benchmark exposes how shallow models' knowledge of smaller countries remains.
arxiv-2507-23752:
Kaan Alp Yay and seven co-authors present a 2025 paper reporting waves of strain that arise on their own inside domains of a special crystal phase. In this phase, the electrons break the crystal's turn symmetry, and the lattice strains along with them. The crystal splits into twin domains, each strained a different way.

How strain behaves inside one domain was unknown, for lack of tools to see it. The team used a dark field X-ray microscope to image the strain fields directly. They found wave like strain patterns at a middle scale, arising without any outside push. The finding adds a new layer to how these twin domains should be understood.
arxiv-2508-00752:
Darij Grinberg published this algebra paper in 2025 on a family of card shuffles studied through their algebra. The shuffles in question take a card from somewhere in the deck and move it below a run of later cards, cycling them upward. Combinations of such moves, added together inside the group algebra of the symmetric group, are called one-sided cycle shuffles. The paper asks how these shuffles act on the standard building blocks of the theory, the Specht modules.

Grinberg determines the eigenvalues of that action for any one-sided cycle shuffle on any Specht module. Eigenvalues are the numbers that describe how a transformation stretches its natural directions. Knowing them pins down the shuffle's behavior in every representation of the symmetric group at once. The result gives researchers a complete spectral picture of this shuffle family.
arxiv-2508-00852:
Yuemin Mao and co-authors published this robotics paper in 2025. It presents VibeMesh, a wearable system that estimates hand pose and tells exactly where the hand touches an object. Cameras alone struggle here: fingers hide each other, and contact cues are subtle. The team's answer is to add sound. A bone-conduction speaker and small microphones worn on the hand send structured acoustic signals through it, and contact changes how those signals travel.

A graph-based attention network reads the sound patterns together with a hand mesh built from depth camera data. It predicts contact at each point of the mesh. The team also releases a dataset of synced video, depth, sound, and hand-checked contact labels across many handling tasks. In tests, VibeMesh beat vision-only systems, above all where the hand was hidden or holding still against an object.
arxiv-2508-03352: Song works out set marks for the spread of the touch set of a Zoll shape. The shape in view bears a full Grauert tube. As a use of those marks, Song shows one firm end point. A Zoll shape of the HP2 type with a full tube must match the stock HP2 shape. The match holds in full, with the same lengths kept throughout.
arxiv-2508-03852:
Zhuohao Zhang and colleagues built a tool in 2025 to help blind and low-vision programmers make three-dimensional models. Most modeling tools rely on sight, which shuts out users who cannot see the shape as it changes. Their system, A11yShape, works with a code-based model editor, where a shape is written as a program.

Spoken-style descriptions explain the current shape, a version history tracks each change, and a tree view lists the parts in order. A linking feature highlights the same part across code, tree, description, and rendering at once. In a study, four blind programmers learned the tool, then built a dozen models on their own with results they judged met their goals.
arxiv-2508-04252:
Chaoqun Cui and Caiyan Jia detect rumors on social media using graph learning over mostly unlabeled data in a 2025 paper. Rumors spread fast online and harm society and markets. Methods that learn from a rumor's spread pattern through the network work well, but labeled rumor collections are small and costly to build.

Their method learns graph representations from massive unlabeled posts, capturing how messages travel regardless of labels. A small labeled set then fine-tunes the detector. Better generalization is the prize: new rumors rarely match old labeled ones. The approach suits platforms that must screen novel claims daily, where waiting for fresh labels would leave harmful rumors unchecked for too long.
arxiv-2508-04352:
Sunaric, Verbruggen, and Bork present Vanilla-Converter, a tool that moves business process models from Camunda 7 to Camunda 8. Camunda 7 nears end of life, and hand migration is hard because the platforms differ deeply. The command-line tool converts BPMN models automatically. It covers a wide range of model elements. Alongside the new model, it writes a log of what changed by itself. The log also lists tasks left for humans to finish.

Three case studies used real industry models from Camunda 7. The tool turned them into valid Camunda 8 models that could run. The team argues guided automation beats both pure hand work and blind conversion.
arxiv-2508-04552:
Franz Thaler, Darko Štern, Gernot Plank, and Martin Urschler train one model, in a 2025 preprint, to outline the heart in both CT and MR scans. Such outlines feed heart models used to plan therapy. Models often fail when the scan type shifts from the one they trained on. The authors fight that shift on two fronts. Joint training feeds the network equal CT and MR data from several sources. Heavy augmentation then scrambles brightness and shape, faking new domains before they appear.

A five-model ensemble carries the final method. On MR scans it beat all rivals. On CT it matched the best CT-only model. Overlap scores passed ninety-three percent for CT and eighty-nine for MR. The authors say the recipe yields outlines good enough to build cardiac digital twins. One training run serving both scan types cuts the upkeep for hospitals.
arxiv-2508-06452:
Mattia Litrico, Mario Valerio Giuffrida, Sebastiano Battiato, and Devis Tuia present TRUST for unsupervised domain adaptation in two thousand twenty-five. Vision models trained in one domain falter in another with no labels. Hard shifts change both scenes and object looks at once. Language holds up better under such complex shifts.

Captions of target images yield pseudo labels for the vision model. A normalized CLIP score gauges doubt in each such label. Loss weights then mute the harm from bad labels. A soft contrastive loss aligns vision and language spaces too. Tests set new best scores on classic and geographic shifts.
arxiv-2508-07752:
J Greenlees wrote a 2025 math paper on rational spectra with group symmetry over select blocks. Spectra are the basic objects of stable homotopy theory, a field that studies spaces through their stable shadows. Adding a group action lets one track how symmetry shapes those shadows.

The paper fixes a set of subgroups whose Weyl groups are finite and which is closed under the right moves. For such a set, the class of spectra whose isotropy lands inside it matches a class of sheaves over the same set. That match gives an algebraic model for the spectra, a rare clean form. The model's injective size is capped by the rank of the group. A second version fills gaps in proofs and notation, as the author notes.
arxiv-2508-08052:
Supriyo Chakraborty and Krishnan Raghavan model how a learning system's usable capacity drifts as it takes on task after task, in work from twenty twenty-five. Continual learning forces one network to absorb new jobs without erasing old ones. The balance point between keeping and adapting is the core tension.

Their measure, effective model capacity, tracks that balance as training proceeds. A difference equation describes how network, data, and optimizer move it over time. The balance point turns out to move no matter the design or training method. When new task data differ from old, room for new tasks shrinks. Tests ran from small plain networks up to transformer language models, backing the theory.
arxiv-2508-08652:
Vishakha Lall and Yisi Liu wrote a 2025 paper on using language models to grade communication in simulation-based training. In safety-critical fields such as maritime operations, trainees must follow communication protocols exactly, and checking compliance against a checklist is part of judging competence. Human grading is slow and inconsistent.

Their method, Prompt-and-Check, uses prompt-based inference with open-source language models small enough to run on consumer graphics cards. Given only the transcript of a trainee's spoken exchanges, the model checks whether each checklist item was fulfilled. A case study in the maritime domain tests the method on participants performing a standard task. A lightweight grader could make simulation training feedback immediate and consistent.
arxiv-2508-09652:
Ponte and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about how rule-based checks shape AI systems that hunt Windows malware. Many systems pair fixed signatures with machine learning models. The two parts are usually built apart and only joined at the end. The team instead trained the learning part only on files that signatures had missed. They asked whether that change makes the whole system stronger or weaker.

Models trained this way resisted crafted files meant to fool them. They also held up better as malware changed over time. The cost was a fixed floor of false alarms from poorly chosen rules. The authors discuss those limits frankly. They suggest adding behavior-based analysis next to harden the system further.
arxiv-2508-10052:
Pallavi Zambare and co-authors present a 2025 paper on NetMoniAI, a team-of-agents framework for watching network security. Threats increasingly arrive as coordinated moves across many machines, which single monitoring points miss. Their design splits the watch: small autonomous agents sit at each node, scanning local traffic for anomalies on their own.

A light central controller then merges the local reports, spotting patterns that suggest a joint attack and keeping a system-wide picture. The authors tested the framework on a small lab testbed and in network simulations. It scaled within tight resource limits, cut duplicated work, and answered faster without losing accuracy. The code is openly released.
arxiv-2508-10352:
Beso Mikaberidze and co-authors used prompt encoders to lift low-performing languages in a 2025 paper. Soft prompts are small trained vectors that steer a big model without touching its weights. Past work tuned them for training stability, leaving their power to carry skill across languages untested.

A language counts as low-performing when even full fine-tuning scores poorly on it. The team pair a light prompt encoder with training drawn from many source languages. Typological traits of the languages guide the mix. The encoder then acts as a bridge into the weak language. Such bridges could serve tongues that big models now fail.
arxiv-2508-10852:
Souhaila Serbout and four co-authors build EvoScat, a tool that shows the whole tale of a software project's change in one view. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Long-lived projects hold vast counts of parts, each changed many times. Those who study how code grows mine sets with millions of such events. Plain views choke at that scale. EvoScat uses a dense scatter view that a user can roam, to give a world view in one frame. It lets a reader see how fast each part ages across years, and how its marks shift with time. Sets can be matched side by side in the same view.
arxiv-2508-11052:
Evey Jiaxin Huang, Matthew Easterday, and Elizabeth Gerber build an AI coach that helps startup mentors and novice founders think better together. Entrepreneurship problems are open-ended: risks hide, assumptions go unchallenged, and uncertainty runs deep. Novices struggle with those mental demands. Mentors lack time and visibility to tailor help. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's system pairs a cognitive model of entrepreneurial risk with a large language model. It proactively poses diagnostic questions to founders. It also helps both sides plan focused, emotionally attuned meetings. Mentors can inspect and edit the cognitive model itself.

A field deployment followed. The system supported novice metacognition and improved meeting depth and focus, the authors report. It also surfaced tensions around trust, misdiagnosis, and expectations of AI. Design principles for proactive collaboration tools are the closing contribution.
arxiv-2508-11552:
Alice Harding, Zorawar Wadiasingh, and Matthew Baring model cascades of particle pairs in the magnetic fields of magnetars, in a research paper from 2025. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, and they emit hard radiation past 200 keV. One proposed source is photons bouncing off fast particles on closed field loops.

The team ran Monte Carlo simulations of what happens when fast electrons are injected at the base of such loops. In the strong fields, photons split and create electron-positron pairs, which then radiate and spawn further pairs and photons. For most viewing angles, light from those pairs outshines the primary signal. The pair light is softer and strongly polarized, which may explain the high polarization seen in some magnetar spectra.
arxiv-2508-13052:
Sourav Raxit and four co-authors plan robot paths by optimizing over windows of reachable speeds. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, targets cluttered, tight settings. Classic planners often stumble on limits like top speed and acceleration. Checking every option in a high-dimensional space is slow. Safety rules shrink the room further.

Their BOW planner uses constrained Bayesian optimization inside each window. It samples control inputs sparingly yet well. Trajectories come out fast and safe. Theory backs the method with convergence toward near-optimal paths. Trials in cluttered scenes show clear wins over rivals. Computation times, path lengths, and solve times all improve. The planner suits robots that must move smoothly among obstacles.
arxiv-2508-14252:
Jeffrey Brock and co-authors harness moving magnetic domain walls for brain-like computing in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Domain walls are boundaries between magnetic regions, and moving them can mimic neuron behavior with little energy. The challenge is getting all the needed behaviors from one material system.

The team uses ferrimagnets, materials mixing two metal families, with locally engineered coupling between neighboring areas. This makes domain walls drift on their own, at speeds set by feature size, mix, and a chiral interaction. Paired with electric torques, the motion yields leaky integration and passive resetting, two core neuron traits. Experiments and simulations back the design as a scalable platform.
arxiv-2508-14352:
Junwei Su and Shan Wu propose a new way to build graphs with computers in a 2025 paper. Graph models that grow networks step by step can create useful fake data. Yet they need huge amounts of memory for large graphs. They also fail to make graphs of sizes they never saw in training.

Their method, called SBGD, first splits a graph into blocks based on common real world patterns. The model then works in that smaller block space instead of the full graph. Tests show memory use fell by up to six times. Quality stayed as good as or better than older methods. The block form also let the model make graphs of new sizes more reliably.
arxiv-2508-14852:
Aleksandr Poliukhin, Nicola Colonna, Francesco Libbi, Samuel Poncé, and Nicola Marzari work out how electrons and lattice vibrations interact, with tools beyond DFT once thought too costly. Their work came out in 2025. Electron-phonon coupling governs transport, superconductivity, and light absorption. Standard density functional theory gives close values for it, but not exact ones. Hybrid functionals, Koopmans functionals, and GW theory promise better numbers. What was missing was one general way to draw couplings out of all of them.

Their finite-difference framework works with any method that gives energies and states. A projection scheme based on energy gaps gets past the old limits of direct finite difference work. Symmetry cuts the number of atomic displacements the method must test, so costs stay manageable. Carrier mobility values can now climb beyond the standard level, and models of real solids gain much sharper inputs.
arxiv-2508-15352:
Sang Kyu Kim and a large team of co-authors report in 2025 a way to control photon number probabilities with phase-tuned interference. Making states with a set number of photons matters for quantum computing and sensing. Beyond single photons, deterministic control has been elusive until now.

Their all-optical protocol turns a single-photon emitter into a generator of zero, one, or two photon states. An interferometer mixes interference effects, with two knobs shaping the statistics. Tuning moves the light from antibunched to strongly bunched. A quantum model maps the results, and the framework may extend to special multi-photon states.
arxiv-2508-15652:
When software agents learn together, team scores hide who actually helped. Ardian Selmonaj and co-authors propose a way to grade each agent without any reward signal at all. Their method, built on information-theoretic Shapley values, watches the policies themselves. It asks how one agent's choices change its teammates' certainty and direction.

The idea borrows from empowerment, the drive to keep future options open. An agent scores well when its actions either sharpen teammates' decisions or preserve their flexibility, whichever the task rewards. Across cooperative and competitive tasks, the scores separated helpful behavior from harmful behavior. They also showed which agents copied each other and which struck out alone. The tool aids explainability for multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2508-15752:
Jon Froehlich and co-authors published a 2025 vision paper on AI agents that can answer questions about what places look like. Digital maps are rich in facts like road layouts and business listings. They cannot say whether a cafe entrance has steps, or where its door sits. Yet such visual details decide whether a place works for a person with a disability.

The authors propose agents that search huge photo collections: street-level views, photos shared on review sites, and images from the air. Combined with normal map data, these could answer fine-grained questions about real places. The paper lays out how such agents might sense and respond, and gives three example uses. It also lists hard problems ahead, from photo coverage to trust in the answers. The work is a research agenda rather than a finished system.
arxiv-2508-17952:
Maryna Manskova, a solo author, wrote a math paper in 2025 on points spread over a sphere. The paper studies how close pairs of points tend to be when the points are placed by random rules. Some rules push points apart at short range, while others do not.

Manskova works out the mean value of a pair-count score for three such rules. Two rules come from a class of processes known for spreading points out. The third rule jitters points on a fixed grid. She compares all three with the case of points placed with no link at all. At short range, the special rules show clear push-apart behavior. At larger range, all cases agree closely with the fully random case.
arxiv-2508-18052:
Silvia Beddar-Wiesing and Alice Moallemy-Oureh extend a classic theory of what graph-learning machines can tell apart, in a 2025 paper. Graph neural networks learn from networks of linked items, and their power matches a famous test that colours nodes by their neighbourhoods. That theory covered networks that change in neat steps. Real networks, such as payment or contact systems, change at ragged times and can split apart.

The authors build a version of the colouring test that runs in continuous time, handling events as they land. They prove it lines up with a matching notion of unfolding trees for such streams. They then define a family of networks that keep the same telling-apart power and can still mimic any target behaviour closely. The work gives builders of time-aware graph models a firm map of their limits.
arxiv-2508-18952:
Saikat Panja, Ayon Roy, and Anupam Singh published a 2025 mathematics paper on raising matrices to powers inside exotic number systems. The setting is the group of invertible matrices over a finite ring of length two, a system like arithmetic modulo a prime squared. Raising each matrix to a fixed power, coprime to the prime, defines a power map. The question: which matrices appear as outputs?

The authors classify the image elements whose reduction, modulo the ring's maximal ideal, is regular semisimple, a well-behaved class. Word maps on matrix groups over fields are classical; over these thicker rings the study is new. The classification tells which powers exist and which are unreachable. Such results feed group theory questions about equations in matrices, with echoes in cryptography and coding. The paper opens a direction: familiar field results must be re-proven, or will fail, when the scalars carry nilpotent fuzz.
arxiv-2508-19052:
Paul Garnier, Jonathan Viquerat, and Elie Hachem present a 2025 computing paper on teaching neural networks to invent numerical schemes. Graph neural networks can imitate the solutions of physical systems, but whether they generalize to new meshes is doubtful. The authors use them for a different job: deriving the scheme itself.

A network trained only on tiny two-node graphs managed to act out a first-order finite volume scheme for the heat equation. The team proves that the scheme's error tracks the network's training loss. Symbolic regression then showed the network had rediscovered the exact classic formula. A second version learned from a physics-based loss alone, with no sample answers. Wider networks went on to find second-order corrections on their own.
arxiv-2508-19452:
Andrea Esposito and co-authors build a formal model in a 2025 paper of the agreement protocol behind the Algorand blockchain. Algorand lets a wide set of users agree on blocks without a central leader. It picks committees by a cryptographic lottery and uses a Byzantine agreement step, which tolerates some faulty or hostile members.

The authors write the protocol in a process algebra and check it with the CADP toolkit. First they confirm the protocol works when no attackers are present. Then they add coordinated hostile nodes that try to force an empty block in place of the proposed one. Their checks use a noninterference frame to see where the attack leaks through. The work maps both the strength of the design and the points where it can be pushed.
arxiv-2508-20852:
Johannes Krotz and Ryan McClarren present a 2025 paper on writing radiation transport equations in curved coordinates. Transport equations track particles or photons streaming through a domain. When the domain is round or bent, the coordinates should follow its shape, but then the streaming term picks up extra twists.

The authors derive a general form for that term in curvilinear coordinates. They describe each particle's direction with a local frame that moves along the path. Direction changes then appear as curvature quantities tied to the geometry of space itself. The framework shows when the angular part can be simplified. It also guides the choice of coordinates that keep both the math and the computing manageable.
arxiv-2509-00452:
Dietmar Ferger, working alone, studies a transform of the Vincze statistic in 2025 and derives its exact and asymptotic distribution. The setting is the one-sided two-sample problem, which tests whether one sample tends to exceed another. A new nonparametric test rests on a transform T of the Vincze statistic, a rank-based measure built from a pair of quantities denoted R and D.

Exact distribution results hold for finite samples, and a limit theorem gives the asymptotic distribution as samples grow. The core idea also extends to the two-sided problem, where deviations in either direction count. There too, a limit theorem is proved. Exact and limiting laws let practitioners compute p-values for the new test at any sample size.
arxiv-2509-00552:
Chengyi Li, writing alone, studies how cosmic photon showers form if space-time has a string-inspired foam, a frothy small-scale structure predicted by some string theory models. Such foam can break Lorentz symmetry, the rule that light speed is the same for all observers, and slow photons slightly.

Li analyzes foam-modified kinematics, the rules for energy and motion, and finds that the slowing can explain photon time delays seen in gamma-ray burst studies while keeping electromagnetic showers intact. Showers are cascades that let detectors identify cosmic photons. Unlike many other Lorentz-breaking models, this foam model can avoid changing shower formation length, so it escapes recent limits from observations.
arxiv-2509-00952:
A J Nayana leads a team of thirty-seven authors on X-ray and radio views of AT 2024wpp. This event is the most luminous known fast blue optical transient. Observations span from two days to most of a year after first light. X-ray emission is luminous and variable throughout. A Compton hump peaks at about fifty days.

The X-ray spectrum evolves from soft to extremely hard. A re-brightening accompanies that change at about fifty days. The properties favor an embedded high-energy source. It shines through asymmetric expanding ejecta around it. Radio emission is modeled as synchrotron radiation from a blast wave. The wave expands into a dense surrounding medium. Inferred outflow speeds increase over time, indicating acceleration. A super-Eddington accretion source with disk winds fits the picture.
arxiv-2509-01152:
Chenjian Wang studies pinned distances, the distances from one fixed point in a set to the other points of that set. The topic grows from a theorem by Bourgain about copies of point patterns inside sets in space. Wang asks whether, for sets with positive upper density, one pinned point can realize all large distances.

The answer is no: Wang gives sets where no single point does that. A weaker result does hold, though. For each point in such a set, its pinned distances still fill a set of positive upper density on the line. Wang also builds an example showing that this weaker bound cannot be improved. The work draws a clear line between global and pinned forms of the problem.
arxiv-2509-01252:
Baruch Meerson studies a tiny particle jittering under Brownian motion in a repulsive potential, a landscape that pushes it outward ever faster. For steep enough potentials, the particle reaches infinity in a finite time, and that blowup time varies at random from run to run. Meerson focuses on very short blowup times.

Earlier work by Krapivsky and Meerson found the leading shape of that short-time tail, which has a sharp essential singularity at zero. Meerson now computes the large pre-exponential factor that was missing, for all integer steepness values. The method applies a WKB approximation, a wave-based estimate, to a transformed equation, at two orders of accuracy. Odd cases need an added fix in a thin layer near the origin, completing a precise statistical picture.
arxiv-2509-01352:
Knowing which features truly cause a prediction, rather than merely track it, can cut bias and sharpen forecasts. Soma Bandyopadhyay and Sudeshna Sarkar propose a generative method to find causally sensitive features, those whose change moves the outcome. Their approach views the problem through interventions and counterfactuals, asking what would happen if a cause were set differently.

A conditional variational autoencoder, a generative model that learns hidden structure, both finds the causal features and serves as the predictor. Removing confounded signals reduces bias in the results. The team tests the method on recommending a user's next location from movement traces in the large GeoLife data set, and on a standard Bayesian network benchmark. Both tests support the claim that the method identifies real causal impact and improves prediction.
arxiv-2509-01452:
Future electron-positron colliders offer a clean setting to hunt for deviations from the standard model of particle physics. Amir Subba and Ritesh K. Singh study how such a machine could bound new effects on couplings between gauge bosons and the Higgs boson. The effects are framed in an effective theory with dimension-six operators that respect the standard gauge symmetries.

The team examines events with three leptons, two jets, and missing energy, using beam polarization as an added handle. Boosted decision trees pick out the phase space of two key processes, triple gauge boson production and vector boson scattering. Polarization asymmetries and spin correlations, joined with total rates, constrain the anomalous couplings. Flavor tagging by neural networks handles jets from W bosons. One-parameter limits at ninety-five percent confidence are reported.
arxiv-2509-01552:
Large vision-language models process images as many tokens, and high-resolution pictures or long videos inflate that count until inference slows sharply. Junjie Chen, with five co-authors, studies token compression inside the model. Their analysis finds two limits in current methods: a bias toward certain positions, and poor fit with fast operators used in deployment.

The team shows that how visual tokens vary during inference follows a pattern that does not depend on the task. Their method, V2Drop, progressively removes the visual tokens with the least variation as the model runs. Dropping near-static tokens cuts computation while keeping the changing ones that carry new information. Chen and the co-authors present variation, long ignored, as a practical signal for speeding up large vision-language models without changing their architecture.
arxiv-2509-01852:
Jef Pauwels and Nicolas Gisin extend an elegant joint measurement from two quantum bits to many. A joint measurement reads several qubits, the basic quantum units, at once in an entangled way. The two qubit version has local shadows that form a perfect pyramid shape and costs little entanglement to run locally. It anchors striking effects in quantum networks.

The pair seek many qubit versions that keep the pyramid symmetry and stay cheap to run locally. For two qubits, those rules pick out the known measurement alone. For three or more, they yield a discrete set of distinct classes. The richer set reflects how multipartite entanglement grows more varied with size.
arxiv-2509-02252:
D G Mazzone leads eleven co-authors in a deep study of vexed magnetism in the Kondo metal YbAgGe. Local spins, vexed links, and free charge mix in this warped kagome metal. Vexed links breed tied ground states with strong shakes, most probed in non metals. Metals add new link paths that theory takes just in stark edge cases.

Mixed free and local charge makes live magnetic links past a set heat mark. Down low, vexed links build slanted short range links in the metal. Long range anti aligned order sets in at last at a low heat with a cut spin size. Local spin models grasp just part of the small scale acts seen. More rich models with free charge paths are in clear need.
arxiv-2509-02452:
Seyedali Mohammadi and six co-authors present a 2025 natural language processing paper asking whether language models truly use label definitions handed to them in a prompt. Models might instead fall back on knowledge baked in during training.

Controlled tests span general and domain-specific explanation datasets. Definition conditions include expert-written versions, model-generated ones, perturbed versions with small corruptions, and swapped versions taken from other labels. Clear definitions did raise accuracy and explanation quality in places. But uptake was uneven and never guaranteed, with models often defaulting to internal habits on general tasks. Domain tasks gained more from supplied definitions. The authors argue that how models blend given knowledge with stored knowledge needs deeper study.
arxiv-2509-02552:
A. L. Shilov and seventeen co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper. It asks what limits electric conduction in twisted bilayer graphene. That material is two graphene sheets rotated to a special angle. Resistance grows with heat as a power law. Rival accounts of that growth have fought for years.

The trick is to heat only the electrons with terahertz light. The lattice stays cold. That splits electron-electron effects from electron-phonon effects. Resistance jumped hugely in magic-angle devices. So interactions rule even where phonons took the blame. Far from that angle, strong effects held at very low densities. At such densities, standard interaction channels are banned. The authors blame broken Galilean invariance in the electron dispersion. Collisions between valleys can then limit the current.
arxiv-2509-02752:
Jiawen Chen, Aritra Halder, Yun Li, Sudipto Banerjee, and Didong Li present a 2025 spatial statistics paper on estimating not just a spatial field but its rates of change across massive datasets. Derivatives expose subtle pattern shifts in environmental and biological data, yet standard Gaussian processes scale cubically and choke on large samples.

Cheap plug-in fixes, fitting a scalable model then differencing, depend on tuning choices and can produce invalid derivative inference. The Nearest-Neighbor Derivative Process instead models field and derivatives jointly inside one scalable Gaussian process. Its cost grows linearly with sample size, making huge datasets feasible. The authors supply supporting theory and test the method in simulations and real data analyses, reporting accurate derivative estimates where older routes struggle.
arxiv-2509-02852:
Frank C. Porter wrote a 2025 research paper on statistics for counting experiments in physics. Its subject is the Poisson distribution, a formula that gives the odds of seeing a given number of random events. Physicists rely on such counts often, yet they report the outcomes in confused or conflicting ways.

Porter set standard reporting methods beside several popular alternatives. He judged each one against traits that a good summary should have. His advice is to report results with the intervals Garwood proposed long ago. Those intervals yield p-values, measures of how surprising data would be under a guess, that behave in steady and sensible ways. He also warns that averaging intervals can mislead when the underlying counts are ignored.
arxiv-2509-03852:
Binqing Wu and three co-authors examine MillGNN, a graph neural network for forecasting several time series at once, in a 2025 research paper. Multivariate forecasting predicts many related quantities together, like traffic at many sensors, and series often lead or lag each other. Earlier methods capture dependencies within and between series, yet miss how lead-lag effects operate at several grouping scales at once.

MillGNN learns those multi-scale lead-lag dependencies. One module builds a lead-lag graph specific to each grouping level, mixing cross-correlation statistics with decaying features drawn from live inputs and time lags. That design keeps the learned relationships statistically interpretable while staying flexible. A second module passes messages hierarchically across scales, propagating lead-lag effects within and between groups. Experiments on eleven datasets, against sixteen leading methods, show MillGNN ahead for both long-term and short-term forecasting, balancing comprehensiveness with efficiency.
arxiv-2509-03952:
A 2025 research paper by Philipp Hanussek and three co-authors compares quantum and classical computers on the same physics tasks. Real-time quantum dynamics is hard to simulate, and matching machines fairly across paradigms is harder still. Their suite converts dynamics into a shared format every solver can attempt.

A parallel-in-time scheme turns the time evolution of an n-qubit Hamiltonian, perhaps non-Hermitian, into quadratic binary problems. Eight dynamical models stress the suite, from single-qubit rotations to entangling gates and exotic generators. The shared scoreboard counts success probability and solving time. Two D-Wave annealer generations face leading standard solvers, including a GPU one. The newer annealer beats its predecessor, while the classical GPU solver keeps the shortest runtimes, reflecting mature heuristics. Large cases near one hundred thousand variables set a hard baseline for future hardware.
arxiv-2509-04152:
Benoît Ronval and two co-authors create fake-but-realistic spreadsheet data using teams of language-model agents in a 2025 research paper. Synthetic tables help train classifiers when real records are scarce or private. Their collection of methods, TAGAL, lets a large language model generate rows, check feedback, and revise, all in a loop. No extra training of the language model itself is needed, and outside knowledge can be fed in during generation.

Classifiers trained only on TAGAL tables performed about as well as those using data from top rival methods. Mixing synthetic rows with real ones also helped. Similarity checks confirmed the tables resemble genuine data. Training-free generation could widen access to useful test and training data.
arxiv-2509-04452:
