Timothée Hornek and two co-authors forecast the direction of electricity prices in fast intraday trading in a 2025 research paper. Wind and solar swings, plus flexible loads like electric vehicles and heat pumps, keep unbalancing power grids. Europe's continuous intraday market lets traders fix positions near real time, but prices jump violently. Most forecasting studies simplify by watching one benchmark price and ignoring the order book, the live list of bids and offers.

Their method predicts price direction for hourly products using short-term features from hourly and quarter-hourly neighbors alike. German exchange data from 2024 and 2025 supplied the tests. Order-book features proved most influential, and overlapping neighbor products sharpened accuracy. Trading simulations suggested profit potential.
arxiv-2509-05152:
Weak gravitational lensing surveys will measure galaxy shapes for billions of objects, and shape errors must stay below one percent. Andy Park, lead author with three co-authors, extend an analytical calibration method in a 2025 astronomy paper. The original framework reaches the needed accuracy but adds noise to images, wasting their depth.

Their deep-field version computes shear responses from much deeper images, preserving the statistical power of wide fields. Tests on simulated isolated and blended galaxies with survey-like seeing and noise meet the strict bias requirement. The method raises the effective galaxy density substantially for simulated ten-year survey data, improving cosmological reach.
arxiv-2509-05252:
Toru Nogayama asks when a basic rule of analysis holds in general function spaces, in a solo 2025 paper on Young's inequality. That inequality bounds how much two functions can overlap when one is slid across the other, a tool used across harmonic analysis.

Nogayama gives a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for the inequality to hold on Banach function spaces, a broad family of spaces defined by size measures. As an application, he studies maximal regularity estimates for heat equations, which say how smooth solutions stay over time. The setting there is Besov spaces built on the same general spaces, widening where the heat estimates apply.
arxiv-2509-05752:
A quantum theory of light sources that feed their own output back through patterned structures is developed by Alex O. C. Davis and Alex I. Flint in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Parametric oscillators are proven sources of quantum light, while distributed feedback structures, using gratings like those in many lasers, offer prized control properties.

Combining the two promises sources of squeezed vacuum, a key resource for quantum technology. The authors give an analytic, fully quantum-mechanical model of such devices. It yields the oscillation threshold, the cavity mode shape, tunability, and the quantum statistics of output modes, including entanglement. Quantum-enhanced sensing with these devices is also discussed.
arxiv-2509-05952:
Reinforcement learning can polish images from flow matching generators, but the usual way of adding randomness hurts the training signal, report Feng Wang and Zihao Yu in a 2025 paper. Online reinforcement learning needs stochastic sampling, so flow models borrow a stochastic differential equation that injects noise. The authors trace visible noise artifacts in outputs to that excess randomness.

Their fix, Coefficients-Preserving Sampling, reworks the sampling process along lines suggested by the DDIM method from diffusion models, removing the artifacts. Cleaner samples mean the reward model grades outputs more accurately. In turn, reinforcement learning optimizers such as Flow-GRPO and Dance-GRPO converge faster and more stably. The paper links a sampling detail to the whole quality of learned image generation.
arxiv-2509-06852:
Routes to chaos in high-dimensional systems may have no bound on their complexity, argue Eran Igra and one co-author in a 2025 dynamical systems paper. The authors revisit problems posed by Yorke using methods in the spirit of Erdős, the famously probabilistic mathematician. Periodic orbits and their bifurcations are the objects of study.

Bifurcations are analyzed as graphs: the authors build collections of graphs that idealize bifurcation diagrams, then color them using the Mallet-Yorke orbit index together with the Lefschetz fixed point theorem. That machinery lets them study how generic routes to chaos are and how complex those routes can become. The headline reading is stark: in high-dimensional systems, a route to chaos can be arbitrarily complex, with no ceiling on that complexity. Graph-based idealizations thus expose wild behavior that direct simulation might never map.
arxiv-2509-07052:
Giulio Audagnotto and Antonino Di Piazza solve a hard motion equation in full in a 2025 paper. A charged mass that speeds up feels its own field push back on it, an effect known as radiation reaction. The DeWitt-Brehme-Hobbs equation gives that motion when both electric and gravity fields are at play.

The pair find the first exact solution of that equation for a charged mass hit by plane waves of both kinds that travel as one. A known limit, the Penrose limit, lets this case stand in for the local view near a path that moves close to light speed in any curved spacetime. They also work out a clean case in full: an electric wave plus a gravity wave of fixed strength. In that case, the gravity wave can change the back-push effect in kind, not just in size.
arxiv-2509-07852:
Seyd Teymoor Seydi tackles wildfire damage mapping in a solo 2025 paper on remote sensing. His method pairs satellite imagery from the AlphaEarth foundation dataset with a Siamese U-Net, a neural network that compares images from before and after an event. The imagery combines optical and heat-sensing views with labelled ground truth.

Training uses a United States burn severity dataset, and testing covers seventeen regions across Europe. Fast, accurate maps of burned land help agencies respond to fires, track environmental harm, and judge climate effects. By learning from two time points at once, the network aims to separate real burn scars from ordinary landscape change, giving mapmakers a quicker starting point after each fire season.
arxiv-2509-08052:
Carolyn McDonald Mill and 4 co-authors tackle a quiet source of bias in precision cosmology in a 2025 paper. Stage IV surveys will measure the universe so precisely that unmodelled flaws can shift conclusions. In three-by-two-point analyses, which combine weak lensing with galaxy positions, wrongly estimated galaxy distances are a prime danger, especially catastrophic outliers whose redshifts are badly misread.

Deep surveys add many faint galaxies whose photometric redshifts are shaky, and intrinsic alignments of galaxy shapes add another systematic effect. The authors work on mitigating the parameter bias these outliers cause. Cleaning such biases decides whether next-generation surveys deliver on their promise of percent-level measurements of dark energy and cosmic structure.
arxiv-2509-08452:
A random colouring of the integer lattice, decided by visibility from a random point, is studied through percolation by Samuel Le Fourn and 2 co-authors in a 2025 probability paper. A lattice point counts as visible from another when the segment between them passes through no third lattice point, a number-theoretic condition tied to coprime coordinates. Colour visible points white and the rest black.

Earlier work by Pleasants, Huck, and Martineau made the random viewpoint precise. The percolation question asks how many infinite connected components each colour forms under a reasonable graph structure on the lattice. Visibility colourings blend geometry, number theory, and randomness, and their component counts reveal whether the white visible world stays connected or shatters.
arxiv-2509-08752:
Vivek Oommen and 4 co-authors learn turbulent flows with generative models in a 2025 paper. Neural operators can mimic fluid systems fast, but standard training smooths out fine turbulent detail. The team tests three hard tasks where that smoothing causes failure.

For jet super-resolution, an adversarially trained operator cuts spectrum error greatly while keeping sharp gradients. For three-dimensional turbulence, it forecasts well for several turnover times and runs far faster than diffusion methods. For sparse sensor data, a conditional model rebuilds full velocity and pressure fields. Together, the results bring near real time flow analysis closer for experiments.
arxiv-2509-09052:
Weather forecasting's best AI models have stopped improving much, so blending them may beat building another. Dibyajyoti Chakraborty and 5 co-authors present MoWE, a mixture of weather experts, in a 2025 research paper. MoWE does not forecast from scratch. It learns to combine the outputs of existing leading models, point by point across the map.

A vision transformer gating network assigns the weights. It conditions them on the forecast lead time, since models age differently into the future. Training MoWE costs far less than training any single expert. The blended forecast beat every individual model and a plain average, with clearly lower errors on two-day horizons. The strategy is efficient and scalable: as new expert models appear, a mixture can absorb them instead of starting over.
arxiv-2509-09152:
Taha Binhuraib and 2 co-authors launch LITcoder, a toolkit for neural encoding models of the brain, in a 2025 paper. Encoding models predict brain signals from stimuli such as text and speech. Each lab tends to rebuild the same core steps from scratch.

LITcoder gives shared tools to align stimuli with brain data, turn stimuli into traits, map traits to brain signals, and score models on held out data. Choices of data, brain zones, traits, and sampling can be mixed and compared in one pipeline. Logging, plots, and links to tracking tools are built in. Fits to three story listening datasets show its range and key design lessons.
arxiv-2509-09352:
Every photograph mixes the colors of surfaces with the play of light across them, and separating the two is a decades-old puzzle. Xiaodong Wang, Zijun He, and Xin Yuan propose a texture-aware solution in a 2025 research paper. The goal is intrinsic decomposition: one layer for reflectance, the true surface color, and one for shading. Complex lighting and rich textures defeat most methods.

The authors noticed that learning-based methods tend to over-smooth, erasing texture. That failure is informative: the smoothed output hints at the lighting, while the missing detail marks the texture. They built a texture-guided regularization term around that insight. The decomposition is then solved as an optimization combining model-based and learned priors. Results beat existing approaches on real-world images. Clean intrinsic layers help relighting, material editing, and any vision task that should not mistake a shadow for a stain.
arxiv-2509-09652:
Prashanti Anderson and 2 co-authors give the first efficient additive approximation scheme for a classic embedding problem in a 2025 algorithms paper. The task fits points in a low-dimensional Euclidean space so pairwise distances match given data as closely as possible, a practice known for decades as multidimensional scaling. Even the one-dimensional case is provably hard, and nothing efficient was known for higher dimensions.

Their scheme runs in polynomial time and lands within a small additive error of the optimum for the k-dimensional metric violation problem. Earlier work had managed only a logarithmic factor in one dimension, and a long-open question asked whether such a scheme existed at all. The result moves a seventy-year-old statistical workhorse onto firmer algorithmic ground.
arxiv-2509-09852:
Chuyuan Li and 3 co-authors use topic signals to guide reinforcement learning for summarising many documents at once in a 2025 language technology paper. A good multi-document summary must merge overlapping sources without drifting off theme or losing coherence. Big language models shine on single documents yet leave clear room to grow when the pile grows.

Simply naming the topic in the prompt already made summaries more informative, a clue the authors turn into machinery. Inside a group-relative policy training scheme, a new reward scores how well a draft's topics line up with the sources. On the Multi-News and Multi-XScience collections the method beat strong baselines throughout, showing topical focus can be trained in rather than hoped for.
arxiv-2509-09952:
Zhi Ying and 3 co-authors automate the craft of digital material design in 2025 with a two-stage system called Chord. Making believable surface materials for rendering takes artists long hours of skill, and recent generators that lean on visual foundation models often sacrifice quality, flexibility, or the user's say in the result. Chord first paints a shaded, tileable texture that follows the user's input, then reads the material back out of that picture.

The reading stage works as a chain: each physical channel of the surface description is predicted in turn, with earlier channels handed along as guidance to a fast image-conditioned diffusion model. The chain holds up on machine-made textures and on wild photographs alike. Text prompts, example images, structural guides, and editing all plug into the same frame.
arxiv-2509-10052:
Yuan-Hao Yang and 13 co-authors demonstrate a new kind of signal converter in this 2025 paper. Many technologies need to turn microwave signals into optical ones and back, from quantum computing links to radar. Existing converters rely on cavities, which boost the effect but limit bandwidth and make scaling hard.

Their device instead uses a traveling-wave design on thin-film lithium niobate, where a hybrid guide carries light and sound together. Continuous phase matching gives very wide working ranges in both the optical and microwave bands. The team converted signals between microwave and telecom wavelengths at room temperature. They also ran nine conversion channels at once in a single device. That is a first step toward dense, chip-scale links between the two technologies.
arxiv-2509-10552:
D. A. Blanco-Mora and 3 co-authors test a brain-signal marker of pain in this 2025 paper. Pain is still measured mostly by asking people, which fails for patients who cannot speak. The team recorded high-density EEG from 59 healthy volunteers who received electrical stimulation under pain and no-pain conditions, then broke each trial down by time and frequency.

One pattern stood out: a drop in beta-band activity over frontal and central electrodes separated painful from painless trials. The size of that drop tracked each person's own pain ratings, with age and gender shaping the link. Run in reverse, the signal predicted ratings across people. The authors offer it as early evidence for report-free pain monitoring, pending tests in patients.
arxiv-2509-10652:
Jie Li and five co-authors study vibe coding inside product teams in this 2025 paper. Vibe coding is a new practice. A team member states an intent in plain language. Generative AI turns it into working prototypes and code. Adoption has been rapid. How it changes teamwork had not been examined closely.

The authors interviewed twenty-two product team members. They came from companies, startups, and universities. A four-stage workflow emerged. Teams dream up an idea, generate a draft, debug it, and review it. Vibe coding speeds iteration. It sparks creativity. It lowers the barrier for non-programmers to join in. It also brings unreliable code and integration headaches. Over-reliance on the AI is a further worry. Deeper tensions surface around trust and responsibility. Skill loss and ownership come up, too. The authors examine all of it through a lens of responsible human-AI collaboration.
arxiv-2509-10752:
Minseok Kim and five co-authors measure the radio channels that future 6G networks will use in this 2025 wireless engineering paper. Sub-terahertz frequencies, between one hundred and three hundred gigahertz, behave almost like light, so models borrowed from lower bands fail. The team ran an extensive measurement campaign in an outdoor street canyon at two frequencies, under clear and blocked paths alike.

Clustering the combined data revealed which reflection paths the two frequencies share and where they diverge, plus how cluster behavior shifts with frequency. From this they build a quasi-deterministic model: fixed geometry supplies the direct path and wall bounces, randomness fills the rest. Standard quantities like path loss, delay spread, and angular spread are reported throughout, giving 6G designers measured ground truth for city streets instead of extrapolation.
arxiv-2509-10852:
A chatbot that remembers you across months of conversation needs memory that thinks ahead. Sangyeop Kim and four co-authors present PREMem in this 2025 paper. Today's systems push too much reasoning into the moment of reply, they argue. Quality then depends heavily on model size.

PREMem reasons before storage instead. It extracts fine-grained memory fragments. The fragments are sorted into factual, experiential, and subjective kinds. Explicit links are drawn between items across sessions. The links record how facts extend, transform, or imply one another. Conversations then read from an already-enriched memory. Experiments show gains at every model size. Small models matched much larger baselines. Performance held up under tight token budgets. The code and dataset are public.
arxiv-2509-10952:
Robots that learn housework from watching people are Yangcen Liu and five co-authors' goal in this 2025 robotics paper. Human videos are plentiful, robot demonstrations expensive, but bodies differ: hands are not grippers, and viewpoints and physics shift too. Their framework, ImMimic, trains across both domains at once and needs only a small set of teleoperated robot demonstrations.

The method maps retargeted human hand poses onto robot joints using dynamic time warping, guided by actions or by vision. Then MixUp interpolation blends paired human and robot trajectories, manufacturing intermediate domains that smooth the adaptation. On four real tasks, picking and placing, pushing, hammering, and flipping, across four different robot hands, ImMimic improved success rates and made execution smoother. The deeper lesson: retargeted hand motion is itself a useful action label.
arxiv-2509-11052:
Ordinary commenters fact-check faster than official systems. Shuning Zhang and eight co-authors prove it at scale in this 2025 study. Community Notes on X attaches crowd-written corrections to misleading posts. Notes arrive slowly, though. The authors analyzed over two million comments. They covered eighteen hundred misleading posts that eventually received notes. A language model pipeline was trained to spot fact-checking comments. Those are replies that correct a post with reasons or evidence.

Nearly every misleading post drew its first fact-checking comment early. Over ninety-nine percent beat the official note's creation. The median first correction took about six minutes. The median note took nearly ten hours. Posts that eventually displayed notes carried significantly more such comments, too. The authors argue for a change. Platforms should treat early corrective comments as an early-warning signal. They are also a resource for faster, synthesized fact checks.
arxiv-2509-11152:
Wajih Boukaram and four co-authors present this 2025 numerical computing paper on solving very large dense linear systems quickly. Their solver uses the H² hierarchical format, which compresses interactions between far-apart parts of a matrix so the whole job grows only linearly with problem size.

The factorization and solution steps are built for fine-grained parallel hardware and can handle many problems in a batch at once. The only inputs are the matrix and the right-hand side, with no extra geometric information needed. Tests on four families of dense matrices up to a million rows showed the promised linear growth in time and memory, with parallel runs on up to sixteen threads. The authors also check numerical accuracy and point out which steps are limited by memory speed.
arxiv-2509-11752:
Hongyuan Zhang and twenty-four co-authors release a foundation model for medical ultrasound in this 2025 biomedical AI paper. Ultrasound AI has been held back by small labeled datasets and by models that each solve one narrow task, so the team trained a generalist on a very large pooled collection.

Their dataset gathers four and a half million ultrasound images from more than twenty-three countries on five continents, across many devices and populations, and the model, EchoCare, learns from it by self-supervision. A hierarchical classifier lets it learn pixel-level detail and whole-image representation together, capturing anatomy at both scales. With minimal extra training it beat state-of-the-art rivals across ten benchmarks covering diagnosis, segmentation, organ detection, landmarks, measurement, enhancement, and report writing. Code and the pretrained model are fully public.
arxiv-2509-11852:
Three open problems about weighted shift operators drive a 2025 mathematics paper by Michal Hevessy and one co-author. Weighted shifts act on spaces of sequences, sliding entries along while scaling each one, and they serve as test cases for how linear systems behave over time.

First, the authors build a shift on a locally convex space that is generalized hyperbolic yet lacks the shadowing property, where true orbits track approximate ones. Next they pin down exactly when uniform topological expansivity holds on a broad class of spaces. Finally they study periodic shadowing on normed spaces and arrive at a condition written purely in terms of the weights, necessary in general and fully equivalent on two classic sequence spaces.
arxiv-2509-11952:
Land cover maps can be built from radar views, optical views, or both. CLAIRE uses both, in a 2025 paper by Debopom Sutradhar and five co-authors. Radar sees through clouds. It also picks up texture that optical images miss. Optical views add color detail that radar lacks. So the network keeps a separate encoder for each kind of image.

A cross-modality attention module merges the two streams of features. A hybrid loss blends focal and Tversky terms. That loss helps rare land-cover classes that plain training tends to skip. Tests span three benchmarks. The best showing came on a cloud-blocked dataset, where radar earns its keep. A small language model then writes a short reason for each label. Users can check why the network named a patch of ground as it did.
arxiv-2509-12152:
Chatbots can guess your age, politics, or health from chat that feels harmless, and Synthia Wang with three co-authors study whether users see that inference risk coming in 2025. The danger goes past leaked training data: models infer fresh facts from innocent text.

Two hundred forty U.S. participants judged snippets for inference risk, rated their concern, and tried rewriting text to block the guesses. Their instincts ran barely better than chance, and their rewrites worked in only about a quarter of cases, beating a dedicated sanitization tool but losing to ChatGPT's own rewrites. Paraphrasing, the most popular strategy, helped least; abstraction and deliberate ambiguity did better. The authors argue for interfaces that warn about inference, not just disclosure.
arxiv-2509-12552:
An exotic particle seen in electron-positron collisions still lacks an agreed identity. It is the phi(2170). Xiang Wei and three co-authors test a new reading of it in 2025. They model its production with an effective Lagrangian approach. The final state holds a phi meson and two pions.

Alongside direct contributions from known mesons, they add a triangle process. A meson pair is produced first. One partner then decays. The remaining pair rescatters into the two pions. A dynamically generated scalar drives that last step. With the loop included, the model matches fresh BESIII measurements well. The match is best around the phi(2170) structure. The fit also pins down properties of two heavier kaon-like mesons.
arxiv-2509-12652:
If a model's politics can be quietly steered, the steering should at least be detectable from outside. Paul Kröger and one co-author adapt a statistical auditing method to that job in 2025, hunting for ideological bias injected into large language models without ever opening the model.

The audit compares output distributions across prompts on a chosen theme; a systematic shift betrays steering toward a political or religious stance. Because the method is model-agnostic and needs only black-box access, it suits independent checks of commercial systems. Experiments validate the approach and frame it as a post hoc accountability tool, separate from the harder questions of prevention.
arxiv-2509-12752:
Niklas Elmqvist leads a large team of 47 co-authors in a 2025 call for Participatory AI, a way to build AI with the people who must live with it. The authors argue that many AI tools today are closed, run from far away, and shaped for profit more than for public good.

They borrow from Scandinavian design work of the 1970s, when workers helped shape new machines. Five shared ideas are applied to four hard problems in automated systems, with real cases to show each step. The aim is tools treated as shared public systems that protect choice, respect, and human values at work and at home.
arxiv-2509-13152:
Lucijana Stanic, Ivan Cardea and 12 co-authors show in 2025 that intensity interferometry can read motion inside stars. The method joins light strength across scopes for sharp views. A time-skewed correlation peak is the new signal.

Models cover two cases: a glow-line disk around a star, and a soak-line binary pair. Peak shift away from zero delay marks inner motion. Tilt, speed symmetry, and inner flows all sway the shift. With fine time steps, the shift yields hard numbers on stellar flows. A fresh window on star dynamics opens if tools reach that speed.
arxiv-2509-13252:
Washington Taylor, Yi-Nan Wang and Yihang Yu sample base polytopes for F-theory in 2025 with a new statistical ensemble. Toric bases for elliptic shapes drive 4D models, but full combinatorics is vast. Focusing on the convex hull alone slims the count greatly.

Monte Carlo draws hulls in fixed boxes with proper weights. In 2D the enlarged set validates against exact counts. In 3D, counts of distinct hulls land near an astronomically high range. Gauge group spreads on those bases are charted. Vertex counts follow a bell curve, as random polytope theory suggests.
arxiv-2509-13452:
David Martínez Torres and Carlos Tomei study the Toda flow in a 2025 mathematics paper. The flow is a classic system of equations whose motion can be tracked through matrices. They work with classes of traceless complex matrices. The eigenvalues of these matrices are all distinct. The pair look for coordinates that make the flow simple.

They construct such coordinates near any diagonal matrix in the class. The coordinates split the non-periodic Toda field into two basic fields. One is radial and one is rotational. Using Lie theory, which studies smooth symmetry groups, they extend the construction further. It reaches all complex semisimple Lie algebras and their real forms.
arxiv-2509-13652:
Yumin Li and Dylan Campbell introduce GARPS in a 2025 computer vision paper. GARPS finds the relative pose between two cameras. It also recovers the true metric distance between them. Classic two-view methods recover direction but not scale. They also struggle with wide baselines and shiny or textureless surfaces.

GARPS skips direct image matching. It reconstructs each view separately into a three-dimensional Gaussian mixture model. A metric depth estimator and a Gaussian scene builder do that work. It then aligns the two models by optimizing a differentiable objective. The objective weighs geometry, color, spread, and semantic features. With no training of its own, GARPS beat classical and leading learned methods on the RealEstate10K dataset. The beaten methods include MASt3R.
arxiv-2509-13852:
Yulun Wu and four co-authors rethink distributed tracing in a 2025 systems paper. Microservice applications record traces of each request's path, but the volume overwhelms storage, so samplers keep only selected traces, usually the abnormal ones, throwing away the normal traces needed for comparison.

Their Trace Sampling 2.0 works at the span level, the individual operations inside a trace, keeping every trace while shrinking each one. The implementation, Autoscope, uses static code analysis to learn the execution logic and preserve the spans that matter without breaking the trace structure. On two open-source microservices it cut trace size by about four fifths while keeping nearly all faulty spans, and it improved root cause analysis accuracy as well.
arxiv-2509-14452:
Sanchita S. Kamath and three co-authors study in 2025 how blind and low vision learners grasp statistical ideas from histograms without sight. Statistics teaching leans heavily on visual cues. Accessible displays exist, but how learners build the underlying concepts is little studied.

Seven blind and low vision participants, blindfold controlled within the study, tried three non visual formats. Formats were tactile swell graphs, shaped patterns on a refreshable braille display, and sonification, turning data into sound. Each learner used all formats across different statistical ideas. Observations reveal strategies learners invent to sense distribution shape, centre and spread. Design lessons follow for statistics tools that teach concepts, not merely render charts in another medium.
arxiv-2509-14752:
Nahyun Lee and three co-authors introduce KAIO in 2025, a harder Korean benchmark for frontier language models. Korean benchmarks are fewer, often translated or narrow, and saturate quickly as models improve. No current Korean test could rank frontier systems, the authors argue.

KAIO is a Korean, maths centred collection stressing long chain reasoning, built to resist saturation and contamination longer than legacy suites. Original Korean questions replace translated imports, cutting both cultural mismatch and leakage from English training data. Frontier progress in Korean needs a yardstick that does not top out within a product cycle. A durable benchmark also protects buyers in Korea from English only capability claims.
arxiv-2509-14952:
Zhuanghua Liu and Luo Luo tackle bilevel optimization when gradient noise has heavy tails in a 2025 optimization paper. Bilevel problems nest one optimization inside another, as in hyperparameter tuning and some reinforcement learning setups. Real gradient noise often produces occasional huge outliers, the heavy-tailed case, which breaks standard convergence arguments.

Their algorithm uses nested loops with normalized stochastic updates designed to tame those outliers. The lower problem is smooth and strongly convex, while the upper one may be nonconvex. They prove how many noisy gradient evaluations suffice to reach an approximately stationary point, with the bound depending on the problem's conditioning and the noise's tail weight. The same idea specializes to minimax problems with a nonconvex objective against a strongly concave one, again with explicit complexity guarantees.
arxiv-2509-15052:
Walker Gosrich and six co-authors coordinate teams of robots whose tasks depend on each other in order, in a 2025 multi-robot systems paper. A task graph spells out precedence: some jobs must finish before others start. Robots may also team up in coalitions, and reward functions capture how coalition size and earlier task outcomes affect later success.

Maximizing total reward is NP-hard, so exact solutions are out of reach for large missions. The authors give network flow-based approximation algorithms instead. Their online algorithm reallocates tasks repeatedly as events unfold, which proves robust to task failures and modeling errors, beating offline plans fixed in advance. Tests span randomized missions, comparison with a mixed-integer solver and a greedy heuristic, and a realistic simulator with physics-based rewards.
arxiv-2509-15352:
Clovis Farley and Bertrand Reulet study small electric noise in a tunnel junction. Such a junction lets electrons cross a thin barrier, and its current flickers. At low voltage, part of that flicker looks like vacuum noise, which is the faint motion left even in empty space. They ask whether this vacuum noise can be uneven, or skewed, as well.

The pair work out the math for a junction in any electric setting at zero temperature. They show the third moment of the voltage noise is always zero above a set frequency. Tests on real junctions match the result. The paper settles a basic question about how quantum devices behave.
arxiv-2509-15552:
Wei Lin, Qingyu Song, and Hong Xu study tuning when only function values can be probed. Some problems give no slope, so each step must guess the slope from a few probes. More probes per step sharpen the guess but eat the budget, leaving fewer steps. The team ask how to split a fixed probe budget best.

They compare two ways to merge probes. One is plain averaging, and the other is a new method built from a local stand in model. Their proofs give clear rates for both across many problem types. The verdict splits: with plain averaging, extra probes per step never pay off. With the new method, extra probes often do pay. The paper settles a basic budget choice.
arxiv-2509-15952:
Gang Yang leads a team that cleans noisy speech in a single generation step. Diffusion and flow models clean speech well, but they need many steps, which costs time and adds error. A recent one step method exists, yet its training is heavy due to costly math in each update. The team adapt that method for speech cleanup.

Their system, COSE, computes the average speed of the flow with a new identity that skips the costly step. Theory stays intact while training cost falls by two fifths. Sampling runs up to five times faster than multi step rivals. Speech quality stays competitive on standard test sets. Code is public. The work suits live cleanup where delay matters.
arxiv-2509-16052:
Who gets to include a trade in the next Ethereum block shapes fees and fairness on the network. Vabuk Pahari and Andrea Canidio study over fifteen thousand proposed blocks from an eight-minute window in December 2024. Only thirty-eight of those blocks joined the chain. They sort trades by whether they appear in blocks from just one builder or stay hidden from the public pool.

Exclusive trades made up most of the fees in winning blocks, by several measures. Yet few senders stick with one builder for long, and some trades switch status across bidding rounds. Some wait with a losing builder, then surface in public, where they face attack risk.
arxiv-2509-16252:
What happens when a slow proton strikes a hydrocarbon molecule depends on both its energy and where it hits. Misa Viveiros and six co-authors simulate these crashes with a time-based form of density theory that tracks electrons and nuclei together. They vary the proton's speed and aim point across the molecular surface in a systematic sweep.

Outcomes range from the proton bouncing off, to being captured, to breaking bonds apart. The balance between electron motion and nuclear motion steers which path each crash takes. Such results help model radiation damage and chemistry in settings where protons meet organic matter.
arxiv-2509-16752:
S. Elham Mousavigharalari and Deniz Türkpençe study phase sensing under noise in a 2025 quantum paper. A phase is a hidden angle that a qubit can encode through a set gate sequence. Noise in real devices blurs that angle. The pair model the probe as it meets a stream of prepared helper particles, one by one.

That stream drives the probe to a steady state that depends on the phase. From that state, a key sensitivity measure can be written in closed form. The route needs no full tomography of the state. It could serve as a test for device quality. Future uses in error repair and control are sketched.
arxiv-2509-17052:
Wataru Nakata, Yuki Saito, Yota Ueda, and Hiroshi Saruwatari clean noisy speech at scale in a 2025 paper. Text-to-speech systems need clean recordings in many languages, which are scarce. Their open model, Sidon, restores rough field recordings to studio-like quality. It scales to dozens of languages and runs fast.

Training a speech maker on a corpus cleaned by Sidon improved synthetic speech quality. That held in a zero-shot setting with no extra tuning. Code and model are released for public use. Cheap cleansing of wild recordings could unlock speech tools for languages that lack studio datasets, widening access to voice technology.
arxiv-2509-17252:
Luke Wisniewski, Thomas Zdyrski, and Feng Fu study how social ties and wealth gaps shape climate action in a 2025 arXiv paper. People choose how much effort to spend cutting emissions, and they often base that choice on forecasts of future harm. The climate then reacts to those choices, which feeds back into what people do next.

The model joins that feedback loop to two social forces: homophily, the pull toward like-minded peers, and wealth inequality. Outcomes range from steady decline to lasting resilience, with waves of public effort in between. Some past work claims homophily always makes warming worse. In this model, homophily can instead block the worst outcomes under the right conditions. Wealth gaps shift who acts and who holds back, so the same climate policy can play out very differently across groups.
arxiv-2509-17552:
Tianle Zhang and five co-authors test whether language models can reason over data that is not text, with no extra training. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that test-time tricks often call outside tools or helper models. Wiring in the output of vision or science models has usually meant costly supervised training, which blocks quick adaptation to new fields.

Their proposal, In-Context Representation Learning, swaps the text in few-shot prompts for representations from a non-text foundation model. The language model then infers over those vectors as if they were examples it had read. The team probes the idea in the molecular domain and asks three questions: how to map the vectors in, what drives the score, and where the limits lie. As a proof of concept, the study maps a training-free route into multimodal reasoning.
arxiv-2509-18152:
Zhenyu Qi and 5 co-authors build a base model for reading well logs, the depth traces used to map rock below ground. Their 2025 model, WLFM, faces messy tool signals, noise, and few tags. It trains on logs from more than a thousand wells, with no tags at first.

Log curves are cut into patch tokens that stand for rock units. Masked-token and contrast steps teach the model rock sense in a self-taught way. Few-shot tuning then fits it to tasks such as pore share and rock type. Scores beat top baselines, and the model shows a learned rock word set.
arxiv-2509-18452:
Huge sparse equation systems sit at the heart of many science and engineering codes. Anton Lebedev and nine co-authors present a faster way to solve them in this 2025 paper. Standard solvers slow down on ill-shaped systems unless a helper, called a preconditioner, reshapes the problem first. Their helper comes from a Monte Carlo matrix inversion method.

That helper works well only with the right settings, and the best settings change from system to system. Hand tuning or grid search costs too much time. The team trains a graph network to predict solver speed from the system and the settings. A Bayesian rule then picks the most promising settings to try. On a new ill-shaped system, the frame found better settings with half the search budget of standard methods. Solver rounds to the answer fell by about ten percent.
arxiv-2509-18552:
Contrastive training teaches models to place matching items close and others apart. Kiril Bangachev, Guy Bresler, Iliyas Noman, and Yury Polyanskiy study the best possible outcomes of the sigmoid version of that training in this 2025 paper. The sigmoid loss powers recent image-text models such as SigLIP. Two knobs, temperature and bias, can be trained along with the model.

The team shows those knobs can drive the loss to zero for a rich family of layouts they call constellations. Each constellation is set by a margin and a relative bias. The layouts link to spherical codes, a classic packing problem. The theory explains SigLIP's strong retrieval scores and the gap seen between image and text clouds. It also gives the dimension needed for high-quality representations. A reworked loss with explicit relative bias trained better in synthetic tests.
arxiv-2509-18952:
Hui-Qiang Liang and three co-authors uncover a new way for odd boundary states to appear in systems that lose energy to their surroundings. Such systems, called non-Hermitian, do not follow the usual rules of quantum physics. Their edge states have been hard to explain. The team traces the new states to a quirk: the equation that rules the boundary is very sensitive to pushes from the bulk of the material, pushes the authors call intrinsic perturbations.

That sensitivity drives a change between two kinds of states. One kind mixes skin effects, where waves crowd at an edge, with topological edge states. The other kind spreads in a scale-free way, and its energy levels shift with system size. Both kinds break the usual size-independent pattern, which gives new handles for controlling edge behavior in such systems.
arxiv-2509-19452:
Search and rescue drones must fly fast through unknown ground and then follow a found target. Alessandro Saviolo, Jeffrey Mao, and Giuseppe Loianno built HUNT, a control method for that job. Older tracking methods lock onto a seen object but fail when nothing is in view. HUNT instead plans from what the drone senses right now, such as tilt, height, and speed.

One pipeline handles the search flight and then shifts to tracking once a target shows up. Field tests took place in dense woods, among shipping containers, and in staged rescue scenes with cars and dummies. The drone held up in spots where methods that need a fixed map position failed. The work points to safer fast flight far from GPS help.
arxiv-2509-19752:
Robot models that see, read, and act need huge sets of demonstrations, and filming humans is slow and costly. Rushuai Yang and ten co-authors let reinforcement learning manufacture the demonstrations instead. A diffusion-based policy explores varied, smooth behaviors on long manipulation tasks. Its rollouts become training data for a vision-language-action model.

Ordinary reinforcement learning often fails on such tasks because rewards are sparse. The denoising process steadies the generated trajectories, lowering their variance. Tests use LIBERO, a benchmark of one hundred thirty long tasks. Synthetic demonstrations could scale robot training the way synthetic text scaled language models. The pipeline keeps a human-free loop from practice to policy. Quality of the generated data, the authors argue, is what makes the swap work.
arxiv-2509-19852:
Speech synthesis based on language models sometimes stutters, repeats phrases, or skips words. ShiMing Wang and eight co-authors trace those stability failures to weak alignment between text and speech tokens. They define an alignment score computed with the Viterbi algorithm, grading how cleanly text maps to sound. That score then guides training of the CosyVoice2 system.

Pre-trained attention values also coach the student model through chain-of-thought style guidance. Tests on two public evaluation sets show fewer repetitions and omissions, with no new side effects reported. Stable synthesis matters for audiobooks, assistants, and accessibility readers that speak for hours. The method improves the base model rather than patching its output. Alignment, the work suggests, is where speech models should be watched.
arxiv-2509-19952:
Shoppers often write 'worst product' while a five-second video shows the true defect plainly. Sarmistha Das and five co-authors define a task around that gap: write the complaint text from the video. They built ComVID, a dataset of over a thousand complaint videos with written descriptions. Each entry also marks the complainer's emotional state.

A new retention metric grades generated complaints in the bargain. The task, named Complaint Description from Videos, helps users who struggle to articulate faults in words. Support teams receive clearer tickets; buyers get faster resolutions. Multimodal complaint mining extends older text-only mining in a practical direction. The dataset gives that direction a benchmark. Product defects are visual by nature, so the framing fits the problem.
arxiv-2509-20452:
The seeds of the first giant black holes are the quarry of Qinyue Fei and nineteen co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. The James Webb Space Telescope has found many huge black holes in the early universe. The smaller seeds that grew into them remain hidden. The team searched some of the faintest distant galaxies yet surveyed, helped by a lensing galaxy cluster.

Using emission line shapes to separate broad from narrow components, they identified ten broad-line active nuclei between redshifts four and a half and seven. Eight are secure and two tentative. Their black hole masses reach down into the intermediate range, a few hundred thousand times the Sun's mass. The ratio of black hole to stellar mass extends down to about a tenth of a percent. An excess of low-mass objects hints they began as direct-collapse seeds, born from massive gas clouds.
arxiv-2509-20652:
Writing a product claim that moves shoppers takes time and money. Po-Yu Liang and three co-authors built Claim Advisor, a generative tool to speed that work, described in a 2025 arXiv paper. The web application uses in-context learning and fine-tuned large language models. It attacks the whole claim workflow: search, generation, optimization, and simulation.

Three functions structure the app. It searches existing claims and visuals that match the consumer's voice. It drafts or polishes new claims from a product description and a consumer profile. And it ranks claims by simulating synthetic consumers' reactions. Trials inside a consumer packaged goods company showed promising results, the authors report. They share their lessons to encourage generative AI adoption in marketing work across industries.
arxiv-2509-20852:
About one newborn in ten needs help to start breathing, so watching the fetal heart during labor matters. Kjersti Engan and six co-authors present FHRFormer in a 2025 paper submitted to an IEEE journal on biomedical informatics. The model fills gaps in fetal heart rate traces and forecasts what comes next.

Wearable monitors let mothers move during labor, but sensors slip and signals drop out. FHRFormer, a self-supervised transformer, learns to repair those missing stretches and predict future heart rate patterns. The authors aim to support earlier detection of abnormal patterns and timely intervention. Large collections of monitoring episodes with diverse outcomes drive the learning. The work connects wearable sensing with safer deliveries.
arxiv-2509-20952:
Flow matching trains generative models by learning a velocity field that carries noise into data. Weili Zeng and Yichao Yan uncover a flaw in that training at very low noise levels in a 2025 paper. They call it the low-noise pathology.

As noise approaches zero, tiny input perturbations can demand huge changes in the velocity target. The learning problem's condition number diverges, slowing optimization. Worse, the encoder spends its limited sensitivity on noise directions instead of meaning, degrading the learned representations. The authors give the first theoretical analysis of this effect. They then propose a contrastive remedy that stabilizes training in the low-noise regime. The work matters for both generation quality and representation learning.
arxiv-2509-21052:
Entanglement tests usually demand pristine optics, and any scrambling in the light path ruins them. Baptiste Courme and four co-authors turn that scrambling into the tool itself in a 2025 quantum optics paper. They violate a Bell inequality by harnessing optical disorder.

One photon of an entangled pair travels through a commercial multimode fiber that mixes its spatial and polarization modes, emerging as a speckle pattern. The other photon stays with the sender. By resolving the speckle pattern spatially, the team extracts measurement settings from the disorder itself. The Bell test then certifies entanglement despite, indeed through, the scrambling. The result suggests quantum certification can survive in messy real-world channels, and even exploit them.
arxiv-2509-21152:
Decentralized exchanges route token trades through chains of liquidity pools, and many trades take a worse path than necessary. Yu Zhang and Claudio Tessone extend a routing method in a 2025 paper on decentralized finance. The base method, from earlier work by Zhang and co-authors, uses a line-graph formulation.

Three extensions bring the method closer to real trading. A breadth-first link iteration rule cuts computation cost and average execution time without sacrificing profit. A route-splitting strategy divides large trades across paths, reducing price impact. A third extension, the authors explain, handles further real-world complexity in pool behavior. Better routing returns more tokens to traders on exchanges that now process billions of dollars in daily trades.
arxiv-2509-21252:
Ecalle senary relation, a deep identity in mould theory, receives a completed proof here. Behind the work are Hanamichi Kawamura. Jean Ecalle presented deep algebraic forms in the study of moulds and resurgence. The senary relation is one such identity, stated in an first form. Dimorphic forms carry two compatible algebraic forms at once. The paper works within Lie algebra theory.

Kawamura gives a completed proof of the senary relation in its first form. As an use, he obtains another proof that the double shuffle Lie algebra injects into the Kashiwara Vergne Lie algebra. He also gives two explicit isomorphisms. Those maps link some dimorphic Lie algebras with their linearized versions. The results clarify links between two major algebraic systems in modern maths.
arxiv-2509-21552:
Pointing a model at the right screen element from a text instruction is called GUI grounding. Yu Zhao and 10 co-authors reframe that task as interactive search in a 2025 paper. Vision language models often fail to output exact numeric coordinates on high resolution screens. Complex layouts make direct prediction worse. A rendered cursor can give the model visual feedback instead.

Their model, GUI-Cursor, moves a cursor step by step toward the target. At each step it identifies the target and judges spatial relations between cursor and target. Movement history conditions the next move. The cursor rendering aligns predictions with on screen locations. Training uses that interactive loop, turning grounding into search with spatial reasoning from visual feedback.
arxiv-2509-21752:
Transient gain in clear atomic media may be smaller in reality than simple models predict. Andrew MacRae and Connor Kupchak study propagation dynamics in electromagnetically induced transparency systems in a 2025 paper. Single atom, in space uniform optical Bloch treatments overshoot gain by missing propagation. Maxwell Bloch model runs including propagation supply the contrast. Two level and three level systems behave in other ways under the fix.

In two level systems, uniform treatments yield incorrect transmission. In three level systems, they predict unrealistically large gain. Doppler averaging in warm vapor suppresses oscillatory ringing and maximum achievable gain. Results explain discrepancies between Bloch outputs and experimental records. Useful limits on transient gain in cold and thermally broadened media are established.
arxiv-2509-21852:
Y. Garay-Solis leads a team of nine astronomers studying how galaxy mergers change star formation across a galaxy. Their paper uses the EDGE-CALIFA survey, which maps galaxies in visible light and in carbon monoxide, a tracer of the cold gas that feeds new stars. They compare a set of isolated galaxies with galaxies caught at four stages of merging.

The team tracked three measures at each distance from a galaxy's center. They recorded how fast stars form per unit mass, how well the gas is used, and how much of the gas is in molecular form. Mergers raised the molecular gas share, but unevenly across the galaxy. What drove stronger or weaker star formation, the fuel or the efficiency, changed with both radius and merger stage. Most of the time efficiency was the main driver. During the closest merging stage, though, the extra fuel took over.
arxiv-2509-22352:
Marie Brockschmidt, Maresa Schröder, and Stefan Feuerriegel present SurvDiff, a diffusion model that generates synthetic patient data for survival analysis. Survival analysis models time until an event, like relapse or death, and it is a cornerstone of clinical research. Its data are awkward to fake: many patients drop out or are lost to follow-up, so their event times are censored. A good synthetic set must reproduce both the event pattern and the censoring pattern. Their 2025 paper claims the first end-to-end diffusion model built for exactly this.

SurvDiff generates the patient covariates, of mixed types, together with event times and censoring indicators, in one process. Across several medical data sets, the synthetic data beat leading generative baselines on how closely it matched the real distribution, and on the scores of survival models trained or tested with it.
arxiv-2509-22452:
Andrea Rotnitzky, Ezequiel Smucler, and James M. Robins settle a conjecture about three ways to estimate the same quantity. The estimators are the one-step, outcome regression, and inverse weighting types. A recent paper showed the first two match exactly for a narrow class of parameters. That class has the mixed bias property, where errors in two nuisance parts can offset each other.

The note proves the match holds for the full, broader mixed bias class. It even allows one nuisance estimate to be nonlinear, not just a linear mix of features. The authors also link their result to older identities found by Robins and co-workers in 2007. Those links tie all three estimator types together.
arxiv-2509-22752:
Hikaru Wakaura solves the traveling salesman problem on far fewer qubits by naming each tour with a compact code. The standard one-hot encoding needs a qubit per city pair and penalty terms that swamp the cost. A Lehmer code labels each tour by a single number, needing only a logarithmic count of qubits and no penalties. Past variational solvers on this encoding stalled at six cities.

Wakaura trains a variational quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network with an exact gradient and a risk-based objective. Basin hopping restarts emerged as the key ingredient that clears the last local minima. The solver found the optimal tour on every test up to ten cities, on polygon and random graphs. One parameter set also generalized across time-dependent graphs.
arxiv-2509-22852:
O. A. Gelfond and M. A. Vasiliev make the nonlinear higher-spin equations in four dimensions respect Lorentz symmetry openly. Higher-spin gauge theory extends gravity to fields of arbitrary spin, set in anti-de Sitter space. Keeping local Lorentz covariance manifest through the calculations has been a persistent chore. Their construction extends the theory with a BRST operator tied to local Lorentz symmetry. BRST is the standard machinery for handling gauge redundancy in quantum field theory.

The setup works with any homotopy scheme for the perturbative analysis, including a recent differential homotopy. It also extends to a variety of richer higher-spin models. Those include versions in three dimensions and models with higher differential forms and Coxeter higher-spin algebras.
arxiv-2509-22952:
Shyam Sundar Ghoshal and John D Towers bound the error of a front tracking method for conservation laws. Their law has a flux that jumps at one point in space, the two-flux case. Front tracking follows each wave front in steps. They prove the error falls with a rate of one half or better.

The fluxes need only be smooth, not convex, monotone, or single-peaked. Only a finite count of flux crossings is assumed. When both fluxes rise or both fall, the rate improves to one. Equal fluxes also give rate one, matching classic results. Their proof uses a new route, not the standard Kuznetsov lemma.
arxiv-2509-23052:
The learning rate schedule can make or break neural network training. Matt L Sampson and Peter Melchior learn schedules from past runs instead of hand formulas. Their method treats training as a dynamical system with a latent state. From current metrics, it forecasts the schedule with the best long-term validation score. The learned schedules depart clearly from the best standard formulas.

Across image tasks and a transformer language task, the method beat all baselines tried. Models trained this way land in flatter loss regions, which aids generalization. The scheduler works with any optimizer. It can sit on top of common experiment tracking tools at low cost.
arxiv-2509-23152:
Picking the best sampled answer fails when the right answer is in the minority. Zhicheng Yang and 6 co-authors train verifiers that critique, not just score. Their Mirror-Critique framework contrasts model solutions with ground-truth ones. A small tuned model writes critique data that says what is wrong and why. Rejection sampling keeps that data high quality.

The critiques cold-start a reinforcement process that sharpens verification skill. At test time, the Mirror-Verifier writes several critiques per candidate. Their aggregate score drives weighted voting or abstention. Accuracy beat majority voting by a clear margin. The solver also grew more honest about its own limits.
arxiv-2509-23252:
Tiny, well-aimed training sets can beat bulk fine-tuning when two models fight to make them. Raviteja Anantha and 3 co-authors present NanoFlux, an adversarial data framework. One model attacks as question writer, and one defends. A tool-augmented judge supervises the duel. The output is multi-step questions with explanations that target set skills.

Under two hundred examples fine-tuned a four-billion-parameter model past full-benchmark training. Math, science, and medical reasoning all gained, with medical up sharply. Compute needs fell by a wide factor. Ablations show a sweet spot for question complexity per domain. Novelty filtering keeps the small set fresh.
arxiv-2509-23452:
A picture request can name where things stand from someone else's point of view, and image models often get that wrong. Tanawan Premsri and Parisa Kordjamshidi built FoR-SALE to fix such errors after a first draft image exists. Their system checks the draft against the text, reads the scene layout with vision modules, and maps the words to a camera view. One shared view then lets the system judge if words and image line up.

When they do not line up, the system plans edits and applies them, with new latent-space moves that turn objects or shift their depth. On three spatial test sets, one round of fixes raised top model scores by up to seven points.
arxiv-2509-23752:
Tiles that cover a lattice with no overlap raise a paired question: can they also serve as a spectrum for signals? Weiqi Zhou, the sole author, proves that any tile in a d-dimensional integer lattice whose size is a prime number must be spectral. The proof runs by contradiction. It shows that the tiling complement of such a tile cannot annihilate all p-subgroups, which forces the spectral property.

Zhou also adds a related result by a simple transformation. Any set of p points in general linear position in the lattice, when the dimension is at least p minus one, must be both tiling and spectral. The paper is short and purely theoretical.
arxiv-2509-23952:
Twisted bilayer photonic crystals promise flat bands and sharp resonances, but they need a theory that covers both near-field coupling and far-field response. Shupeng Xu and 2 co-authors build that general theory on a perturbation framework for non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. A universal form for interlayer coupling emerges, tied to Fourier transforms of the single-layer Wannier functions. At the K point of hexagonal lattices, the coupling reduces to the Bistritzer-MacDonald form known from graphene.

For a honeycomb slab with air holes, the theory predicts a fourfold band splitting in the far field, confirmed by simulation. The authors also propose a wide-angle, high-Q flat band cavity design.
arxiv-2509-24552:
Hybrid models that mix local sliding-window attention with a long-term memory beat either part alone, but the window size has a surprise in store. Loïc Cabannes and 8 co-authors study that interplay in a hybrid of window attention and a linear recurrent memory. Larger windows hurt long-context performance, they find, because the model leans on local attention and starves its long memory of training.

Short windows force the memory to learn, yet windows that are too small hurt even short tasks. Their fix trains with window sizes that change at random, so both stores get exercised. Hybrids trained that way beat fixed-window rivals on short and long problems alike.
arxiv-2509-24852:
Alexandre Queant, Ulysse Rançon, Benoit R Cottereau, and Timothée Masquelier teach recurrent spiking networks to learn their own signal delays. Their 2025 paper works with networks of artificial neurons that fire brief spikes, prized for low energy use. In brains, both connection strength and transmission delay adapt, and theory says delays add expressive power.

Until now, delay learning mostly covered one-way networks. Their method tunes delays in recurrent loops together with the weights, using a smooth approximation that gives usable gradients for fractional delays. On a chaotic series prediction task it beat all baselines. On four other time-based data sets it stayed competitive. Studying the trained networks shows delay tuning builds depth-dependent timing structure, echoing how real circuits organize signals in time.
arxiv-2509-24952:
Amandla Mabona and colleagues introduced a scoring fix for protein fragment identification in 2025. Mass spectrometry tools can read peptide sequences directly, without a reference database, which opens up less-charted parts of the proteome. The catch is trust: each tool reports its own confidence score, the scores are often poorly calibrated, and there is no principled way to estimate the false discovery rate.

Their framework, Winnow, works with any sequencing model. A small neural network converts raw scores into calibrated confidences using features of each match, then estimates error rates for single matches and for the whole experiment without decoy data. Both instant and dataset-tuned calibration are supported.
arxiv-2509-25852:
Zitong Bo and colleagues published a robotics paper in 2025 on teaching vision-language models to plan robot actions. Long tasks from spoken instructions remain hard for robots. Planners often fail because training data for multi-step plans is scarce. Rewards for good plans are also hard to define.

Their framework, REVER, trains a planner that reasons step by step. Demonstrations were captured with a hardware-independent recording setup. An automatic engine labeled each demonstration with instruction and plan. A verifiable reward scores plans by matching them against true skill sequences. Good ordering and coverage earn higher reward. The trained planner aims for plans that are physically plausible. It was released for real-world manipulation research.
arxiv-2509-26052:
Nikolaos Angelinos builds, in a 2025 paper, a model of three-dimensional quantum gravity out of the simplest kind of topological field theory. In his construction, the gravity path integral sums over every bulk shape whose boundary is a surface of a chosen genus. For the abelian theory he uses, each single shape prepares a stabilizer state, a tidy quantum state borrowed from error-correction theory.

The shapes sort into finitely many classes, each sharing one such state, and the classes further group into orbits under the surface's symmetry group. One orbit, the handlebodies, averages to a known vacuum series; the others add genuinely new topologies. The result can be rewritten as a weighted average of boundary theory partition functions, with a matrix of weights linking bulk and boundary. Angelinos shows those weights are fixed by the theory's allowed boundary conditions, and works the machinery through examples.
arxiv-2509-26452:
Turan, Moret, and Bardow build a tool that maps every nearly-best design of an energy system, not just the winner in this 2025 paper. Models leave out real-world concerns, so planners want the whole shelf of options within a small margin of optimal. Older search methods wander that shelf by heuristic and cannot say what they missed.

Their method leans on convexity to guarantee coverage. A new metric both measures how complete the map is and points where to explore next. Refinement stops at a chosen tolerance, after which any near-optimal design can be produced almost for free. On a coupled model of Switzerland's energy system, theirs was the only method that could promise full coverage. The heuristics, by contrast, skipped large regions entirely. The authors warn that missed regions mean real transition options never reach the table.
arxiv-2510-00052:
Mallick and colleagues test whether the sound of breathing alone can screen for sleep apnea. The disorder where breathing repeatedly pauses in sleep, without the expensive overnight laboratory study that is the current standard. Using 18 audio files from the MIT-BIH Polysomnographic Database, they convert respiratory sounds into spectrograms and train a ResNet-based convolutional network. Deliberately optimizing for recall first so that almost no true apnea event is missed.

Oversampling the rare apnea segments and applying class weights counter the dataset's imbalance, and the model reaches 90.55 percent recall for apnea detection. At the deliberate cost of low precision and 36.42 percent overall accuracy in the reported results. The authors position the system as a cheap, device-independent pre-screening tool for homes and basic clinics. Where a false alarm can be resolved by confirmatory testing but a missed case cannot.
arxiv-2510-00452:
Dalal Alharthi of the University of Arizona wrote this 2025 paper on automating cloud forensic investigations with AI. After a cloud attack, investigators comb logs by hand, a slow and error-prone process. The proposed framework, called CIAF, uses a language model guided by a formal rulebook of forensic terms. Inputs are cleaned and standardized first, so log entries get read consistently.

The framework was tested on Microsoft Azure logs containing ransomware-related events. Simulated attacks measured how much the framework improved detection over the baseline. Precision, recall, and F1 all landed near ninety-three percent in the reported experiment. The modular design should adapt to other attack types beyond ransomware, the author argues. Standardized inputs also make findings easier to reproduce and defend later. The paper presents the framework as a foundation for AI-driven forensic workflows across cloud platforms.
arxiv-2510-00652:
Ouyang, Xiang, Wang, and Ding at Huawei's Singapore research centre present OTTER in this 2025 arXiv paper on multimodal tagging. Organizing personal and enterprise media needs labels, but a fixed category list cannot capture everything users care about, while fully free tagging drifts into inconsistency. OTTER unifies both worlds, pairing a curated taxonomy with an open layer of user-driven tags. The team built a large hierarchically organized dataset of images and text, labelled by vision-language models and refined by humans.

A multi-head attention architecture aligns visual and textual inputs with embeddings for both fixed and open-set labels. On two benchmarks, OTTER reached overall F1 scores of 0.81 and 0.75, ahead of the next-best systems. Its open-set tagging was near perfect, while predefined label quality stayed competitive with closed-set rivals.
arxiv-2510-00852:
Sotudeh and three co-authors test the Hadrosymmetric Twin Higgs model against cosmological data in this 2025 arXiv paper. Twin Higgs models solve the little hierarchy problem by adding a twin sector whose particles are neutral under ordinary forces. Unlike the mirror version, the hadrosymmetric variant copies only the quarks into the twin sector, adding no light twin photons or neutrinos. That restraint keeps it clear of limits on extra relativistic species, and colliders can barely see it.

The team implemented the sector in the CLASS code and fitted it with Markov Chain Monte Carlo runs. Against Planck cosmic microwave background data plus local Hubble measurements, the Hubble tension fell from over four sigma to about two and a half sigma. The matter clustering discrepancy eased at the same time. The authors argue cosmology may be the sharpest probe of this deliberately elusive model.
arxiv-2510-00952:
Farhadipour and six colleagues from the University of Zurich describe their team's entries to the NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluation of 2024 in this 2025 arXiv report. Speaker recognition systems decide whether two recordings share one speaker, a task that degrades with short clips, language mismatch, and poor audio. The Zurich team, called CL-UZH, entered both the fixed and open conditions of the challenge.

For fixed-condition audio trials they used an X-vector system built with the Kaldi toolkit, trained from scratch on the CTS superset data. Face recognition with FaceNet supplied the visual side for audio-visual and visual-only trials. For the open condition they submitted models pretrained on the large VoxBlink2 and VoxCeleb2 datasets. The report compares development and evaluation performance across these systems and conditions for other challenge participants.
arxiv-2510-01052:
Mahdipour Aghabagher and Momtazi at Amirkabir University of Technology build a hybrid dialogue state tracker for Persian chatbots, in this paper published in Computer Speech and Language. Dialogue state tracking keeps a running record of what a user wants during a multi-turn conversation. Pure rule-based trackers cannot adapt to free, human-like exchanges, which hurts languages with fewer ready-made tools. Persian is one such language, and the authors target it directly.

Their system combines rules with several learned parts, including BERT for slot filling and intent detection, XGBoost for intent validation, and a GPT model for state tracking itself. Online agents generate answers in real time on top of that state. Evaluated on a broad Persian multi-turn dialogue dataset, the hybrid clearly improved accuracy and coherence over existing Persian methods. The authors credit the mix of structure and learned flexibility.
arxiv-2510-01252:
Mahran and Simbeck trace how a language model's training books quietly become its social assumptions. Models absorb patterns from massive corpora, but evaluations rarely connect outputs back to sources. Sparse autoencoders offer a lens, splitting dense activations into readable features.

As a controlled case, the team trained a small GPT-style model on nineteenth-century novels by women. Features were probed against eleven social and moral categories. Gender and kinship formed a stable backbone, with associations entangling deeper in the network. The pipeline generalizes into an audit tool for any corpus's cultural fingerprint. Thirty-seven novels by ten authors form the deliberately narrow corpus. Marriage, class, and morality join gender among the probed themes. Depth entangles associations that early layers keep separate. Stable backbones suggest some themes organize the whole representation. Auditing data through models beats auditing outputs alone every time.
arxiv-2510-01352:
Blower and Malham solve the full noncommutative version of a classic hierarchy of wave equations. The KP hierarchy describes shallow-water and plasma waves through infinitely many coupled equations. Replacing ordinary multiplication with noncommutative operations produces a far harder system.

A linear integral equation carries the solution, with scattering data obeying the linearized hierarchy. Two routes confirm the match, one through classical dressing transformations. The second runs through an exotic nonassociative algebra tied to descent algebras of permutations. Working inside that stranger algebra, the final identity lands back in the ordinary associative world. Direct linearisation is the strategy that tames the infinite system. Gelfand-Levitan-Marchenko is the integral equation at the method's core. Semi-additive scattering data unlock the direct substitution route. Grafting products give the descent algebra its unusual multiplication. Completeness is the claim, the whole hierarchy at once.
arxiv-2510-01552:
Tang and co-authors automate the ranking of cyber threats with a language-model pipeline called Polar. Over eleven thousand new vulnerabilities appeared in a single recent year, far more than analysts can grade by hand. Older scoring tools miss context and drift as attacker behavior shifts.

Polar works in four stages, from triage through static and exploitation analysis to mitigation advice. It turns messy threat reports into structured severity scores and forecasts of exploitation chances. Evaluations on real-world threats showed better ranking accuracy than prior approaches. The explanations it writes also help analysts decide, rather than merely trust, each ranking. Structured outputs plug into existing ticketing and patch queues without reformatting. Disclosure details and standard attack mappings drove much of the accuracy gain. Hallucinations appeared in predictable spots and yielded to simple validation rules. Prioritization decides what gets patched tonight.
arxiv-2510-01852:
Ironmonger and Ruškuc build a general decision framework for pattern-avoidance questions in this 2025 combinatorics paper. They order structures by consecutive embedding, where neighbors in a small structure must stay neighbors in the larger one. An avoidance set collects all structures that dodge a finite list of forbidden patterns. Two questions matter: whether such a set is well quasi-ordered, and whether it is atomic.

Well quasi-ordering rules out infinite families of mutually incomparable structures. Atomicity asks whether the set splits into two strictly smaller avoidance sets. The authors extend recent methods into one framework that settles both questions at once. It applies across a wide range of structure types. Graphs, directed graphs, and collections of relations all fall inside its scope. The result turns case-by-case arguments into a reusable machine for consecutive orders.
arxiv-2510-01952:
Llosa Isenrich, Schesler, and Wu build simple groups with carefully prescribed finiteness behavior in this 2025 group theory paper. Finiteness properties grade how close a group comes to having a finite classifying space. Exotic examples separate those grades one rung at a time. Simple groups, which admit no proper normal subgroups, rarely cooperate with such fine control.

Starting from any finitely generated linear group over the rationals, they construct a simple group sharing its finiteness properties. The original group even sits inside the new one as a quasi-retract. One application is a simple group of type FP-infinity that is nevertheless not finitely presented. For every n, they also produce a simple group of type FP-n that is neither finitely presented nor of type FP-(n+1). The constructions arise as Röver-Nekrashevych groups. They answer a standing question of Zaremsky about what finiteness patterns simple groups can realize.
arxiv-2510-02052:
Bajnoková and eight co-authors catch a solar flare warming up minutes before it erupts in this 2025 astronomy paper. The event was a modest C1-class flare in September 2022. Geometry helped: the NuSTAR telescope saw it hidden behind the solar limb, while the STIX instrument viewed it face-on. That pairing let the team study faint coronal emission without the flare's glare.

NuSTAR detected nonthermal emission and plasma heated above ten million kelvin starting seven minutes before the flare. The signal implies electrons were already accelerating continuously in the corona during that quiet onset. Matching type III radio bursts from a ground array supported the same story. Model parameters stayed steady through the onset, pointing to one persistent process. STIX spectra of the main flare showed similar electron distributions with a higher low-energy cutoff. The onset may therefore be an early fingerprint of the flare's own acceleration engine.
arxiv-2510-02252:
Araújo, Ze, Xu, Wu, and Liu show that retargeting quality decides humanoid tracking success in this 2025 robotics paper. Humanoid robots learn to move by copying human motion mapped onto their bodies. That mapping leaves artifacts: sliding feet, self-penetration, and impossible poses. Learning policies then burn effort correcting bad references, amid heavy reward tuning.

The authors suppress that extra tuning and measure retargeting quality directly. Cleaner reference paths yield better tracking policies under the same learning setup. Sloppy retargeting caps what the policy can achieve, regardless of training time. The results reorder priorities for teleoperation pipelines. Effort belongs upstream, in the mapping stage, not in compensating rewards. Teams building humanoid datasets now have evidence for investing in conversion quality first.
arxiv-2510-02552:
Cruz-Garcia and co-authors simulate how cooling shapes eerily even patterns in superconductors. Their 2025 physics paper studies hyperuniform vortex arrangements. Hyperuniform matter suppresses density wobbles at large scales. Superconductor vortices can settle into that hidden order. Experiments saw finite size and disorder disturb the pattern. The team models vortices as layered elastic lines in three dimensions. Their cooling protocol mimics the real laboratory procedure. Slow cooling from liquid to solid mirrors the experiments. Finite thickness limits the even pattern in equilibrium already.

Cooling dynamics add a second, stronger limitation. Which effect dominates depends on cooling rate and thickness. Disorder slows the long waves that would heal the pattern. The results map a realistic route to synthetic hyperuniform materials. Host media thickness must enter design calculations early. Interpreting vortex images also becomes safer with this frame. Hidden order is fragile in specific, predictable ways.
arxiv-2510-02852:
Akbari-Moghaddam and co-authors rethink bed planning for intensive care units. Hospitals must guess future demand under deep uncertainty. Babies and patients arrive at uneven rates. Stays vary widely by case and by site. A common rule keeps average use under eighty-five percent. The authors show it can mislead planners badly. Units can meet the average target yet overflow on many days.
