arxiv-2602-00352: Li Siyan and team introduce DETOUR, an interactive benchmark for dual agent search and reasoning. Recalling information in conversation often takes multiple turns, yet existing benchmarks for tip of the tongue search cover only single turn settings. A Primary Agent, the subject of evaluation, identifies the recollected entity by querying a Memory Agent held consistent across evaluations. Results show leading models still struggle, reaching only 36 percent accuracy across all modalities, text, image, audio, and video, underlining the need for stronger underspecified search abilities.
arxiv-2602-00452: X. Z. Zhang presents a minimal dissipation plan for the particle-hole Hubbard model, asking whether superconducting order can form as an attractor of open dynamics. By applying a rotated jump operator, a local eta-pair operator, on one site, Lindblad evolution drives the system from the vacuum into a steady state. That state exhibits large scale eta-pair long-range order. A single local seed establishes long range order across the lattice, unlike extensive reservoirs. The mechanism rests on dark state selection and removal of excursions from hopping.
arxiv-2602-00552: V. V. Glinskiy and colleagues present a drift-kinetic PIC model for plasma confinement in mirror traps. The one-dimensional two-velocity electrostatic model extends a semi-implicit PIC method with energy and charge conservation to collisional plasma and floating-potential walls. Coulomb tests match theory, and the model reproduces the ambipolar potential profile to the walls and the near-wall jump despite grid steps. It matches Debye sheath theory and the Bohm criterion, while electron kinetics in expanders shifts temperature, potential, and density by about 15% against MIDAS.
arxiv-2602-00652: Kyung Yun Lee and colleagues present RIRFlow, a training-free Bayesian method for room impulse response problems like denoising and deconvolution, where learned priors need large data sets and generalise poorly. They derive an analytic prior from impulse-response statistics, modelling them as a Gaussian process whose variance decays exponentially. This yields a closed-form Wiener denoiser for minimum mean squared error. That denoiser serves as the prior inside a flow-based inverse solver using guided posterior sampling, extended to nonlinear cases by a local Gaussian approximation.
arxiv-2602-00952: Jing Wang and colleagues treat fine-tuning under a tight label budget as a game between learner and task setter. The learner, acting first, commits to a scoring rule and a plan for asking for labels, while the task set then picks hard cases in reply. Their method works with full feedback and keeps a finite label budget inside the learning goal. A Largest-Latency-First gate then screens which labels to ask for, keeping spend inside the budget. The result adapts large language models with few labels.
arxiv-2602-01152: Zhuolin Du and Yisheng Song build a memory-slope plan for extreme M-values of elastic-type tensors. Such values steer work on springy matter and quantum tie-ups. The team first turns the value hunt into a chain of free-form tune tasks with a shift knob. A memory-slope plan then chases those extreme values, with a proof of global convergence. Broad number tests back the plan's power and steadiness.
arxiv-2602-01352: Xingzu Zhan and co-authors build T2M Mamba, a text-to-motion plan tying beat and keyframe weight together. Past motion plans treat beat and keyframe weight apart, drifting on long runs, and crumble when rewordings shift text vectors. Their beat-salience Mamba gauges keyframe weights via boosted density-peak grouping and FFT-sped self-match, catching linked motion cheaply. A periodic align module then firms text-motion links. Tests on HumanML3D and KIT-ML confirm gains, with an FID of 0.068 and lifts elsewhere.
arxiv-2602-01652: Takeshi Fukumoto and colleagues roll spheres down a granular slope, varying speed, slope angle and sphere density, to map friction in a roll. Spheres sink into the bed while slowing at a constant rate, and sinking depth relative to radius scales with density relative to bulk density. To price energy loss they define a friction coefficient, which falls as slope angle and slip ratio rise. Tests across densities show that coefficient grows linearly with normalized depth, with a base term falling with slip ratio and a near constant slope.
arxiv-2602-01752: Yidan Wang and colleagues embed several bits in language model text, extending zero bit schemes beyond mere spotting. Methods extend zero bit schemes with fixed logit shifts and counting reads, which degrade text quality and read robustness at larger payloads. Their WorldCup framework models sampling as a structured channel, embedding bits through layered contests. Entropy aware tuning preserves quality, and confidence aware reads using token scores enable message recovery. Tests show a balance across capacity, robustness and quality, beating baselines and offering a base for future marking.
arxiv-2602-01852: Zeyan Wang and colleagues remove client data from a federated model, tackling utility and leak risks. Multi client erasure adds gradient conflicts that degrade forgetting, so their FUPareto framework uses Pareto optimization. An MBS loss pushes the target logit under the best non target logit, improving efficiency and cutting inference risk. Pareto gains keep utility, Pareto expansion guarantees forgetting, and a null space projected gradient method decouples client gradient conflicts. Tests show it beats federated unlearning methods on both efficacy and retained utility.
arxiv-2602-01952: Wenjia Jiang and colleagues build SQLAgent, a two stage framework mapping a database before generating SQL. Existing methods fail in complex settings because SQL reasoning needs familiarity with schemas, semantics and join paths. Exploration uses a Monte Carlo Tree Search strategy over the schema to build a database knowledge base, generating schema fragments, queries and natural language descriptions. Deployment uses a dual agent system to retrieve information and generate SQL queries from user questions, using collected knowledge as examples. Benchmark tests show accuracy well above strong baselines.
arxiv-2602-02252: The CMS team reports a family of all-charm tetraquarks emerging from the double J/psi mass spectrum. A clearer picture comes from proton-proton collision data of 315 inverse femtobarns, yielding far more double J/psi pairs than previous CMS studies. All three structures, with their interference, exceed five standard deviations. Interference implies common quantum numbers, squared masses line up linearly with a resonance index, and natural widths decrease with index. These features fit radial excitations of tetraquarks built from two diquarks with spin 1 and no orbital excitation, disfavoring interpretations.
arxiv-2602-02352: Petr Jancar and colleagues revisit well-formed free-choice Petri nets, a field established in the 1970s by Commoner and Hack. The authors give a new characterization by introducing semi-T-components, dual to semi-S-components, which correspond to minimal siphons. Highlighting the symmetry between the dual concepts, they derive classical coverability results for T- and S-components. They also derive the duality theorem: a free-choice net is well-formed exactly when its reverse-dual is also well-formed, all through highly symmetric arguments.
arxiv-2602-02652:
Writing in 2026, Neel Kolhe and 7 co-authors examine how ram pressure distorts the rotation of WLM, an isolated dwarf irregular galaxy. WLM has avoided major interactions for eight billion years, yet it is losing gas to pressure from the surrounding intergalactic medium, like wind stripping a moving car. That same pressure should perturb the gas kinematics, especially at the outskirts.

The observations confirm an asymmetric rotation curve between the approaching and receding sides. The galaxy decomposes into two components. A compact inner part rotates like a solid body, resembling a bar, and is barely affected by ram pressure. An extended disk, marked by a double-horn profile, has its dynamics considerably reshaped. The lesson is methodological: mass estimates for such dwarfs must model both components and the asymmetry, or the numbers will mislead.
arxiv-2602-02752:
Srinath Srinivasan and 1 co-author compare four ways of feeding domain knowledge so language models can warm-start high-dimensional software engineering tuning, posted to arXiv in 2026. Models do well on tuning problems with few features but lose to Bayesian methods when the dimension count grows. Whether structured knowledge can bridge that gap was unclear.

Four architectures are tested on data sets stratified by dimensionality. Human-in-the-loop prompting uses delayed expert feedback. Adaptive multi-stage prompting finds and validates constraints sequentially. Dimension-aware refinement tunes in progressively expanding feature subspaces. A hybrid approach mixes statistical scouting with retrieval-boosted prompting. Performance is measured by Chebyshev distance to known optima and ranked with Scott-Knott clustering against a known rival for model-generated warm starts. The study pits human-supplied knowledge against machine-generated knowledge head-on, asking which source helps a model start closer to the optimum.
arxiv-2602-02952:
Transformers that know when they are unsure are the goal of Elias Hossain and 6 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Language models are often overconfident, assigning high certainty to wrong answers. Adjusting output probabilities after the fact leaves the internal computation unchanged, while ensembles cost much more training and storage.

Their framework, UAT-LITE, injects uncertainty directly into self-attention at inference time. Monte Carlo dropout creates varied forward passes, and the spread estimates token-level uncertainty. That signal then modulates attention without changing pretrained weights. A layer-wise analysis tracks how uncertainty builds with depth. Across question answering and classification benchmarks, calibration error fell by about a fifth while accuracy held.
arxiv-2602-03052:
Hybrid classic-quantum models trained across many clients are stabilized by Yueheng Wang and 6 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Federated learning trains collaboratively without centralizing private data. Adding quantum parts could ease computation and communication burdens. Uneven data across clients, called non-IID data, still degrades results badly in hybrid settings where spreads differ sharply between sites.

Their system, FEDCOMPASS, groups clients by class spread similarity using spectral clustering. Classic trait extractors are aggregated within each cluster. Quantum settings use circular mean aggregation with changing tuning for stable updates. Tests on three benchmark datasets followed. Score improved by up to about ten percent over strong federated earlier methods, and settling stayed more stable under non-IID cases.
arxiv-2602-03152:
Long inputs exhaust language model memory, and Yifei Wang heads a team of 8 other researchers with a frequency-based fix. The key-value cache grows with input length and bottlenecks deployment. Token pruning keeps only a critical subset, but static choices risk irreversible loss while dynamic heuristics miss how importance depends on the query being answered for each new request.

Their framework, FASA, predicts token importance in a query-aware way. The key insight concerns rotary position embeddings, where a few dominant frequency chunks agree strongly with full attention behavior. Those chunks identify critical tokens cheaply, and focused attention runs only on them. Across long-context tasks, FASA beat token-eviction baselines and neared oracle accuracy. It kept near-full performance while retaining only a small cache fraction.
arxiv-2602-03252:
Yury Bliokh's solo analysis examines when waves push particles and when they pull them. Ponderomotive forces act on small particles inside propagating wave packets, or pulses. Bliokh considers simple point particles plus composite dipole and dumbbell particles. The fields are forward-propagating packets, where phase and group velocities align, and backward-propagating ones, where they oppose, changing how momentum transfers to a particle in each case.

Depending on the packet's characteristics, particles may be pushed away from the source or pulled toward it. Dynamics in a beat wave, formed by two forward waves with slightly different frequencies, are also examined. Such a beat wave emulates a periodic sequence of forward or backward pulses. That provides a simple mechanism for pulling forces, as used in optical and acoustic tractor beams.
arxiv-2602-03552:
G. G. Motorina and 4 co-authors examine millimeter radio emission lingering after a solar flare's main burst. Their 2026 paper studies the M5.7 flare of May 4, 2022. It was observed at 93 gigahertz by a radio telescope at Bauman Moscow State Technical University. The later phase is less well known than the explosive start of a flare.

The team compares the radio signal with extreme ultraviolet emission and with temperature and emission-measure data from two space missions. The enhanced emission rises together with the ultraviolet signal, tying it to moderately hot plasma near a million degrees. Their emission-measure calculations pin down the plasma parameters. They conclude that thin coronal plasma that light passes through supplies roughly a fifth of the millimeter signal.
arxiv-2602-03752:
Tiny printed lenses lose precious light to reflections at their surface, a serious tax for faint astronomical signals. Ishan Rana and 3 co-authors coat microlenses with grass-like alumina to stop those losses in a 2026 paper. The lenses are printed by two-photon polymerization in a new resin, IPX-Clear, prized for visible-light work.

The coating is a forest of nanoscale alumina blades grown by atomic layer deposition. It eases the refractive index gradually from air to bulk resin, which is nearly the ideal antireflection condition. On glass such coatings already lift transmission dramatically. Here, coated microlenses lose only about three tenths of a percent of photons to reflection across the visible band. The authors outline wider-band tests and protective overcoats as next steps.
arxiv-2602-03852:
Graduate students under strain rarely queue for counseling, but a therapy chatbot is always awake. Chan-in Sio and 4 co-authors interview ten Chinese postgraduates about AI-powered cognitive behavioral therapy chatbots in a 2026 qualitative study. Little was known about how this population perceives such tools, which promise low-barrier mental health support.

Semi-structured interviews, analyzed thematically, show students are cautiously open to the tools. Round-the-clock access and perceived usefulness encourage adoption. Privacy worries, emotional safety concerns, and doubt that a chatbot fits complex problems hold students back. Stigma, peer views, digital literacy, and language quality also shape intentions. The authors turn the findings into design guidance on transparency, safeguards, and step-by-step care pathways for deployment that respects local culture.
arxiv-2602-04252:
Labeling every image in every new class batch wastes most of the effort. Aditya R. Bhattacharya and 2 co-authors combine active learning with class incremental learning in a 2026 paper. Continual learning systems meet classes episode by episode and cannot revisit old data, yet standard setups assume full annotation of each episode anyway.

Their ACIL framework selects only the samples worth labeling, using active learning criteria tuned to the incremental setting. Most samples in an episode would never be seen again, so labeling them buys little. Choosing salient examples cuts annotation cost while fighting catastrophic forgetting. The pairing targets real deployments, where classes arrive over time and labelers are scarce.
arxiv-2602-04352:
Splitting a model into fragments can beat shipping it whole. Sayan Biswas and 9 co-authors introduce Mosaic Learning for decentralized training without a central server in a 2026 paper. Devices each hold pieces of the model and spread fragments independently across the network.

Fragmentation cuts redundant communication among correlated parameters and diversifies how information propagates, at no extra communication cost. Theory gives state-of-the-art worst-case convergence and shows parameter correlation speeds contraction. Across four tasks, node-level accuracy beat a leading epidemic learning baseline by up to twelve points. The framework suits collaborations where data cannot be centrally hosted, from hospitals to phone fleets.
arxiv-2602-04552:
Hao Xu extends a basic law of thermodynamics in a 2026 paper on Landauer's principle. The principle links erasing information to a minimum heat cost. It seemed to fail when a heat reservoir is replaced by a squeezed thermal state, which carries extra usable resources.

Xu defines an effective Hamiltonian, an energy description adapted to the transformed reservoir. With it, he proves a generalized inequality that reduces to the classic principle for ordinary reservoirs. The framework also defines entropy production and proves it cannot be negative. An example detector moving through a quantum field confirms positivity by direct calculation. The result gives a tool for quantum thermodynamics in unusual settings.
arxiv-2602-04652:
Ryan Barker and 5 co-authors measure how graphics processors speed up a key 5G decoding task in a 2026 paper on edge communications for vehicles. Roadside units must decode signals within strict timing limits while also hosting other services.

The workload is LDPC decoding, an iterative error-correction step whose cost grows with parallelism and iteration count. The team built a reproducible benchmark with telemetry from an existing 5G baseline. They varied processor types, batch sizes, and iteration counts. Offloading to graphics processors raised throughput greatly and cut average decode time. That freed the central processor and left spare computing margin. The findings support GPU-equipped compact base stations for dense vehicular workloads.
arxiv-2602-04752:
Andrew Lee and 3 co-authors open up transformer attention in a 2026 paper on query-key interplay. Attention decides which tokens a model looks at, but why one token wins has lacked good tools for explanation.

The authors study the joint space formed by queries and keys, the two vectors whose match yields attention scores. Their contrastive covariance method splits that space into low-rank parts that humans can read. High attention arises when query and key traits align inside those parts. After tests in theory and simplified settings, they apply the method to large language models. It found readable subspaces for semantic groups and binding traits. Attention scores could then be credited to specific traits.
arxiv-2602-05052:
Solving partial differential equations the usual way means building large sparse matrices, a step that can eat most of the compute cost. Shizheng Wen and 7 co-authors attack that snag in this 2026 paper with TensorGalerkin, a toolkit built on the Galerkin method. Their design splits assembly into a map stage over mesh parts and a reduction done by sparse matrix multiplication.

Both stages live inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation, so the assembly graph keeps a fixed count of nodes no matter how big the mesh grows. That trait lets one engine serve three jobs: fast numerical solving, end-to-end differentiable tuning under PDE limits, and physics-informed operator learning. Tests on two- and three-dimensional tasks, covering elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic cases on messy meshes, showed clear gains in speed and accuracy over a range of rivals.
arxiv-2602-05152:
Retrieval systems learn from each query and then forget the lesson, recomputing the same expansions forever. Yuntong Hu and 3 co-authors propose Evolving Retrieval Memory in this 2026 information retrieval paper, a training-free framework that banks query-time gains into the index itself. Query expansion works, but stateless systems pay for it on every single request.

The method updates document keys using feedback that is gated on correctness, credits each expansion signal to the keys it actually helped, and keeps updates bounded so the index stays stable. The authors prove query and key expansion are equivalent under standard similarity scores, and that their selective updates converge, effectively baking the best expansion into the index with zero added inference cost. Across 13 domains in the BEIR and BRIGHT benchmarks, retrieval and generation both improved, most on reasoning-heavy tasks, at native retrieval speed.
arxiv-2602-05352:
Neural networks that learn physics on curved surfaces work with meshes and graph convolutions, and those convolutions have a smoothing habit. Edward Berman and 3 co-authors study that habit in this 2026 machine learning paper, presented in its ICML 2026 camera-ready form. A known fix, unitary convolutions, preserves features exactly by construction, but the authors question whether preservation is what physics wants.

For diffusion-like processes, smoothness naturally grows over time, so a convolution forbidden from smoothing is overconstrained. The authors prove unitary convolutions hurt on such dynamics tasks, then propose relaxed unitary convolutions that balance preservation against the smoothing a system physically needs. Both versions are generalized from graphs to meshes. On heat and wave equations over complex meshes, and on weather forecasting, the relaxed method beat strong baselines including mesh-aware transformers and equivariant networks.
arxiv-2602-05552:
Flying a drone indoors by spoken instruction, with no GPS to lean on, is the goal of VLN-Pilot, a framework by Bessie Dominguez-Dager, Sergio Suescun-Ferrandiz, and 3 co-authors. A large vision-language model acts as the pilot, reading free-form commands and grounding them in what the drone sees. The system plans and adjusts flight paths on its own, reacting to obstacles and surprises along the way.

Unlike rule-based planners, the approach uses semantic understanding to pick context-aware behaviors with little task-specific engineering. Tests run in a custom photorealistic indoor simulator built by the team. The agent scored high success rates on complex tasks, including long routes with several semantic targets in sequence. The authors argue that language-guided pilots could cut operator workload for jobs like inspection, search and rescue, and facility checks.
arxiv-2602-05852:
Finding communities in a network gets easier when nodes carry extra data, such as labels or attributes. Amir Asadi, Akbar Davoodi, Ramin Javadi, and Farzad Parvaresh find the exact point where recovery becomes possible. Their setting is the Data Block Model, a stochastic block model augmented with node associated data. The question is exact recovery: naming every node true community with high probability.

The authors introduce a new divergence measure, the Chernoff TV divergence, and use it to characterize a sharp threshold for exact recovery. They give an efficient algorithm that achieves the threshold, plus a matching converse showing recovery is impossible below it. Simulations confirm the theory and show the benefit of vertex data as side information. It speaks to practitioners in social and biological networks, where side data is common but its value was unquantified.
arxiv-2602-06252:
Matrix multiplication dominates the cost of running large language models, especially ones squeezed to very few bits per weight. Ahmed J Abdelmaksoud and 3 co-authors propose D-Legion, a many-core chip design built for exactly that work. Its cores are systolic arrays, grids that pass data rhythmically, and they adjust their precision to the numbers at hand.

Cores group into Legions that handle dense and sparse quantized multiplication in several modes. Partial sums are accumulated in parallel to cut memory traffic, and matrix tiles are broadcast across Legions to reuse data. A design sweep picked the best grouping. On attention workloads from two tiny-bit models, latency and memory use fell sharply.
arxiv-2602-06452:
Fake faces made by modern generators are so clean that detectors based on texture or frequency traces fail. Hongyan Fei and 4 co-authors look instead at specular reflection, the sharp highlight component of light on skin. In the Phong lighting model, that component depends on many parameters in a nonlinear way, making it the hardest part to fake faithfully.

Their method first separates the specular layer from face texture using a Retinex-based estimation. Clues then live both in the reflection itself and in how it relates to texture and direct light. A detection network with two-stage cross-attention reads those relationships. The authors aim for detection that generalizes to entirely synthetic faces, not just edited ones.
arxiv-2602-06552:
Combining several fine-tuned models into one versatile model avoids retraining, but current merging methods treat each model as an indivisible block. Haiyun Qiu and 3 co-authors present MERGE, a method that merges at the component level instead. Attention layers and feed-forward layers, they note, merge differently and tolerate merging differently.

MERGE formulates component-wise merging as a two-goal optimization balancing cross-task performance against storage cost. A surrogate-assisted evolutionary search finds the Pareto-optimal configurations, the trade-offs where neither goal can improve without hurting the other. Good configurations can be reused, and modules can be recombined on demand for a given input. The design restores efficient batch inference that instance-specific merging had sacrificed.
arxiv-2602-06652:
A vision-language model can give the same answer twice while its inner picture of the input has shifted a lot. Farooq Ahmad Wani and eight co-authors argue that standard robustness checks miss this. Their framework tracks drift in the model's inner states, how it reacts to changes at fine and coarse scales, and how smooth its vision tokens stay, next to the usual answer-based scores.

Applied to modern models on three public benchmarks, the checks reveal a clear pattern. Small changes like text overlaid on an image can push the inner state as far as a wholly different image would, even when the final answer stays put. Bigger models scored higher but were no steadier, and some changes even cut false alarms by making models more cautious. The authors say answer stability alone is weak evidence of real robustness.
arxiv-2602-06852:
Jonathan Pan built a tool for tracing how chatbots recall facts, layer by layer. Inside a model, a few true signals hide in a thick mix of noisy, shared signals, so it is hard to say which parts do the recall work. His Quantum Sieve Tracer starts with old-style causal tracing to find key layers, then maps head signals into a vast quantum space for a sharper look.

Tests on two open models, a small Meta model and a small Alibaba model, gave a split result. One model's seventh layer acted as a plain recall hub, while the other's ninth layer held recall back, so cutting its heads oddly made recall better. The work shows quantum kernels can tell a build-up part from a hold-back part, giving a fine map of attention.
arxiv-2602-06952:
Manan Agarwal and seven co-authors map the shocked plasma of Cassiopeia A, the youngest known Galactic core-collapse supernova remnant, with the XRISM X-ray observatory. Understanding a remnant's plasma conditions reveals its explosion mechanism, ejecta structure, and large-scale asymmetries. The team used more than 350 kiloseconds of high-resolution microcalorimeter data, producing the first plasma parameter maps of any supernova remnant from such an instrument.

They divided the remnant into one-arcminute squares and fit each spectrum with two pure-metal ejecta components, intermediate-mass and iron-group elements, plus nonthermal synchrotron radiation. A new Bayesian framework, UltraSPEX, yielded full posterior distributions and exposed parameter degeneracies. Findings include enriched argon and calcium ratios near the silicon jets, a high nickel-to-iron ratio at the northeast jet base, and faster, broader iron-group ejecta, consistent with strongly clumped ejecta models.
arxiv-2602-07352:
Singly ionized ytterbium already serves quantum information and searches for new physics, and narrower transitions would sharpen both.  Patrick McMillin and three co-authors report three semi-forbidden transitions from the metastable state of Yb+, with sub-hertz widths owed to the long lifetimes of the states involved.

They measure absolute frequencies, isotope shifts, hyperfine structure, and quadrupole transition moments. They find spontaneous lifetimes limited by slow magnetic dipole emission to lower odd-parity states, one of which looks like an attractive long-lived qubit host.  Atomic experts get new precision lines and a candidate qubit hiding in the decay path.
arxiv-2602-07452:
Simulating plasma around black holes needs a particle-in-cell code that stays regular at the event horizon.  Claudio Meringolo and one co-author present FPIC, a general-relativistic particle-in-cell method written in Fortran with MPI parallelism for fields and particles.

Spherical Kerr-Schild coordinates encode the problem's topology while remaining regular at the horizon, and a finite-difference time-domain Maxwell solver with leapfrog stepping evolves the fields.  Several particle pushers are implemented, plus a novel hybrid that switches scheme based on Hamiltonian energy violation.  Astrophysical plasma teams get a documented, horizon-safe code for stationary axisymmetric black hole spacetimes.
arxiv-2602-07552: Helly-type theorems say when a family of sets must share a common point, and their topological versions replace convexity with homological rules.  Pavel Paták and one co-author survey recent advances in that topological setting. They compare two proof strategies side by side: arguments built on the nerve lemma and arguments built on non-embeddability.  The overview is concise and technical, aimed at readers who want the current state of topological Helly theory and the tools driving it.
arxiv-2602-07752:
Polymer solutions are often modeled as elastic dumbbells, but simulating their full distribution is costly because the equations live in high dimensions and blow up at the boundary. Runkai Feng and two co-authors develop two fast spectral methods for the spatially homogeneous FENE model that handle that singularity cleanly.

Their Jacobi spherical-harmonic schemes use weighted formulations to resolve the boundary behavior, march in time with a stable second-order method, and reduce to sparse linear systems that solve efficiently. Numerical tests confirm spectral convergence, and the solvers provide trustworthy reference solutions for benchmarks. Researchers modeling complex fluids gain both a tool and a yardstick for cheaper closure approximations.
arxiv-2602-07852:
Fine-tuning language models on narrowly harmful data can make them broadly misaligned, answering unrelated prompts in stereotypically evil ways, a surprise that expert surveys failed to predict. Anna Soligo and three co-authors investigate why emergent misalignment arises, using it as a window into how models generalize.

They find models can learn just the narrow task, but the general misaligned solution is more stable, more efficient, and more influential in pretraining data. They trace both narrow and general solutions to linear representations in the model. Comparing those representations shows general misalignment achieves lower loss and greater robustness. The paper deepens our grasp of a safety-relevant inductive bias in large models.
arxiv-2602-07952:
Quantum chaos shows up in how operators grow and spread, and the Brownian spin SYK model offers a tractable laboratory for that growth. Tingfei Li and two co-authors study the full distribution of operator sizes, not just its average, for Hamiltonians with interactions of order two up to L.

They derive a closed master equation for the Pauli-string coefficients and recast it through generating functions, diagonalizing the leading evolution operator exactly for arbitrary initial distributions, including decoherence effects. A systematic expansion in inverse system size then captures higher-order corrections to scrambling and late-time behavior. The work shows those corrections matter, and that the whole size distribution probes chaos more finely than averages alone.
arxiv-2602-08052:
Factory scheduling with unrelated parallel machines, release dates, setups, and eligibility rules must balance late jobs against setup time, a multi-objective puzzle that defeats simple rules. Bulent Soykan and three co-authors propose a deep reinforcement learning method pairing proximal policy tuning with a graph neural network that represents jobs, machines, and setups.

Guided by a multi-objective reward, the agent learns a direct scheduling policy minimizing total weighted tardiness and total setup time as one. On benchmark instances it beats both a standard dispatching rule and a metaheuristic, achieving a better trade-off between objectives. Manufacturing teams gain a scalable scheduler for the messy, constrained problems that real plants actually face.
arxiv-2602-08252:
As split and political violence grow, grasp self fusion, the merging of own and group self that predicts will to act very, becomes urgent. Devin R. Wright and two co-authors test a mental language score that gauges fusion from language patterns, large language models, and hidden image.

Across data from the United Kingdom and Singapore, the method beats ready ways at guessing checked fusion scores. Applied to extreme texts, it reveals two distinct high-fusion routes to violence: ideologues frame themselves through the group, forming kinship bonds, while grievance-driven individuals frame the group through own self. Psychologists and extremism teams gain a scalable reading tool and a refined theory of divergent pathways.
arxiv-2602-08552:
Subjective ratings are noisy, so even a perfect model cannot correlate perfectly with human judges, yet that ceiling is rarely measured. Fredrik Cumlin proposes rho-Perfect, an estimate of the highest correlation a model can achieve on subjectively rated data. His arXiv paper derives the estimate under heteroscedastic noise, the common case where noise varies across items.

Squaring rho-Perfect estimates test-retest correlation, which validates the approach. A speech-quality demonstration shows how the measure separates model shortcomings from data-quality problems. Readers get a practical yardstick: before blaming a model, check whether the ratings themselves cap its score.
arxiv-2602-08852:
Erin Carmody defines a new ranking, called Mitchell rank, for supercompact cardinals, some of the largest infinities in set theory. The rank counts layers of fine measures on collections of small sets, building a ladder of strength above a given cardinal. Her 2026 paper then asks how far down that ladder forcing can push a cardinal.

She shows how to force a measurable cardinal's degree down to any chosen level at or below its starting degree. The same soft-touch forcing can lower the Mitchell rank for supercompactness to any desired degree, with side results for strongly compact cardinals. It is pure set theory: measuring giant infinities and reshaping them with care.
arxiv-2602-09052:
Stall cells are spanwise-periodic structures that appear on wings near stall and scramble the load distribution. Rishabh Mishra and three co-authors simulate them in three dimensions with a hybrid RANS-LES turbulence model, validating global loads against experiments and simpler simulations. Spanwise variation in where flow separates drives uneven loading: mid-span separates early through flow bifurcation, while attraction near one chord length outboard keeps flow attached longer.

The separated shear layer rolls into a vortex tube that wobbles through a Crow-type instability against the trailing-edge vortex, bending tubes and shear layer and driving spanwise flow. A new finding: peaks of spanwise velocity rotate about fixed spanwise axes, with angle growing linearly downstream. The study clarifies structures experiments struggle to capture.
arxiv-2602-09452:
Inverse synthetic aperture radar images from car radars reveal target shape and size, but road clutter and uncorrected target motion blur them. Multiple-input-multiple-output radar can sharpen the signal, yet motion compensation methods proven for single-channel images had not been tested much for multi-channel ones. Devansh Mathur and three co-authors evaluate three popular compensation techniques on multi-channel data in their 2026 paper.

Entropy minimization, cross-correlation, and phase gradient autofocus were tested on measurements from a commercial millimeter-wave multi-channel radar. Cross-correlation compensation wins in the multi-channel setup, improving overall quality by more than a third over the alternatives. The paper thus identifies which standard compensation method carries over best when automotive radar gains extra channels.
arxiv-2602-09552:
Chat-based question answering leans on search-grounded writing, but most studies test methods alone and on single turns. Klejda Alushi and three co-authors compare search methods in order for multi-turn chat QA in their 2026 paper, where chat history, pronoun links, and shifting intent complicate search. Eight varied datasets across multiple domains share one test setup, with search quality and answer writing both scored.

Robust yet simple methods, re-ranking, hybrid BM25, and HyDE, steadily beat vanilla search. Several advanced techniques, by contrast, gain nothing and sometimes fall below the no-search base. Dataset traits and chat length strongly shape search success, explaining why no single strategy rules everywhere. Effective chat search, the authors conclude, depends less on fancy build than on matching strategy to dataset structure.
arxiv-2602-09652:
The BESIII Team reports the first sighting of a charm particle decaying into a pair of neutral cascade baryons. Using about ten billion particle events taken with the BESIII machine at the BEPCII ring, the team finds the rare decay signal in their 2026 paper. The result adds a new decay mode to the known ways of charm states.

Analysis accounts for overlap between the direct path through the charm state and a non-direct path making the same final bits. Both paths fold into fits of the pair mass spectrum. Decay rates are set under both adding and clashing overlap cases, with stat and setup errors given apart. The first sighting of this decay opens a fresh window on how charm couples to baryon pairs.
arxiv-2602-10252:
Datacenter networks suffer a tyranny of the single objective: fabrics hardcoded for one metric shine when application and network goals align but fail badly when they diverge. A 2026 paper led by Sanjoli Narang, with three co-authors, proposes DMart, a decentralized scheduling framework treating network bandwidth as a competitive marketplace. Applications encode traffic urgency and importance into autonomous bids, letting diverse objectives coexist natively on the same fabric.

DMart runs distributed per-link, per-round-trip auctions without integer programming, centralized schedulers, or complex priority queues, meeting datacenter scale and sub-microsecond demands. Packet-level simulations against specialized schedulers show DMart matching them on their home turf while also optimizing secondary metrics. Against pFabric and Sincronia, it halves deadline misses and cuts coflow completion times by over one and a half times, while matching pFabric short-flow completion times.
arxiv-2602-10352:
Self-interpretation asks language models to describe their own inner states, but hyperparameter sensitivity makes them unreliable. A 2026 paper led by Keenan Pepper, with eight co-authors, shows that training lightweight adapters on interpretability artifacts, with the language model fully frozen, yields dependable self-interpretation across tasks and model families. One scalar affine adapter with barely more parameters than model dimension is enough.

Trained adapters generate sparse autoencoder feature labels beating the training labels themselves, seventy percent versus fifty percent scoring at seventy-billion scale. They identify topics with ninety-four percent recall at one versus one percent for untrained baselines. They also decode bridge entities in multi-hop reasoning appearing in neither prompt nor response. The learned bias vector alone accounts for eighty-five percent of improvement. Simpler adapters generalize better than expressive alternatives, and self-interpretation gains outpace capability gains from seven billion to seventy-two billion parameters.
arxiv-2602-10452:
Zhaoye Pan and four co-authors study networked agents that must optimize jointly under shared constraints in a 2026 paper. Most prior work assumes costs and constraints split neatly into per-agent pieces. Real network control problems do not: the global cost and the long-term constraints couple the agents' decisions in ways no single agent sees alone.

The paper proposes a distributed online primal-dual recipe built on belief consensus. Each agent maintains a local belief about the joint decision, exchanges it with neighbors, and updates it from full-information feedback. The authors analyze the method's results on time-varying problems, showing that agents can coordinate on nonseparable objectives and constraints through local communication alone.
arxiv-2602-10552:
Dongyang Li and seven co-authors steer brain activity with images in a closed loop in a 2026 paper. Most brain-computer interface research decodes neural signals into conduct. The reverse direction, using stimuli to guide brain states, is far less understood. Vision is the hardest case: desired subjective states lack clean measures and EEG feedback is noisy.

Their system, MindPilot, uses EEG signals as tuning feedback for naturalistic image making. Treating the brain as a black-box function, a pseudo-model guidance process iteratively refines images without stated rewards or slopes. Unlike prior work confined to invasive settings or flicker stimuli, the system uses non-invasive EEG and natural images. That opens a path toward brain modulation through ordinary visual experience.
arxiv-2602-10652:
Yongshi Ye and nine co-authors unify how AI agents build and maintain memory in a 2026 paper. Self-evolving memory acts as trainable settings for language-model agents, but current methods optimize memory management while treating extraction as static. Agents then accumulate instance-exact noise instead of robust memories that transfer.

Their system, UMEM, jointly optimizes a language model to extract and manage memories jointly. Meaning neighborhood modeling plus a neighborhood-level marginal utility reward counter overfitting to single instances. By judging a memory's utility across its meaning neighborhood, the system keeps memories that transfer and discards ones that merely fit one episode. The paper reports improved transfer for agents that must learn continuously.
arxiv-2602-10752:
Mischa Huisman and four co-authors harden cooperative cruise control against vehicle doubt in a 2026 paper. Cooperative adaptive cruise control enables platooning through inter-vehicle communication, improving traffic speed and safety. Usual designs rely on feedback linearization assuming exact vehicle settings, but real long-run motion carries parametric doubt.

Applying nominal-model linearization yields imperfect cancellation, model mismatch, and degraded results with off-the-shelf controllers. Instead of redesigning the control law, the authors model the mismatch between ideal and actual closed-loop motion explicitly. Toughness becomes a path-matching problem: cut the energy of that mismatch so the unsure system behaves as closely as possible to the design ideal. The approach upgrades toughness without replacing deployed controllers.
arxiv-2602-10852:
N. A. Cockton and fifteen co-authors reconstruct hole dispersions in gallium arsenide quantum wells in a 2026 paper. Rashba-split heavy-hole subbands in flat hole gases resist tested access. Heavy-hole and light-hole mixing produces non-parabolicity and breaks the usual density-to-wavevector correspondence. Low-field magnetotransport offers a way in.

Using undoped heterojunction devices in an accumulation-mode field-effect shape, the team sustains strong out-of-plane electric fields. It keeps high mobilities and large spin-orbit tilt. Fourier analysis of Shubnikov-de Haas swings resolves single subband densities, and temperature dependence of the Fourier amplitudes yields strong masses and dispersions. The readings give a detailed picture of spin-split hole bands under strongly asymmetric confinement.
arxiv-2602-10952:
Linus Ekstrøm and five co-authors improve quantum multi-objective tuning with archiving in a 2026 paper. Finding best trade-offs among conflicting objectives matters daily in industry, and variational quantum multi-objective tuning has drawn interest as a quantum route. The authors improve it with a Pareto archive and dominated-answer substitution, clearly improving hypervolume settling at extra quantum and older cost.

They propose RMNK landscapes as a unifying testbed for benchmarking quantum multi-objective methods. Such landscapes are common in the older field, and the authors devise a generic older-to-quantum mapping of them. Number hyperparameter tuning of the quantum method greatly enhances its results. Final comparisons against older plans assess where quantum multi-objective tuning now stands.
arxiv-2602-11152:
Voting rules are judged by how much welfare they lose when voters rank but do not score. Hamidreza Alipour and Mohak Goyal resolve a long-standing tension in that distortion frame by moving to chance-based voting. Under noisy Plackett-Luce rankings, Copeland and Borda both achieve distortion bounded by a heat-like setting, free of candidate count.

Those bounds sit within a factor of two of the known lower bound for randomized rules, and improve the prior Borda bound. Rules that use only top choices fare worse: Plurality and Random Dictator keep a dependence on candidate count, and veto variants do not remove it. The authors also bound all fixed tournament rules. The lesson is that chance-based voting aligns distortion with normative intuition.
arxiv-2602-11252:
Measuring Fermi surface volume in underdoped cuprates is blocked by heat and disorder. Alexander Nikolaenko and four co-authors propose Sondheimer swings as a robust other probe. These semiclassical swings in thin-film magnetoresistivity arise from matching cyclotron radius to film thickness.

They need no Landau rounding and survive at moderate fields and higher temperatures where quantum swings fade. Their rates depend only on Fermi surface settings, not on spread details, and they separate pocket parts in rate. Computed spectra for three scenarios, unreconstructed, spin-density-wave reconstructed, and fractionalized, show distinct universal traits, including a shape-dependent phase shift between longitudinal and transverse signals.
arxiv-2602-11552:
Sheets of material only atoms thick can carry current with no resistance, but finding versions that stay stable and let engineers tune that behavior is hard. Jakkapat Seeyangnok and one co-author use first-principles calculation to survey MXene sheets made from molybdenum carbide and nitride, coated with halogen atoms such as fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine. Only the bromine and iodine coated carbide sheets prove stable under vibration checks.

Both stable sheets are metals whose electron states near the key energy level are rich enough to support strong coupling between electrons and vibrations. That coupling yields superconducting transitions near 13 and 18 degrees above absolute zero, well above the bare carbide sheet. Adding charge or stretching the sheet pushes those temperatures past 21 degrees, marking the coated sheets as tough, tunable superconductors.
arxiv-2602-11852:
State-of-the-art language models surpass most humans in certain domains, yet their reasoning stays largely opaque, reducing trust and raising risks of deception and falsehoods. Yordan Yordanov and eight co-authors introduce the Prototype Transformer, an autoregressive architecture that replaces the square-cost attention module with a linear-cost module based on prototypes, learned parameter vectors. Pattern vectors create communication channels that gather context at different time scales.

That structure leads pattern vectors to capture nameable concepts, such as woman, during training, offering a path toward reading model reasoning and making targeted edits to behavior. Compared with baselines, the Prototype Transformer scales well with model and data size, resists input noise, and performs well on text generation and downstream tasks including GLUE. It is a promising step toward language models interpretable by design rather than by after-the-fact accounts.
arxiv-2602-12252:
If huge ripples in the early universe collapsed into planet-mass black holes, they should also have left a faint gravitational wave hum. D. Blas led this work with six co-authors, tracing that scalar-induced background in the microhertz band, where future lunar and satellite laser ranging could hear it. The Moon, in effect, becomes a listening post.

From a null detection, the team derives projected limits on the planet-mass black hole population, including shifts caused by the electroweak phase transition in the early universe. They also link those limits to recent microlensing views of Andromeda by the HSC team. A quiet result from lunar ranging could thus tighten what we know about tiny ancient black holes.
arxiv-2602-12352:
Almost complex manifolds carry metrics that almost, but do not quite, fit the Kähler mould. Their Lee forms encode the mismatch. Ethan Addison led this work with two co-authors. They study pluricanonical locally conformally almost Kähler metrics.

Such a metric comes from a locally conformally symplectic structure of the first kind. Its Lee form has an anti-invariant derivative. Its Nijenhuis image is orthogonal to a spanned distribution. On compact complex manifolds, pluricanonical locally conformally Kähler metrics have parallel Lee forms. The same holds for Chern-Ricci flat Gauduchon metrics. The paper generalises both facts to the almost Kähler case. It shows no compatible symplectic form exists when the Lee form is non-trivial. It notes the fundamental two-form is a Hodge Laplacian eigenform. It proves the derivative vanishes for Gauduchon metrics with real holomorphic Lee direction.
arxiv-2602-12852:
Web agents that research online often wander through long, looping tool-call trajectories, wasting time on dead ends. Junjie Wang and eleven co-authors propose WebClipper, which compresses those trajectories by treating search as a state graph. It mines a minimal directed acyclic graph that keeps essential reasoning while cutting redundant steps. Training continues on the pruned trajectories, steering the agent toward leaner search habits.

The payoff is concrete: tool-call rounds fall by about 20% while accuracy improves, and a new F-AE score measures the balance between accuracy and efficiency. Experiments confirm that pruned trajectories preserve performance while cutting cost. For deep research systems, the message is that how an agent searches matters as much as what it finds, and shorter, cleaner paths can also be better ones.
arxiv-2602-14252:
Osher Elhadad and two co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv method for recognizing an agent's goal from its behavior. Goal recognition matters for aligning AI with human intent, but standard methods assume an optimal goal-directed policy, which may differ from how the actor truly behaves. That mismatch can mislead recognition.

GRAIL learns one goal-directed policy per candidate goal from demonstration trajectories, using imitation learning and inverse reinforcement learning. It can capture suboptimal and systematically biased behavior, yet still scores a partial trajectory in a single forward pass. Across tested domains, GRAIL raised F1 by over 0.5 under biased optimal behavior, and by about 0.1 to 0.3 under suboptimal behavior.
arxiv-2602-14352:
Zihui Ma and seven co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv setup for disaster feeling across cities. Social media gives a real-time lens on public feeling during disasters, but text-only models often back city-first skew and miss left-out groups. The paper adds movement-informed acts and city-likeness data boost to cross-city learning.

Focused on the January 2025 Southern California wildfires, the model reached top scores and showed varied feeling patterns, above all where fire exposure overlapped or emergency replies lagged. Feeling words tracked positively with real-world movement shifts, showing the worth of joining acts and text. Mixed fusion and city-aware training lifted both exactness and fairness, arguing for context-aware feeling models.
arxiv-2602-14652:
Moving mass across a network takes time, and start and finish times often matter. Anqi Dong, with Karl H. Johansson and Johan Karlsson as co-authors, extends optimal transport to schedules with departure-arrival constraints. Classical theory assumes all mass leaves at once and arrives at once.

Two cases are treated: rates fixed separately at sources and sinks, and travel times fixed per particle. The first case becomes a multi-marginal transport problem; the second fits unequal-dimensional transport. For line graphs, the authors study when the path exists and is unique. For general graphs, they reduce to a chosen path set and optimize over it.
arxiv-2602-14752:
Naeem Akhtar and others craft finer sub-Planck shapes from SU(1,1) round states for sharper sensing. Quantum states with sub-Planck marks can feel tiny shifts past the usual quantum bound, a boon for sensing.

Old compass states, built from four Perelomov coherent states on a curved plane, gave uneven marks, sharp one way and dull the next. The new build stacks at least six such states, evenly spaced round a ring path, so sharpness evens out in all ways. Sensing gains a rounder tool, keen in each direction alike.
arxiv-2602-14852:
Chris Gartland and Mikhail Ostrovskii study lower estimates for L1 distortion of transportation cost spaces, the earth mover's distance between distributions on a finite metric space. Low-distortion embeddings of earth mover's distance into L1, pioneered by Charikar and by Indyk and Thaper, underpin algorithms in computer science and vision, with an O(log n) upper bound long in question.

Grid graphs, especially planar grids, are a fundamental test case, and the authors press the lower-bound side of that question. Their estimates mark how far embeddings can be squeezed before distortion must grow. Optimal transport geometry gains a sharper sense of its embedding limits.
arxiv-2602-15352: Bezdek gets better findings on even shrinks of overlaps and joins of equal balls, thereby growing earlier part proofs of the Kneser-Poulsen guess in these cases. Also, the paper proves Blaschke-Santaló-type bounds for r-ball shapes. Both results cover balls of equal size and how their overlaps and joins act under uniform contractions.
arxiv-2602-15552:
Merabishvili and colleagues test whether trimming the latent space of a generative model yields better test inputs for image classifiers. They work with style-based GANs and judge generated inputs on three fronts: whether they are valid, how diverse they are, and how often they expose faults. The test ground is boundary testing of classifiers on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR-10.

Two trimming routes are compared: mixing latent codes with binary search, and random latent truncation for open exploration. Code mixing wins, giving a higher fault detection rate while also improving diversity and validity. The paper offers testers a practical rule: shape the latent space with care, since how inputs are sampled changes what bugs surface.
arxiv-2602-15952:
Barai uses cosmological simulations to separate two ways that central supermassive black holes grow: merging with other black holes, and pulling in gas. Her simulated black holes start as seeds of a hundred thousand solar masses. They first grow mainly by mergers, reaching around ten million solar masses while gas intake stays low.

After seven to nine billion years, gas accretion reaches the Eddington rate. A fast growth phase then lasts several hundred million years, lifting masses by factors of a hundred to a thousand. Feedback from active nuclei then drains gas from galaxy centres, capping growth near ten billion solar masses by today. The same history explains recent JWST Little Red Dots: normal mass objects grew mostly by mergers, while overmassive ones went through bursts of rapid gas accretion.
arxiv-2602-16652:
Erik Hansen, Prerana Sharma, and Swadesh Mahajan study nonlinear frequency shifts in incompressible Hall magnetohydrodynamic turbulence. Magnetized plasma turbulence stems from wave links, and adding the Hall effect makes MHD waves dispersive, changing which nonlinear links matter. The turbulent state that emerges should thus differ from plain MHD.

The authors build a reduced model of wave-wave links, zeroing in on those that alter a wave's linear dispersion in a phase-coherent way. Those special links add an amplitude-tied term to the dispersion law, giving nonlinear frequency shifts. Resonance-driven shifts rule, adding damping or growth that sets the nonlinear time scales for energy spread. Those scales, joined with a critical balance guess, can gauge the energy spectrum.
arxiv-2602-16752:
Yu Yin, Shuai Wang, Bevan Koopman, and Guido Zuccon study how prompt injection attacks threaten language-model-based rankers. Simple injected prompts hidden in a candidate document can sharply shift ranking decisions, posing serious security risks for ranking pipelines. How far that weakness spans model families, designs, and settings was largely unexplored.

The paper runs a broad empirical study of jailbreak prompt attacks on rankers. Two tasks frame it: preference vulnerability, gauged by attack success rate, and ranking vulnerability, gauged by ranking quality impact. Three ranking paradigms and two injection variants are tested, along with scaling across families, position sensitivity, backbones, and cross-domain robustness. Search engineers get a map of where ranker vulnerability holds and where it fades.
arxiv-2602-16852:
Minh Duc Bui and co-authors present the first natural language processing study of Meenzerisch, the dialect of Mainz and the traditional tongue of its carnival. Meenzerisch is near dying out, a fate shared by many German dialects. Language technology could aid preservation and revival, yet no prior NLP work had addressed this dialect.

The team builds a digital dictionary from an existing 1966 resource, with over two thousand dialect words paired with Standard German meanings. Tests then ask if state-of-the-art language models can generate definitions for dialect words, or generate dialect words from definitions. Models fail at both: the best definition score is only about six percent, and the best word generation score is under two percent. Dialect preservation researchers get a dataset and a stark baseline.
arxiv-2602-17452:
Wyatt Benno led a four-author team presenting Jolt Atlas, a zero-knowledge machine learning framework for checked inference. Jolt Atlas extends the Jolt proving system to model inference, adapting Jolt's lookup-centric approach to ONNX tensor operations rather than copying CPU instruction execution as zero-knowledge virtual machines do. The ONNX model removes the need for CPU registers and eases memory consistency checks.

Lookup arguments built on the sumcheck protocol suit non-linear functions, key building blocks in modern machine learning. Optimizations such as neural teleportation shrink lookup tables while preserving accuracy, alongside several tensor-level verification optimizations detailed in the paper. The team shows Jolt Atlas can prove inference in memory-constrained environments, a prover property called streaming, and achieves zero-knowledge through the BlindFold technique from Vega. Proofs are succinctly verifiable and can run on-device without specialized hardware, suiting privacy-centric and adversarial settings.
arxiv-2602-17552:
Tripti Agarwal led an eight-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on compressing data from large HPC runs keeping its shape. Error-bounded lossy compression is essential for massive outputs of such runs. Leading tools such as SZ and ZFP bound errors well, but they often fail to preserve topological structures like minima, maxima, and saddle points. Older topology-aware tools fix that gap at a steep compute cost.

TopoSZp, built on the high-throughput SZp compressor, keeps critical points and links while staying light. It combines fast critical point detection, keeping local order, and targeted saddle point fixes, all inside a relaxed but strict error bound. On data sets, it keeps far more critical points intact than rivals, with no false alarms or wrong critical point types. It runs far faster in both directions than older topology-aware tools, while size savings stay strong.
arxiv-2602-17952:
Hu Lou and team propose a hardware-friendly approach to one-dimensional function approximation, a basic computing and engineering problem. Neural networks approximate well, yet their tuning stalls on flat loss landscapes caused by parameter mirrors, slowing convergence and hurting transfer for high-frequency parts.

Inspired by symmetry breaking in physics, the team augments a 1D input with constant values to form a higher-D vector, breaking parameter mirrors without adding parameters. They test the method on ten 1D functions, including smooth, discontinuous, high-frequency and non-smooth functions. Results show input-space expansion speeds training convergence. It cuts LBFGS rounds by about twelve percent on average. It lifts fitting scores, cutting final MSE by about sixty-six percent for the best 5D expansion. Cut-out studies show effects of expansion size and constant choice, with pi beating other constants. Readers gain a low-cost technique for algorithm design.
arxiv-2602-18152:
Ortal Hadad and five co-authors ask whether machine-written text carries a statistical fingerprint. Their 2026 paper tests a simple idea: lossless compression, the same trick that shrinks files, can measure how patterned a text is. More patterned text packs down smaller, and that packing behavior may mark text made by chance-based sampling.

Across three test worlds, from controlled human-machine continuations to a machine-made encyclopedia beside Wikipedia and synthetic social forums beside Reddit, machine text packed down tighter than human text. The gap held across models, tasks, and topics, yet it faded in short, broken-up chats, where small samples hide the pattern. The paper offers a plain, model-free yardstick for how machine generation reshapes written language, and where that yardstick stops working.
arxiv-2602-18252:
Rishika Bhagwatkar and three co-authors probe a weak spot in discrete image tokenizers. Their 2026 paper notes these tokenizers, which turn pictures into token strings for multimodal models, have never been tested against adversarial attacks, unlike CLIP encoders. The team is first to study the gap.

They design attacks that nudge tokenizer features just enough to flip the extracted tokens, cheaply and without tailoring to any one task. The attacks work across classification, retrieval, and captioning. For defense, they retrain popular tokenizers with unsupervised adversarial training while freezing everything else. Robustness jumps against both unsupervised and full supervised attacks, generalizes to unseen tasks and data, and can use unlabeled images. The work flags tokenizer safety as a core piece of trustworthy multimodal models.
arxiv-2602-18352:
Tung T. Ngo and four co-authors test an on-device coding assistant for qualitative researchers. Their 2026 paper introduces ChatQDA, a framework powered by open-source language models for privacy-preserving open coding. Qualitative analysis is labor-heavy, yet privacy risks often rule out commercial models for sensitive research.

A mixed-methods user study rates the system highly for ease of use and felt efficiency, but trust proves conditional: users value it for surface-level extraction while doubting its nuance and consistency. Even with local deployment technically secure, participants report epistemic uncertainty about data protection, suggesting invisible security does not by itself build trust. The paper closes with design recommendations for local-first tools that stress verifiable privacy and method rigor.
arxiv-2602-18452:
Gaia A. Bertolino and four co-authors build a benchmark for answering questions about breathing sounds. Their 2026 paper notes that conversational AI tools increasingly process patient data for health checks, yet question answering on breathing audio remains underexplored. Existing studies test narrowly and lack real-world variety across data types, devices, and question types.

The team introduces RA-QA, with a standard data pipeline, a large multimodal question-answer set, and one shared scoring protocol. RA-QA merges public breathing-audio datasets into nine million format-diverse question-answer pairs covering diagnosis and context. Testing general audio-language models and domain-specific designs sets repeatable reference points and shows how current methods fail under varied conditions.
arxiv-2602-18552:
Amaya Sinha and eighteen co-authors test whether close binary stars pollute stellar chemistry. Their 2026 paper uses SDSS-V APOGEE data to measure how close binarity affects surface chemistry across the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. The team derives membership and orbits for one hundred three single-lined binaries in open clusters, analyzing motion with The Joker and UltraNest.

BACCHUS covers fourteen chemical species, from silicon to neodymium. Assuming open clusters share chemistry, the team compares binaries with single stars at similar states. A subset with strong UV excess shows carbon-to-nitrogen ratios higher than expected, inflating age estimates and pointing to pollution from an evolved companion. At population level, binaries prove statistically alike with single stars, with no link between orbital separation and enrichment, and co-eval stars within about five parsecs count as homogeneous regardless of makeup.
arxiv-2602-18652:
Nina Hosseini-Kivanani tackles idioms that trip models. Her 2026 paper presents PolyFrame for the MWE-2026 AdMIRe2 task on idiom disambiguation. Idioms carry meanings not following from their words, a problem growing across languages. PolyFrame runs one pipeline for image-plus-text and text-only caption ranking.

All variants keep frozen CLIP-style encoders plus the multilingual BGE M3 encoder, training light modules only: logistic regression and sentence-type prediction, idiom synonym substitution, distractor-aware scoring, Borda fusion. From a CLIP baseline, idiom-aware paraphrasing and sentence-type classification lift English top-rank accuracy to sixty percent, with the same score in zero-shot Portuguese transfer. On the multilingual blind test across fifteen languages, systems average roughly one third top-rank. Ablations point to idiom-aware rewriting as the main driver, with sentence-type prediction and fusion adding robustness. The findings show effective idiom disambiguation is possible without fine-tuning encoders.
arxiv-2602-18852:
A cell membrane is only four nanometres thick, yet its electrical behaviour is complex. M. M. B. Sheraj, with one co-author, presents a three-slab model in 2026 for the dielectric permittivity of a lipid bilayer. The membrane is treated as three dielectric slabs. One slab covers each head-group region. The third covers the lipid tails.

Equal and opposite bound surface charges surround each head-group slab. They account for the membrane dipole potential. Parameters come from molecular dynamics simulations. They capture both the zero-field potential and the response to applied fields. The tail region behaves almost like vacuum. The head-group region is highly anisotropic. Averaging over slab widths gives the out-of-plane permittivity a meaningful continuum reading, overcoming a limit of microscopic theories.
arxiv-2602-19052:
The pygmy dipole resonance still hides its true character. W.-L. Lv, with two co-authors, probes it in 2026 through gamma decay of lead-208 states. Two questions drive the work. What is its isospin character? How collective is it? A Skyrme particle-vibration coupling model supplies the answers.

Gamma decay from pygmy states to a low-lying excited state is strongly suppressed. Decay from the giant dipole resonance is far stronger. That contrast reveals a mostly isoscalar character. Detailed diagram analysis finds a real presence of one-particle-one-hole configurations coupled to a phonon. A quantitative method then sizes complex-configuration components in the wave function. That component is smaller in the pygmy resonance than in the giant dipole case, and far smaller than in the giant quadrupole case.
arxiv-2602-19152:
How do Picard bundles behave when restricted to a curve inside its Jacobian? Usha N. Bhosle, writing alone in 2026, studies that restriction for twisted Picard bundles. The curve is irreducible and projective, with at most nodes as singularities, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Its compactified Jacobian hosts the bundles.

For genus two and rank at least three, a two-dimensional family of stable ACM bundles emerges on the compactified Jacobian, with the Picard bundle in its limit. An embedding of the generalised Jacobian into a moduli space of stable vector bundles uses a twisted restriction. Under suitable conditions, the universal bundle restricts stably to curve times Jacobian. For smooth curves twisted by a line bundle, the Picard bundle restricts with semistability or stability above explicit degree thresholds. Theta divisor restrictions are also determined.
arxiv-2602-19452:
Hardware trends toward reduced precision computing have revived interest in sharper floating point arithmetic. Longfei Gao and Frimpong Baidoo study compensated summation methods, which sharpen sums beyond what hardware natively supports, above all when addends are not known in advance. Complete accounts of error behavior are given for these methods.

The analysis traces the link between results at two back-to-back summing steps, showing which operation caps the result. That insight guides the design of more nuanced methods. The work builds on Dekker's 1971 floating point number system. It drops the rule that number representations be unique, a strange-looking choice that proves powerful for error analysis.
arxiv-2602-20052:
Language models produce text one symbol at a time. That makes their output a symbol source of the kind information theory studies. A 2026 arXiv paper by Marco Scharringhausen, working alone, treats model output as a stationary source over a finite alphabet and measures its entropy per word.

The comparison set is natural language, written and spoken, drawn from the Open American National Corpus. Model word entropy comes out lower than natural speech entropy in both written and spoken form. The longer-term aim is to make precise our intuitions about information and uncertainty in large language training. That includes judging what happens when models train on text other models generated, especially text scraped from the world wide web.
arxiv-2602-20352:
Vinit Singh and four co-authors review quantum machine learning for complex systems, a field moving from theory toward real use. Their review surveys basic models, including variational quantum methods, quantum kernel methods, and neural-network quantum states, focused on complex quantum systems. Neural-network quantum states get focus as rich models for linked matter, systems out of balance, and open quantum systems.

The review also covers hard parts of training and sampling, quantum-boosted sampling, and checks of learning dynamics, including information-theory tools for scale and ease of training. Use-driven methods in drug research, cancer biology, and agro-climate work show where complex data call for hybrid quantum and non-quantum methods. The authors close with shared quantum machine learning as a path to spread-out, private quantum intelligence. Overall, the review offers a unified view of the promise and limits of the field.
arxiv-2602-20452:
Quantum machines built from identical particles need error fixes rebuilt from scratch. S. L. Wu and Lian-Ao Wu present a general fault-tolerant design based on same-particle qubits, finding that first-order effects between such qubits and their bath differ deeply from the usual qubit-bath case. That gap forces current decay-fighting methods to be redone.

The authors propose that the simplest quantum error code can live inside the real qubit, if fixing and repair are generalized beyond unitary steps to real undo steps. Logical and real qubits then stand on equal footing. Dynamic shielding still works in this unified picture, and a decay-free-subspace-like structure appears. An exactly solvable model plus numerical tests back the methods.
arxiv-2602-20752:
Muscle-bone ills are a large global health burden and a leading cause of harm, yet MRI reading remains challenging. Tian Lan and ten co-authors built OrthoDiffusion, a unified diffusion-based model for multi-task MRI reading.

The system uses three view 3D models, pre-trained in a self-taught way on nearly sixteen thousand unmarked knee MRI scans. It learns body-part features from side, front, and top views. Those view features support tasks, including body-part mapping and multi-label calls. Tests show it achieves results segmenting eleven knee structures and detecting eight knee flaws. The model shows strength across centers and field levels, always topping older models. Where tagged data was rare, it kept high test hits using only ten percent of labels. Features learned from knee imaging proved mobile to other joints, with diagnostic results across eleven ills of the ankle and shoulder.
arxiv-2602-20952:
Searching encrypted geo-textual data usually means juggling separate indices for each query type, which is costly and awkward. Zhen Lv and six co-authors propose RISK in this 2026 arXiv paper, a single model for rich spatial-keyword queries on encrypted data. It works textual-first, then spatial, on a new nearest-neighbor quadtree that embeds representative and regional neighbors, encrypted with standard cryptographic tools.

RISK supports both secure range queries and secure nearest-neighbor queries, carries a proof of security under the IND-CKA2 model, and extends to multi-party settings and dynamic updates. Experiments on three real datasets and one synthetic dataset show it beating the state of the art by wide margins in response time. Readers get one index where several incompatible ones used to be needed.
arxiv-2602-21052:
In-order tip models usually add place tags at the input, but that trick only weakly teaches order. Timur Nabiev and Evgeny Frolov argue the flaw runs deeper in this 2026 arXiv paper. With no place signals, focus is unchanged by reordering, and added tags tangle place with item meaning while fading in deep nets. Their answer is a kernel self-focus tool.

A learnable place kernel works purely in place space, untangled from meaning likeness, and tunes focus weights straight. Applied per focus block, it allows tunable multi-scale in-order model work. Tests on standard next-item trials show steady gains over strong base cases. Readers get a cleaner way to teach sequence models about order.
arxiv-2602-21252:
Security watchers usually flag stats-based oddities, but crypto breaches are set by policy: no key reuse, no step-downs, bounded key life spans. Rahul Ray recasts spotting around those rules in this 2026 arXiv paper with INTACT, a policy-tuned setup. Instead of a static edge over conduct-based traits, the model scores breach odds given both seen conduct and stated security intent.

Conduct-based and intent coders fuse into codes that yield a breach score, giving a family of choice edges dial-set by policy. Tests on a real network-flow set and a two hundred ten thousand-trace fake multi-intent set show matching or beating strong base cases. Telling apart is near-perfect on real data, with a steady edge on link-based and mixed breaches. Intent tuning lifts telling apart, readability, and toughness.
arxiv-2602-21652:
Minhao Jiang and five co-authors propose Sparsity Induction for accurate post-training pruning of large language models. Large language models excel at text generation, while growing parameter scales strain compute and memory efficiency. Post-training pruning cuts model cost by removing weights from dense networks, but native dense matrices lack high thinness, so direct weight removal disrupts model states and yields poor recovery even after post-tuning.

Sparsity Induction pushes models toward higher thinness at spread and feature levels before pruning, to push pruning limits. At spread level, thinness grows through mathematically equivalent scaling transforms, fully absorbable with no extra parameters or inference-time overhead. At feature level, a Spectral Norm Loss promotes feature thinness from a low-rank view. Tests across varied model designs and tasks show the method further boosts thinness-friendliness, achieving superior pruning scores over existing methods.
arxiv-2602-21752:
Optimal control over radio networks usually assumes real-time channel state information, yet exact channel data is hard to obtain in advance because radio channels vary over time. Minjie Tang and three co-authors propose a pilot-free design in which control commands come from plant states plus control-aided channel guessing. For linear plants over OFDM links, guessing uses a Kalman filter. The optimal policy follows from the Bellman principle.

To tame the curse of size, the answer is built with a coupled Riccati rule, run fast by random method. The team proves both the guesser and the closed-loop system stay stable, gives rules for a unique stable near answer, and proves the method settles. Moved to nonlinear plants with a KalmanNet guesser and a Markov-tuned deep fixed policy gradient control, the pilot-free approach beats benchmarks in both control quality and guessing quality.
arxiv-2602-21852:
Traffic light research is slow. Training a control system in SUMO can take hours. Setting up runs again can take days. That slow pace makes it hard to test a design many times with fresh random seeds. Much of the delay is waste. For timing lights, what matters most is how queues build up and clear. A flow model called the Cell Transmission Model captures just that part.

Haoran Su and one co-author built LightSim. It is pure Python and installs with pip. It works with Gymnasium and PettingZoo. On one CPU, it runs over 20000 steps each second.
