Tests covered single crossings, grids, main roads, and six real city nets. Rankings from SUMO held up for old-style and learning controls. Training ran 3 to 7 times faster. It ships free with nineteen cases, seven controls, and full learning tools. It cuts setup from days to minutes.
arxiv-2602-22252:
The Fermi paradox asks why a galaxy that should teem with life seems silent, and one answer is that technological civilizations simply do not last. Sohrab Rahvar and Shahin Rouhani explore that answer, asking what the silence implies if intelligent life is common on Earth-like planets. Under optimistic assumptions about life's emergence, the absence of contact itself becomes evidence.

Their analysis caps technological lifetimes at a few thousand years in the most optimistic scenario, with longer-lived civilizations making the silence ever harder to explain. Our light cone already spans the galaxy's history over the past hundred thousand years, deepening the puzzle. The authors stress these are upper bounds from the paradox, not predictions of any civilization's fate.
arxiv-2602-22452:
Embodied agents must first judge which candidate actions are physically possible, before any planning begins. Chayan Banerjee argues that supervised fine-tuning trains action scorers poorly for that job: it scores each candidate independently and never teaches discrimination between subtly wrong and right actions. He proposes the Contrastive World Model, which fine-tunes a language model as a scorer with a contrastive objective and hard-mined negatives.

The key idea pushes valid actions away from invalid ones in scoring space, emphasizing hard negatives that look similar but are physically incompatible. Intrinsic tests on hundreds of hard-negative pairs from the ScienceWorld benchmark measure affordance judgment directly. The approach gives embodied pipelines a feasibility filter that knows not just what is likely, but what is possible.
arxiv-2602-22752:
Nils Schwager and three co-authors test whether language models can stand in for social media users. The shift from exploratory tools to silicon subjects in social science needs validation of operational validity, the match between simulated and real behaviour. Their task, Conditioned Comment Prediction, asks a model to predict how a user would comment, judged against authentic digital traces.

Tests on open-weight 8-billion-parameter models in English, German, and Luxembourgish reveal a form-versus-content split in low-resource settings. Fine-tuning aligns surface form, length and syntax, yet weakens semantic grounding. Explicit conditioning from generated biographies also turns redundant under fine-tuning, as models infer latently from behavioural histories. The guidance: favour authentic behavioural traces over descriptive personas.
arxiv-2602-22852:
Oliver Larsson and three co-authors introduce buoyancy, a new lens on workload performance in shared, mixed-hardware computing. Simple gauges like CPU use or app-level metrics miss how resource fights and noisy neighbours degrade performance, since bottlenecks can hide in any shared resource.

Buoyancy blends app-level metrics with system-level views of shared-resource contention, capturing bottlenecks and headroom across resources at once. That holistic picture supports orchestration that respects both app needs and resource realities, in a form meant to be intuitive, extensible, and portable across platforms. Tests on representative multi-tenant workloads show buoyancy flagging bottlenecks about nineteen percent better than traditional heuristics on average, and it drops into existing metric slots.
arxiv-2602-22952:
Yuan Tang and three co-authors take over the riskiest step of bedside tracheostomy. The windpipe procedure serves ICU patients on long breathing help, and its needle puncture can cause major bleeding or back wall piercing when off-target. Manual puncture without guidance today errs by about five mm and thirty degrees.

A speed-ruled robotic arm now drives needle entry, guided by two magnet-based sensors, one at the needle tip and one inside the trachea. A self-tuning bounded driver tunes shaky motion values live while dodging bumps with body and nearby tissues. Tests checked the driver, then four hundred trials on a dummy showed median place error under two mm and midline drift about four degrees, hinting at feasible robotic puncture.
arxiv-2602-23252:
Maximilian Kalcher and one co-author derive a scaling law linking analog-to-digital converter bit depth to effective bandwidth for signals with 1/f-to-the-alpha power spectra. Quantization adds a flat noise floor, and where that floor meets the falling signal spectrum sets an effective cutoff frequency. Each added bit extends this cutoff by a factor of two to the power 2/alpha, roughly doubling bandwidth per bit when alpha equals two.

The law needs quantization noise to be nearly white, and the authors show the minimum bit depth for that condition depends on alpha. Tests on synthetic 1/f-to-the-alpha signals for alpha of 1.5, 2.0, and 2.5 give prediction errors under 3 percent with the theoretical noise floor, and about 14 percent when the floor is estimated from the quantized spectrum itself. An illustration on real EEG data shows the practical stakes.
arxiv-2602-23552:
Armen Gulian and two co-authors report that copper-oxide high-heat superconductors can break time-flip balance with no outside field. Using Tl2Ba2CaCu2O8 tiny bridges, they observe a strong superconducting diode effect at 100 K under strictly zero-field settings.

The one-way response stays the same in fields up to plus or minus 100 Oe. The results match recent reports of zero-field diode effect in Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8, and jointly they suggest time-flip balance breaking may be built into the cuprate superconducting state. The findings sharply constrain theory models of high-heat superconductivity that rely on time-flip-balanced workings.
arxiv-2602-23852:
Zhaowen Wang and five co-authors present ULW-SleepNet, an ultra-lightweight network for scoring sleep stages from multiple physiological signals. The 2026 paper notes that many sleep models are heavy and built for a single brain-wave channel, limiting their use on full overnight polysomnography data.

The network uses a dual-stream separable convolution block, depthwise separable convolutions, shared channel parameters, and global average pooling to slash compute while keeping accuracy competitive. Tests on two Sleep-EDF sets give strong accuracy with only a tiny parameter count and modest arithmetic cost, cutting parameters by nearly all versus leading methods at small accuracy loss. The design suits real-time sleep monitoring on wearables and small connected devices, where power and size are tight.
arxiv-2602-24152:
Gongyu Ni and three co-authors study scheduling strategies for distributed quantum computing jobs, where circuits run across multiple connected quantum devices. The 2026 paper notes that scaling qubit counts across devices demands not only circuit compilation but also execution management. It is a hard problem because quantum-specific constraints join the usual goal of shortening job batches.

Constraints include quantum processing unit utilization, the rate of non-local gates that span devices, and queue latency for distributed jobs. The authors propose, simulate, and evaluate a range of strategies. Heuristics maximize resource use. Node selection uses heterogeneous network connectivity. Nodes release asynchronously when jobs finish. A reinforcement learning scheduler uses proximal policy optimization. Benchmarks against traditional first-in-first-out and list schedulers, across job types and network conditions, map which strategies best allocate distributed jobs to devices. In short, the best plan wins. The win is clear..
arxiv-2602-24252:
Moritz Woelk and two co-authors propose a neural Luenberger state observer for nonautonomous nonlinear systems, a model-free method for estimating hidden system states from input-output data. The 2026 paper trains the observer offline on historical or simulated state measurements, extending the Kazantzis-Kravaris/Luenberger observer structure to systems with manipulated inputs.

An additional input-affine term is added to the linear observer-state dynamics, determining a nonlinear injective mapping of the true states. Both that term and the mapping from observer states back to system states are learned with fully connected feedforward neural networks. The authors theoretically prove that trained networks, given new input-output data, can observe states with a guaranteed error bound. Case studies on a bioreactor and a Williams-Otto reactor validate the synthesis method. The proof holds.
arxiv-2603-00052: Wang's team presents RBF-Gen, a knowledge-guided surrogate method for high-dimensional design optimisation under scarce data. Data-driven stand-ins falter there, since experts hold domain knowledge few methods can use with little data. It builds a radial basis function space with more centres than training samples. It uses the null space through a generator network, coding shape links and spread priors as factors. It beats standard radial basis stand-ins on low-dim shape problems and a semiconductor factory dataset, guiding answers toward physics-true results.
arxiv-2603-00152: Sun and colleagues revisit GRPO training for visual large language models, questioning the assumption that language-reasoning training transfers cleanly to visual perception. Using reasoning segmentation as a test case, they surface two neglected factors: a broader output space, and fine-grained stable rewards. Their Dr. Seg framework adds a confirm-by-looking step and a distribution-ranked reward module, with no architectural changes, plugging into existing GRPO-based visual models. Experiments show it improves complex visual scenarios while keeping strong generalisation.
arxiv-2603-00252: Albergo and Kanwar discuss a Monte Carlo method for evaluating flow fields in lattice field theory, where learned field transformations may ease critical slowing and signal-to-noise troubles. Field transformations come from flow fields solving a local transport problem exactly, within an annealed sequence of distributions. Defining the estimator with coupled Langevin noise greatly cuts statistical noise in the required integrals. Demonstrations cover U(1) transport and an SU(N) glueball correlator, and the fields can also seed unbiased training data for machine learning.
arxiv-2603-00352: Purcell and Brown present magnetic moments, quadrupole moments, and B(M1) and B(E2) values for 50-neutron nuclei between nickel-78 and tin-100, a benchmark for the nuclear shell model. New Hamiltonians for this model space come from valence-space in-medium renormalization-group methods with two- and three-nucleon interactions. Singular-value-decomposition fits to experimental binding and excitation energies refine them, yielding Hamiltonians called p35-i2, p35-i3, and p30-i3. Results from the various Hamiltonians are compared with experiment to assess theoretical uncertainties.
arxiv-2603-00452: Shen and five colleagues treat text as a material to be shaped, grown, and pruned, arguing that rigid linear writing tools hide what generative models can do. A formative study finds users reason readily with the material metaphor, feeding a framework that links metaphors to shifts in how writers picture, carry out, and judge work. Two probes test the idea: a clay probe refined by hand gestures, and a plant probe where ideas sprout over time. The work widens the design space for writing tools built around living, workable text.
arxiv-2603-00852: Hiraishi and eight colleagues probe how hydride ions move in lanthanum oxyhydride, a material with high ionic conduction. Muon measurements on a sample near one quarter oxygen show implanted particles hopping mainly between tetrahedral sites, gated by empty neighboring octahedral spots. Their jump energy, about a tenth of an electronvolt, clashes with the far larger value implied by conductivity at high heat, pointing to fluid-like, glassy motion rather than simple Arrhenius hopping.
arxiv-2603-00952: Zhang and five colleagues untangle motion from shape in 4D Gaussian splatting for moving scenes. Their VeGaS framework adds a velocity-based shearing matrix that models complex nonlinear motion while keeping geometry separate. A deformation network then refines shapes and orientations from space-time context and velocity cues. Tests on public sets give leading results, fixing flaws that arise when motion and geometry share one covariance form.
arxiv-2603-01052: Huang and Dhami resolve causal uncertainty with CausalSAGE, a plan that sharpens partial ancestral graphs into full directed acyclic graphs. Observational data alone pins the true graph only up to a Markov equivalence class, leaving many later uses stuck with maybe-arrows. Their method expands variables into state-level forms, constrains search with structural knowledge and soft priors, and optimizes one smooth objective, combining results while enforcing acyclicity.
arxiv-2603-01252: Sun and six colleagues generate medical follow-up questions with KG-Followup, pairing a language model with a structured medical knowledge graph through active in-context learning. The graph patches the model's limited domain knowledge with professional expertise for pre-diagnostic assessment. Tests show it beats leading methods by 5 to 8 percent on recall benchmarks, easing the intensive patient-clinician interaction load of clinical diagnosis.
arxiv-2603-01352: Tadaki reports a highly super-Eddington accretion state in a heavily obscured nuclear region, offering dynamical backing for the idea that the fastest stretches of black-hole growth can unfold there. ALMA observations of a hyperluminous galaxy hidden by dust, W2305-0039, at redshift over three show nuclear CO(11-10) far more excited than CO(7-6). X-ray-dominated region models reproduce excitation, while photodissociation-region models fail to match it. Modeling the position-velocity diagram gives a black-hole mass near log eight and gas dispersion of 277 kilometers per second.
arxiv-2603-01552:
Ayantika Das, Keerthi Ram, and Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam model how Alzheimer disease changes the brain over time in this 2026 work. AI tools that fake future brain scans can help track decline, if staff can steer them well. Patient facts beyond the scan, like age and scores, should shape the fake scan in clear ways.

Their auto-encoder pairs diffusion, a method that builds images step by step, with strict alignment rules. One loss forces the model to focus on brain zones where the disease changes tissue most. Separate code spaces hold disease-linked facts apart from traits that mark the person, which keeps identity stable. Tests judge the fakes by image match scores and by zone-by-zone volume checks on real Alzheimer scan sets.
arxiv-2603-01752:
Ihor Kendiukhov traces causal links inside single-cell foundation models in this 2026 study. Such models read gene activity in single cells, yet how their internal features affect each other was unknown. Sparse autoencoders split model activity into readable features, which gives the study its handles.

Kendiukhov ablates, or switches off, single features and watches how downstream features respond. Applied to two large models across four conditions, the method maps tens of thousands of causal edges. Both models show about half their links as biologically coherent, plus a strong tilt toward inhibitory links. Shared domain pairs across models are far more common than chance, and disease-linked domains join that shared set often. Gene-level lab checks, though, suggest the links encode co-expression more than true causal control.
arxiv-2603-01852:
Kristian Stolevik Olsen bounds how strongly a hidden shared driver can make a large system fluctuate. His 2026 work studies many-particle systems where one unseen factor acts on all parts at once. Particles may never interact directly, yet the shared driver can still link their behavior tightly.

Olsen derives a universal upper bound on relative fluctuations for a broad class of observables. The bound uses a generalized mutual information between the observed states and the hidden variable. Mutual information measures how much one signal reveals about another, here applied to collective response. Worked cases include non-interacting Brownian gases under several kinds of dynamical disorder. The inequality gives a general rule for when global disorder can, and cannot, sustain large-scale swings in big systems.
arxiv-2603-02052:
Elena Koung, Yunhan Liu, Zinan Zhang, and colleagues study how teenagers guard themselves during risky interactions on Discord. Their 2026 work draws on interviews with teenage users of the chat platform. Discord mixes private messages, semi-private voice channels, and public servers, which creates layered safety risks.

Teens exercise vigilance by screening suspicious contacts before accepting friendships with strangers. Safety tools and controlled risk-taking help them protect privacy while still socializing online. At community level, selective server participation and vigilant governance structures add a second shield. The findings frame vigilance as active agency, not passive exposure to platform hazards. Teen-centered design lessons follow, aimed at safer environments that support, rather than override, those strategies.
arxiv-2603-02252:
Mandip Goswami releases a speech benchmark for echo-filled rooms in this 2026 paper. Speech tools often fail when voices bounce off walls, a flaw called reverberation. His data set pairs each clean recording with the same clip echoed by a real room. Rooms vary in echo length and in how much direct sound survives.

Five sizes of the Whisper model were tested on sixteen hundred clips. Echo hurt every model, but not equally. The penalty in word errors ranged from small for the largest model to large for the smallest. The biggest model, large-v3, handled echo best of the five. Goswami releases the data, test code, and baseline scores so others can build tougher speech tools.
arxiv-2603-02552:
Anirudh Lanka, Juan Garcia-Nila, and Todd Brun make holonomic quantum gates fault-tolerant in this 2026 paper. Holonomic gates steer a quantum system along a path to enact logic. Continuous measurement offers a route to such gates inside error-correcting codes. Noise, though, constantly threatens the evolving logical state.

Their framework pairs continuous measurement with real-time feedback. One noise type is suppressed intrinsically by the quantum Zeno effect. Other errors are decoded from measurement records, revealing which syndrome sector the state entered. That knowledge steers the holonomic path mid-flight toward the target gate. Speeding up beyond slow adiabatic motion creates its own errors. An analogous protocol corrects those too. Faster, fault-tolerant holonomic gates become feasible.
arxiv-2603-02652:
Cheng Tao Yang and Johann Rafelski examine how one basic physics constant could shift the story of the early universe. Their 2026 paper centers on the Weinberg angle, a free value in the standard model of particle physics. With radiation corrections included, this angle helps set the Fermi coupling, which controls weak-force rates.

Those rates fix both how long a free neutron lives and how many neutrons existed when the first light elements formed. The authors work out how changes in the angle flow through to both quantities. If the angle can drift with heat or cosmic conditions, early-universe predictions drift with it. The paper maps that link clearly for later tests.
arxiv-2603-02852:
Jiaxin Han reviews how astronomers should draw the edge of a dark matter halo. The classic picture treats a halo as a settled ball ending at the virial radius. Yet halos keep growing, and fresh material piles into a layer outside the settled core as infall orbits shrink over time.

Newer boundaries describe that growth layer from different angles. The splashback radius marks where infalling matter first turns around, the depletion radius tracks where the surroundings are being emptied, and the turnaround radius encloses the whole infall zone. Together they recast the halo as a layered, stratified object. Han reviews how each edge is found in data and theory, notes where unified predictions still fail, and supplies a Python package for the key collapse models.
arxiv-2603-02952:
Ihor Kendiukhov opens up two single-cell foundation models to see whether they learned biology or just correlations. Geneformer and scGPT are trained on millions of cells, but causal regulatory logic is harder to prove than pattern matching. His 2026 study trains sparse autoencoders on every layer of both models to split tangled signals into readable features.

The atlases hold tens of thousands of features, nearly all invisible to simpler analysis. Many features map to known pathways and protein networks, and they group into modules with layered organization. Yet against genome-scale gene-silencing data, almost no features responded specifically to a regulator's true targets. The models clearly store organized biological knowledge, but very little cause-and-effect regulatory logic.
arxiv-2603-03052:
Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen argues that buildings themselves are becoming robots. His 2026 paper traces human-building interaction beyond smart thermostats and facades toward whole spaces that physically move. Robotic furniture, swarm robots, and shape-changing rooms show that walls, desks, and partitions can now reconfigure themselves.

In the proposed shift, several building layers act in sync to serve occupants and save energy at once. The agenda doubles as a test bed for human-robot interaction with strange robot forms, even treating the whole building as one robot. The author calls for joint work across computing, psychology, cognition, and architecture. The temporal, spatial, and social complexity of lived spaces is the core challenge to solve.
arxiv-2603-03252:
Mark Goadrich, Achille Morenville, and Éric Piette build a card table where game AI can be compared fairly. Algorithms for imperfect-information games are usually judged game by game, hiding whether a method is robust or just lucky. Card games are a natural testbed because hands are hidden and draws are random.

Their testbed, Valet, packages twenty-one traditional card games spanning genres, cultures, player counts, and deck types. Every game's rules are encoded in one description language, so different systems play identical games. Random simulations characterize each game's branching and length, and baseline scores for a Monte Carlo tree search player against random opponents show the suite is usable. The standard setup should sharpen future comparisons.
arxiv-2603-03552:
Tom Hoekstra, Sander A Mann, and Jorik van de Groep formalize what happens when a light-bending surface is too small for its own waves. Nonlocal metasurfaces steer narrow bands of light and boost near-fields, serving augmented reality, biosensing, and nonlinear optics. Their modes travel far sideways, so real devices, which are small, suffer edge damage to performance. Their 2026 paper models the damage directly.

A spatiotemporal coupled-mode theory shows that when a mode's propagation length is capped by the device size, the scattered field grows interference fringes and its spectral line broadens. A quality-factor formula gains an extra edge-loss channel, and stored energy and lifetime scale exponentially with interaction length. Experiments with position- and momentum-resolved spectroscopy on a metasurface only tens of micrometers wide confirm the predictions. Designers get concrete handles for shrinking the effect.
arxiv-2603-03752:
Chuang Zhang and seven colleagues split reasoning work between a small model and a large one, and teach the small one to know its limits. Large models reason better but cost far more. Their 2026 system, COREA, lets a small language model answer first, stating its answer plus a spoken confidence score. Anything below a confidence threshold is handed up to the large model for a second, stronger attempt.

The trick is making the confidence honest. A reinforcement learning stage adds a calibration reward, aligning the small model's self-assessment with its real accuracy while also improving its reasoning. Across varied datasets and model families, the cascade cut costs by about a fifth on unfamiliar mathematics, with a drop in success of under two percentage points. Similar savings held outside mathematics.
arxiv-2603-04052: Cheney and others first characterize plasma settings and carbon decontamination rates experimentally in superconducting radio rate cavities. In-situ plasma processing restores cavity results against field emission, using noble-gas and oxygen plasma for hours to strip hydrocarbon contamination. Despite extensive research, plasma settings and cleaning rates under varied terms had never been straight measured. The team measured plasma settings with a Langmuir probe and cleaning rates with a carbon-coated quartz crystal microbalance. Results across a large setting space yield processing guidelines, plus discussion of cavity-as-reactor challenges.
arxiv-2603-04552: Mafi and colleagues recast user experience for society-in-the-loop AI systems. AI now decides in key settings where unsure outputs and human checks shape use. Old UX plans built for fixed systems miss how people and rules mix. A mixed methods study pairs a close read of 269 stakeholder views with a live video trial. People meet AI through risk, rules, and capacity to act, while detection and alert routing set the level of human checks and work. A new yardstick centers accuracy, speed, adaptation time, and trust.
arxiv-2603-05052: Sarthak Girdhar and team study interference of Laughlin quasiparticles in the fractional quantum Hall regime inside a Fabry-Pérot interferometer. The Aharonov-Bohm phase along the loop gains sin(2πλ)/2 per quasiparticle present, where πλ is the exchange phase. This contribution comes from time-domain braiding as quasiparticles pass the interferometer's quantum point contacts. With symmetric injection, tunneling current noise shows Aharonov-Bohm swings against injected current, giving access to the exchange phase. At large injection, a wide Fano factor shows power-law scaling with a distinctive phase shift.
arxiv-2603-05352: Diego Armando Resendez Prado proposes psyche-driven Ailed. Chess engines passed human strength, yet play unlike humans. Static personality and dynamic psyche from five positional factors drive behavior. An audio-inspired chain reshapes move probabilities. The chain accepts any move-probability source and needs no search. Across 12,414 Maia2-1100 games, a monotonic agreement gradient from stress to overconfidence proves chain-driven variation. Overconfidence leaves vanilla Maia2 alone; stress lowers scores.
arxiv-2603-05452: Gupta and colleagues ask how well global features of quantum bit strings can be read when each qubit is measured alone, without joint processing. They test a greedy rule that applies the best single-system measurement to every part and guesses the Boolean value from the outcomes. The rule matches an unrestricted global measurement exactly when the target function is affine, apart from finitely many exceptions. Its success rate never falls below the square of the optimal global rate.
arxiv-2603-05552: You and team present TEGA, a touch-boosted grasping helper for assist robots that fuses EMG-based intent-to-force guessing with visuotactile sensing mapped into vibrotactile feedback on a wearable haptic vest. Exact finger placing alone misses grasp force control, vital for objects of diverse hardness, texture, and shape. Users with upper limb disabilities lack natural tactile feedback. The vest gives real-time tactile feedback for natural, matching force tuning during handling, and user studies confirm much improved steady grasp and task success.
arxiv-2603-05652: Sakaue and Carlon develop a clear scaling theory for tagged-monomer mean-squared shift in active chains via a layering formula. The monomer shift equals a lone active bit's shift, shaped by links holding tension spread along the backbone. This splits motion from links and reveals new moving regimes clearly. They test guesses against exact math for broad active chain models with varied noise stats, showing toughness across tiny details. The result is a simple structure that can grow for complex systems too hard to solve by math.
arxiv-2603-05752: Xu and team explore green 6G waveforms weighing non-right angles with right angles for backward fit and new ideas. As 6G grows, demand grows for ITU-defined jobs and powers, needing standards-fit waveforms. They look into SC-OFDM and SC-NOFS, in 1D and 2D forms. Both use 1D/2D pre-coding, giving bigger range, simpler handling, and delay-Doppler toughness. SC-NOFS in 2D improves thrift and reduces latency, making it a 6G pick. It offers powers spanning high data rate, movement, low-latency talk, and greenness.
arxiv-2603-05952: Liu and team present VINE for few-shot splitting under mis-match and cross-view clash. Few-shot splitting spreads to novel classes with limited guidance, yet struggles across views. VINE models shape sameness and foreground telling apart, tuning models. A space-view graph captures local layout and spreads view-fixed meaning. A telling prior from support-query gap shifts SAM features toward key regions. Enhanced SAM and ResNet traits blend through masked cross-focus into class-steady models. Tests back power and toughness under viewpoint shifts and complex structures.
arxiv-2603-06252: Pleiss and his team set out Synthetic Monitoring Environments, a suite of continuous control tasks that give reinforcement learning white box diagnostics. Environments tangle complexity and lack ground truth metrics, making failures hard to diagnose. SMEs offer configurable tasks with optimal policies, giving instant regret math and strict state bounds for within and out of distribution evaluation. Strip-downs of PPO, TD3, and SAC show how action and state space size, thin rewards, and policy complexity shape scores in distribution regimes. SMEs give a clear testbed for RL tests.
arxiv-2603-06352: Martínez and Ros-Oton study singular sets in parabolic obstacle problems with general blocks, proving Hausdorff dimension at most n minus 1. Before this, the result was known only when the Laplacian of the block equaled minus 1. Their approach joins monotonicity bounds and a truncated frequency formula, and by steps shows saturation for every cut parameter between 2 and 3.
arxiv-2603-06552: Sage and Greco describe KCLarity's CLARITY entry, a shared task on ambiguity and evasion classification in political discourse. They investigate two formulations: predicting the clarity label, and predicting the evasion label then deriving clarity through the task taxonomy hierarchy. They explore auxiliary training variants and zero-shot decoder-only models under the evasion-first formulation. In all, the two formulations perform comparably; among encoder-based models, RoBERTa-large leads the public test results, while zero-shot GPT-5.2 generalizes better on the hidden evaluation set.
arxiv-2603-06652: Li and colleagues address process hallucinations in multimodal reasoning, where models reach correct answers while misperceiving visual evidence. They propose PaLMR, aligning process and outcomes through a perception-aligned data layer and an optimization layer. The data layer builds reasoning data with pseudo-ground-truths and visual facts; the optimization layer fuses rewards with process-aware scoring for visually faithful chains-of-thought. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B reduce hallucinations and improve visual reasoning fidelity, reaching top results on HallusionBench while staying strong on MMMU, MathVista, and MathVerse.
arxiv-2603-06952: Song and colleagues study whether graph thinning can speed graph neural network flows without losing scores. As graphs grow to billions of nodes and edges, learning workloads strain under multi-hop walks over areas. Method tweaks help, yet data handling and flow remain jams at scale. Thinning cuts edges to create sparser areas, and may serve as a prep step for these jams while keeping scores on node sorting tasks. They build a setup to test thinning methods, running the study of GNN training and use over thinned graphs.
arxiv-2603-07052: Sekhmani and colleagues work out exact black hole shapes in a model where a Kalb-Ramond field breaks a key space-time symmetry. The field sits with a fluid that pushes in different ways along and across the radius. By setting the radial push to match dark energy and letting the side push vary, they cover dust, light-like matter, and dark-energy-like cases. They check curve measures for a true core flaw and test energy rules, which shift with field strength, fluid density, and the side-push choice.
arxiv-2603-07152: Posva and colleagues study linear alpha-p actions on affine spaces and their quotient singularities, using explicit stacky resolutions. They sort the singularities into log canonical, canonical, or terminal cases, and compute their stringy motivic invariants. A conjecture by the second author and Fabio Tonini says these invariants match those of linear Z-over-p quotients. The new approach reduces that conjecture to matching explicit multi-sets, checked for many primes by computer, with a general proof in an appendix.
arxiv-2603-07552: Yu and colleagues rebuild driving scenes fast with ReconDrive, a feed-forward 4D Gaussian splatting framework. Per-scene optimization is accurate but slow, while existing feed-forward methods lose visual quality. ReconDrive extends a 3D base model with hybrid guessing heads splitting spatial and look fitting, plus a static-dynamic mix capturing motion through velocity tracking. It beats feed-forward baselines on driving benchmarks and rivals per-scene tuning at far greater speed.
arxiv-2603-07752: Barzykin studies an over-the-counter FX market-making problem where a dealer streams size-dependent quotes and manages inventory risk. Adverse selection comes through latency-driven price moves, and the dealer can reject trades when slippage breaches a tolerance threshold. Slippage tolerance is treated as a control optimized with quotes, making each trade akin to an embedded option on the latency price move. Rejection feedback via an EMA score modulates future client intensity, and an adiabatic-quadratic approximation yields closed-form quotes and thresholds.
arxiv-2603-08052: Chiarelli and colleagues study a variant of Cops and Robbers with one cop and one robber, where the cop follows a fixed patrol walk chosen before play begins. The robber is omniscient and knows the patrol in advance, and capture happens when the robber comes within a set distance of the cop. They define the patrol capture radius as the smallest radius that lets the cop always capture the robber on a connected graph under optimal play. The work opens a systematic study of this parameter across several graph classes.
arxiv-2603-08352: Gallo and colleagues generalize the Kuramoto model of synchronization to higher dimensions, moving from scalar to matrix coupling. In the classical formulation, oscillators move on the unit circle, each with a scalar phase and a natural frequency, interacting through sinusoidal coupling. The authors propose a d-dimensional generalization in which oscillators are unit vectors on the d-minus-1 sphere. They interact through a matrix-weighted network, a framework where links carry a matrix weight instead of a scalar weight. This opens synchronization analysis to vector-valued states.
arxiv-2603-08452: Alekseev and colleagues classify unital cubic maps from the cyclic group of order 3 into an arbitrary non-abelian group. They show the universal group admitting such a map is infinite and give a concrete presentation of it. They also build an infinite representation of it in PSL3(C) whose image is an arithmetic lattice commensurable with PSL3(Z[omega]), where omega is a primitive cube root of unity. So finite nilpotent groups of arbitrarily large nilpotency class admit a unital cubic map from C3 whose image generates the group.
arxiv-2603-08552: Emanuele Borgonovo and colleagues study how to invest over time when payoffs bend and beliefs stay cloudy. Their frame handles bent payoffs, many tastes for risk, and shifting doubt, with learning built in. A robust rewrite turns the doubt-averse task into a doubt-neutral one with skewed priors, giving plain trading rules. A fund-manager case shows doubt tilting beliefs toward bad states and trimming risky bets.
arxiv-2603-08652: Haodong Li and colleagues reason about image making in code rather than in loose words. Word-only plans lack the precision that tangled layouts, structured visuals, and dense text demand. Their CoCo frame writes runnable code for the scene layout and runs it in a sandbox to draft the picture. Fine edits then polish that draft, beating plain generation on three test benches.
arxiv-2603-08752: Sumit Mukherjee offers electoral_sim, an open Python frame for comparing voting systems across voter landscapes. Voters and candidates sit as points in a two-dimensional ideology space, and ballots follow distance, scored against the voter median. Tests span consensus to polarized electorates over 200 trials per case, plus a Boltzmann softmax mechanism as a theoretical ceiling, not a policy pitch.
arxiv-2603-08852: Sunil Prakash offers LDP, a protocol for multi-agent language-model systems that knows who each delegate is. Current protocols hide model traits like identity, reasoning profile, quality scores, and cost, blocking smart hand-offs. LDP adds identity cards, agreed payload modes, governed sessions, origin tracking, and trust domains, cutting delay and tokens in tests while warning that raw confidence notes harm results.
arxiv-2603-09452: Xiangsen Chen and colleagues introduce CyberThreat-Eval, a benchmark testing whether language models can automate real-world cyber threat research. Analysts triage open source intelligence, search deeply, and draft reports, yet existing benchmarks pose multiple-choice tasks unlike real workflows and grade by word overlap. This expert-annotated benchmark, drawn from a leading company's daily workflow, covers all three stages. Its analyst-centered metrics score factual accuracy, content quality, and operational cost.
arxiv-2603-09552: Paolo Leopardi and colleagues weigh the costs and gains of task specialization in multi-robot systems through an evolved foraging task. Earlier work saw specialization emerge under evolution but asked if it was feasible, not what it cost. With a fixed evaluation budget they evolve neural networks as generalists for the whole task and as specialists for subtasks. The generalists tune well, while the specialists cooperate poorly and score worse, so specialization need not pay when the budget is tight.
arxiv-2603-09952: Ruihan Xu, Jiajin Li and Yiping Lu ask how neural network optimisers should scale as networks grow wider. They view tools such as AdamW and Muon as steepest descent under matrix operator norms. Standard norms break layerwise composition, blocking width free bounds in deep nets. A new family of mean normalised norms restores it, yields rescaled variants, and recovers muP scaling as one special case.
arxiv-2603-10152: Francesco Giancaterini and coauthors introduce a regularised test for serial dependence in high dimensional non Gaussian time series. The test checks the null claim that no linear or nonlinear serial dependence is present. Their approach extends a portmanteau test by Jasiak and Neyazi into the high dimensional setting, adding shrinkage regularisation to handle the many series at once. The abstract frames the method as the paper's central contribution.
arxiv-2603-10652: Yangfan He, Changgyu Boo, and Jaehong Yoon ask whether video reasoning models are ready for the outdoors, where weather, occlusion, and camera motion disturb what they see. Their ROVA framework trains for robustness with a consistency reward under spatio-temporal corruptions, and a difficulty-aware strategy that re-estimates sample difficulty as the model improves. A new benchmark, PVRBench, adds real-world perturbations to embodied video data. Rival models lost large chunks of accuracy under such disturbances, while ROVA cut the losses and even improved clean scores.
arxiv-2603-10852: Yali Zhu and coauthors build a team of AI agents that work together. The team reads breast ultrasound images in the order a clinician uses. It first finds the lesion. It then assesses its signs. It then assigns a category. The main agent joins the four structured signs to output a BI-RADS category. It also gives a benign-or-malignant call, and each step stays reviewable. Training runs in stages, with the sign agent taught first. Corrective trajectories are added later. Tests show gains over strong vision-language baselines.
arxiv-2603-10952: Anastasios Tzanidakis and James Davenport report a young F-type star, Gaia-GIC-1, whose light swings wildly as dusty material crosses in front of it. They argue the dust is debris from a recent planetary collision, forming a clumpy cloud on a bound orbit. A periodic modulation of 380.5 days in earlier Gaia data fits an orbiting clump, and the system has stayed infrared-bright for over four years. The fresh debris measures around 900 kelvin, and follow-up spectroscopy shows no prominent features, likely because the system varies so strongly.
arxiv-2603-11052: Haoze Song and coauthors measure uncertainty in neural operator surrogates for partial differential equations. They argue the bands should track the residual patterns that drive downstream risk. They do not perturb weights all over the network. They inject randomness only into the lifting module of the network's lifting-propagation-recovery anatomy, so the learned solver stays deterministic. Two light lifting-level changes plus calibration give more reliable coverage and tighter bands on hard benchmarks, including discontinuous-coefficient Darcy flow and three-dimensional car aerodynamics surrogates.
arxiv-2603-11252: Benedikt Schwab and Thomas Kolbe build radiometric fingerprints of city surfaces by pooling repeated mobile laser scans of the same semantic objects under different distances, angles, conditions, sensors, and campaigns. Semantic 3D city models are detailed but rarely record materials, while every laser return carries material information. The authors link hundreds of millions of beams from four campaigns and five sensors to 6,368 modeled objects across four inner-city streets. The fingerprints show recurring patterns within object classes, evidence that class-dominant materials can be read from scan data.
arxiv-2603-11352: Sravan Kumar Ankireddy and coauthors give time series transformers a variable-resolution tokenizer, patching sequences where the signal demands it instead of at fixed intervals. Point-wise tokens preserve detail but scale badly, while fixed patches can slice through natural transitions and blur local dynamics. Their TimeSqueeze runs a lightweight state-space encoder at full resolution, then segments by content. Short patches go to information-dense stretches and long patches to smooth ones, and the scheme beats point-wise and fixed-patch rivals in long-horizon forecasting.
arxiv-2603-11452: Aktar, Pan, and Okuda simulate gas falling onto spinning black holes in active galactic nuclei. Their flows reach the magnetically arrested disk state, where magnetic flux chokes the inflow. The model uses one temperature and counts bremsstrahlung as its radiation process. That arrested state holds at every spin they try, from none to near max. Spin, they find, has little effect on how the flow moves or on its spectrum. Post-processing with two temperatures shows very hot electrons in the jet region.
arxiv-2603-11952: Deoli and co-authors compare image registration methods for pairing RGB and near-infrared images in off-road forests. Registration underpins sensor fusion and off-road autonomy, but dense woods stress it hard. NeMAR, tried in six configurations, partly succeeds, though its GAN loss wobbles and geometry can slip. MURF aligns broad features well during shared information extraction, yet loses fine detail in thick vegetation. This early study, the authors say, shows the field needs sturdier multi-scale methods before forest use.
arxiv-2603-12052: Lolck, Thorup, and Yan sharpen a classic pivot method for correlation clustering. The classic algorithm earns a factor of three, and known tight cases rest on very good clusters. Their twist strips out all good clusters before each pivot step runs. That change pushes the proven approximation ratio just below three. Tests on synthetic data also look strong. The method beats both the classic pivot algorithm and the routine that locates good clusters.
arxiv-2603-12352: Zhang, Patnode, and Lee model how microbial links shift with covariates in a Bayesian frame. Microbiome counts bring discreteness, over-dispersion, and high dimensionality at once. Their factor model lets the covariance matrix vary with outside factors. A lower-dimensional loading matrix carries that change in a form that stays in reach. Dirichlet-Horseshoe priors induce joint sparsity for robust estimates in wide data. Mean abundance gets its own regression, and mock plus real data show the method performs well.
arxiv-2603-12452: Lazarotto and Ragazzo build a dissipative point-mass N-body model that preserves total angular momentum. Their forces drain energy between masses, as tidal effects do in real systems. Total angular momentum stays fixed by construction in this setup. For central configurations, a chosen distance law makes the motion match a lossy two-body problem. Poincaré tools then map the topology of solutions for that two-body case. Averaged equations show no effect of the dissipation on periapsis precession over Keplerian motion.
arxiv-2603-12552: Faris Chaudhry studies how the temperature setting shapes contrastive learning with the InfoNCE loss. He models how embeddings move under Langevin dynamics on a curved space. With slow cooling, in line with classic simulated annealing, the model is shown to reach the best set of representations with high chance. Faster cooling can leave it stuck in poor local minima. The results give a clear base for how to set and tune such schedules.
arxiv-2603-13152: I Maillette de Buy Wenniger and co-authors measure which-path information in light absorption and emission by a quantum dot. Two pulses excite the dot in a Ramsey-like sequence with a tunable phase gap. The dot then emits superpositions of zero- and one-photon states into two time bins. The first bin acts as a which-path detector for the interferometer. Its stored information cuts the contrast of Ramsey fringes over time. Later emission into the second bin is steered by that same record.
arxiv-2603-13352: Xi Chen, Maojun Zhang, Yu Liu, and Shen Yan propose SpectralMoE for domain generalization in semantic segmentation. Spectral shifts across capture conditions hurt models sent to unseen domains in remote sensing. Global fine-tuning of foundation models treats all land cover the same way, which causes confusion. SpectralMoE instead refines foundation model features locally, place by place. A dual-gated Mixture-of-Experts routes visual and depth features to top experts for tailored fixes. Cross-attention then fuses the refined depth cues into the visual stream.
arxiv-2603-13452: Gideon Popoola and John Sheppard introduce MESD, a metric for explanation fairness across intersectional subgroups. Outcome metrics like demographic parity cannot show whether a model reasons in different ways for different groups. That gap breaks procedural fairness, and fairness gerrymandering can hide it in single-attribute checks. MESD measures gaps in explanation quality across subgroups formed by multiple protected attributes. It joins label-aware aggregation, empirical-Bayes shrinkage for small groups, and CVaR weighting for worst cases. Tests show it reveals disparities that outcome metrics miss.
arxiv-2603-13552: Piyush Sao studies complex singularities that limit safe step sizes in cross-entropy training. Optimization analyses use local Taylor models, which hold only inside the Taylor convergence radius along the update direction. That radius is set by the nearest complex singularity, not real-line curvature alone. For cross-entropy, zeros of the softmax partition function create logarithmic singularities he calls ghosts of softmax. He derives closed-form radius formulas under logit linearization for binary and multiclass cases. Across six architectures, no model failed below the normalized threshold.
arxiv-2603-13852: Xiotidis and co-authors test AMD Versal AI Engines for physics setups that demand fixed, microsecond-scale latency. These chips place AI co-processors beside programmable logic in one package. The team runs a boosted decision tree and a convolutional neural network in vectorized form on the engines. A further network, built for the ATLAS Phase-II trigger, is checked on open data. They conclude the engines can add useful compute to FPGA systems and may replace some logic-based designs.
arxiv-2603-13952: Chen and co-authors use language model feedback as the reward for audio-visual speech enhancement. Standard scores like signal-to-noise ratio track perceived quality poorly and explain little. An audio language model describes the enhanced speech in words, and a sentiment model turns that text into a rating from one to five. That rating trains the enhancement model with PPO reinforcement learning. On the AVSEC-4 dataset, the method beats supervised and DNSMOS-based baselines on quality metrics and listening tests.
arxiv-2603-14152: Wang and co-authors add precise skeleton control to native 3D generation with SK-Adapter. Text and image prompts stay vague about exact pose and joint layout. Their light adapter turns joint positions and bone links into tokens that a frozen 3D backbone reads through cross-attention. The base model keeps its shape and texture quality while following the skeleton. A new dataset, Objaverse-TMS, gives 24,000 text, mesh, and skeleton triples for training. Tests beat prior baselines and extend to local 3D editing.
arxiv-2603-14552: Palethorpe and co-authors pin down the makeup of small transiting exoplanets in six systems. Exact mass and radius values reveal planet makeup and history. The team joins new CHEOPS transit data with older K2 and TESS photometry. Radial velocity data come from HARPS-N, HIRES, ESPRESSO and more. Joint fits reach errors under 15% for mass and 5% for radius. Found worlds range from rocky planets to steam-rich and low-density cases. Some systems hide extra companions seen only in velocity data, they note.
arxiv-2603-14852: Yamamoto and co-authors plan surgical robot paths in joint space on a Riemannian manifold. Robotic forceps must pivot around a fixed insertion port. Angle limits bind the arm during minimally invasive work. The belly cavity surface is mostly non-concave, a costly shape in position space. Mapping position into a manifold reframes the search. An edge cost function guides the path hunt in joint space. Gradient descent finds near-best paths with ease on that shape. Joint travel shrinks versus position-space plans, they report.
arxiv-2603-15252: Lellouch and co-authors detail the integrals behind a three-loop calculation of hadronic vacuum polarization. Each integral gets a full treatment. They explain how to compute every one and lay out the math behind the method. The work ends in a fast numerical code. That code gives accurate values for any complex photon virtuality. The account supports the companion physics result published earlier.
arxiv-2603-15552: Oumarou and co-authors build a fair way to compare two early fault-tolerant methods for molecular energies: statistical phase estimation and Krylov subspace diagonalization. Both methods feed on expectation values of Chebyshev polynomials of the Hamiltonian. For the Krylov route, they optimize shot allocation and keep the spanning states nonlinear enough. For phase estimation, tighter error bounds cut circuit depth by about a third. Scaling checks reach active spaces of 54 electrons in 36 orbitals, using tensor network tools.
arxiv-2603-15752: Kim and co-authors image cool hydrogen gas around 22 gas-rich Seyfert galaxies. The hard X-ray picked hosts hold at least 10^9.7 solar masses of HI. About 80 percent have HI-detected neighbors nearby. Many show lopsided gas, one-sided tails, or bridges to companions. Size and star formation follow known scaling relations with no odd offsets. Hosts are often the biggest systems in their groups. Wider HI disks pair with stronger AGN activity. The team reads this as gas gained from neighbors fueling the nuclei.
arxiv-2603-15852: Anwar and Georgalos test whether chat sustains cooperation against an AI partner. Some 234 people played repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games against GPT-5.2. Groups got no chat, one pre-play chat, or chat before each round. A fourth group faced a human under the same chat rule. One chat exchange lifted cooperation from 49 to 84 percent. Extra chats added under one point more. Cooperation with the AI matched the human case. Strategy style still shifted by partner type, though. People reciprocated humans but cooperated flatly with the AI.
arxiv-2603-16452: Wang and co-authors study peak heat flux for the first mode of a convex domain. Their scale-free ratio compares boundary flux against the first eigenvalue. For convex shapes, they bound the flux by a constant times that eigenvalue. Layer potential tools give shape-derivative formulas for fast computing. Numeric searches over rounded polygons point to one winner. The semidisk likely maximizes the ratio, with peak flux mid-diameter. They prove the semidisk is a critical point under small arc changes.
arxiv-2603-16552: Bobadilla and Camjayi find a route to spin-polarized currents in plain antiferromagnets. Antiferromagnets suit spintronics but their balanced spins long blocked active use. A selection rule states what a polarized dc current needs. Both particle-hole symmetry and sublattice equivalence must break at once. In the Hubbard model, doping and a magnetic field break one each. Correlations then turn uneven scattering into a sizable polarization. It peaks deep in the ordered phase and flips sign.
arxiv-2603-16752: Van Caelenberg, Stratigakos, and Spyrou build day-ahead scenarios that keep power reserves deliverable. Congestion often blocks reserves when forecast errors hit in real time. Adding error patterns as extra cases can guard the plan. Older methods missed how grid layout and the schedule shape that congestion. Their two-stage robust model ties day-ahead choices to real-time stress. A search loop builds cases from the worst error pattern it can find. On the RTS-GMLC test grid, blocked reserves fell sharply. The case count shifts with each schedule.
arxiv-2603-17052: Zhao and co-authors investigate collapse problems in vector quantization, a method that turns continuous representations into discrete tokens. Such tokenization underlies many language and diffusion models, yet its failure modes are little studied. Using synthetic and real data, they map two collapse types: tokens collapse and embeddings collapse. They identify triggers such as random initialization and limited encoder capacity. They then propose fixes aimed at each collapse type. The authors call this a first full study of representation collapse in vector quantization.
arxiv-2603-17652: Jiang, Zhou, Liu, and Sun present VectorWorld, a streaming world model for driving policy tests. Log replay cannot react, and older generative models drift or lag in closed loop. VectorWorld paints ego-centric vector-graph tiles of lanes and agents as the run unfolds. A gated VAE builds a start state that matches history-aware policies. One-step masked completion keeps generation real time. Closed-loop runs stayed stable past one kilometer, they report.
arxiv-2603-17952: Manna and co-authors test gender handling in decoder-only translation models. Languages mark gender in unlike ways, so translation must often guess what the source left vague. Their framework adds a Prior Bias score for a model's default gender lean. Decoder-only systems did not clearly beat encoder-decoder ones on gender metrics, they find. Extra post-training sharpened context use and cut the masculine lean. Scale alone did not fix the bias.
arxiv-2603-18052: Malarchick maps how small dense Lindblad propagation runs on near-term quantum control hardware. At Hilbert sizes 3, 9, and 27, cache limits and launch costs matter more than peak speed. He tests two CPUs, two NVIDIA GPUs, and a low-cost FPGA. Gaps trace to thread forks, strided reads, PCIe transfers, and propagator uploads. A GRAPE-style test shows fast propagation does not mean fast control tuning; the propagator build dominates at size 27.
arxiv-2603-18252: Samorzewski and Kliks study where to place reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in a Poznan mobile network. They map radio propagation across the city for a 5G/6G access network with eight base stations. Simulations cover line-of-sight and blocked paths among high-rise buildings, with SISO and MIMO cells. Strategic surface placement cuts path loss and lifts coverage where base stations alone fall short. Fewer new base stations are then needed, lowering network cost.
arxiv-2603-18452: Yu, Alajaji, and Gharesifard introduce Polya threshold graphs, a random graph model built from an urn process. Each new node is universal or isolated, set by a draw from a two-color Polya urn. The adjacency matrix has an explicit form in terms of the draw sequence. They derive the exact degree distribution, a decay centrality expectation, and the Laplacian spectrum. Consensus dynamics on these graphs are analyzed as an application.
arxiv-2603-18752: Rio-Torto, Cardoso, and Teixeira build WeNLEX, which explains chest X-ray labels in plain sentences. Most explanation systems train on large sets of human-written rationales. Those texts can sound right while missing the model's true reasons. WeNLEX needs as few as five true examples per diagnosis. Images rebuilt from its explanations must match the source scan in feature space, which enforces faithfulness. A small clinician database keeps wording plausible. Validation covers faithfulness, diversity, and plausibility. Joint training even lifts classifier AUC by 2.21 percent over the plain classifier.
arxiv-2603-18852: Marburger and co-authors measure the stretch factor in hydrogen-air flames hit by thermodiffusive instability. A rod anchors a V-flame in a laminar premixed flow. Near the rod, the flame stays smooth with a clear angle and burning rate. Downstream, it breaks into cellular wrinkles at a sharp transition. OH-PLIF imaging tracks both branches and their surface angles. Three methods estimate the wrinkled area growth over a smooth reference. The stretch factor falls from about 1.2 to about 0.85 as the fuel share rises, matching theory.
arxiv-2603-19052: Patel shows that the Hodge bundle over the space of curves of genus at least two holds no proper sub-bundles. The bundle is a basic object in the study of curve families. A sub-bundle would split its structure in a way the result rules out. The paper also notes a striking fact. The math content was generated by Aletheia, a custom AI agent built on Gemini Deep Think. That makes the work a case study in AI made proof.
arxiv-2603-19552: Yu and co-authors present StreetForward, a feedforward system that rebuilds dynamic street scenes fast. Driving tools need quick scene reconstruction without slow per-scene tuning. StreetForward needs no camera poses or trackers as input. A temporal mask attention module, built on the VGGT design, captures motion across frames. Static and moving content share one 3D Gaussian Splatting model. On the Waymo Open Dataset, it beats prior methods on new views and depth. Zero-shot tests on CARLA confirm it generalises.
arxiv-2603-19952: Malcolm and Bogenberger ask how much traffic future lane-free city streets could carry. Self-driving cars may not need fixed lanes at all. A simple analytic model shows lane-free flow beats lane-based flow for the same street width. It also shows capacity grows smoothly with width, not in lane-sized steps. They then simulate signal-free intersections run by automated management. Their OptWULF approach uses conflict-based search across agents plus a window-based planner. OptWULF used the whole drivable area evenly and handled uneven demand well.
arxiv-2603-20052: Effenberger and Knutti trace where uncertainty in wind and solar forecasts comes from. They study 31 pairings of regional and global climate models. A variance split, resolved by place and season, separates each model's share. For the base climate fields, regional models dominate the spread. For projected wind changes, the driving global model matters most, except in mountains. Solar radiation flips by season: regional models rule in summer, global ones in winter. The results guide how to build ensembles for energy planning under climate change.
arxiv-2603-20352: Middlehurst and co-authors expand a key archive for multivariate time series classification. The old UEA archive held 30 data sets and saw heavy use. Their Multiverse archive grows it to 133 classification problems. Cleaned versions of messy data sets bring the total to 147. The archive merges other collections and lone data sets into one repository. A smaller core subset helps teams start without huge compute costs. Baseline tests with established and recent classifiers set benchmarks for future work.
arxiv-2603-21052: Zhao and Wang settle a conjecture on the Erdős-Ginzburg-Ziv constant of finite groups. The constant is the smallest length that forces any sequence in a group to contain a full length subsequence whose product, in some order, is the identity. Gao and Li had conjectured a bound of three halves of the group order for non-cyclic groups. The authors confirm it for all non-cyclic groups whose order is not divisible by four. Equality holds exactly for groups with a cyclic subgroup of index two.
arxiv-2603-21152: Liu and co-authors introduce TRACE, a multi-agent system that does physical reasoning for seismology on its own. Modern seismic networks record earthquake sequences in fine detail, but explaining how big quakes emerge stays hard. TRACE plans and runs workflows while keeping auditable evidence chains from data to interpretation. On the 2019 Ridgecrest sequence, it built a high resolution catalog and recovered delayed cascading between the two main shocks. On the 2025-2026 Sanriku sequence, it formed a testable account of progressive destabilization in a segmented megathrust.
arxiv-2603-21252: Owusu-Ensaw and co-authors characterize where a modified Hardy operator stays bounded on integrable functions. The classic Hardy operator is not bounded on L1 of the positive half-line, nor is its discrete form on summable sequences. They subtract a natural corrective term to build a modified operator. They then find the largest subspace on which it maps integrable functions to integrable functions. The sharp condition is a logarithmic integrability requirement, whose weight reflects obstructions at both small and large scales.
arxiv-2603-21552: Dong asks whether human mobility can look like an equilibrium system when viewed at coarser time scales. Using five years of intercity flow data covering millions of travelers, Dong finds short-term flows are strongly asymmetric. As flows are averaged over longer windows, over half of city pairs settle toward balance. Directional imbalance decays as a power law. The rest show steady drift or a crossover between regimes. A stochastic model splitting drift from correlated fluctuations reproduces all three behaviors.
arxiv-2603-21752: Hannula and co-authors speed up Bayesian inference for Kuramoto models, the standard tool for synchronization in oscillator networks. Full Bayesian treatment is slow here, since state spaces are large and likelihoods are hard to compute. Their amortized approach trains a neural network on simulated phase data to mimic the posterior at once. Later inference then needs no fresh sampling or optimization per dataset. On synthetic Kuramoto networks, the method tracked posterior shape and uncertainty well, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-21852: Odrzywołek shows that one binary operator can generate every function of a scientific calculator. The operator, called eml, takes exp of its first input minus the log of its second, plus the constant one. From this single node he builds e, pi, and i, plus arithmetic and the usual transcendental functions. Each formula becomes a binary tree of identical nodes, a grammar as spare as hardware's NAND gate. He found the operator by exhaustive search. Shallow eml trees can recover exact formulas from numeric data by gradient training.
arxiv-2603-21952: Mathur and co-authors pick small variable sets for generalized linear models in biomedical data. Exact best subset selection cannot be computed at high dimension. Their COMBSS-GLM method relaxes subset choice into continuous weights, optimized by a Frank-Wolfe scheme fed by envelope gradients. Each step needs one penalized fit. Theory marks a curvature regime where the relaxed problem's minima sit at binary corners. In simulations and two real studies, rice genome and cancer data, it matched known loci and scored perfectly with few genes.
arxiv-2603-22252: Ueda and co-authors present SelfTTS, a speech system that moves speaking style across voices. Most systems lean on pre-trained speaker or emotion encoders. SelfTTS needs neither. It separates speaker and emotion information with gradient reversal layers and a cosine similarity loss. A contrastive method then clusters the speaker and emotion embeddings by label. The system also refines its own output through self-augmentation, using its voice conversion skill. Tests show stronger emotional naturalness than top baselines. Target timbre and emotion also stay more stable.
arxiv-2603-22452: Bittner builds a geometric account of slow thermodynamics in open quantum systems. He places the dynamics on a control manifold of steady states. In that picture, the work over a cycle equals the flux of a curvature form. For thermal steady states the curvature vanishes, matching the area laws. States that keep quantum coherence reshape the curvature, making it uneven and sign-changing. Work then depends on where a cycle sits and how it is oriented, and coherence can cut or even reverse net work.
arxiv-2603-22552: Tonapi and Paquin ask whether a network's node labels can stay coprime along every edge while the network changes over time. They define dynamic coprime labeling as a chain of one-to-one labelings driven by a fixed rule that preserves coprimality. Their main result is an equivalence: a graph has such a dynamic labeling exactly when it has a classical coprime labeling. They describe families of allowed rules and build labelings for paths, wheels, cycles, and hypercubes. An application to Carmichael's theorem closes the work.
arxiv-2603-23452: Sheng unifies the ways of solving the inverse Kohn-Sham problem. The problem asks for a local potential whose ground state gives a target density. Past schemes speak in split tongues: penalties, iterations, PDE constraints, and more. Sheng anchors them in a fixed-density constrained search with density-potential duality. In that frame, the potential acts as a dual object tied to matching the density. He sorts methods by how they treat the state equations. The map shows where ambiguity and weak-gap trouble enter each design.
arxiv-2603-24252: Karimov and co-authors solve a sub-diffusion problem with a regularized Prabhakar fractional derivative. They study the first initial-boundary value problem for that equation. A superposition step splits it into two simpler boundary problems. They then write the solution in explicit form, along with its Green's function. That function uses a two-variable Mittag-Leffler type function. They prove the formula they obtain truly solves the problem posed. The work gives a closed-form route for this class of fractional diffusion problems.
arxiv-2603-24352: Domingos and co-authors study totally umbilical real hypersurfaces in products of complex space forms. In single complex space forms with nonzero curvature, such hypersurfaces do not exist. The authors ask what happens in products of these spaces. They prove rigidity and nonexistence results for the product setting. If a hypersurface has no local product structure, its shape operator cannot be parallel. They also classify the umbilical cases that do carry a local product structure. Those turn out to be totally geodesic or extrinsic hyperspheres.
arxiv-2603-24652: He and co-authors explain when network pruning works by looking at representation hierarchies inside language models. Pruned models often keep performance on non-generative tasks but fail at generation, and the reason was unclear. They split the model's computation into embedding, logit, and probability spaces. Embeddings and logits prove largely robust to pruning damage. The nonlinear step from logits to probabilities amplifies small deviations, which then build up across time steps during generation. That explains why retrieval and multiple-choice tasks survive pruning while open-ended generation degrades.
arxiv-2603-24952: Iles and co-authors present a new way to tell which stars belong to a galaxy's central bar. Their test uses dynamical actions, quantities tied to a star's orbit. Stars in a bar feel a lopsided pull, so their actions fail to stay constant. The team turns that failure into a star-by-star rule, checked within measurement error. Tests on simulated galaxies recover bar length and angle close to what the eye finds, with length off by about nine percent on average.
arxiv-2603-25052: Miao and Ungar probe why a language model's stated confidence often misses its true accuracy. Probes and steering tests show two signals live inside the model. One tracks how likely an answer is right. The other drives the confidence the model says out loud. The two run at right angles, so they barely interact. Asking the model to reason while it scores itself warps the spoken signal and worsens the mismatch. Their two-stage steering reads the inner estimate and bends the spoken score to match it.
arxiv-2603-25352: Błaszak, Marciniak, and Szablikowski grow soliton hierarchies from pencils of special algebras. They define Novikov algebras of Stäckel type, tied to classic separable metrics in Viète coordinates. Pairs of these algebras, mixed as pencils, can extend to matching Poisson operators. Those operators then spawn whole families of soliton equations. The harvest includes coupled Korteweg-de Vries and coupled Harry Dym chains. Triangular versions of both chains appear as well. The route turns an algebraic pencil into rich integrable systems.
arxiv-2603-25452: Konan and Aman bring a new calculus to the control of delayed random systems. Their target is the stochastic Volterra equation, where the present state sums the whole past, with delay added. They use Hida-Malliavin tools to study the best control. The partner adjoint process turns out to obey an anticipated backward Volterra equation. From that shape they prove maximum principles of both kinds: one that any best control must obey, and one that certifies a control as best. The frame is broad and rigorous.
arxiv-2603-25552: Bortolotti and co-authors ask whether bent spacetime can blur the line between identical particles. Noncommutative spacetime twists the rules of Poincaré symmetry, and with them Bose and Fermi statistics. They build a field theory on the broadest oscillator algebra that fits that twist. Pure twisted statistics would spark Pauli-forbidden atomic jumps at rates labs have already ruled out. A quon-like variant damps those jumps enough, but only if sector walls break down. Particle sameness itself starts to crack, which motivates sharper Pauli tests.
arxiv-2603-25752: Liu and co-authors propose a model for recognizing emotion in multimodal conversations. Noise in audio and video can distort features and skew fusion. Text also carries more emotion cues than the other streams, a point past work often ignores. Their model first denoises audio and video with a differential transformer. It then builds relation graphs within and across modalities to track speaker-linked emotion patterns. A text-guided diffusion step spreads audio and video cues into the text stream. The authors report more robust and better aligned fusion.
arxiv-2603-26052: Chen and co-authors present MaLSF, a framework for verifying multimodal media by checking local details. Global fusion can wash out small clashes between image and text. MaLSF instead uses mask-label pairs as anchors between pixels and words. A two-way module lets text query the image and the image query the text. This cross-checking pinpoints the exact conflicts. A second module gathers those signals for the final call. The authors report top scores on the DGM4 and fake news tasks.
arxiv-2603-26152: Soares and Peres review the quantum and topological traits of graphene plasmonic systems. Plasmons are collective waves that couple light with charge motion in a material. The authors cover single-layer graphene and twisted bilayer graphene. Other stackings of graphene sheets are included as well. They also treat several built structures. These include gratings, grids, chains of graphene disks, and the kagomé lattice. The article maps how twist, topology, and quantum effects meet in this family of platforms.
arxiv-2603-26252: Xiao and Holloway propose a three-layer plan for AI tools that support teamwork among people with mixed abilities. Most access tools serve one person facing one barrier, they note. Yet many hard tasks get done through partners whose skills fit together. Their layers cover sharing facts across abilities, mediating workflows between partners, and acting as a bounded partner toward shared goals. The plan builds on the Ability-Diverse Collaboration framework and grounding theory.
arxiv-2603-26452: Mlkvik, Spaldin, and Ederer present a unified first-principles account of vanadium dioxide across its phases. They combine density-functional theory with dynamical mean-field theory, using an unusual bond-centred orbital basis. That basis lets one setup cover the rutile, M1, M2, and T phases without pre-sorting vanadium pairs. In the M2 phase they find two distinct insulating states on its two chain types, one singlet and one Mott. The two stay strongly coupled, so both switch together at the metal-insulator transition.
arxiv-2603-27052: Yang and co-authors map the barriers to generative AI adoption across disciplines and roles at one university. Rather than blaming personal attitudes, they test whether barriers are built into the system itself. The survey covered 272 academic and professional services staff at a Russell Group university. Regression, structural modeling, and text clustering gave a multi-level picture. Non-STEM academics stressed ethics and integrity concerns most. STEM and services staff stressed governance and infrastructure limits instead. The authors urge governance by role over generic training.
arxiv-2603-27352: Liu asks which structural correlations make covalent network glasses rigid at the Maxwell threshold. Four candidates are tested against a tree-like, order-free baseline model. Enthalpic stress delays rigidity instead. Chemical defects need fractions near 40 percent, far above real values. Geometric linking does not set the threshold either. Only medium-range order proxies restore rigidity at real strengths. Chalcogenide phase data and silica ring counts support medium-range order. DNA networks rule out pure entanglement as the cause.
arxiv-2603-27452: Fisk and co-authors give robot fingers a way to tune grip friction. Each fingertip holds small rollers that spin freely or lock. Free rollers let objects slide along one line. Locked rollers grip like a plain fingertip. The rollers can also pivot to new angles. A gripper with these tips passed hard tests. It slid and turned parts inside the grasp. It also held mixed parts and coped with unsure contact points. The design stays simple and cheap to build.
arxiv-2603-27552: Pranav M R and co-authors introduce BLOSSOM, which lets scattered clients train one multimodal model together. Real clients often lack some data types entirely. Most federated methods assume all clients share all types. BLOSSOM accepts any subset of modalities per client. Shared blocks merge across clients each round. Task-specific blocks stay private on each device. That split yields partial personalization for each site. In sparse settings, scores rise 18.7 percent over full merging. Tests span several diverse datasets.
arxiv-2603-27752: Yu and co-authors catch hallucinations in retrieval-augmented answers claim by claim. RT4CHART splits each answer into checkable claims. Each claim is judged against the retrieved context. Labels mark claims as entailed, contradicted, or baseless. Checks run from local spans up to the whole answer. Verdicts map back to exact answer spans. Context evidence is returned for each call. Tests on RAGTruth sets lead rival detectors.
arxiv-2603-28052: Lee and five co-authors argue that an AI system's harness, the code that stores and feeds it context, shapes results as much as the model itself. Harnesses are still written by hand, so they built Meta-Harness to search over harness code on its own. The searcher reads past code, scores, and run traces from a filesystem. Found harnesses beat a top context system by 7.7 points and topped hand-built baselines on coding tasks.
arxiv-2603-28252: Kumar, Dash, and Alexandropoulos analyze secret key rates for a quantum key system boosted by a smart reflective surface. The setup sends Gaussian-modulated light at terahertz frequencies through direct and reflected MIMO links. They model an eavesdropper who can tap only some path segments, a realistic limit on access. Their formulas cover every access pattern, and a swarm search tunes the surface phases for the best rate. The sender-to-surface leg proves the most security-critical.
arxiv-2603-28352: Pratiher gives a light trigonometric test for how many roots of a quintic equation are real. Quintics have no general formula, thanks to the Abel-Ruffini theorem, so a cheap root census is handy. He rewrites a depressed quintic through a Chebyshev identity into an equation in cosines. The shape of that equation reveals the split between real and complex roots. The method extends a known quartic trick and needs little computation.
arxiv-2603-28752: Jankowski, Palumbo, and Slager report a universal topological dichroism in chiral three-dimensional systems. The response depends on the chirality of the light itself. Chiral topological invariants produce integer-quantized differences in dichroic excitation rates. The effect also arises more generally from coupling optical chirality to higher tensor Berry curvatures. Dixmier-Douady invariants and Hopf indices enter that broader picture.
