Youngmin Oh studies learning from duels when the world cheats and the mail is late. In linear dueling bandits an agent picks pairs and learns from which won. Here the context that matters arrives only after serving, feedback lands after unknown delays, and an adversary corrupts some of it within a total budget.

His algorithm learns a predictor of the post-serving context from what is known before serving. It weights past observations adaptively, clipping feature vectors so corrupted and stale duels do limited harm at once. The regret bound he proves does not care which delay regime is in force, and its cost splits additively between corruption and delay rather than multiplying, the usual fate of such analyses. Matching lower bounds for adversarial delay, up to a mild factor, say the price is near forced. Code is public.
arxiv-2605-02452:
Xiyuan Wang and four co-authors ask a flipped question in a position paper on large language models. Much work uses these models to help graph tasks. The authors ask instead how graphs, the networks of linked nodes used across computing, can help the models work better and fail less often.

Three routes get the focus. Graphs can supply fresh, checked facts to cut false claims. Graph-shaped prompts, from chain forms to tree and graph forms, can guide step-by-step thought. Graphs can also help models read structured data in shops, code, and databases. The paper closes with future ideas, such as sparse model designs drawn from graphs and memory systems modeled on the brain.
arxiv-2605-02552:
Firas Mohamed Elamine Kiram and four co-authors test whether memory helps a learning controller set chemotherapy doses when the patient's full state cannot be seen. Dose choice is a sequence of trade-offs between shrinking a tumor and limiting harm. Most learning approaches assume the state is fully observed, which clinics rarely have.

The team uses a recurrent deep method with memory networks for both actor and critic, and compares recurrent and non-recurrent variants on a standard chemotherapy benchmark. Patient variation is held fixed so that only hidden state and noisy readings differ. Memory gave a small edge when the state was fully known, but a much larger, steadier edge when it was partial. Tumor control was more consistent, and healthy cells were better preserved.
arxiv-2605-02752:
Giacomo Pacini and five co-authors show that text-guided counting models often count the wrong thing. Such models count objects of any class named in a written prompt, a flexible idea for open-world use. Standard tests, though, use single-category images and score only the count, so they never check whether the model grounded the prompt in the right class.

Several leading models, the team finds, often fail to tell which class should be counted, giving spurious counts and weak real-world reliability. Their fix is a new evaluation frame: a test suite with a negative-label test and a distractor test, plus new metrics for each. A fresh dataset of real multi-category images, with rich annotation, supports the tests. The message is that counting accuracy without grounding is not trust.
arxiv-2605-02852:
Savik Kinger and four co-authors infer which neurons in a circuit actually drive each other, and at what delay, from population recordings. Neural circuits compute through directed, fast interactions that play out across time scales and settings. The problem is to recover those local links from sampled activity without assuming a simple form for the underlying dynamics, which real brains rarely obey.

Their method trains denoising score models on windows of consecutive brain states. Products of scores across blocks recover the sensitivity map between states, which is turned into calibrated, directed edge tests. Multi-block windows that condition on middle time points separate effects by lag and avoid a bias of pairwise analysis. Applied to whole-brain imaging of a small worm, the method recovered lag-specific structure that current methods miss.
arxiv-2605-02952:
Mengman Wei and Qian Peng propose a systems frame for how teen mental health and substance use develop over time. Genes, life exposures, and brain processes interact across years, and single snapshots miss that motion. Their model casts genes as the base state. Exposures act as inputs that vary with time. The brain serves as a middle processor, and behavior emerges as the output.

Data come from a large long-term study of teen brain development. Harmonized measures cover acting-out and inward-turning behavior, plus first use of alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, and any substance. Gene-based risk scores, broad exposure features, and brain imaging summaries feed the frame. Both smooth tracking over time and event-time modeling share one data structure. Domain-level summaries keep the results readable.
arxiv-2605-03052:
Zhejian Zhou, Tianyi Zhou, Robin Jia, and Jonathan May probe how large language models handle negation inside, not just in their final answers. Open models often answer negation questions wrong, yet the authors test whether some internal parts still process the negation correctly.

Experiments on Mistral and Llama models show late attention layers push simple shortcuts that cause many errors; removing them raises accuracy sharply. Probing further, the models use two routes at once: heads that attend to the negated phrase, and a stronger route that builds a full representation of the negative phrase itself.
arxiv-2605-03552:
Stefano Della Fiore studies how short a source code can be when blocks of symbols, not just single symbols, are counted. He uses a Pareto-type test of finite-block optimality, which compares codes through the full sequence of their expected block lengths. His test case is a four-symbol constrained Markov source, a source where only certain symbol strings are allowed.

Della Fiore builds a canonical code that orders allowed strings by their information cost and assigns binary strings in shortlex order. He proves the expected lengths fall below the natural per-symbol rate for blocks of length two or more. The result shows that a well-known code for this source is not Pareto-optimal.
arxiv-2605-04152:
Timothy Trott studies what consistency alone forces on the basic forces of particle physics, by demanding that scattering amplitudes behave properly in a unitary, local theory in four dimensions. For particles without mass, new limits come from how amplitudes split apart in a controlled complex setting.

Those limits recover the full structure of gluon interactions, including restrictions on the underlying symmetry algebra and on parity and time-reversal behaviour. For massive particles, Trott calculates scattering for spins up to one in full generality and maps where the energy growth becomes dangerous. The results explain how massive vector boson scattering is softened, and what lies beyond.
arxiv-2605-04252:
Daniel Bath and three co-authors give a recipe for smoothing the singularities of configuration hypersurfaces, shapes defined by polynomials that generalise ones from graph theory and particle physics. These shapes are usually highly singular, which makes related integrals hard to evaluate even in simple cases.

Their two-step method first passes to a blow-up variety linked to work of Bloch, then builds a smooth tropical compactification using combinatorics of a special matroid family. They construct the needed maps explicitly for every configuration. Along the way they show the blow-up has a strong regularity property in positive characteristic.
arxiv-2605-04352:
Igor Rivin builds a benchmark for testing deep structural reasoning in language models, based on hard problems about subgroups of a matrix group over the integers. Each problem gives a subgroup by listing its generators and asks for a number-theoretic property of that subgroup.

The construction hides information that makes the answer a quick closed-form check for the maker, while a solver without it must do serious algebraic analysis. Rivin reports traces from two leading models, including one that spent over two hours on a single case and named the bottleneck itself. The gap separates models with real algebraic knowledge from those relying on general computation.
arxiv-2605-04552:
Brielen Madureira and three co-authors study what makes Brazilian disasters newsworthy abroad. Media coverage shapes disaster response. Yet the drivers of foreign attention to local events are poorly understood. Brazil has also lacked a broad, checked news data set for studying them.

The authors analyse about two thousand items on Brazilian fires and landslides in German newspapers from 2000 to 2024. Using time series splitting, they detect peaks of attention. They check how well those peaks line up in time with events in national and global disaster records. Their peak analysis is a step toward explaining which Brazilian disasters reach foreign headlines.
arxiv-2605-04752:
Eugene Kofi Okrah Denteh and three co-authors build a hybrid system for classifying traffic congestion that joins two kinds of evidence most earlier work treated separately. Camera-based methods read the scene but lean on static appearance and crude time pooling, while signal-based methods capture motion dynamics yet cannot locate congestion within a scene.

Their framework lets dense optical flow, the measured motion between frames, guide attention over image features so the model focuses on moving, relevant regions. In parallel, aggregated flow statistics form motion traces that are decomposed by empirical mode decomposition into natural temporal components. The fused representation aims to classify congestion with both spatial grounding and data-adaptive timing.
arxiv-2605-04852:
Emmanuel Avila and three co-authors estimate properties of exploding stars from gravitational waves given off when a rapidly rotating stellar core bounces. They aim to recover the ratio of rotation energy to gravity and to probe the equation of state, which describes matter under extreme pressure. Their work uses real detector noise rather than clean simulated noise.

An added timescale parameter improves how well their template matches waveform databases. Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo on hundreds of simulated signals, they recover the rotation measure with a median error near twelve percent. They also show real noise can bias results, while better prior choices can cut that bias sharply.
arxiv-2605-04952:
Klaus-Rudolf Kladny and three co-authors cut the routing cost in mixture-of-experts language models, where each token is sent to only a few specialist sub-networks. Using many tiny experts improves performance, but scoring every expert for every token becomes the dominant cost. Their routing design borrows the inverted index idea from search engines.

First, tokens are matched to quantisation codewords to build a shortlist of candidate experts. Exact scores are then computed only within that shortlist, closely approximating full routing with no added constraints on expert design. Tests showed a better accuracy-to-compute trade-off than existing routers, even with more than a million tiny experts.
arxiv-2605-05052:
Elias Haslauer and six co-authors train interpretable neural networks to predict the momentum carried by mountain-driven gravity waves in the atmosphere. Climate-scale models cannot resolve these small waves directly, so their effects must be approximated by formulas. Better learned approximations could improve those models if scientists can see what the networks rely on.

Trained on a full year of reanalysis data and tested on another year, the networks predicted momentum fluxes with moderate to good accuracy across four wave selections. An explainability analysis using SHAP values suggested the networks had learned physically meaningful relationships. The authors also give guidance on when such learned parameterisations can be trusted.
arxiv-2605-05352:
Shauvik Biswas and Sayan Chakrabarti study how electromagnetic waves ring around parametrised wormholes, and what that ringing reveals about the wormhole's shape. Quasinormal modes are the decaying tones of a perturbed spacetime. Using a standard parametrisation, the authors describe static, spherical wormholes, including Damour-Solodukhin and braneworld examples, through far-field and near-throat parameters.

They first map where the parametrisation stays valid for isolated wormholes, finding non-smooth metric functions can limit it and distort the main ringdown signal. They then embed a wormhole in a dark matter halo and constrain its parameters using the observed shadow of the galactic centre black hole. Within that allowed range they compute the fundamental ringing frequencies.
arxiv-2605-05652:
Simulation-based inference learns to estimate parameters from a simulator, but real data rarely match the simulator exactly. Joon Jang, Eunho Jeong, Kyu Sung Choi, and Hyeonjin Kim propose SPIN, which uses unlabeled real data to bridge that gap. Simply matching distributions can blur exactly the traits that fix the parameters.

SPIN instead translates simulator outputs toward the real domain and back, training the round trip to preserve parameter-relevant information. The mapped data then trains the network. The design aims for posterior odds that stay sound even when the simulator is off.
arxiv-2605-05852:
When an earthquake kills ground base stations, satellites and high-altitude platforms could keep a 6G network alive. Donglin Wang and three co-authors present a system-level simulator for exactly that fallback. Their lightweight tool models linked ground and space networks under a partial-failure disaster case.

The simulator breaks ground stations at random and moves services to satellite, platform, or drone links. Users can then measure how coverage and service degrade and recover. The aim is building resilience before the disaster, not improvising after it. The tool stays light, so many scenarios can be run and compared side by side.
arxiv-2605-05952:
Pedro Vergara sets out a vision for digital twins in power systems, in a self described position paper. A digital twin is a model that mirrors a real grid and helps guide choices. Power grids act across many time scales and places, yet twin research has so far stayed far from real use, he argues.

Vergara proposes Foundation Twins, which join foundation AI models with reinforcement learning systems that support decisions. The foundation side brings broad generalization across cases, while the learning side handles choices at varied speeds and scopes. His aim is a twin that can speed and improve grid decisions rather than sit as a lab concept. The paper maps how such systems could be built.
arxiv-2605-06152:
Hanqing Liu and three co-authors trace periodic loss spikes in long neural network training to floating point precision limits. These spikes, called the Slingshot Mechanism, were usually blamed on the dynamics of optimization itself. The authors prove a different trigger that appears once training reaches a high confidence stage.

When the correct class logit pulls too far ahead, its gradient can round to exactly zero in backpropagation while rival gradients stay nonzero. That breaks a zero sum balance and sets up a feedback loop they call Numerical Feature Inflation. Classifier and feature means then grow exponentially until gradients reappear and the loss spikes. Even without a visible spike, partial absorption can still drive abnormal growth of parameter norms.
arxiv-2605-06452:
Matthew Simon Tan, Marco Tomamichel, and Ian George study how fast quantum channels make states indistinguishable. Data-processing inequalities say post-processing can only blur differences between distributions. Strong versions use constants that bound how quickly a Markov process contracts toward its fixed point, in both classical and quantum settings.

Working with quantum f-divergences, the authors prove a local reverse Pinsker inequality. It implies the long-run contraction rate is bounded by a strong data-processing constant from a chi-squared type divergence. Under quantum detailed balance they give conditions for the bound to be tight, then apply the results to several named f-divergences, strengthening some known findings.
arxiv-2605-06552:
Michal Kobiela, Diego A. Oyarzún, and Michael U. Gutmann design genetic circuits under two kinds of uncertainty at once: random molecular noise inside cells and varying laboratory conditions. Bayesian design cycles handle this but need costly model fitting after every test, slowing the loop. Their framework instead trains a reinforcement learning policy up front across a spread of possible conditions.

Simulator models based on differential equations or jump processes generate the training experience. The trained policy then suggests experiments that adapt immediately to observations, with no fresh inference step. Tests on gene expression and repressilator circuit models show it handles both molecular noise and cross-lab variability well.
arxiv-2605-06652:
Sushant Gautam and eight co-authors tackle comparing language models for safety when no labeled benchmark exists for the language or sector at hand. They formalize benchmarkless comparative safety scoring and the fixed conditions, from scenario pack to rerun budget, under which scores count as deployment evidence. Validity rests on an instrumental chain rather than agreement with labels.

Their SimpleAudit tool checks that scores respond to a controlled safe-versus-weakened contrast, that model identity dominates scoring noise, and that results stabilize across reruns, shown on a Norwegian safety pack. A public-sector procurement case then shows the safer model can depend on scenario category, so scores must be reported with their full context.
arxiv-2605-06752:
M. Gomilšek and twenty-four co-authors name a three-dimensional magnet as a strong candidate for a quantum spin liquid, a state where spins stay linked and never order even near zero. Theory says bond anisotropy can hold such a state even on bipartite lattices, but no material had been proven. Their compound arranges strongly coupled copper trimers into a three-dimensional bipartite network of effective half-spins.

Tests by heat data, neutron scattering, and resonance methods find no freezing or symmetry breaking down to twenty millikelvin, instead showing a gapless dynamic state. Math explains it: a modest fifteen percent microscopic anisotropy is amplified at the trimer level to sixty percent or more, stabilizing the liquid.
arxiv-2605-06852:
Rokas Veitas, Ahmed Khalifa, Francisco Machado, and Shubhayu Chatterjee show that quantum fluctuations can stabilize a chiral ferromagnet, a magnet whose order twists with a handedness. Ferromagnets usually have a simple unfrustrated ground state, so fluctuations are weak and phenomena are limited. Naturally occurring couplings that do not conserve magnetization change that picture fundamentally in their analysis.

Classical reasoning predicts only straight, achiral states, yet the quantum system forms phases including a ferromagnet with large orbital chirality and a chiral stripe. The chirality emerges spontaneously from spin-orbit interactions rather than from field-induced canting. These states carry an enhanced thermal Hall signal and connect to moiré materials, Rydberg arrays, and non-Kramers spin systems.
arxiv-2605-07152:
Alfo Borzi and Guofeng Zhang shrink large linear quantum systems while preserving their physical rules. Model reduction must respect commutation rules and the quantum input-output structure, which blocks standard projection methods. Their approach uses a symplectic projection that satisfies those physical realizability rules by construction.

Inside it, a repeated rational Krylov algorithm builds richer search spaces and extracts a symplectic basis at each step. Tests on oscillator chains and a Kitaev-chain-inspired system kept that structure with no visible loss. Accurate reduced models came at modest cost, though quality depended on energy-loss patterns, channel placement, and the chosen reduced size.
arxiv-2605-07452:
Maurice Funk, Jean Christoph Jung, and Tom Voellmer extend a data-driven way of learning logical concepts to richer description logics. Bounded fitting learns formulas from labeled examples with generalization guarantees and can run through SAT solvers, but it was developed for a basic logic. The authors study versions adding inverse roles, counting restrictions, and feature comparisons.

They determine when the favorable theoretical properties survive in that richer setting, and implement the method with a SAT solver. Comparisons with leading concept learners give encouraging results. The work presents bounded fitting as a practical route to learning expressive logical concepts from examples.
arxiv-2605-07552:
Zepeng Yang and six co-authors estimate three-dimensional human poses by fusing camera images with data from wearable motion sensors. Transformer models do this well but are too slow for long sequences in real time. Their system, VIMCAN, combines a Mamba sequence model, which is fast, with cross-attention, which handles spatial relations between the two data streams.

VIMCAN reached mean joint position errors of 17.2 millimeters on the TotalCapture dataset and 45.3 millimeters on 3DPW, beating earlier transformer-based and other leading approaches. It also runs at over sixty frames per second on consumer hardware, fast enough for live use. The authors published the source code in a public repository for others to test and extend.
arxiv-2605-07752:
Min Gao and four co-authors bring machine-learning practice to quality checks in semiconductor plants. Process drift, equipment wear, and raw material shifts degrade models in this setting over time, so the retraining strategy matters as much as the model. They tested strategies on five years of real production data.

A simple fixed cadence, retraining every five production batches without retuning settings, beat fancier strategies across abrupt and gradual drift at far lower compute cost. They also add conformal prediction, which wraps forecasts in confidence intervals with firm guarantees. Judging when intervals sit inside allowed control limits turns reactive quality control into a predictive one, and the paper distills usable rules for factories.
arxiv-2605-07852:
Victor K. Khamesi and three co-authors detect changepoints in many-variable time series by watching dependence itself, not averages. The hardest changes to spot are shifts in how variables move together and in temporal dynamics, which leave means and variances nearly untouched. Error-based methods measure such change only at one remove, and scalar summaries can be too coarse.

Their method, CHASM, tracks the truncated eigenvalue sequence of a step-by-step estimated dynamic mode decomposition operator. It aligns eigenvalues across time with an optimal assignment scheme and an extended monitoring design for complex-valued series. It is online, unsupervised, and assumes nothing beyond finite moments. Across synthetic and real datasets, including video and text, it matched or beat modern competitors.
arxiv-2605-07952:
J. Kombe and J. D. Pritchard probe how much of a quantum computer's supposed workload classical prep work can quietly erase. Rydberg atom machines encode maximum independent set problems on unit-disk graphs, the kind drawn from atoms' interaction ranges. Kernelization methods can shrink such problems before any quantum hardware is involved.

Many small or sparse instances reduce away in full. Dense graphs keep finite cores that will not shrink even after deep reduction. Longer interaction ranges make reduction work less well, while vertex weights help it. The surviving kernels mark the demanding regime most relevant for testing quantum hardware. For the quantum side, running those kernels would need non-native embeddings with heavy overhead, so running the original native instances may be more practical.
arxiv-2605-08152:
Divya Gupta presents a hardened design for federated learning, where many sites train one model without pooling their raw data. Standard setups remain exposed to poisoned gradient updates from bad nodes, and the central aggregation step can become a bottleneck at scale.

The proposed architecture wraps each node's computation in a zero-knowledge proof, so updates are verified cryptographically before aggregation without anyone inspecting the raw gradients. That check neutralizes model poisoning at the door. The design also leans on optimized big data processing to keep aggregation fast across distributed edge networks, and the study evaluates how the system performs as it scales.
arxiv-2605-08252:
Ankit Sanjyal tackles skewed emotion data in multimodal emotion recognition. On the CMU-MOSEI corpus, happy samples make up about two thirds of the data. Fear, disgust, and surprise together stay under seven percent. Standard fusion models learn to ignore the rare feelings entirely.

Affect-Diff joins three jointly trained parts. A causal graph learned with NOTEARS reweights each modality before fusion. A beta-VAE bottleneck compresses the latent space in a regularized way. A one-dimensional diffusion prior resists collapse onto the majority class. Balanced accuracy rose eighteen percent over the strongest baseline. That baseline scored zero on the three rarest emotions.
arxiv-2605-08452:
Jian Lan, Zhicheng Liu, Xinpeng Wang, Yuhao Zhou, and coauthors diagnose how vision-language models reason about moving objects. Strong spatial and physical reading is a foundation skill for such models, yet their kinematic physics answers mix genuine derivation with lucky guessing, and their confidence numbers are rarely checked.

The FACT diagnostic separates three abilities: seeing the scene faithfully, knowing the physical law, and grounding events in time. A companion method, NICE, calibrates confidence using neighborhood information and new reliability metrics. Across six recent state-of-the-art models, the decomposition shows where quantitative physics reasoning breaks, giving builders specific failure points rather than one blurred score.
arxiv-2605-09052:
Alexander Grayver and Joachim Saur ask how spacecraft could probe the inside of Enceladus, Saturn's icy moon, without drilling. Beneath its ice shell sits a salty ocean, and deeper down a rocky core that may be warm and porous. Electric and magnetic measurements offer a way to sense these hidden layers.

The authors set out the physics of electromagnetic sounding for this moon and model one-dimensional and three-dimensional structures. Changes in the ice shell's thickness leave marks on the magnetic field whose size depends on how conductive the ocean is. An orbiter could measure the ocean's overall conductivity, while a lander using a wide range of periods could sound both the ocean and the core.
arxiv-2605-09152:
Jucheng Hu leads eleven co-authors in introducing Meow-Omni 1, an open model built to infer what a cat is likely feeling or intending. Their 2026 work targets a core problem in animal behavior study: the same signal, such as a purr, can mean very different inner states depending on body context. Ordinary multimodal models miss high-rate body data, so they rely on surface pattern matching.

Meow-Omni 1 joins video, audio, body time-series data, and text in one system, using special encoders tied to grounded body signals. On MeowBench, a new expert-checked benchmark, the authors report the best intent recognition score among the models tested, well ahead of leading vision and omni-modal rivals. They release model weights, training code, and a cat dataset. The aim is a scalable path toward tools for veterinary diagnosis and wildlife work.
arxiv-2605-09352:
Zhang and six colleagues ask why networks trained apart in different senses end up sharing representations. Past evidence uses similarity scores that work the same both ways, spotting sharing but missing its direction.

The team introduces one-way sharing analysis with cycle-kNN, an uneven alignment score, used on dozens of unimodal models trained apart, covering point clouds, vision, and language. They find a steady one-way tilt: senses other than language drift toward language's local layout far more than the reverse, across all model families and scales, yet same-both-ways measures miss it entirely. A look at the mechanism traces the tilt to uneven feature density, with language representations in the tightest regions of the space. Under the Information Bottleneck view, squeezing representations drives them toward discrete, compositional structures typical of language. That is the Wittgensteinian Representation Hypothesis: language's meaning structure is the end point of multimodal sharing.
arxiv-2605-09652:
Dikshant and five colleagues extend RDEx-CSOP, a differential evolution variant that topped the CEC constrained optimization track, with three changes targeting stagnation and late stage variance. The second scale factor in the usual branch is now drawn independently from a truncated Cauchy distribution. A small feasible only archive is added and sampled with probability tied to its size. After 180 generations without improvement, a stagnation counter triggers three local overrides on the standard branch.

Those overrides pull toward the global best, raise the archive sampling floor, and saturate the crossover rate when the population success rate runs low. The exploitation biased branch and every other component stay untouched. On the CEC suite, the extended method matches its parent and rivals on feasibility aware quality. It improves time to target on most problems, showing that small, targeted changes can beat wholesale redesign.
arxiv-2605-09752:
Beßner and five colleagues built a scheme that pairs quantum math with atom-scale models for repeating systems, like crystals and liquids at electrodes. The quantum zone, handled with density functional theory, links to water molecules described by a multipole model with direction-dependent response and fixed multipoles up to the hexadecapole. Each side shifts in reply to the other, so polarization runs both ways.

Near- and far-field expansions were tuned so the periodic interaction potential converges smoothly and fast, matching full quantum accuracy. Short-range electric forces are damped to screen the link and stop runaway polarization. In motion simulations, a flexible inner zone with elastic scattering keeps the radial pattern smooth across the zone edge. Electrode-liquid interfaces are the target use.
arxiv-2605-09852:
Popoola and Sheppard mapped a blind spot between two fields. Algorithmic fairness targets equitable outcomes. Explainable AI targets interpretable reasoning. Their survey shows a model can meet every standard fairness test in its outputs while staying profoundly unfair in its reasoning. They call this procedural bias, and argue explanation fairness deserves study as its own object.

The core idea is a conditional invariance framework. Explanations should be indifferent to protected traits once task inputs are fixed. That single rule yields today's explanation fairness scores as partial versions. The survey adds a seven-part map, three ways explanation inequity arises, and a six-step workflow for auditing explanation fairness in practice.
arxiv-2605-10052:
The openJiuwen Team and the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence at Renmin University of China propose Swarm Skills, a portable specification for teams of AI agents. Single-agent skills can already ship as reusable assets, but multi-agent coordination rules usually stay trapped inside one framework's code or fixed settings. As work shifts from single-agent prompt engineering to multi-agent coordination engineering, that lock-in blocks sharing and steady improvement.

Swarm Skills builds on the Anthropic Skills standard, adding multi-agent meaning, packaging roles, workflows, execution bounds and a structure for self-evolution into distributable assets. A companion algorithm distills successful runs into new skills and patches old ones, scored on effectiveness, use and freshness, with no human in the loop. A case study on the open-source JiuwenSwarm system shows agent teams porting coordination strategies across frameworks and evolving them on their own.
arxiv-2605-10652:
Yuxuan Guo and Yuto Ashida look at two-dimensional Dirac fermions set in a deep-subwavelength cavity made by high-impedance metasurfaces. Unlike plain metal walls, metasurfaces host quasielectrostatic transverse-magnetic modes linking two-dimensional electrons over long range. Joining static electronic screening with Dyson-Schwinger analysis, the authors show this built link can change Dirac matter ground-state traits basically.

Below a key fermion flavour count, the link drives an excitonic insulating phase through an infinite-order quantum phase shift and makes a mass gap alone. Above that key count, the set stays gapless but enters a non-Fermi-liquid key regime. There, the quasiparticle residue is crushed to zero and the Dirac cone shows a nonanalytic spread. Under a straight-on magnetic field, cavity wobbles lift the zeroth Landau level split for all flavour counts, marking metasurface cavities as good sites for building linked Dirac matter.
arxiv-2605-10952:
Vinayak and Ajeet Kumar derive the large-scale behavior of rod-like metamaterials, structures built by repeating a rod network in one direction. Their scheme captures the nonlinear response of the smoothed structure as a plain rod, using exact Cosserat rod theory at both scales.

Assuming uniform large-scale strain along the arc length reduces the full problem to a single micro unit under helically periodic edge conditions. Solving that unit with joint constraints yields the smoothed rod's forces, moments, and stiffnesses. Tests on square, cross, and helical-rod units validate the method and point toward artificial-muscle uses. Metamaterial designers get a rigorous bridge from microstructure to rod behavior.
arxiv-2605-11152:
Indranil Biswas and Jacques Hurtubise build theta functions for singular curves. Start with X, an irreducible singular Riemann surface, and its desingularisation X-tilde. Its generalised Jacobian J(X) fibers over the Jacobian of X-tilde, and an Abel map of X-tilde to J(X) lifts the Abel map to the smooth Jacobian.

The authors construct a theta function over a compactified generalised Jacobian, and it supplies a section of a fitting positive line bundle. Translation on J(X) then yields all line bundles of that degree. Shifting the theta function and restricting it to the Abel image yields one section that works across all line bundles of that degree over X. This extends Riemann's classical result to the singular case. Algebraic geometers get the classical theta construction where curves are allowed to be singular.
arxiv-2605-11252:
Chong Qi and Mário B. Amaro examine quantum tunneling, global phases, and limits of classical action reconstructions. A recent proposal claims the Schrödinger wave function rebuilds exactly from a discrete sum of action branches weighted by densities, without semiclassical approximations.

The authors test this claim for passage through finite barriers and quantum phase phenomena. Although consistent when Hamilton-Jacobi admits global real branches, the claim breaks down in off-limits regions with no real action. Using rectangular and Coulomb passage in alpha decay and nuclear fusion, the wave function needs a non-vanishing quantum potential, or else complex action. The growing barrier component fixed by global boundaries is needed for transmission; it cannot come from local real trajectories alone. Berry phase, flux quantization, Josephson tunneling, and dc SQUID interference also impose global phase constraints absent from local action transport. Foundations readers get a clear limit for reconstruction.
arxiv-2605-11352: Hassan Tavakoli, Thinh Nguyen and Bella Bose study estimating a channel whose sender picks inputs to maximize mutual information under the true parameter. From output observations alone, they aim to recover both the capacity-achieving input distribution and the true channel parameter. They propose two efficient methods based on Blahut-Arimoto optimality: a bilevel fixed-point method and an augmented Lagrangian method. Both recover the true values in tests, where a plain maximum-likelihood approach ignoring the maximization constraint fails.
arxiv-2605-11552: Xin Peng, Bing Wang and Zhenjian Wang study torus fibrations under first Betti number restrictions. They examine torus bundles with affine structure groups. First, they prove rigidity: when the first Betti numbers of bundle and base differ by exactly the dimension gap, the bundle can be classified. Second, they give necessary and sufficient conditions for topological splitting of principal torus bundles. The results clarify the geometry of collapsing sequences under Betti number constraints, extending prior work by Huang-Wang.
arxiv-2605-11752: Qijun Hou and three colleagues tackle federated learning when the server can see only some clients each round. They treat client choice when only some clients are visible as a partially observable Markov decision process and build a reinforcement learning method with spatial-temporal attention over past models and client identities. Across several datasets it beat existing baselines in uneven, partly visible settings.
arxiv-2605-12352: Alaee, Khuri and Kunduri prove sharp lower bounds for the mass of toric four-manifolds. These manifolds are asymptotically locally Euclidean or locally flat. For complete manifolds with nonnegative curvature, the mass is at least the matching instanton's mass. A further term comes from angle defects of spheres that generate its second homology. The bound extends to manifolds with conical and orbifold singularities. It suggests a refined total mass that never falls below the instanton's mass.
arxiv-2605-12752: Pasquali and nine colleagues propose SLICE for LoRA adapters in continual learning. LoRA is used for continual fine-tuning of language models for its small size, mixing and fit with replay plans. Yet LoRA continual learning remains open to sudden loss, whose size depends on how next task slopes mix. When next slopes conflict, plain starts channel updates into spaces that erase old ways. SLICE gathers slopes from the task and a replay store of earlier tasks, fixes them through a projection, and splits the result via cut SVD.
arxiv-2605-13352: Mayank Nautiyal and four colleagues propose GeoFlowVLM, an adapter that adds uncertainty estimates to frozen vision-language models. Such models place images and text as points on a shared sphere. Yet they normally reveal neither cross-modal ambiguity nor ignorance of unfamiliar inputs. The adapter learns the joint distribution of paired embeddings on that sphere through Riemannian flow matching. From it they derive a retrieval entropy for ambiguity and a typicality score for unfamiliarity, both calibrating well.
arxiv-2605-13652: Namrata Shivagunde and three colleagues compare five low-rank pre-training methods against full-rank training, asking whether rank limits change the solutions reached. They test GaLore, Fira, CoLA, SLTrain and ReLoRA on 16 metrics across loss landscape, checkpoint interpolation, spectral structure and activation similarity. Low-rank methods are neither equivalent to full-rank training nor to each other, even at close perplexity, and each lands in a geometrically distinct basin. Full-rank training sits in a sharper basin along random directions, while GaLore tracks full-rank most closely.
arxiv-2605-13952: Arias-Tamargo and three co-authors link edge rules to categorical symmetries in two-dimensional fermion theories. They pin down every anomaly-free invertible global symmetry of two free complex Weyl fermions, each taking Zk form for a primitive Pythagorean triple. Gauging any one of them leaves the theory self-dual, so each brings a non-invertible topological defect. Any conformal boundary condition imposed on two Dirac fermions that keeps U(1) squared symmetry can be built by dressing one trivial Dirichlet boundary. One such defect does the dressing.
arxiv-2605-14152: Lee and fifteen co-authors present ROK-FORTRESS, a bilingual, culturally adversarial benchmark for national security and public safety risks. Multilingual safety is usually tested through translation-only benchmarks that keep the underlying scenario, leaving language-geopolitics interactions largely unexamined. The benchmark uses the English-Korean pair and the United States-Korea geopolitical axis as a case study. A transcreation matrix separates language effects from geopolitical grounding, testing adversarial intents across English versus Korean language and United States versus Korean entities, institutions and operational details.
arxiv-2605-14252: Sun and six co-authors propose Selective Alignment Knowledge Distillation for spiking neural networks with unequal treatment. Current distillation aligns all steps, assuming all predictions should be treated equally. SNN predictions vary over time, and middle steps need not each be correct. SeAl-KD aligns class and temporal knowledge, equalizing rival logits at wrong steps and reweighting alignment by score. Tests on image and neuromorphic datasets show improvements over older distillation methods.
arxiv-2605-14352: Schneider, Steuber, Schneider and Dreo Rodosek propose a transformer-based model projecting a text's political orientation on a left-to-right spectrum, as a scalar d between minus 1 and 1. Four corpora were used: Bundestag plenary notes, Wahl-O-Mat, 33 newspaper articles, and 535,200 tweets from 597 Bundestag members. In-domain, DeBERTa-large scored highest at F1 0.844, and on X at accuracy 0.864; on newspapers, Gemma2-2B excelled with MAE 0.172. Transformer models recognize political framing in German news at poll level, and architecture and training data can matter as much as size.
arxiv-2605-14652: Lupo and Tantalo expand a method for extracting smeared spectral densities from Euclidean lattice correlators without Backus-Gilbert regularisation. The solution splits into a sum of terms, echoing singular value decomposition, where the terms that add the most statistical noise add the least to the central value. The task then becomes finding the best truncation, so the signal saturates before noise explodes. The approach is tested alone and as a complement to stability analysis.
arxiv-2605-14952: For trials whose volunteers differ from the wider eligible population, Lan Wen, Issa J. Dahabreh, and Yu-Han Chiu estimate treatment effects that vary with patient traits. Average effects can hide differences that matter for clinical and policy choices. The team builds pseudo-outcomes from conditional influence functions, then fits the effect curve by local linear regression. Sample splitting guards against overfitting, and simulations plus a heart-surgery study illustrate the method.
arxiv-2605-15152: Xiaohua Zhan and four colleagues demonstrate the first quantization-conditioned attack that survives advanced LLM quantization schemes. Earlier attacks failed against popular methods like AWQ, GPTQ, and GGUF I-quants. The new attack injects large outliers into specific weight blocks, exploiting the shared property that outliers can force neighboring weights to round to zero. A model that looks benign in full precision can therefore turn malicious once users quantize it, across a broad range of schemes and behaviors.
arxiv-2605-15352: Shangqun Yu and six colleagues train a diffusion-based visuomotor policy for the full door-opening-and-passing task with a nonholonomic mobile base and dual arms. Pulling heavy self-closing doors demands coordinated handle rotation, gap widening, holding, arm switching, and passage with clearance. Hand-crafted state machines fail to generalize across real conditions. A single end-to-end learned policy instead executes the long, constrained sequence, demonstrating simultaneous base-and-arms coordination that no prior visual action model had shown for this complete task.
arxiv-2605-15452: Peter Müller gives a direct build for a long-open sphere problem in algebra. The task is a matrix whose first row holds the sphere coordinates. Past work showed such a matrix exists just when the field has Stufe at most four. That settled the 2-adic case, but the proof gave no example. Müller builds the matrix from four field elements whose squares sum to minus one. He also shows how he found it.
arxiv-2605-15752: Rungployphan Kieokaew and three colleagues forecast megaelectron-volt electron flux in Earth's belt. Such electrons threaten satellites, so forecasts aid operations. Their pipeline trains regression, convolutional, memory, and Transformer models on satellite and solar inputs. It targets MeV flux in L-shells from L-shell 2.8 through L-shell 6.0 in the test range. TimesFM+Cov scores best with mean R2 0.9 across L-shells, versus under 0.78 among rivals in the test set. R2 stays above 0.9 for lower L-shells and falls to 0.77 at the highest shell, beating rivals by up to 48 percent.
arxiv-2605-15852: Leyang Chen and three colleagues present GHOST, a training-free way to manage the key-value cache in streaming 3D reconstruction from long monocular video. Older methods either cut the cache to fixed anchor frames, hurting quality, or use attention scores blind to 3D structure. GHOST ranks token value in tiers, shields special tokens from eviction, and sets layer budgets by cosine similarity, guided by the model's own geometry outputs. Tests show it keeps reconstruction quality while halving the cache and speeding inference 1.75 times over state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2605-16052: Kordjamshidi and four colleagues test whether language models truly reason about tax law or merely recall tainted training data. They build a detection protocol and a fresh test suite of unseen cases and rule changes. Stand-alone models look inflated by taint. Hybrid neuro-symbolic systems, which turn statutes into formal rules for a symbolic solver, generalize better.
arxiv-2605-16152: Borbényi, Terlov, and Tóth prove measurable analogues of Whitney's theorems on weak isomorphisms of finite graphs. For locally finite graphings, a weak isomorphism is an edge-measure-preserving Borel bijection that preserves cycles and hyperfinite subgraphs. Their rigidity theorem shows every weak isomorphism of a weakly 3-connected, infinitely-ended graphing comes from a graphing isomorphism. They also prove a full measurable Whitney theorem via six measurable Whitney operations.
arxiv-2605-16452: Li and twelve others present Peak-Detector, a framework using instruction-tuned language models for cross-modal, explainable peak detection across cardiac signals. Peak detection across ECG, PPG, BCG, and BSG matters for heart care but is hurt by noise. A peak-representation technique condenses time-series data while preserving critical events. Two-stage optimization — supervised fine-tuning then reinforcement learning — builds self-explanation on a custom dataset. Across four modalities and seven data sets, Peak-Detector hits best or tied-best detection.
arxiv-2605-16852: Grašič and colleagues introduce the d-capacity of a graph. It is the maximum number of players that can simultaneously traverse the graph, each visiting all vertices while keeping distance at least d under various movement rules. They determine capacities for paths and cycles and give bounds for bipartite graphs. They also characterize topfull graphs, where 1-capacities reach their theoretical maximum, linking them to graph factorizations and connectivity.
arxiv-2605-16952: Rosain and Cailler present TableauxRocq, a deep embedding of free-variable tableaux in the Rocq prover. The free-variable tableau method automates proofs across many logics, and many provers rely on it, yet its results had never been formalised in a proof assistant. Their calculus is proved sound and offers a modular Skolemization system enabling Skolemization-based optimisations. They also adapt the Goeland prover to export proofs in TableauxRocq form, giving a fully certified proof checker whose checks run as fast as Goeland's own terms, and faster with Skolemization optimisations.
arxiv-2605-17052: Chetverikov, Sørensen and Honoré fix the variance rules for trimmed least-squares and trimmed least absolute deviation methods in two-period panel models with cut-off data. The published rules rest on extra rules the first work left unstated, and one fails when the parameter vector is zero. The authors work out the right Hessian and long-run variance, give a plug-in rule for it, and add a bootstrap that needs no tuning for the second method. One published rule, they note, already aims at the fixed variance.
arxiv-2605-17152: Alam, Chowdhury and Prince run a half-day tutorial on multilingual, multimodal language models for languages with little data or computing power. The session covers cheap data creation, adapter stacks that align text, speech and vision, and evaluation that respects culture rather than centering English. Participants also practice tuning a compact vision-language model and wiring a speech-to-text-to-model pipeline.
arxiv-2605-17352: Zhang and colleagues present AMATA, a multi-agent frame for knowledge-heavy question answering that aligns agent paths instead of letting agents drift. Six expert agents reason together with outside tools, guided by within-path preference learning and cross-agent dependency learning. Tests on five known benchmarks show it beats plain baselines, knowledge-augmented systems and rival path systems, while also cutting token use.
arxiv-2605-17452: León-Cardenal and colleagues study poles of zeta functions for finite morphisms between normal surfaces. They prove poles of the motivic zeta function for the target lie inside those for the source. Examples show the inclusion is strict. They also show topological poles admit no general inclusion either way. For quotient maps from finite abelian group actions on the complex plane with trivial differential divisor, they prove equality on both levels. They also give a criterion for the topological target zeta to be a multiple of the source's.
arxiv-2605-17652: Chaparala and colleagues test ten workflows for speech summarization, varying input mode, audio, transcript or both, and editing, self or peer-editing. Human audio-based summaries prove less informative and more compressed than transcript versions. Iterative peer-editing with audio, however, mitigates this gap, enabling audio-based summaries to match transcript counterparts and language-model ones on detail. The findings support peer-editing among human annotators for benchmark making informed by lexical and prosodic information, for dataset collection even without transcripts.
arxiv-2605-17752: Jiande Cao, Yexiong Zeng, Franco Nori, and Ze-Liang Xiang design a neural network made entirely of light. This avoids the slow electrical conversions that usually supply nonlinearity. Phase-tuned interference in a giant cavity sets adjustable connection strengths, while an integrator in the bad-cavity regime sums signals over time. Transient Rabi dynamics in a driven two-level system supply the nonlinear kick. Full-physics simulations score highly on handwritten digits and colored-object recognition, clearing a path to fully optical neuromorphic computing.
arxiv-2605-17852: Yiqin Deng and six colleagues design CA3D, a joint 3D plan for UAVs that must finish delay-sensitive tasks. Their theory shows computing accessibility links placement to task completion, while drone spacing trades access against completion odds. The plan balances access, completion odds, and redundant overlap between drones. Simulations with varied node capacities beat Random, Fixed, and Greedy baselines under hotspot and random user layouts. With eight drones under hotspot users, CA3D nears full completion, about 3.3 times the Random rate.
arxiv-2605-17952: Benedict Florance Arockiaraj and three colleagues count machine washer parts in images. Counting suffers from overlap, scale variation, occlusion, and changing light. Their method extends FamNet with an extra loss component, trained on the given dataset. They compare three baselines: a traditional image processing pipeline, instance segmentation, and density map estimation. Scoring by mean absolute error and root mean squared error against true counts, their approach reaches 1.96 mean absolute error.
arxiv-2605-18352: Tara Azin and three colleagues compare human and language-model judgments on conditional sentences and their presuppositions, the background assumptions a sentence carries. With ratings from 120 people and four models, their May 2026 study finds people blend probability and pragmatic cues, while models align unevenly. Strikingly, the models matching human ratings best often show the weakest coherent reasoning.
arxiv-2605-18452: Ya-Qi Wei and twelve co-authors show squeezing-induced stochastic resonance in a 2026 paper, in a trapped ion acting as a Duffing oscillator, boosting weak electric-field signals. Squeezing the ion's phase noise boosts its swing size, hitting resonance with no added noise source. The trick lifts the signal-to-noise ratio by 4.28 decibels over old noise-driven resonance under a matched test setup, promising better atomic ion sensors.
arxiv-2605-18752: Vicente Amado Olivo and seven co-authors test, in a 2026 study, statistical versus AI methods for finding expert reviewers. They frame expert finding as retrieval, using an observatory's peer review system, with proposal authorship as proxy ground truth for expertise. Six methods are tested across observatories and conferences. Old methods win: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency puts an expert in the top 25 about eighty percent of the time, versus fifty-two percent for GPT-4o mini. Vocabulary, they argue, is blurred by semantic smoothing in generative methods.
arxiv-2605-19052: Tung Quoc Le, Anh Tuan Nguyen, and Viet Anh Nguyen give a theory for learning Lagrangian relaxation multipliers for mixed-integer linear programs from data. They derive a generalisation bound for the learned multipliers. They prove a matching lower bound. It shows a linear link to the number of coupling constraints cannot be avoided. They also show averaged stochastic gradient ascent attains the optimal rate. Finally, they extend the work to warm-start learning, proving a faster optimal rate and an edge over predicting multipliers directly.
arxiv-2605-19352: Subba Reddy Oota and colleagues compare how vision-language and action models line up with brain activity during video gameplay. Most brain-alignment work uses language or passive viewing, while interactive studies stuck to reinforcement learners. Using scans from players of Atari-style games, they test prompts that stress action versus reasoning. Both model families beat reinforcement baselines, and prompt gains run larger in frontal, parietal, and motor-planning areas than in early visual cortex. Action models lean heavily to action, while vision-language models stay more balanced.
arxiv-2605-19452: Dallot and team study Byzantine agreement when nodes carry a predictor flagging suspects. They fully characterize the consistency-robustness trade-off in both plain and authenticated settings. With n nodes and a tuning parameter, their methods handle a set fraction of faulty nodes when the flags are right, and fewer when they are wrong. Authenticated robustness roughly doubles the plain bound. The bounds are exactly tight: one more faulty node makes agreement fail. Resilience also degrades linearly as predictions go wrong, halving the loss rate under authentication.
arxiv-2605-19552: Alexandrov, Klemm and Pioline use new Gopakumar-Vafa data for Calabi-Yau threefolds. They study 5D indices, stable pair values and Donaldson-Thomas invariants at large charges. Below a critical momentum the 5D index matches the entropy of spinning BMPV black holes, with subleading terms. Above it, black rings with minimal dipole charge rule. Stable pair invariants show a ring-hole transition at negative momentum plus two more transitions at positive momentum, to a plateau, then power growth. Donaldson-Thomas invariants transition to a D0-brane-ruled phase.
arxiv-2605-19652: Rathnasuriya and team present the first systematic study of code generation bugs in tile programs, the frameworks behind high-performance GPU kernels for deep learning and scientific computing. Multi-stage compilation pipelines create bugs tied to input shapes, data types and backend targets, often surfacing as silent wrong results or slowdowns. From 401 GitHub bug reports they isolate 301 tile-program codegen bugs, characterizing root causes, symptoms, triggering inputs, detecting oracles and fix strategies. The study grounds future debugging, testing and repair tools for tile compiler infrastructure.
arxiv-2605-19752: Krzakala and colleagues tackle the hard job of naming small molecules, called metabolites, from mass spectrometry data. Their MSAlign model lines up two frozen foundation models, one reading spectra and one reading molecules, and a score blend lifts accuracy further at little extra cost. The team also untangles a testing trap: how data are split trades hidden leakage against shifts between training and test sets. They measure that shift, test existing splits, and release data, splits and code.
arxiv-2605-20052: Ying-Jia Lin and five co-workers label radiology reports with little training data using a system called PromptRad. It reframes multi-label classification as masked language modelling and enriches category meanings with synonyms from the UMLS Metathesaurus in a multi-word verbalizer. Fine-tuning the language model without extra classification layers needs far less labelled data than standard fine-tuning. On liver CT reports it beats dictionary and fine-tuning baselines with only thirty-two labelled examples, and it handles complex negation patterns better than existing methods.
arxiv-2605-20252: Orgest Zaka introduces a Clifford setting for Julia dynamics via the geometric product. The iteration raises a vector to a power along a unit direction and adds a constant. Though the geometric product creates higher-grade parts, a grade-reduction mechanism collapses to the vector subspace. The Clifford Julia operator is closed on the space, defining a well-posed system in any dimension. The work extends Julia dynamics past the complex plane and into higher-dimensional geometric algebra, opening a new path for fractal-type dynamics in Clifford algebras.
arxiv-2605-20352: Reina-Campos, Speagle and Harris test whether globular clusters trace dark matter in galaxy clusters. They model cluster positions as a spatial Poisson point process and apply the method to Abell 2744. Bright clusters roughly follow the three main clumps of that cluster, matching mass maps more closely than other galaxy parts. Bright blue clusters match the weak-lensing mass map alone, giving a second route to map mass in such clusters.
arxiv-2605-20452: Wiesnet studies limits of recursive classification in proof theory through the refined A-translation. That translation, due to Berger, Buchholz and Schwichtenberg, rests on recursively defined formula classes in minimal arithmetic. Wiesnet shows none of the four related properties admits a recursive characterization. He also extends the framework with conjunction, re-states the translation theorem, and uses a Rust prover for the theory as a case study on Rust for proof assistants.
arxiv-2605-20552: Tomas Kocak and four colleagues tackle online recommendation on graphs, where neighbouring items should earn similar ratings. Their spectral bandit methods use a small effective dimension, a count that stays low on real graphs. Both methods grow linearly in that dimension instead of scaling badly with the total number of items. Trials on real recommendation data learn good taste profiles for thousands of items from only tens of rated nodes.
arxiv-2605-20652: Sarah Garcia Jones and nine colleagues show nonlinear behaviour in a tungsten silicide weak link inside a three-dimensional RF-SQUID. Nonlinearity matters for encoding quantum states, running gates, reading qubits, and mixing signals. Their narrow neck, made from a glassy material with high kinetic inductance, acts like a Josephson junction with a sawtooth current-phase link. They also measure how long metastable persistent-current states last in potential wells.
arxiv-2605-20852: Shu-Cheng Chang and three colleagues confirm the Hamilton-Tian claim for the Sasaki-Ricci flow in a compact transverse Fano quasi-regular Sasakian 5-manifold. Their paper first proves the claim in that setting with klt foliation singularities. It then derives a compactness theorem for Sasaki-Ricci solitons on transverse Fano quasi-regular Sasaki 5-manifolds. By the second Sasakian structure theorem, the claim follows for a compact transverse Fano Sasaki 5-manifold, with uses for gradient soliton objects.
arxiv-2605-21052: Cesar Bernardes summarizes recent CMS measurements at the LHC on the thermodynamic properties of hot QCD matter. The analysis extracts the squared speed of sound of strongly interacting matter at extreme heat from the multiplicity dependence of mean transverse momentum in ultra-central lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV. It yields a squared speed of sound of 0.241, with statistical error 0.002 and systematic error 0.016, at an effective temperature of 219 MeV. That result agrees well with lattice-QCD calculations, and complementary proton-lead studies are also presented.
arxiv-2605-21152: Mohan Bhupal and Burak Ozbagci give a Legendrian surgery description of the canonical contact structure on links of normal complex surface singularities. They show it is the unique consistent diagram-realizable contact structure on those spaces, up to isomorphism. A closed-form formula for Gompf's theta-invariant follows in the Seifert fibered case, with a recursive leaf-to-root formula for general plumbing trees. The Seifert formula recovers known cases and matches the Némethi-Nicolaescu expression.
arxiv-2605-21252: Haitang Yang proposes an exact kinematic sector of holography, distinct from holographic dynamics, on a CFT on an open solid torus in the Weyl frame. The torus supplies an intrinsic scale, manifest in the Weyl frame as an extra bulk direction. The construction needs no crutches — no cutoff, large-N limit, strong-coupling assumption, or heavy-operator approximation — and its bulk-boundary pairs come out exact and finite. Standard dictionary entries return only as singular limits, and Weyl-frame two-point functions define entanglement entropy without replicas.
arxiv-2605-21452: Juliette Alimena and co-authors test the proposed FCC-ee collider's reach for axion-like particles at all planned energies. They focus on particles coupling mainly to electroweak gauge bosons, produced with a photon and decaying to two photons. Sensitivities are computed for masses from five to three hundred twenty gigaelectronvolts, reaching a few times ten to the minus six per gigaelectronvolt at the Z pole.
arxiv-2605-21552: Jinzong Dong, Zhaohui Jiang, and Bo Yang propose Expectation Consistency Loss, rethinking trust tuning under covariate shift. Trust tuning for sorting models is vital in safety-critical decisions. Yet general methods assume training and test data are of the same kind, limiting power under shift. They derive an exact rule for tuning under shift, named Expectation consistency rule. This gives a sound basis for a new tuning loss.
arxiv-2605-22252: Liang and colleagues present LineageFlow, a model that drafts new protein sequences true to a chosen family. Most discrete generators start from blank or masked noise. They must then rebuild conserved parts from scratch. LineageFlow instead starts from lineage priors drawn from ancestral sequence reconstruction, so generation becomes guided mutation from an evolved scaffold. Family validity nears that of natural held-out sequences, and structural confidence beats uniform and masked baselines. A midway rerouting trick adds further gains without step-by-step predictor guidance.
arxiv-2605-22352: Fatoyinbo and Jeong analyse Canadian wildlife surveillance records for highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) from 2022 to 2026. The study covers 2,657 detections across 13 provinces and territories. Most detections were in birds, led by waterfowl and raptors, while mammals formed a smaller but notable share. Burden peaked in 2022 and rose in autumn and spring. Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia emerged as hotspots, and reassortant Eurasian-North American lineages dominated. Year, season and lineage proved the key predictors, supporting risk-based One Health surveillance.
arxiv-2605-22652: Jabłonowski builds a network of 47 inequalities among 33 integer knot invariants. He propagates them with parity rules, alternating evaluations, ribbon status and interval bounds for prime knots through 13 crossings. He proves the propagation sound, terminating and order independent in every case. Under a source bound hypothesis, the database yields unknotting numbers for 36 thirteen crossing knots and doubly slice genera pinned down for 72 of them. A leading coefficient obstruction to skein tree depth, with Conway polynomial tests as a special case, fixes 11 skein depths exactly.
arxiv-2605-22752: Kominers and others study lines through points pairing each index with its prime, asking how few segments cover the first n points. They prove the covering number grows like n times log log n over log n, near Sloane's conjectured n over log n. They show one line can cover at least a constant times log n points. Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, they bound the line cover above and push the covering number below by a power of n. The results sharpen both sides of a prime covering problem.
arxiv-2605-22852: Schönherr and five coauthors study the expressive power of Deep Homomorphism Networks for learning over relational databases, motivated by limits of message-passing graph networks. Relating these networks to fragments of first-order logic, they tie max, sum, and mean aggregation variants to the unary negation fragment plus counting and ratio quantifiers. Through the logic-SQL correspondence, the results clarify how these networks relate to SQL queries. They also settle decidability of emptiness and subsumption problems for the networks.
arxiv-2605-22952: Vologdin, Tao, and Gilad build a framework for gauging database unfairness under differential privacy, where noise and limited access hide bias. They set three rules for unfairness scores: positivity, monotonicity, and DP computability. Three matching scores put them into practice. One uses mutual information with a total variation proxy. One repairs data via weighted MaxSAT. One ranks tuples by impact, isolating the key records. Privacy-preserving algorithms follow, with sensitivity, accuracy, and efficiency checks. Tests on real datasets show the scores track their non-private versions.
arxiv-2605-23352: Gavrielov identifies the even strontium isotopes from mass 90 to 100 as a case of intertwined quantum phase transitions, where two kinds of change happen at once. Using the interacting boson model with configuration mixing, he shows normal and intruder nuclear shapes cross between mass 96 and 98. The intruder shape itself shifts from near-spherical to deformed across that range. The ground state thus jumps from a weakly collective normal form to a deformed intruder form, matching data on energies, isotope shifts, and transition strengths.
arxiv-2605-23452: Marcela Grcić, Daniel D'Orazio and Martin Pessah model how a lopsided binary star pair stirs eccentricity into the gas disk around it. Where the binary pull dominates, disk eccentricity wobbles around the value for a lone test particle, shrinking inversely with distance. Where gas pressure dominates, it breaks from that pattern and shrinks with the square of distance, matching recent simulations. The team extends the model to heavy disks and wobbling binaries, proposing that the inner cavity settles where the slowest trapped mode rings in step with the binary wobble.
arxiv-2605-23552: Johnson, Marijuán, and Pisonero study when a list of numbers can arise as the eigenvalues of a matrix with no negative entries and no block split, that is, an irreducible nonnegative realization. After background and fresh notes, they show such matrices exist in several broad cases. They then look at sizes below five, where the inverse eigenvalue problem is already solved. Last they treat the trace-zero case, using graph tools to say which lists work, and discuss the linked positive case for trace-positive lists.
arxiv-2605-23852: Xu and Jagadish study memory effects in quantum systems ruled by Weyl maps, which move states around a grid of phases. Using the Hermite normal form, they classify subgroups of that grid and pin down which isotropic maps generate memory-free evolution. Uneven anisotropic maps cannot, they show. Their result is that mixing maps that never lose memory can yield memory-free evolution, so memory is not additive under mixing, while some mixtures stay eternally memory-bound. Three-level examples trace the shift among the three regimes.
arxiv-2605-23952: Bogdan and de Valois-Franklin propose Machine Psychometrics, a way to study artificial agents by their inner structure rather than by capability scores alone. They steer between two errors: dismissing any inner organization in them, and reading human-like inner life from fluent behaviour alone. Its core is the Machine Mindprint, a profile listing calibration, source integrity, suggestion resistance, context stability, and grounding. A Trust Protocol turns such records into deployment choices through probes, perturbation tests, and monitoring, judging them because they are not human.
arxiv-2605-24152: Kapitonova and Ball present Inverter, a brain-inspired frame for embodied planning and control built on paired forward and inverse models and hierarchical action organization. Inverse Learning bridges reinforcement-learning-style amortization, which emits one action per pass, and optimal-control-style planning over whole trajectories. Single Inverters and two-level stacks match or beat offline baselines across maze variants by about 24 percent on average, at far less inference compute. A Pulse Inverter also synthesizes single-qubit gates matching GRAPE at over a thousand times less compute per gate.
arxiv-2605-24252: Polche and eight co-authors test hybrid quantum-classical forecasting of electricity use, on 103 smart-meter series and IBM's Marrakesh chip. One model, a kernelized quantum reservoir computer with repeated measurement, uses 114 qubits and beats its classical analog by about a third. The second model, a projected quantum-kernel Gaussian-process design, predicts 100 values with 100 qubits. Nearly half the outputs reach high accuracy. Average error falls about three-fifths on simulator and two-fifths on hardware. Together they show hybrid quantum forecasting feasible at 100-plus qubits.
arxiv-2605-24352: Ahmad, Nakisa, and Rastgoo launch Partner-Aware Skill Discovery, learning skills shaped by partner conduct. Standard layered methods chase agent-centred rewards and miss partner conduct, so skills exploit stray signals instead of tuning. The new frame adds a contrast inner reward catching partner-play patterns, lining up skills across like partners while keeping plans distinct. Shaping skills by partner play curbs shortcuts and builds steady, nimble teamwork. Tested in Overcooked-AI with varied partners and human-proxy models, it beats crowd and layered rivals.
arxiv-2605-24452: Ovcharov tests language drift by fine-tuning models on Ukrainian rulings from three epochs. Each model trains on one epoch and is tested on three. Forward drop is severe: pre-war models lose up to about 27 points on war-era rulings. Drop is one-way, with backward transfer tough. Legal-domain prep shrinks drop and tilt, not scores. Time-ordered learning wipes out loss for XLM-R and lifts war-era scores by 17 to 19 points. Reverse time-ordered training forgets badly. Swiss prep lifts scores but not time drop.
arxiv-2605-24552: Luoyu Chen and colleagues defend language models against jailbreaks from the opposite direction: instead of learning from harmful examples, they protect benign behavior. Their test-time Ellipsoid Control nudges activations toward refusal with projected gradient descent, while an ellipsoid fitted to benign data limits distortion of benign geometry. Across several models, attacks, and benign tasks, the defense strengthened safety while preserving utility better than blacklist-style methods. The 2026 white-list approach thus avoids dependence on incomplete, shifting harmful samples.
arxiv-2605-24752: Andrej Risteski asks how hard it is to learn generative sampling from Ising models. He and Thuy-Duong Vuong build narrow computational models just past a known spectral threshold. They prove sampling from them is hard under standard crypto assumptions, even with full settings. Below the threshold sampling is tractable, so it marks a sharp easy-hard split. Sampling can thus be harder than learning settings, and fast learners must echo training distributions or favor memorization-hallucination patterns.
arxiv-2605-25052: Yoav Gur-Arieh, Ana Marasovi\ć, and Mor Geva ask whether faithfulness metrics for chains of thought actually measure faithfulness. Such traces often fail to reflect the computations behind predictions, and ground truth is scarce because internal computations cannot be observed. The authors build tasks whose outputs reveal the required computations, plus an automated labeling pipeline. That yields BonaFide: 3,066 labeled chains across 13 tasks and 10 models. Most metrics perform near chance and degrade on longer chains. The best reaches only 0.70 AUROC at chain level, another 0.59 at step level.
arxiv-2605-25352: Konstantinos Emmanouilidis and colleagues design models with formal robustness proofs from latent structure in learned codes. Ad-hoc defenses lack guarantees, while proof-based methods often give overly cautious bounds, ignoring data structure. The team first studies Gaussian mixtures, giving conditions for robust models and a closed-form proof. Their main result shows exact structure is unnecessary: if a latent spread sits close to a Gaussian mixture, certified scores fall slowly, with a bound. Tests on two image benchmarks reach top or strong certified scores with strong clean results.
arxiv-2605-25452: Nil Ayday, Mahalakshmi Sabanayagam, and Debarghya Ghoshdastidar survey how theory explains generalization in graph neural networks. They identify three broad frameworks: learning-theory bounds tied to hypothesis size and graph-isomorphism power. Approximations use Gaussian models, tangent kernels, and graphon operators, while random-graph analyses yield concrete error rates. The survey highlights key results, limitations, and open questions for each perspective, showing what theory now guarantees about networks deployed from social nets to drug discovery.
arxiv-2605-25552: Muhammad Kashif and Muhammad Shafique test variational quantum circuits after hardware build. That step reshapes circuits through qubit mapping, routing, and basis splitting, yet most studies judge expressibility and trainability only before building. Looking at logical and built circuits across ansatz families, qubit counts, and depths, they find design-driven shifts, with expressibility gaps above one hundred percent and trainability swings up to a quarter. Plain designs prove sturdier, while highly tangled ones shift most, and the trade-off between the two traits can itself change.
arxiv-2605-25652: Akarajaradwong and colleagues test whether agreement is a ceiling for grading Thai bar-exam essays, and whether matching it proves an LLM judge stable. Three Bar Council-trained examiners and 26 LLM judges score the same 15 answers. On ten cells with both rubric axes prescribed, all 29 raters converge tightly. On five cells where the rubric stays silent on a correct answer that omits a decisive citation, humans split into two readings. 22 of 26 LLMs cluster near the majority band, and none match the minority reading.
arxiv-2605-25752: Landry studies static spherically symmetric spacetimes in teleparallel F(T) gravity with electromagnetic sources. From the coframe pair he derives field equations and conservation laws, which limit the allowed setups. A general reconstruction method builds nonlinear models for any coframe choice. For power-law setups, he finds constant-radius, black-hole-like and wormhole-like cases, and studies their horizon and stability traits. The new charged cases extend Reissner-Nordström spacetimes, with changed horizon and distant behavior.
arxiv-2605-25852: Laplante tackles conditional coverage: prediction sets should cover every subgroup, not just on average. Exact conditional validity needs assumptions. Yet for data drawn independently and identically it comes down to a feature-free score. His PIT-CP turns any base score into a nearly invariant one, keeping its shape and coverage. The task then becomes 1D density estimation on the score, rather than full estimation. On varied datasets PIT-CP matches or beats strategies.
arxiv-2605-25952: Wu and five colleagues say fast multimodal systems lose too much visual detail. They squeeze images into few tokens using a single clue. Their VEN-VL framework first enriches the visual picture by combining several viewpoints. It then compacts the picture step by step through specialist routing experts that raise information density. Extra visual supervision guards key details during compaction. Tests report strong results with few condensed tokens, narrowing the speed-quality gap.
arxiv-2605-26252: Abdelghny Orogat and Essam Mansour argue that long-term agent memory should be a governed data workload, not storage. Systems pin rightness to records, embeddings, or graph edges, yielding four failures: unchecked growth, stale meanings, forced forgetting, and lookup that never writes back. Their Governed Evolving Memory, or GEM, swaps record work for four state operators that take in, revise, forget, and fetch, under six rules for correct change. A prototype called MemState shows the design can work and what a native engine must still add.
arxiv-2605-26352: Mingchen Li and six colleagues tackle credit assignment for interactive retrieval agents, which inspect evidence, rephrase queries, and search again in loops. Their critic-free RICE-PO framework turns retrieval interactions into local learning signals. It picks uncertain executable actions as anchors, testing local counterfactual branches with retrieval metrics. Credit passes to hidden reasoning steps only when influence is strong and later effects stay stable. On BRIGHT and BEIR, RICE-PO beats prompt-based agents and group-based baselines under the same retriever.
arxiv-2605-26452: Dhruv S. Kushwaha and Zoleikha A. Biron build a filter for actor-critic robot learning under state/input limits in training and deployment. Robust Koopman-CBF SAC learns a Koopman predictor from data, forms affine barrier constraints in lifted space, enforced through a quadratic-program layer. A residual margin from held-out rollouts tightens the barrier against approximation error. The critic learns from safe actions, while the actor drifts toward the feasible set.
