Amin and colleagues build a framework for auditing synthetic data in a 2026 privacy paper. Synthetic datasets promise the utility of real data without exposing real people, yet generators can memorize and regurgitate private records. Telling a true leak from a coincidence is the auditor's core problem.

Their framework separates true disclosures, where a person's information is genuinely reproduced, from phantom disclosures, where similar data arises by generalization or chance. Splitting real data into training and holdout parts, then applying careful statistical tests, checks whether observed matches exceed what strict baselines like zero learning or a stated differential privacy bound would allow. The audit needs no model access, no planted canaries and no reference training, only synthetic output and a held-out control set. In effect it works as a membership inference attack with tighter leakage bounds than earlier data-based audits, at far lower computing cost.
arxiv-2606-17052:
Khan, Mora and Vellojin analyze a finite element method for vibration problems in a 2026 numerical analysis paper. The Laplace eigenvalue problem, finding natural frequencies of a membrane or cavity, usually enforces its boundary condition strongly. The Nitsche method imposes it weakly instead, through penalty-like terms built into the formulation.

Three variants are studied through compact operator theory. The discrete solution operators converge in norm, so Babuška-Osborn spectral theory applies, giving error estimates for eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Rates depend on the variant: the symmetric one is optimal for eigenfunctions and double-order for eigenvalues, while the nonsymmetric ones lose ground. The paper also builds a residual error estimator for the symmetric method, driving adaptive mesh refinement where error concentrates. Tests confirm the predicted convergence, stability and robustness, and map how the penalty parameter shapes results in practice.
arxiv-2606-17252:
Ding, Quan, and Tu present a 2026 arXiv paper giving diffusion models a thermodynamic reading, linking their training goal to entropy production. Diffusion models turn data into noise, then learn a reverse process that rebuilds data from noise. Their training uses score matching, which estimates the gradient of the data density at each noise level, and this paper asks what that objective means in physics terms.

The authors define a trajectory-based quantity, time-asymmetry entropy production, from the forward and reverse dynamics together. It obeys exact fluctuation theorems, the precise symmetry laws of stochastic thermodynamics. A classic score-matching kernel turns up naturally as one fluctuating part of that quantity. Its average is exactly proportional to the score-matching objective itself, and its fluctuations measure how unevenly a model covers the data manifold.
arxiv-2606-17352:
Hossain and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on spotting out-of-distribution inputs, the unfamiliar cases where neural networks often answer with misplaced confidence. Their detector, MM++, works after training is done and needs no examples of the odd inputs at all. It builds on Mahalanobis distance methods, which judge how far an input's features sit from each class centre in a learned feature space during use.

Rather than trusting only the final layer, MM++ hunts for informative middle layers by watching where feature entropy drops sharply, a sign of strong semantic compression. Those layers are fused with the final features, and a regularised shared covariance keeps distance estimates stable in the joint space. The method is scale-invariant, so feature size alone cannot skew the scores it reports. Tests report robust detection for both near and far odd inputs across model designs.
arxiv-2606-17852:
Chang and colleagues test whether quantum circuits help a generative model invent new crystal materials, in a 2026 paper. Finding stable new crystals is a hard search problem, and classical generative models often collapse onto a few repeated structures. Quantum versions promise wider exploration, but near-term hardware is small, so the team uses a split-head design that separates lattice bounds from atomic positions.

Tested on the tight magnesium, manganese, and oxygen system, their quantum model faced a classical twin with the same architecture. The classical twin won on thermodynamic precision, while the quantum circuits more than doubled the share of geometrically valid structures and covered far more near-stable chemical space. The study cleanly separates what the architecture contributes from what the quantum hardware adds.
arxiv-2606-18352:
Omoruyi and colleagues introduce the TNG SAM, a semi-analytic model of galaxy formation tuned to mirror a major hydrodynamical simulation, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Full simulations track dark matter, gas, stars, and black holes together but are costly, while semi-analytic models run fast by simplifying the same physics.

The team rebuilt parts of the Santa Cruz semi-analytic model around measurements from IllustrisTNG. The rebuild updated how halo gas is accreted and cools, how outflows move at galaxy and halo scales, how efficiently stars form, and how metals circulate. Calibrated on feedback-dominated galaxies, the new model reproduces the simulation's flows of gas and metals. It matches galaxy and halo properties, such as stellar mass and hot halo gas, to within about thirty percent out to early cosmic times. The authors present it as a flexible bridge for studies needing simulation-like behavior across much larger volumes.
arxiv-2606-18652:
Jiang and colleagues calculate how often hyperons should decay into a pion or photon plus an invisible dark particle, within a low-scale baryogenesis scenario called Mesogenesis, in a 2026 particle physics paper. In Mesogenesis, ordinary hadrons can produce dark baryons that carry a hidden baryon number, potentially explaining both dark matter and the matter-antimatter asymmetry at energies directly testable by current experiments. Hyperon decays offer a clean place to look.

Using an effective Lagrangian approach with final-state interactions, the authors computed tree-level and one-loop triangle contributions. They found the loop diagrams are as significant as the tree diagrams and cannot be ignored for several channels. The resulting branching ratios for hadronic decays come out around one in a hundred thousand for the leading modes. The radiative decays sit below one in ten million, giving experimental searches concrete targets.
arxiv-2606-18852:
Muhamad and Sari improve the detection of hate speech that hides its intent, in a 2026 paper. Implicit hate works through insinuation, sarcasm, and euphemism, rather than slurs. Posts that attack the same group can share topical wording with innocent posts. So contrastive methods learn surface shortcuts that work in one dataset, and fail to transfer to others.

Their scheme ImpSH uses triplet learning that aligns each post with its implied statement, the insinuation behind it. It mines semi-hard negatives bounded by context, aiming training at near confusions. A variant forms positives through data augmentation. Tested on three datasets with BERT and HateBERT encoders, under matched prep and tuning, ImpSH was a viable option to supervised contrastive baselines. It often improved cross-domain performance. Representation analysis showed tighter positive pairs with balanced global spread, for a stable mapping from posts to their insinuations.
arxiv-2606-19052:
Muller and colleagues present an integrated approach to forecasting and stress-testing credit risk in 2026. Banks must gauge how loan books behave under stress, yet classic stress tests often skip how loans are produced. They also miss how risk measures move together. The authors join a loan production part with a credit risk part in one framework that can be extended and fit to real data over time.

A full portfolio is simulated with realistic loan terms and distributional assumptions. Cash flow histories are then generated in a multistate probabilistic framework, and portfolio default and loss rates are computed. Stress scenarios vary the loan terms inside a broader Monte Carlo setup, giving a range of portfolios to compare. Loan terms can also be modeled as functions of input variables with any fitting method. That dynamic, flexible setup aims to sharpen stress-testing practice beyond static, one-off exercises.
arxiv-2606-19152:
Zhang and colleagues present AdsMind in 2026, a multi-agent system that finds low-energy adsorption setups on catalyst surfaces. Finding how a molecule best sits on a surface is key to modeling catalysis. Exhaustive search with ab initio methods is far too costly, and machine-learning force fields speed relaxation but leave the vast search space as a bottleneck. Open-loop language model agents cannot correct bad first guesses without physics feedback.

AdsMind closes the loop. Agents propose setups, a learned force field relaxes them, and the feedback drives self-correction across rounds. Across four language model backends, success rates are very high on two benchmarks. The system needs only a handful of relaxations per case, a large cut versus heuristic enumeration. Spot checks with density functional theory validate the best setups. Such closed-loop search could speed catalyst screening.
arxiv-2606-19252:
Singh and colleagues optimize rigid and flexible nozzles for pulsed jet propulsion in 2026, inspired by squid and jellyfish. Those animals use flexible funnel deformation for rapid acceleration and maneuvering at low energy cost. The study asks how nozzle geometry trades impulse against energy input in engineered pulsed jets. A multi-objective Bayesian optimization framework, joined with three-dimensional fluid-structure simulations, searches designs that raise impulse while cutting jet energy.

Rigid and flexible nozzles show fundamentally different performance characters. Rigid designs reach the highest impulse amplification over a baseline cylindrical nozzle, about fivefold, but at much higher energy cost. Flexible designs peak lower, at about two and a half times the baseline impulse, yet achieve far better propulsion efficiency. Their best impulse-to-energy ratio is well above the rigid best. The contrast gives designers a clear map. Pick rigidity for raw thrust, flexibility for efficient cruising.
arxiv-2606-19552:
Sangmyeong Lee, Shun Inadumi, and Koichiro Yoshino release LaViSA in 2026, a benchmark for vision-language models facing ambiguous sentences. Structural ambiguity arises when one sentence allows several valid readings from its syntax alone. A picture of the scene can show which reading fits, if the model can use it.

LaViSA pairs ambiguous sentences with clarified versions and images drawn for each clarified reading. Seven ambiguity categories structure the test set. The team evaluate a wide range of vision-language models, both proprietary and open-source, across sizes and reasoning styles. Recent models do use visual scenes to settle some readings, the results show. Yet certain ambiguity types and faint visual contrasts still trip them up. The gaps mark where joint language-vision understanding still falls short. LaViSA gives builders a sharp tool for tracking progress on that weakness.
arxiv-2606-19652:
Chao Yin and Antoine Lesage-Landry train shallow neural networks by convex optimisation in 2026. The goal is robustness against adversarial attacks, small input tweaks that flip a network's output. Lipschitz regularisation bounds how fast outputs can change, but training stays nonconvex.

Yin and Lesage-Landry swap the hard program for a convex restriction solvable to global optimality. The scheme works as post-processing: start from a pretrained network, then solve the convex program. The resulting network is guaranteed no worse than the starting one on the target objective. Experiments on real regression datasets run under adversarial settings. The convex route posts lower objective values than existing methods. On certain datasets its networks are both more accurate and more robust. Guaranteed improvement steps are rare in network training, making the certificate the core appeal.
arxiv-2606-20352:
Sriram Kalathoor and Joseph Oefelein map the invisible skeleton that organizes mixing in a supersonic reacting shear layer. Their 2026 paper analyzes time-resolved mid-plane data from a 3D direct simulation of hydrogen and air burning as they shear past each other. The tools track moving fluid parcels: finite-time Lyapunov exponent fields reveal repelling and attracting transport barriers, while Cauchy-Green measures and geodesic structures cross-check the same pattern.

They measure ridge geometry, crossings, and how long ridges last, and tie that pattern to temperature, mixture fraction, and a reaction product. Forward and backward ridges overlap in localized patches, scalar gradients are strongly enriched along it, and scalar responses lag the flow only slightly. Coherent structures, the picture shows, actively organize where fuel and oxidizer meet and react.
arxiv-2606-20552:
Kevin Grosvenor and Subodh Patil compute the renormalization group flow of active flocks to all orders. Their 2026 paper works with the Toner-Tu theory of Malthusian flocks: polar-ordered active fluids that do not conserve momentum, where density relaxes so fast it drops out as a hydrodynamic variable.

Using the MSRDJ action formulation for stochastic systems, in the limit of isotropic diffusion in two dimensions, the authors renormalize the couplings and their anomalous dimensions. Ward identities from a nonlinearly realized rotation-shift symmetry, plus a nonlocal redundancy of the representation, make the all-orders result possible. Exact RG control over a canonical active-matter theory sharpens every perturbative prediction built on it.
arxiv-2606-20652:
Kristina Kehrer and Tim Conrad present a hybrid model of COVID-19 spread across Germany in 2026, linking three kinds of simulation at once. Agent-based models track individuals in detail and can use mobile phone mobility data, but they run slowly. Equation-based models using partial and ordinary differential equations run faster, yet describe crowds more coarsely. Their framework couples all three so detail is kept where it helps most.

Movement between regions enters through data-driven jump processes that transfer people between local models. Berlin is compared in agent, partial-equation, and ordinary-equation form inside a national run, letting the authors test travel bans to and from selected states. They also evaluate Zero-COVID and No-COVID strategies. The experiments show how mobility shapes outcomes, and give planners a tool balancing accuracy against cost.
arxiv-2606-20952:
Filippo Scaramuzza and Damian Tamburri report a field study in 2026 of tiny machine learning operations for cyber-physical systems, such as offshore wind equipment. Machine learning operations is becoming a software discipline. Its tiny variant targets microcontrollers with tight memory. Opaque models, noisy mixed data, and safety stakes hinder adoption. Most decisions in such settings still rely on human experts.

Their end-to-end pipeline fuses domain physics, expert judgment, and sensor streams. It builds explainable, small models that run on the device itself. Steps include automated data cleaning, knowledge-driven features, interpretable models, and rolling validation under drift. Data come from two offshore wind cable-trenching campaigns. A classifier predicts harmful load peaks up to three minutes ahead. Its footprint fits in a tiny memory budget. Field evidence matters because lab pipelines often fail when sensors, weather, and machines interact in real operations.
arxiv-2606-21152:
Jun Jiang and three colleagues study spin correlations and quantum entanglement in 2026 for top quark pairs produced by photon-photon collisions at a polarized photon collider. Photons come from Compton backscattered laser beams. Predictions cover cross sections and spin observables. Next-to-leading order corrections in quantum chromodynamics are included under several beam polarization settings.

Those corrections raise the total cross section significantly. Spin observables move only slightly. The spin density matrix of the top pair is then used to study entanglement and Bell nonlocality. Entanglement is strongest near the pair production threshold. Both effects depend sensitively on beam polarization. Top quarks decay before hadronizing, so their spins carry clean quantum information. Photon colliders could thus become a controlled laboratory for quantum correlations at the highest energy scales.
arxiv-2606-21252:
Talha Ilyas, Deval Mehta, and Zongyuan Ge built a seizure detection system in 2026 that can explain its own alarms, a gap in earlier video-based tools. Their neurosymbolic design first extracts skeleton sequences of patients in epilepsy monitoring units with a prompt-guided foundation model. It then predicts simple motor concepts drawn from clinical semiology guides, the signs doctors use to read seizures, and combines them through differentiable logic into plain Boolean rules.

On two public seizure video benchmarks, the system reaches about 90 and 85 percent sensitivity, with well under one false alarm per ten hours. Non-seizure clips are split into normal activities, which sharpens training and cuts false positives. Every alert can be traced to the motor signs seen, the rules used, and each rule's weight in the decision.
arxiv-2606-21452:
De Smet and ten colleagues show in 2026 that moving spin qubits around a chip can itself perform quantum operations, not just transport them. In conveyor-mode shuttling, traveling-wave voltages carry electrons across a semiconductor device while preserving their spin. The team uses that motion as the control knob in two distinct schemes for single and two-qubit gates.

In conveyor EDSR, spins shuttle resonantly through sideways magnetic field gradients at their Larmor frequency, producing high-fidelity rotations. In diabatic conveyor gates, tilts of the quantization axis give tunable bang-bang control instead. Adding exchange interaction switched by the motion yields a family of two-qubit interactions, selectable by shuttling speed and distance. The results point toward reconfigurable processors where transport and computation merge into one mechanism.
arxiv-2606-21652:
Omri Lesser and Chao-Ming Jian propose a trial wavefunction in 2026 for a fractional quantum spin Hall insulator with Z4 topological order. Fermions of opposite spin in half-filled conjugate Chern bands interact in ways their Landau-level cousins escape, because inter-species collisions rule out the standard Halperin wavefunctions. The Z4 order is the minimal one compatible with charge and spin conservation, time-reversal symmetry, and the fractional spin Hall response hinted at by twisted MoTe2 experiments.

Their construction condenses an anyonic exciton built from neutral fermions of a decoupled Moore-Read Pfaffian pair. A variational mass captures both inter-species s-wave and intra-species p-wave pairing of composite fermions. Monte Carlo energetics on a sphere, including the Landau-level-mixing kinetic penalty, show the Z4 state winning over sizable parameter regions.
arxiv-2606-22152:
Ahmad and colleagues bridge, in 2026, phase-field modelling and deep learning to predict how alloy microstructures evolve in two and three dimensions. The test case is ternary spinodal dealloying, a self-organization process used to fabricate nanoporous materials with complex internal structure. Phase-field simulation is faithful but slow, so the authors teach a network to continue its trajectories.

The learning workflow has three parts. A dimensionality-reducing autoencoder compresses high-resolution microstructure images into compact codes. An attention-augmented convolutional LSTM then learns the spatiotemporal patterns of the evolution. A slice-by-slice strategy extends the model to three-dimensional systems. In the hybrid scheme, the phase-field model handles the rapid early stages and the network predicts late-stage coarsening. The trained model stays accurate up to four hundred timesteps ahead. It also generalizes to compositions outside its training distribution.
arxiv-2606-22352:
Zihui Zhao, Yuanbo Tang, and Yang Li study dictionary learning in this 2026 paper, a technique that represents data as combinations of a few learned building blocks called atoms. Many methods force sparsity, meaning few atoms stay active for each input. Their focus is a family that simply caps the total number of activated atoms, a global rule whose theory has lagged behind its practical success.

The authors show this parsimonious approach matches a probabilistic model where hidden variables govern which atoms switch on together. Reading it as maximum a posteriori estimation, a standard Bayesian fitting rule, lets them prove generalization guarantees that were hard to reach before. The analysis spells out how sparsity, storage cost, and reconstruction accuracy trade off. That tradeoff yields data-driven settings, removing manual tuning. Their algorithm reconstructs images better at similar sparsity on visual benchmarks, and it speeds up inference for vision-language models.
arxiv-2606-22552:
F. Herz realizes a radiative version of the Mpemba effect in this 2026 physics paper. The Mpemba effect is the counterintuitive finding that a hotter system can sometimes cool faster than a colder one. It is known in convective, conductive, and quantum settings, but a version driven by thermal radiation had not been explored.

Herz creates the effect with a vanadium dioxide nanoparticle sitting near a silicon carbide substrate. The particle's phase change shows hysteresis, meaning its state depends on its thermal history. An analytic onset condition is derived, and the phase space of the effect is mapped. Latent heat, the energy stored during the phase change, acts as a thermal buffer and enables both the ordinary effect and an inverse one. Near-field coupling to the substrate governs the relaxation time. The substrate's reflection stores the memory of the initial state outside the particle, making the effect passive.
arxiv-2606-23052:
Chun-Wei Chen and colleagues make speech language models listen to sound rather than guess from words in a 2026 paper. Such models reason about spoken input, yet they lean on language habits and ignore acoustic detail. A decoding trick called contrastive decoding fixes this by comparing outputs with and without the audio. That trick doubles the work at answer time and slows replies. Their framework, CAAD, instead bakes the contrast into a student model during training.

Chen and colleagues add a synchronized teaching strategy to keep that training affordable. The teacher produces its contrastive output for a whole sequence at once, guided by shared pseudo ground truths. The student then absorbs the audio-aware signal directly into its weights. On the Dynamic-SUPERB benchmark, CAAD gained about eight percent over standard distillation in relative terms. It also reduced language bias on a second benchmark.
arxiv-2606-23152:
Jakub Gregorek and colleagues release ShotcreteDepth, a dataset for robot depth perception on construction sites, in a 2026 paper. Shotcrete is concrete sprayed onto surfaces to reinforce tunnels and repair structures. Automating the spraying needs robots that can judge depth reliably. Real sites fight the sensors with dust-filled air and poor lighting, leaving depth readings incomplete and noisy. The dataset records an active shotcreting process alongside general construction scenes. It pairs stereo color images with LiDAR point clouds gathered under those harsh conditions.

Gregorek and colleagues collected over eleven thousand time-synchronized samples. Two hundred twenty carry hand annotations for evaluation. A lightweight labeling tool for LiDAR clouds ships with the release. The dataset supports stereo matching plus depth completion and estimation under conditions that mirror real industrial sites.
arxiv-2606-23552:
Bajand and Vakili study the quantum behavior inside a charged black hole, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. The Reissner-Nordström geometry describes a black hole with electric charge. It has an outer event horizon and an inner horizon, and its interior region behaves much like a small universe. Classical theory predicts a singularity there, where the equations break down, so a quantum treatment is needed.

The authors shrink the full geometry to a minisuperspace model, keeping only a few changing variables. They then apply affine quantization, a method built for positive quantities such as a radius, which cannot drop below zero. The main equation separates neatly. One sector gives Hermite-polynomial modes, and the other gives smooth radial solutions. Building wave packets, the team shows that affine quantization adds short-distance terms. Those terms change how the wave function behaves near the center, and charge shapes the resulting probabilities.
arxiv-2606-23652:
Möbus, Bergamaschi, França, and Rouzé present a protocol for learning how an open quantum system evolves, in a 2026 paper on quantum information. Real quantum devices leak into their surroundings, and their dynamics follow a Lindblad generator, a rule combining internal evolution with dissipation. When interactions act on at most a few qubits at a time, the generator is local, and learning it matters for diagnosing noise.

The protocol needs only simple tools: preparing product states, brief evolution, and single qubit measurements, with no prior knowledge of the interaction pattern. It estimates every coefficient to a chosen accuracy, with sample counts that grow manageably with system size. A projection step then rounds the estimates into a valid generator. If the important interactions are sparse, the cost can drop to logarithmic in system size.
arxiv-2606-23752:
Brito dos Santos Filho presents a shared memory layer that lets several different AI coding agents continue each other's work, in a 2026 paper on software engineering tools. Developers now switch among coding assistants such as Codex, Grok, and Claude Code as context windows fill. Each tool keeps its own private log, so goals, decisions, and open tasks drift. Copying context by hand is lossy and expensive.

The system, ESAA Conversational, treats the visible conversation as an event store. Hooks and watchers capture turns mechanically into one append only log. Deterministic projections then produce handoff, state, decision, and task files any agent can read. A case study with five hundred seventy logged events shows heterogeneous agents collaborating through the shared log alone. The public release ships with an empty log, preserving the privacy of the development history.
arxiv-2606-24052:
Quigg traces an unlikely line from a wave seen on a Scottish canal in 1834 to the force holding quarks inside particles. Written for Gerard 't Hooft's eightieth birthday, this 2026 essay follows John Scott Russell's solitary canal wave into the Korteweg-de Vries equation, which describes robust wave packets called solitons. A single soliton turns out to mirror a special potential well holding exactly one bound state.

Combining several solitons yields symmetric reflectionless potentials, wells that trap waves without reflecting them, holding many bound states at once. That construction solves an inverse scattering problem: rebuilding a potential from the states it binds. Quigg then applies the machinery to quarkonium, heavy quark-antiquark pairs, building approximate confining potentials for the interquark force. The approximations also let him test whether that force stays the same across different quark flavours, as theory expects.
arxiv-2606-24252:
Agrawal and colleagues carve precise one-dimensional channels into layered crystals, for future nanophotonic devices. Sharp edges confine light tightly. But ordinary lithography and dry etching roughen edges and ruin repeat runs. Anisotropic wet etching of van der Waals crystals, such as transition metal dichalcogenides, leaves sharp zigzag edges by itself. Yet it leaves them only inside lone triangular or hexagonal shapes, set by the crystal's symmetry.

A lithography-guided framework breaks that limit. It forces neighbouring etched holes to interact in a controlled way. In multilayer tungsten disulfide, merging etch fronts sustain long-range zigzag facets. They unlock a straight edge alignment once thought impossible. Designers thus gain junctions at two angles instead of one. The team fabricates proof-of-concept nanochannels with the method. Agrawal's 2026 results present these channels as building blocks for high-index photonic structures, exact by construction, not by polishing.
arxiv-2606-24852:
B. A. Weaver measures how strongly Lyman alpha emitting galaxies cluster in three dimensions, using spectroscopy from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, DESI. The galaxies were picked from an intermediate band imaging survey taken with the Blanco telescope's DECam camera. Weaver computes the power spectrum and the two point correlation function, plus cross correlations with DESI quasars.

Two modelling routes interpret the measurements. Analytical modelling and halo occupation distribution modelling, the latter simulation based, agree on a linear bias between roughly two point three and two point six. That range covers redshifts from roughly two point three to three point four, when the universe was young. The analytical route also constrains how radiative transfer effects distort the signal. Weaver also quantifies non perturbative clustering effects such as Fingers of God. The results feed the design of future high redshift surveys, including a planned DESI successor.
arxiv-2606-25052:
G. Apostolovska and five colleagues present a portrait of the main belt asteroid (300) Geraldina. Two decades of archival photometry from the Rozhen observatory anchor the study. Dense lightcurves since 2017, archive data, and sparse Gaia measurements complete it. Lightcurve inversion yields the rotation period, a shape model, and the spin axis tilt. The rotation is confirmed as prograde. Two mirror image pole solutions fit equally well, an ambiguity the authors state openly.

Orbit runs show Geraldina stays stable for a hundred million years. It passes near Jupiter's 2 to 1 resonance without capture. Instead it interacts with an unidentified higher order resonance supporting its long term stability. Its spectrum marks it as a primitive carbonaceous C type body with low albedo. Stability, composition, and darkness point the same way. Apostolovska and colleagues conclude Geraldina is likely an ancient asteroid, a survivor from the early solar system on a quiet orbit.
arxiv-2606-25152:
Detectors that separate human writing from AI text are usually trained once on labelled data, then deployed into a shifting world. Kevin Ren, Manish Raghavan, and Nikhil Garg identify three continual shifts: adversarial humanisation of AI text, new language models appearing, and slow drift in how humans write. Labelled data for the shifted text is rarely available.

Their alternative adapts at test time. Semi supervised learning exploits a signal of machine generation, the sameness of outputs observed together at inference, to adjust without labels. State of the art supervised detectors fail badly under the shifts, in adversarial and natural forms alike. One commercial detector catches only about a quarter of adversarial AI text, where the test time approach catches about nine tenths. The team releases its code publicly.
arxiv-2606-25352:
A wide field X-ray telescope sweeps up genuine cosmic flashes mixed with instrument glitches and cosmic ray hits. Lang Chen and colleagues built M-EPDet in 2026 to vet that candidate stream for the Einstein Probe's Wide-field X-ray Telescope in real time. Three stages cascade. One neural filter is shaped for the telescope's cross like image arms, and a two branch filter targets cosmic rays in time and spectrum. A variability screen that respects the local background finishes the chain. Each stage's scores are reported separately.

On real in orbit data, the cascade kept over ninety eight percent of genuine astrophysical sources. It rejected about ninety three percent of instrumental artifacts and over ninety eight percent of cosmic ray events. A final variability step cut the surviving candidate volume by more than ninety nine percent, easing the human inspection load.
arxiv-2606-25452:
Keeping a team of robots in formation while it moves usually means stacking a safety controller on top of a formation controller, then tuning the pair. S Saharsh and Pushpak Jagtap fold both jobs into a single constraint in 2026. Their control barrier function style condition is extended so it also guarantees reaching the target formation in finite time, not just staying safe. The whole rule sits inside a quadratic program solved in real time using only neighbour relative positions.

No separate nominal controller and no hand tuning are required, which removes the clashes that can make layered schemes infeasible. Agents may differ from each other and follow nonlinear dynamics. Simulations of moving formations under a leader follower setup validate the approach. The authors stress the method's lean sensing diet suits settings where global position fixes are unavailable or unreliable.
arxiv-2606-25552:
Voice assistants must extract intent and slots from speech, and one utterance can carry several intents at once. Po-Yen Chen and Berlin Chen tackle the unreliability of prompt based language models on such input in 2026. Sampling the model repeatedly gives self consistency, but conflicting answers come as whole structured frames that flat majority voting cannot merge. Their framework instead breaks predictions into intent specific frames, groups them by domain and intent, and clusters the slots inside each group.

Each cluster is scored by how much supporting path evidence backs it, a reliability measure the authors call path support. Trustworthy frames are kept and reintegrated into one final prediction. Zero shot tests on a multi intent benchmark improved slot scores and overall accuracy over single pass inference. Intent accuracy stayed broadly stable, suggesting the gains come from cleaner slot assembly rather than lucky intent guesses.
arxiv-2606-25752:
A bump on a hypersonic vehicle's skin takes pressure, heating, and shear loads. In thin air those loads may depend on gas far from the wall. Elyas Lekzian and Ehsan Roohi quantify that reach in 2026 for triangular protrusions. They use direct simulation Monte Carlo fields, across Mach four to eight and a range of rarefaction. Around every wall point they summarised growing circular neighbourhoods of the flow. Then they asked how large a neighbourhood a diagnostic needs before its predictions nearly match using the whole domain.

No single information length emerged. Full field knowledge cut pressure errors from about forty six to fourteen percent. Heating errors fell from about seventy three to thirteen percent. Shear improved far less and stayed hardest to pin down. It saturated at shorter radii. Heating showed the clearest nonlocal support, on the protrusion's own scale. Pressure often needed more than three times that.
arxiv-2606-26052:
Jaume de Dios Pont, Lukas Liehr, and Mitchell Taylor answer a standing question about Gabor frames. A Gabor system shifts one window function across a lattice in time and frequency. Frames give stable, redundant representations of signals. The existence problem asks whether nice windows can generate frames on lattices of density above one in higher dimensions. Candidate windows live in respected spaces like the Schwartz space and the Feichtinger algebra.

Negative is the answer, under explicit criteria. For every dimension above one, the team lists lattice conditions under which a frame cannot be generated by any function with a continuous Zak transform. The result rests on characterizing when quasiperiodic functions share a common zero. That characterization may interest other problems too. A Lean 4 formalization of the main result accompanies the paper. Time-frequency analysis loses a hoped-for construction, but gains a sharp boundary for where to stop searching.
arxiv-2606-26152:
K. K. Nandi, R. N. Izmailov, R. Kh. Karimov, and A. A. Potapov examine black holes that carry an imprint of a fifth dimension. Braneworld models, inspired by string theory, place our four-dimensional world on a brane inside a larger space. Gravity from the extra dimension leaves a tidal charge in the black hole solution of Dadhich and colleagues. The charge looks like electric charge in the equations, but it can take either sign, and no electricity is involved.

Strong-field effects carry the signatures. Gravitational lensing near the hole shifts measurably with the tidal charge. Ringdown tones, the quasinormal modes a disturbed hole rings with, shift too. The two sign variants are compared against each other and against plain Schwarzschild. One variant's light orbits prove less stable than Schwarzschild's. Its accretion disks should therefore shine brighter. The Sagittarius A-star case anchors the discussion in a real target.
arxiv-2606-26252:
Westley Brown and colleagues compare galaxy shapes in dense clusters and in the open field, at redshift near one point six. Three clusters from the SpARCS survey anchor the cluster side. Field galaxies come from the 3D-HST survey. Sérsic index, a measure of how concentrated a galaxy's light is, sorts the galaxies into disk-like, bulge-like, and in-between forms.

Crowding already shapes galaxies at that era. As local density rises, bulge-like galaxies grow commoner and disk-like ones rarer. The trend holds in clusters and in the field alike, with matching slopes. Mass pushes the same way: higher stellar mass means a higher Sérsic index on average. Most galaxies stay disk-like until a high mass threshold, reached sooner in clusters than in the field. A morphology-density relation was already in place that far back.
arxiv-2606-26552:
Yangjun Wu and seven colleagues present ForeAgent, an agent system for spotting AI-generated images. Generative models now produce highly realistic fakes at scale. Detectors struggle to notice fine forensic traces. Language-vision models look promising, but many rely on fixed training examples written by frontier models. That supervision is costly and rigid.

ForeAgent splits the job into perception and verdict stages. The perception stage gathers cues about meaning, space, and frequency patterns in the image. A large multimodal model then weighs those cues into a reasoned verdict. Improvement comes from a hindsight strategy. The agent attempts training cases, then studies its failures using the known answers. It rewrites weak reasoning into better examples. A dual-expert filter keeps only high-quality new examples. The loop lets the detector refine itself over time.
arxiv-2606-26752:
Huchan Lee and Sin Kyu Kang scan a particle physics model that tackles three open problems at once. The scotogenic model generates neutrino masses through a dark sector loop. It also supplies dark matter candidates. The minimal extension studied here also addresses the instability of the Standard Model vacuum at high energies. The authors test the model against a wide battery of data.

Checks include vacuum stability and theory consistency bounds. Flavour and precision data matter most: rare muon and lepton decays, conversion rates, and boson decay measurements. The scan found viable fermionic dark matter in a mid-range mass window. A partner scalar is confined to a heavier window. One striking conditional result emerged: a recent cosmological bound, if confirmed, would rule out the inverted ordering of neutrino masses in this model.
arxiv-2606-27052:
Bentley and colleagues search millions of research abstracts for signs that large language models are reshaping scientific writing. Language models now help draft and revise papers, and their output feeds back into training data for later models. That loop could slowly shift shared writing habits across science. Abstracts from arXiv between 2010 and 2025 form a natural experiment, with early 2023 as the turning point. The team tracks word-pattern laws and a combined style index linked to model-like writing, in a study appearing in 2026.

After early 2023, the style index jumps sharply. Core word laws, named for Zipf and Heaps, shift only slightly in their exponents. Two subtler changes stand out more clearly. Turnover among the most-used words speeds up markedly. Also, the link between model-like style and three complexity measures flattens after 2022. Together, the patterns suggest human and model writing now form one mixed, evolving system.
arxiv-2606-27252:
Dobson and colleagues bring rigorous Bayesian model choice to exoplanet mass measurement from radial velocity data. Planet hunters fit star wobble curves, but choices about orbit shape, noise, and trends sway the masses they report. Information criteria, the usual comparison tool, lack a built-in Occam's razor and ignore prior knowledge. The learned harmonic mean estimator computes Bayesian evidence straight from existing sampling output. No refitting procedure needs changing in this exoplanet methods paper of 2026, the estimator's first radial velocity use.

Eighteen model variants are fitted to each of six single-planet systems. A seventh system gets seventy-two variants for a planet-count comparison. No single model wins everywhere, confirming that per-system comparison is essential. The open-source harmonic package makes the method drop-in for current workflows. Robust masses follow from honest model doubt.
arxiv-2606-27452:
Do, Brown, and Pokorný trace where the millimetre-sized meteoroids hitting Earth come from, comets or asteroids. Orbit-based rules exist, but their reliability for tiny meteoroids was never strictly checked. The team tests several known criteria, including the classic K and Pe rules, the Tisserand invariant, and a recent aphelion-distance scheme. During 2026, backward-integrating swarms of orbital clones for three hundred eighty-six observed meteoroids evaluates each one's origin.

The K and Pe criteria prove best at finding a meteoroid's parent type. A dividing speed emerges: below about seventeen kilometres per second, Earth-impacting grains released in the last two hundred thousand years are mostly asteroidal, whatever the criterion. Cometary dominance arrives only above about twenty-seven kilometres per second in the reported analysis. Thermal processing near the Sun further scrambles material signatures. Sporadic meteors gain a solid family tree.
arxiv-2606-27552:
A pipe can wobble violently once fluid flows through it fast enough, and more so when the pipe also spins. Ali Fasihi and three colleagues study this case in 2026. Their pipe cannot stretch. One end has a fixed pin, and the other a sliding roller. That support change removes the usual stretching-based restoring force.

The team derives new equations of motion. The nonlinear terms come from the no-stretch condition and from bending curvature. Two independent methods are used. One expands the curvature to ninth order. They show ninth order is the lowest that captures the true amplitude. The common third-order shortcut greatly overstates the deflection. The second method is a modified Hencky bar-chain model. It models the pipe as a chain of rigid links with exact angle mathematics. Both methods agree closely. The stability boundary forms an ellipse-like curve of flow speed against spin speed.
arxiv-2606-27652:
Thinking aloud does not always help an emotion recogniser. Zhiyuan Han and ten colleagues found this paradox in multimodal emotion recognition in 2026. Fast answers often beat slow, deliberated answers. Fast thinking raises recall with broad, confident predictions. Slow thinking raises precision by filtering wrong categories out. Their framework, MER-R1, turns that contrast into a training signal.

MER-R1 is built with reinforcement learning. Dual-objective disentanglement splits recall and precision into two signals. They can then be optimised jointly instead of traded off. A calibration step aligns the final slow answer with fast intuition. Correct emotions get strengthened, and incorrect ones get suppressed. The authors also give a theoretical justification for the synergy. It reduces variance-driven interference during optimisation. Experiments on MER-UniBench and MME-Emotion reach state-of-the-art results. Reasoning finally benefits emotion recognition in their tests, they report.
arxiv-2606-27852:
Gravitational-wave event GW241011 poses a formation puzzle. Its binary black holes have an extreme mass ratio near zero point three. The primary also spins rapidly. Hierarchical mergers explain high spins naturally. They rarely give such extreme ratios, though, and recoil kicks can eject the merged black hole. Rui-Chong Hu, Ying Qin, and Bing Zhang test an alternative in 2026: mass-ratio reversal in isolated binary evolution.

Population synthesis with COMPAS quantifies the channel. The authors vary stellar-evolution and binary-interaction assumptions. They find the conditions under which mass-ratio reversal can make GW241011-like systems. A small fraction of such binaries overlap the event's credible region. These systems show low mass ratios and positive effective spins. Only models with high common-envelope efficiency produce them. Lower-efficiency binaries tend to merge during the common-envelope phase instead. The channel thus stands as a viable alternative under identifiable conditions.
arxiv-2606-27952:
Multistate models track how people move between health states over time. Occupation probabilities say how likely each state is at a given time. Niklas Nyboe Maltzahn, Gergely Dániel Lukáts, and Kjetil Røysland derive estimators for them in 2026. Two levels of coarsening complicate the data. Right-censoring is one level. Baseline exposure is the other. The key assumption is coarsening at random. Time-varying confounders are allowed, and no Markov property is required.

The estimators use augmented inverse probability weighting. That method blends outcome modelling with weights for the chance of being observed. The resulting estimators are robust and efficient. Theory proves both claims. A simulation study shows them in practice. Tools from causal inference and the missing-data literature are combined. The target is settings where states are only partly observed in practice. Expected length of stay is among the quantities such estimators support.
arxiv-2606-28452:
Andreas Wichert, writing alone, speeds up quantum tree search. Amplitude amplification, the generalization behind Grover's famous search algorithm, is usually analyzed as if every branch of a search tree were as wide as the widest one. Real trees are uneven, and Wichert shows the cost is governed by the average branching instead.

Building the tree dynamically, his construction reaches a query complexity set by the square root of the average branching raised to the depth, improving on the worst-case figure. He also pushes back on the fashion for quantum backtracking, noting it fits only problems with a natural backtracking shape. Because the dynamically built tree hides its own structure, he proposes sampling methods to estimate it. He also adds a quantum greedy search guided by a lookahead heuristic borrowed from the Soar cognitive architecture.
arxiv-2606-28652:
Zitian Zhou and Nan Lin keep sparse regression learning as data streams in. High-dimensional quantile regression predicts conditional quantiles rather than means and tolerates heavy-tailed noise. It must run online here, updating with each observation while keeping the model sparse. Its nonsmooth loss makes the online problem genuinely hard.

Their Adaptive Iterative Hard Thresholding alternates random subgradient steps with thresholding that prunes small coordinates, on a set schedule. Early on, thresholding is delayed so weak yet useful coordinates can build up evidence; later, projections grow frequent to steady the estimate and exploit local curvature. Theory places the iterates in an inflated sparse cone, with two-phase convergence and logarithmic regret for a sliding-window target. Computer runs and schedule ablations back the design against standard online sparse-learning baselines.
arxiv-2606-29052:
Lei, Peng, Zhang and Xu design a scheduler that decides which pieces of meaning deserve radio bandwidth when devices cooperate on a task. In task-oriented semantic communication, devices send compact semantic features rather than raw data. Radio resources are scarce, channels fade fast, and end-to-end delay budgets are strict. Older solutions either optimise too heavily to run live, or assume channels change slowly.

Their framework, iCoTASC, mixes offline preparation with light online decisions. Attribution-based importance scores guide which embedding dimensions each device sends, acting as a practical control signal. A data-driven utility function captures how extra quantisation detail yields diminishing returns. Per-transmitter lookup tables are computed offline, so online scheduling is mostly table lookup plus low-cost refinement under changing channels. The design supports real-time, channel-adaptive allocation across distributed devices. Crucially, the underlying task model never needs retraining when the scheduler adapts.
arxiv-2606-29552:
Pandey leads a large team refining line-by-line radial velocity measurement, a technique that reads each spectral line of starlight separately instead of blending them. Blending through cross-correlation loses information about line shape changes caused by stellar activity. Reading lines independently preserves that detail, which matters when hunting planets by the tiny wobble they induce in their star.

Using 383 days of NEID solar observations, the team measures more than three thousand eight hundred spectral lines. Their full line list already edges out a cross-correlation approach on the same lines. Careful subsets chosen by line depth and scatter do better still. Their iterative algorithm, FLARES, preferentially removes whichever lines most reduce the weighted scatter. It reaches a scatter near one metre per second with just twenty-four lines. Monte Carlo simulations show the selection is robust and reproducible.
arxiv-2606-29652:
Zerhoudi, Roegiest, Mitrović, and Granitzer argue for local-first information retrieval, search that runs on the user's own device instead of remote servers. The most valuable material to search is also the most sensitive: personal documents, legal files, and medical records. Current retrieval-augmented generation systems still send such content to outside servers by default.

Their framework organizes retrieval architectures by three dimensions: privacy and control, capability, and accessibility. Experiments on consumer hardware span five benchmarks and collections from one thousand to one million documents, testing dense retrieval, BM25, and hybrid fusion. In those tests dense retrieval keeps over ninety percent of its ranking quality up to one hundred thousand documents. Approximate indexes extend that to a million documents with small quality loss. A seven-billion-parameter local model comes within a few points of a cloud baseline for answer quality.
arxiv-2606-29852:
Li Cai, Jingsong Chai, and Yadi Liu work on Bessel distributions in pure mathematics. These distributions attach special functions to representations of a group. Their setting is a split reductive group over a p-adic field. A p-adic field is a number system built from a prime. The question is whether these distributions act like ordinary smooth functions.

Cai and colleagues derive germ expansions for Kloosterman integrals tied to the group. Germ expansions are local approximations near special points of the group. Using them, they prove the distributions are regular for every generic representation. That result needs one condition on smaller building block groups. Kloosterman sums for every Levi subgroup must admit nontrivial bounds. Such bounds would feed back into the relative Langlands program, a broad web of conjectures linking representations and number theory, where these distributions first arose.
arxiv-2606-29952:
Seonghwan Park, Hyunji Jung, Dongyeop Lee, and Namhoon Lee address out-of-distribution detection. The task is spotting inputs unlike anything a network trained on. Reliable systems must flag such inputs instead of guessing confidently. One clue, explored in their 2026 paper, is curvature of the loss landscape. Earlier curvature methods were slow and rested on untested assumptions.

Park and colleagues show that unfamiliar inputs produce larger Hessian curvature. Hessian curvature measures how sharply the loss surface bends. The gap over familiar inputs grows as the shift strengthens. Their detector, Fold, combines the feature Hessian with partial feature normalization. It runs at roughly the cost of one forward pass. A variant, AutoFold, invents fake unfamiliar samples by masking model outputs. No outside data is needed for calibration. On standard benchmarks, Fold improves detection scores and lowers false alarms.
arxiv-2606-30152:
Huanping Xiao, writing alone, separates two kinds of gender signal inside contextual language models. In languages like Spanish, nouns carry grammatical gender by rule. Models also absorb social gender stereotypes from their training text. The two signals become tangled in the learned representations. Debiasing methods built for English ignore that tangle entirely.

Xiao builds balanced datasets of inanimate nouns for the study. Both controlled sentence templates and natural Wikipedia contexts are used. Three estimators then extract a grammatical gender direction from embeddings. They are a centroid method, a support vector machine, and linear discriminant analysis. New dual-objective metrics weigh two goals against each other. One goal suppresses grammatical gender leaking into inanimate nouns. The other preserves real semantic gender for occupation terms. Unweighted controlled contexts yield the purest gender direction. The simple centroid estimator beats the trained rival methods.
arxiv-2606-30252:
Maxime Riché, Daniel Tan, Vili Kohonen, and Niels Warncke protect fine-tuning from teaching models unwanted traits. Fine-tuning on narrow bad data can produce broadly misaligned models, a failure called emergent misalignment. Inoculation prompting fights this by naming the bad trait during training. That drains the pressure to learn the trait deeply. Their inoculation adapters move the same idea into model weights.

An adapter is first trained on the undesired trait alone. It is then frozen while a separate task adapter trains. The task data show both desired and undesired traits together. At deployment, the inoculation adapter is discarded entirely. Only the task adapter ships with the model. Across six model families, undesired traits are suppressed better than with prompting. Traits that no prompt can reliably elicit can also be suppressed. Surprising backdoors under probing are fewer as well.
arxiv-2606-30752:
Amy Smock and six colleagues use stellar ages to read the history in the Milky Way's spiral arms. Passing spiral patterns leave signatures, ridges or wrinkles in the space of stellar actions, but motion alone has not revealed what made them. The team ran tracer-particle simulations with varied recipes for spiral arms, then asked which stars populate the wrinkles each recipe creates.

Nonwinding spirals produced signature overdensities at high radial action, a region usually linked to older stars. Yet the wrinkles were filled by stars that began on nearly circular orbits. Near-circular starts correlate with younger stellar ages. So a wrinkle's age mix can betray when a spiral pattern passed through the solar neighbourhood. The simulations suggest one pattern could stock a wrinkle with zero-age stars sitting in orbits typical of stars much older than the Sun. The authors propose age as a clock for spiral episodes.
arxiv-2606-31152:
Alhomsi and two colleagues build a numerical scheme for the perturbed Boussinesq system, equations for buoyancy-driven flow in a stratified fluid. Their version subtracts a stable layered resting state, so the scheme tracks departures from balance. Each time step should stay cheap and the method should not demand tiny steps for stability.

Their second-order consistent-splitting scheme uses a generalized scalar auxiliary variable and treats convection, advection, buoyancy, and stratification terms explicitly. Each step then solves only a few separate linear systems. They prove unconditional weak stability and optimal second-order error bounds for velocity, pressure, and temperature. Tests confirm the order and reproduce internal waves plus slow relaxation to balance, though the error constant grows sharply as viscosity or diffusivity shrinks.
arxiv-2606-31352:
Zhao and five colleagues present Dualformer, a feature extractor for blind analysis of communication signals. Tasks such as automatic modulation recognition and signal structure parsing must work without prior knowledge of the signal. Complex-valued signals carry in-phase and quadrature parts, and most models handle them awkwardly or at double cost.

Dualformer follows the DualNN idea: one shared network processes both channels of the complex signal, which provably cuts generalization error while keeping expressive power. Signals are split into patch tokens, and multi-granularity features are captured across scales. Against three transformer baselines and four deep learning rivals, Dualformer wins steadily on modulation, scheme, and structure tasks. The same design also transfers to blind source separation and low signal-to-noise spectrum sensing.
arxiv-2606-31452:
Bromboszcz studies arrangements of conics and lines whose crossings stay simple, set in the complex projective plane. Only nodes, tacnodes, and ordinary triple points are allowed. The shape of such an arrangement controls its homological algebra, above all the Jacobian syzygies of its defining curve.

For plus-one generated conic arrangements with defect three, the first part derives numerical restrictions and tests them against Bézout's theorem, the Dimca-Sernesi bound, and Hirzebruch-type inequalities. The possible numbers of conics end up bounded, with low-degree exceptions split from cases still open. For arrangements of total degree at most six, the second part identifies the weak and strong Ziegler pairs in a recorded database, pairs that share numbers yet differ in syzygies.
arxiv-2606-31552:
Götz and five colleagues test whether the realism of simulated rooms changes how well speech enhancement models learn. Training data for multichannel enhancement is often augmented with room-acoustic simulation, and most pipelines use fast geometrical acoustics. Wave-based simulation is slower but tracks the physics of sound far more closely.

They train SpatialNet on data from geometrical methods, from a high-fidelity wave-based and hybrid set, and compare all models on measured recordings. The high-fidelity training data cut the median word error rate by up to 38 percent relative to the low-fidelity sets. Simulation quality, not just quantity, drives the gain. Enhancement teams should treat acoustic realism as a training variable in its own right, the results argue.
arxiv-2606-31752:
Janson and three others look for signatures of the circular Unruh effect in the transitions of a multilevel atom. The effect predicts that a detector moving in a circle through an electromagnetic vacuum becomes excited. An atom on such a path serves as the detector, and its electric and magnetic dipole transitions compete as channels.

Unlike the usual focus on electric transitions, magnetic dipole transitions dominate, the team shows. Comparing free-space and cavity setups, they find sensitivity improves by shrinking the mode volume while guarding the mode density. A new scheme uses the atom's multilevel structure to suppress spontaneous emission. That suppression could bring the faint circular Unruh signal within experimental reach.
arxiv-2606-31852:
Aghamov and three colleagues determine the modal logics of full products of neighborhood frames. Neighborhood semantics generalizes Kripke semantics for weak modal logics. On a product frame, three neighborhood functions arise naturally: a horizontal one, a vertical one, and a genuine product one combining both coordinates.

Two tri-modal logics are axiomatized, for frames validating the logic T and for frames validating D. Each turns out to equal a threefold fusion of the base logic plus one interaction principle, called mix. Over S4 the two candidate principles, sub and mix, coincide. That equivalence yields an axiomatization of the logic of full products of topological spaces as a by-product of the main theorems.
arxiv-2606-31952:
Spencer and two colleagues speed up a bottleneck in near-term quantum computing: writing a classical matrix as a combination of Pauli strings. Quantum algorithms for chemistry, optimization and linear algebra usually assume the input already arrives in that form. For a general matrix, recovering the decomposition takes time exponential in the number of qubits, which can erase any quantum speedup before the device even runs.

Their randomized classical algorithm targets matrices promised to use only polynomially many Pauli strings, accessed through sparse queries. It recovers the exact decomposition with success probability at least one minus a chosen error level. Query and runtime costs stay polynomial in the qubit count, the number of Pauli terms and the logarithm of the inverse error.
arxiv-2608-00152:
Shoeibi and Yousefi ask whether in-distribution success can be trusted in CRISPRi prediction. A benchmark win inside one distribution may fail under shift. An endpoint may also entangle with a design factor. They study both risks in perturbation-effect prediction. A frozen Geneformer representation is tested under a locked protocol.

Heads and model choice were frozen before test evaluation. Outcome labels stayed withheld until final unblinding. In-distribution, the representation beat a random-feature control by 0.1645 in R squared. It then failed zero-shot transfer on both external screens. Its correlations there were negative, below the control on each. A count-only model explained the benchmark endpoint strongly. Much of the magnitude signal overlapped with cell count, they find.
arxiv-2608-00352:
Wang and Bai present AETHER-P3, a machine learning model for global thermospheric density forecasts. Density in the thermosphere governs drag in low Earth orbit. It is a prime source of error in orbit prediction and conjunction checks, above all during geomagnetic storms. Their model forecasts up to six hours ahead from a three-hour input window. Uncertainty estimates come with each forecast.

The task is framed as sequence-to-sequence regression. Inputs include recent space weather plus future times and locations from the user. Physics model estimates from JB2008 and NRLMSISE-00 add consistency at future points. Dual recurrent encoders and an evidential output head produce mean and uncertainty. Test skill reached R of 0.95 in quiet periods. Extreme storms degraded skill to about 0.89, as expected. Uncertainty stayed well calibrated across all regimes.
arxiv-2608-00452:
Kahirov, Deshpande, and Sundararaman ground lexical retrieval in semantic evidence with CE-QE. BM25 catches exact keyword matches and corpus-wide term weight. It is blind to the semantic vocabulary gap, though. A relevant document phrased differently is never retrieved. No reranking downstream can recover a document outside the candidate set.

Cross-Encoder Query Expansion reads token attributions from a cross-encoder over top semantic results. It picks the terms the cross-encoder treats as decisive and appends them to the BM25 query. Every expansion term is copied verbatim from a retrieved passage. That blocks vocabulary the corpus does not contain. On seven BEIR data sets, recall rose sharply where vocabularies diverge. Natural Questions Recall@100 climbed from 0.32 to 0.47. The BM25 index itself stays unmodified.
ashmole-theatrum-chemicum-britannicum-16:
Elias Ashmole, the antiquary whose museum still bears his name at Oxford, edited the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum in 1652. The anthology gathers English alchemical verse from the Middle Ages and the Tudor age. Ashmole meant to prove that England had its own noble line of adepts.

The poems of Thomas Norton, George Ripley, and the writers who used the name Lully fill its pages in their old spelling. Ashmole adds notes, lives of the authors, and a defense of the art against its mockers. The book preserved the canon of English alchemy that later scholars still study from his pages.
averroes-renan-averroes-et-laverroisme-1:
Ernest Renan published Averroes et l'averroisme in French in 1852, the first modern study of Averroes and his followers. Renan was a young French scholar when he wrote the book as his doctoral work. Averroes, the twelfth-century thinker of Cordoba, had been half forgotten in the West despite his fame as Aristotle's great commentator.

Renan traced how Averroes read Aristotle and how Latin followers turned his teaching into a bold doctrine of reason's independence from faith. He followed that influence through both Muslim and Christian schools. The book put a daring medieval mind back at the center of philosophy's history. It also launched Renan's career and set the pattern for later studies of how Greek thought passed through Arabic hands into Europe.
braid-magic-witchcraft-animal-magnetism-:
Braid's mature statement came in Magic, Witchcraft, Animal Magnetism, Hypnotism, and Electro-Biology, in its enlarged third edition of 1852. Witch trials, demonic possession, and mesmeric marvels crowd its pages. Braid rereads them all as misunderstood nervous and mental phenomena. What ages blamed on demons, he assigns to trance, suggestion, and disease.

The book gathers his whole demystification project between two covers. History supplies his cases, and his physiology supplies the keys. Electro-biology, a stage name for hypnotic shows, gets its share of analysis. The work caps a decade in which he remade the field. It shows a surgeon arguing with centuries of fear. The argument stays humane throughout.
buckley-life-and-adventures-1852:
William Buckley lived wild for thirty-two years, and his Life and Adventures, out in 1852, tells how. Buckley was a felon sent to the far south land who fled to the bush in 1803. The Wathaurong folk took him in. He dwelt as one of them till new white men came in 1835 and he stepped out of a lost age, a giant in skins.

John Morgan shaped his tale for print. Midst wars, hunts, and rites stands talk of the bunyip, the dread beast of the swamps. The book is a rare guest's tale. It grips throughout.
centuria-chymica-hoc-est-tractatus-aureu:
An anonymous Latin verse treatise on the philosopher's stone, printed in 1652, calls itself a golden tract and a hundredfold chemical work. Its short numbered poems warn that writers on the art speak in riddles on purpose. Secrets, the opening verses insist, are for the sons of the art, not for the unready crowd.

Poems then ask where the stone's matter is found, and answer through cabala, number, and name. Adam, red earth, mercury, and the sun carry hidden counts. Salt, sulphur, and mercury form the three principles; fire, air, water, and earth the four elements. Nature and the craftsman argue in dialogue near the end. The old long-s type, roughly scanned, slows the Latin down.
chadwell-memo-1952:
A CIA science chief urged Washington to take the flying saucers in earnest in September 1952. Marshall Chadwell's memo to the Director of Central Intelligence asks the National Security Council to act. Chadwell ran the Office of Scientific Intelligence in a summer of mass sightings.

He warns that the saucer reports touch air defense and public calm at once. His ask set in train the Robertson Panel, which met the next winter in secret. That panel taught the agency to calm and debunk the reports in public. The memo is the paper that made UFOs a Washington question.
cia-0000008652:
Quang Yen district, in Quang Ninh province, is named in a June 1974 report on a dead American pilot sighted there. Quang Ninh borders China and holds Ha Long Bay's coast, far northeast of Hanoi. The sighting reached the files well after the 1973 ceasefire.

Reports from remote districts tested the reach of the postwar accounting system. A witness account had to travel far before analysts could match it to a loss. Many never matched, yet all were kept. Keeping them mattered because later evidence sometimes completed an old fragment. This file is one such fragment, preserved with its place and date.
cia-0000010252:
A living American prisoner and the body of a helicopter crewman appear in the same January 1974 item, from a place the title cuts off. The pairing compresses the postwar search into one report: one man to keep seeking, one to bring home. Helicopter crews left many such paired cases.

Mixed reports forced two kinds of follow-up at once, hope and recovery. Analysts split the item and sent each half down a different channel. Both halves stayed linked by the shared incident. This file preserves the pairing as it arrived, a small emblem of the accounting's double duty in 1974.
cia-0000010552:
The situation in the Khe Sanh area, with refugees and the Laotian side of Khe Sanh named in its heading, fills a January 1968 spot report. Khe Sanh was a Marine combat base near the Laotian border, weeks from its famous siege. Spot reports carried fresh, local detail rather than finished analysis.

Refugees in the heading remind readers that civilians filled the ground armies fought over. The Laotian angle mattered because supply routes and sanctuaries crossed that border. A spot report's value is its nearness to the moment. This one preserves the Khe Sanh area as seen just before the siege began.
cia-0000013852: A CIA note dated June 3, 1967, reports an American prisoner held in NVN, the short code for North Vietnam. The title gives no name, camp, or town. Still, the place mattered: prisoners in the north entered a camp system run from Hanoi. Short notes like this helped map where captured men were being held.
cia-0000015352: A meeting of the OSI advisory group on UFOs fills a CIA file dated January 3, 1953. The meeting ran from January 14 through 17 that year. OSI was the agency's science office. Those four days match the famous panel that judged the saucer evidence and called for calm study. The meeting file of the OSI group is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015452: Nothing But the Facts on UFOs, or Which Novosti Writer Do You Read, is the teasing title of a CIA item dated March 2, 1968. Two articles came with it, judging by the clipped title. Novosti was a Soviet news agency, so its saucer writing drew American notice. The entry shows Moscow and Washington each reading the other's press on even so odd a topic.
cia-0000022152: Two American pilots were held captive in Khang Khay, in Xieng Khouang Province, in May of a year the clipped title cuts off. The CIA record is dated in 1967. Khang Khay was a town on the edge of the Plain of Jars in Laos. Captivity reports from that highland war were checked name by name against the lists of the missing.
cia-0000022652: Sightings and reported casualties of American prisoners in Bien Hoa and Binh Duong provinces fill a CIA record dated in 1974. The two provinces neighbor each other north of Saigon. After the 1973 peace, such tallies served the accounting for men who never came home. The record joins hopeful sightings and grim casualty reports in one postwar ledger.
cia-0000036852:
An FBIS dispatch dated October 1, 1967 carries John Sydney McCain's remarks about his capture at Truc Bach Lake. McCain's plane went down over Hanoi, and he was pulled from the lake and taken prisoner. FBIS was the American service that monitored and translated foreign broadcasts.

The dispatch preserves what McCain was reported to have said about the day he was captured. His words reached the file through enemy media, then through American translators. Few records show a famous prisoner so close to the moment his captivity began. McCain would spend more than five years as a prisoner before he finally came home in 1973.
cia-0000037152:
Six alleged American prisoners were reported seen in a detention camp near Thao La, in a CIA record dated October 3, 1983. The sighting came a full decade after the Vietnam War's prisoners were released. Claims of men still held kept arriving, and each one entered the files.

The record preserves the claim as reported: six men, one camp, one named place. Officials had to weigh such reports without proof either way, a hard and painful task. The file shows why the live-sighting question stayed open in the public mind for years. A camp sighting was the strongest kind of claim, and also the hardest kind to prove or dismiss.
cia-0000042352:
Results of a youth poll on religious issues are reported in a CIA record dated March 2, 1989. A poll of the young on faith can show where belief is heading. The record preserves the survey's findings as they were published at the time.

Inside, the young respondents' answers on religion are set out in summary. Such polls interested officials watching societies change from within. Belief among the young was a live question in the late 1980s. States built on official atheism were loosening, and surveys like this one measured what a new generation actually thought about faith.
cia-0000045152:
Guerrillas issued a communique on the killing of Marines, in a CIA record dated May 6, 1985. The Marines died in the Zona Rosa attack in San Salvador. American servicemen killed in a cafe district shocked the United States.

Inside, the guerrillas' statement on the killings is preserved as issued. Claiming such an attack was a claim to reach and daring. It told Washington the war could touch its own people anywhere. The file holds the rebels' message from that spring, in a conflict where statements were fired like rounds and read as closely as battle reports.
cia-0000045252:
No movement marked the kidnapping negotiations, in a CIA record dated August 6, 1985. Standstill reports filled the long middle of the crisis. Movement, when it came, would be measured against weeks like this one.

Inside, the frozen state of the talks is recorded without decoration. A system that files even its empty days gives history a full clock. This entry is one tick of that clock from August 1985. It shows the case as those living it mostly knew it. They knew it in mornings when the answer was that nothing had changed at all.
cia-0000049052: Lt. Col. Sigifredo Ochoa Perez is the named subject of a CIA item from 1983, filed with the Truth Commission records. Ochoa's name also appears in this series tied to the Romero murder investigation. Dossiers on single officers were how the files turned a huge war into persons who could be judged.
cia-0000049252: The killing of Dr. Ignacio Ellacuria fills a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. Ellacuria, rector of the Central American University, was murdered with five fellow Jesuits, their housekeeper, and her daughter that November. His name titles this file alone, as the best-known of the eight dead.
cia-0000107452: Observations Concerning Palestine and the Arab Countries is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107452, dated February 2, 1949. The heading uses the plain word observations, a watcher's notes rather than a verdict. Palestine and the Arab countries share the title evenly. The brief record is an observations item from the winter of 1949 in the Middle East files.
cia-0000112352: Prc: Scientists Identify Xinjiang Ufo As Plasma Fireball is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112352, dated March 3, 1988. PRC shortens People's Republic of China at the front of the title. Its scientists name the Xinjiang object a plasma fireball, a plain answer in the heading. The brief record is an identification item from the spring of 1988.
cia-0000112752: South Africa's Turn to Heavy Water Technology: History and Implications Delete is the heading, with its ending deleted, on CIA document 0000112752, dated March 1, 1984. The title traces a turn: South Africa moving to heavy water technology, with its history and implications. The deleted ending is marked in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the deletion mark as released.
cia-0000115452: Growth and Prospects of Leftist Extremists in el Salvador -- Interagency Intell is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000115452, dated January 1, 1980. The title tracks growth and prospects for leftist extremists in El Salvador, in an interagency paper. Intelligence breaks off at Intell in the released heading. The brief record is a growth assessment item from the first day of 1980.
cia-0000117852: Fbis Trends - Vietnam - Introduction; Paris Talks is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000117852, dated July 3, 1969. FBIS names the Foreign Broadcast Information Service at the front of the title. The heading pairs an introduction on Vietnam with the Paris talks, joined by a semicolon. The brief record is a broadcast trends item from the summer of 1969.
cia-0000118652: USSR: Olympic Games Preparations is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000118652, dated January 3, 1980. The heading tracks how the Soviet Union was getting ready for the Olympic Games. Preparations is the title's word for that work, in the heading itself. The brief record is a games buildup item, filed at the start of the Olympic year 1980.
cia-0000119752: Current as of 5 p.m. on November 7, 1956, this CIA report covers Hungary three days after the Soviet assault began. Organized resistance was over and the reckoning had started. The report documents the first days of the aftermath. Three days after the assault, reporting turned toward the reckoning: arrests of fighters, a new government installed, and a population stunned into silence.
cia-0000132652: Dated January 6, 1961, this CIA study weighs how other nations might react to possible American moves, with Cuba the apparent target named in its title. Papers of this kind tested the diplomatic cost of action before leaders chose it, in the weeks after Washington cut ties with Havana. The declassified text, cataloged as document 0000132652, comes through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132752: Cuba and the Caribbean are paired in a CIA paper dated January 4, 1961. Its headline misspells the region as Carribbean, a slip kept from the original. The Caribbean that winter stood on the front line of the Cold War. The islands formed the revolution's own neighborhood, feeling each shock first. The short paper surveys Cuba and the region around it together.
cia-0000134252: Two foreign ministers possibly resigning over a regional meeting fill item 12 of a CIA series dated August 4, 1960. The ministers served Venezuela and Peru.
