The meeting belonged to the Organization of American States, and the Cuba debate ran through it. That debate was costing ministers their posts that year. The short item reports the talk of resignations.
cia-0000135952: The CIA cable of 5 January 1954 is about a request for a list of compromised cryptonyms and pseudonyms, and it survives in declassified form. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136052: With a date of 2 February 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with current information on the sixth military zone at Quiche. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136352: Negotiations broke off over unacceptable demands on both sides, LINCOLN tells CADICK in this 4 July 1954 cable. CALLIGERIS insists on the right to enter the capital at the head of his liberation army, while Monzon demands to remain number one for thirty days. Both demands are unreasonable, headquarters judges, and CALLIGERIS must be turned around quickly or he will lose his friends. His triumphal march would antagonize the army he needs for support.
cia-0000136552: A Spanish document dated 3 July 1960 is among the earliest items in this slice of the 2506 Brigade files. In mid-1960 the CIA was only beginning to build the exile force that became Brigade 2506. The catalog names no subject for the document. Preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated record from the operation's first summer, when the brigade existed as a small, secret training program rather than an army.
cia-0000136952: Wide press coverage is requested of LINCOLN in this May 1954 cable, though the transcription is heavily garbled. Headquarters is attempting wide coordination of themes including a Montenegro plan, peasant and labor mobilization, and suppression of liberty, and asks the station to follow up with resistance groups taking open actions. It also requests details on a continued basis of any future SYNCARP actions that could be exploited and would gain wider support. The cable is press exploitation planning with its specifics partly lost.
cia-03185152:
Belgium leads the surviving brief pages of the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 15 August 1960. Prime Minister Eyskens announced on 9 August that Congo events force a revision of Belgium's NATO commitments. Political pressure builds for a defence cut of 120 million dollars, a third of the budget. Cancelling the F-104G fighter programme and pulling troops from West Germany are the likely first steps.

A senior defence official calls the forces' whole future fluid, hinging on the Congo and on public reaction to losing the Kamina base. Laos takes the next item. King Savang has named Souvanna Phouma to form a government, accepting the Somsanith cabinet's resignation on 14 August. A rebel-held assembly in Vientiane had forced the no-confidence vote. The king acted, the brief judges, to avert a worse break.
cia-06232652:
Central Intelligence Bulletin for 29 November 1958, marked Top Secret, leads with the Shah's account of a Soviet offer to Iran. The bulletin reports the Shah saying Ambassador Pegov offered almost unlimited aid if Iran would drop its military ties with the West. Tehran would also need to adopt a friendly or neutral policy, according to that account.

Asia-Africa items report the United Arab Republic giving Tapline until 6 December to meet Syrian demands for more revenue. In Morocco, Istiqlal leader Allal el-Fassi might succeed Balafrej as premier, amid unrest in the Rif. Moderate North African leaders are reported troubled by growing pro-Nasir influence. Iraq items cover a new National Front with Communist support. Western pages cover reactions to the Soviet Berlin proposal and Chile rejecting a Chinese Communist copper approach.
culpeper-english-physician-1652:
Nicholas Culpeper was a London herbalist who broke the physicians' monopoly by translating their Latin pharmacopoeia into English. His English Physician, published in 1652, is his herbal, the guide that put physic in every English household. Culpeper assigns each plant its ruling planet and its virtues together.

He describes hundreds of English herbs, where they grow, when to gather them, and what ills they cure, in plain words for poor readers. His astrological frame tells the user which herb fights which disease by the stars' sympathy and opposition. No medical book of the age reached more homes, or stayed in print so long.
douglass-fourth-of-july-1852:
Frederick Douglass spoke in Corinthian Hall at Rochester, New York, on Monday, July 5, 1852. The speech was printed as a pamphlet the same year. He opens by confessing nerves and doubt about his powers before so large a crowd.

Then he turns to the hard question in his title: what the Fourth of July means to the slave. For those still in chains, he argues, the day mocks them with talk of freedom they cannot share. Born enslaved himself, Douglass answers with fierce and exact logic. The address still stands among the greatest speeches in American history.
dupotet-magie-devoilee-1852:
Dupotet unveils occult science in La Magie devoilee, in French from 1852, his flagship work. France's great magnetizer argues that the magnetic trance opens doors to hidden powers. Mesmerism and occult lore meet and merge across its confident, crowded chapters of doctrine and marvel.

He claims an ancient wisdom behind his modern practice of magnetism. Spirits, fluids, and secret traditions all find a place in his system. Later occultists cited the book across the rest of the century. It marks the bridge where the magnetic movement passed into the occult revival, a crossing that shaped French alternative science for decades.
el-dorado-an-adventure-of-the-scarlet-pi:
Baroness Orczy's El Dorado, an adventure of the Scarlet Pimpernel, opens with a foreword separating her hero from the historical Baron de Batz, with whom students had confused him. Sir Percy Blakeney's league now aims at the most precious life in Europe: the Dauphin, the lost child of Louis XVI, held in the Temple prison. Armand St Just, Percy's brother-in-law, falls in love and into betrayal.

The contents move through the Theatre National, Mademoiselle Lange, Chauvelin's pursuit, and certificates of safety, while Blakeney bullies a poor lad out of carrying a message indoors. Orczy stretches her hero's disguise and nerve to their limit. El Dorado is generally counted the strongest of the Pimpernel sequels, darker than the first.
england-in-america-1580-1652:
Lyon Gardiner Tyler tells the first seventy years of English America in England in America, 1580-1652, published by Harper in 1904. Twenty chapters move from the genesis of colonization through Gilbert and Raleigh's ventures to the founding of Virginia. Maryland, Plymouth, and Massachusetts each get their founding and their contentions.

Tyler, a Virginian and college president, writes narrative history with a critical essay on authorities at the end. Chapters cover social and economic conditions, religion and government, and the New England Confederation. The frontispiece shows Sir Walter Raleigh, whose colonies open the story. Maps of Roanoke Island, Jamestown, and St. Mary's face the Virginia chapters. The book serves the student who wants one clear volume on the colonial beginnings.
europmc-pmc10057852:
Jin and co-authors review nanobodies and their uses in diagnosis and therapy in a 2023 paper. Nanobodies are tiny antibody fragments taken from the unusual antibodies of camels and llamas. Their small size and simple structure let them bind targets that standard antibodies cannot reach.

The review covers how nanobodies are made and where they are now used. Uses span lab tests, imaging, and treatments for infection and cancer. The authors also note limits, such as fast clearance from the body. The paper gives a clear entry point to a nimble class of tools.
europmc-pmc10763652:
Zhang and co-authors read the shapes of spike proteins from three SARS-CoV-2 variants in 2021. The spike is the club-shaped part the virus uses to enter cells. Delta, Kappa, and Gamma each carried changes in that part. The team used a cold electron scope to map each spike in full.

Delta's spike fused with cell walls more readily than the rest, Zhang reports. It did so even when few entry locks, called ACE2, were at hand. Fake viruses with the Delta spike entered cells far faster than all other variants. Changes in each variant reshaped the spike's head, a main target of antibodies. The body-lock zone changed only in small local ways. The maps help explain Delta's fast spread and antibody escape.
europmc-pmc10858952:
Wang and colleagues review a cell type that shields tumours from drugs in this 2024 paper. Macrophages are immune cells that eat germs and clear dead cells. Inside tumours, many of them shift to a form called M2-like, which calms immune attack. That calm helps cancers spread and shrugs off drugs meant to kill them.

The review explains the tricks these cells use to protect tumours. It then surveys treatments that aim at them, often paired with standard anti-cancer drugs. Some of these paired plans are in human trials now. Other sections map drug designs that block these cells, drain them, or push them back to an attacking form. Several pairing plans are already in human trials, the authors note.
europmc-pmc1140952:
Saha, Chant, Welham, and McGrath systematically review how common schizophrenia is worldwide in this 2005 paper. Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness with delusions and disordered thought. Knowing its prevalence matters for planning health services and for studying risk factors. The team searched databases, citations, and authors for studies with original data published from 1965 to 2002.

Studies were sorted into core, migrant, and special group types. Filters separated discrete estimates by kind: point, period, lifetime, and lifetime morbid risk. Cumulative plots showed how estimates distribute when ranked. The authors then tested how sex, urban living, and migrant status shift the figures. Migrant groups and urban settings tended to show higher prevalence. The review gives planners a consolidated evidence base rather than single-study numbers.
europmc-pmc1240052:
Greulich and colleagues studied mutant growth receptors in lung cancer in 2005. Changes in the EGFR gene are common in one lung cancer type. Tumors with those changes often respond to two blocker drugs. Which exact changes cause cancer, and which resist drugs, was unclear.

Mutant receptors turned normal cells cancerous without outside growth signals. They formed tumors in mice with weak immune systems. Most mutants stayed sensitive to the two blocker drugs. One change in a key segment caused resistance instead. Greulich maps which mutations predict drug response or failure.
europmc-pmc1257652:
Lanphear and colleagues pooled seven child lead studies worldwide in 2005. Lead is a proven nerve toxin even at low levels. Open questions covered harm below 10 micrograms per deciliter. Data covered 1,333 children followed from infancy to age 5 to 10.

Peak blood lead averaged 17.8 micrograms per deciliter in early childhood. About 18 percent of children never topped 10 micrograms. After adjustments, higher lead tied to lower IQ in a clear inverse pattern. The pooled design lets low-dose effects show through. Lanphear supplies strong evidence that no lead level looks safe for IQ. By age five to seven, average peak lead fell to 9.4.
europmc-pmc1410752:
Extra drug treatment after breast cancer surgery saves lives, but many women get it without need. Pawitan and co-authors sought a gene test to sort who truly needs it. In 2005 they profiled tumors from 159 women in Sweden and tracked who stayed well for five years.

A set of 64 genes split patients into three groups. One group did well with treatment, one did well without it, and one did poorly despite it. The gene test beat grade, stage, and age at sorting risk. Pawitan checked the test on fresh groups in Sweden and the Netherlands. It held up, hinting some women can safely skip harsh drugs.
europmc-pmc1420652:
Wnt proteins guide how embryos grow and how cells change fate. Mikels and Nusse purified one of them, Wnt5a, in 2006 to study how it sends signals. Wnt5a had been classed as acting outside the main Wnt route, which steadies a protein called beta-catenin.

Pure Wnt5a blocked the main route when a second Wnt drove it. It did so through a lone receptor named Ror2, without changing cell calcium. Yet with a different receptor, Frizzled 4, Wnt5a switched the main route on. Mikels proposes that the receptor a cell carries, not the Wnt itself, decides what the signal does.
europmc-pmc1440852:
Diets rich in fat and sweet foods are spreading across the developing world. Hawkes traced that shift in 2006 to the merging of world markets. The change, called the nutrition transition, feeds rising obesity and long-term disease. She asked how trade and business rules reshape what people eat.

Hawkes points to three routes. Trade rules raised the use of plant oils. Foreign cash in food plants and shops spread processed foods. World ads pushed the same goods. She focuses on middle-income lands, where the shift bites fast. Her aim is to help policy makers see which rules drive diet change, so they can craft food laws that guard health.
europmc-pmc1472552:
Snake bite kills and maims many people in warm regions each year. Gutiérrez, Theakston, and Warrell argued in 2006 that the world largely ignores it. Antivenoms exist on every continent, yet the burden stays heavy in Africa, Asia, Oceania, and Latin America. Health bodies give the problem little heed.

The trio call snake bite a major neglected disease of this century. They urge a global partnership to confront it. Better supply of antivenom, training, and public attention form the core need. Gutiérrez frames the issue as one of fairness: the victims are often poor farmers far from care.
europmc-pmc1559652:
Comparing two genes by what they do needs a fair yardstick. Schlicker and co-authors built one in 2006 from the Gene Ontology, the standard word set for gene functions. Their method scores how alike two sets of function terms are.

One measure, simRel, compares biological processes across species groups. A second, funSim, finds functionally related gene products within or across genomes. The scores matched sequence-based methods, yet also linked proteins with no shared ancestry. Schlicker mapped the whole function space of yeast proteins. The map gives a global view of how gene jobs relate.
europmc-pmc1570152:
Viewing a protein's shape next to its gene sequence speeds insight. Meng and co-authors added such linked tools to UCSF Chimera in 2006, a popular molecular graphics program. Sequences from an alignment attach to their structures on import, so a click in one view lights up the other.

One tool overlays two proteins with no prior alignment, using sequence and shape cues together. It can match proteins sharing very few identical letters. Another builds sequence alignments from structural overlays. Meng stresses the program stays open: users can plug in their own data and annotations without writing Chimera code.
europmc-pmc1636652:
Some trials roll out a treatment in waves rather than all at once. Brown and Lilford reviewed the stepped wedge design in 2006, finding just 12 studies or protocols using it. Clusters start the intervention at staggered, random times until all receive it.

The design suits cases where withholding a likely-good treatment seems unethical. It also suits rollouts that logistics force to be gradual. The reviewed studies spanned many diseases and settings, with a niche in developing countries. Brown notes the design lets analysts model how effects change over time, yet it remains little used.
europmc-pmc1866352:
Kaltenbach, Hughes and co-authors hunted in 2007 for proteins that change the course of Huntington's disease. The disease is a fatal brain degeneration caused by an overlong glutamine stretch in the huntingtin protein. Its toxicity is thought to flow partly through the protein's many binding partners.

Using two screens, a yeast interaction test and pull-downs read by mass spectrometry, they built a set of 234 high-confidence huntingtin partners. They then tested 60 of those genes in a fruit fly model of the disease. Twenty-seven passed as strong genetic modifiers, confirmed with more than one gene variant each. That 45 percent hit rate far exceeds random gene sets. The result backs the idea that huntingtin's interaction web holds levers that speed or slow neuron death.
europmc-pmc2124952:
Hideyo Noguchi of the Rockefeller Institute reported in 1912 the first pure culture of Spirochaeta refringens. Schaudinn and Hoffmann had described the organism in 1905, in the same paper that announced the syphilis germ. It is a coarse spirochete of surface genital lesions, found in syphilitic and non-syphilitic sores alike, plumper than the pallidum, with fewer, irregular curves, and quick to take dyes.

Isolating it had defeated everyone before him. Noguchi's strain grew alone at last, and he records its shape and habits in culture. The living body, he finds, is cylindrical, not ribbon-like as Schaudinn thought. Waves of bending run along it from one end. The strain caused no disease in rabbits or monkeys. Readers get a common but elusive germ finally pinned down in pure form.
europmc-pmc2125252:
Hugh A. Stewart and Samuel C. Harvey of Columbia's pathology department sorted the blood's opposing pushes on arteries in 1912. Plasma, they find, carries a dilator substance that acts specifically on the kidney's vessels. It is a protein of the albumin class, brought down by boiling and by alcohol, and it is present in serum too.

Clotting then adds the opposite agent. As blood clots it frees a constrictor that acts on kidney and limb vessels alike. The constrictor is no protein: it survives boiling, dissolves in alcohol, and works directly on the artery's muscle coat, as the dilator also does. Their dilator, they note, works at the vessel wall itself and appears in the serum of every laboratory animal tried. Readers get shed blood shown to carry both an opener and a closer for arteries.
europmc-pmc2125452:
Herbert L. Celler and William Thalhimer of Mount Sinai Hospital in New York reviewed and extended the hunt for the gastric ulcer's cause in 1916. Everyone's attempts to make a chronic ulcer in animals, they note, had failed. Injure the stomach lining any way you like and it heals promptly, unless the blood supply is cut off entirely, which brings infarction and perforation instead.

Their own position is deliberately unconvinced. Non-hemolytic streptococci are present in nearly all gastric ulcers, and Rosenow's recent work pressed their claim. Yet presence is not proof: the authors cannot satisfy themselves that these organisms either start the ulcer or keep it from healing. One rabbit's stomach, two days after injection, showed bleeding patches with a shallow V-shaped defect and large bacilli invading, but no streptococci. Readers get a fashionable germ theory respectfully left unproven.
europmc-pmc2125652:
Eugene L. Opie published these autopsy findings in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1917. Working from lungs examined after death, he asked when the small, healed spots of tuberculosis first appear and how they relate to the lung-apex disease that kills adults. He traced lesions by age, from early childhood into old age, and compared focal spots with apical ones.

Opie found that focal lung lesions mostly begin in childhood, and that more than half of all people gain them between the ages of ten and eighteen. By early adult life nearly everyone carries such a lesion somewhere. Spots away from the apex tend to heal and stay quiet, while apex lesions appear later, grow more common with age, and account for nearly all fatal cases after age ten.
europmc-pmc2130952:
Paul A. Lewis and Dorothy Loomis asked whether the anaphylactic response, like resistance to tuberculosis, runs in guinea pig families. Their paper is the second on allergic irritability, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925, from Princeton. Their breeding stock had already been shown by Wright and Lewis to differ by inheritance in tuberculosis susceptibility.

The inbred lines that differ against tuberculosis differ in their anaphylactic responses as well. Families relatively resistant to tuberculosis appear somewhat more resistant to one or more phases of the anaphylactic reaction too. The authors define allergic irritability as a general character of the animal, the basis on which it reacts to antigenic stimuli of every kind, helpful, harmful, or indifferent. If one inherited constitution governs both disease resistance and shock response, the two fields share a root. The paper reports the family pattern and leaves the mechanism open.
europmc-pmc2131252:
Leonard Rowntree and Takuji Shionoya, at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, opened a 1927 series on clotting outside the body. Postoperative lung embolism, a clot that travels to the lungs, drove the work, since it caused a clear share of deaths after surgery at their clinic. Part one presents a method, not yet results on causes.

Blood is run through an artificial loop outside the body while staying alive in the circuit, so clot formation can be watched directly. Many conditions in the loop can be held or changed at will. The setup also lets the team study white clots and fibrin deposits apart from each other. The two may form as separate processes, the authors note.
europmc-pmc2131452:
Ronald Christie, at the Hospital of The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, wrote part six of the diathermy study series in 1928. Diathermy heats tissue with high frequency currents. Earlier parts dealt with whole limbs and organs. This part asks a finer question: does the current pass through the living cell itself, or only around it?

Christie describes a method to measure the relative impedance, the electrical opposition, of living cells to these currents. The current does enter the cell, so heat is made inside cells as well as between them. A small part of the cell's impedance makes no heat. He also warns that saponin raises the conductivity of a salt fluid, so it spoils such measurements on living material.
europmc-pmc2409852:
Isenring, Capra, and Bauer trialled intensive diet support during radiotherapy in 2004. Patients getting radiation to the gut or head and neck often eat poorly and lose dangerous amounts of weight. The trial randomised 60 outpatients starting at least 20 radiation sessions to intensive help or usual care.

The intensive group got personal counselling from a dietitian, following a set protocol, plus food supplements when needed. Usual care meant general advice and a booklet. After 12 weeks, the counselled group had lost significantly less weight and kept better nutrition scores. Their overall quality of life also declined less, with firm statistics behind each gap. Lean tissue differences favoured counselling but were not conclusive. The authors said the goal in this setting should be holding weight steady, not gaining it.
europmc-pmc2533652:
King and colleagues reviewed population studies in 2008 on the mental health of lesbian, gay, and bisexual people. Earlier work hinted at higher rates of mental illness and self-harm than in heterosexual people, but the studies varied in quality. The team searched a wide range of databases and kept only studies with a heterosexual comparison group and sound definitions.

Twenty-five studies covering over 11,900 non-heterosexual and 214,000 heterosexual people qualified. Suicide attempts were about 2.47 times as common over a lifetime in the lesbian, gay, and bisexual group, and depression and anxiety ran at least 1.5 times higher. Alcohol and drug dependence were also about 1.5 times higher. Risks were sharpest for substance dependence in lesbian and bisexual women and for lifetime suicide attempts in gay and bisexual men.
europmc-pmc2592352:
Köbel and colleagues showed in 2008 that the four subtypes of ovarian carcinoma behave like different diseases, with direct consequences for biomarker research. Most studies and treatment protocols pool serous, clear cell, endometrioid, and mucinous tumours together. The team measured 21 candidate biomarker proteins in a population-based series of 500 ovarian cancers collected between 1984 and 2000.

Twenty of the 21 biomarkers differed significantly between subtypes but not between stages within a subtype. Nine markers predicted survival in the whole cohort. Yet only three stayed prognostic within the largest subtype. None did within clear cell tumours. One marker, WT1, flipped direction entirely: unfavourable across the whole cohort, but favourable within high-grade serous cancers, with a risk ratio of 0.5 there against 1.7 overall. The authors urge analysing each subtype separately.
europmc-pmc2612752:
Altenhoff and Dessimoz benchmarked the leading orthology projects in 2009, the databases that decide which genes in different species are counterparts inherited from a common ancestor. Such calls underpin comparative genomics, yet the projects had rarely been compared head-to-head. The team mapped predictions from nine major projects and two simple standard methods across millions of sequences.

They scored every method with six tests covering both family-tree accuracy and conservation of function. For family-tree work, OMA and Homologene performed best. The same held for high-specificity function analysis. For broader coverage at lower specificity, OrthoMCL beat Ensembl Compara and Inparanoid. EggNOG offered the widest coverage but too little precision for detailed work. Surprisingly, a simple method often won. The bidirectional best-hit method beat projects with far more complex algorithms.
europmc-pmc2686252:
Sansom and colleagues showed in 2009 that the dose of a single gene, Pax6, tips young brain stem cells between copying themselves and becoming neurons. Pax6 is a master switch of the developing cortex, the brain's outer sheet. The team mapped where it binds DNA in mouse cortical stem cells and which genes answer to it.

Pax6 directly switches on whole teams of genes: some that keep stem cells dividing, some that make intermediate builder cells, and some that finish neurons. It works in a core network with three other regulators, Neurog2, Ascl1, and Hes1. The system proved exquisitely dose-sensitive. Extra Pax6 pushed cells toward making neurons and builders, at the cost of self-renewal. Removing it starved the cell cycle machinery and shrank the stem pool. Building a cortex, it seems, is partly a matter of keeping one switch at the right setting.
europmc-pmc2702752:
Lima and co-authors introduced a new lab method in 2009 for naming which brain cells are firing during live recordings. Normal probes can hear spikes, which are brief electric pulses from brain cells, but they cannot tell which type of cell made them. Their method is called PINP, short for photostimulation-assisted identification of neuronal populations.

PINP puts a light-sensitive channel, called channelrhodopsin-2, into one chosen group of cells only. A brief flash of blue light then makes just those cells fire at once, so they stand out in the record. The team proved it in mouse cortex, the outer brain layer, and in rat hearing cortex, where tagged cells replied to sound in a distinct way.
europmc-pmc2790452:
Subramanian, Krishnan, and Sethuraman reviewed lab-made scaffolds for repairing damaged nerves in 2009. Nerve injuries can leave lasting harm, and grafts taken from a patient's own body are limited by supply, size mismatch, and new growths at the donor site.

A good scaffold should copy the natural support mesh around cells, the review argues. It must be safe in the body, break down slowly, resist infection, and carry the chemical and surface cues that help nerve cells stick and grow. Many designs also carry growth factors such as NGF and BDNF, proteins that coax nerve fibers to sprout and lengthen. The authors weigh materials and building methods meant to guide new nerve fibers across a gap, giving injured nerves a path to heal along.
europmc-pmc2798952:
Hilty and co-authors compared the bacteria living in the airways of adults and children with asthma against healthy controls in 2010. Asthma flares are often set off by infection, yet the normal airway community was barely known. The team read a bacterial marker gene from airway samples of forty-three subjects.

The bronchial tree proved far from sterile, holding about two thousand bacterial genomes per square centimeter of surface. One broad group, the Proteobacteria, and in particular Haemophilus types, appeared much more often in asthma and in chronic lung disease called COPD. A second group common in healthy airways, including Prevotella types, thinned out in patients. The same shift appeared in children with asthma.
europmc-pmc2809052:
Giri and colleagues tested in 2009 a way to put a number on swelling inside heart muscle using magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI. Swelling, called edema, marks fresh heart damage, but standard weighted scans vary with coil placement, bright blood, and motion, and reading them is a matter of judgment.

The team compared methods on test objects, then scanned healthy volunteers, three pigs, and three patients after heart attacks. Their mapping method measured a heart tissue value that held steady across people and did not shift with heart rate. In every heart attack case, the injured zone scored clearly higher than healthy muscle elsewhere in the heart.
europmc-pmc2825552:
Akcay, Nguyen, and Edelstein reviewed in 2009 the inflammatory messengers that drive acute kidney injury, a sudden loss of kidney function that still raises death risk on its own. Injury from low blood flow, sepsis, or toxins first changes the kidney's vessel lining and tubule cells. Those cells then release signals that pull in white blood cells.

Neutrophils, macrophages, natural killer cells, and lymphocytes flood the injured kidney, the review explains. Signals called cytokines and chemokines, made by tubule and vessel cells, do the recruiting, and the invading cells extend the damage. Inflammation thus shapes both the opening phase of injury and its spread, making these messengers prime targets for future treatment.
europmc-pmc2848652:
Kringos, Boerma, Hutchinson, van der Zee, and Groenewegen systematically reviewed the primary care literature in 2010 to pin down what a primary care system actually consists of. Everyone calls front-line care the linchpin of health systems, yet nobody had mapped its parts from evidence. The team searched seven databases for studies from 2003 to mid-2008 and kept eighty-five.

Ten core dimensions emerged. Structure rests on governance, economic conditions, and workforce development. The care process runs through access, continuity, coordination, and comprehensiveness. Outcomes show up as quality, efficiency, and equity in health. Across the studies, strong showings on these dimensions tracked better overall system performance and population health, letting the authors define primary care as one multidimensional system.
europmc-pmc2958552:
Komar and colleagues infected twenty-five North American bird species with the New York 1999 strain of West Nile virus in a 2003 study, using mosquito bites to mimic natural spread. Knowing which birds amplify the virus guides surveillance and control.

Songbirds and shorebirds proved the strongest reservoirs, with blue jays, grackles, house finches, crows, and house sparrows topping the list. Eight species died, many shed virus from mouth or droppings, and some passed it to cage mates or by mouth. Virus also persisted in tissues of many survivors. The ranking helps officials predict which species drive outbreaks.
europmc-pmc2996852:
Shimizu and colleagues showed in 2010 that rice needs two cooperating receptors to sense chitin, a fungal wall material that triggers plant defences. One partner, a binding protein called CEBiP, and a kinase receptor from a related plant were each known, but their teamwork was unclear.

Quietening the rice kinase OsCERK1 sharply blunted defence responses to chitin fragments, proving it essential alongside CEBiP. Pairing tests showed the two can join each other and themselves. After chitin treatment, cell membrane samples contained a joined complex of both. CEBiP also pairs with itself even without the signal, ready for assembly.
europmc-pmc3012052:
Oonincx and colleagues measured greenhouse gas and ammonia output from five insect species proposed as food or feed in a 2010 experiment. Livestock farming emits heavily, and edible insects were floated as a cleaner protein source.

Mealworms, house crickets, migratory locusts, and two beetle species differed widely in gas output and growth speed. Even so, the insects grew faster per input and emitted greenhouse gases at rates matching or below pigs and far below cattle, with ammonia output also much lower. Carbon dioxide per unit of weight gained likewise favoured insects, supporting their case as lower-impact protein.
europmc-pmc3029252:
Treangen and Rocha asked in 2011 how bacteria gain new protein families, by copying their own genes or by picking up genes from neighbors. Copying, called duplication, is the classic route in larger organisms. The team compared closely related bacteria with small, medium, and large genomes to separate the two routes cleanly.

After setting aside mobile DNA and virus genes, they found that most family growth came from transfer between cells, not from copying. Imported genes tended to persist longer, perhaps because they bring truly new abilities. Copied genes were used more heavily and changed more slowly once kept. The authors argue that transfer brings novelty while copying mainly raises dosage, so evolution studies must treat the two very differently.
europmc-pmc3072352:
Adams, Johansen, Powell, Quig, and Rubin compared in 2011 gut symptoms and stool microbes in children with autism and typically developing children. Gut complaints are reported far more often in autism, but their link to behavior was unclear. Stool from nearly a hundred children was tested for bacteria, yeast, digestion markers, and fatty acids, and parents rated gut and autism severity on standard checklists.

Gut symptom scores tracked autism severity closely: children with worse gut scores had markedly worse autism scores. Children with autism had lower levels of the short fatty acids that gut bacteria make from fiber, and lower counts of one helpful bacterial group, while another group ran higher. Digestion markers were otherwise similar between groups. The authors are careful not to claim cause. Still, the tight link suggests gut problems deserve treatment in their own right in autism care.
europmc-pmc3102752:
O'Hara, Virág, Varró, and Rudy built in 2011 a computer model of the electrical pulse of a healthy human heart ventricle cell, long a missing tool in arrhythmia research. Most experiments use animal cells or human proteins in foreign cells, and species differences distort the answers. The team gathered fresh measurements from undiseased human heart tissue for the key ion currents and built them into one model cell.

The simulated pulses matched real recordings in shape, in how they shorten as heart rate rises, and in how they recover after extra beats. Variants modeled the three wall layers of the ventricle. The model reproduced drug block effects, dangerous early extra pulses under one blocker, and the beat to beat alternation seen at very fast rates in real hearts. It also showed which currents drive each behavior. Cardiologists and drug testers now have a human based test bed.
europmc-pmc3138752:
Fran Supek and colleagues built a web tool that tames long gene-function lists in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Big experiments end with statistical lists of what changed genes do, but those lists run long and repeat near-identical terms, making them hard to read. Their server trims such a list to a clear representative set.

The tool groups terms by how close their meanings sit, then keeps a slim set that still covers the findings. Results can be viewed as maps, graphs, tree-style charts, or word clouds, each showing how topics split and relate. The server is free online. For researchers drowning in redundant output, it turns an unreadable list into a picture that can guide the next experiment.
europmc-pmc3190352:
Mei Yang and colleagues showed that immune cells parked in breast tumours hand cancer cells tiny invasion-boosting packages in a 2011 paper in Molecular Cancer. Tumour-associated macrophages are known to help breast cancer spread, but the delivery route was unclear. Growing the two cell types together without contact let the team watch molecular parcels cross between them.

Labelled small RNAs visibly travelled from the activated macrophages to the cancer cells inside shed membrane sacs. One macrophage-specific small RNA rose sharply in recipient cancer cells and made them more invasive through a known growth pathway. Blocking that RNA in the macrophages cancelled the invasion boost. The study names parcel delivery as a concrete mechanism behind a long-observed partnership in metastasis.
europmc-pmc3221052:
John Ashburner and Karl Friston presented a faster algorithm for aligning brain images in this 2011 paper in NeuroImage. Registration warps one brain scan to match another, and the most accurate approaches allow large, smooth warps that never tear or fold the image. Those methods were slow and memory-hungry, limiting routine use.

Working within the established large-deformation framework, the authors reformulated the problem so only an initial velocity field is estimated, with the full warp following from a geodesic path. A Gauss-Newton fitting scheme then converges in fewer steps and with less memory. Tested on freely available, hand-labeled datasets, the algorithm matched up well against other inter-subject registration methods tested on the same data, making high-quality alignment more practical.
europmc-pmc3257652:
Sofia Forssten, Marika Björklund, and Arthur Ouwehand reviewed the bacterium Streptococcus mutans and tooth decay in this 2010 article in Nutrients. Cavities and dental plaque are among the world's most common diseases, caused by microbes and food debris together. Acid-producing bacteria, above all S. mutans, colonize tooth surfaces and damage the hard structure when fermentable sugars such as sucrose and fructose are present.

The authors first lay out the evidence linking this species to the decay process. They then turn to laboratory simulation models of caries, systems that reproduce the mouth's conditions for testing how decay develops. Such models let researchers measure how cariogenic different food substrates are and how well S. mutans colonizes surfaces, without experimenting in people's mouths. The review presents the models as a valuable route to understanding and eventually preventing a near-universal disease.
europmc-pmc3281852:
Xin Gao and colleagues characterized a checkpoint molecule on immune cells inside lung tumors, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. TIM-3 is a brake on T cells, known to mark exhausted killer cells in chronic infection and cancer. What it does on the helper T cells infiltrating tumors was unclear, so the team analyzed immune cells from fifty-one patients with non-small cell lung cancer.

TIM-3 was strongly raised on both helper and killer T cells inside tumors but barely present on the same patients' blood cells. Killer cells carrying it made less of an antiviral cytokine. Most strikingly, about seventy percent of the TIM-3-carrying helper cells were regulatory T cells. These are the suppressors of immune attack. TIM-3 levels on helper cells also tracked with lymph node spread and advanced stage. The authors cast TIM-3 as a regulator acting mainly through these regulatory cells.
europmc-pmc3348152:
Levy, Ziv, and Siegal showed that identical yeast cells spread their bets by making unequal amounts of a stress shield, in a 2012 study. Cloned cells grown in identical conditions still differ wildly in gene activity, and whether that spread is mere noise or a survival strategy is a classic puzzle. Using a new tracking approach, the team watched single unstressed yeast cells over time.

Cells settled into a range of growth states that matched their levels of a regulator of trehalose production, a sugar that protects against stress. The pattern also tracked cell age, with older lineages favoring the protected state. Crucially, a cell's state before any trouble predicted how well it survived a later stress. The authors call this bet hedging: the population sacrifices some growth in good times so that someone is always ready for bad times.
europmc-pmc3373052:
Yu and a large study team described in 2006 an unusual human outbreak of Streptococcus suis infection in Sichuan, China. The germ normally lives in pigs and only rarely sickens people, usually one case at a time. In July 2005 a farmer fell ill with high fever and coma a day after slaughtering a pig that had died unexplained.

Investigators found more patients in nearby hospitals, many with similar contact with sick or dead pigs. Blood cultures grew the germ in some cases, tying the cluster to pig exposure. Human infections before this event numbered only about two hundred reported cases worldwide. The outbreak's size made pig-linked spread a public health concern, not just a job hazard.
europmc-pmc3398752:
Marks and a large team profiled stem cells in 2012 to define the ground state of pluripotency, the most basic form of a cell that can become anything. Mouse embryonic stem cells grown in serum are a mixed bunch. Cells kept in a defined brew with two kinase blockers, called 2i, look more uniform and naive.

The two growth styles produced clearly distinct gene-activity and chromosome profiles. The 2i cells quieted lineage genes and carried fewer of the poised, both-ways marks at gene switches. Yet both cell types could still specialize equally well. A pause in gene reading near the start line kept developmental genes in check in 2i, suggesting promise without priming.
europmc-pmc3480952:
Leask and colleagues built a practical guide for talking with parents about vaccination, in BMC Pediatrics in 2012. Parents' talks with health workers shape their choices more than leaflets do, and heavy-handed persuasion can backfire. The team reviewed studies to sort parents into five positions, from ready acceptors to firm refusers, and matched advice to each.

For every group they set goals and tactics grounded in consent rules and interviewing science. Hesitant parents call for a guiding style that draws out their own reasons to vaccinate, not debates. Some families need a second visit or a specialist clinic. Leask's group stresses rapport and honest answers throughout. The framework aims to protect trust while helping parents reach sound decisions.
europmc-pmc3484052:
Welch and colleagues presented reporting rules for reviews that ask how health programs affect fairness, in PLoS Medicine in 2012. Averages can hide harm: a program that lifts overall health may still widen the gap between rich and poor. Yet few systematic reviews report effects on equity at all, and those that do give too little detail to copy.

The PRISMA-Equity guidelines, built by group agreement, tell reviewers what to report when fairness is in view. They cover reviews of programs for disadvantaged groups, programs meant to narrow gaps, and general programs whose fairness effects matter. Welch's team expects wider use to build better evidence on who gains and who loses. That evidence, they argue, serves the global push for fairer health.
europmc-pmc3535352:
The spinal cord's protective barrier leaks in ALS, and Ethan A. Winkler, Jesse D. Sengillo, John S. Sullivan, Jenny S. Henkel, Stanley H. Appel, and Berislav V. Zlokovic test human tissue for the damage in this 2013 study. Rodent work had already shown barrier breakdown and red cell escape before motor symptoms.

All eleven cervical cords from ALS patients show deposits of hemoglobin and iron-rich hemosiderin outside vessels, typically 10 to 50 micrometers wide; none of five control cords do. Perivascular hemoglobin deposits run 3.1 times higher in ALS. Staining confirms stray red blood cells, and the barrier's support cells, pericytes, are reduced in motor regions. Barrier failure, the authors argue, is part of human ALS, not only of mouse models.
europmc-pmc3623852:
Babette Weksler, Ignacio Romero, and Pierre-Olivier Couraud assessed a lab-grown model of the blood-brain barrier in Fluids and Barriers of the CNS in 2013. The barrier's vessel lining decides what reaches the brain, and researchers need a human version they can grow. Real human brain vessel cells are scarce, since tissue is rare. The cell line hCMEC/D3 was built in 2005 from vessels in a piece of human temporal lobe removed during epilepsy surgery. It filled that gap and had powered over one hundred studies.

Chapters recount how the line was made immortal and cloned, judge it trait by trait: barrier tightness, transporter proteins that pump drugs back out, and responses to infection and inflammation signals. Strengths include easy growth and a brain-like vessel character; limits include leakier junctions than the real barrier. The verdict is a qualified endorsement for drug transport and disease mechanism work.
europmc-pmc3637052:
How well a one-line health rating matches lab facts is tested in a 2013 BMC Public Health study by Shunquan Wu and six colleagues. Data came from 18,000 adults picked at random in five cities in China. Each person rated his or her own health on a five-step scale, from very good to very bad, and staff checked diseases, lab values and daily habits.

Disease rates rose step by step as self-ratings fell, most sharply for heart and brain vessel disease and for poor sight. Lab values and life factors lined up with the ratings in the same way. The end point of the study is that a person's own rating tracks real health well. It can serve as a quick, broad health measure when large groups are surveyed.
europmc-pmc3661552:
Hard-to-run protein software opens to all comers through a shared web server, Lyskov and a large team report in a 2013 PLoS One article. The software, Rosetta, predicts the shapes of proteins and designs new ones, Yet its steep learning curve and hunger for computing power kept it in few hands. The team built a web frame, called ROSIE in the text, to run Rosetta jobs through a browser.

ROSIE gives all tools one face for users, one clean way for builders to add tools, and a back end that borrows cluster power from member sites. A central group keeps it running. Nine tools from six builder teams were live at launch, spanning docking, RNA building, antibody work and protein redesign. The frame, the authors say, cuts the cost of putting lab software online to near zero.
europmc-pmc3665452:
Species lines for microbes can be drawn from genome reads, Meier-Kolthoff, Auch, Klenk and Göker show in a 2013 BMC Bioinformatics article. For 25 years the gold test for splitting bacteria and kin into species was a lab method that mates DNA from two strains, a slow craft from the 1970s. Their digital method, called GBDP in the text, infers distances between genomes and converts them into values that mimic the lab test.

Tests of methods and settings show GBDP still matches the lab test best, and new models lift its accuracy further. The upgrade adds confidence intervals, ranges that mark how sure a distance call is, built two ways. Model-based ranges held steady, while resampling ranges swung with the distance rule used. A free web service hosts it. Sound species lines need such honesty about doubt built in.
europmc-pmc3667752:
How much of human variety is in the genes gets a fresh count from Zaitlen, Kraft, Patterson, Pasaniuc, Bhatia, Pollack and Price in a 2013 PLoS Genetics study. The team used Iceland's population-wide family records, long gene reads and health measures for 38,167 people. They scored 23 traits, 11 measured on a scale and 12 yes-or-no traits, across pairs from siblings to cousins.

Their heritability counts came out well below twin-study figures, with extra likeness tracing mostly to shared homes, not gene interplay. A new joint method let them count both total heritability and the share caught by common gene markers. Those markers explained over half the heritability across the 23 traits, more than earlier work had found. The rest likely hides in rare variants that standard gene chips do not read.
europmc-pmc3672752:
Blocking one cartilage-cutting enzyme slows joint decay in mice, Wang and six colleagues report in a 2013 Arthritis Research and Therapy study. The enzyme, MMP13, cuts the collagen that gives cartilage its strength, and joint disease osteoarthritis has no drug that changes its course. The team bred mice whose cartilage cells could have the enzyme gene switched off after birth, then injured their knees to trigger the disease. A blocking drug was tested too.

Mice with the gene off showed slower joint decay at 8, 12 and 16 weeks after surgery, with less cartilage loss on blind scoring. The blocker cut enzyme activity by over 85 percent in dish tests. Injected into mice, it slowed decay too and cut cartilage cell death. The enzyme, the authors say, is a true driver of the disease, and blocking it is a sound drug strategy in this model.
europmc-pmc3932552:
Wanqing Li, Xiaoqin Mai, and Chao Liu review the default mode network and social thought. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. This network is active when the brain rests. It turns up again and again in social tasks. Those tasks include reading emotions, feeling empathy, and guessing what others think. Moral judgment belongs to the list as well.

One hub does much of the work: the medial prefrontal cortex. Its parts split the jobs. A lower part, tied to emotion zones, supports emotional engagement with others. A front part helps keep self and other apart. A top part works with a junction zone on perspective taking. The review also touches on autism and psychopathy. In both, this social machinery behaves in atypical ways.
europmc-pmc3975152:
Deborah Doens and Patricia L. Fernández review the receptors that let the brain's immune cells respond to amyloid beta in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2014. Alzheimer's disease combines amyloid deposits, tangled tau protein, and chronic inflammation. Microglia, the brain's resident macrophages, sit in the middle: they clear amyloid, which helps, yet they also release toxic mediators that harm neurons. Which role dominates may decide how the disease moves.

Amyloid switches microglia on through several innate immune receptors on their surface. The review explains how those receptors work together to recognize the deposits, swallow them, and set the cell's activation level. Understanding that receptor teamwork, the authors argue, is a route to therapies that keep the clearing function while muting the harmful one.
europmc-pmc3986552:
Deborah Chiabrando and four colleagues review heme control in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2014. Heme is the iron-bearing ring at the heart of hemoglobin. It is essential kit for many tasks. It carries oxygen and moves electrons. It helps process drugs and steroids. Loose heme is toxic, though. It drives oxidative stress and chews up membranes. In the end it can kill cells. The body must keep its levels on a tight leash.

The review follows that leash step by step. Cells scavenge stray heme from outside. They make heme and load it into proteins. They break the excess down for disposal. They ferry heme across membranes through named importer and exporter proteins. That transport story is the newest part of the field. Failures at any step surface in disease. Anemias and tissue injury are among the results.
europmc-pmc4044952:
Jina Yun and seven colleagues uncover a backup pathway that guards mitochondria when the Parkinson's-linked PINK1 and parkin genes fail, in eLife in 2014. Both genes protect mitochondrial quality. Their loss causes inherited Parkinson's disease. Finding other routes to the same protection could suggest new treatments.

In fruit flies, raising a protein called MUL1 rescued the defects of PINK1 or parkin mutants. MUL1 tags mitofusin, a protein that fuses mitochondria, for disposal. Too much mitofusin is itself toxic in these mutants. MUL1 clears the excess by a separate route that runs parallel to PINK1 and parkin. Removing MUL1 on top of either gene loss proved lethal in flies and damaging in mouse brain cells. The two routes thus back each other up on a shared target. The authors flag the MUL1 pathway as a promising drug target for Parkinson's disease.
europmc-pmc4045152:
Gabriele Berg, Martin Grube, Michael Schloter, and Kornelia Smalla survey the state of plant microbiome research, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014. Plants host dense microbe communities on and inside their tissues. Together, host and microbes act as one meta-organism. The microbes form a second genome for the plant.

Soil microbes around roots have drawn most study so far, though microbes colonise nearly every plant compartment. Decades of work link these partners to growth, health, and stress protection. The mini-review looks back at how the field grew and what it has established. It also names the gaps: how plants select their microbes, how communities shift, and how findings can serve farming. Uses on the horizon include microbe-based crop protection and growth support for a changing climate. The authors frame plant microbiomes as a young field with direct value for sustainable farming.
europmc-pmc4167952:
D. Grinsell and C. P. Keating reviewed nerve repair in BioMed Research International in 2014. Nerves outside the brain and spinal cord heal slowly after injury, and healing is often partial. Fewer than half of patients who have a torn nerve sewn back regain good movement or feeling, and basic surgical methods have changed little in over 60 years.

Their review walks through current surgery, then newer options. Nerve transfers, where a working nerve branch is rerouted, show promise for injuries close to the spinal cord. The authors also cover lab-stage ideas from molecular work and tissue engineering that aim to clear the blocks that stop fibres from regrowing. The gap between what science knows and what surgery can do frames the whole piece.
europmc-pmc4187052:
Vincent T. van Hees, Søren Brage, and eight co-authors offered a fix for wrist and hip motion sensors in the Journal of Applied Physiology in 2014. Small accelerometers worn for days record how active people are, but factory calibration drift makes studies hard to compare. Extra lab calibration visits are costly and often impossible.

Their method finds still moments in the wearer's own data, when the sensor should read plain gravity, and uses those moments to correct itself. Tested in cohorts from the United Kingdom, Kuwait, Cameroon, and Brazil, 1,552 people in all, the correction cut calibration error sharply in every group. Adding the sensor's temperature readings helped only slightly. Corrected data changed standard activity scores by large margins in some cohorts, which shows how much the drift had distorted results.
europmc-pmc4222452:
Dagmar A. Kuhn, Barbara Rothen-Rutishauser, and six co-authors compared how two cell types swallow nanoparticles in the Beilstein Journal of Nanotechnology in 2014. Particles meant for medicine must enter the right cells, and cells have several doors: engulfing, gulping fluid, or two kinds of coated pits. Which door a particle uses shapes its fate inside.

Working with mouse macrophages and human lung epithelial cells, the team tuned blockers for each door and tracked tagged marker proteins. The two cell types stocked the door machinery differently: macrophages carried much of one raft protein and the clathrin coat, while caveolin was absent in one line's profile. Uptake routes for the same particle differed by cell type, a warning that drug carriers must be tested in the cells they target.
europmc-pmc4307252:
Lucia Marseglia and eight co-authors review oxidative stress as a driver of the diseases that travel with obesity. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. Excess fat raises the risk of diabetes, heart disease, fatty liver, and several cancers, and fat tissue itself is now seen as an active hormone making organ, not a mere store.

Fat packed with immune cells and strained by growth produces reactive oxygen species beyond the body's defenses. That imbalance damages vessels, blunts insulin action, and feeds the metabolic syndrome. The review gathers evidence from human and animal work on how this stress builds and where antioxidants or lifestyle change might interrupt it.
europmc-pmc4314252:
Aaron van Donkelaar, Randall V Martin, Michael Brauer, and Brian L Boys built world maps of fine particle air pollution from satellite data. Their study appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2015. Ground monitors are sparse across much of the world, while satellites watch everywhere and hold more than a decade of records.

The team merged readings from three satellite instruments and used a chemical transport model to convert the view from orbit into ground level particle levels, checked against ground measurements gathered worldwide. The maps cover 1998 to 2012 at fine scale. They let health researchers estimate long term exposure for whole populations, including places with no monitors at all.
europmc-pmc4334652:
Erica M Schulte, Nicole M Avena, Ashley N Gearhardt, and Tiffany L Weir asked which foods people most link with addictive like eating. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. The authors propose that highly processed foods act a little like drugs of abuse: concentrated doses of fat and refined carbohydrate hit the blood fast, a pattern captured by glycemic load.

Undergraduates and a larger online sample rated thirty five foods for problem eating signs using a food addiction scale and forced choices. Processed items rich in fat and fast sugars, such as pizza, chocolate, and chips, topped the list, while plain foods ranked low. The pattern supports processing level, not calories alone, as the trait that makes foods hard to stop eating.
europmc-pmc4355952:
Justin Cotney and a large team studied the gene regulator CHD8 and its links to autism, in Nature Communications in 2015. CHD8 changes how DNA is packed, and harmful new mutations in it turn up again and again in people with autism spectrum disorder. Risk genes for autism tend to switch on together in the fetal brain. The team mapped which genes CHD8 binds in human fetal brain, human neural stem cells, and mouse cortex.

Genes bound by CHD8 were strongly enriched for other autism risk genes in both human and mouse tissue. When CHD8 was knocked down in human neural stem cells, many of those risk genes changed their activity. Adding CHD8 binding data to risk models also improved the detection of risk genes. Loss of CHD8 may thus disturb an old gene network as the brain forms.
europmc-pmc4370852:
Kim van der Zwaluw and co-authors presented a cheap new test for dangerous bacterial enzymes, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Some Gram-negative bacteria make carbapenemases, enzymes that destroy carbapenem drugs, a last-line defense. Finding these producers fast matters for infection control, but the standard test is costly. The new Carbapenem Inactivation Method gives a result within eight hours using simple lab steps.

The method matched gene-test results closely for the main enzyme families, including KPC, NDM, and OXA types. It worked across common gut bacteria such as Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli, and also in tougher species like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii. The authors describe it as robust and cost-effective. Labs with small budgets gain a practical screen where the standard test is out of reach.
europmc-pmc4377852:
Mihaela Angelova and co-authors profiled the immune landscape of bowel cancers, in Genome Biology in 2015. Large cancer projects had catalogued mutations, but paid little heed to whether those mutations provoke immune attack, or how tumors evade it. The team applied a joint strategy to 598 colorectal cancers, mapping immune cells inside tumors, the altered proteins those cells might target, and the genes behind each pattern.

Immune cell mixes tracked with distinct molecular types of tumor. Shared cancer-germline antigens appeared in all patients, while new antigens from mutations were rarely shared, so vaccines would need to be personal. Tumors escaped in two broad ways: heavily mutated ones raised immune brakes, while quieter ones drew in suppressive cells and lowered display signals. Network analysis across 11 more groups flagged BCMA as a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc4432652:
Glenn Cowley and a large team of co-authors shared results of gene shutdown screens in more than two hundred cancer cell lines in Scientific Data in 2014. To grow, each cancer depends on some genes more than others, and those weak points can guide drug design. The team used viruses to deliver short RNA pieces that silence one gene at a time, across the genome.

Each line was tested for how silencing each of thousands of genes changed cell growth after many doublings, read out by sequencing. All lines were screened under the same conditions, so their weak points can be compared fairly. Paired with each line's genetic profile, the data let researchers link a dependency to a mutation or cell type. A software tool provided with the data helps find such links, in straight or curved patterns.
europmc-pmc4455052:
Weidong Bao, Kenji Kojima, and Oleksiy Kohany updated Repbase, a database of repetitive DNA, in Mobile DNA in 2015. Genomes of complex organisms are full of repeated sequences, including transposable elements that copy and move themselves. A trusted, hand-checked reference set of those repeats underpins almost every genome analysis, from masking repeats before gene hunting to studying genome evolution.

Repbase began in the early nineteen-nineties as a set of human repeats and grew under its founder, the late Jerzy Jurka. The update explains how entries are now submitted and revised, with a tool that guides contributors, and shows short examples of using the data. The authors invite the wider research community to submit repeat sequences from more species, so the reference keeps pace with the genomes being read.
europmc-pmc4471552:
Ning Huang, Xiong Chen, Rajamani Krishna, and Donglin Jiang turned a layered porous material into a strong carbon dioxide trap, reporting in Angewandte Chemie in 2015. Covalent organic frameworks are crystalline polymers with ordered channels that could soak up gases. In the flat, two-dimensional kind, dense stacking of layers leaves little pore space, which had so far limited their use for capturing carbon dioxide.

Rather than fight the dense stacking, the team used it: they decorated the channel walls with many functional groups, packed in tightly because the layers sit close. The decorated framework captured carbon dioxide with high capacity, could be reused, picked carbon dioxide out from flue gas mixtures selectively, and separated it productively. The authors propose wall decoration as a general, simple strategy for making two-dimensional frameworks into high-performance gas storage and separation materials.
europmc-pmc4515552:
Wei Wang, Amy K. Erbe, Jacquelyn A. Hank, Zachary S. Morris, and Paul M. Sondel review how natural killer cells help antibody drugs kill cancer, in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015. NK cells are immune cells that can attack without prior training. Lab-made antibodies can coat a tumor cell and mark it for them.

NK cells carry Fc receptors that grip the tail of a bound antibody. That grip switches the cell on: it bursts the target and releases signals like interferon gamma that call in other immune cells. The review covers this antibody-dependent killing, used against cancers such as neuroblastoma, breast cancer, and B cell lymphoma. It also explains the KIR receptor family, which brakes or frees NK cells, and how gene variants in these systems change response.
europmc-pmc4533152:
Simon Roux, Steven J. Hallam, Tanja Woyke, and Matthew B. Sullivan mined public microbe genomes for hidden viruses, in eLife in 2015. Viruses shape microbial ecology, yet most viral sequence space is uncharted 'dark matter,' and which virus infects which host is often unknown. Viral genomes tucked inside bacterial and archaeal DNA offer a way in.

The search pulled out 12,498 high-confidence viral genomes, each linked to its microbial host, enlarging public sets tenfold. Thirteen bacterial groups gained their first known viruses, and 7 to 38% of unknown sequences in virus surveys could now be named. Network checks matched accepted virus taxonomy, suggested 264 new genera, and measured how often cells carry spare viruses or suffer coinfection.
europmc-pmc4569652:
Wouter Peeters and six co-authors survey traumatic brain injury across Europe, in Acta Neurochirurgica in 2015. Brain injury from blows and falls is a major public health and economic burden, yet countries count it so differently that a European picture barely existed. The team reviewed incidence studies that gathered European data between 1990 and 2014.

Twenty-eight studies from 16 countries qualified, with wide gaps in how cases were defined and found. Falls and road traffic accidents were the two leading causes, falls ahead in most studies, and incidence peaked in the oldest age groups. The pooled analysis gives an overall European rate while exposing how badly the field needs one counting standard.
europmc-pmc4598952:
How mesenchymal stem cells, known as MSCs, handle damaged power plants inside the cell is the subject of a 2015 study by Donald G. Phinney and colleagues. These stem cells support blood stem cells and calm immune activity, but how they survive stress was unclear. The work appeared in Nature Communications and focuses on mitochondria and macrophages.

MSCs push worn-out mitochondria to their surface inside small vesicles. Macrophages then swallow and reuse that material, which boosts their energy output. At the same time, MSCs release packets carrying microRNAs that quiet macrophage activation through toll-like receptor signals. Together, the hand-offs link stem cell survival with macrophage behaviour and may explain part of how MSC treatments help injured tissue.
europmc-pmc4640152:
Working with colleagues, Elena Viganò published a 2015 study uncovering how human monocytes release inflammatory signals in one fast step. Monocytes are early responders to infection. Most cells need two steps to activate the inflammasome that matures the cytokine IL-1 beta. Monocytes react to bacterial lipopolysaccharide alone. The work appeared in Immunology and Cell Biology.

Two enzymes, caspase-4 and caspase-5, proved to drive the release of IL-1 alpha and IL-1 beta in this pathway. Caspase-5 was cut into active pieces soon after stimulation, including one new fragment tied to secretion. The pathway needs uptake of the bacterial signal through CD14 and TLR4, plus a signalling enzyme and calcium flow. Naming these drivers offers targets for calming endotoxin shock.
europmc-pmc4650752:
Fatemeh Momen-Heravi and colleagues' 2015 study centres on how liver cells hurt by drink send word to immune cells in tiny sacs called exosomes. Liver harm and immune cell swelling drive a severe liver illness in heavy drinkers. A small RNA named miR-122, common in liver cells, was their focus.

The sacs rose in the blood of healthy people after binge drinking and in mice fed drink. Sacs from liver cells grown with drink carried miR-122 and were taken up by immune cells. The RNA shut down a shield pathway and made the cells react more strongly to germ toxin, sending out more swelling signals. Blocking miR-122 in the sacs stopped the effect. The route shows how drink can prime immune cells for worse liver harm.
europmc-pmc4712552:
Rosalinda D'Amore, Umer Zeeshan Ijaz, Melanie Schirmer, and seven colleagues benchmarked methods for profiling microbial communities in BMC Genomics in 2016. Studies of microbes lean on the 16S ribosomal RNA gene as an identity marker, but labs differ in platforms, primers, and preparation, and results shift accordingly. The team built two fake communities, one with strains in even shares and one uneven, then ran them through four sequencing platforms and three preparation designs across nine gene regions.

Every combination distorted the community picture somewhat. Error rates and false hybrid sequences depended on how libraries were prepared, and the region chosen changed what could be told apart. Yet one hopeful pattern held: relative shifts in abundance between samples were still recovered faithfully. The authors advise trial runs on several regions before big projects, and fake communities as routine controls. Their benchmarks help labs choose designs with open eyes.
europmc-pmc4729952:
Ronald J. A. Wanders, Hans R. Waterham, and Sacha Ferdinandusse reviewed how peroxisomes cooperate with other cell compartments, in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology in 2015. Peroxisomes run several unique jobs: building special membrane fats, shortening very long fatty acids, making bile acids and the brain fat DHA, and handling reactive oxygen. Genetic defects in these jobs cause severe diseases, often fatal early in life. None of the jobs, though, is finished inside the peroxisome alone.

Half-done products shuttle to mitochondria for final burning, and helper molecules must be recycled for the assembly line to continue. The review goes pathway by pathway through the handoffs between peroxisomes, mitochondria, and the endoplasmic reticulum. Redox shuttle systems that keep the chemistry balanced get detailed treatment. The picture that emerges is of organelles as trading partners, which explains why one broken compartment can sicken the whole cell.
europmc-pmc4834552:
Barbara W. Sódar leads a broad author team in Scientific Reports in 2016 with a warning for blood vesicle research. Tiny vesicles shed by cells circulate in blood and are chased as disease biomarkers. Isolating them cleanly is the field's known headache; this team shows one contaminant hides in plain sight by imitating the vesicles themselves.

Most particles in the vesicle size range in blood plasma lacked vesicle markers. They proved to be low-density lipoprotein, the cholesterol carrier, which shares the vesicles' size and weight behavior and rides along through every standard isolation method. Under the microscope, the lipoprotein even stuck to true vesicles in mixed samples. No current method yielded a lipoprotein-free preparation, so the authors urge designers and readers of blood vesicle studies to reckon with the impostor.
europmc-pmc4864252:
Justin C. Brown, Michael O. Harhay, and Meera N. Harhay studied sarcopenia and death in community-dwelling older adults in 2016. Sarcopenia means low muscle mass and slow movement. Whether it predicts specific causes of death, and whether the risk differs by sex or body weight, was unclear. The study followed 4,425 older adults from a national United States health survey run in 1988 to 1994.

Average age was 70.1 years, and 36.5 percent met the sarcopenia definition. Sarcopenia went with higher death risk overall in both men and women. In women it also tracked with higher heart and vessel death. Muscle checks may thus flag older adults who need closer care and strength support.
europmc-pmc4880952:
Farman Rashid, Aasim Shah, and Ge Shan reviewed long non-coding RNAs that work in the cell cytoplasm in 2016. These long RNA strips do not build proteins, yet they steer many cell events. Outside the nucleus, they act through several routes. Some steady or doom the messages that do build proteins. Others tune how fast those messages are read.

Cytoplasmic strips can also soak up tiny regulator RNAs like a sponge, serve as raw stock for making those tiny regulators, and alter proteins after they are built. Well-studied cases anchor each route. The review closes with open questions on how these quiet RNAs are sorted, timed, and targeted in health and disease.
europmc-pmc4882852:
Angela Glassing and co-authors warned in Gut Pathogens in 2016 that lab kits themselves carry bacterial DNA that can distort microbe surveys. Sensitive DNA methods now scan samples with very few bacteria, such as tissue. At that scale, germ DNA hiding in extraction kits and reaction mixes can swamp the true signal. The team catalogued contaminants in common kits.

Against earlier reports, they found 88 more bacterial genes riding in reagents. In rich samples the noise matters little, but in low-biomass samples it can fake whole communities and false germ finds. Blank controls and contaminant lists become a must. The study is a standing caution for placenta, blood, and other near-sterile sample claims.
europmc-pmc4999852:
Susan Hall and ten co-authors review the cellular effects of pyocyanin, a toxin secreted by the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Their review appeared in Toxins in 2016. The bacterium causes severe hospital acquired infections in many body systems. Pyocyanin is a redox active pigment it releases, able to generate reactive oxygen species inside host cells. Studies link it to harm in the respiratory, cardiovascular, urological, and central nervous systems, mostly in cell culture work.

Respiratory effects are the best studied, given how the bacterium infects lungs. Newer work shows damage in other systems as well, driven by free radicals and inflammatory cytokines. The authors note the evidence leans heavily on in vitro studies. Whether the toxin crosses membranes freely in the body, as its chemistry suggests, is still untested. They call for high quality animal studies to map what pyocyanin exposure really does to whole organs.
europmc-pmc5009152:
Richard D. Beger and a large group of co-authors present a white paper in Metabolomics in 2016, arguing that metabolomics belongs inside precision medicine. Metabolomics measures the full set of small chemicals in cells, tissues, and body fluids. That chemical state reflects genes plus diet, surroundings, and gut microbes, and gives a direct read on health. Clinics today test only a narrow slice of it.

The paper, written for a Metabolomics Society task group, urges big health studies to add full chemical profiling. Wider profiling could describe diseases and their course more exactly and sharpen the sorting of one illness from another. The authors give advice on which lab platforms to pick, how to collect and store samples, and how to keep measures standard across sites. They also cover how the data should be read and shared.
europmc-pmc5044952:
Karen Duis and Anja Coors review microplastics in the environment in Environmental Sciences Europe in 2016. Tiny plastic particles now appear in water, sediment, and soil. The review gathers what is known about their sources, travel, and effects, with special attention to care products such as scrubs, a publicly debated source.

Care products turn out to be a minor share; wear and breakup of larger plastic goods matter far more, the authors judge. Most creatures that swallow microplastics pass them quickly, and there is no clear proof of buildup up the food chain. In lab tests, harm took doses far above levels measured in sea water, though beach sediment levels came closer to effect levels in worms. Pollutants hitchhiking on the particles seem unlikely to add much to body burdens. Even so, because the particles persist and concentrations keep rising, the authors urge cutting plastic release worldwide.
europmc-pmc5239552:
Fan Zhang and colleagues traced how the signal TGF-beta pushes macrophages toward a tumour-friendly state in Oncotarget in 2016. Macrophages, immune cells that settle in tumours, can take an attacking M1 form or a calming M2 form that helps tumours grow. TGF-beta was known to favour the M2 form, but the inside route was not clear.

In human macrophages, TGF-beta raised the anti-inflammatory signal IL-10 and lowered the inflammatory signals TNF-alpha and IL-12, the M2 pattern. The switch ran through a protein called SNAIL: adding SNAIL alone produced the M2 pattern, while removing it forced the M1 pattern and cancelled TGF-beta's effect. Two signaling routes, SMAD2/3 and PI3K/AKT, were needed for TGF-beta to raise SNAIL. Blocking the TGF-beta to SNAIL path restored inflammatory output, which the authors flag as a possible anti-tumour target.
europmc-pmc5254452:
D. P. D. Wilkie, of Edinburgh University, reviewed ulceration after gastro-enterostomy in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1910, reporting work from the Royal College of Physicians laboratory funded by the Carnegie Trust. The operation joins stomach to jejunum to bypass a blocked outlet, but a peptic ulcer at or beyond the join had emerged as a grim sequel. About ninety cases were on record, with the complication's true frequency still unknown.

Two forms are set apart: ulcers at the join itself, by far the commoner, and true jejunal ulcers at a distance. They can appear weeks or years after surgery, usually with a return of stomach symptoms, though sudden perforation is sometimes the first sign, and perforation kills often. Every recorded case followed surgery for non-cancerous disease. Wilkie's experiments close the paper: excess stomach acid alone, he found, will not ulcerate the jejunum after the operation.
europmc-pmc5285552:
David M. Greig, conservator of the Royal College of Surgeons' Museum in Edinburgh, recorded a case of meningeal naevus with adenoma sebaceum in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1922. The patient, John E., an eighteen-year-old in Greig's ward at Dundee Royal Infirmary in February 1913, had suffered fits for fifteen years and paralysis of the right side for eleven. The naevus is a vascular tumour of the membranes over the brain, paired here with a skin condition of small facial growths.

His history was troubled from the start: convulsions at fourteen months, late sitting and walking, and fainting turns that settled into regular morning and evening fits. Schooling ran off and on to age fourteen while the weakness slowly deepened. Greig notes that surgery had unexpectedly eased the case over nine years, the surprise that emboldened him to publish alongside a similar report by Campbell and Ballance.
europmc-pmc5324652:
Malte C. Kremer, Christophe Jung, Sara Batelli, Gerald M. Rubin, and Ulrike Gaul mapped support cells in the adult fruit fly brain in Glia in 2017. These cells, called glia, were long seen as mere glue between nerve cells. Work in the embryo had charted them well, but the adult brain map was thin. The team used hundreds of genetic driver lines to light up glia types.
