Glia make up about one tenth of the cells in the fly nervous system. They wrap every part of every neuron: body, input branches, and output fibers, plus the whole system as a shell. A few plain rules shape them. Each glial cell shuns its glial neighbors, hugs neurons tight, and molds its form to the part it wraps. No fixed spatial pattern links glia to set neurons. The paper's full atlas and tool kit set up fresh work on what adult glia do.
europmc-pmc5397452:
Juliet Compston leads the National Osteoporosis Guideline Group writing group in a 2017 paper in Archives of Osteoporosis. The paper is a major update of the United Kingdom guide on osteoporosis, the bone-thinning disease that raises break risk. It covers women past menopause and men aged fifty or over. Past guides came out in 2008 with a refresh in 2013, and proof was graded by strength for each advice point.

Advice spans how to spot the disease, how to rate break risk, daily life steps, and drug choices. It covers how long to give the main bone drugs and how to check they work, bone loss caused by steroid drugs, bone loss in men, and care after a break. The guide, cleared by the national care standards body, aims at all staff who treat the disease.
europmc-pmc5408452:
Gabrielle Lindsay Smith and four co-authors review social support and physical activity in older adults in a 2017 paper in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. Staying active cuts death risk and wards off many chronic ills, yet few older people move enough, and activity falls with age. The team searched five databases for studies linking support, or loneliness, to activity in healthy adults over sixty.

Most of the studies that met their rules looked at one point in time rather than following people forward. Support aimed at activity itself, such as a walking partner or praise for effort, went with higher activity, above all when it came from family. General support, support from friends, and loneliness showed no clear link. Leisure activity showed the tie more often than mixed measures did.
europmc-pmc5446752:
Efthymiou and Goate review gene studies that tie late onset Alzheimer's disease to the brain's immune cells. Alzheimer's is the form of the disease that starts after age 65. Most drug work has chased amyloid plaques, with no success so far. The authors ask what other paths may drive risk.

They walk through large gene scans and gene network studies. Many risk genes, such as TREM2, CD33, and ABCA7, act in microglia. These are the brain's own immune cells. The review weighs what each gene does in those cells and in the disease. The authors argue these genes may raise risk apart from amyloid. That shift could point drug hunts toward immune paths.
europmc-pmc5482052:
He, Zhu, and Mo report a modeling study in Nature Communications on super-ionic conductors. These solids carry ions far faster than most solids do. They are prized for safer batteries and fuel cells. Why so few materials reach that speed was not understood. The team used first-principles computer models to probe the cause.

The models show that fast flow does not come from single ions hopping alone. Instead, many ions move together in a concerted way, they report. That shared motion faces low energy barriers. Special ion layouts and strong ion interactions create the effect. The authors offer this as a general design rule. It may guide the search for new fast conductors.
europmc-pmc5591952:
Sicard and co-authors review gut bacteria and intestinal mucus in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. The gut lining wears a mucus coat. Its main ingredient is mucin, a sugar-heavy protein. Most gut microbes live inside that layer.

Mucus works two ways at once. It shields the gut wall from damage and invaders. It also feeds and houses friendly bacteria. Microbes grip mucin sugars as anchor points. Some form biofilms on it. Others clip off its sugars for food. Signals in mucus can even switch pathogen genes on or off. Bacteria, in turn, reshape the mucus itself. The layer keeps renewing as a moving trap. Readers get the two-way traffic between microbes and their mucus home.
europmc-pmc5632352:
Urdaneta and Casadesús wrote a review in Frontiers in Medicine. Their subject is the two-way tie between bacteria and bile salts. Bile salts are made in the liver from cholesterol. Gut bacteria reshape them, and they reshape gut bacteria in return. The balance helps keep the gut and liver healthy.

The review explains how bacteria change bile salts. Some enzymes split them apart, and others alter their structure. Bile salts can also kill bacteria by harming cell membranes. Resistant species survive by rebuilding their outer layers. They also pump the salts out and switch on stress responses. One case is Salmonella, which can infect the gall bladder for years. The authors say this knowledge may guide new treatments.
europmc-pmc5636952:
Gastegger, Behler, and Marquetand present a methods study in Chemical Science. They combine neural networks with molecular dynamics. The aim is to simulate infrared spectra of molecules. Standard quantum simulations capture motion well but cost too much. They also struggle with large systems and long runs. Static methods miss anharmonic effects and heat effects.

The team trained high-dimensional neural network potentials on reference data. Forces helped build the potentials, and sampling picked data points. A new scheme modeled dipole moments as well. Methanol served as an early test case. Other organic molecules followed. The authors report spectra that include anharmonicity and temperature effects. Their approach keeps quantum-level accuracy at far lower cost.
europmc-pmc5643552:
Lemaçon and co-authors report a companion study in Nature Communications. It also concerns BRCA proteins and stalled replication forks. Without BRCA protection, the MRE11 nuclease degrades reversed forks. That damage drives sensitivity to chemotherapy. The team combined electron microscopy with DNA fiber methods. They traced exactly how the breakdown starts and proceeds.

CtIP starts MRE11-dependent attack on unprotected regressed arms. The EXO1 nuclease then extends the degradation. Limited cutting creates a tail that MUS81 can cleave. That cleavage enables a rescue route needing POLD3. Rescued forks restart through a break-induced replication process. The pathway held in BRCA2-deficient cells, not BRCA1-deficient ones. The authors propose targeting it to tune drug response.
europmc-pmc5661652:
Peng and Croce present a review in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. It covers microRNAs in human cancer. MicroRNAs are small noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression. Their levels go wrong in many tumors. Causes include gene copying changes and faulty transcription control. Epigenetic shifts and broken processing machinery also contribute.

A microRNA can act as an oncogene or a tumor suppressor. The effect depends on context and targets. Faulty microRNAs touch every hallmark of cancer. They sustain growth signals and help cells evade suppression. They also resist cell death, invade tissue, and spur blood vessel growth. The authors review microRNAs as candidate biomarkers. Uses include diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy design.
europmc-pmc5686552:
Wlodarczyk and co-authors report a mouse study in The EMBO Journal. It finds a special microglial subset in the newborn brain. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. A subset marked by CD11c dominates areas forming myelin. Myelin is the sheath that wraps nerve fibers. These cells carry a distinct gene profile. Their genes support survival, movement, and growth of young brain cells.

The subset is the main source of growth factor IGF1. Removing IGF1 from these cells impaired early myelination. Toxin tests that target CD11c cells gave matching results. Similar cells appear when adult brains repopulate after cell loss. Those adult cells lack the newborn growth program, though. The subset thus looks unique to development.
europmc-pmc5744552:
Wood describes a small, very painful lump under the skin in this 1812 paper. He was a surgeon in Edinburgh, writing on cases seen over one year. The lump, or tubercle, is no bigger than a coffee bean. Skin over it looks normal, and it can be found only by touch in most cases.

Despite its size, the lump causes severe, at times excruciating, pain. It grows to a set size and then stays much the same for years. It most often forms in the limbs. Patients traveled far and accepted surgery to be rid of it, he reports. His cases give an early full account of the condition.
europmc-pmc5754852:
Newsome and co-authors present updated guidelines on abnormal liver blood tests. The guidance comes from the British Society of Gastroenterology. It updates a first version from 2000. It serves doctors in primary and secondary care who face odd liver results in children and adults.

The guidelines first define what counts as an abnormal test and a standard test panel. They then set when tests should be checked and how long results should be watched. A set of graded recommendations follows for the response. They cover which scans, blood checks, and screens to run for each patient. The guidelines do not treat the liver diseases behind the results.
europmc-pmc5772852:
Wongrakpanich and co-authors review the use of NSAID pain drugs in older adults. These drugs are among the most prescribed for pain and inflammation. They also carry known harms, from gut bleeding to heart and kidney injury. Older patients use them at very high rates.

The review covers how the drugs act and move through the body. It sets out current guidelines for their use in the elderly. Side effect profiles and clashes with other common drugs get full treatment. The authors aim to give clinicians a complete picture for safer prescribing in later life.
europmc-pmc5785952:
Lundqvist and co-authors study bursts of brain rhythms during working memory in monkeys. Working memory was long pictured as steady firing. Single trials instead show brief gamma and beta bursts. Gamma bursts carry the stored items in spikes. The monkeys held two objects in mind and matched later sequences.

Before a needed object appeared, gamma and item coding rose while beta fell, they report. That readout pattern showed only for relevant test items. When items were no longer needed, beta rose and gamma fell. Slips from this pattern predicted errors. Beta may gate what working memory reads out.
europmc-pmc5891552:
Mokkink and co-authors adapt the COSMIN checklist for systematic reviews. Their article appeared in Quality of Life Research. The original checklist judged single studies of measurement quality. This version serves reviews of patient-reported outcome measures. It asks whether included studies risk biased results. The steering committee debated each standard for adaptation. A pilot test used a review of hand osteoarthritis measures.

Key changes reordered the properties under review. Standards on mere reporting were dropped. Item response theory standards were merged into property sections. Teams must now state their hypotheses in advance. Labels in the four-point rating system also changed. The tool now fits review work alone.
europmc-pmc5905152:
Strain and Paldánius review diabetes, heart disease, and the microcirculation. Their review appeared in Cardiovascular Diabetology. Heart disease is the top cause of death in type 2 diabetes. Standard risk factors do not explain the full burden. High blood pressure is far more common in diabetes than expected. Its harm also hits harder there.

The review compares vessel changes in diabetes with those in other people. Large and small vessels suffer together, limiting backup routes. That joint damage may explain part of the excess risk. Effects of diabetes drugs on small-vessel outcomes are reviewed. Shared causes of pressure and heart risk are explored. Readers get a vessel-level view of diabetic risk.
europmc-pmc5981252:
Zoidis and co-authors review selenium-dependent antioxidant enzymes and the properties of selenoproteins. Their review appeared in Antioxidants. Selenium enters proteins as selenocysteine, the twenty-first amino acid. Any protein carrying it counts as a selenoprotein. Their production depends on cofactors and on dietary selenium. In farm animals such as chickens, intake shapes performance and immunity.

Many selenoprotein functions are still unknown, the authors note. Faults in their genes or low selenium link to many diseases. Heart, immune, muscle, bone, and brain disorders all appear. Heavy metal poisoning lowers their message levels. The review updates the field with focus on chicken results.
europmc-pmc6065152:
Ren and co-authors review how the tumor microenvironment drives pancreatic cancer spread. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. Pancreatic cancer kills most patients soon after diagnosis. Tumors grow inside dense scar-like tissue called desmoplasia. Immune activity there is held in a suppressed state.

Cancer and stromal cells build this setting together. It shields tumors from chemotherapy, radiation, and immune attack. It also feeds blood vessel growth and cell migration. Cells use it to prepare niches in distant organs. The review traces each step of that partnership. Readers get targets for combination therapy. Breaking the shield, the authors argue, may lift survival.
europmc-pmc6098152:
Napolitano and co-authors show how cells switch off the cleanup factor TFEB after feeding. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. TFEB drives autophagy and lysosome building during starvation. It works inside the nucleus. How it leaves again after nutrients return was unknown.

The team found TFEB shuttles constantly in and out. Export, not entry, is the slow step. The export carrier is CRM1. Nutrient signals through mTOR tag two serines in order. Those tags sit beside an export signal. With food restored, tagged TFEB ships out and shuts down. Readers get a new role for mTOR in nuclear export.
europmc-pmc6159552:
Robertson and Nash present a software article in Microbial Genomics on MOB-suite, tools for studying plasmids in bacteria. Plasmids are small DNA circles that bacteria trade, often carrying drug resistance. Draft genome assemblies tend to break plasmids into pieces. That makes their content hard to analyse.

MOB-suite clusters, reconstructs, and types plasmids from draft assembly data. On test genomes with known content, it found plasmid pieces with 95 percent sensitivity and 88 percent specificity. The tools are modular, so each step can run on its own. The authors compare the suite with rival tools. The work helps labs track resistance plasmids through bacterial populations.
europmc-pmc6204752:
Thiele and Bellgrove wrote a review on brain chemicals and attention. Attention lets people pick out key inputs and ignore the rest. Faults in attention mark many brain and mental disorders. The review appeared in Neuron. It links cells, circuits, and behaviour.

The authors sum up how attention changes single nerve cells. They then show how networks of cells change. Four chemicals get the most focus. They are acetylcholine, dopamine, noradrenaline, and serotonin. Each one tunes circuits in its own way. That tuning helps direct attention to the right event. The authors point to tests that could fill key gaps. Such tests could guide new drugs for attention faults.
europmc-pmc6213552:
Bach Knudsen and co-authors review butyrate, diet, and gut health. Butyrate is a short fatty acid made in the large gut. Gut microbes make it from dietary fibre. Low fibre intake limits its production. The review appeared in Nutrients.

Butyrate supports colon health and calms inflammation. It acts through the NF-kB pathway and related signals. Diet type and fibre mix change how much is made. The authors review effects on the gut barrier. They also review effects on inflammation markers. Benefits look strong and steady in the gut itself. Effects in distant tissues look weaker and less steady. The authors link that gap to lower butyrate levels far from the gut.
europmc-pmc6220752:
Gjerstad and co-authors review feedback control of stress hormones. The HPA axis governs these hormones in mammals. Adrenal glands release glucocorticoids in response to stress. At rest they also follow daily and hourly rhythms. The review appeared in Stress.

Broken hormone rhythms link to disease in humans and rodents. Feedback signals keep the hourly pulses in shape. The authors review the role of two receptor types. They also cover a chaperone protein called FKBP51. Recent work shows feedback inside the adrenal gland itself. Receptors there help control hormone synthesis. The review pulls these threads into one account. It shows why rhythm, not just level, matters.
europmc-pmc6317252:
Repana and co-authors present an updated catalogue of cancer genes. The resource paper appeared in Genome Biology. The catalogue is called the Network of Cancer Genes. It lists 2,372 genes with known or likely driver roles. Entries were hand-curated from 275 publications. The source screens covered over 100 cancer types.

Those screens drew on samples from 34,905 donors. The new edition holds over 1.5 times the old content. Each gene carries notes on its properties. These include expression, evolution, and interaction partners. Protein function and essentiality are annotated too. The catalogue is free online for researchers. It helps labs judge which mutations matter in a tumor.
europmc-pmc6323052:
Mills and Rahal review the growth and habits of genome-wide association studies. The scientometric review appeared in Communications Biology. It covers 3,639 studies published up to 2018. Those studies spanned 3,508 traits. Sample sizes and discovery rates climbed steeply. Ancestry diversity moved up and down over time.

Participants stayed mostly of European ancestry. They made up 88 percent in 2017. Three countries supplied most discovery samples. United States agencies funded 85 percent of the work. Women held senior author roles less often. The authors built a field-specific impact index. They close with ten policy recommendations. Funders, editors, and scientists all get guidance.
europmc-pmc6335852:
Schrempft and co-authors test whether lonely older adults move less. Their study appeared in BMC Public Health. Social isolation and loneliness may harm health partly through habits. The team used data from a long-running English ageing study. Participants were 267 adults aged 50 to 81. Each wore a wrist accelerometer for seven days.

Isolated adults recorded lower total activity over 24 hours. The gap held after accounting for health and mood. Mobility limits and depressive symptoms were also factored in. Sedentary time and light activity were examined as well. Loneliness showed its own links to activity patterns. The measures were devices, not self-reports of exercise. That makes the activity picture harder to bias. The work ties social life to daily movement in later years.
europmc-pmc6415852:
Reiss and co-authors report the German BELLA cohort study in PLoS ONE. Children from poorer homes show more mental health problems than richer peers. The team asked how family status and stressful life events work together on that risk.

Data covered 2,111 young people aged seven to seventeen at the start. Three survey rounds ran between 2003 and 2008. Low family status tied directly to more mental health problems. Stressful events added to the load, and the two risks interacted. The authors argue support must reach poor families before problems harden. Schools are one setting they name.
europmc-pmc6494952:
Zheng and co-authors test whether lipoprotein(a), the blood particle that ferries oxidized phospholipids, actively drives aortic valve calcification rather than merely marking risk. They followed 145 patients with aortic stenosis using PET imaging of calcification activity, CT calcium scoring, and echocardiography, and treated valve cells with the particle in culture.

Patients in the top Lp(a) third showed hotter calcification activity at baseline and far faster calcium accumulation, 309 versus 93 arbitrary units per year. They also had quicker hemodynamic worsening and a hazard ratio of 1.87 for valve replacement or death. In the dish, Lp(a) pushed valve interstitial cells toward bone-like differentiation through its oxidized phospholipids, an effect an antibody against those lipids blocked.
europmc-pmc6520952:
Smith and co-authors review how food marketing shapes children's attitudes and eating. Their systematic review appeared in Nutrients. It covers children from birth to age 18. Marketing of unhealthy food is a known risk factor for childhood obesity.

The team searched five databases for studies up to September 2018. They found 71 eligible articles. Studies showed clear harmful effects across many techniques. Marketing boosted attitudes toward the foods, liking for them, and intake. Effects were strongest for television, movies and product packaging. The authors say the evidence supports limits on marketing to children. Gaps remain on new media methods and long-term effects on weight.
europmc-pmc6523452:
Pinu and co-authors share the metabolomics community's view of multi-omics integration. Their article appeared in Metabolites. It grew from a peer session at the ANZMET 2018 conference in Auckland. Multi-omics work joins genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Joining such data sets stays hard, since each type differs by nature.

Metabolites sit downstream of genes, transcripts and proteins. So metabolomics tools may help bind the layers. The authors give methods, software and database guidance. They list design needs, from sample choice to shared standards. They also name open challenges, funding limits among them. The piece serves as a guide for teams planning joint studies.
europmc-pmc6593152:
Prüss-Ustün and co-authors update the health burden from poor water, sanitation, and hygiene. Their analysis appears in the International Journal of Hygiene and Environmental Health. The focus is on low- and middle-income countries. For each disease, they paired exposure levels with exposure-response links. The shares of deaths tied to these risks were then worked out. The outcomes went well beyond diarrhoea. Lung infections, poor nutrition, and schistosomiasis were in the set. Malaria, worm infections, and trachoma rounded it out.

Diarrhoea caused most of the tied deaths. It accounted for 829,000 deaths in 2016. That is 60 percent of all diarrhoeal deaths. Children under five lost 297,000 lives. Across all the diseases, the toll reached 1.6 million deaths. That is nearly three percent of all deaths worldwide.
europmc-pmc6606852:
Bussi and Gutierrez review how tuberculosis bacteria live inside human cells. Their article appears in FEMS Microbiology Reviews. Mycobacterium tuberculosis kills more people than any other single infectious agent. It claimed close to 1.7 million lives in 2017 alone. Its hidden life inside cells makes it hard to clear.

The authors follow the bacillus from inhaled droplets to the alveoli. Macrophages swallow it, yet it can survive inside phagosomes. Some bacteria escape into the cytosol or persist in granulomas. Spread can reach lymph nodes, fat, and bone marrow. The review maps host defenses such as autophagy against bacterial evasion tricks. It also flags the technical hurdles that slow study of human infection.
europmc-pmc6667152:
Margolis and Sadovsky survey what remains unknown about extracellular vesicles. Their essay appears in PLoS Biology. Cells release these membrane vesicles constantly. They carry proteins, nucleic acids, and metabolites between cells. The field once dismissed them as platelet dust. New tools revealed defined biological functions instead. Publication growth has outpaced solid evidence, though. The authors sort established facts from attractive hypotheses.

Open mysteries structure the essay. How cargo gets selected for loading is unclear. Release, targeting, and uptake routes remain murky. Delivery efficiency claims often lack proof. Shared names hide deep vesicle diversity. Standards for separation and analysis still lag. The authors pose hard questions for the field.
europmc-pmc6683152:
Sun and co-authors test faecal transplant therapy in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Their study appears in Translational Psychiatry. The mice carry APP and PS1 transgenes. Alzheimer's has been linked to abnormal gut microbiota. The team gave healthy donor faeces daily. Treatment lasted four weeks by stomach tube. Memory, amyloid deposits, and tau changes were assessed. Synaptic proteins and brain inflammation markers followed.

The authors report broad gains after transplant. Memory deficits eased in treated mice. Brain amyloid build-up fell measurably. Tau phosphorylation and Aβ40 and Aβ42 dropped. Synaptic markers PSD-95 and synapsin I rose. Inflammation markers COX-2 and CD11b fell. Gut microbes and short-chain fatty acids normalised. The authors propose transplant as a candidate strategy.
europmc-pmc6711452:
Smith and co-authors examined how best to compute brain age delta. Brain age is how old a brain scan makes someone look, judged against a large reference group. Delta is the gap between that estimate and a person's real age. A positive gap may signal faster aging, a negative one resilience.

The note shows that the common way of computing delta is biased. The authors test fixes on simulated and real data. They then check corrected delta against 5,792 non-imaging measures in about 19,000 UK Biobank participants. Their method gives cleaner links to health, life factors, and thinking test scores.
europmc-pmc6721852:
Han and co-authors give an overview of mesenchymal stem cells for regenerative medicine. These cells are drawn easily from bone marrow, fat, and joint tissue. They can turn into many cell types as a treatment requires. They also slip past immune watch, so transplants rarely face rejection.

The paper covers how the cells are extracted and guided to mature. It then surveys lab and clinical uses across regenerative medicine. Past work grew from the spindle-shaped marrow cells found in the mid-1970s. Cases include a tissue-engineered windpipe transplant that still worked at five years. The authors close with challenges that remain before wider use.
europmc-pmc6754952:
He and co-authors showed that exosomes from stem cells help skin wounds heal. Mesenchymal stem cell transplants speed wound repair, mostly through signals the cells release. The missing piece was how the stem cells interact with macrophages at the wound. Removing macrophages early delayed healing in their tests, proving the cells were required.

Stem cells from bone marrow and jaw marrow traveled to wounds in mice. There they pushed macrophages toward the M2 form, which calms inflammation and rebuilds tissue. Exosomes carried the effect. A small RNA in the exosomes, miR-223, drove the switch by targeting a gene called pknox1. Stem cells stripped of exosomes healed wounds more slowly.
europmc-pmc6778852:
Liebschner and co-authors describe recent developments in Phenix, a software package for macromolecular structure determination. Knowing a molecule's 3D shape explains how it works. Phenix handles the main experimental routes: X-ray, neutron, and electron diffraction, plus cryo-electron microscopy. The paper reviews what is new in the package.

Restraint systems for ligands and linked groups have grown more automatic. Metal and carbohydrate geometry can now be handled without hand tuning. The authors explain each method's basics for non-experts as they go. Structures solved with Phenix feed the public Protein Data Bank. X-ray diffraction remains the dominant source of deposits, with cryo-EM rising. The update aims to keep the tools current across all three probes.
europmc-pmc6791352:
Glenn and co-authors present a universal indexing system for Illumina DNA sequencing libraries. Massively parallel sequencing is powerful but costly to start and to run at small scale. Sample preparation is only part of the expense. Their system breaks library building into reusable parts. It extends a standard dual-indexing scheme to 768 primers.

Those primers yield 384 unique dual indexes, or 147,456 combinations when mixed freely. Indexes stay eight letters long, many matching Illumina standards. In validation, 206 of 208 primers passed quality checks, a 99% success rate. Hundreds of libraries were built in varied scenarios. One universal adapter serves every library type, cutting start-up and per-sample costs for sequencing labs.
europmc-pmc6811952:
Chan and co-authors review human papillomavirus and cervical cancer in the Journal of Oncology. HPV is a common virus spread by close contact. A small set of its types can cause cancer over time. Cervical cancer stays a major health problem in many regions despite good screening tests.

The review covers how often HPV occurs in different places and age groups. It explains how the virus drives cancer and how Pap tests and HPV tests find risk early. It also covers vaccines that block the worst types. Rates of disease and death vary widely by region, and the authors stress gaps in data from many countries.
europmc-pmc6844052:
Jing and co-authors review low oxygen in cancer treatment, in Molecular Cancer. Solid tumours often outgrow their blood supply, leaving inner regions starved of oxygen. That state, hypoxia, rewires how cancer cells behave. It is tied to poor outcomes for patients. It also blunts chemotherapy and radiation, which both work less well without oxygen.

The review explains how hypoxia reshapes the tumour's surroundings, from immune cells to blood vessels. It drives cells to burn more sugar and to dodge death signals. Damaged DNA repair and dormant states add to resistance. The authors then survey treatments designed to exploit or reverse low oxygen. They judge this a promising route against resistant cancers.
europmc-pmc6853652:
Kamat and co-authors announce a major update to PhenoScanner, in Bioinformatics. The tool is a database of results from large genetic studies in humans. A researcher can look up a DNA variant and see every trait it has been linked to, a so-called phenome scan. Such checks help judge whether a variant's effects are broad or narrow.

Version 2 holds over 150 million genetic variants and more than 65 billion associations. The first version held 350 million associations, so the growth is vast. Links now span diseases, gene activity, metabolites, proteins, and epigenetic marks. New searches by gene, region, or trait were added. A programming interface lets other software query the database directly.
europmc-pmc6881452:
Singh and co-authors present a new predictor of RNA shape, in Nature Communications. Most of the human genome is copied into noncoding RNAs whose jobs are unknown. Their folding patterns, or secondary structures, give the first clues. Classic folding algorithms have barely improved in over a decade. Only a few hundred high-quality RNA structures are known, which limits training data.

Their method, SPOT-RNA, learns from those structures with an ensemble of two-dimensional deep networks. Transfer learning stretches the small training set further. It predicts unusual pairings too, including noncanonical pairs and pseudoknots that older tools miss. Tested structures came out close to the true folds in the study's examples.
europmc-pmc6991252:
Sheetz and co-authors chart how fast robotic surgery spread across common operations. Their cohort study appeared in JAMA Network Open. Robotic operating keeps diffusing into new procedure types. Critics note higher costs, up to 25 percent above keyhole surgery in some reports, and thin proof of benefit for some uses.

Regulators had warned against robotic surgery for breast and cervical cancer care, citing missing real-world data. The team used a statewide Michigan registry covering 73 hospitals and over 90 percent of surgery in the state. Trained abstractors, not billing codes, recorded how operations were done. Robotic use rose steeply across general surgery procedures in the registry years. Growth was fastest in areas with limited evidence of advantage, such as hernia repair. The pattern, the authors argue, deserves scrutiny.
europmc-pmc7001252:
Dadi and co-authors review the global burden of depression during pregnancy and its effects on babies. Their umbrella review appeared in BMC Public Health. Depression before birth is among the most common mood disorders in women of childbearing age. Mental health still gets little attention in pregnancy care, above all in poorer countries.

The team combined ten reviews covering 306 studies and 877,246 participants for prevalence. Reported rates ranged widely, from 15 to 65 percent worldwide. Abuse and violence exposure, weak partner or social support, and personal or family mental illness history stood out as risk factors. Six more reviews, with 75,451 participants, covered birth outcomes. Babies of depressed mothers faced higher risk of low birth weight and early birth. The authors urge policy to take antenatal mental health seriously.
europmc-pmc7015852:
Zhang and a large team of co-authors report a genome study in Nature. Their subject is the blue-petal water lily, Nymphaea colorata. Water lilies sit near the base of the flowering plant family tree. A genome from this branch can test ideas about how flowers first evolved.

The team assembled a genome of 409 million bases and annotated 31,580 protein-coding genes. Their family-tree analyses place two early lineages as successive sisters to all other living flowering plants. They also find an ancient whole-genome doubling shared within the water lily order. Genes that guide flowering and flower shape survive from that doubling. Scent and colour genes seem to have evolved in parallel with those in core flowering plants.
europmc-pmc7029452:
Bernard Stoecklin and co-authors report the first COVID-19 cases in France in Eurosurveillance. France stepped up surveillance on 10 January 2020. The aim was to catch imported cases early and stop further spread. Three cases were confirmed on 24 January, the first known in Europe.

The report describes the surveillance system and the response. Contacts were sorted into three risk groups, with follow-up matched to each group. Five contacts were judged low risk, and 18 were judged moderate or high risk. By 12 February, two patients had been discharged. The third still had a cough. No onward transmission had been found. The authors stress close teamwork between health agencies and hospitals.
europmc-pmc7059252:
Czeszumski and co-authors review hyperscanning in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. Social interaction is central to human life, but studying the brain during real interaction is hard. Hyperscanning tackles it by recording brain activity from more than one person at the same time, looking for links between their neural signals. The authors evaluate two decades of work with the method.

Three recording tools dominate: functional MRI, magneto- and electroencephalography, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Each carries trade-offs in precision, freedom of movement, and cost for paired recording. The review then surveys analysis methods used to estimate brain networks and synchronisation between partners. Finally it walks through findings by cognitive function, from joint action and cooperation to communication, weighing what inter-brain synchrony actually proves. The authors aim to give newcomers and practitioners an honest account of what hyperscanning can and cannot show.
europmc-pmc7071652:
Ajayi and Akhigbe update methods for staging the estrous cycle in laboratory rodents in Fertility Research and Practice. Knowing which phase of the reproductive cycle a female rat or mouse is in matters for experiments on fertility and for testing how drugs and chemicals affect reproduction. Bringing an animal into heat on schedule is equally useful.

The review describes the phases and their variations in detail, then the ways to tell them apart: visual inspection, vaginal smears and cytology, tissue histology, vaginal wall impedance, and urine chemistry. A vaginal smear, for example, mixes three cell types, and their proportions reveal the phase. Methods for artificially inducing estrus so females become receptive to males are also covered. The authors frame the guide as a teaching and research reference, consolidating scattered practice into one current account for reproductive scientists.
europmc-pmc7084952:
Wang and co-authors surveyed the general public in China on the mental effects of the early COVID-19 outbreak, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Their online survey ran from 31 January to 2 February 2020 and gathered 1,210 replies from 194 cities. Standard scales measured the event's impact plus depression, anxiety, and stress.

In total, 53.8% of respondents rated the outbreak's psychological impact as moderate or severe. Moderate to severe anxiety symptoms appeared in 28.8%, and depressive symptoms in 16.5%. Most people stayed home 20 to 24 hours a day and worried about family members catching the virus. The results gave officials early evidence for planning mental health support.
europmc-pmc7139552:
Wang and co-authors review what liver-specific knockout mice reveal about PPAR proteins as metabolic regulators, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. PPARs come in three forms, alpha, beta/delta, and gamma, and together they manage fat handling in the body. The liver steers whole-body energy balance, so its PPARs matter greatly.

Deleting each form only in the liver exposed distinct jobs: alpha runs much of liver fat metabolism, while the other two act more elsewhere yet still shape liver disease. Faulty signalling feeds fatty liver, its inflamed form, scarring, and even liver cancer. The authors pull the mouse evidence together into a guide for how each receptor might be targeted.
europmc-pmc7201952:
Ganyani and co-authors estimate the generation interval of COVID-19 from symptom onset records. Their study appeared in Eurosurveillance. The generation interval is the time between one infection and the next in a chain. It feeds models that guide control measures. The team used cluster data from Singapore and Tianjin, China, from March 2020.

They allowed for uncertainty in incubation time and in who infected whom. From the generation interval they derived the serial interval between symptom onsets. They also estimated how much spread happens before symptoms. A warning runs through the work: reproduction numbers built on serial intervals can be biased. Careful estimation matters for judging interventions. The paper gives modelers a firmer footing for early pandemic numbers.
europmc-pmc7273352:
Pak and co-authors argue that COVID-19 is an economic crisis as well as a health one, and that the world was not ready for either. Their commentary appeared in Frontiers in Public Health. Lockdowns and illness cut incomes, raised unemployment, and disrupted transport, services, and manufacturing across the globe.

Most governments, they write, underestimated how fast the virus would spread and reacted only after damage was done. The costs of past outbreaks were already known, yet investment in preparedness stayed low. Because new outbreaks are certain to come, the authors call for proactive international cooperation and proper financing of collective defenses. Preparing early, they argue, protects both lives and economic prosperity.
europmc-pmc7282252:
Papadopoulou, writing alone, reviews sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and function. Her review appeared in Nutrients. Sarcopenia raises the risk of disability, falls, hospitalization, and death in older adults, yet it often goes undiagnosed. Reported prevalence ranges widely, from 5% to 50%, depending on age, sex, health, and the definition used.

No single standard exists for judging or treating the condition, which makes comparisons hard. The review covers how common sarcopenia is, what causes it, and how it might be prevented or treated. Physical activity and nutrition stand out as the best-studied defenses, with better outcomes where they are applied. The author argues for sharper diagnosis and care tailored to each older person.
europmc-pmc7301352:
Iba and co-authors define what makes COVID-19's clotting disorder distinct from other coagulopathies doctors know. Their review appeared in Critical Care. Clots and abnormal clotting tests are frequent in COVID-19, but the pattern does not match bacterial sepsis or classic disseminated intravascular coagulation.

In COVID-19-associated coagulopathy, D-dimer and fibrinogen rise sharply while clotting time and platelet counts stay nearly normal at first. Vein and artery clots are more frequent than in sepsis-driven disease. Features overlap partly with hemophagocytic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome, and thrombotic microangiopathy, but not fully with any of them. Sorting these similarities and differences, the authors argue, is what allows correct diagnosis and anticlotting treatment.
europmc-pmc7319552:
Chang and co-authors release miRNet 2.0, an upgraded web platform for working out what microRNAs do. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. MicroRNAs are small regulators of gene activity, and understanding them requires placing them in networks of the genes they target. The first version, from 2016, had been used by more than 20,000 researchers.

Version 2.0 widens the context: it adds transcription factors and genetic variants that affect microRNAs or their targets, and expands the underlying databases more than five-fold. New tools build and explore multi-part networks, with functional analysis available on the spot. The interface and workflow were rebuilt for speed, and an R package ships alongside for programmers. The platform stays free for systems biology research.
europmc-pmc7442652:
Agarwal and co-authors build a single-cell atlas of the human substantia nigra, a brain region lost in Parkinson's disease. They sequenced about 17,000 nuclei from matched cortex and substantia nigra samples. The atlas shows which genes each cell type uses.

Common Parkinson's risk tied to gene activity in dopaminergic neurons. The linked pathways cover mitochondria, protein folding, and protein disposal. A second link tied risk to oligodendrocytes. Unlike Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's risk showed no tie to microglia or astrocytes. That hints that inflammation plays a smaller causal role here. Substantia nigra neurons also linked with several mental health disorders. Distinct disorders used distinct gene sets but met at shared spots in oligodendrocyte lineage cells.
europmc-pmc7454352:
Paterson and co-authors present a case series of brain and nerve problems tied to SARS-CoV-2 infection. Reports of such problems grew as the pandemic spread. The series gathers clinical, scan, and lab findings in one place.

The series covers 43 patients with neurological complications of the infection. Syndromes included encephalopathies, where brain function clouds, and encephalitis, where the brain inflames. Some patients had acute disseminated encephalomyelitis with bleeding changes. Others had transverse myelitis of the spinal cord. Ischaemic stroke appeared in the group as well. Guillain-Barré syndrome, a nerve weakness illness, was also seen. The authors sketch a wide spectrum of nervous system harm. Their set helps doctors spot these patterns early in care.
europmc-pmc7468152:
Hablitz and co-authors show that brain fluid flow follows a daily clock in mice. The glymphatic system moves cerebrospinal fluid into the brain and clears waste. The water channel aquaporin-4, set in astrocyte endfeet, supports the flow.

Flow and clearance peaked during the mid-rest phase of the mice. Drainage from the brain to lymph nodes varied in the opposite pattern. Aquaporin-4 placement at vessel walls was highest in the rest phase too. Mice lacking aquaporin-4 lost the day-night gap in both flow and drainage. The results say spinal fluid spread is under circadian control. Sleep timing, not just sleep itself, shapes brain cleaning. The work links body clocks to waste control in the brain.
europmc-pmc7489852:
Meltzer and co-authors test if vitamin D status links with COVID-19 test results. The cohort held 489 patients at one center. Each had a vitamin D level drawn in the year before testing.

The relative risk was 1.77 times greater for likely deficient patients than for those with likely sufficient status in this cohort. That gap was statistically significant in the team's analysis. Age, race, and other traits were weighed in the models. Still, a cohort study cannot prove that vitamin D changes infection risk. The authors call for randomized trials to settle the point. Trials could test both broad public steps and targeted help for groups low in vitamin D. The work adds a lead, not a verdict.
europmc-pmc7663252:
Zhu and Zhu review the main subsets of CD4 helper T cells. These white blood cells direct much of the adaptive immune response. Five major subsets are now known: Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg, and Tfh cells. Each is set apart by its signals and master control genes.

Each subset fights a distinct class of threat, from germs inside cells to worms. A related family, innate lymphoid cells, mirrors three of these subsets. The authors link each subset to human diseases, with stress on cases caused by single gene defects. The review shows how a skewed subset mix can drive illness.
europmc-pmc7778952:
Köhler and co-authors describe the Human Phenotype Ontology in 2021. The ontology, called HPO, gives a shared logical standard for describing abnormal traits seen in human disease. It launched in 2008 and is now a worldwide standard for exchanging phenotype data.

Recent growth covers neurology, kidney disease, immunology, and lung disease. Newborn screening terms were also expanded. The seizure section now follows the guidelines of the International League Against Epilepsy. The team explains how HPO defines diseases apart from their traits. They also align HPO terms with phenotype ontologies for animal models. Such alignment should sharpen tools such as Exomiser. Translation into indigenous languages and use in health records are covered as well.
europmc-pmc7845152:
de Sena Brandine and Smith present Falco, a fast stand-in for the FastQC sequencing checker. Quality control is the first step in reading sequence data. Most centers build it into their standard pipelines. The checks are simple but add up at scale.

Falco copies FastQC's work at higher speed. On average it runs three times faster. Results match the original tool. It also uses less memory while it runs. Report displays are more flexible in HTML form. Big sequencing centers gain the most from the savings. The tool drops into existing pipelines with little fuss. Speed matters when data arrive by the terabyte.
europmc-pmc7968452:
Bahadoran and co-authors present a review of dietary polyphenols as possible aids in managing diabetes. Polyphenols are plant compounds found in many foods. Growing proof suggests they can act like mild, food-based medicines. The review weighs their effects on the metabolic faults of type 2 diabetes and on its long-term damage. The evidence comes from cell work, animal studies, and some human trials.

The compounds ease high blood sugar, poor lipid profiles, and insulin resistance, the authors report. They also help fat tissue work better and cut oxidative stress and inflammation. Over time, such effects may guard against heart disease, nerve damage, kidney damage, and eye damage. The review sorts the compounds by family, from phenolic acids to lignans. It closes with a caution: the best dose and course in patients are still unknown.
europmc-pmc8000752:
Roth and co-authors present a review of tryptophan metabolism and the gut-brain balance. Tryptophan is an essential building block the body cannot make. It is the sole source of serotonin, a signal vital for mood, hunger, sleep, and pain. It also feeds gut motion and secretion. Its breakdown path, the kynurenine route, steers nerve activity and body-wide inflammation at once.

Gut microbes shape how tryptophan is used, both directly and at one remove. Shifts in its products can shift behaviour and thought in turn. Faulty handling of the compound sits near the root of many brain and mental disorders. The review traces its roles in health and disease across both nervous systems, brain and gut. It frames the microbiome as a treatment target where tryptophan plays a lead part.
europmc-pmc8012052:
Chmielewska and co-authors synthesize how the COVID-19 pandemic affected mothers and newborns. Their systematic review and meta-analysis searched MEDLINE and Embase for studies comparing outcomes before and during the pandemic. The search found 3,592 citations, of which 40 studies qualified. The outcomes covered stillbirth, maternal death, preterm birth, and mental health.

The authors report that stillbirth rose during the pandemic, with a pooled odds ratio of 1.28. Maternal death also rose, at 1.37. Preterm birth did not change overall, but it fell in high-income countries. Postnatal depression scores were higher than before. Surgically managed ectopic pregnancies increased sharply. The harms fell hardest where health systems had least to spare.
europmc-pmc8039952:
Liu and Sun review how to turn cold tumors into hot ones by drawing in T cells. Immune checkpoint inhibitors have reshaped cancer care. Their power depends on T cells that enter the tumor and kill its cells. Cold tumors lack that infiltration, so the drugs fail there. Hot tumors, rich in T cells, respond far better.

The review explains why tumors stay cold. Faulty T-cell priming and weak homing signals share the blame. The authors then collect the strategies that heat tumors up. Each works by raising priming, guiding T cells in, or both. Nanomaterials earn a closing section of their own. Paired with immunotherapy, they sharpen antigen display and T-cell entry. Combination treatments built on these ideas may widen who benefits.
europmc-pmc8050952:
Bharat and co-authors report lung transplantation for patients destroyed by severe COVID-19. Some patients develop end-stage lung fibrosis with no path back. For them, a transplant may be the only treatment. Doubts ran deep, from virus hiding in the old lung to bodies weakened by long ventilation. The team proceeded with three consecutive patients anyway.

All three had needed prolonged mechanical ventilation and ECMO support. Recovery had been judged unlikely in each case. The transplants were carried out successfully. The team then studied the removed lungs in fine detail. Postmortem tissue from patients who died of COVID-19 ARDS added comparisons. Imaging cleared tissue to reveal the scarred matrix. Molecular probes searched for leftover viral RNA. The work sets early ground rules for a last-resort option.
europmc-pmc8126852:
Morselli and co-authors build a network medicine pipeline to rank old drugs against COVID-19. New drug development takes a decade, far too slow here. Algorithms offered rival shortcuts with unproven accuracy. The team ran AI, network diffusion, and proximity methods side by side. They ranked 6,340 approved drugs for expected effect. Then they did what most studies skip: a large lab check.

The lab screened 918 of the ranked drugs experimentally. That ground truth exposed how each method truly performed. A consensus algorithm blended the methods and beat them singly. Top-ranked drugs then faced live virus in human cells. Six drugs cut viral infection in those tests. Four of them could be repurposed for patients right away. The strategy, the authors stress, travels beyond COVID-19. Neglected diseases with no drug pipeline could use it tomorrow.
europmc-pmc8137852:
Søvold and co-authors call for the mental health of healthcare workers to become a global public health priority. Frontline staff absorbed the pandemic's worst shocks firsthand. Stress, burnout, and moral injury rose across the workforce. Depression and trauma symptoms climbed with them. Crisis conditions magnify every standing strain in the job. The authors gather the evidence for that burden.

They then sort the defenses that might actually help. Personal self-care strategies form the first layer discussed. Evidence-based interventions for teams form the second. Organizational measures carry much of the real weight, though. Staffing, scheduling, and leadership culture shape daily strain. Long-run systemic change is the paper's true demand. Policy recommendations target health leaders directly. Empowerment, not resilience slogans, is the proposed direction. A workforce treated as expendable will eventually break. Protecting carers is protecting care itself.
europmc-pmc8346252:
Oblak and co-authors give a full evaluation of the 5XFAD mouse model for Alzheimer's testing. Animal models shape what therapies reach patients. Each model shows only part of the human disease.

The MODEL-AD consortium was formed to vet such models deeply. The 5XFAD mouse is a widely used transgenic line. The team measured its traits across age and assay types. They checked how its changes match human Alzheimer's disease. Gaps are named as plainly as matches. Preclinical teams can now judge when this model fits a question. Shared standards should cut wasted trials.
europmc-pmc8416852:
Nøst and co-authors test whether blood markers of body-wide inflammation predict later cancer. Such markers had been linked to cancer risk and death, but few studies measured them before diagnosis. Early markers could help spot disease sooner.

The study used the UK Biobank cohort of about 440,000 people recruited between 2006 and 2010. Four markers built from blood cell counts were checked against 17 cancer sites. Higher marker levels linked to higher risk for seven cancers. The ties were strongest for colorectal and lung cancer. Links also grew stronger for cases found within a year of joining. A low lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio linked to lower risk.
europmc-pmc8417352:
Hug and co-authors estimate stillbirth rates and trends for 195 countries from 2000 to 2019. Stillbirths mark the quality of care around pregnancy and birth. Global plans call for an end to preventable stillbirths, but rates first need standard measurement.

The team built a data set of 2833 country-year points from 171 countries. Sources included health records, household surveys, and population studies. After quality checks, 1531 points fed a Bayesian model. A stillbirth was defined as a death at 28 weeks of pregnancy or later. The results let countries judge their progress over two decades. Gaps in data remain part of the story.
europmc-pmc8490152:
Avsec and co-authors build Enformer, a deep learning model that predicts gene expression from DNA sequence. How noncoding DNA sets gene activity in each cell type is a big open problem. Human genetics work depends on better answers.

Enformer reads long-range contacts up to 100 kilobases away in the genome. That reach sharply raised prediction accuracy over past models. Variant effect calls improved for both natural variants and lab-made changes. The model also learned enhancer-promoter contacts straight from sequence. It matched methods that need direct lab data as input. The authors expect gains for disease mapping and for reading regulatory evolution.
europmc-pmc8507252:
Jiao and co-authors show how neutrophil exosomes worsen sepsis-linked lung injury. Neutrophils play a big role in this lung damage. Their tiny released packets, called exosomes, may link their inflammation to tissue harm. The exact role of these packets was unclear.

The team spurred mouse neutrophils with a key sepsis signal and harvested their exosomes. Those packets pushed macrophages toward the inflammatory M1 state. They also primed macrophages for pyroptosis, a fiery cell death. A small RNA inside the packets carried much of the effect. It raised levels of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Results held in live mice and in cell co-cultures.
europmc-pmc8809252:
Guilliams and co-authors map liver macrophage niches with spatial proteogenomics across species. The liver is the body's largest solid organ, yet parts of it stay poorly charted. The team combined four data types on healthy and obese human and mouse livers. That mix let them place every liver cell type in space.

They found lipid-linked macrophages gathered at the bile ducts. Aligning data across seven species showed shared programs for two macrophage kinds. Local lipid exposure drove one kind to form in fatty regions. The resident kind depended on signals from stellate cells through a conserved route. The atlas gives validated ways to tell liver cells apart.
europmc-pmc8822752:
Yang and co-authors examine targeted therapy for glioma, a common brain tumor. Care today depends on the tumor's molecular type. Circumscribed gliomas often yield to full surgical removal. Diffuse gliomas and glioblastoma are far harder to treat. Glioblastoma care pairs surgery with radiation and temozolomide chemotherapy. Results remain poor, so new targets matter.

The review walks through classic targets such as EGFR and the p53 pathway. It explains why many of those efforts failed. It then turns to immune-based options, from checkpoint drugs to CAR-T cells. The tumor microenvironment gets its own treatment. The authors stress biomarkers that match a drug to a patient. They call for more trials to test these pairings.
europmc-pmc8894452:
Chen, Kang, and Tang explain how the protein HMGB1 leaves the cell and what happens next. Inside the nucleus, HMGB1 tends chromosomes like a chaperone. In the cytoplasm, it can spur the cleanup process autophagy. Once outside, it acts as a danger signal. Extracellular HMGB1 stirs inflammation and immune responses. Its exit is tightly controlled. This minireview focuses on that control.

Chemical edits to the protein help decide its route. Acetylation and phosphorylation are among them. Cell death programs offer passive exits. Apoptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis each release it differently. Active secretion uses its own machinery and signals. The authors map the transporters and pathways involved. They close with drug prospects. Blocking HMGB1 release could treat inflammation and tissue damage.
europmc-pmc8942852:
Suzuki and co-authors probe why Omicron spreads fast yet sickens less, using models, cells, and hamsters. Statistical modeling suggested Omicron outran Delta in several countries. Cell culture tests measured fusion between infected cells. Omicron proved less fusogenic than Delta and the ancestral strain. Its spike protein was cut less efficiently. That cutting step powers cell merging. Hamsters then tested disease in a living host.

In hamsters, Omicron infected lungs less well. It caused milder disease than Delta and the ancestral virus. The authors join the levels into one picture. Rapid growth in people is one trait. Lower fusion and weaker lung harm are others. They can coexist in one variant. The study is a multiscale portrait of Omicron. It warns against judging a variant by spread alone.
europmc-pmc9005552:
Whitaker and co-authors measure lasting COVID-19 symptoms in a huge community study in England. The REACT-2 survey sampled adults across the country. Rounds three to five held 508,707 people. A later round added 97,717 more for a check. The team counted symptoms lasting 12 weeks or more. They also hunted for who faced the highest risk. A learning method grouped people by symptom patterns. The total study took in 606,434 people.

At 12 weeks, 37.7% of infected people in the main rounds still had a symptom. The later round found a lower share. Women faced higher odds of lasting symptoms. Age, obesity, and smoking raised the odds too. Hospital care for the first illness was a strong marker. Poverty and health work also raised risk. One cluster stood out with mostly breathing symptoms. The authors warn that long-term care needs will stay large.
europmc-pmc9117152:
Cao and co-authors set out a general way to design proteins that bind a chosen spot on a target protein. The method starts from the target's three-dimensional shape alone. It first scans a vast range of possible binding modes. It then searches hard near the most promising modes.

The team designed binders for 12 diverse protein targets with unlike shapes and surfaces. All the binders were smaller than 65 amino acids and proved very stable. After lab tuning, they bound their targets at nanomolar to picomolar strength. Crystal structures of five binder-target pairs closely matched the design models. Data from vast design sets also show where the method still falls short. The work opens a route to binders for therapy and diagnosis.
europmc-pmc9223652:
Thangavel and co-authors overview recent insights into harm from fine particulate matter, PM2.5, in humans. These particles are smaller than 2.5 micrometers across. They enter through the lungs, reach the alveoli, and can pass into the bloodstream. Recent data link them to nearly 4 million deaths worldwide each year.

Once inside, the particles stir reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and oxidative stress. That sparks lung inflammation and promotes many illnesses. Heart disease, lung disease, cancers, and preterm births are all tied to exposure. The review describes causal links, toxic effects, and the molecular pathways involved. Readers get a concise account of a global air pollution threat.
europmc-pmc9461252:
Huang, Hong, and Wei review the epithelial-mesenchymal transition and its part in tumor spread. This shift is normal in embryo growth and tissue repair. When it restarts in cancer, cells gain motion and invasion skills. They also gain stem-like traits and drug resistance.

The authors map the control network behind the shift. Transcription factors lead the network. Post-translational control and epigenetic changes add layers. Noncoding RNAs fine tune the process. The shift is dynamic and not a simple on-off state, they stress. Partial states matter in real tumors. Chapters link the process to circulating tumor cells and tumor stemness. The last part weighs therapy plans that aim at the shift. It also lists why chemo and immune therapy struggle against it.
europmc-pmc9500552:
Buchan and co-authors estimate COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness against Delta and Omicron in Ontario, Canada. The study used a test-negative case-control design. It drew on linked provincial health and testing databases. Adults with symptoms who took a PCR test in December 2021 formed the study group.

Two doses held up well against symptomatic Delta infection. Effectiveness ran 89% soon after the second dose and 80% after 240 days or more. Against Omicron, two doses faded fast, from 36% down to 1% by 180 to 239 days. A third dose lifted Omicron protection to 61%. It lifted Delta protection to 97% as well. Severe outcomes stayed better guarded than mild infection. After a third dose, effectiveness against severe outcomes was 95% for Omicron and 99% for Delta.
europmc-pmc9508552:
Badmus and co-authors analyze the lipid pathways behind metabolic associated fatty liver disease. The disease joins fat buildup in the liver with metabolic faults. Obesity and insulin resistance are the usual partners. Heart disease risk climbs with it, they note.

Liver fat balance rests on four flows of lipid traffic. Fatty acids flow in, are made new, are burned, or flow out. When the flows tilt, fat piles up in the liver. Long strain can then spark inflammation and scarring. The review details the molecules that run each flow. Transporters such as CD36 and FABP1 get close study. A therapy part maps drugs onto these paths. Options span diabetes drugs, fat making blockers, and PPAR agonists. Thyroid hormone based drugs are also weighed.
europmc-pmc9542252:
Wilding and co-authors track weight regain after semaglutide withdrawal in the STEP 1 trial extension. The main trial randomized 1961 adults with obesity to weekly semaglutide or placebo. Treatment ran 68 weeks next to lifestyle support. The extension then stopped all treatment and watched for a year.

The extension covered 327 participants from the main trial. By week 68, mean weight loss was 17.3% on semaglutide and 2.0% on placebo. After withdrawal, the semaglutide group regained 11.6 percentage points by week 120. Net loss from the start was then just 5.6%. Heart and metabolic gains also slid back toward baseline. The authors read this as proof that obesity is chronic. Lasting gains need ongoing treatment, they conclude. The subset came from sites in five countries with top recruitment.
europmc-pmc9710552:
Chaumeil and co-authors present GTDB-Tk version 2, a memory friendly update of a genome classification toolkit. The tool assigns taxonomy to bacterial and archaeal genomes. It follows the Genome Taxonomy Database frame for its calls. Growth of the reference tree had pushed its memory needs too high.

The old build needed about 320 GB of memory to run. The bacterial reference tree alone held 62,291 genomes. That load shut out many labs and slowed wider use. The update splits the job into two placement rounds. User genomes first land in a family level tree sketch. They then move into a class level subtree with species picks. Memory needs drop sharply under the new scheme. The authors report next to no loss in call quality. The toolkit is free under an open licence for all users.
europmc-pmc9873552:
Kotani and co-authors assess circulating tumor DNA as a marker after colorectal cancer surgery. More than 30 percent of patients relapse despite standard treatment. Blood tests for tumor DNA may flag risk and guide added chemotherapy. The GALAXY study forms part of the CIRCULATE-Japan program.

The team tracked tumor DNA before and after surgery in 1,039 patients with stage II–IV disease. Median follow-up was 16.74 months. Positive tumor DNA four weeks after surgery carried a hazard ratio of 10.0 for recurrence. It was the strongest prognostic factor in stage II or III disease. Positive patients also gained clear benefit from added chemotherapy. The results support blood-based risk testing after surgery.
falscher-und-wahrer-lapis-philosophorum-:
Unknown hands produced Falscher und wahrer Lapis philosophorum, a German alchemical tract dated 1752. Its long title promises a noble Christian philosopher's priceless instruction. He recounts what befell him in his costly search for the Stone of the Wise. The title claims to prove the stone's reality and its means, under divine aid.

The body text is set in Fraktur, and its scan reads roughly. A middle sample names sulphur, salt, and spirit as one thing in essence. It calls them the three stones of the wise in their books. Sol, Luna, and Mercurius stand for gold, silver, and quicksilver there. Arnoldus de Villa Nova, Geber, and Raymundus Lullius are cited as lights. The tract teaches classic tria prima doctrine in German dress.
five-treatises-of-the-philosophers-stone:
A second text of the five treatises on the philosopher's stone stands here, its authorship left unknown. The copy opens with a French note from a bookseller. It calls the work very rare, uncited by the bibliographers, and escaped even by specialist dealers. The five treatises, the note says, were likely never printed apart before this.

The last treatise, on the names of the stone, is laid by the note to Guillaume Grataroli, the Italian physician and alchemist, his name deformed in print. The sampled body is the same working text as the English edition of 1652. It warns the worker to keep the fire temperate. If the fire is set before the time, the matter is made red too soon, and the work is spoiled. Solution of the body and congelation of the spirit call for a light decoction and forty days of moist putrefaction.
florus-epitome-roman-history-watson-1852:
Lucius Annaeus Florus cast the whole history of Rome as the life of one man, from youth to age, in his Epitome of about 120 CE. John Selby Watson's English version came out in 1852, with a notice on Florus. The short work runs from Romulus to Augustus.

Rome grows through childhood wars in Italy, storms to manhood in the Punic and eastern wars, then turns its strength on itself in civil strife. Florus writes with heat and color, more poet than clerk. His book was read all through the Middle Ages. It gives the quickest bold sketch of Rome's rise that Latin kept.
frus-1861-d152:
On 10 September 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton as part of a matched round of orders. The letter is document 152 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to London and Paris within the same mid September days. The twinned orders kept the two great posts in one harness. For Dayton the note was part of a matched set, proof that France and Britain were handled as one problem. One problem, two capitals: the matched orders kept the wall in Europe even. An even wall in Europe was the aim of nearly every letter Seward sent that year.
frus-1861-d252:
Dated 11 September 1861, a report from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 252 in the President's message volume for 1861. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d52:
On 8 June 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to Charles Francis Adams. It is document 52 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters to one envoy on one day mark a busy desk in Washington. Seward split his points into short papers, each fit for its own file. The pair shows how the Secretary broke a wide front of work into small, clear tasks for his man in London. Two letters in a day also kept each subject apart for the clerks who filed the record.
frus-1862-d152:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 September 1862. The dispatch is Document 152 in the official Foreign Relations volume for that year, the printed record the State Department gave to Congress.

By late September, British ministers were debating whether to step into the American war, and Antietam had just checked the Confederate advance into Maryland. Adams reported from inside that debate. His letters home helped Washington decide how hard to press London, and they remain a prime source on how close Britain came to acting. British backing for the South would have brought Richmond credit, ships, and fresh hope at once.
frus-1862-d252:
A Dayton report dated 12 February 1862 stands as Document 252 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

That week, British and Spanish forces were growing cool toward the joint venture in Mexico, while France pressed on alone. Dayton watched that split from Paris and reported what it might mean. His letter belongs to the early record of a French adventure in Mexico that would trouble American policy for years. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d352:
On 1 January 1862 Henri Mercier wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward, in a letter printed as Document 352 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The catalog title spells the French minister's name Merrier.

A New Year's Day letter between a minister and a secretary of state was often formal, but form itself carried meaning in diplomacy. Mercier began 1862 as France's voice in a capital at war. The year would take him on a famous trip to Richmond and into the middle of the truce debates, and his file starts here. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks.
frus-1862-d452:
On 4 March 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to John Lothrop Motley in Vienna. It is Document 452 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Early March 1862 found the Union advancing in the West and preparing the great campaign in Virginia. Motley's task in Austria was thankless but real: keep a skeptical empire from lending the Confederacy any countenance. Seward's instructions to Vienna mixed war news with firm statements of American rights at sea. Read beside Motley's replies, they show how the Union argued its case even where it expected little warmth. The principle was plain. No court should be left to Confederate agents alone.
frus-1862-d52:
Seward's incoming mail for 25 April 1862 held a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 52 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d552:
On 29 October 1862 Roest van Limburg sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward, the last Dutch ministerial note in the year's printed file. It is Document 552 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The late-October note closes a Washington exchange that began in June with a burst of daily letters and settled into a steady rhythm. Through it, the Netherlands kept its rights on the record and the United States kept a useful friend correctly informed. Paired with Pike's reports from The Hague, the Van Limburg file gives the full circuit of Dutch-American dealing in 1862. It ends quietly, which for both governments was the desired result.
frus-1862-d652:
On 1 August 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Townsend Harris, the American minister in Japan. The letter appears as document 652 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It belongs to the first year of the Civil War, when Seward ran American foreign ties from Washington.

Outward letters like this one told an envoy what his government wanted and what it could not do. Harris, at the far end of a mail route that took months, had to act on such word long after it was sent. The letter is a small, clear look at how orders moved from a war-time capital to a lone post in Japan.
frus-1863p1-d152:
On 10 April 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, and a second letter to him bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 152 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's pairs that spring kept the London brief oiled as the ship fight turned. Each sheet took a head: a claim here, a word of tone there. This letter opens the pair of 10 April. It shows Washington working the file in its set rhythm. It ran ten days behind the news from London and ten days ahead of the talks to come.
frus-1863p1-d252:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 29 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 252 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d352:
On 6 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 352 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d452:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington wrote this official letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 8 April 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d52:
On 30 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to Stephen R. Mallory. Memminger ran the Confederate treasury; Mallory ran its navy office. The letter is document 52 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, in the Confederate group printed there.

Letters between the South's money chief and its navy chief dealt with the cost of the sea war. Ships built abroad ate cash the treasury did not have. This one shows the two men at their desk work in Richmond, weighing bills against a shrinking purse. It is a home-office piece among letters to Europe, and it rounds out the group with the view from inside.
frus-1863p1-d552:
On 6 June 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d652:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent an official note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 30 October 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.
