That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d152: On November 21, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill, the day before the Cairo Conference opened. The letter is Document 152 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Last letters before a meeting tend to fix times and tempers, though this record names no topic. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, at the very threshold of the conference chapters, where the volume's long correspondence at last becomes a meeting.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d252:
Ambassador Averell Harriman wrote a secret memorandum at Cairo on 23 November 1943 recording a talk with Soviet official Andrey Vyshinsky. While waiting to see the President, Harriman had sounded him out, at Harry Hopkins' request, on Soviet views of several Mediterranean problems.

On Lebanon, Harriman said bluntly that America could not let the French Committee wreck world trust in its pledges of freedom, and Vyshinsky answered that his government could hold no other view. On Italy's king, Vyshinsky kept an open mind but leaned against keeping him, saying any institution blocking the Moscow principles must move aside. Both men agreed that Yugoslav leader Mihailović had been not merely useless in the war, but harmful.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d352:
Steve Early, the President's secretary, sent Harry Hopkins a longer telegram from Washington on 2 December 1943, supplementing his earlier report of that day on the Cairo communiqué's reception. It returns to the Reuters leak that had scooped the official release.

Early reports bitter resentment among American newspapers. He reports formal protests to Minister Bracken and to Ambassador Halifax. He reports a heated debate in the House of Commons that day, where Bracken disclaimed responsibility. The Reuters story had gone out generally some thirty-three hours early, though British censors kept it out of English papers. It gave away nearly the entire Cairo story except the communiqué's text. Washington reporters, Early says, blame the British, not the Americans, and kept their own correspondents' fuller accounts unpublished until the release hour.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d452: At number 452 the Cairo-Tehran volume pauses for an editorial note. The Foreign Relations series relies on such notes to bridge its documents. Editors explain background, identify people, and note where related records sit. That guidance helps inside a dense summit record. In November and December 1943, Allied leaders met in Cairo and Tehran. Their talks set strategy against Germany and Japan. The note serves readers working through those talks.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d52: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 22, 1943, while Hull, Eden, and Molotov were deep in their Moscow sessions. His message is Document 52 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister followed the Moscow talks with care, since their outcome shaped the Tehran agenda. The catalog record gives the date and the two names only. The letter's text in the Foreign Relations volume holds its business.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d552:
Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek sent a secret message to President Roosevelt on February 3, 1944. Chiang led China's war against Japan from Chungking and had met Roosevelt at Cairo the previous November. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

China's position had weakened since Cairo: promised operations in Burma had been scaled back, and Chungking felt its claims slipping behind Europe's. A secret Chiang message carried that pressure directly to the President. For readers, it is the voice of the alliance's fourth power at a low moment, insisting that the Pacific war and China's survival stay near the top of Washington's agenda.
frus-1944-quebec-d152:
The Combined Intelligence Committee reported on September 9, 1944, on the prospects of a German collapse or surrender. The estimate, current as of September 8, reviewed the fronts, bombing damage, and German manpower losses. It then forecast the form the end would take and the date by which organized resistance would stop.

The committee judged that no German recovery was now possible, yet the Nazi government was unlikely to surrender and party control remained strong. Collapse would probably come as piecemeal surrenders by field commanders. Organized resistance under the German High Command, it concluded, was unlikely to continue beyond December 1, 1944, and might end even sooner. A long appendix supports the judgment front by front.
frus-1944-quebec-d252:
Stettinius supplemented his voting report on September 15, 1944, by sending Roosevelt the exact text of the compromise formula three governments were studying. The size of the majority was left blank in the draft: the Russians wanted 51 percent, the British two-thirds. Everything else in the Dumbarton Oaks voting dispute turned on the formula's distinctions.

Enforcement action, regional arrangements, disarmament, and admissions would all require a majority including the permanent members' concurring votes. For pacific settlement of disputes, however, the votes of members party to the dispute would be excluded, even permanent members. Stettinius called adoption a substantial concession to the Soviet view, justifying an American push for the two-thirds majority.
frus-1944-quebec-d52:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on September 3, 1944, as Brussels fell to the advancing Allies. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

The speed of the advance that week raised hopes the war might end in 1944, and the leaders' letters carried that excitement alongside their preparations for Quebec. Roosevelt wrote to a partner then on the ocean, coming to meet him in Canada. For readers, the message catches the alliance at a moment of high confidence, nine days before its leaders sat down to plan the end.
frus-1945-50-intel-d152:
President Truman addressed a memorandum to Secretary of War Patterson on 16 May 1946. Readers meet it as document 152 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d252:
On 9 December 1947, the Executive Secretary (Souers) sent a memorandum to the Members of the National Security Council. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 252, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The ink on the National Security Act was barely dry, and both the CIA and the Council were finding their feet.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d352:
A memorandum from the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination (Wisner) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 13 September 1948. Readers meet it as document 352 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Reform of the CIA was in the air, with the Dulles survey under way and each agency guarding its own role.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d52:
Minutes of the 171st meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 29 November 1945, two days after the 170th. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Three committee meetings in ten days close the State Department's November. The minutes record the department settling its line as the White House plan took final shape. Readers can use the run of minutes, 168th through 171st, as a frame for the month. Papers came in, the committee chewed them, and the department's position hardened. Such records are dry by design. Their value is precision about what was decided, and when, inside one of the contest's main camps.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d152:
Churchill's speech in the Commons on Poland put Washington on the spot, and Stettinius reported the damage on 15 December 1944. His top secret memorandum to the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Churchill had stressed his agreement with the Soviet frontier proposals.

Worse, the prime minister seemed to imply that a settlement was hard because the United States had not clearly stated its attitude. Stettinius says he has declined to comment, having seen only the early press reports. He then reminds the President of the letter sent to Mikolajczyk on 17 November, which Churchill saw before Harriman delivered it. Its points, summed up again here, were the American position all along.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d252:
Pacific plans could be shared with Churchill, Roosevelt ruled on 11 October 1944. These excerpts from his telegram number 83 to Harriman are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. They settle who may see what in Moscow, and who commands in the Far East.

General Deane, the President writes, holds all the information on American plans that is available. He has given it, or will give it, to the Soviet staff. Unless Deane thinks it unwise just now, Harriman may pass the same material to Churchill. The Pacific campaign will remain under American command, Roosevelt states. Churchill may tell the Soviets that the British fleet and British land and air forces will take part where their services tell most against Japan.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d352:
The world security body and Poland shared the plenary table at Yalta on February 6, 1945, in Bohlen's minutes. Stettinius first reported the foreign ministers' work: the word "dismemberment" would go into Article 12 of the surrender terms. Molotov had dropped extra phrases he had wanted added.

More time was needed, Stettinius said, on reparations and on how a French zone would relate to the control commission. Churchill then began to speak as the record breaks off. The minutes show the conference working two tracks at once — building a peace body while deciding how to carve up the enemy's state.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d452:
Agreement on Poland, with two points outstanding, is Eden's news in Matthews's minutes of February 10, 1945. The meeting opened late, delayed by a private talk between Churchill and Stalin. Roosevelt asked Eden to report the foreign secretaries' sessions of the night before and that morning. Eden read the Polish formula, which was agreed after debate on wording.

Churchill then raised a gap: the formula said nothing about frontiers. The world at large would ask about them, he warned. All three were agreed on the eastern frontier, he said, and in principle on the western. Only the exact line, and how much to say, remained. Matthews catches the settlement's soft spot.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d52: Admiral William Leahy, the president's chief of staff, wrote to Roosevelt on 12 January 1945. His message is document 52 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Leahy sat at the center of military planning in Washington, so a note from him in departure month ties the summit record to the armed services preparing it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d152:
Acting Secretary Grew sent Truman the State Department's comments on the British agenda on June 14, 1945. His memorandum, with a long attachment, is document 152 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew had offered the comments when he delivered Churchill's list on May 30.

Grew finds the British subjects sound and urgent, but their form unfortunate. Churchill's list reads largely like a bill of complaints against the Soviet government, he warns. That is hardly the right approach to the meeting. And Churchill would surely want it reworded before Stalin saw it. Some problems may settle before the summit anyway. Grew lists the briefing books now in preparation. They cover American questions to raise and policy papers on every British topic. They also cover papers on points Stalin might raise, and a full set of maps.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d252:
A briefing paper argued for joint action on Korea's interim rule, dated July 4, 1945. The paper is document 252 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It addresses what should follow Japan's defeat in Korea, a Japanese colony since 1910.

Joint action is important and necessary, the paper holds, because China and Russia border Korea and have long-standing interests there, and because the Cairo Declaration promised Korean independence in due course. Naming any single power as trustee would be extremely hard and might cause serious international consequences. The State Department therefore recommends some form of interim international supervisory administration or trusteeship, with the United States, Britain, Russia, and China all taking part. An appendix lists the advantages of preparing Koreans for self-rule under such a body.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d352:
Exports from Germany before any reparations deal are covered in an extract from the briefing book paper on policy toward Germany. Each occupying power, it notes, may need to supply countries in its care with German goods at once. Relief and rebuilding cannot always wait for formal reparations agreements to be signed.

Washington therefore wanted two pledges from its partners. Such exports would be limited to goods urgently needed for relief and rebuilding in the freed countries, with stress on railway stock, coal, and textiles. And a complete record would be kept of everything taken out of Germany for this purpose, so early takings could be squared with the final reparations account.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d452:
Greek consent is reported to Secretary Byrnes in Grew's cable from Washington of July 14, 1945. MacVeagh and his British colleague had called on the Greek Prime Minister on July 13. They presented identical notes. America and Britain, the notes said, stood willing to act if Athens agreed. They would invite the Soviet Union and France to join in supervising the Greek elections. The step rested on the Yalta undertakings and the Varkiza Agreement.

The Prime Minister, Grew reports, immediately produced his signed statement: on behalf of the Royal Hellenic Government, I agree. Grew suggests the Secretary may wish, in consultation with the British, to inform the Soviets and express the hope that Moscow will aid in carrying out the Crimea responsibilities.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d52:
Stalin stayed out of the date dispute in a top secret personal message to Churchill on June 5, 1945. It is document 52 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had urged that the Big Three meet earlier than July 15, and Stalin answers from Moscow.

Stalin points out that July 15 was Truman's proposal, and that he had simply agreed to it. Since Churchill and Truman are now writing to each other on the subject, he says, he will make no new proposals of his own about the date. The short note left the decision with Washington and London, and it shows Stalin content to let his two allies argue between themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d552:
State Department staff wrote a top secret briefing paper on Yugoslavia dated July 4, 1945. It is document 552 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The paper comments on the British agenda and urges a firm line with Marshal Tito.

It says Tito's regime ignores the Yalta terms on Yugoslavia. The joint government holds only six men who are not partisans, and just three of them speak freely. The partisan congress acts of 1943 are now treated as a basic law. Free speech, it says, is crushed, and the coming vote is being rigged in advance. The paper wants the three powers to press Tito hard and to act jointly if he goes on as before.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d652:
Acting Secretary Grew gave written orders for the Tangier talks in a secret letter of June 20, 1945. Addressed to Henry Villard, chief of the African Affairs desk, it is document 652 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Villard would lead the U.S. side in the talks.

Grew allows Villard some latitude in bargaining. Any drastic departure from the orders, above all on legal points, must first be referred to Washington. The letter grounds the U.S. role in its new weight in world affairs and its long interest in Morocco. It notes that U.S. military and naval chiefs agree with the State Department here. The United States should take an active part in restoring the Tangier zone and in running it in the interim.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1052:
Britain's delegation presented this note to the conference on August 1, 1945. A file notation says Stalin asked for time to study it. The note recalls a standing pledge. British and American commanders are supplying their Berlin zones with food and coal. The rates are 40,000 tons of food a month and 2,400 tons of coal a day. The pledge runs for thirty days from July 15.

Until a deal sets the Soviet deliveries owed under the reparations agreement, the Control Council should act at once. It should draft a six-month import program for Greater Berlin. The program would cover the food, coal, and fuel needed to lift the whole city's people to an agreed standard. The Soviet government would furnish those amounts as an advance delivery.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1152:
One day after its last paper, the American team tabled another proposal, dated 30 July 1945. Back-to-back papers in the final days show a team racing the clock. The summit would close on 2 August, and every unsettled line was being fought over.

Late proposals traded the last gains and closed the last gaps. Some won their points; others were dropped to save the deal as a whole. This paper is one more American move in that endgame. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it lets readers follow the drafting of the final protocol almost hour by hour.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1252:
A second Hurley message to the President and the Secretary of State bears the date 26 July 1945. Two dispatches in a day from the China post show a file moving fast. The ambassador split his subjects across them as events demanded.

That day the Allied terms to Japan went out from Potsdam. China would feel their effects at once, in its war and in its politics. Hurley's twin reports belong to that charged moment. This one is the day's companion piece, and together the pair shows an envoy working at full stretch on the summit's most crowded day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1352:
Ambassador John Winant cabled the acting secretary of state from London on 18 July 1945. Winant had served in Britain through most of the war and knew its leaders well. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

London's reading of events carried special weight in Washington, and Winant was trusted to give it plainly. His cable arrived as the Potsdam talks got under way, when British views on Germany and the Soviets mattered hour by hour. For readers, the message is a window on the alliance at work. One capital telling another what it sees, in the middle of a summit that would set Europe's shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-152:
The United States delegation issued this memorandum on July 31, 1945, as the conference worked toward its final text. Memoranda on the last day served the closing push. They carried checks, fixes, and last views between the team's offices. The paper entered the second Potsdam volume of the official Foreign Relations series.

A final-day memo shows staff discipline under strain. Writers had no time for polish, so they wrote plain. That plainness helps readers now: the memo states needs and facts without a gloss. It belongs to the inner record of how the American side finished its largest wartime conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-52:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes record the approval of their 197th meeting's conclusions, from July 20, 1945. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Two amendments to the record are set out in the part printed here.

One amendment concerns command in the Southwest Pacific and Southeast Asia. It now records that the British chiefs would seek the agreement of three governments to the new set-up. Those governments are Australia, New Zealand, and the Netherlands. A second amendment quotes General Marshall's condition for accepting the directive. The British chiefs, he said, must be responsible for winning that approval. Those governments had been parties to the original arrangements, so their consent was owed. The chiefs then turned to the long-running debate on basic objectives, strategy, and policies.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d752:
George Kennan, the American chargé in Moscow, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. Document 752 opens the volume's Moscow thread. Kennan was already known for hard, clear views of Soviet aims. With Harriman at Potsdam, Kennan held the embassy. His letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A Kennan dispatch rewards attention. He wrote to be read, in prose that cut through routine. Readers get the view from inside the Soviet capital as the summit opened. The document also shows the odd split of that week: the ambassador bargained with Stalin in Germany while his deputy watched Stalin's capital.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d852:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 17, 1945, the opening day at Potsdam. Document 852 stands among the volume's first-day texts. The American team led with paper from the start. Its drafts framed the talks' early shape. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Opening proposals from the same day can be read as a set. Together they show the breadth of the American agenda. Readers can sort which topics the team pressed first. The document also shows summit craft: table early, table in writing, and make the others react. Potsdam's two weeks of argument grew from first-day texts like this one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d952:
American drafters prepared two rival conference statements in this undated working paper, filed with the July 25, 1945 papers. One draft fits agreement on reparations; the other fits failure. Both were written ahead of the Potsdam outcome, so the delegation could move fast either way.

The agreement draft favors quick deliveries of existing capital equipment to cut Germany's war potential. The Soviet Union would also draw equipment from the Ruhr, while sending food and raw materials west. The failure draft lets each occupying power take interim reparations from its own zone. Both drafts stress shrinking the metals, machinery, and chemical industries, and helping lands ruined by German attack.
gao-gaoreports-b-297452:
SERAPH protested a Coast Guard award for sea threat training in GAO decision B-297452, dated January 12, 2006. The winner was CACI Premiere Technology. The work helps the Guard spot, track, and stop terror threats at sea. The firm said two key staff were marked wrong on past skill. That mark was its lead claim.

GAO denied the protest. The mark on those two staff did the firm no harm. Its bid was not marked down for those two. It was cut for flaws on a new point. The firm did not fight that point. A flaw that did not drive the loss cannot win a protest. Harm is the gate.
gao-gaoreports-b-297552:
Computers Universal protested a purchase order for a vehicle track system in GAO decision B-297552, dated February 14, 2006. The winner was WINTEK IT. The buyer ran schools for Defense families in Korea. The system tracks school vehicles. The firm's quote was marked up in review. A fee rise from a new deal was added to its price.

GAO sustained the protest. The added fee may have been in the quote price in full. The agency did not check with the firm first. Adding a cost with no check skewed the price match. Price marks must rest on checked facts. A guess add-on that lifts a quote past a rival cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-299452:
Rothe Computer Solutions, doing business as Rohmann Joint Venture, protested an Air Force buying path. The work covers visual information services for the Air Force Academy. The Small Business Administration took the need into its 8(a) program. GAO ruled in B-299452 on May 9, 2007.

Placement in that program can need a harm check. Such a check asks if a current small firm would be hurt. The agency judged the services a new requirement. On that call, no harm check was owed. GAO found the new-requirement call fair. The firm had held linked work since 2002, but the slice at issue stood apart. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309752:
Protests of a global Army logistics award were upheld (GAO decision B-309752, dated October 5, 2007). Contingency Management Group, LLC and IAP Worldwide Services, Inc. fought the awards. The Army Sustainment Command sought logistics aid on a global scale. The wins went to three firms under one call for offers. The losers said the scoring was skewed.

GAO found deep flaws in the scoring. One winner's plan rested on facts that clashed with the call's own script. The clash drew no note in the score file. A like plan from a rival drew a demerit. The math on staff mixes lacked firm support. GAO sustained the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-310552:
Singleton Enterprises-GMT Mechanical, A Joint Venture won its protest in GAO decision B-310552, dated January 10, 2008. The Veterans Affairs office sought new main transformers at its Lexington, Kentucky hospital. The call was set aside for firms owned by hurt veteran small owners. The agency tossed the joint bid as unfit on its face. The toss turned on the firm's status claim.

GAO sustained the protest. Status as a fit firm of that class is not the buy agency's call. That call sits with the Small Business Administration alone. The bid's face was not the flaw. The agency used the wrong tool to judge the firm.
gao-gaoreports-b-311452:
Hydro Fitting Manufacturing Corporation lost its protest (GAO decision B-311452, dated July 8, 2008). The Defense Logistics Agency sought valve stem kits for the HMMWV truck fleet. The kits count as a key safety item. A bad kit can leave a tire soft and the truck at risk of a crash. Fit sources must pass set tests to sell the kits.

GAO denied the protest. The firm had its chance to meet the test rules. It chose not to heed them in full. A firm that skips the test path can be kept off the fit list. Safety parts earn strict gates for good cause.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-252:
Clean Air Act, GAO-05-252 of February 28, 2005, reviews the math behind two ways to curb a toxic metal from power plants. Mercury can harm the brains of young children. In January 2004, the Environmental Protection Agency put two caps on the table. One sets a fixed cap for each plant. One lets plants trade credits. A final rule was due in March 2005.

The agency must weigh costs and gains for big rules, and it did so here. Over 680,000 written views came in on the plan. GAO tests if the agency's sums help chiefs choose. It made no sums of its own.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-452:
Medicaid payments to health centers and rural clinics are examined in GAO report GAO-05-452, released on June 17, 2005. A 2000 law set a prospective payment system for Federally Qualified Health Centers and Rural Health Clinics. Rates were to rise with inflation and changes in services offered. States could use a different method only if it paid at least as much. GAO surveyed the states and studied four of them in depth.

State use of the new system raised problems. Some states applied inflation updates and service changes in ways that did not match the law. GAO found too little proof to judge whether rates needed to be rebased or refined. Federal oversight was also weak. Guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services did not ensure that states followed the law in a consistent way. It shows how a payment reform can drift in practice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-552:
Federal computer security under the 2002 security law is graded in GAO report GAO-05-552, dated July 15, 2005. The law, known as FISMA, set duties for agencies, inspectors general, the standards institute, and the budget office. GAO's periodic report to Congress judges how well agency safeguards work in practice. It also rates how far the government has come in carrying out the law as a whole.

Weaknesses run through all 24 major agencies, GAO found. Access controls often fail. Rules for changing software are not always in place. Duties that should be split between staff are often merged. Plans for keeping work going after a failure are thin. Full security programs are rare. These gaps leave data open to tampering, fraud, and disclosure, and operations open to disruption. Progress is real but uneven. Agencies report more required practices in place each year. Watchdogs have done their yearly reviews, and guidance has kept to schedule.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-652:
First responder readiness after the 2001 attacks is reviewed in GAO-05-652, a report of July 11, 2005. The homeland security department has granted $11.3 billion in 4 years to state and local crews. It built three national frames: a response plan, a command system, and a preparedness goal. Plans follow for rating local skills, ranking investments, and shared training. Each faces hard rollout problems.

Most skills serve every hazard: 30 of 36 target capabilities match for terror attacks and disasters alike. The split comes in prevention, which aims only at attacks. Grant rules stress terror, though the gear serves all hazards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-852:
U.S. efforts against Islamic extremism are catalogued in GAO-05-852, issued September 16, 2005. Experts call the spread of extremism the top threat the nation faces. Some sources allege Saudi Arabia has funded that spread. GAO was asked what U.S. agencies do to spot, track, and counter such support. It also asked what has been reported about Saudi and other sources. And it covered steps the Saudi government has taken.

GAO found the spy agencies and Defense focus on spotting and tracking the threat. Their work centers on counterintelligence and force protection. The State Department counters through diplomacy and public outreach. The aid agency runs development programs meant to ease the conditions that feed extremism. A fuller classified account was in preparation, GAO noted. Agency technical comments were folded into the report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-952:
Who serves in the military is profiled in GAO-05-952, a report from September 22, 2005. Heavy operations and recruiting strain have sharpened interest in the force's makeup. Concern runs that some groups bear an unfair share of fighting and dying. GAO compared troops with the civilian workforce. It checked recruiting results and retention for fiscal years 2000, 2002, and 2004. Combat deaths and wounds were also covered.

Since the all-volunteer force began in 1973, troops have grown older and better schooled. Minority, female, spouse, and parent shares have all risen. The force is younger than the civilian workforce. Women hold 16 percent of posts, versus 48 percent of civilian jobs. Hispanic share rose from 5 percent in 1993 to 9 percent in 2004, still below the civilian 11 percent. The department has not fully adopted 1997 race and ethnicity standards, GAO found. That blurs direct comparison for Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-352:
Cleaning up a former nuclear weapons site can teach hard lessons. Dated July 10, 2006, GAO-06-352 studies the cleanup of the Department of Energy's Rocky Flats site. In 2001 the work was late and over cost. By October 2005 the contractor said the job was done far sooner and for less than expected five years before.

GAO asked what drove that early finish. It also checked work still left, total costs, and health and safety proof. The report tests whether the cleanup met the agreed level of protection. It then draws lessons for Energy's other sites. Readers learn what helped at Rocky Flats and what still needed care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-52:
Riders who speak little English rely on transit more, and agencies must reach them. GAO wrote GAO-06-52 on November 2, 2005, about transportation access for people with limited English proficiency. More than 10 million people in the United States speak English not at all or not well. An executive order directs agencies to guide grantees on access. The Transportation Department issued its guidance in 2001. Revised guidance was pending.

GAO reviewed language services that transit agencies and planning groups provided. It weighed the effects and costs of those services. It checked how the department helps and monitors its grantees. Better sharing and oversight of guidance could improve access, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-852:
Moving United States forces around the globe is planned in GAO-06-852, which GAO issued on September 13, 2006. The Defense Department's global posture plan reshapes where forces are based overseas. The changes will cost billions of dollars. They come while the department fights in Iraq and realigns bases at home. GAO examined how fully the department has built its strategy and how it reports progress and costs to Congress.

GAO found that the department stated its posture strategy across four main documents. But those documents did not fully show the traits of an effective national strategy. GAO's past work lists six such traits, from clear goals to measures of results. Without them, execution and success are hard to judge. GAO called for a comprehensive strategy and annual reporting on progress and costs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-152:
Leaking fuel tanks under old gas stations can foul soil and groundwater for years. GAO studied who pays for those cleanups in GAO-07-152, issued February 8, 2007. Tank owners must pay by law, but many rely on state cleanup funds. Those funds work like insurance for owners who cannot pay. GAO surveyed every state on costs, funding, and fund health.

States expected public funds to cover a large share of known leaks, GAO found. Cleanup of about 54,000 of roughly 117,000 known releases would cost about $12 billion in public money. The average cleanup costs about $125,000. State funds took in about $1.4 billion in 2005, mostly from gasoline taxes. Yet only about one-third of states checked yearly that owners kept coverage. GAO gave the environmental agency four steps to tighten oversight. It also flagged weak data behind how federal cleanup funds are split among states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-352:
Washington's close-in airport could squeeze in more flights, but gates, not runways, set the limit. GAO updated its slot study in GAO-07-352, issued February 28, 2007. Reagan National works under takeoff and landing slots. Laws in 2000 and 2003 added 44 slots. Of those, 24 allow flights past the 1,250-mile perimeter. Six western cities gained service. GAO asked how much room remains. It also tracked fares and shares at three area airports.

Some room exists without new slots, GAO found. Seventy-eight current slots sit unused, mostly at off-peak hours. Bigger planes on commuter slots could carry more people. Airlines with the long-haul slots won big shares on those routes. Rival airports felt no clear effect. Dulles traffic grew and its fares fell from 1999 to 2005. Baltimore's airport saw little change. The airports authority disputes the transport department's capacity math.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-52:
Foreign doctors fill gaps in U.S. care through visa waivers, and GAO-07-52, a GAO report from November 30, 2006, counts the flow. Many towns struggle to draw physicians. Doctors who train in the United States on J-1 visas must normally go home for a time. A state or federal agency can waive that rule if the doctor agrees to serve a needy area. In 1996, GAO found the waivers were a major supply line but poorly tracked.

GAO surveyed states and agencies on waivers sought in fiscal years 2003 through 2005. It logged the doctors' fields, work settings, and locations. Waiver doctors now serve more needy areas than the National Health Service Corps places. Yet the health department keeps no full data set on them. GAO told the health secretary to collect and use that data when it marks shortage zones and posts its own doctors.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-652:
Bird flu readiness in U.S. poultry is the subject of GAO-07-652, a GAO report released June 11, 2007. A deadly strain has reached nearly 60 countries in a few years. It has killed millions of birds and more than 170 people. The Department of Agriculture leads planning for outbreaks in U.S. flocks, with state help. Homeland Security coordinates the wider federal reply.

GAO read plans and laws, toured poultry sites, and met officials in five states that had faced outbreaks. It also reviewed 19 state plans. Real steps stand out: stockpiles, drills, and cull plans exist. The seams show in who leads when a case hits, and in how fast birds can be culled and paid for. The report urges the two departments to nail down roles now. A virus will not wait for a turf fight to end.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-752:
Social Security numbers in public records are examined in GAO-07-752, dated June 15, 2007. Property and court records often carry the numbers in full. Record keepers have begun to post such records on the web. That shift makes the numbers far easier to harvest for fraud. In one Ohio case, a ring stole data from a keeper's website. The theft caused over $450,000 in losses. GAO traced how federal records feed numbers to state and local keepers.

Federal agencies supply many records that local offices then make public. Steps at the federal level could cut how many numbers flow out that way. GAO weighed what the federal government can do on its own records. Other risks remain, though. Numbers already sit in old records and in private hands. The report maps where federal action can help most. It frames the balance between open records and fraud risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-252:
Military ties to states and the Guard are probed in GAO report GAO-08-252, dated April 16, 2008. U.S. Northern Command leads homeland defense and civil support. The National Guard Bureau is its formal bridge to the states. State guard leaders know local officials and terrain from years of disaster work. Sound links between them can speed any federal response.

GAO surveyed every state adjutant general and won a full response. It asked how far joint planning, drills, and readiness work have come. Steps to improve coordination are real, the title notes. Gaps remain between the command and the states it would serve in a crisis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-452:
Medicare Part B imaging services are studied in GAO report GAO-08-452, issued June 13, 2008. Imaging is one of the fastest-growing parts of Part B, which covers doctor and outpatient care. GAO read claims data from 2000 through 2006 and asked private health plans how they manage imaging.

Spending on imaging under the physician fee schedule more than doubled over the period, reaching about $14 billion. Advanced scans such as CT and MRI grew far faster than X-rays and ultrasound. The share of imaging done in doctors' offices rose from 58 percent to 64 percent. In-office spending per patient varied almost eight-fold across states, from $62 in Vermont to $472 in Florida. GAO recommended that the Medicare agency weigh added safeguards such as prior approval for scans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-52:
Air Force business system investments are the focus of GAO report GAO-08-52, dated October 31, 2007. Congress in 2004 ordered tiered accountability for defense business systems. GAO scored the Air Force against its own investment management framework, built on the Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996.

The service has set up an investment board and basic project-level structures. It has fully met three of nine key project-level practices. It has met none of the five portfolio-level practices, such as keeping a complete investment portfolio. Policies for picking and re-picking investments, board duties, and joining funding to selection are not fully written down. Officials say new guidance is being drafted. GAO urged the service to define these policies in full. Defense officials noted work under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-852:
Grant money for homeland security flows by risk, not by head count alone. Since 2002 the homeland security department has sent out almost $20 billion for readiness. GAO-08-852, dated June 27, 2008, reviews the risk method behind about $1.7 billion in fiscal year 2007 grants.

The method weighs threat, weakness, and harm in three steps, then checks each bid's worth. For 2008 the map changed: risk was scored for the 100 largest metro areas, as a 2007 law required. GAO calls the overall method sound. Its weak point is the weakness score, which barely varies by place. A better gauge of local weakness is the fix GAO seeks.
goodwin-graeco-egyptian-magic-1852:
Charles Wycliffe Goodwin published the first English rendering of a Greek magical papyrus in 1852. His edition presents papyrus PGM V from the British Museum's Anastasi collection. Greek text, English translation, and notes appear together in the volume.

The papyrus holds a working handbook of spells from Roman Egypt. Love charms, dream-sending rites, and prayers to Egyptian gods fill its columns. Goodwin, an Egyptologist and judge, recognized the text's importance early. His edition opened serious study of ancient magic to English readers. Historians of religion still treat the publication as a landmark. The spells mix Greek and Egyptian traditions freely.
guillaume-clerc-bestiaire-divin-hippeau-:
Guillaume le Clerc, a Norman poet, wrote the Bestiaire divin around 1210. It is a bestiary in French verse, each beast matched with its Christian meaning. Hippeau's edition of 1852 supplies this text of the great thirteenth-century poem.

Guillaume treats lion, unicorn, pelican, and dozens more in rhyming lines. He describes each creature's nature, then draws the lesson for the soul. His verse is graceful, and his morals are aimed at ordinary hearers. The poem stands among the finest of the verse bestiaries. Hippeau's careful edition kept it available to scholars. Together, poem and edition preserve a high point of medieval animal lore.
gulistan-eastwick-1852:
Edward B. Eastwick published his English Gulistan in 1852, the first translation of Saadi's Rose Garden into prose and verse together. Saadi of Shiraz wrote the Gulistan in Persian in 1258, after a lifetime of travel and study. Eastwick adds a life of the author drawn from the Atish Kadah.

Kings, dervishes, schoolboys, and wrestlers pass through eight chapters of tales and maxims. Each short story lands on a line of counsel about mercy, contentment, speech, or power. Saadi mixes prose with verse morals in the Persian manner, and Eastwick follows him. Persians have quoted the Gulistan for seven centuries as their handbook of wisdom. Eastwick's pioneering version opened it to the English world.
hahnemann-lesser-writings-1852:
Samuel Hahnemann wrote far more than the Organon, and The Lesser Writings of 1852 gathers that scattered work in one place. R. E. Dudgeon edited the volume, with notes by Richard Hughes. Essays, letters, and case notes sit side by side, spanning Hahnemann's long career as the founder of homeopathy and its first arguer.

Some pieces argue with critics, while others record single cures or early drug trials. Together they show his ideas forming well before the famous system took shape. Students who know only the Organon find a fuller Hahnemann here: sharper, more restless, and always testing his rules against practice.
hawthorne-blithedale-romance-1852:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Blithedale Romance in 1852, his novel of a utopian farm community. The book is a roman à clef of Brook Farm, where Hawthorne had lived in 1841. It is the first great American novel of utopian community and its discontents in fiction.

Poet Miles Coverdale, the narrator, spies on his fellow reformers from trees and hermitage hides in Blithedale. Hollingsworth, a stern prison reformer, bends the commune to his single driving cause of reforming criminals. Zenobia, proud and passionate, and meek Priscilla fall into a triangle that ends in river death. Coverdale's voyeur gaze makes him the least trusted teller Hawthorne ever built into a tale here. The book asks if reformers love mankind or only their own grand schemes.
hugo-napoleon-the-little-1852:
Victor Hugo wrote this attack on Napoleon the Little, meaning Napoleon the Third. The title page brands him deposed by the wish of law, destroyer of the Second Republic. A Protestant Episcopal clergyman translated it from the sixteenth French edition. The New York issue is dated 1870.

Hugo writes from exile, in a fury of scorn and detail. Police seizures fill some pages: a man named Viguier is chained by the wrists till his hands swell blue. Such scenes build Hugo's case that the empire rests on force. The prose runs from ledger to thunderclap. It remains the great literary indictment of a coup d'état.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-mari-ben-m:
Abba Mari ben Moses ben Joseph, called Don Astruc of Lunel, led the fight against the rationalism of the Maimonists in the Montpellier controversy of 1303-1306. Born at Lunel, he moved to Montpellier. There he found the young dropping rabbinical study for science and thought, and sermons that turned Scripture into allegory. That trend, he held, put faith and the Law at risk.

In letters later printed as "Minḥat Ḳenaot," Abba Mari appealed to Solomon ben Adret of Barcelona, the most powerful rabbi of the time. He asked for a ban on the study of philosophy and on allegory that denied miracles. Ben Adret backed him, and a decree was prepared barring the study of physics and metaphysics before the age of thirty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abomination-352:
Abomination explains English Bible wording for Hebrew terms about things loathed on religious grounds. The chief term, to'ebah, marks the strongest offense. Other terms cover detested things and stale sacrificial flesh.

Examples show the range of the word. Egyptians shunned eating with Hebrews, and shepherds drew scorn. Unclean food, idols, magic, and sexual offenses all earn the label. One lesser term applies to forbidden animals named in Leviticus xi. Moral faults count too: lying lips, pride, false measures, and unjust judges. Even a blemished sacrifice offends. Prophets add that a sacrifice offered without a pure motive is also an abomination.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-isa: Abraham ben Isaac of Granada was a Cabalist of the thirteenth century. He wrote Sefer ha-Berit, a work on the Cabala quoted by Moses Botarel. His Berit Menuhah won high praise from Isaac Luria for its deep comments. Its speech and its use of Simon ben Yohai as speaker look much like the Zohar. He may have had a larger Zohar text than the one now known. A third work, Megalle ha-Ta'alumot, is known from his own mention of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-prochow: Abraham Prochownik, the Powdermaker, is a legendary figure said to have been named prince of Poland in 842. The entry tells the tale as legend, not as settled fact. After Prince Popiel died, the Poles met at Krushwitz and failed to agree on a successor. At last they chose a rule: the first man to enter the city next morning would rule. That man was Abraham. Proclaimed prince, he declined the honor and pressed them to elect the wise Pole Piast, founder of the Piast line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abu-abdallah-mo: Abu Abdallah Mohammed al-Nasir was an Almohade sultan. He ruled Morocco and southern Spain early in the thirteenth century. Under his father, Abu Yusuf Ya'aḳub, Jews had to wear a black gown and a coarse veil. Jews of the Maghreb asked the new sultan to lift that rule. He changed only the color. He ordered them to wear yellow. The entry calls this the start of a marked dress for Jews in the Middle Ages. European lands soon copied the practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acts-of-parliam:
Acts of Parliament relating to the Jews of England lists the laws that set the place of Jews in English life. England's will as a law maker sits in the Statutes of the Realm. Jews were cast out in 1290, before Parliament took its modern form. So few early laws name them. After their return, more laws deal with wedlock and civil bars.

The list runs year by year. A 1694 act taxes Jews who live as man and wife. A 1702 act makes Jews keep their Protestant children. It was repealed in 1846. An act of 1740 opens the American colonies to settlers, Jews among them. In 1753 one act lets Jews be made citizens by Parliament. A year later a new act wipes that act out, after a No Jews outcry. Later acts ease bars in Jamaica and Barbados. Rules on votes and shops close the list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adoption-852:
Adoption, as Roman law knew it, is not found in Bible or Talmud law. Roman adrogatio let a man make a stranger his child in law. Jewish law has no such act. Yet its sages praise the man or woman who raises a child. More so, they praise those who teach a child virtue and fear of God. Such carers should be held as parents, the Talmud says.

Proof texts build the case step by step. Merab bore sons, but Michal raised them, so Scripture calls them hers. Ruth bore a son, but Naomi raised him, so he bears her name. Jacob sired his sons, but Joseph fed them, so they take his name. Moses taught Aaron's sons, so they are set down under Moses' name. Mordecai took Esther as a daughter when her parents died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-b-tahlifa-9: A Babylonian amora of the fourth and fifth centuries, Aha b. Tahlifa was a disciple of Raba. He was a friend of Aha b. Ika and a senior colleague of Rabina II. The entry gives only these ties of teacher, friend, and colleague, with no teaching or incident of his own recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aksenfeld-israe:
Israel Aksenfeld was a Judaeo-German writer, born in Russia in the last quarter of the eighteenth century. He died about 1868. In his first years he lived among the Hasidim. He was a disciple of Nahman of Bratzlav and a companion of Nathan, that teacher's editor. Later he left those circles and settled in Odessa.

By his own study he gained wide knowledge of law, letters, and science. He worked as a notary public and wrote fiction in volume. About twenty works came from him, though only five were printed. His drama of 1862, "The First Jewish Recruit," shows the shock in the Russian ghetto when Jewish military service was first enforced, in 1827. His novel "Das Sterntuchel" attacks the seamy side of Hasidism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-samue: Samuel Alexander was a metaphysician and psychologist. He was born in Sydney on July 6, 1859. He studied at Wesley College and Melbourne University. In 1877 he won a Balliol scholarship. Two years later he took a double first. In 1881 he became a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford. He tutored there, then resigned in 1890 to study psychology at Freiburg. In July 1893 he took the philosophy chair at Owen's College, Manchester. His book "Moral Order and Progress," of 1889, joins evolution with Hegelian ethics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aman-1352: Aman is a name found in the Apocrypha alone. It shows up in the book of Tobit, chapter fourteen. There Aman is called the foe of Achiacharus. The entry warns that the reading is not firm. Other copies give Nadab in that place. Still others give Accab or Adam. A second Aman shows in the added parts of Esther. For that name the entry sends readers to Haman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anaiah-the-lord: Anaiah is a name borne by two men in Nehemiah. The name means the Lord hath answered. The first man stood by Ezra as he read. That scene is told in chapter eight of Nehemiah. In Greek dress his name is Ananias. The second man sealed the pact with Nehemiah. That act is told in chapter ten. The entry holds that the two may be one man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anna-bekorenu-1: Anna Bekorenu is a pizmon, a liturgical poem, for the Eve of Atonement in the Sephardic rite. It fills the place held by Omnam Ken and Ki Hinneh Ka-homer among the Ashkenazim. David Ibn Bekodah wrote the prayerful hymn in the twelfth century. He plainly meant it to be sung back and forth between cantor and congregation. Its old tune comes from Spain and holds an Arab flavor. The entry prints the version sung at Bevis Marks and praises the tune's build and rhythm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apophis-1652:
Apophis is the name of the Egyptian king under whom, some early writers say, Joseph came to Egypt. Syncellus places him in the sixteenth century before the common era. Josephus makes him the second king of the Hyksos dynasty, while Julius Africanus makes him the sixth.

The monuments clear up the clash, the entry says. They show two Hyksos kings of the name, with different royal names, matching the second and sixth places. One of them reigned at least thirty-three years by the monuments, forty-nine by Manetho, down to about 1570 B.C. Yet the entry warns that tying him to Joseph rests on a mistaken Hyksos theory, so the dates built on it cannot be trusted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aretas-in-arama:
Aretas IV was a Nabataean king who reigned from 9 B.C. to the year 40. His full title in the inscriptions runs Aretas, King of the Nabataeans, Friend of his People. As Judea's strongest neighbor, he often took part in its affairs and shaped the fate of its rulers, the entry says.

His surname set him against the usual Friend of the Romans style, and Augustus was slow to recognize him. Yet in the year 4 B.C. he joined Varus's expedition against the Jews with a large army. Later his daughter married Herod Antipas. When Herod put her away for Herodias, hatred and a border quarrel over Gilead brought open war between them, the entry recounts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenaz-1952:
Germany bears the name Ashkenaz across medieval rabbinical writing, and this second entry asks how that usage began. Its root is obscure. Zunz cites the ritual of Amram Gaon, about 850, as perhaps the oldest source, though that work was padded by later hands. Mentions in Yosippon and in Hasdai's letter to the king of the Chazars would carry the sense down to the tenth century.

Firm ground comes later. In the first half of the eleventh century, Hai Gaon answers religious questions sent to him from Ashkenaz, and he plainly means Germany. Rashi, in the second half of that century, speaks of the language of Ashkenaz. From those uses the name settled as the standard Hebrew word for Germany and its Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-astronomy-2052:
Astronomy here means what the Bible and later Jewish books say about the sky. The opening part treats the stars, planets, and fixed stars. The sky itself is a raḳia', a solid plate set in the midst of the waters. It split the waters above from the waters below. The stars were made, not created, from light that already was.

In the Bible's picture the stars are living beings. They march like soldiers, stand before God's throne, and praise him. Later parts of the entry take up the seven heavens and the huge counts of stars in rabbinic speech. One saying gives each of twelve signs of the zodiac armies of stars beyond counting. The Talmud, like all teaching before Copernicus, puts the earth at the center, with the stars moving around it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ba-al-shem-tob-:
Israel b. Eliezer, known as the Ba'al Shem Ṭob, founded the Ḥasidic movement. He was born about 1700 and died at Miedzyboz on May 22, 1760. The entry warns that the few facts of his life come wrapped in legend and miracle tales. Even his birthplace is unsure. His parents were poor and pious, and the community raised him after they died.

As a boy he shunned the schoolroom for the woods. His guardians gave up on making him a rabbi and set him to walk children to school. Later he worked as an arbitrator in Jewish courts, where his honesty and his feel for people won him a rich patron's daughter in marriage. The entry then follows his rise as a teacher. His core idea was cleaving to God: the ideal man, in his words, is himself a revelation, one who sees himself as a showing forth of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baginsky-benno-:
Benno Baginsky was a German doctor born at Ratibor, Prussia, on May 24, 1848. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1870 and served as an army doctor in the Franco-Prussian war. After the war he practiced for a time, then turned wholly to diseases of the ear, nose, and larynx from 1880. In 1884 he became a docent at Berlin in those fields, and in 1897 an honorary professor.

Most of the entry is a list of his papers, which it says won him standing at home and abroad. The topics run from his 1870 thesis on syphilitic disease of limb and skull bones to studies of the inner ear, the cochlea, and vertigo from ear lesions. He also helped with a large encyclopedia of the medical sciences and wrote for many leading journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-banu-kainuka-a-:
Banu Ḳainuḳa'a was a Jewish tribe in north Arabia, apparently the first Jews to settle at Medina. Before Islam it was the strongest of the Jewish tribes of the peninsula. Its men formed a guild of goldsmiths. Their market-place served as the general market of the city until Mohammed laid out his own. The tribe also held two strong castles in the north of Medina.

After Mohammed came to Medina, he tried to win the Jews to Islam. When that failed, he turned to threats and made war first on this tribe. The Jews shut themselves in their fortresses and held out through a siege of fifteen days. Then they surrendered. Mohammed had the men chained and wished them killed, but was persuaded to spare them if they left the town, leaving their goods behind. They settled at Adra'at in the north.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barruchius-baru: Valentinus Barruchius was a Spanish poet who lived probably in the twelfth century and is said to have been a native of Toledo. He wrote in clear and ornate Latin the history of the Count Lyonnais, Palanus, an old romantic legend recounted by early Catalonian chroniclers and found in folk-tales of many countries. In England its most popular form is a Norman ballad of William of Malmesbury. Voltaire used the story in "Artémire" and "Tancrèd." Boaistuan, prefacing his own version of 1596, praises Barruchius' work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bat-sheba-2652:
Bat-Sheba here names a family of printers in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, not the wife of David. The name comes from a woman's name, Bath-sheba. Mattathia Bat-Sheba, who died at Salonica toward the close of 1600, is the first known bearer.

His sons kept the Salonica press going from 1592 to 1605, with backing from patrons in Venice. Their mark was a figure half lion and half eagle, with crowns. The entry links the family to a Damascus book of 1606 and to later printers at Prague. A single book printed at Damascus in 1606 came from the house of Abraham there, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-elim-2752: Beer Elim is a Moabite town named in the lament for Moab, in the eighth verse of the fifteenth chapter of Isaiah. That is nearly all the entry can say of it. It adds one careful guess: the town is probably the same as the Beer met in the desert wanderings, in the sixteenth verse of the twenty-first chapter of Numbers. No site, size, or later history is offered for the place in this very short notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bemoza-e-menuha: Bemoza'e Menuhah is the name of a hymn sung as part of the penitential prayers on the first Sunday of the week before the New Year. A special melody honors it there. Its first verse is also chanted in some German congregations at the closing service of the Day of Atonement. The tune is by no means ancient, the entry says, yet it keeps old traits of Hebrew melody. Like most such hymns, it is woven from Bible phrases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedictions-he:
Benedictions are prayers of thanks and praise, said in the service or on set occasions. Rabbinic tradition credits the Men of the Great Synagogue, the elders of Ezra's time, with fixing their form. Early thanks in the form Blessed be the Lord appear in Genesis, Ruth, Samuel, and the Psalms.

The long entry traces the growth of these prayers in Temple and synagogue use. It lists the eight blessings of the high priest on the Day of Atonement and the blessings set around the Shema. It also sorts blessings by kind, as Maimonides did, and prints many of the set forms in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berenstein-issa: Issachar Baer Berenstein, a Dutch rabbi, was born in Leeuwarden, in Holland, in 1808. He died in The Hague on Dec. 13, 1893. The son of a chief rabbi of Amsterdam, he served as a judge there for ten years after his father's death. In 1848 he became chief rabbi of The Hague and held the post for forty-five years. He built up communal bodies there, among them an orphan home and a Jewish hospital. The state honored him with the Order of the Golden Lion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstorff-chri:
Christian Günther, Count of Bernstorff, was a Danish and Prussian statesman. He was born in Copenhagen on April 3, 1769. He died on March 28, 1835. He entered diplomacy in 1787. He served in Berlin and then Stockholm. From 1797 he led Denmark, first as secretary of state. He then served as prime minister until 1810.

The entry stresses his support for Jewish emancipation. At the Congress of Vienna he urged it for Holstein's Jews. In 1818 he offered help when Lewis Way presented a memorial for the Jews. That year Prussia made him minister of foreign affairs. He held that post until 1832.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blaser-isaac-b-:
Isaac b. Solomon Blaser was a Russian rabbi and educator. He was born in Wilna about 1840. He was Israel Lipkin's foremost pupil. He best expounded Lipkin's moral teachings. About 1864 he became rabbi of St. Petersburg. He held that post for sixteen years. Then he settled in Kovno.

At Kovno he headed the Perushim, men set apart for study. Berlin's Caspar Lachman endowed them richly. Blaser sent emissaries to collect more funds. He also led the Mussar movement of moralists. His book "Peri Yiẓḥaḳ" appeared at Wilna in 1881. Russian Jews knew him as Reb Itzele Peterburger.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bochner-hayyim-:
Hayyim b. Benjamin Ze'eb Bochner was a Cabalist, Talmudist, and grammarian born at Cracow in the first quarter of the seventeenth century. He died at Fürth on Feb. 2, 1684. He sold his share of his father's business to study.

Bochner ran a free rabbinical school in his own house. He served as rabbi at Ebenfurth and Lackenbach, then lived in Vienna till the expulsion of 1670. His chief book, Or Hadash, collects the laws on blessings. He also edited works on Hebrew grammar and prayer. His other works treat grammar, diet, and prayer. One book on diet came out at Cracow in 1669 under another man's name by error.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-braun-solomon-3: Solomon Braun was a French lieutenant of artillery born at Paris in 1868. He died in Togbao, in the Sudan, in 1899. His father, a poor pedler, saw his gift for learning and sacrificed much to school him. Solomon passed the hard entrance test for the Ecole Polytechnique. In 1897 he won leave to join Major Bretonnet's expedition to Lake Tchad. Tuaregs surprised that party and slaughtered every member of it. The entry rests on a note in the Archives Israélites of Feb. 13, 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bruchsal-3752: Bruchsal is a city in the grand duchy of Baden where Jews lived as early as the start of the twelfth century. In 1337 its Jews joined others in paying 700 marks a year to the bishop of Speyer in place of taxes. Many Jews there were martyred at the time of the Black Death, in 1348-49. The community stayed small for centuries, at one or two hundred persons. By 1902 it held about 100 families. The entry names David Friedberg of Mosbach, rabbi there from 1857 to 1871, as its most famous rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burger-theodor-: Theodor Bürger was the pen name of Daniel Pillitz, a rabbi and preacher in Szegedin, Hungary, from 1843 to 1847. Two years into his post he published a book denying the authority of the Talmud. Its theme caused a stir. Despite the pen name, readers traced the book to him at once. He was forced to resign his rabbinate and left his congregation for private life. Before leaving he held memorial services for Archduke Joseph in 1847. In 1849 he published a prayer book for Israelites of both sexes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bush-solomon-38:
Solomon Bush was an American soldier born in Philadelphia, son of Matthias Bush. His father had signed the non-importation agreement of Oct. 25, 1765. Solomon served as an officer in the Pennsylvania militia from 1777 to 1787. On July 5, 1777, he became deputy adjutant general of the state militia.

In September 1777 a skirmish wound in the thigh left him badly hurt. When the British took Philadelphia that December, he became a prisoner and was later paroled. Unable to earn a living, he stayed at his father's home. Pennsylvania promoted him to lieutenant colonel in 1779. In 1785 the council, under Benjamin Franklin, granted him a pension for his services.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-campanton-isaac: Isaac Campanton, son of Jacob, was a Spanish rabbi born in 1360. He died at Penafeel in 1463. He lived through the dark years of Ferran Martinez and Vicente Ferrer, when Talmud study sank among Spanish Jews. Historians still call him a gaon, and one names him the gaon of Castile. His pupils included Samuel al-Valensi and Isaac Aboab. He left a single work, a method guide for teaching the Talmud. It was printed again and again across three centuries. A fresh edition by Isaac Weiss appeared at Vienna in 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carmoly-issacha:
Issachar Bar ben Judah Carmoly, an Alsatian rabbi, was born at Ribeauville on Sept. 15, 1735. He died at Sulz in May 1781. At age ten he could already follow the lectures of Jonathan Eybeschütz. He later studied at Frankfort and at Metz, where Samuel Helman gave him the title of rabbi.

Back home, Carmoly began medical study under Jacob Assur of Nancy. Talmud study drew him away, though he kept a fair grasp of mathematics. Marriage into a banker's family led to a new rabbinate at Sulz, and Carmoly filled it. His printed work was Yam Yissakar, a commentary on the Tosefta to Beẓah, issued at Metz in 1769. Many more works stayed in manuscript. They cover Talmud, law, the calendar, mathematics, and the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catherine-ii-41:
Catherine II, empress of Russia, was born at Stettin on May 2, 1729, and died at St. Petersburg on Nov. 17, 1796. Wife and successor of Peter III, she took the throne on July 9, 1762. Within a week she faced a Senate decree giving Jews free admission to the interior of Russia.

Catherine leaned liberal, but she owed her throne to the Orthodox party. She put off a decision, citing a note by Elizabeth Petrovna: no profit from the enemies of Christ. Jews were left out of her edict of Dec. 15, 1762, which let foreigners settle in Russia. Yet a letter of May 11, 1764, told a governor to let certain foreign merchants live and trade at Riga on equal terms. Their clerks and workmen were to get passports whatever their religion. The merchants named in that letter were Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-charleston-s-c-:
Charleston is the chief city of South Carolina, in the United States, founded in 1670. The colony's charter, drawn up in 1669 by John Locke, granted liberty of conscience to all settlers. It named Jews, heathens, and dissenters in plain words. The earliest record of a Jew at Charleston comes in 1695, when one served as interpreter for the governor.

By 1702 Jews appeared in numbers and voted at a general election. Arrivals from Georgia in 1740-41 swelled the community. The first synagogue, Beth Elohim, was founded in 1750, with Isaac da Costa as its first minister. A Hebrew Benevolent Society also dates from early days. Before 1786 the city held both a Portuguese and a German congregation. Charleston Jews grew rich and won distinction. In the war for independence, many served in the field, several as officers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chorin-franz-43:
Franz Chorin, a Hungarian deputy and grandson of Aaron Chorin, was born at Arad on May 11, 1842. He studied law at Arad, Budapest, and Vienna, then practised in his home city. Elected to the Hungarian Parliament in 1870 for Arad, he stayed a member for twenty-one years in a row.

The entry credits him with the Exchange Law of 1876, wholly his work. He also pushed for years to reshape Hungarian criminal procedure on more liberal English lines. In 1896 he was picked to draft that bill, and it passed. From 1881 he directed a coal-mining company and turned to labor questions. Szatmár made him an honorary citizen in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coffee-4452:
Coffee, a drink made from the berry of Coffea Arabica, likely came first from Abyssinia and entered Arabia in the fifteenth century. It spread through the Islamic world into Europe. Among Egypt's Jews it grew so common that it was called the Jewish drink. London tales credit a Greek in 1652, but Anthony Wood's diary has Jacob, a Jew, selling coffee at Oxford two years sooner.

Dutch growers carried the plant to Java about 1690, Surinam about 1718, and Jamaica in 1728, with Jews active in the trade. Jewish law questions fill the second half: coffee before morning prayer, coffee at Passover and at the Seder, and coffee-house visits on the Sabbath, which were generally barred.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cordovero-gedal: Gedalyah ben Moses Cordovero was a Talmudic scholar who lived at Safed in the sixteenth century. He was a son of the famous cabalist Moses Cordovero. On his mother's side he was a nephew of Solomon Alḳabiẓ. He studied under Solomon Sagis. His work was chiefly editing. He prepared three works of his father for print at Venice. Two carried his own prefaces, in 1585 and 1586. He also edited an anonymous work in 1588. In 1616 he published a glossary of non-Hebrew words in the Bible, with Spanish equivalents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crescas-astruc-: Astruc Don Crescas was a Provençal scholar. He lived probably at Perpignan, in the fourteenth century. The entry is very short and rests on a single manuscript. Samuel, son of Solomon Shalom of Perpignan, consulted Crescas on a point of law. The case was a complicated one about marriage. Both the inquiry and Crescas' answer survive in manuscript. Nothing else is stated here: no dates, no books, and no other rulings. A Bodleian manuscript catalogue is the one source given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-b-jacob-o: David ben Jacob of Szczebrzeszyn was a Polish scholar known only as the author of one commentary. His work explains the Targum Jonathan and Targum Yerushalmi on the Pentateuch, and the Targum Sheni on Esther. The entry calls it really a glossary. It was printed at Prague in 1609 and reprinted there in 1781 and 1789. A reported Prague edition of 1537 would place the author in the first half of the sixteenth century, but Steinschneider denied that such an edition exists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-del-bene-david-:
David Del Bene, also known as Mehabob, was an Italian rabbi born at Mantua in the later sixteenth century. Gifted as a speaker and well schooled in secular learning, he preached as a youth in his home synagogue. His sermons drew crowds, partly because he quoted Italian poets. That style angered strict critics, who pushed to have him excommunicated.

David left the pulpit and turned to rabbinical study under Menahem Azariah of Fano, who had once judged him. He built a strong Talmudic name and was often consulted on hard legal questions. Ferrara then made him its rabbi, a post he held for thirty-six years. He died at Ferrara early in the seventeenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-devenishki-5152: Devenishki is a village in the government of Wilna, Russia, shown here through the census of 1898. It held 1,877 people, of whom 1,283 were Jews. Among the Jews, 277 were artisans. About 66 women and girls earned a living knitting stockings, which were sold in Wilna. About 93 people worked as day-laborers, and the rest were in business. The village had a poorhouse and other charities, plus a Jewish library. Its schools included a free school with 84 pupils.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dodavah-r-v-dod: Dodavah, read in the Revised Version as Dodavahu, meaning loved of God, is named only as a father. His son was Eliezer of Mareshah. The entry tells that Eliezer preached against the alliance of Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah. He read the wreck of Jehoshaphat's ships as God's punishment for that alliance. The entry cites Second Chronicles xx. 37, notes the Septuagint's different form of the name, and suggests it may be a corruption of Dodayahu.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dueren-isaac-be:
Isaac ben Meïr of Dueren was a German rabbi and codifier of the late thirteenth century. He took his name from the town where he lived. Contemporaries ranked him among Germany's leading Talmudic authorities. His Sha'are Dura, on the dietary laws, became the standard code.

Later giants of the law added notes to Sha'are Dura. Israel Isserlein, Solomon Luria, and Isserles are among them. With those notes the book was printed again and again, from Cracow in 1538 onward. Zunz suggests Dueren also wrote Tikkun Shetarot, on the forms of legal documents. That work survives in manuscript at Vienna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eglon-5452: Eglon was a king of Moab who beat the Israelites in war. The entry is four lines long. It says he took the city of palm-trees, likely Jericho. He held Israel under his rule for eighteen years. Then Ehud rose against him and killed him, ending the subjection. The entry gives no reign dates, no capital, and no family. Its whole story is the conquest, the eighteen years, and the assassination by Ehud's hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-ben-per:
Eleazar ben Perata the First was a tanna of the second century. He lived in a time of harsh Roman bans. Circumcision, study of the Law, and feast keeping all drew cruel penalties. He was once arrested and thrown into prison. There he met Hananiah ben Teradion, a fellow prisoner. In the end Hananiah was put to death, and Eleazar was cleared.

The entry gives samples of his teaching in law and homily. One homily warns against the evil tongue. It points to the spies in the desert, who spoke ill of mere trees and stones. If they were punished so hard, he argues, far worse waits for one who slanders a fellow man. On a Sabbath, men hunted by Rome asked if they might flee. Eleazar sent them to the tales of Jacob, Moses, and David. See what they did, he said, in the same straits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esdras-books-of:
Books of Esdras are apocryphal writings ascribed to Ezra, and the entry sorts out their tangled numbering. In the Greek Bible the Greek Ezra stands before Ezra and Nehemiah. Jerome rejected it from the canon, and later counts shift between I, II, and III Esdras. The English Bible calls the Greek book I Esdras. Two Latin versions of it exist, plus Syriac, Ethiopic, and Armenian ones.

Eight of its ten sections copy parts of Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. One section, found nowhere else, tells of three courtiers of Darius debating, with a Jewish youth winning. The entry then treats the Apocalypse of Esdras, built from seven visions. An angel named Uriel answers questions about Israel's suffering. A vision of a mourning woman is explained as Zion, and a restored city appears in her place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezekiel-book-of:
The Book of Ezekiel is among the most original books in Israel's sacred writing, the entry claims. Its marks are a tight plan and a single tone throughout. Two halves match the prophet's two themes: chapters one to twenty-four press repentance and judgment. Chapters twenty-five to forty-eight promise rescue and renewal. A vision by the river Chebar opens the book.

In the first half Ezekiel acts out the siege of Jerusalem in signs. He shows the Temple fouled, and God's glory leaving the city to the flames. False prophets lead the people astray, he charges, and no true prophet could now save them. Jerusalem is a useless vine fit only for burning. Each person is judged for his own sins, not his fathers', the entry stresses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-feilbogen-josep: Joseph Feilbogen was an Austrian rabbi born in 1784 who died at Strassnitz, Moravia, on March 3, 1869. He served in turn at Piesling, Pirnitz, Kanitz, Great Meseritz, and Holleschau. His peers ranked him among Moravia's keenest Talmudists, the entry says, and a great master of pilpul, or sharp legal debate. He wrote many notes on Talmudic treatises. At Great Meseritz he taught Isaac Hirsch Weiss, later author of a famed history of tradition. No birth town is given for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischer-nicolau:
Nicolaus Wolfgang Fischer was a physician and chemist born on Jan. 15, 1782, in Great Meseritz, Moravia. He died at Breslau on Aug. 19, 1850. He studied at five universities and took his doctor's degree at Erfurt in 1806. He settled there to practise medicine the next year. In 1813 he became assistant professor of chemistry at Breslau. A year later he was made professor and head of its chemistry institute.

Fischer held that post until his death. He wrote many chemical papers for learned journals. His books treat mercury drugs, tests for arsenic, and the action of light on silver chloride. Later works cover chemical affinity and galvanic electricity. In 1815 he and his whole family embraced Christianity. He then backed the Christian mission in the Jewish quarter of Breslau.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fould-edouard-m: Edouard Mathurin Fould was a French politician born at Paris on Dec. 18, 1834. He died at Moulins on April 8, 1881. This is one of the shortest entries in its stretch, and it reports only his record at the polls. On June 1, 1863, he was elected deputy for Allier. In that seat he supported the empire. He resigned in 1868. In 1876 he stood again, at Montluçon. There the Republican candidate defeated him. One short source line closes the notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gabriel-ben-jud: Gabriel ben Judah of Vitry was an Italian physician who flourished in the sixteenth century. His name points to Vitry in France, though one scholar reads it as Vittoria in Italy. He lived at Sienna in 1530 and at Castro from 1552 to 1563. He rendered several medical works into Hebrew.
