Shah and four co-authors rank new cancer marks for made-to-fit guard cures in this twenty twenty-three review. Such marks spring from cell code flaws found in one sick folk's tumor. Their odd form makes them prime marks, yet few prove fit to strike.

Inside, gene scans list code flaws, but hand picks must sift the true marks out. The team weighs scan-first hunts gainst full screens of all named marks. A top snag is to find the T-cell locks that fit each mark. Lone-cell tests now read lock-to-mark fits with far more fine grain. Cast tools that guess lock picks close the tour of the field.
pmc-10750052:
Kyuhyun Kim and co-authors review, in a 2023 paper, how carbon dioxide buried deep underground can turn into solid minerals, the most lasting form of storage. Buried gas can also sit in rock pores, dissolve in water, or stay trapped by cap rock, but only minerals lock it away for good. The review covers basalt, sandstone, carbonate, and shale hosts.

Mineral growth depends on rock type, heat, fluid mix, the gas phase, and rival reactions. It can also change a rock's pores, flow paths, and strength, which feeds back on how much gas can be injected and kept safe. The authors close with open questions and study directions for storage design.
pmc-10750352:
Keyong Peng and Jinghua Pan wrote this 2023 editorial introducing a research collection on markers that predict who benefits from cancer immunotherapy. Immunotherapy has transformed cancer care, yet many patients do not respond, and guessing wrong costs time and harm. The collection, a second volume, gathers studies hunting for predictive signals.

One highlighted study scored four proteins in liver cancer tissue and found two that flagged patients likely to gain from checkpoint drugs. Another tracked a blood protein in patients during treatment. The editors argue that tissue-based scoring has the practical edge of fitting routine lab workflows. They frame the volume as a step toward matching each patient to the immune treatment most likely to work.
pmc-10751952:
Altan and a large team report a study from twenty twenty-three on blood signs that may flag harm from immune cancer drugs. Such drugs can trigger the immune system to attack healthy organs. The team asked if self-attacking antibodies in blood before care hint at later harm. They tracked fifty-eight patients with late lung cancer on two immune drugs. Blood was drawn at set times and again when side effects struck.

The team screened blood against one hundred twenty targets for two antibody types. Distinct starting patterns linked to later harm in distinct organs. One antibody linked to lung harm, one to skin harm, and one to liver harm. The authors say these signs merit more study. They could one day flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-10762652:
Ai Fujii and four colleagues report a kidney disease that vanished after a colon cancer was removed, in a case study from twenty twenty-three. Membranous nephropathy is increasingly linked to malignancy when a certain protein, NELL-1, is present. Their patient was an eighty-year-old Japanese woman with nephrotic syndrome. Her kidney biopsy showed an unusual double staining pattern.

Screening then found advanced cancer in her sigmoid colon. After surgical removal of the carcinoma, her kidney disease entered complete remission within about half a year. Five years later she remained in remission without recurrence. Re-examination showed very strong NELL-1 staining in the kidney and tumor tissue. A second marker stained the kidney but not the tumor. The case highlights how autoantibody markers can guide diagnosis and treatment of cancer-linked kidney disease.
pmc-10772652:
Gabriel and five co-authors wrote an invited perspective in twenty twenty-three on ChatGPT and health information in urology. Urology covers the urinary tract and male reproductive organs. They discuss a study that tested ChatGPT 3.5 as a patient information tool in this field.

In that study, eighteen sample patient questions covered benign, cancer, and emergency topics. Three certified urologists scored each answer for accuracy, completeness, and clarity. About seventy-eight percent of answers were judged appropriate, with clarity scoring highest. Yet the reading level was harder than guidelines advise for patient material. The authors note limits, such as few questions and taking only the first answer each time.
pmc-10781652:
Writing as a commentator, Michael Kreissl weighs a study that used a radioactive tracer scan to diagnose and grade prostate cancer. The study scanned one hundred thirty-eight men whose signs pointed to prostate cancer. The tracer binds to a protein found on prostate cells, lighting them up on the scan. Kreissl places the work in a wider shift away from needle biopsies, which can hurt and cause harm.

He notes the scan can show not just where a tumor sits but how aggressive it may be. It can also catch spread or return of disease earlier than standard imaging. The comment weighs what such a virtual biopsy could change in care planning. It also frames the questions the study leaves open.
pmc-10803952:
Bente Vilming and eleven colleagues published a 2023 real-world study of niraparib, a maintenance drug for recurrent ovarian cancer. Patients whose cancer responded to platinum chemotherapy can take niraparib to delay its return. Most trial evidence comes from patients with inherited BRCA mutations; this study covers those without them.

The retrospective cohort included 94 patients with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer and no known germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation, treated through an individual access program in Norway. The main outcome was the time from starting niraparib to the start of the next treatment, a practical measure of benefit. Real-world data of this kind shows how a drug performs outside the strict conditions of trials.
pmc-10823352:
Domenico Della Rocca and a large team compare three ways to treat a common heart rhythm fault in this two thousand twenty-three study. Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation comes in bursts and is often treated by isolating the lung veins. One option, pulsed field ablation, uses electric pulses rather than heat or cold. The team matched patients across centers by their health profiles. They then compared the pulsed system with a freezing balloon and with point-by-point radiofrequency burning.

Matching keeps the comparison fair despite different patient mixes. Outcomes cover how well each method worked and how safe it was. A non-thermal method that kills only heart tissue could spare nearby structures. The study feeds a fast-moving debate in heart rhythm care. Electrophysiologists choosing ablation tools are the readers.
pmc-10830652:
Eduardo Navas and four co-authors present a soft robot gripper for picking small fruit in an article whose text is dated 2023. Harvest work is hard to automate because ripe fruit bruises easily, and a stiff claw can spoil the crop or snag on plants. Soft grippers bend and squeeze gently, which makes them a good fit for this job.

The gripper is printed on a 3D printer from a flexible plastic filament and driven by air pressure. That makes it cheap, compact, easy to copy, and simple to swap out. It is built both for harvesting small and medium fruit in the field and for pick-and-place work after picking, while staying safe around people.
pmc-10845352:
Elizabeth Slaney, Renee Modica, Leandra Woolnough, Dina Kafisheh, Denise Heather Bell-Brunson, and Melissa Elder wrote a case report on a child whose immune system turned dangerously overactive. The head dates the paper to 2023, though the catalog gives 2024. The child had a joint disease of childhood and developed macrophage activation syndrome, a storm in which immune cells attack the body.

Standard steroids and immune drugs usually control this syndrome, but this case resisted them. The team escalated to high-dose anakinra, a newer antibody drug, and a chemotherapy agent, alongside care for an adenovirus infection that may have stoked the crisis. Reports of such resistant cases guide other teams facing the same emergency.
pmc-11045952:
Noorjehan Joosub, Gert Kruger, and Pieter Basson design a service model for brain injury rehabilitation in South Africa, in this 2023 paper. The country sees many acquired brain injuries, yet survivors often get little rehab because services are scarce and acute care takes priority. A model built for rich countries would not fit local limits and cultures.

The authors used program theory to build the model in four linked layers. It weaves together proven frameworks, the realities of the South African setting, the role players the system needs, and evidence based steps for whole person care. The stated aims are quality, access, fit, and efficiency. The paper offers the model as a guide for future research and service planning in similar low resource settings.
pmc-11143552:
Rita Motidost Komleh, Homa Yousefi Khoshsabegheh, and Ali Davoudi Kiakalayeh report a 2023 study of drowning in Iran. Drowning ranks among the top ten causes of death for people aged 1 to 24 worldwide, yet most cases can be prevented. In Iran, children and teenagers face the highest risk.

The team gathered records for the first half of 2020 and 2021 from health centers, forensic offices, hospitals, and rescue services. Cases rose from 977 people in 2020 to 1,081 in 2021, and roughly two thirds died each year. Men and boys made up more than three quarters of cases. June and July were the peak months in both years. The data break down by sex, place, and outcome to guide prevention work.
pmc-11225452:
Makafui C I Akpah and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three assessment of malnutrition in chemotherapy patients in Accra, Ghana. Poor nutrition worsens cancer outcomes, and early diet support is recommended for all patients. How common malnutrition was at the national oncology centre was unmeasured.

About one hundred twenty patients with varied cancers and stages took part. A standard patient-rated nutrition tool scored weight loss, food intake, and symptoms. Only a small share were well nourished, while many were suspected or confirmed malnourished. Scores tied to triage urgency and treatment cycles. The study argues for routine screening at treatment start.
pmc-11250552:
Douglas Mack, writing alone in 2023, argues for standard ladders to reintroduce milk and egg to allergic children. Many children with these allergies can already tolerate the foods when heavily heated. Baking changes the proteins so they provoke less reaction. A ladder then steps the child from baked goods toward plainer forms. Tolerating the heated form is an early sign of outgrowing the allergy. Yet ladders in use vary widely between clinics.

Varied steps and doses make outcomes hard to compare and may risk safety. A shared standard would keep the climb gradual and monitored. The piece is a call for agreed protocols, not a trial. It weighs best practice for dietitians and allergy clinics. Families gain a clearer, safer path to broaden a child's diet. Most children do outgrow these allergies in time.
pmc-1140952:
Saha, Chant, Welham, and co-authors review studies on how common schizophrenia is around the world. Knowing the share of people affected shapes both health service planning and research into causes. Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness, and counts of it vary widely between places and studies.

The team searched in a systematic way for all sound studies, gathered them in one place, and summed up what they found. A careful overall picture helps planners decide how many services and staff are needed. It also gives researchers a firm base for asking why rates differ between groups.
pmc-11532552:
Vijayaragavan and co-authors present, in a 2024 paper, a hybrid deep learning system that reads customer sentiment in online shopping reviews. Knowing whether buyers feel positive, neutral, or negative helps stores lift satisfaction, and automatic reading must handle the tangled wording of real reviews.

Their pipeline cleans the text, turns words into vectors with word2vec, and classifies feeling with a weighted parallel model that merges two classic components. The design is framed for smart city retail platforms, where review streams are huge and constant. The authors report their approach sorts sentiment with the accuracy such services need to track public mood about products.
pmc-11536652:
Zhe Chen and co-authors built a precise lab assay in 2024 for checking the cancer drug tepotinib in rat blood, then used it to test a food contact. Tepotinib treats certain lung cancers, and naringenin, a compound in grapefruit, can interfere with drug metabolism. The team developed an ultra-results liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry method with a related drug as internal standard. Acetonitrile separated the drug from blood proteins before reading.

The assay proved linear across a wide range, from a tenth of a nanogram per milliliter up to five hundred, with an excellent link. Accuracy stayed within a few percent across days, and the finding floor was very low. With the method checked, the research staff dosed rats to test how naringenin changes tepotinib levels. Reliable contact data guide dosing advice for patients who eat grapefruit or take supplements.
pmc-11536852:
Jingjiao Li, Jie Hu, Danni Jin, Haonan Huo, Ning Chen, Jiaqi Lin, and Xueguang Lu wrote a 2024 paper on the fat particles that carry mRNA into cells. Vaccines and gene drugs ride in these particles, and their key ingredient is a fat that can charge up. Small changes to that fat's shape can make or break delivery.

Using one fast chemical reaction, the team made six hundred twenty-three versions of the fat and tested each one. The best had long chains of a set length, a bend in the chain, and a certain head group. Changing the chain or the bend weakened delivery. Converting one bond type in the winners made them work even better in animals. Mixing the best with a known strong fat raised output further, giving makers clear rules for design.
pmc-11541552:
Stefan Steinlechner and Kerrin Witt argue that smelter leftovers are an overlooked metal reserve for Europe, in this 2024 paper. Supply policy leans on mines and scrap, yet slag heaps, dusts, and sludges from aluminum, zinc, copper, and lead works hold real metal value.

Past efforts usually chased one element or dumped the rest into building material, losing the metals for good. The authors lay out the mixed physical, chemical, and metallurgical steps real recovery needs. Deep characterization of each stream comes first, so target elements can be steered out. The paper frames residues as local secondary mines.
pmc-11552452:
Lopez and co-authors survey the body surfaces of wasps, bees, and ants for ideas engineers can steal, in this 2024 paper. These insects carry tools on their skin: grippers, drills, sound makers, scent sensors, and venom injectors. Each solved a hard physical problem long ago.

The review gathers recent biomimetic work drawn from these surfaces and rates what each feature does now. It then maps where the tricks could travel next, from medical devices to robots and field sensors. The authors argue the family's huge diversity is an untapped catalog of surface design, and they outline the most promising paths.
pmc-11556652:
Mohamed Mai, Melinda Witbreuk, Pieter de Witte, and Christiaan van Bergen published a 2024 survey on care for developmental dysplasia of the hip in the Netherlands. In this condition, a baby's hip socket forms too shallow, so the joint can slip out of place. Diagnosis and treatment used to vary widely between hospitals.

Two national guidelines were introduced to give a uniform protocol for children under one year of age. The authors repeated a questionnaire first run in 2011 among pediatric orthopedic surgeons. They asked whether diagnostic methods and treatment pathways had actually changed since the guidelines arrived. Comparing the two surveys shows whether written guidance succeeds in standardizing real clinical practice across a country.
pmc-11573552:
Hailing Qiu and colleagues recorded muscle electrical activity in children after surgery for a neglected elbow fracture pattern in 2024. A Monteggia fracture with a dislocated radial head, when treated late, needs open surgery plus cutting and grafting of the ulna bone. The question was how arm muscles recover afterward, measured with surface electrodes rather than needles.

Function scores after surgery were significantly better than before. One forearm muscle tied to grip strength, though, still showed low electrical activity on the affected side and had not reached the expected recovery in the study window. Readers get both reassurance on overall function and a clear target for rehabilitation follow-up.
pmc-11575052:
Yiping Chen and colleagues build an indicator system promoting physical activity in older adults who notice their own cognitive decline. Their 2024 study uses expert consensus methods to create targets for interventions and policy.

Activity lowers Alzheimer's risk in this group, yet these adults tend to move less than peers. Starting from literature and a systems framework, the team drafted fifty-nine indicators across three levels. Fifteen experts were invited; eleven completed all three consultation rounds in early twenty twenty-four. Consensus settled on three top-level dimensions with nine secondary items and a detailed third level beneath them. Expert authority and agreement statistics supported the final weighted system.
pmc-11577952:
Muharrem Kanar and co-authors compare two ways of measuring the frame settings used to correct bone deformities with smart circular fixators. Getting the assembly numbers into the planning software takes precise radiographs, and poor images mean repeat X-rays and delays. One group of patients had the measurements taken during surgery from fluoroscopy, corrected with neural network software. The other group was measured from radiographs after surgery.

The review covered 84 patients treated from 2013 to 2022. Measuring during surgery lengthened the operation by about 25 minutes on average. In return, those patients needed far fewer radiographs afterward, about 29 against 56. The time until the deformity was fully corrected did not differ significantly between the groups. Radiation dose from fluoroscopy was also similar. The authors argue that in-surgery measurement trades a longer operation for fewer images and quicker, more accurate corrections afterward.
pmc-11580552:
Fang and seven colleagues link a growth factor to a class of immune cells in bowel inflammation in twenty twenty-four. The disease group covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, both long term gut inflammations. The growth factor helps repair blood vessel walls during inflammation. The team measured it and a cell marker in blood and gut tissue from sixty patients and controls.

Both the factor and the marker ran high in active disease, in blood and in colon tissue. Their levels rose and fell together across patients. Together, the two colon measures flagged active disease with fair accuracy. Each also stood as a risk factor on its own in their models. The pair may help doctors judge disease activity.
pmc-11586452:
Yurong Ou and five co-authors study two cell-protection proteins in colorectal cancer in a 2024 paper. One protein guards cells against a form of iron-driven death. The other helps manage a key antioxidant. Both may interact with a signaling protein that often drives tumor growth.

The team examined tissue from 120 patients who had surgery in 2017 and 2018. Staining showed how strongly each protein appeared in tumor samples. High levels of both protective proteins tracked closely with the signaling protein's presence. The authors also linked expression patterns to clinical features and patient survival. Such links could point to new treatment angles that strip tumors of their defenses.
pmc-11587752:
Xuemei Yang and seven co-authors report a large cohort study from 2024 on heart rhythm faults and later health. They followed more than 141,000 adults in the Kailuan study in China. Heart checks with a standard tracing test found two faults: a fast, uneven beat and a block in the heart's signal path.

Over a mean follow-up of more than twelve years, both faults were linked to higher risk. People with the faults had more heart and vessel disease, more heart failure and stroke, and higher death rates than people with no fault. The links were stronger in younger adults. The authors urge steps to prevent such faults.  The study draws on health records, death records, and active follow-up visits to track outcomes.
pmc-11589752:
Shimin Jiao and seven colleagues build an optomechanical MEMS geophone sensitive enough for oil and gas exploration, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Geophones underpin seismic monitoring and resource surveys. Optical measurement offers higher sensitivity in smaller packages than traditional designs. Their sensor uses a tiny Fabry-Perot cavity with a movable mirror.

The device reached a very low noise floor across its working band, close to the thermal limit. Balanced detection canceled common noise from the laser and environment. Bandwidth spanned hundreds of hertz with a useful measurement range for ground motion. A compact packaged version only forty millimeters across was demonstrated. High sensitivity plus robust packaging suit field deployment. The authors see strong potential for exploration and seismic monitoring work.
pmc-11590252:
Mu and coauthors improve neural detection of sheet structures in electron density maps. Many nets have been built to find protein structures in such maps. Standard loss functions suffer when classes are imbalanced. Sheet voxels are far rarer and harder than helix voxels.

Five loss functions were tested in one network design. The data set held 1,355 cropped map and structure pairs. A new loss blends focal and dice terms in one function. That blend gave the best overall detection accuracy. Sheet detection gained the most from the new loss. The method may sharpen protein model building.
pmc-11594852:
Kishimoto, Fujimoto, and Ihara study fever as a predictor in Kawasaki disease, in work from twenty twenty-four. Kawasaki disease is an acute vessel inflammation of childhood. First treatment is immunoglobulin by vein, and response varies.

Records for more than three hundred patients at one institution were reviewed. Children were grouped by whether fever persisted or settled at the end of the first treatment, and at a second time point. The aim was to see if temperature at treatment completion predicts disease severity. A free, instant marker like fever status could help doctors escalate care early for the children who need it.
pmc-11595852:
Angelo Torrente and co-authors ask migraine patients how COVID-19 changed their disease. The infection has been tied to the worsening of pre-existing conditions, and migraine is sensitive to stress and infection alike. The team built a questionnaire asking patients to compare their migraine before and after infection. One hundred and two patients who had been infected at least once took part.

Fifty-four patients reported worse migraine after the infection. Forty-five noticed no change, and three improved. Twenty-one patients had to switch preventive therapy because the old one stopped working. Among those who worsened, the most effective new treatments were monoclonal antibodies against a migraine-related peptide. The authors note the impact varied from person to person. They present the survey as a patient's-eye view of how an infection wave reshaped a neurological condition, with newer drugs offering relief to those hit hardest.
pmc-11599752:
Katherine Harper leads a team on virus changed nuclear bodies in cells. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with paraspeckle like condensates. The nucleus holds many such membrane free bodies.

A herpesvirus drives new, larger forms of these bodies. Their protein mix differs from the normal version. They are required for the virus to copy itself well. The bodies sit next to virus replication centers. They may act as hubs that process viral RNA. Protein trapping into them drives genome instability. That harm is part of the infection story.  The scaffold RNA is named in the text.
pmc-11600752:
Yuan Ding, Ming Cheng, and Chunxiu Gong present two cases of a rare inherited disorder in Chinese children in this 2024 paper, with a review of past cases. Type I sialidosis is caused by a faulty enzyme that breaks down certain sugars. One case was an eleven-year-old girl whose main sign was short stature. The other was a ten-year-old boy who gained weight fast and had failing vision. Genetic tests confirmed the diagnosis in both children.

The team compared their cases with sixty-nine confirmed cases from thirty-one papers. Clinical and electrical test traits were set side by side. The two children show how varied the first signs can be. Short stature as a lead sign is easy to miss as a clue. The review aims to sharpen doctors' eye for this rare disease. Earlier naming can guide family counseling and care.
pmc-11602752:
Ruijie Zeng, Joseph Sung, and Jun Yu present a new suspect in stomach cancer in a 2024 paper. One germ, Helicobacter pylori, is the long established top risk factor. Yet few infected people ever develop the cancer. Erasing that germ also fails to cut risk once early gut changes set in.

The team mapped microbes across stages of stomach disease. A different germ, Streptococcus anginosus, stood out at every stage. It lingered even after the first germ was cleared from the stomach. Lab work showed it can settle in the stomach lining. There it keeps inflammation alive over time. The authors argue this germ helps drive the march toward cancer. It may offer a fresh target for prevention in high risk patients.
pmc-11603252:
Robert Goldstein and co-authors find hidden heart weakness in patients recovering from COVID-19 hospital stays, in this 2024 pilot paper. Routine tests usually look normal after discharge, yet cardiac events stay elevated. Exercise ultrasound may expose what rest tests miss.

Fifteen recovering patients without heart inflammation exercised to breathlessness or fatigue. Their resting measures matched healthy data, bar a faster pulse. At peak effort, pumping strength ran lower and filling pressure markers ran higher than in healthy peers doing the same work. The authors argue stress testing should join follow-up for hospitalized survivors. The authors argue stress testing should join follow-up for hospitalized survivors, at least in larger confirmatory studies.
pmc-11603352:
Antonia Beiersdorfer, Markus Rothermel, and Christian Lohr wrote this 2024 commentary on how the human brain codes smell. Most of what science knows about smell comes from animals, and single-cell data from people have been scarce. The authors discuss a recent Nature study that recorded single neurons in awake human patients.

That study found cells in the smell cortex and the amygdala that answer to specific odors and rate how pleasant they are. Surprisingly, some of the same cells also fired for pictures and words tied to those odors. The commentary explains the known wiring from nose to brain and why such shared coding matters. It suggests the brain stores smells as concepts, not just as sensations.
pmc-11604052:
Khan and Broce present in twenty twenty-four a case of muscle damage caused by a widely used diabetes and heart drug. The drug class helps the kidneys shed sugar and is prescribed for diabetes, heart failure, and kidney disease.

A man in his late forties with diabetes and heart failure started the drug and soon developed muscle pain and weakness. Tests showed a raised muscle enzyme, confirming drug-induced myopathy. Stopping the drug cleared both the symptoms and the enzyme rise. The authors note this harm is not on the drug class's listed side effects, apart from scattered case reports. They urge doctors to keep the rare risk in mind when starting such therapy.
pmc-11605252:
Sushan Pokharel and co-authors report a case of steroid triggered psychosis in a thirteen year old boy with kidney disease, in work from twenty twenty-four. The boy had nephrotic syndrome from a scarring kidney condition and started oral prednisolone. Steroid psychosis is rare in children and counts as a severe side effect.

Three weeks into treatment he grew anxious and fearful and saw a threatening figure in his room. Sleep fell away. Doctors tapered the steroid over six weeks and switched him to another immune drug. Added drugs calmed the psychosis, and he went home after a week. At four weeks the psychosis had cleared and the kidney disease had improved. Close watch of children on steroids is urged.
pmc-11608052:
Rheumatoid arthritis brings joint damage, pain, and bone loss that do not move in lockstep. Qi Liu and co-authors track all three over four weeks in arthritic rats in a 2024 study designed to find the best window for testing new drugs.

Groups of rats were examined week by week after arthritis was induced. Swelling and pain sensitivity were scored by behavior, while CT scans measured joint injury and bone thinning. Muscle pull and squeeze strength added a mechanical readout. Mapping how inflammation, pain, and bone loss rise and diverge tells experimenters when a treatment can fairly prove itself against each symptom. Timing, the authors argue, is half the experiment.
pmc-11608252:
Xianghe Meng and co-authors make a way to print, in three dimensions, with a magnetic field, for soft machines with thin walls and spaces in them. Their 2024 study aims to copy the hollow build of organs, and how they act as they move.

The printer uses magnetic arrays and a solenoid to make a uniform field that can be set. That field sets the way ferromagnetic particles point. Patterned ultraviolet light then makes each layer solid, with magnetisation set in code. A plan for support, and a mix of materials tuned for the work, lifted how firm the printing was and how often it worked. Machines that were printed showed peristaltic propulsion and one-way transport of fluid. They also showed pumping in cycles, and shifts in shape as they took fluid in and pushed it out. Hollow ratios hit very high levels.
pmc-11608352:
Lukas Kriesch and Sebastian Losacker published this data paper in 2024. It offers a global data set of patents tied to the bioeconomy, the shift from fossil resources to renewable biological ones. That shift spans farming, chemicals, energy, and more, which makes its progress hard to track.

Patents are a standard gauge of new technology, but no one had sorted them for this theme. The authors used a transformer language model, which reads patent abstracts for meaning, to flag bioeconomy inventions. A topic study then grouped the flagged patents into clear technology fields. The data set can be joined to other patent records, adding inventor, firm, and place details. The authors aim it at policy makers and researchers who chart how the bio-based transition is actually moving.
pmc-11609452:
Wu and co-authors weigh eye care by video against in-person visits inside a large California health system after the first pandemic wave. The study covered more than 174,000 patients seen between late 2020 and mid 2021. The main question was how often a first visit, remote or not, led to a follow-up visit in person.

Twenty-seven percent of video patients needed a later in-person visit, against thirteen percent of those first seen in person. Video care carried more than double the risk of a return visit. Yet chart review found remote diagnoses right 93 percent of the time, and most video patients never needed more. Use patterns differed by sex, race, language, and age, with the youngest and oldest patients using video least. The authors conclude telemedicine handled most eye needs well and deserves a lasting place in eye care.
pmc-11610152:
Aishwarya Raj and six co-authors watch brain support cells, astrocytes, turn from protectors into promoters of Parkinson's style damage when overwhelmed by the disease protein, in this 2024 study. The protein, alpha-synuclein, spreads between cells, and astrocytes are first responders that swallow it. The team fed rat and human stem cell astrocytes both loose and clumped forms of the protein.

Early on, the cells coped: small forms went to the proteasome shredder, clumps to enzymes and self digestion, and nearby dopamine neurons stayed healthy. Prolonged exposure broke all three disposal routes. The stressed astrocytes then leaked material that collapsed neuron branches and hurt survival. The authors map which disposal path handles which protein form, and where the system fails, as a guide for therapies that support the cleaners.
pmc-11610352:
Yu Fang and co-authors study how blocking an iron export protein stalls bone-forming cells, in a cell study from 2024. The protein, SLC40A1, is the cell's main gate for sending iron out. Too much iron inside a cell can drive oxidative harm, so the gate's role in bone growth was worth testing.

In mouse bone precursor cells, silencing the gene trapped iron inside and raised markers of oxidative stress. Bone formation signs, from enzyme stains to mineral deposits, all fell. Boosting the gene did the reverse. Two blockers, one against iron-driven cell death and one against a stress pathway switch, each undid much of the harm. The authors trace the chain from iron buildup to a stress pathway named PERK/ATF4/CHOP.
pmc-11612052:
Liria Yamamoto-Rodríguez and a large team test a scan tool that measures the choroid in a long-term eye disease. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The disease, called VKH for short, swells the back of the eye in phases. Its course is most often judged by eye, with dye tests and scans read in a rough way.

Their tool reads thickness on its own from a swept-source scan, over three years of care. When the layer thins, sight tends to gain with treatment. When it thickens, sight drops and a relapse is at hand. The scan catches some silent relapses that sight tests miss, and dye tests back those finds. The tool may cut the need for dye tests.
pmc-11615252:
Muhammad Bangash and five colleagues report a case of a woman hit by three respiratory viruses at once, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The thirty-four-year-old came to the emergency room with fever, nausea, vomiting, and loose stools after a suspected bad meal. Tests found COVID-19, a parainfluenza virus, and an enterovirus or rhinovirus together. She then grew short of breath, her blood pressure dropped, and sepsis set in.

Scans showed fluid-filled bowel loops, pointing to gut infection or swelling. Antibiotics were started, but blood cultures came back clean and she slowly improved with basic support care. A steroid course helped her breathing, and she went home in stable shape. The case shows how hard care becomes when several viruses strike together.
pmc-11617052:
Prasan Shankar and co-authors present three cases of liver cirrhosis, at the stage where the liver fails to keep up, treated with Ayurvedic and integrative care. Cirrhosis is late-stage scarring; standard care can treat causes, but long-term reversal is still an open question. In Ayurvedic terms, liver disease falls under the heads Kamala and Udara. The three patients were treated at an Ayurveda hospital with herbal drugs and outside therapies.

Care included Panchakarma, a detox and renewal protocol, plus a diet with salt and fluid limits. Patients were checked at intervals with standard tools. All three felt better and lived better. Abdominal pain, ankle swelling, and fatigue all eased. Liver blood tests improved by a clear margin. Three cases cannot prove a cure. But it sets out a full traditional regimen in a form others can judge and repeat.
pmc-11618752:
Qi Ye and a large team of co-authors found the switch that ships a DNA guard out of the nucleus. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with 53BP1, a protein that steers how double strand breaks heal. A partner, TIRR, holds it back. How that pair is ruled when damage hits was not known. The team shows TIRR is sent to the cell's outer zone and worn down after damage.

A tag at one lysine by the enzyme DTX3L is the key step. That tag drives the export and sets which heal path runs. It also sets how keen tumors are to PARP block drugs. The tag enzyme runs high in prostate cancers. Readers get a fresh drug lever in DNA care.
pmc-11623452:
Hong Lin and seven co-authors explore whether eating more thiamine links to lower diabetes risk in a 2024 study. Thiamine is a B vitamin, and earlier work on its relation to type 2 diabetes conflicted. The team analyzed a national United States survey from 2007 to 2020, covering over fifteen thousand adults aged forty five and older.

After adjusting for many possible confounders, higher dietary thiamine intake tracked with lower odds of diabetes. Each unit rise in the transformed intake measure came with about fourteen percent lower risk. The pattern held across subgroups split by age, sex, race, smoking, drinking, blood pressure, body size, and heart disease. The authors caution that a one time survey cannot prove cause.
pmc-11626052:
Rania El-Tanbouly and co-authors published this study in 2024. It works with Catharanthus roseus, the Madagascar periwinkle, a plant that makes prized cancer and blood pressure drugs. Breeding new plant lines uses a soil bacterium to insert genes, but results vary with the bacterial strain. The team compared three strains carrying a marker gene, inserted by syringe into plant tissue. They then checked the changed plants at the molecular level.

One strain, GV3101, changed the most plants, at about sixty-one percent. Yet its cuttings regrew the worst, at ten percent. Another strain changed fewer plants but regrew them well. Marker gene activity ran highest in the GV3101 plants. DNA fingerprint checks showed wide variation among the new lines. The authors suggest picking the strain to match the goal: change rate or regrowth.
pmc-11626252:
Jen-Te Hsu, Ju-Feng Hsiao, See-Khong Chin, Yu-Cheng Hsu, and Meng-Huan Lei study a heart tracing pattern that flags danger in stress cardiomyopathy. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. In this condition, often called Takotsubo, the heart weakens suddenly, and dangerous fast rhythms sometimes strike in hospital.

Fifty-five patients meeting set criteria were split by whether their tracing showed the critical convex pattern. Fast rhythm attacks hit the pattern group far more often than the others. Hospital death was also more common in that group. Combined, rhythm attack or death split the groups sharply. Multi-factor analysis kept the pattern as an independent warning sign. A quick tracing check at admission could mark who needs the closest monitoring.
pmc-11626452:
Abel Walekhwa and colleagues run a mock anthrax outbreak in a rural Ugandan district and grade the response, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Anthrax, a bacterial disease of animals that can spill into people, is a standing risk in the Namisindwa district. The team paired the drill with interviews of key officials and workers, read through a model of what drives behavior.

Much was in place: staff knew the disease and the response steps, guidelines existed, and communication channels worked. The gaps were plain too. Borders leak unregulated animal trade, protective gear was short, and there was no money for surveillance or response drives. The verdict was partial readiness: strong people, thin purse. The authors urge regular drills of this kind, livestock vaccination, and funding that matches the plans on paper. Then the next real outbreak would meet a district ready in fact, not just in form.
pmc-11628252:
Peng Wang and colleagues published a 2024 review comparing steroid drugs for severe pneumonia. Steroids can calm the lung inflammation that kills patients. Several steroid types are used in hospitals. Guidelines do not say which works best. The team compared them through a network analysis.

Trials of different steroids were linked statistically. Death within a month was the main outcome. Need for breathing machines also counted. Safety checks covered bleeding and new infections. The network method ranks drugs never tested head-to-head. Hospitals gain a clearer basis for choosing. Severe pneumonia leaves little room for guesswork in intensive care.
pmc-11629452:
Youchao Xiao and co-authors study how fluid from a brain tumour type drives obesity through leptin resistance, in work published in 2024. Craniopharyngioma patients often gain severe weight, and their cyst fluid is rich in inflammatory signals. The team injected cyst fluid, or one key signal from it called CXCL1, into rat brains without damaging the appetite centre.

Treated rats gained weight and body fat measures, stored more liver fat, and showed worse blood sugar and lipid profiles. Their leptin levels rose, yet injected leptin stopped working: a classic resistance pattern. A known inflammatory pathway switched on and raised a suppressor protein that blocks leptin signalling. A salicylate drug preserved leptin sensitivity in cell tests. The authors identify a targetable mechanism for this tumour's obesity.
pmc-11629752:
Ardiana Nurrohman and co-authors use computer simulation, in a 2024 study, to learn why a double change in a flu virus protein makes the drug oseltamivir fail. The drug blocks neuraminidase, a protein the virus needs to spread. One known change weakens the drug greatly, and a second change weakens it far more.

The team simulated the normal protein, each single change, and the double change, then tracked shape, flexibility, and binding strength. Their energy results matched lab data. In the double mutant, a key contact with the drug faded and a stabilizing bridge broke apart. The detail helps explain strong resistance and may guide better drug design.
pmc-11631852:
Qi Zhang and co-authors grow stealth killer cells from stem cells to hunt B-cell blood cancers, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The cells carry a built sensor for a B-cell mark and edits that hide them from host attack. A missing tag gene plus a calm-down tag do the hiding.

The grown cells bore the usual killer gear and poured out attack signals when they met tumor cells. Mixed with foreign immune cells, they dodged T cell attack and quieted rival killers. They wiped out marked cancer lines and fresh patient cells in dishes. Grafted animals showed strong tumor control too. Readers get a shelf-ready cell therapy sketch.
pmc-11631952:
Diksha Sharma and nine colleagues show that clay minerals help carry phytoplankton carbon out of the surface ocean, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Mineral dust landing on the sea boosts carbon sequestration somehow. The interaction with microbes was poorly understood. Experiments used Gulf of Maine bloom seawater sprayed with clay.

Every clay treatment raised sticky polymer particle levels tenfold. Those particles glue cells and clay into sinking flocs. Dinoflagellates fell sharply while diatoms rose. Genetic checks confirmed dinoflagellates were removed inside the flocs. As much as half the phytoplankton carbon was stripped out. The authors trace a pathway from dust to deep carbon export. It gives the biological carbon pump a mineral assist.
pmc-11634352:
Américo Gusmão Amorim, Olival Cirilo Lucena da Fonseca, Raimundo Hugo Matias Furtado, and a wider team wrote this case report, published in 2024. It describes blocking two veins of the liver's right side at once, to grow the left side before a major cancer operation.

Big liver resections fail when too little liver would remain. Plugging the veins that feed the doomed lobe pushes the other lobe to grow. In this patient, imaging showed too little tissue would be left after removing an intrahepatic bile duct cancer. Doctors blocked the right portal vein and the right hepatic vein in one strategy. The patient recovered without liver failure. Three years after surgery, the cancer had not returned. The authors say knowing this combined block can widen which tumors count as removable and cut complications.
pmc-11636252:
Spent car batteries will soon pile up as electric cars spread, and rules for their reuse lag behind the tech. Min Liu and seven co-authors bridge the two in 2024, weighing the laws of Europe and China against the ways labs now reclaim old cells. Europe will soon force set shares of reused lithium, nickel, and cobalt in new batteries. China pushes take-back and second-life use of spent packs.

Three reclaim routes get a close look: water-based, heat-based, and direct repair. Most past studies lean on models or lab data, since plant-scale facts are scarce. The team also unpack the carbon math that Europe's rules apply to each route. Their point is plain: good tech alone will not close the loop. Rules must be built to match what plants can truly do.
pmc-11637452:
Juliana Almeida Oliveira and three co-authors review a drug for postpartum depression in a 2024 paper. The drug, zuranolone, is the first pill approved for this condition. It offers care outside a hospital, which matters for new mothers. The team asked how well it works and how safe it is.

The authors searched three large databases in September 2023. They kept only trials that compared the drug with a placebo. Two trials with 346 women met the rules for the review. The drug raised response and remission rates at several time points. It also cut the need for other antidepressant doses. Sleepiness was the main added risk and grew with dose. The authors call the drug promising but say safety needs more study.
pmc-11638252:
Weiß, Paelecke, Mussel, and Hein present a study from twenty twenty-four on brain responses to personality-typical faces. People prefer faces matching certain traits, past surveys suggest. Participants rate faces built to look high or low on key traits. They also say how much they would like to interact. Brain signals are recorded during the ratings. Faces seen as outgoing or agreeable draw stronger interaction interest. Faces seen as anxious draw less interest.

Agreeable viewers favor agreeable faces even more strongly. A late brain signal grows with preference for agreeable faces. An early face signal shows no such pattern. The authors stress both viewer and face traits shape social pull.
pmc-11639752:
Xiaoxian Tang and colleagues puff persimmons into chips with hot air and pressure swings, and tune the process by response surface, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Variable-temperature pressure-difference puffing explodes moisture outward, leaving a crisp, porous snack. Four knobs, pressure, holding time, temperature, and drying time, were optimized together.

The winning recipe used about zero point four six megapascals for ten minutes, then ninety-four degrees for ninety-two minutes. It gave chips at three point six percent moisture, with high crispness and a sensory score above ninety. Their pores were cavernous: pore volume beat microwave and vacuum methods by fifty-eight to two hundred thirty-eight percent, and dwarfed vacuum frying most of all. The authors crown pressure-difference puffing the method for airy, high-quality persimmon chips.
pmc-11639852:
Satoshi Mizutani and co-authors describe a demanding pancreas operation in a 2024 paper. Some pancreatic cancers are judged inoperable at first, yet shrink enough with drug therapy to allow surgery. Removing them fully can mean cutting out the celiac axis, a major artery branch, and rebuilding it. The authors lay out the key steps for doing that safely.

Success, they say, rests on a clear front view of the great vessels in the belly during the operation. The rebuilt artery must be short and free of tension so blood keeps flowing. From 2014 to 2024, sixteen such patients had conversion surgery with a major artery removed. Five needed the artery rebuilt. Four of those five had the most advanced local stage. Four fifths had all cancer cleared at the margins. One patient had a serious complication, and none died.
pmc-11640152:
Shenfei Long, Shad Mahfuz, and Xiangshu Piao present a two thousand twenty-four feeding study in pregnant sows and their newborn piglets. The supplement tested was an active form of vitamin D. It was fed from late pregnancy until birth.

Forty sows were split evenly between a normal diet and the supplemented one. Groups were balanced for weight, parity, and back fat. Supplemented mothers produced richer first milk with more protein and fat. Their piglets were born heavier on average. Protein digestion and antioxidant defences also improved. The trial shows late-pregnancy diet can lift both sow and litter outcomes.
pmc-11640452:
Anna-Katharina Meissner and colleagues assess image quality and reliability of artificial intelligence tumour classification using stimulated Raman histology on biobank samples. Their 2024 study asks whether previously frozen tissue works for this rapid optical imaging method.

Twenty-five brain tumour patients provided samples imaged fresh and after thawing from frozen storage. An experienced neuropathologist rated image quality for both versions. Two classification systems predicted the tissue diagnosis from the images. Frozen samples matter because biobanks could supply larger, more varied datasets for training, including rare tumour types underrepresented in current data. No prior data existed on frozen tissue suitability for this analysis, which the study now addresses.
pmc-11640552:
Removing a spinal tumor can leave the back unstable and the wound hard to close, especially after large cancers are cut out. Casey Martinez and co-authors describe spino-plastic surgery in this 2024 paper, a team approach pairing spine surgeons with plastic and reconstructive specialists.

Case reviews show the method restores the spine's working shape using living bone grafts and muscle flaps fed by their own blood supply. Patients gained mobility, hurt less, and saw fewer healing failures like nonunion or infection. The authors present the collaboration as a growing pillar of cancer reconstruction and call for wider study of its techniques.
pmc-11641052:
Karina Zolotareva and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four computer-based study of genetic markers in primary open-angle glaucoma. The disease damages the optic nerve and can end in blindness. The team focused on promoter variants that change how strongly a key protein binds DNA.

They first sorted glaucoma-linked genes by evolutionary age, before and after camera-type eyes appeared. Computer predictions then flagged thousands of candidate variants altering that binding. Such variants could raise or lower gene activity in the eye. Readers get a screened list for later lab testing, plus a view of which glaucoma genes are ancient.
pmc-11641152:
Yan Zeng, Yulong Yin, and Xihong Zhou review how gut microbes and the host talk to each other through tiny packages called extracellular vesicles, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. These sacs carry small gene-control pieces known as microRNAs. The exchange helps keep the gut in balance.

The review gathers what is known about vesicles from food, from gut microbes, and from the host's own cells. It explains how they guard the gut wall, calm immune responses, and steady the microbe mix. It then covers their roles in gut diseases, from diarrhea to bowel inflammation and colon cancer. The authors see the sacs and their cargo as possible tools to prevent, spot, and treat such diseases.
pmc-11641452:
Minali Prasad and a large team of co-authors test whether blocked retinal vessels go with dementia in a study from 2024. The team compared 474 patients with a blocked retinal vein or artery against 948 matched patients without blockage. Odds of dementia were worked out after adjusting for heart, demographic, and eye factors.

Patients with a blocked retinal vein had more than twice the odds of dementia overall, and higher odds of vascular dementia. Both central and branch vein blocks showed the link. Artery blockage showed no such link, and no blockage type linked to Alzheimer's disease. The authors read vein blockage as a warning sign worth noting.
pmc-11641752:
Corneliu Toader and six co-authors wrote this 2024 review of the molecular roots of brain wasting diseases and the newest treatment ideas. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and ALS advance slowly and still lack strong therapies. Behind them sits a web of faults: misfolded proteins, chronic inflammation, failing cell power plants, and gene errors.

The review pulls together what is now known about how those pathways intertwine to erode neurons. It then surveys the most promising ways to intervene. Delivery systems built at the nano scale can ferry drugs past the brain's barrier, a long standing block. Gene and cell based approaches also feature in the outlook.
pmc-11641952:
Chilmon, Kalinowski, and Jackiewicz-Rek test how mineral fillers change air cleaning cement in twenty twenty-four. The cement carries a nano catalyst that breaks down traffic nitrogen oxides in light. Tests mimicked Warsaw's autumn air and light. Swapping part of the binder for fillers was the variable.

More filler meant fewer pores in the surface, and weaker cleaning power. The reaction's product mix also grew less selective as filler rose. Full binder mixes kept the best cleaning traits. The team backs richer binder content for photo active surfaces. City air gains hang on such surface details, they note.
pmc-11642152:
Ilaria Arciero and four colleagues build a three-dimensional printable cell array for modeling breast cancer in the lab, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Breast cancer often spreads to bone in advanced stages. Tissue stiffness and microenvironment remodeling influence progression, but remain poorly understood. Their platform mimics bone-like conditions on a small, tunable scale.

Highly metastatic breast cancer cells were embedded in hydrogel spheres inside the array's cavities. As stiffness increased, the cells trans-differentiated toward bone-like cells. They also produced breast microcalcifications, a clinical hallmark. The array doubled as a drug-testing platform for chemotherapy sensitivity. Drug resistance in the cells decreased over time in the device. The authors offer the array as a reproducible model of the bone metastatic niche.
pmc-11642352:
Alina Khlebnikova, Anna Kirshina, Natalia Zakharova, Roman Ivanov, and Vasiliy Reshetnikov review work on messenger RNA vaccines against germs, in work from 2024. Such vaccines proved their worth against viruses in recent years. Germs, though, are far more complex than viruses, and they hide from the immune system in more ways.

The review covers nine germ species for which these vaccines have been built and tested in animals. For each, it lays out body features and tricks the germ uses to dodge defense. Results from animal tests are weighed, and ways to make the vaccines stronger are debated. The authors call the review one of the first full maps of this young field.
pmc-11643452:
Adam Lubojański and co-authors published a review in 2024 on a mineral nanomaterial used across medicine. The material copies the main mineral of bone and teeth, ground to particles under one hundred nanometers wide. At that size its surface area balloons, which makes it handy both as a rebuilding scaffold and as a carrier for drugs.

The review gathers the latest work on the particle's physical and biological behavior. Uses covered range from regenerative repair of bone to targeted delivery in cancer therapy. The authors stress that the promise is broad but the evidence is still young. Their survey gives researchers a single map of what is known and what needs testing next.
pmc-11643652:
Yan Mo and a team of co-authors build a sensor for a sedative that is being abused in e-cigarette liquids, in two thousand twenty-four. The drug is a hospital anesthetic, and its spread into vaping liquids has raised social concern. Fast, on-site checks are needed to screen suspect samples.

It also cuts through interference from the complex liquid mix. The team present it as a first screen, with standard lab methods used to confirm flagged samples precisely.
pmc-11644152:
Zhou Yan, Jia Guo, and Xi Zou heat-treat 3D-printed stainless steel to see what annealing fixes and what it costs, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Directed energy deposition builds metal parts layer by layer, leaving internal stress and fine cellular structures. Post-build heat treatment is the standard remedy.

Annealing at rising temperatures grew the cells until the cellular structure vanished at the highest range. Strength fell as temperature rose, a trade against stress relief. Separately, laser pulse frequency and duty cycle influenced residual stress, with moderate settings reducing it most. The results map processing choices for printed 316L steel parts. Engineers balancing strength against distortion now have temperature-specific evidence rather than habit.
pmc-11644252:
Endah Kristiani, Tzu-Hao Yu, and Chao-Tung Yang build a live monitoring system for large sport motorcycles. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Mechanical faults and risky riding cause crashes that warning systems could prevent.

Working with professional mechanics, the team chose what to measure and how to mount sensors without harming the bike or breaking Taiwan's rules. A narrowband radio link sends data over long distances with little power. A lean messaging protocol and clear dashboards present the data. The system watches for abnormal behavior and faults in real time. Instant alerts reach the rider through messaging apps. The authors expect fewer failures and safer riding from constant oversight.
pmc-11644652:
Jaehyeok Yun and Jong-Eun Kim test broccoli sprout extract as a shield for skin cells against city dust, in this 2024 paper. Fine particles in polluted air push skin toward aging and inflammation. The team traced the effect to one kinase, p38, a stress switch inside the cell. The extract grabs that switch directly, without fighting for its fuel slot, and turns its volume down. Downstream signals tied to aging and inflammation faded with it. The authors propose the extract as a working ingredient for skin care aimed at pollution damage.
pmc-11644852:
Wojciech Jarmołowski and co-authors hunt for faint ionosphere signals that might track earthquakes over the Aegean Sea, in a 2024 study. The ionosphere is a charged upper layer of air that can react to changes below, a link called lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere coupling. The spectrum of the filtered signals proved rich and varied by instrument type. Only some bands seemed sensitive to seismic activity. Choosing the right bands is a key step before any earthquake link can be claimed. The study offers a careful method for that selection, in a region where strong quakes are a real threat.
pmc-11646952:
Knowing fast whether a germ resists antibiotics can save lives in sepsis care. pmc-11647052:
Farahani and nine co-authors reviewed cell stress in urological cancers in this paper from twenty twenty-four. The endoplasmic reticulum folds proteins and balances calcium inside cells. The authors map targets for new therapies.
pmc-11647852:
Ricardo Soto and Sebastián Godoy automate skin cancer screening with heat cameras, removing the expert hand that earlier versions needed. pmc-11648052:
Vlachou, Johnson, and Hoffman-Censits review aim-drug pairs for spread sac growth. The growth is fierce, with poor odds once it spreads wide. Plat drugs held the front line for scores of years. pmc-11648552:
Xin Xue and co-authors report a 2024 study of oxygen levels and frailty in older patients with sleep apnea. In this condition, breathing stalls through the night and blood oxygen dips. Frailty, a state of weakness and low reserve, is known to track with the condition.

The study drew on 1,006 older patients tested at several centers between 2015 and 2017. Over a median follow-up of 52 months, 275 patients became frail. The authors grouped patients by their mean overnight oxygen level and modeled the risk with flexible curves. The link came out U-shaped: risk was highest at the lowest oxygen levels and rose again at the top. Patients in the lowest group had a frailty risk about 43 percent above the middle groups. pmc-11650452:
Naotaka Kishimoto, Toru Yamamoto, Simon Tran, Takuro Sanuki, and Kenji Seo report, in a 2024 letter, a low-cost way to train dental staff for medical emergencies using phone screens and video links. Emergencies such as fainting, severe allergy, and choking can strike during dental care. Practice on robot patients works but costs a great deal. pmc-11650752:
Chelsea N Miller and Katharine L Stuble report a two thousand twenty-four community-science study of how warm spring days affect flowering stages in woodland herbs. Climate studies stress average warming, yet brief hot spells may compress delicate life stages. Understory herbs flower fast and early.

Volunteers monitored nearly two hundred plants of fourteen species twice weekly across five botanic gardens. Each plant's stage changes were timed against daily temperature departures from thirty-year norms. Warmer-than-usual days related to shorter reproductive stages. Such compression could misalign flowers with pollinators even when average seasonal timing looks unchanged.
pmc-11651552:
Haimin Li and ten colleagues published a virology study in two thousand twenty-four on a circular RNA that fights viral infection. Circular RNAs do many jobs in cells, but their role during infection was mostly unknown. Pseudorabies virus, a herpes-family virus of pigs, served as the model.

pmc-11652052:
Suhong Zhao and co-authors build a scan-based test for breast cancer type in this 2024 study. Some tumors carry low levels of a growth marker called HER2. The network reached fair accuracy at both hospitals in held-out tests. A benefit check suggested the tool could aid real decisions. The authors offer it as support for planning, not a stand-alone test.
pmc-11653552:
Tiziana Bruno and co-authors wrote this 2024 commentary on new molecular leads against multiple myeloma. pmc-11654652:
Jehanzeb and five co-authors compare two screw methods to fix spine breaks at the chest-waist junction, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Both methods use screws through small skin cuts. At six months, the short-span group held its curve a bit better. No screw failures occurred in either group. The team backs the short-span method for single-level breaks.
pmc-11655352:
Nimmo, Kleine, and Morbidelli argue the Moon is older than most rock dates say. Moon rocks give ages from four point three five to four point five one billion years. Which set is right hinges on what each rock date marks. Rock ages may mark a later melt, not the first freeze.

Grain dates spike at that same time, which fits the claim. The first freeze may sit well before that date. Their model joins orbit math with rock facts.
pmc-11655652:
Yulv Zhou and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether a plant compound can boost aspirin's effect against bowel cancer. It also stalled the cell cycle and pushed more cancer cells to die. The team points to one signaling route as the main path, and suggests new aspirin-like drugs built from the plant compound.
pmc-11656052:
Ryan Lewis and co-authors report a 2024 study in rats on breathing muscle control. A toxin model kills breathing motor neurons in a selective way. pmc-11656252:
Junmei Wang and five co-authors use computer theory to design a better catalyst for making ammonia from nitrogen, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. Turning nitrogen gas into ammonia with electricity would be a cleaner route to fertilizer. A molybdenum carbide material shows promise, but it grabs nitrogen weakly, and a rival reaction that makes hydrogen steals the current.

The surface also favors nitrogen over hydrogen, which cuts the rival reaction. Two paths to ammonia were compared, and one clear route won. The work gives design rules for future catalysts.
pmc-11656352:
Alexandre Brolo and Nathan Lindquist introduce a special journal issue marking fifty years of a light-based method for studying surfaces, in a 2024 essay. The story starts in Southampton, where a team wanted to watch chemistry at an electrode in water. To boost their odds, the team roughened a silver electrode to hold more of the test chemical on its surface. The signal came back far stronger than expected, and it changed with the applied voltage. That surprise launched the field of surface-enhanced Raman scattering. The essay notes the effect was not grasped as new physics at the time, and it frames the issue's papers as a look back at the field's growth.
pmc-11656452:
Stefanie Enriquez-Geppert and co-authors reviewed executive functions in pilot performance in a 2024 paper. Flying asks the brain to juggle many tasks in a fast-changing sky. Executive functions, the mind's control suite for focus, switching, and holding back impulses, look central to that juggling.

The review gathered studies that tie each such function to how pilots perform. Which functions forecast flight skill best turned out murky across the evidence. The answer matters for pilot selection, cockpit design, and brain training. Sharper tests could one day make both hiring and skies safer.
pmc-11656652:
Xiaowan Xie and co-authors asked whether patients whose immune treatment caused side effects also fared better against advanced lung cancer, in a 2024 study. The side-effect group answered treatment far more often, with response and disease control rates roughly double the other group's. Their cancer also stayed quiet longer, and they lived longer by the reported medians. Smoking status was the one baseline trait that differed. The authors suggest the side effects may signal a more awakened immune attack on the tumor.
pmc-11656752:

pmc-11657552:
Shuning Zhang, Zhangjie Chen, Meihuan Chen, and Hailong Huang present a 2024 analysis of thalassemia burden across Asia from 1990 to 2021. Cost and spending data joined the health data for a fuller view. The maps can guide screening and care funds to the lands where the burden bites hardest.
pmc-11658252:
Yishan Yan and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on how master's nursing students in China view living wills, the documents that record end-of-life wishes. Students wanted better training and flagged family and cultural hurdles. The study maps what educators should teach first.
pmc-11658352:

pmc-11659752:

pmc-11660652:

pmc-11663852:

pmc-11668552:

pmc-11669552:

pmc-11673652:

pmc-11674252:

pmc-11674952:

pmc-11675052:

pmc-11675252:

pmc-11675652:

pmc-11675752:

pmc-11675852:

pmc-11676252:

pmc-11676452: Dmitri V. Krysko, Irina V. Balalaeva, and Tatiana A. Mishchenko wrote a 2024 review of photodynamic therapy for cancer in a medical journal. pmc-11676552:

pmc-11676652:

pmc-11677652:

pmc-11677752:

pmc-11677852:

pmc-11678452:
