Regression weighs body weight, stem size, and placement error. Scores and complications complete the comparison. The results counsel care when offering short stems to heavier patients.
pmc-11678652:
Chao Xie and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on what makes a plastic paint film keep water out. Such films guard steel and concrete on bridges and ships. The team made five films that differed only in how much thinner was mixed in. They then soaked the films and tracked how water moved inside and how strength held up.

Fine tools let them weigh the tiny open spaces in each film and spot water-loving groups in its chemistry. More thinner first shrank those spaces, then grew them again past a point. Water resistance rose and fell with the same curve. The mixes with a fifth and a quarter thinner did best of the five. They let in the least water and kept the most strength after soaking. Two scoring methods ranked them the same. The work can guide film design on real projects.
pmc-11679052:
Adnan Elahi Khan Khalil, Jesus Arturo Perez-Diaz, Jose Antonio Cantoral-Ceballos, and Javier Antelis wrote a 2024 paper on using brain waves as an ID check. Passwords can be stolen, but a person's brain response is hard to copy. Their system uses the P300 signal, a brain wave that fires when a person spots a chosen character.

The scheme has two stages: first naming who the user is, then confirming the claim. A neural network reads features drawn from the signal's strength across five frequency bands. Recordings are stored in a database for quick matching. Brain-based login is still a research field, and studies like this test how far a simple network can take it.
pmc-11679752:
Malgorzata Kaczorowska, writing alone in 2024, sifts new green stuff to split lithium, rubidium, and caesium ions from water by soak-up. The review takes in the most fresh work on stuff, in the main from twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four.

Need for these light metals grows through goods with charge craft, through care, and through flight and space craft. But ores in the wild are in scant store, which pushes work to win them back from salt waters, from waste water, and from waste soups. Groups of stuff sifted take in ion sieves and soak goods based on a light metal. They take in stone soak goods, joined goods, and resins. Each is weighed for its main good points and its weak points. Acts on the wild world get marked heed. The review aims to guide growth of green split ways that can be used at plant scale.
pmc-11681852:
Tamirat Getachew and six co-authors ask how herbal medicine use during pregnancy links with harm to the unborn child in eastern Ethiopia. Herbal remedies are widely used in pregnancy around the world, yet evidence on fetal risk is thin. Most past work was based in clinics, which miss mothers who never attend checkups. Their 2024 community study visited homes and randomly selected 882 mothers.

About 43 percent had used herbal medicines in their last pregnancy. Three plants led the list: a basil relative, pumpkin fruit, and a rue relative. Use ran higher in rural homes, in women with problems in the last pregnancy, and in women whose last birth ended badly for the child. The team stops short of claiming cause. They call for safety testing first, and for joint work by healers, communities, and clinics.
pmc-11682952:
Allan Busuulwa, Simon Riley, Alexandra Revynthi, Oscar Liburd, and Sriyanka Lahiri test whether common strawberry sprays leave residues that harm the predatory mites farmers release. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Florida is the second biggest strawberry state, and a tiny thrips pest drives much spraying.

Three mite species that eat the pest were exposed in lab cells to eight commercial products, from standard chemicals to plant extracts and fungi, plus a water control. Survival, feeding, and egg laying were tracked as residues aged. All products wore the mites down over time to some degree. The ranking helps growers time mite releases around sprays so the two control methods reinforce rather than cancel each other.
pmc-11683252:
Victor Caso Moreira and co-authors share a data set in 2024 on the surface of a titanium alloy used in aircraft. The alloy, called Ti6Al4V, is prized for being strong yet light and slow to rust. Joining it to plastic composites could make parts that are both tough and green, but the bond needs the right surface texture.

The data record surface profiles and roughness made by two methods. One uses a laser to etch the surface, and the other uses electric sparks to erode it. Teams who weld metal to polymer with friction methods can use the data to pick a texture that grips well. The set supports work on lighter, stronger joined parts.
pmc-11687252:
Clare French and five co-authors published a 2024 systematic review of primary care programs meant to stop pain patients from sliding into opioid dependence. Nearly a third of adults with long-term non-cancer pain take prescribed opioids worldwide. The team searched five databases for trials and comparison studies of prevention tools used in primary care, excluding dose-tapering programs. Eighteen studies qualified, eight of them randomized trials.

Most programs bundled several parts. Of the stronger trials, five showed a benefit on at least one outcome. Four of those five included a nurse care manager or other specialist support. Two trials, covering automated symptom checks and a phone app, showed no benefit. The authors say the evidence is sparse and uneven, and call for larger, better trials before firm guidance is possible.
pmc-11688052:
Walid Bakeer, Marwa Gaafar, Ahmed El-Gendy, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It compares strains of Staphylococcus aureus, a common bacterium, sorted by how they stand up to two key antibiotics, methicillin and vancomycin.

From 250 clinical samples, the team found sixty-two with the bacterium, and twenty-seven of those resisted methicillin. Every one of those twenty-seven resisted several drugs at once. Most still fell to vancomycin, but seven strains resisted it too, and those showed even broader drug resistance. The team paired lab drug tests with genetic typing and checks for harm-causing genes. They argue that knowing these profiles helps doctors pick treatments and helps public health programs slow the spread of hard-to-treat strains.
pmc-11688252:
Burgos and eight co-authors review a neglected suspect in cattle inflammation: D-lactate, a mirror form of a common fermentation acid. Grain-rich feeding can flood a cow's rumen and blood with this acid, a state tied to lameness and joint trouble. The acid itself, not just the souring, may drive the inflammation.

The review gathers evidence that D-lactate alters the behavior of joint lining cells, white blood cells, macrophages, and T cells. Each cell type sits on the path from rumen upset to body-wide inflammation. The authors argue this lens sharpens the picture of ruminal acidosis. They call the molecule's role an enigma worth direct testing.
pmc-11688352:
Healthy pigs grow faster and use less feed, which also lightens the climate cost of pork. Julia Gickel and co-authors review trials of vaccines against four common pig infections and ask whether vaccination shrinks the carbon footprint of fattening pigs. They pooled performance data from dozens of European trials and fed the numbers into life cycle assessment models.

Vaccinated herds came out ahead across the board. The footprint fell by up to 12.1 percent with the circovirus vaccine, with smaller cuts for the other diseases and their combinations. The authors argue that keeping animals healthy is a practical climate tool for farms, since better growth means fewer resources spent per kilogram of pork produced.
pmc-11689252:
Jessica Krok-Schoen examines, in 2024, resilience among women aged eighty and older in a large health study. Nearly thirty thousand women, median age about eighty-four, answered resilience measures. Scores did not differ by race or ethnicity, but women in poorer neighborhoods scored slightly lower than those in richer ones.

Older age, more schooling, better self-rated health, lower stress, and living alone all tracked with higher resilience. Social support mattered for White, Black, and Asian women but not Hispanic women. Some links, like smoking and spirituality, appeared only in middle-income neighborhoods. The author argues the many shared patterns can guide support programs for a diverse aging population.
pmc-11689352:
Brenna Renn and Kristopher Kern present a symposium report from 2024 on mental health care for older adults. The older population is growing and growing more diverse. The authors argue that care and training must serve people from groups long pushed to the margins.

The symposium gathers talks from a society for the study of aging and mind. One talk covers fair mentoring for trainees. A second shares findings on care that respects culture and fights bias. A third reports a national survey on widening the workforce. A discussant ties the talks together and presses for change in both training and daily care. The group stresses steps that clinics and schools can take at once.
pmc-11689452:
Clarissa Shaw and co-authors build training for talking with nursing home residents while masked in this 2024 paper. Face masks muffle speech and hide expressions, which strains care for residents with dementia. Masks still return during outbreaks of lung infections. The team created a thirty-minute web course called CHATO-PPE from a literature scan and interviews.

Short videos show a care visit going wrong, then right, using clear speech and person-centered habits. Twenty-six nursing home caregivers piloted the course. Their confidence in dementia care rose clearly after it. Nearly all said they would recommend it and use its tips. Learners also said the habits help even without masks.
pmc-11689852:
Sandy Alcantar argues in 2024 that trauma is being missed in older Hispanic patients, and dementia blamed instead. Post-traumatic stress disorder can mimic or worsen memory problems. Yet clinicians often skip asking this group about trauma, whether suffered before or after immigration.

Barriers include language, weak links with community providers, and assessment habits. Alcantar calls for routine trauma screening in this population, done with cultural and language care. Better teamwork between providers and community partners could cut misdiagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. The piece also urges periodic review of how assessments and treatments are working, so care keeps improving.
pmc-11689952:
New York City packs more than a million older adults into a small area, and the pandemic plus the climate crisis have raised the stakes of every emergency. Elana Kieffer summarizes a 2023 city report in this 2024 conference presentation, drawing on interviews with older New Yorkers and the professionals who serve them.

The report shows how partnerships, clear teaching, efficient programs, and ready access to resources helped neighborhoods bounce back after COVID-19 and earlier storms. The findings are framed through strengths rather than deficits. Kieffer argues the lessons can guide advocacy and policy so older residents are better backed before the next disaster.
pmc-11690252:
Carmelina Oyales and Victoria Apuan present a 2024 study on elder abuse inside families in the Philippines. Respect and care for older people are strong values in Filipino culture, which makes the hidden abuse of elders a striking topic. The study asks why such abuse stays invisible in society.

The authors interviewed ten victims of elder abuse in depth. They also held group talks in five localities with thirty-two local officials and welfare workers. Victims reported shock, anger, depression, and a sense of helplessness. The most common harms were emotional abuse, neglect, abandonment, and money exploitation. Poverty and age bias made things worse. Family secrecy and weak reporting systems kept help from arriving on time.
pmc-11690352:
Barış Sevi, Adil Supiyev, Angela Gutierrez, and Graciela Muniz Terrera tested whether personality predicts allostatic load, the body's cumulative wear from chronic stress, in older Hispanic Americans. This group faces higher average load and related health gaps. Using a national retirement study, they followed 319 adults aged fifty and over across eight years and three measurements. Of the five major traits, only conscientiousness predicted load: more conscientious people started with lower wear.

No trait predicted how fast load changed over time. The team then tested the healthy neuroticism idea, that worry harms health unless paired with conscientiousness. The data went the other way: people high in both traits started with higher load, not lower. The authors say personality does matter for stress wear in this population, but the popular buffering hypothesis failed its test. Health programs, they imply, should not count on that combination to protect anyone.
pmc-11690452:
Xiayu Chen and six co-authors study loneliness among older caregivers in California in a 2024 paper. Adults past sixty-five form the second largest group of family caregivers in the United States. Caring for others while aging oneself raises the risk of isolation.

The team analyzed a statewide health interview survey from 2020. About a fifth of the older respondents had provided care in the past year. Fifteen percent of those caregivers reported loneliness. Weighted statistical models compared caregivers with non-caregivers and split caregivers by dementia care. Caregivers proved more likely to feel lonely. The study maps which traits tie most tightly to loneliness in each group, aiming policy at the loneliest caregivers first.
pmc-11690552:
Frank Infurna and co-authors compare how midlife pain has shifted across birth groups in the United States and peer nations, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Matched survey data covered the United States, thirteen European nations, South Korea, and Mexico. The question was whether rising pain in later-born Americans mirrors trends abroad.

Later-born midlife Americans did report more pain, and the rise started earlier in midlife for them. Parts of Europe shared the rise, in both mainland and Nordic states. England, Mediterranean Europe, South Korea, and Mexico instead saw pain fall across groups. Possible causes span health gaps, care use, and the costs of western life. Readers get a map of where midlife hurts more now.
pmc-11691052:
Kristin Miller, Kelsey Weitzel, and Naomi Meinertz describe a 2024 program that brings health classes to rural older adults. Many rural elders face isolation as family moves away and transport stays scarce, which harms health and independence. The Cooperative Extension system links these adults with community programs, yet how such partnerships work is rarely written down.

The talk uses a strength-training program run across several states as its model. It lays out the teamwork between campus researchers, local agents, and community partners. A current project adapts the classes for elders with limited mobility, guided by a local advisory group. The authors argue this model helps research make a real difference in rural life.
pmc-11691352:
Jenny Walker and five co-authors count hospital stays that good outpatient care might have prevented in adults with dementia, in a 2024 study. The team used a national United States hospital database from 2016 to 2019. They flagged eight conditions that timely clinic care can often head off, from infections to injuries. Among millions of stays for older adults with related conditions, about one in nine patients also carried a dementia diagnosis.

Preventable stays in the dementia group piled up at older ages, with over four in five past age seventy-five. Sepsis, injuries, urinary infections, and heart failure led the list. Urinary infections sent dementia patients to hospital at more than twice the adjusted rate of others. The authors urge prevention plans that single out dementia patients, above all for infection care.
pmc-11692252:
Oonjee Oh and three co-authors ask, in twenty twenty-four, if the timing of problem-solving therapy matters for hospice family care partners. The therapy can ease stress and low mood, but the best time to start is not clear. They looked back at data from a therapy trial with more than two hundred care partners.

Some care partners got the therapy face to face, some by a mix of in-person and video calls, and some got an added form that stressed the good sides of care. Starting near the move to hospice or later both helped low mood in the face to face group. Worry fell for all groups, at both times. In the added form, only the later start helped low mood. The authors say timing needs more care in real hospice work.
pmc-11692452:
Mallory Johnson maps where certified nursing assistants work across the United States, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. These aides give much of the daily hands-on care in nursing homes and other care settings. Johnson uses pay records, census data, and state training lists to study county patterns.

Most counties had aides, but a few hundred had none at all. Those places tended to be rural, with fewer people, fewer hospitals, and fewer training sites, yet more older residents. Having more hospitals and nursing home beds went with having more aides. Need alone did not explain where aides work.
pmc-11693252:
Brett Burrows and three co-authors read a stepped exercise plan for veterans with knee joint wear plus back pain, in 2024. Back pain makes the knee ill's drag on life worse. The plan starts with three months of home exercise backed by the web. Those who lag then get phone coaching, and those still short get hands-on therapy.

Three hundred forty-five veterans were split two-to-one between the plan and a mailed-facts arm. Three in four had back pain at the start. In that back-pain set, the plan arm beat the facts arm by about ten points on a knee score at nine months. The gap cleared the stats bar with room. In the no-back-pain set, the arms did not split. A cheap stepped plan may thus help most where two pains meet.
pmc-11693352:
Doria Qu and co-authors describe in 2024 how an arts curriculum was adapted for Mandarin-speaking older adults. The English program, called Creativity Circle, had earlier reduced social isolation. The adapted version ran for eight weeks with sixteen participants in the group.

Changes included Cantonese songs, Chinese poetry, and clay modeling of traditional items. Fifteen people finished the program, and they found it helpful and culturally fitting. Participants valued happiness, health, and family over material goals. Loneliness scores eased after the series, though the change was not statistically significant. The study shows adapted arts can support well-being.
pmc-11696652:
Alaa Aldeen Joumah, Assef Jafar, and Chadi Albitar present a 2024 study of robot modeling with Bayesian neural networks. A 6-RSU parallel manipulator moves a platform with six linked arms. Predicting its forward geometry, where the platform sits for given joint settings, must be exact for safe work. Bayesian networks learn such models and also report their own uncertainty. Earlier learning studies predicted the geometry but gave no confidence range. The team modifies a NARX-style network, which uses past inputs and outputs, into Bayesian form.

The blend pairs strong prediction with honest error bars. Simulation and bench experiments test the model. Robotics engineers get position estimates that know when to distrust themselves. Uncertainty is a safety feature in shared workspaces: a robot unsure of its pose should slow down. Parallel robots are fast but geometrically tricky, so learned models with confidence are a practical advance over fixed formulas.
pmc-11696752:
Zongyang Li and five co-authors study the fluid behavior of a large offshore condensate gas reservoir in China's Bohai Sea, and how it affects gas flow through the rock. Their paper came out in 2024. In such reservoirs, falling pressure makes liquid condense inside the pores, a setback that traps valuable liquid and blocks gas.

Laboratory experiments on real rock cores tested how injecting dry gas changes the fluid mix. Injection drew out condensed liquid, lowered its share in the pores, and improved recovery. Injecting earlier and at higher pressure worked best. Damage tests showed that condensed liquid hurt flow most in tighter rock, and cracks made the harm worse. The results supply parameters for planning gas injection in similar deepwater fields.
pmc-11697552:
Acid eats away at aluminium used in industry, so cheap ways to slow that damage are in demand. Onukwuli and co-authors test an expired drug, danacid, as a protective coating in a 2024 study set in strong acid.

The team weighed metal loss, ran electric tests, and modeled the drug's molecules on a computer. The drug clung to the metal surface in a thin layer and slowed damage sharply, with top test scores above ninety percent. Math models used to tune the dose agreed that the effect was strong. Computer results backed the lab findings. The study suggests that some expired drugs could find a second life guarding metal instead of going to waste.
pmc-11701452:
Eun Ji Park and co-authors compare how much body stress follows three ways of removing colon cancer, in a 2024 study. The three ways are open surgery, keyhole surgery, and robot-assisted surgery. The team wanted to see if the robot's technical strengths show up as a gentler recovery for the patient.

They reviewed cases from one large Korean hospital, treated between 2006 and 2012, and matched patients so the groups were alike at the start. Each group held 66 patients. Blood tests after surgery showed the lowest white cell counts in the robot group and the highest in the open group. A nutrition-linked score also favored the robot group. Patients passed gas and returned to soft food fastest after robot-assisted surgery.
pmc-11704852:
Jun-Won Seo and Joon Young Song reply to a comment on their long COVID guideline in a 2024 letter. The exchange concerns how chronic COVID can be diagnosed and treated. The authors address points raised by a commenter and add evidence on vaccination and long term symptoms.

They note that vaccines can prevent or reduce long COVID risk, possibly by lowering initial severity and speeding viral clearance. Studies found lower symptom risk in vaccinated people, even when vaccination followed infection. A large veterans study found new long COVID cases fell with each variant, with most of the drop attributed to vaccination.
pmc-11709752:
Ryan Dacey and a large team ask whether epigenetic clocks, blood measures of how fast the body is aging, predict cognitive decline by eroding resilience rather than by driving degeneration itself. Their study came out in 2025, using the long-running Framingham Heart Study.

In more than two thousand participants, one clock that paces aging predicted faster decline in executive function and higher risk of mild impairment and dementia. Two other clocks predicted lower starting scores instead. The results barely moved when a blood marker of neurodegeneration was added to the models. That stability suggests the clocks carry information about resilience, the ability to cope with damage, rather than about damage alone. The distinction matters for choosing prevention strategies.
pmc-11710152:
Ana Guerrero gives a 2025 conference talk abstract on worn-out cells as a drug target in Alzheimer's disease. Cells that stop dividing but refuse to die build up with age and feed many age-linked illnesses. Guerrero asks how much this buildup matters inside the brain during the disease, where the picture is still unclear.

Her team built a mouse model that pairs amyloid buildup with tools to track and remove these worn-out cells on command. The talk surveys drug plans that kill such cells or tame what they release. It also shares early data from the new model on when the cells appear near amyloid deposits.
pmc-11710352:
Claire Delpirou Nouh and co-authors report the case of a young patient whose illness looked like one brain disease but proved to be two others, in a paper published in 2025. The woman, in her late fifties, had growing trouble with hand control, writing, and space tasks over a year. Scans showed uneven shrinkage on one side of her brain.

Her state worsened fast, and she died four years after diagnosis. A brain exam after death found heavy Lewy body disease in mid-brain areas plus strong Alzheimer's changes. Cases like hers are rare for this syndrome, the authors note. The report warns that mixed brain diseases can hide behind one set of signs, which matters for care and for trials.
pmc-11712152:
Aygun Badalova reports a trial of an app that retrains name recall in people with dementia in a 2025 study. Losing the names of loved ones, called proper name anomia, is a common and painful problem in dementia. The Gotcha app trains one face a day from family photos, using proven methods of error-free learning and spaced recall.

The trial compared six weeks before therapy with six weeks of training, with weekly free-naming tests. A speech checker gave feedback in real time. Of the first twenty users, eighty percent named better during training, and eight improved by a clear margin. Group analysis also showed a firm training effect. Badalova notes that freely naming a relative again can mean a great deal to families.
pmc-11712852:
James A C Myers and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on how being alone in life relates to thinking scores in people with dementia in the United Kingdom. They used marital and living status, pulled from health records, as rough signs of social isolation. Records covered patients aged fifty and up over nearly three decades.

People who had stayed single all their lives started with lower scores on a standard thinking test. Those living in supported housing lost ground faster over time than those in other setups. The authors note that isolation can be changed, unlike many risk factors. Clinics may want to ask about living setup when they plan a patient's care.
pmc-11713452:
Hughes and co-authors check the steadiness of a web-based thinking test people take at home, in this 2025 paper. The battery runs on phones, tablets, or computers without a tester present. It joins a word-list memory test, a speed and planning test, and a combined score.

The study included nearly thirteen hundred adults who took the battery two to four times. Most were healthy, with an average age near seventy-one. The authors test whether scores stay steady across sessions, which a screening tool must do to be trusted. Steady home scores could let clinics and trials check thinking often without office visits.
pmc-11713552:
Ashley Powell and co-authors study links among personality, heart health, and thinking in older African Americans, in this 2025 paper. African Americans carry a heavier load of both heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. A trait called neuroticism, a tendency toward worry and stress, has been tied to worse outcomes in both areas.

Eighty-three healthy older adults from a healthy aging study gave blood samples and took fitness and body measures. They also completed personality surveys and learning tasks. The authors test whether high worry scores and weak heart health together signal early thinking problems tied to Alzheimer's risk, an area they say has been studied too little in this group.
pmc-11713652:
Xi Yu and co-authors use brain age models to weigh how chronic illness speeds brain aging in a 2025 paper. Long-term diseases like diabetes raise dementia risk, but the path is unclear. A brain that looks older than its years may be the link. The team uses detailed scans that show the fine wiring of white matter.

The study covers 1,123 adults from a Mayo Clinic aging project. Most were healthy, while others had mild memory loss or Alzheimer's. Health records listed each person's chronic conditions. Scan-based models then estimated how old each brain looked. Comparing conditions side by side shows which ones tax the brain most. That ranking can guide which illnesses doctors treat first to guard memory.
pmc-11713752:
Wiesje van der Flier and co-authors compare patients across world regions in two large drug trials in a 2025 paper. The trials test semaglutide, a diabetes drug, in early Alzheimer's disease. Patients join from Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, and other regions. If the groups differ at the start, the drug's effects may be hard to read fairly.

The team pooled the starting data and split it by region. They compared age, schooling, memory scores, and brain health markers. One trial also let in people with more small-vessel damage in the brain. Regional gaps in who joins such trials can shift what the results mean. The paper gives readers a clear map of those gaps.
pmc-11714252:
Tak Youn, Hea Jeong Park, and Hyong Sook Jun ask whether brain wave links can foretell drug response in Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 conference paper looks at links recorded when drug care first began. Doctors now have no firm way to guess long term response when they first write the script.

The team recorded resting brain waves from 56 patients as they began drug care, then split them into good and poor response groups after about two years. The poor group showed stronger links in fast brain waves between spots in the right half of the brain at the start. Slow wave links also set the groups apart. The authors say these early wave patterns could help doctors pick and adjust drugs sooner.
pmc-11715052:
Heather Kwan and three co-authors asked whether a rich social life goes with more brain tissue in old women. Low social contact is a known risk for dementia, and women face more risk than men. The team drew on a long study of healthy aging in women in Australia. Brain scans let them weigh tissue volume zone by zone.

One hundred fifty-one healthy women past age sixty had scans and filled in a short form on social life. Across the whole brain, tissue volume did not track the social score at a clear level. Some zones at the back of the brain leaned that way but fell short of the bar. A close look at one zone at the brain's base, the cerebellum, did find a clear link. The group urges more work on which zones gain from social life.
pmc-11715252:
Kim Caf and Martin Rakusa asked whether stroke patients know when their thought skills have slipped. Thought loss after a stroke is common and easy to miss in a busy ward. The team paired a self-report form with a scored test of thought skills. They also used a scale that helps tell vessel-based loss from other kinds.

Seventy-four patients took part soon after an acute stroke. By both the self-report and the scored test, sixty-three percent showed thought loss. Yet the two reads often named unlike people. Thirty-one patients knew of their loss, while sixteen denied loss the test could plainly see. Sixteen more claimed loss their scores did not back. Self-report caught the state with only fair skill, so the team urges staff to test rather than ask.
pmc-11715852:
Masroor Anwar and colleagues measured four blood proteins in a large multicenter study of dementia and its early stages. Early and pre-symptom changes in the brain are poorly understood, which slows diagnosis and treatment. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team used an ultrasensitive single-molecule test platform to measure two amyloid proteins and two proteins tied to nerve damage and brain support cell activity. Participants included people with Alzheimer disease, people with mild cognitive impairment, and older controls, followed across centers over time.

Two proteins, one from nerve fibers and one from support cells, were clearly higher in both patient groups than in controls, and both rose with age. The support cell protein also rose stepwise across older age groups in Alzheimer patients. The amyloid measures did not separate the groups. The authors propose the two raised proteins as candidate markers of risk and progression.
pmc-11715952:
He-Ying Hu, Hao Hu, and Jin-Tai Yu explore links between the heart and Alzheimer's disease in this 2025 study from the CABLE cohort in China. All participants had normal thinking, yet some already showed quiet changes in heart structure on ultrasound scans. The team asked whether those changes track with spinal fluid markers of the disease.

The study covered 1,244 adults with an average age of about sixty-five. A larger or thicker left side of the heart went with higher levels of tau proteins in spinal fluid and with poorer thinking scores. The tau changes partly explained the heart-to-thinking link. Heart measures were also higher in early disease stage groups than in healthy controls. The results support close ties between heart health and brain health.
pmc-11716052:
Vaatausili Tofaeono describes early work to define dementia risk in American Samoa, in this 2025 paper. The territory's adults face high rates of smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, and diabetes, all tied to dementia risk, yet that risk had never been measured there. The study plans to assess more than a thousand adults aged fifty and older.

The project uses the Talanoa framework, a Samoan approach built on open face to face talk, respect, and service to the community. A consensus group of Samoan clinicians used it to agree on a fair way to judge each person's risk from test data. Early results from twenty-six people found about sixty-two percent at high risk, with diet and low activity as key factors. The approach aims to make research fit local values.
pmc-11716352:
Paul Yushkevich and co-authors report 2025 work on a brain disease of old age that lacks a good test in living people. The disease, known by its short name LATE, harms a protein in brain cells and often comes with Alzheimer's disease. With no scan or fluid test for it, proof comes only after death.

Groups have scanned brain tissue taken after death with strong, fine scans and mapped how thick the outer brain is. Both the LATE protein and tau, the Alzheimer's protein, link to thin spots in the inner side brain. The two patterns look alike in part but differ in part too. The hope is that these maps will lead to a test that works while a person is alive.
pmc-11716952:
Sarah Bauermeister describes a 2025 training effort that tries to open dementia research skills to early career researchers everywhere. Many workshops cost too much for staff at smaller schools or in lower-income countries, so access to good training has stayed uneven.

The program runs through Dementias Platform UK. It offers hands-on data workshops where researchers work with large cohort data, classes in study design at basic and advanced levels, and a twelve-week mentoring scheme. More than 200 researchers from 11 countries have taken part over five years. Bauermeister argues that shared, low-cost training can widen who gets to do this research.
pmc-11717152:
Devi Nair, editor in chief of a heart rhythm journal, closes 2024 with a letter looking back on a busy year in cardiac rhythm care. The field saw strong trial results and new tools aimed at steadier, safer treatment of irregular heartbeats.

Nair singles out pulsed field ablation, a method that uses electric pulses rather than heat to treat atrial fibrillation. Trial wins and new approvals during the year sped its spread to clinics. Progress in pacing that works with the heart's own wiring also gets attention. The letter thanks readers and authors while setting up the work the journal plans to feature next.
pmc-11727752:
Romina Aspera-Werz and ten colleagues published a 2024 study of printed scaffolds for bone repair. When bone cannot heal alone, surgeons graft replacement material. The patient's own bone remains the gold standard, but printed synthetic biomaterials offer high availability and designs matched to the target tissue.

The team printed calcium phosphate scaffolds in a gyroid structure, a porous, curved lattice resembling natural bone architecture. They varied two production factors: the particle size of the starting powder and the sintering temperature used to fuse it. They then measured how these choices affected the scaffolds' mechanical strength and compatibility with living cells. The results guide the manufacture of bone substitutes that are both strong and cell-friendly.
pmc-11728852:
Olga Pawełczyk and co-authors track a dog disease in a 2024 study from southern Poland. Babesiosis, spread by ticks, can kill dogs, and the local picture of exposure was patchy. The team reviewed blood samples sent to a commercial lab from clinics that suspected the disease, over four years from 2018.

Of just over three thousand samples, about nine percent tested positive under the microscope. Cases peaked twice a year, in April and October, matching tick activity. Pure-bred dogs tested positive more often than mixed breeds. One region around Częstochowa supplied the most positives. The authors urge vets in the area, above all in that region, to keep the parasite in mind when dogs fall ill.
pmc-11731252:
Riza Hayati Ifroh and three co-authors survey university students in Indonesia on support, lifestyle, and well-being in a study from 2024. Data came from 348 students in ten cities in East Kalimantan who filled an online questionnaire in 2023. Measures covered perceived social support, healthy lifestyle, felt well-being, and health-related quality of life.

All four measures were linked to each other. A healthy lifestyle also carried part of the effect of social support on both well-being and quality of life. The authors suggest that youth lifestyle deserves a place in population studies of well-being, alongside social support, when student health programs are planned.
pmc-11734252:
Vitaliano Gomes de Araujo-Neto and co-authors review how acid strength affects bonding to glass-ceramics in this 2023 paper. Dentists etch glass-ceramic crowns with hydrofluoric acid before cementing them. The question was whether weaker acid, under five percent, bonds as well as stronger mixes. Four databases were searched for lab studies up to mid-2021. Nearly a thousand papers were found and screened. Seventeen made the review, and twelve fed the pooled analysis.

The pooled results compared bond strength between low and high acid groups. Standardized gaps between the groups were the main measure. Lab studies on ceramic samples stand in for real teeth here. A finding for weaker acid would mean safer handling in the clinic. The acid is harsh and can burn skin and tissue. The authors aim to settle a practical protocol choice for dentists.
pmc-11773652:
Ruaa Jadallah and Shatha Hammad compare two cooking oils in a 2024 feeding trial. Blood fat after meals is a risk marker for heart disease. The length of fat chains may change that response and appetite. Coconut oil is rich in medium chains, palm oil in long chains.

Twenty healthy adults took part in the crossover trial. Each person ate biscuits made with one oil, then later the other. Blood samples tracked fats for six hours after each meal. Triglyceride and cholesterol rises were lower after coconut oil. Hunger and fullness ratings did not differ between the oils. Later meals also came out much the same in size. The authors say chain length shapes blood fat more than appetite.
pmc-11779552:
New mothers with low incomes face trauma and daily stress that can feed post-traumatic stress, and the mix differs by background in ways flat averages hide. Yasmin Kofman and co-authors sort that mix in a 2024 study of mothers from five United States regions, spanning Black, Latina, and White groups. They group mothers by the pattern of what they faced in the past year.

Four patterns emerged, from low exposure to high daily stress, injury and illness, and violence. Any pattern above the low one came with stronger symptoms across nearly every symptom family at six months. Which pattern hurt most shifted by racial and ethnic group. The authors say screening after birth should read the whole pattern of a mother's load, not single events alone.
pmc-11782552:
Wagaye Alemu and co-authors follow children hospitalized with pneumonia in southern Ethiopia in a 2024 study. Pneumonia is a leading killer of children, especially where care access is limited. The prospective study tracked 484 children across several centers in the Gedeo Zone. The team measured time to poor outcomes and searched for predictors using survival analysis.

About seventy nine percent of children recovered, while a small share died, transferred, or left against advice. Poor outcomes occurred at a rate of four per hundred patient days. Other illnesses at admission, age, nutrition status, and residence each predicted poor outcomes. Very young age carried a particularly high risk. Readers see which hospitalized children need the closest watch.
pmc-11784052:
Siriphorn Chimplee and co-authors test mangrove bark and leaf extracts against a harmful amoeba, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The amoeba lives widely in nature and can cause lasting infections in people and animals. Current single drugs often fail, and some strains resist standard drugs that target a key cell protein.

Extracts from leaves and bark stopped most growth of two amoeba types in lab tests. Both extracts also cut how well all tested types could stick to surfaces, by a large share. Computer models predicted how plant compounds bind the target protein. At the safe dose found, the extracts did not harm mammal cells in tests.
pmc-11792152:
Heather Suttor and co-authors present a study of how schoolgirls in Bali seek menstrual health facts online. The head of the text dates the work to 2023. Good facts support girls' health and rights, and many now find them on websites, social media, or health apps.

The team ran group talks, deep talks, diary tasks, and observation in four junior high schools. Girls aged thirteen to fifteen took part. They found facts through search engines and met them on social media, above all a short video app. Girls liked the privacy, ease, and fun of online facts. But too much content raised worry, and false claims fed myths about periods. The authors urge programs to teach sharp health and digital skills.
pmc-11794252:
Solomon Debela Bekeko and co-authors present a study on depression and anxiety among displaced people in the Metekel zone of Ethiopia. The head text dates the study to 2024. People forced from their homes face trauma, lost work, and isolation, all of which strain mental health.

Nearly one thousand respondents were chosen by systematic random sampling and interviewed with a structured questionnaire. About eighty percent screened positive for depression and about seventy-five percent for anxiety. A structural model linked higher scores to older age and to the death of a loved one. Formal education and some job types were tied to lower scores. Prior mental illness and trauma scores also shaped the outcomes.
pmc-11795552:
Yufen Zheng and others built a chart to forecast survival in breast cancer in 2025. Survival after surgery depends on many traits. Standard staging captures only some factors. American records data fed the model. Chinese hospital data checked it from outside. Many clinic traits were joined.

The chart foretold survival well. All checking cohorts did well throughout. Choice analysis showed maximum net benefit. Per-person forecasts become handy for doctors. Treatment plans can be tuned per patient. Talks about outlook gain a concrete tool. The authors claim it is more exact than staging. Multi-centre evidence supports the model.
pmc-11811752:
For patients with post-traumatic stress who face a high risk of suicide, doctors lack a clear ranking of which antidepressant is safest to start. Oshin Miranda and co-authors build a stand-in trial from real-world records in a paper whose head record gives 2024. They follow patients who began a drug within weeks of a suicide-related event and watch for the next such event.

One drug stood out: patients starting it had notably fewer new suicide-related events than those starting three other common choices. The gap held after the team adjusted for other traits and for the many comparisons made. The authors urge care in prescribing for this group, since the choice of first drug may carry real risk weight. A true randomized trial remains the test that would settle it.
pmc-11818752:
Padmaja Kumari Rani and nine co-authors published a public health evaluation in twenty twenty-five of a mobile-phone diabetes prevention program in rural Andhra Pradesh, India. The mDiabetes program sent fifty-six voice messages in the local language over six months, backed by village health meetings and leaflets. Over one hundred thousand rural residents were reached in a year.

Five hundred forty-five people completed surveys before, right after, and three months later. Diabetes awareness climbed from about eighty-three percent to nearly universal and stayed there. Diet and activity habits were tracked alongside knowledge. The quasi-experimental design cannot fully exclude outside influences. Still, the results suggest cheap voice messaging plus community workers can shift awareness at population scale.
pmc-11841652:
Yuanheng Liu, Xianglin Luo, and Hao Xu link money control to movement in older Chinese adults in this paper. Older people move less for many reasons, and finances are one suspect. Having economic autonomy means deciding over one's own money. The team analyzed a national aging survey from two thousand eighteen. It covered one thousand nine hundred sixty-one people aged sixty and above.

They sorted participants by autonomy and recorded activity type, frequency, length, and purpose. Autonomy went with more light and moderate activity. The link to hard exertion was weaker or absent. Financial independence may support daily habits like walking and chores. The findings speak to aging policy as much as to health advice. Gerontology readers are the audience.
pmc-11888752:
Upasana Reddy and a team of co-authors ran a six-month trial on tooth decay after radiation for head and neck cancer, in two thousand twenty-four. Radiation harms the glands that make saliva, and dry mouths decay faster. More than one hundred patients took part and were split into three care groups.

One group used virgin coconut oil, one a calcium-rich tooth mousse, and one a fluoride mouthwash. Decay scores were checked at the start and after six months. The tooth mousse group fared best, with less new decay and slower growth of old lesions. It beat both other options by a clear margin in the trial's tests.
pmc-11935552:
McKenzie Jancsura and co-authors ask whether an inflammation-stoking diet after pregnancy harms heart health more in women who had troubled pregnancies, in a 2024 study. Data came from a large first-pregnancy cohort revisited about three years after delivery, 3,249 women in all. Diet was scored for its inflammatory load. Troubled pregnancies included early birth, small babies, pregnancy diabetes, and blood pressure disorders.

Higher inflammatory scores tracked with higher weight, wider waists, higher blood pressure, worse fats and insulin, and more inflammation markers. Some links shifted depending on whether a woman had suffered a troubled pregnancy. The authors argue the post-pregnancy years are a window where diet quality matters doubly for women whose pregnancies went wrong.
pmc-11935652:
Xiaoying Wang and eight co-authors show a super-switch drives syndecan-4 to spur lung press ill in low air. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Genes that drive talks tween lung tube cells were the hunt. A fresh super-switch gene, syndecan-4, lit high in low-air tube cells and in blood of sick folks. A growth switch drove it through its super span.

The part fires cell growth by sway of a kin part's fate, and rides out in small sacs that mar the mate cell kind. Block of it in low-air beasts eased tube rework and ill growth.
pmc-11970152:
Juliana D'Sa leads a team that tests a breastfeeding class for pregnant women. Their study from twenty twenty-four was run at a hospital in Riyadh. What a mother knows before birth shapes how she feeds.

Women took a knowledge test, then the class, then a test by phone. Scores rose a lot by the second test, the team found. Traits that guess knowledge scores were also sought. The class ran over a short span in one summer. Such classes may help new mothers start feeding well. The group was drawn from one large hospital.
pmc-12352452:
Ben Gabrielson, Hanlu Yang, Trung Vu, Vince Calhoun, and Tülay Adalı published this 2024 methods paper on shrinking tensor decompositions to a chosen core of the data. Tensor methods split multiway arrays into simple rank-one pieces, but modern data are huge, and most fast methods sample randomly. The team instead select coresets, small mode subsets whose reduced tensor still approximates the whole.

Both random and deterministic selection rules are offered, scored by how closely the coreset stands in for the full tensor. The deterministic route doubles as feature selection: the kept slices are the meaningful ones, which the authors demonstrate on brain imaging data from fMRI. There, the selected features carry the signal while the computation sheds the bulk. The authors pitch mode coresets as efficiency with an explanation attached, a rare pairing in large-scale analysis.
pmc-12479852:
A 2023 Korean health report tracks how rates of felt depressive symptoms differ across cities and provinces from 2013 to 2022. The figures cover adults aged nineteen and older. A case counts when deep sorrow or despair kept a person from daily life for two weeks.

In 2022 the lowest rate was in Sejong-si and the highest was in Incheon. The gap between the highest and lowest rates grew slightly from the year before. Rates were adjusted for age using a standard population so places could be compared fairly. The short report, drawn from a national community health survey, gives officials a quick view of where need is greatest and how the spread has moved over time.
pmc-12664152:
Konstanze Schoeps and colleagues set out a 2025 study plan for SEL4@ll, a school program that builds social and emotional skills in teens. The program runs through a serious game, mixing learning goals with game design that keeps students engaged. Schools in four European countries will take part in a randomized trial.

About one thousand students aged ten to sixteen will join from Germany, Italy, Spain, and Finland. The plan pairs six weeks of solo game play with class sessions led by teachers. The team will measure skills, school well-being, and social inclusion before and after. The design lets the group test whether game-based learning can lift these skills at scale. Results should guide schools that want to teach more than test content.
pmc-12666152:
Pablo Jimenez-Labaig and co-authors pool trials on long-horizon endpoints after immune therapy for cancer in two thousand twenty-five. Immune drugs that block the PD-1 path can keep working through later lines of care. Standard endpoints stop at the first setback, which may miss that long benefit.

Second-event endpoints track time from the draw to a setback or death on the next therapy after the first. The review gathers trials of these drugs in solid tumors that report such endpoints. Pooled ratios compare immune arms with control arms, and extra analyses probe what shifts the effect. The team also tests how well the long endpoints stand in for overall survival.
pmc-12696952:
Dong-Xue Rao, Xin-Yue Sun, and Rong Chen compare lung wash findings in severe pneumonia patients with and without ARDS in this 2025 study. ARDS is the syndrome where lungs fail under inflammation. One hundred sixty patients at one hospital were enrolled. Half had ARDS and half did not. Lung fluid was tested with a broad genetic pathogen hunt. Immune cell subsets in the fluid were also counted.

Twenty-eight-day outcomes completed the picture. The ARDS group's fluid held more of one gut bacterium, among other contrasts. T cell depletion patterns differed between the groups. Such profiles may help predict who fares worst. The study is a retrospective cohort analysis. It links microbes, immunity, and prognosis in one dataset.
pmc-12698652:
Wenlong Cheng and co-authors study deep tillage with organic additions on soil carbon, nitrogen, and wheat yield, in a research paper from 2025. Soil carbon and nitrogen stocks set how well farm soil produces. Long-term practice shapes those stocks inside soil clumps, called aggregates, which protect stored nutrients.

A six-year field trial paired rotary or deep tillage with straw, manure, or both. Mixed additions raised carbon and nitrogen in large aggregates near the surface. Deep tillage with single additions raised stocks in deeper layers. Deep tillage also shrank large aggregates, which cut some gains. The paper weighs yield links and guides tillage choice.
pmc-12699852:
Short repeated DNA stretches sit in every genome, but how common they are across life's branches was unmapped. Nikol Chantzi and Ilias Georgakopoulos-Soares count them in a 2025 study spanning nearly one hundred eighteen thousand organisms.

Repeat frequency varied hugely, and the variation followed taxonomy more than anything else. Simulated genomes showed bacteria and archaea hold about as many repeats as chance predicts. Complex-celled organisms, by contrast, carry orders of magnitude more than chance. In some groups the repeats cluster at working gene sites. Brand-new complete ape genomes showed repeats thick and variable near chromosome centers. The authors conclude these repeats expanded along the complex-cell and viral branches of life.
pmc-12701052:
Xinming Xu and co-authors link diet quality to how fast bodies age in a 2025 paper. Bodies age at unlike rates in each organ, and the team built age scores for the whole body plus the heart, kidney, liver, and muscles. Scores were trained to forecast death risk from survey data. Diet was graded with five well-known scoring systems based on one-day food recalls.

Better diet scores tracked with slower aging on both body-based and gene-mark-based measures. The team then built new diet scores aimed straight at slow aging. Foods high in vegetables and fruit were the strongest signs of a youth-keeping pattern. The work ties daily food choices to aging at the level of single organs.
pmc-12702452:
Nicholas Brooke and co-authors track poison enquiries in the United Kingdom through the COVID-19 pandemic in a 2025 study. The National Poisons Information Service answers calls about exposures and poisonings, and its call pattern is a live gauge of harm at home. Lockdowns changed daily life sharply, so the team asked how the calls changed too.

They pulled all enquiries from the national database for 2018 to 2020 and sorted them by caller, patient, and exposure traits. In the first lockdown, calls about deliberate exposures fell as a share of the total, which may reflect fear of attending health facilities. Calls about dental painkillers rose in the same span, as dental care shut its doors. The patterns can guide public health moves in future crises.
pmc-12708652:
David Vizarraga and co-authors trace in 2025 how a pneumonia bacterium steals the fats it needs to live. Mycoplasma pneumoniae cannot make some essential lipids, so it must take them from its host. The bacterium also turns up in burst artery plaques, which hints at a wider role.

A surface protein called P116 pulls cholesterol from blood fat carriers and from host cells. An antibody aimed at part of P116 blocked that theft and slowed bacterial growth in the lab. It also stopped the bacteria from binding to human artery lesions. In mice, the bacteria homed to the liver and to plaques, a targeting trick the authors say could be put to medical use.
pmc-12709852:
Qi Liu and colleagues reviewed in 2025 how blocking DNA repair has become a weapon against cancer, increasingly in combination with immunotherapy. Healthy cells constantly repair DNA damage through a network called the DDR pathway, which also pauses the cell cycle for repairs. Tumors often carry defects in this network, a weakness that makes them depend on the repair routes they have left. Drugs that inhibit those remaining routes can kill cancer cells selectively.

PARP inhibitors such as olaparib and its relatives are already approved and in clinical use. Inhibitors aimed at ATM, ATR, DNA-PK, checkpoint kinases, and WEE1 are moving through trials. The review explains synthetic lethality, the principle behind these drugs, and surveys combinations with other anti-tumor therapies. Pairing repair blockers with immunotherapy is a particular focus, since accumulated DNA damage can make tumors more visible to the immune system.
pmc-12712852:
Freja Frankenhaeuser and co-authors followed a Stockholm cohort for thirty-five years to ask whether gum disease predicts earlier death. In nineteen eighty-five, clinicians examined one thousand six hundred forty-three people; two hundred eighty-six had periodontitis, a deep gum infection. National registers then tracked deaths, including cancer deaths, through twenty seventeen.

Those with gum disease at the start died sooner overall, and cancer deaths stood out in particular. Losing two or more teeth by midlife, heavy tartar, and inflamed gums also flagged higher risk. Certain drug purchases, from metabolism medicines to cancer and immune drugs, tracked with higher mortality too. The authors link long-standing mouth inflammation with lifespan.
pmc-12717252:
Daniel Roll and co-authors present a 2025 data report on a rare set of telescope images of low Earth orbit. The Frigate data set holds wide-view still frames packed with satellites and debris. Such space surveillance images are seldom public, since most are held by firms or governments with their own sensors.

A commercial provider, ExoAnalytic Solutions, collected the images with ground-based telescopes and shared them by agreement. Raw frames carry lens glare, vignetting, and edge decay. The team also releases cleaned versions with glare removed, backgrounds subtracted, and detail sharpened. Usage notes suggest stacking frames, finding streaks, and auto-labeling objects. The set can train machine learning tools for tracking satellites and spotting debris. Open data of this kind is scarce.
pmc-12717952:
Habibeh Matin, Parvin Sarbakhsh, and Abdolreza Shaghaghi adapt a questionnaire on treatment self-drive for Persian-speaking patients with type two diabetes. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. The drive to manage one's own care, freely chosen, supports lasting healthy habits.

The team translated the form back and forth by the standard method, then had fifteen health specialists judge its face and content fit. Patients with diabetes filled it in so the team could test its structure and steadiness. Consistency scores were strong, and repeat scores were near identical. Factor checks explored how its items group. The authors conclude the Persian version is sound for use in Iran. It gives clinicians a way to measure how self-driven their patients feel about treatment.
pmc-12718252:
Iraide Sáez-Zamacona, Rosa María Martínez-Espinosa, and Guillermo Grindlay put a salt-loving archaeon to work cleaning industrial wastewater. Haloferax mediterranei thrives in brines and already showed talent for removing nitrogen compounds and metals. The team grew it in desalination and textile effluents, supplemented with minimal nutrients.

Growth slowed and the cells visibly stressed, pumping out up to ten times more carotenoid pigment on textile waste than in ideal medium. The microbe still stripped sixty to ninety percent of nitrate from the wastes, among the best rates reported at such salinities. The authors pitch a circular strategy: wastewater treatment that also harvests valuable pigment, pending better waste blending.
pmc-12719952:
Jiyeon Lee looks at what keeps registered nurses in their jobs at care homes in Korea, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Homes need steady nursing staff, since nurses who stay know the residents well and give better care. Lee weighs both the traits of the nurses and the traits of the homes they work in.

The data came from 163 nurses and 38 home heads, who filled in set forms in August of two thousand twenty-two, plus records kept by the homes. Answers from each nurse were grouped by home, so each home was the unit in the tests. Homes run for profit kept fewer nurses. Nurses who had stayed longer, and those with more strength to bounce back from strain, were more apt to stay on. Lee urges steps that build that strength and keep staff in post, which should also lift the care residents get.
pmc-12721552:
Nicole Pauli, Marco Roller, and Marcus Clauss study breeding seasons in camels and their relatives in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Seasonal breeding times births for good conditions, using day length as a cue. The team compares Old World camels with South American camelids such as llamas and alpacas.

They gathered conception data from past studies and zoo records. All species could breed year round, with domestic South American forms the least seasonal. Old World camels leaned toward breeding in long days, as expected. South American species leaned unexpectedly toward short days. The authors link this to climate and plant growth in their native habitat, and they note that day length seems to play a partial role.
pmc-12723952:
Naffisah Hassan and four co-authors measure health-related quality of life among urban children living in poverty in Malaysia. Quality of life here spans physical, psychological, family, friend, and school domains. Their 2025 survey took 855 children aged 7 to 17, under parental supervision. It asked how sex, age, number of siblings, internet access, and family healthy living style play into the scores.

Boys scored lower than girls in the psychological, family, peer, and school domains. Age groups differed in the physical, friend, and school domains. Sibling count split scores across all domains, with the no-sibling and two-sibling groups apart from the six-or-more group. Internet access and a healthy family lifestyle each tied to higher scores. The team links the map to child development theory and pitches it for intervention plans built for poor urban children.
pmc-12729152:
Pan Chen, Xiaoyan Yin, and Lei Ren build a model to predict an irregular heartbeat in a heart failure group. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, works at one hospital in Fuyang, China. The patients have heart failure with preserved pumping strength. The rhythm problem, atrial fibrillation, is a common and risky add-on for them.

Three hundred thirty-four patients were followed for one year to see who developed the rhythm fault. Data split into a larger build set and a smaller check set. A pruning method picked the key risk traits. Heart disease, body weight index, and a thyroid measure stood out. Checks of accuracy and fit judge how well the model can serve clinic use.
pmc-12730652:
Aruna Chandra Singh and co-authors present a sensitive test for immunity to cytomegalovirus in this 2025 paper. The virus often stays hidden in the body after first infection. Knowing who carries antibodies helps protect patients with weak immune systems. Current tests can miss small amounts of antibody.

Their sensor uses gold nanopillars that boost a fluorescent signal. Short peptides on the surface catch only antibodies against this virus. Tests showed the sensor could detect a small fraction of the antibodies found by a standard method. The device is small, fast, and can test many spots at once. The same design could be adapted for other infections where peptide capture works.
pmc-12731152:
Antonio Cigliola and eight co-authors review where treatment of muscle invasive bladder cancer is heading, in this 2025 paper. The standard, bladder removal plus platinum chemotherapy, cures some patients at high cost in toxicity and relapse. The review searched the major databases and conference records for trials adding newer weapons around surgery.

Immune checkpoint drugs added to chemotherapy raised the share of patients whose tumors vanished before surgery. Antibody drug conjugates, which deliver poison directly to cancer cells, and targeted drugs also showed promise alone and in combinations. Blood based tumor DNA and tumor gene profiles are being tested to pick who needs what. The authors judge the field mid transformation: encouraging results everywhere, but the biomarkers that would personalize the new arsenal are not yet proven.
pmc-12731452:
Raquel Diaz and a large clinical team described in two thousand twenty-five a rare wound complication after breast cancer surgery. A woman in her late sixties had a mastectomy with immediate reconstruction. Soon afterward, a large sterile ulcerating inflammation spread across the breast that antibiotics and repeated cleaning surgery failed to help.

Tissue study showed a dense white-cell infiltrate without infection, confirming post-surgical pyoderma gangrenosum, an immune-driven skin disease. Strong steroid treatment healed the wound fully, and final reconstruction succeeded. Breast surgeons learn a vital lesson: not every angry post-surgery wound is infected, and cutting further can make this condition worse.
pmc-12732652:
Florencia Gayo and colleagues reviewed oral bacteria and stroke in 2025. Gum disease may raise stroke risk through vessel inflammation. It may also promote clots and irregular heart rhythm. The team gathered population, antibody, and molecular studies. They searched for mouth bacteria and their products in patient samples. Blood, saliva, and removed clots were all examined. The question was whether oral germs shape stroke course. Outcomes and outlook after stroke were also weighed.

Blood antibodies to gum pathogens tracked with new strokes. They also tracked with poorer outlook after stroke. Clots held DNA from common mouth bacteria groups. Classic gum pathogen DNA was absent there, though. Antibodies to one gum pathogen inside clots marked weaker reopening. Other bacteria in clots marked more early harm. The authors support a real link, with caveats. Weak samples limit DNA proof, they note. Better molecular methods must clarify the mechanism.
pmc-12733052:
Simpson, Kelly, and Murphy develop an injectable gel that slowly releases a bone-friendly drug in this 2025 study. Weakened vertebrae are hard to treat locally: the bone is spongy, the spinal cord sits close, and material must stay put. Their gel flows as a liquid, then sets at body warmth inside the bone.

Tuning the gel recipe gave a set point of 29 degrees, easy injection, and kind behavior toward cells. Adding a bone-like mineral kept the gel stable for a month. Loaded with simvastatin, it released the drug over 35 days. In dishes, the release blocked bone-eating cell formation but did not boost bone building, a dosing puzzle the authors flag for future work.
pmc-12734752:
Dušan Arsić and co-authors pick the best base stock for fix welds by two rank ways at once. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Three stocks were tried for a build gear fix in one firm, all laid by hand arc welds. Four marks set the weights: wear track width, cost, mass loss, and laid coat hardness.

A best-worst weigh way set the mark weights, and two rank ways then ran in step. Both rank ways put the same stock, E DUR 600, on top. The team pitch the twin way check as a sound path for such firm picks.
pmc-12736552:
Daniil Golubchikov and co-authors present a 2025 materials study on making a common silicone rubber water-friendly. PDMS is a staple of microfluidic chips and medical devices, but water beads on its surface, which limits its use. Coatings of polyethylene glycol can fix that, and the team asked which chain length works best.

They grew the coating straight from the surface using short PEG chains of weight 400. The treated surface reached a very low contact angle, near nine degrees. Under flows mimicking arteries and capillaries, the coating held for three days with only modest drift. Roughness, stiffness, and clarity of the rubber stayed unchanged. The results favor short chains for stable, clear, water-loving surfaces in biomedical tools.
pmc-12736952:
Jumanah Alyoubi and a team including Paolo Nesi propose a way to make fake network traffic data that can train security tools, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. Tools that spot devices on a network learn poorly when some device types appear far less often than others in the training data.

Their method first maps how traffic features relate to each other, using three kinds of links. Those maps guide a generative model that makes new data while keeping the real patterns. A large language model then sets rules for each class, such as sane value ranges and links between features. The aim is synthetic traffic that looks real and stays valid. That could help guard key systems where real traffic data is scarce or private.
pmc-12737152:
Kamar and colleagues weigh full sleep drugs against local numbing for bone surgery in weak-brain patients in this twenty twenty-five review. Such patients face high rates of slow wake, wild mood, and mind fog after full sleep drugs. Bone work is among the most common rush surgery types in wards.

Inside, the review pulls proof from three decades of ward and lab work. Weak-brain patients showed far higher rates of slow wake and wild mood after full drugs. The paths run through brain scent shifts, blood flow slips, and swelling waves. Local and spine numbing kept brain flow steadier and cut such ills in the proof. The team urges local routes first when the case allows them.
pmc-12737752:
Flu strains that jump from animals to people can kill many of those they infect, and vaccines are the main shield.
