It rests on literature reviews, expert talks, and lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic. Speed of vaccine design improved greatly in that crisis, while fair access lagged.

The priorities call for vaccines that protect across many strains. They also seek better markers of protection, faster factory methods, and smarter strain picking. Trust and uptake need direct work with communities. The roadmap ties animal and human health into one plan.
pmc-12743152:
Yuan Shen and nine co-authors track how well stroke patients in China stayed on preventive drugs, in a 2025 study. After a stroke or a brief mini stroke, long term drugs lower the chance of another event. The team used a national stroke registry covering the years 2007 to 2018, with two large patient groups.

Sticking with all prescribed drugs rose over time. At three months after discharge, adherence grew from about sixty seven percent to about eighty one percent. At twelve months, it rose from about thirty five percent to about sixty percent. Gains were real but left a large gap at one year. The authors study which patient traits shaped adherence, to guide further quality work.
pmc-12745452:
MacDonald and co-authors gather what force and motion studies say about holding a handstand in this 2025 review. The handstand is a balance feat run from the wrists, and coaches teach it largely by feel. A shared biomechanical picture could sharpen that teaching.

The reviewers searched three databases to August 2025 and kept twenty-one studies that measured the handstand directly. Most mapped forces and joint motion; a third studied balance tactics, and a few measured muscle activity. The shared finding is a wrist strategy: tiny wrist corrections keep the body stacked and still. When that fails, shoulders, elbows, and hips join in a mixed rescue. Eyes closed clearly hurt stability, and bending the neck did too. Stronger gymnasts balanced better, and skill level and age shaped control. The authors offer the synthesis as a base for training and testing.
pmc-12746452:
Haidara Nadwa and four co-authors trace the first steps of a disease protein's misfolding in a 2025 paper. The protein is the main precursor of a serious amyloid disease, but the earliest trigger was unclear. Using two advanced simulation methods, they watched a disease-relevant fragment of it move over long simulated times and many temperatures. The free-energy maps told a clear story.

One helix came undone first, before the others loosened, while the whole bundle stayed compact. During that stage, a hidden aggregation-prone stretch briefly surfaced. The authors argue that this local exposure, not full unfolding, starts the disease process, and they name stabilizing that helix as a drug strategy.
pmc-12747352:
Spencer Poodiack Parsons, René Torenvlied, and Matteo Bodini offer a two thousand twenty-five simulation study of noise in human and algorithm decisions. Algorithms are praised for steady judgments, unlike variable humans. How steady but biased advice interacts with noisy human judgment was little explored.

Their agent-based model pairs decision makers with advisers of varying bias and noise. Surprisingly, human noise softened the harm of biased algorithms. Noisy advice pushed people back onto their own prior beliefs. When beliefs were polarized, people answered only matching advice. The results complicate the simple story that consistency is always better.
pmc-12748752:
Matheus Braga and seven co-authors test an old drug as an early treatment for brain injury in rats. No drug today truly treats traumatic brain injury. The drug, biperiden, blocks one signal type in the brain and has shown hints of protecting nerve cells. The team struck the rats' brains with a fluid pulse, then gave the drug in three doses over the first day.

Treated rats showed fewer dying nerve cells, lower blood levels of two damage markers, and calmer support cells than untreated rats. Movement scores on the first day did not differ clearly. The paper argues the drug's cell-level protection earns it further study for the hours right after injury.
pmc-12748852:
Aye Myint and seven co-authors compare dialysis policies for Brunei in a 2025 study. Kidney failure rates there are among the world's highest, and demand for treatment and skilled staff keeps rising. A policy favoring home-based dialysis on the abdomen has seen low uptake. The team modeled three policies, counting costs, health gains, and staffing needs over five years.

Both home-first options beat current practice on cost and health. The automated home option came out best from both government and wider social views. Current practice would need many more specialists and nurses, while home-first policies cut that need sharply. The authors urge planners to fold staffing into policy choices.
pmc-12750852:
Jiao Lin and co-authors present a 2025 study of what predicts embryo success after surgery for severe womb scarring. Intrauterine adhesions can block fertility, and cutting them away is standard before IVF. Even then, many transfers fail, and the reasons were not mapped.

The team reviewed 229 patients treated at one hospital from 2020 to 2024, all of whom had the surgery before embryo transfer. Repeat operations hurt both implantation and pregnancy chances. Years of infertility, adhesion scores, and fluid in the cavity also lowered implantation. Estrogen dosing patterns mattered for pregnancy itself. A thicker lining on transfer day protected both outcomes. The authors build the findings into a predictive model for counseling patients.
pmc-12751952:
Catherine Behzad and nine co-authors test a simple body index against fatty liver disease in northern Iran, in a 2025 study. The index, called the lipid accumulation product, combines waist size with blood fat levels. Fatty liver disease not tied to alcohol is common and often silent. The study drew on the second stage of the Amol Cohort Study and covered three thousand one hundred twenty adults. Liver fat was confirmed by ultrasound scans.

The team compared the index across thirds of the population and modeled its link with disease while adjusting for other factors. A second liver score was checked in parallel. If a cheap index flags likely cases well, clinics can reserve scans for those who need them most. The study supplies numbers for a region with little prior data.
pmc-12753752:
Magda Abouelanwar and Mohamed Mahmoud build a pull-based nano stuff that takes out harsh chromium and curcumin dye from waste water. Their 2025 study joins a changed sheet stuff with gel from psyllium seeds into one life-based soak good.

Chromium harms the guard kit of the body, the liver, and the kidneys. Plant-based foul goods such as curcumin show up more in plant waste water. Chem tests made firm that the two parts link firm. In strong acid states, take-out hit near ninety-eight in each hundred for chromium. It hit near ninety-seven in each hundred for curcumin. Soak-up tracked models that hint at mixed face coats, through charge pull, hydrogen bonds, pore fill, and a shift of the chromium form. The stuff kept more than ninety-three in each hundred of its work at the end of ten fresh-use rounds.
pmc-12756052:
Alex Youn, Abbott Gifford, and Ishaan Swarup assess compartment syndrome rates and risk factors in children's tibial tubercle fractures. Their 2025 retrospective study uses a nationwide paediatric hospital database covering twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-three.

Over sixty-eight hundred patients aged eighteen or younger with these fractures were included. About four percent carried codes for compartment syndrome, the related surgical release, or both. Only about one percent had both a syndrome diagnosis and the release procedure coded. Older and male patients showed higher rates in initial analysis. Compartment syndrome is a limb-threatening complication, yet its incidence in this specific paediatric fracture had been largely unexplored.
pmc-12763852:
You Wu and eight co-authors show that cinnamic acid, a spice plant compound, lifts insulin sense in prediabetic mice. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Poor insulin sense marks the early path to type two diabetes and ties to fat gain. The compound is rich in cinnamon and like foods, but its guard role at this early stage was vague.

Fat-fed mice got the compound for twelve weeks. Sugar tests got better, fast sugar fell, and fat gain eased. Gene and waste reads showed faster break-down of branched-chain amino acids in fat, with low marks in blood too. The compound also curbed fat swelling and revived a key sugar gate. The team backs food-based early guards.
pmc-12764252:
Huan Li and co-authors test two drugs, alone and paired, for guarding lungs during bowel cancer surgery, in a 2025 trial. Lung injury around surgery can spoil recovery from belly operations. Each drug had shown some lung protection on its own.

One hundred seventy-six patients at one hospital split into four groups: neither drug, each drug alone, or both. The main score was a ratio that grades how well oxygen crosses into blood at the end of dosing. Both drugs lifted that score on their own, and the pair interacted in the analysis. Other scores covered lung strain, later lung trouble, recovery quality, and inflammation markers.
pmc-12771752:
Whether two proteins touch steers much of cell life, and lab tests for each pair are slow and dear. Kamal Taha, writing solo in 2025, weighs a family of learning tools that guess the touches from data: forests and boosted trees that vote in packs. Four such tools get a deep review and a head-to-head trial. The pack design lets weak learners cover for each other, which lifts the calls past lone tools.

Two tools shared the crown. One, LightGBM, took the top score on all three test sets and scaled best to big data. Its close kin won on steadiness, with built-in brakes on overfitting. Plain forests read most clearly, a plus when labs must explain a call. Taha frames the four as a shelf of picks, traded off by size and need.
pmc-12772552:
Jane Ellen Carland and co-authors review the first three years of a short-stay assessment unit at St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney, in a 2025 paper. The PANDA Unit opened in 2020 for people who arrive at the emergency department drunk, drug-affected, or disturbed in behavior, often with other health or mental health needs. The team reviewed unit records from 2020 to 2023 and interviewed patients about their stay.

Over those years, 2,473 patients had 4,108 stays at the unit. Most stays involved alcohol or stimulant use, suicidal thoughts, or both, and the typical stay lasted about 21 hours. Most patients went home afterward, and about 15 percent returned within 28 days. The paper reports what the unit does, who it serves, and how patients felt about the care they received.
pmc-12775752:
Asmamaw Ketemaw Tsehay and co-authors published a study in 2025 on digital health records in Ethiopia. Electronic records can raise care quality, but most public facilities in the country still use paper. The team asked how willing health workers are to use the new system and what shapes that will.

The survey covered 322 workers at five facilities in a northwestern city that had adopted the system. About seventy-three percent showed good acceptance of the records. Ease of use was the strongest single predictor of acceptance. Long work experience, owning a personal computer, and past training in the system all helped. Unhappy pay pulled acceptance down. The authors call for better system design, targeted training, and wider access to computers.
pmc-12784852:
Nine researchers led by Kailun Ma gauged inbreeding and gene variety in Xinjiang Brown cattle, one of China's five big dual-purpose breeds raised for both milk and beef. They read gene chips from seven hundred fifty cattle on three breeding farms. Two yardsticks were compared: family records and long matching gene stretches in the DNA itself.

Gene variety ran fairly high overall, and one farm showed the richest mix. DNA-based inbreeding ran higher than record-based figures, and close kin pairs appeared within the herd. Short matching stretches were the most common, hinting at older shared ancestry. The authors say the data can guide mating plans that guard the breed's variety.
pmc-12785952:
Zou, Zhou, and Zhang reviewed tiny gene regulators in diabetic kidney disease for this paper from twenty twenty-five. The disease is a major cause of kidney failure worldwide. MicroRNAs are short RNA strands that tune gene activity. Their levels shift in set patterns inside the kidney's many cell types.

Some microRNAs drive scarring by boosting a well-known growth pathway. Others protect the kidney's filters and surfaces by holding scarring back. Because these strands are stable in blood and urine, they may serve as painless markers of damage. The review maps the cell-by-cell networks now known. It also weighs their promise as tests and as drug targets for more precise care.
pmc-12789452:
Li and co-authors present a detector that helps drones spot objects using both visible and heat images, in this 2025 paper. Such detection aids traffic control and disaster response in smart cities. Heat images often blur object edges, though, which makes targets hard to separate from their background.

The system adds three parts to a standard detector. One part sharpens edges, one merges features at several scales, and one blends the two image types using attention. Together they help the drone find objects of many sizes even as flight height changes the view. Tests in the paper weigh how much each part adds to accuracy.
pmc-12796952:
Hiba Abdelkafi and co-authors present a 2025 study of how watching video changes the feedback students give each other in sport. Peer feedback helps learning, and video is widely used to support it. What video does to the feedback itself, rather than to final skill, was unexamined.

Forty-one sports science students learned the long jump over four sessions, then worked in pairs. One jumped while the other watched live and gave thirty seconds of feedback. The observer then watched a recording and gave thirty seconds more. Video viewing nearly doubled the amount of feedback given. The team also sorted comments into descriptive and prescriptive kinds and checked the advice for accuracy. The findings show video reshapes the coaching talk that drives learning.
pmc-12803752:
A large team of co-authors reports a case in two thousand twenty-five of spine surgery done in two stages through a scope, under local anesthesia. The patient, a man of seventy-five, had two narrowings squeezing nerves in his lower back at once. Standard care would fuse the spine under general anesthesia, a heavy option for an older, high-risk patient.

Scans showed one narrowing beside the spinal canal and another at the exit hole for the nerve root, caused by a slipped vertebra that was stable. The team freed each spot in turn with full endoscopic surgery while the patient stayed awake. The case shows the stepwise route can find and treat both lesions.
pmc-12805752:
Min Woo Lee and ten co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a pre surgery step for bile duct cancer near the liver. Big liver cuts are the cure path, but the left over liver can fail. Blocking a portal vein branch ahead of time grows the safe remnant. The team looks back at patients with the high forms of the disease over a decade.

Three groups form: cut with no block, cut after block, and block with no cut. Survival was alike for the two cut groups. The no cut group fared far worse. Age and the remnant share after the block tracked with survival in both block groups. The step makes big cuts safer, they say.
pmc-12812752:
Nora Berg Bjørnevoll and Karl Bjørnar Alstadhaug read how well a drug keeps multiple sclerosis quiet at a Norwegian hospital. Their study deals with cladribine, an immune tuning drug for the relapsing form of the disease. Few watch based studies have weighed it. The team read charts of all patients treated at Nordland Hospital from twenty eighteen to late twenty twenty-four. Sixty patients took at least one round.

The mark was NEDA-3: no sign of disease acts on three fronts at once. Most had the relapsing form; two had other early forms. The team tracked how long that quiet held. Readers who treat this disease get real ward proof next to trial data.
pmc-12813152:
Yueran Li and co-authors present a study, published in 2025, of how blood levels of the antifungal drug voriconazole relate to benefit and harm in elderly patients. The drug fights invasive fungal infections, but its levels swing widely between people, and older patients are fragile. Too little invites treatment failure; too much poisons the liver.

The retrospective study covered thirty-seven elderly patients whose drug levels were monitored during therapy. Liver markers rose after treatment while inflammation markers fell. Drug concentration correlated negatively with albumin and calcium, among other measures. The authors use these links to argue for level-guided dosing tuned to the elderly, rather than one dose for all.
pmc-12815952:
Wild fruit trees feed many poor households, and Tesfaye Gebre and co-authors examine one of them, Bauhinia thonningii, in northern Ethiopia. They collected pods and seeds from two zones in the Tselemti district, warm moist lowlands and cooler mid-highlands, and compared their shapes and food value. The team measured pod size, seed counts, nutrients, and mineral content.

Zone mattered for nearly every trait. Lowland pods grew longer, near 18.3 centimeters, carried about 51 seeds, and held more protein, fat, fiber, and minerals than highland pods. The seeds were the richest part, reaching about 30.7 percent protein in the lowlands, while highland samples held slightly more moisture. The authors link the lowland edge to warmth, humidity, and richer soil movement. They argue the tree deserves a place in food planning, and that knowing how zone shapes its value can guide its protection, farming, and breeding.
pmc-12816252:
Xinmei Li, Minghong Qu, Haizhi Li, and Te Li simulate blood levels for two potassium supplements given together to heart emergency patients, in work from twenty twenty-five. Low potassium threatens the heart, and pairing a slow release chloride tablet with citrate granules is a common fix. Dose timing guidance was thin.

Records from three hundred thirty patients at one hospital fed a standard curve analysis. Peak times grew with dose count, from about five hours to about six. Each dose lifted blood potassium by a set small step. Total exposure rose in a near straight line with dose. Data fit a one compartment model. The authors offer the numbers as a base for safe, rational dosing.
pmc-12817452:
Monica Hruzd and co-authors report a 2025 study of ankle sense and movement. Proprioception is the body's sense of joint position. Its loss links to poor balance and falls in older adults. Standard tests of that sense can be clumsy and blunt. The team built a sensor-based tracking game for the ankle. A moving target on screen guides real-time foot tracking.

Nineteen young adults and ten older adults played the game. A small gyroscope taped to the foot bone tracked motion. Each leg tried three tracks of rising difficulty. Vibration on leg muscles disturbed the sense on purpose. The design lets deficits show as tracking errors. Rehab teams get a sensitive, game-like measure that patients may enjoy. Minor deficits that old tests miss could surface early, when training helps most.
pmc-12821952:
Noah Olasehinde, Patricia Ajayi, and Oluwaseun Oloyede studied in 2025 why Nigerian households cook with the fuels they do, and what that costs their lungs. Nigeria produces oil, yet much of its population still cooks over firewood and other polluting solid fuels. The smoke drives indoor air pollution and acute respiratory infections. The team analyzed a nationally representative household survey covering more than twenty-six thousand homes.

Because families commonly stack several fuels rather than switching cleanly, the authors modeled fuel choice with a method that allows that behavior. They then linked the primary fuel to respiratory illness in the household. The work connects energy poverty to health in hard numbers. It also shows which household factors push families toward gas or electricity, giving policymakers levers beyond simply urging cleaner cooking.
pmc-12822052:
Valérie Schuermans and co-authors check whether two laboratories, measuring neck motion their own ways, arrive at the same story, in a 2025 study. When the neck extends, each vertebra contributes in sequence; that sequence may reveal dysfunction, but tracking it on moving X-ray films is hard. Two centres built independent tracking methods. Twelve volunteers without symptoms, young and older, bent their necks under each protocol.

One centre let people move freely; the other guided the motion. Twenty-six frames from the second half of each extension were analysed both ways. Agreement statistics, correlations, and difference plots compared the segment-by-segment sequences from the fourth to seventh neck vertebrae. Agreement ran high despite the protocol differences, the authors report. Cross-validation like this is what turns a research measurement into one clinics could trust.
pmc-12823752:
Min Wu and a large team of co-authors examine star shaped brain cells under long term low blood flow in a 2025 mouse study. White matter suffers most when brain blood flow stays chronically low, and astrocytes help drive the resulting myelin damage. Using a surgical model that narrows both carotid arteries, the team inspected astrocyte interiors with electron microscopy.

Activated astrocytes in the brain's main white matter tract showed heavy stress: altered mitochondria, fragmented internal membranes, swollen compartments, plus stepped up waste eating and recycling. Deleting a membrane protein called caveolin-1 only in astrocytes softened all these stress signs. Most importantly, it also reduced myelin loss. The protein emerges as a lever on astrocyte tolerance.
pmc-12831252:
Pan Wang and colleagues studied a small RNA switch in glioblastoma in 2025. Glioblastoma is a highly malignant brain tumour. Low oxygen makes it more aggressive. A methyl mark can silence one small RNA. The team traced how that silencing helps tumours. Oxygen sensing played a central role.

Public data, patient tissue, and cell work were combined. Silencing lifted a chain of active proteins. That chain strengthened tumour growth signals. Blocking the chain weakened tumour traits again. Treated mice lived longer in tests. Cell results matched the animal findings. The authors suggest epigenetic treatment ideas. Personal treatment approaches may follow later.
pmc-12831352:
Jiajin Hu and nine co-authors follow pregnant women trimester by trimester to see how physical activity relates to preterm birth, in a two thousand twenty-five prospective cohort study. Exercise in pregnancy is encouraged, yet the timing and dose questions persist.

Two thousand eighty women were recruited early and followed through delivery. In every trimester, the most active third had markedly lower preterm birth odds than the least active. A cumulative score rewarding sustained activity showed a dose-response pattern, strongest for medically indicated preterm births. Spontaneous preterm birth showed no such link. The authors argue for guiding activity from early pregnancy and sustaining it throughout.
pmc-12835052:
Spent catalyst from oil cracking ends its life in dumps, though its bones are the stuff cement loves. Paweł Niewiadomski and five co-authors ground Polish refinery waste into cement pastes in 2025, swapping it for up to a fifth of the cement. The waste is near nine-tenths glass and alumina, and bench tests showed it hungry to bind lime, the mark of a true cement helper.

Pastes with the swap set as firm as plain ones, and their crush strength rose by up to a sixth at the best shares. Flow, bend, and soak stayed near par. Three water shares told the same tale. The team frame the swap as a double win: less dump fill, less fresh cement burned.
pmc-12835452:
Yuhong Liu and co-authors report a single center study from 2025 on advanced liver cancer. The cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma. Patients received immune checkpoint inhibitors plus targeted drugs and radiotherapy as first treatment. The team asked whether an immune score and tumor growth in the portal vein could predict survival.

The study covered 143 patients, split by score and by vein involvement. Patients with low risk scores lived longer without the disease getting worse. Patients with tumor in the vein did worse. Those with both risk factors had the shortest survival. Using the score and vein status together predicted survival better than either one alone.
pmc-12837952:
Çetinkaya and Batırel review a last-resort surgery for leaking lymph in the chest in a 2025 case series. Chylothorax, where milky lymph fluid floods the chest, usually yields to diet changes or tying the main duct through the chest. When anatomy is altered or both sides leak, those routes can fail, so the surgeons instead tied the duct's root, the cisterna chyli, through the abdomen.

Fourteen patients treated between 2011 and 2025 had stubborn, high-output leaks after earlier measures failed. Half the leaks followed surgery; others stemmed from blood cancers or no clear cause. Tying the root stopped the leak in eleven of the fourteen, with a median hospital stay of nine days after surgery. Follow-up stretched past six years for half the group.
pmc-12840352:
Prasanta Bandyopadhyay, Samidha Shetty, and Gordon Brittan sketch in 2025 a theory of comparative, evidence-based model choice. Decision theory has been shaped by subjective Bayesians and frequentist schools. Evidential approaches often keep a subjective tilt, which the authors reject for their new account.

On their account, models are judged by how well data and background support them, compared by relative distance. The framework aims to serve both prediction and explanation as twin goals. They identify statistical tools to measure that support. The theory is contrasted with interval probability approaches that lack the dual aims.
pmc-12840952:
Paula Chappell and four co-authors pilot a method for learning why people die by suicide in Cornwall, a mostly rural and coastal area of England. Their study came out in 2025. They tested whether recordings of official inquests could yield useful lessons during the pandemic period.

The team analyzed thirty inquests chosen evenly across the months studied. Common risk factors included isolation, anxiety, broken daily routines, low mood, and money strain. Working from home in a rural area affected both patients and health staff. Lockdown pressures hit hardest those already at risk of poor mental health. The authors call for earlier spotting of decline, trauma-informed care for all ages, and fairer community support.
pmc-12843052:
Nine radiation oncologists argue an ignored structure deserves protection in cervical cancer treatment in a paper from 2025. The bulboclitoral complex matters for sexual health but appears in no planning guideline as an organ at risk. The team re-planned twenty patients two ways: standard, and with the structure outlined and spared. Doses to the complex were then compared directly.

Sparing cut the median maximum dose from about forty-nine to about twenty-nine gray. The share of the structure receiving the full prescription dose fell from over a third to zero. Other targets stayed covered by design. The authors ask whether sparing improves patients' sexual health. That clinical question now needs a trial.
pmc-12843252:
Federica Cariati and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five retrospective study of semen quality in men with blood cancers. The hormone system behind sperm production is disturbed in these diseases. Whether each cancer type harms sperm in its own pattern matters for fertility saving.

Records came from men who banked sperm at one Italian center before treatment. Earlier work shows leukemia often damages semen clearly. Lymphoma results are mixed, with some men fully normal before therapy. Comparing types helps counsel each patient individually. Fertility teams get disease-specific grounding for personal preservation plans.
pmc-12844052:
Ahmad Ali and colleagues published a 2025 study of antibiotic resistance on Florida beef farms. They collected fecal samples from cows and calves. Nine cow-calf operations of different sizes took part. Thousands of E. coli isolates were tested. Eight antibiotics were used in the tests.

Resistance was common for several older antibiotics. Nearly half the isolates resisted some of them. Resistance stayed low for a few other drugs. Farm size comparisons were a central aim. Such data show where stewardship matters most. Resistant farm bacteria can reach people through food and water. Monitoring herds helps protect both animal and human treatment options.
pmc-12849252:
Qiajun Du and three co-authors show that how much a liver cancer patient's inflammation scores wobble between visits predicts survival, in this 2025 study. The scores alone say less than their instability does. The cohort held 780 patients, of whom 528 lived past the ninety-day mark used for analysis. Blood tests from the first ninety days supplied the wobble measure.

Each standard rise in the wobble of the systemic immune-inflammation index came with about twenty-six percent higher death risk. Patients in the top quarter of wobble faced about seventy percent higher risk than the bottom quarter. Adding wobble to standard forecasts sharpened accuracy at one and two years. The authors call for prospective checks of the marker.
pmc-12853752:
Guoquan Wen, Yi Zeng, and Yu Sun build, in twenty twenty-five, a survival model for early triple-negative breast cancer based on how inflammation changes after surgery. This cancer type lacks three common drug targets, which limits therapy. Baseline inflammation markers link to prognosis, but how they evolve after surgery was underexplored. The team reviewed two hundred ninety-six patients who had surgery then chemotherapy. Endpoints were time free of disease and survival from breast cancer specifically.

They used the yearly slope of inflammation indices as a new feature. Values were log-transformed, and overlapping predictors were screened out. Survival models were paired with time-dependent accuracy curves, resampling checks, and an explanation method that attributes risk to each feature.
pmc-12855852:
Huang and nine co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on how distant tumors reshape fat storage in the liver. Cancer acts body-wide, sending factors that alter far organs. The team use an advanced light microscope to read liver chemistry in tumor-bearing models. They find an odd buildup of vitamin A-rich fat droplets in the liver. Deeper spectral reads show higher unsaturation and abnormal vitamin A forms. Blocking secretion from the tumors erases those liver changes. A protein in tumor-shed vesicles emerges as a key mediator of the effect.

The findings reveal a systemic arm of cancer progression. Tumor-driven fat and vitamin A shifts may aid spread and blunt therapy. The authors frame the liver changes as a new facet of metastasis biology.
pmc-12864952:
Saddaf Razzaq, Aayesha Riaz, Naila Siddique, and four colleagues build a DNA vaccine for a poultry plague in this two thousand twenty-five study. Newcastle disease virus is a top threat to chickens worldwide. Normal vaccines cut deaths but do not fully stop infection or shedding of the virus. A vaccine matched to the local strain may do better. The team took the fusion gene from a genotype seven strain found near Rawalpindi, Pakistan, and cloned it into a DNA plasmid.

They checked the gene was in place and cells made the protein. Then one hundred twenty chickens were split into four groups: the DNA vaccine, an empty plasmid, a salt solution control, and an untouched control. Blood antibody levels were tracked for four weeks, then the birds faced the live genotype seven virus. The study tests whether a strain-matched DNA shot can protect where standard vaccines leak.
pmc-12876152:
RuiFang Lyu reviews how deep learning is reshaping the reading of brain-wave recordings, in a paper whose text dates to 2025. The recordings, called EEG, are cheap and painless but noisy and hard to interpret. Neural networks promise faster, more accurate reads for clinics.

The review tours five model families, from image-style networks to memory-equipped and attention-based designs, plus hybrids. Uses covered include diagnosing brain disorders, tracking recovery, assessing mental health, and driving brain-computer interfaces. Three obstacles recur: signals vary wildly between people, labeled data are scarce, and the models cannot explain themselves. Lyu closes with trends and open problems, aiming to give newcomers a map of a fast-growing crossroads.
pmc-12879752:
Sirlei Pereira Nunes and four co-authors published this study in 2025. It follows heart valve surgery patients in Brazil and asks how they themselves rate their quality of life over time. The patients were cared for under a structured care line model at a large heart center.

A psychology team checked each patient three times: before surgery, just after the intensive care stay, and six months after going home. Patients filled in two standard quality of life forms. Scores rose strongly by the late check, above all for movement, pain, self-care, and mood. Several parts of the longer form, such as energy and general health, also improved. The authors say the gains support team-based, long-term follow-up built around the patient's own view.
pmc-12907352:
YiWen Chen published a 2025 study of how autistic children play and interact with others, read as sequences of behavior during structured play time. How those sequences flow, and why they stall, was not clear. Most earlier assessments read the child at one static point. The present study reads the actions in their flow, as a live stream.

Chen observed sixty autistic children and forty typically developing peers, with video coding and physiological signs in hand. The autistic group showed far less complex sequences of behavior. Their play fell into a loop of avoidance and rigid actions. A classification tool found three play patterns: high interaction, medium interaction with rigidity, and low interaction with high avoidance. The low group benefited least from intervention. Chen concludes that the sequences can serve as targets for care plans.
pmc-12927252:
Yang and Shen examine in 2025 how streetscape visuals link to public emotions around West Lake in Hangzhou. Streets shape daily life and quality of life, yet their emotional pull is hard to measure. They paired social media posts with street view images from two historic districts.

Posts on Sina Weibo were sorted into positive and negative sentiment. Street images were segmented into nineteen elements, and seven visual space measures were computed. Rider elements and enclosure tied positively to emotion, while traffic lights and openness tied negatively. Effects also varied with building type, which suggests design cues that planners can test.
pmc-12929552:
Channapur and a large team hunt in twenty twenty-five the genes that let tropical maize roots withstand aluminium poisoning in acid soils. The metal stunts roots and caps yields across the tropics. Growing two hundred and fifty diverse maize lines in water culture under a tuned dose, they measured root length, area, and branching, then scanned the genome for linked markers.

Stress shrank most root traits by a quarter to over a third, while roots thickened slightly. Dozens of markers across eight chromosomes explained a tenth to a fifth of the variation, clustering into hotspots on two chromosomes. Candidate genes included detox and transport helpers known from stress biology. The authors offer the spots as targets for breeding aluminium-tough maize.
pmc-12973452:
Badr El Kassimi and Abdelkarim Kharroubi review varicose vein surgery at a regional hospital in Agadir, Morocco, in a 2025 study. The paper's catalog title is in French, while the text itself is presented in English. Varicose veins are widened, twisted veins, common in rich countries and a frequent reason for clinic visits in Morocco too. The team looked back at all patients operated on between April 2021 and September 2022.

Fifteen patients had surgery, with an average age of about forty-four and a near-even split of men and women. Records covered the reason for the visit, a standard severity class, and the operation performed. Leg pain with heaviness was the main complaint. Small reviews like this document local practice and help hospitals plan vascular services.
pmc-13037652:
Yasmin and five co-authors test plant oils against Salmonella in chickens, in work from twenty twenty-five. Salmonella in broiler chickens harms bird health and can reach people through food. Plant essential oils are being tried as an option besides antibiotics.

More than a hundred chicks were split into nine groups. Diets held cinnamon bark oil or eucalyptus oil from the first day. Birds were then infected with two Salmonella types. The team counted bacteria in droppings and tracked weight gain, feed use, immune response to vaccines, and gut shape. The design tests both germ control and growth effects in one trial.
pmc-13116352:
Milagros Alvarado and co-authors map community mental health care in three provinces of northern Peru, in a 2026 study. National reforms aim to move care out of big hospitals and into local community centers tied to primary care. How that shift lands in rural Andean districts was little known. The team reviewed policy, ran focus groups, and interviewed 31 providers, users, and community members.

Local views of mental health mixed cultural beliefs, social norms, and money worries. pmc-13118352:

pmc-13126852:
Kelsey Reider and six co-authors share a data set on microbes in soil left behind by a shrinking glacier, in a paper published in twenty twenty-six. Some ground was freed recently; some had been bare since the Little Ice Age. Each sample was tagged by season, height, and exposure age. DNA was pulled and a marker gene was read to name the microbes. The set is offered for studying how ecosystems form on new land.
pmc-13130752:

pmc-13135552:
Jiazhennan Zhang and five colleagues published a 2026 study on a gene called SNRPB2 and its role in breast cancer. Laboratory tests on breast cancer cells then probed what the gene does, and RNA sequencing traced the pathways it affects. Their findings link SNRPB2 both to control of the cell cycle and to how the tumor interacts with the immune system.
pmc-13139452:
Pulling names, dates, and figures out of scanned business documents is slow work when layouts vary and pages are stained or stamped. pmc-13144552:
Lijuan Nie and eight co-authors test pachymic acid, a compound from a medicinal fungus, against fatty liver disease in cells and mice, in this 2026 study. pmc-13147452:
Jaime Mazón-Ruiz and three colleagues appraise a rare success story in dialysis care: the PISCES trial, which found that high-dose fish oil cut cardiovascular events in hemodialysis patients. Most prevention trials in this population have failed, so the authors ask what PISCES did differently.

pmc-13147652:
Christina Elling-Lueder and co-authors report a 2026 study of how social anxiety shapes the inner, mental side of sexuality in adults. Their sample held 242 adults with the disorder, compared with controls without it.

Men in the group differed from women on some scores. The authors say these mental patterns may help explain sexual problems and can guide care.
pmc-13148652:

Transcripts were coded in stages, from open notes to focused themes. The analysis names what helped participation, time, trust, clear benefit, and what blocked it, then compares those factors with earlier literature. Lessons target recruiters directly.
pmc-13153252:
Bennett Amaechi and six co-authors tested toothpaste formulas against early decay in a 2026 lab study. Early cavities begin as soft spots in enamel, and the right paste may harden them again. The team compared pastes built on calcium hypophosphite, on hydroxyapatite, and on standard fluoride.

The authors present the blend as a strong option for repair of early lesions.
pmc-13153652:
García-Gimenez and a large team review lab models that mimic sepsis to test drugs against stray histones in twenty twenty-six. Flat cell dishes miss tissue layout, and rodents translate poorly to humans.

Three dimensional models step in: organoids, printed tissues, and organ chips with flow. Chips add shear, oxygen slopes, and cross organ talk. These rigs can screen histone blocking agents at scale. Drugs like heparin kin and anti histone antibodies are named. The team sees a path to sharper intensive care.
pmc-13157752:
Fati Kirakoya-Samadoulougou and her team set out a protocol for a review of too-large baby births. Their plan from twenty twenty-six covers births in low and middle income lands. Babies born too large put both mothers and newborns at risk at birth. Which risk factors count most in poorer lands has had too little study.

For each cause, the team will work out its population attributable fraction. Those shares show where work to stop such births buys the most health. Diabetes, body weight, and access to care are likely causes in view. The protocol fixes the methods before any results are pulled in.
pmc-13159752:
Nanyuan Jiang and co-authors report a small breast repair in a 2026 paper. A 68-year-old woman had a sebaceous cyst beside the nipple that grew over six years. Removing it left a defect of about two centimeters across.

The authors add a literature review and praise the method's fit, mild impact, and hidden scarring.
pmc-13167252:
Cornelius Bauer and five co-authors test a new radiation dose sensor in a 2026 study. During electron beam therapy, the dose at the skin surface is hard to watch live. It stayed linear, steady across dose rates, and even from all angles, with repeat readings tight. Surface doses on test blocks and a body phantom matched chamber and film readings within a few percent. The authors judge the sensor fit for clinic use and for live checks on patients.
pmc-13169152:

The search ran across thirty-two antigens of one virus and its kin. Readers get a map of mimic spots that could drive self harm in the brain.
pmc-13174952:
Amol Mehta and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, emergency stent treatment for a fast-moving form of pressure buildup inside the skull that threatens sight. In this fulminant form of idiopathic intracranial hypertension, swelling at the optic nerve can blind a patient within weeks.

The team searched four databases and found seven studies covering twenty-three patients treated urgently with a stent in the brain's venous channel. Patients were mostly young women with severe swelling and fading vision, often after medicines had failed. Every case had a narrowed channel with a pressure gap across it. After stenting, swelling eased in nearly all, and vision held steady or improved.
pmc-13175752:
Jung-Hyun Kim presents a 2026 review proposing a life course nutrition strategy for Korean teens and young adults. These years set habits that echo for decades, yet eating in this group is shaped by school, first jobs, and tight budgets. Generic advice rarely moves behavior.

Following quality rules for narrative reviews, the author searched the literature from 2015 to mid 2025 plus policy papers from global and Korean agencies. The synthesis ties nutrition to behavioral science: what nudges choice, what sustains change. The proposed model is community based and personal, with support that follows a person across life stages rather than ending with a single program. Forty sources anchor the plan.
pmc-13177652:
Graham Mecredy and Jessica Jordao describe a training program that builds health data skills inside Indigenous communities in a 2024 article. Population health data can serve Indigenous peoples well only under Indigenous data sovereignty, and a baseline of data knowledge is usually demanded before access is granted, a gate that itself creates inequity. Their institute created a training program to lower that gate from the community side.

Graduates gain the knowledge to request, govern, and use health data for their own organizations' priorities. Capacity built inside communities, rather than advice delivered from outside, is the program's defining aim.
pmc-13179452:
Mahmoud Bahari and a team of co-authors test how well single-shade fillings match tooth color, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. They worked on thirty-two pulled front teeth with deep class III holes cut on both sides. Each hole was filled with Omnichroma or a multi-shade resin, with or without a thin blocker layer.

Color was judged by eye with a shade guide and by a light-measuring device. Skipping the blocker hurt the match for the multi-shade resin in large holes. Adding it changed nothing for Omnichroma. The single-shade resin also matched better by eye. The findings guide filling choice for front-tooth repairs.
pmc-13183752:
Mehmet Akif Sahin and six co-authors test bone fixation methods in a lab study from twenty twenty-six. Breaks near the top of the shin bone, outside the joint, are hard to fix. A short top fragment and a wide bone canal make a central nail prone to tilt.

The team used fifteen model shin bones with the same standard break. One group got a nail alone. One got a nail plus two Poller screws. One got a nail plus a small one side plate. They compared how stable each build was under load. The results can help surgeons pick the best add on when a nail alone may not hold alignment.
pmc-13184552:
Sung and Cheong review quantum biology from mechanisms to medicine. Quantum effects were long thought too weak in warm, noisy cells. Proof now shows they shape many living processes. Effects hold coherence, tunneling, and spin dynamics.

The review sums up fresh lab, math, and theory advances. Tools hold fast spectroscopy, quantum sensors, and simulations. Systems span light capture, enzyme action, and DNA pairing. Sense organs and cell power chains also show quantum roles. Disease links and medical uses are mapped in depth. The team sees quantum tools as a rising medical frontier.
pmc-13196252:
Nabila Y Al-Tamimi and colleagues present a 2026 case report on low vision care. Their patient was a 70-year-old woman with age-related macular degeneration in both eyes. That disease harms the center of the retina, the light-sensing layer, and blurs central sight.

Tests showed weak distance and near sight, central blind spots, and warped vision. Glasses alone gave only slight gains. Care then added a small telescope for distance and a lighted hand magnifier for reading. Staff also advised home changes and glare filters, plus food guidance and checks with a grid card. At three months her vision held steady. The case shows how tailored aids can help a person stay independent.
pmc-13196952:
The editors of PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases update an earlier concern notice about a study of ticks in Algeria. The study reported finding bacteria that cause relapsing fever and other diseases in soft ticks. After it appeared, questions arose about its ethics approval. The journal looked into whether the work met its research ethics rules.

The ticks were gathered over three years from farms, gull nests, and animal shelters across four Algerian areas. The paper named a ministry committee as its approver but gave no permit numbers. The lead author said the work followed the laws of Algeria and France. The editors found the papers provided too thin to settle the matter. This note records the state of that open concern for readers.
pmc-13197652:
Ricardo Fernández-Ferreira and colleagues present a 2026 case report on stomach cancer spread to the skin. Skin spread from stomach cancer is rare and marks late disease. Their patient also carried the HER2 marker, a growth signal that targeted drugs can block.

A three-drug regimen included the HER2-targeted drug trastuzumab. By the sixth cycle the scalp patch had cleared fully, and the back lump had shrunk by more than half. Gains held at one year. Fewer than twenty such scalp and neck cases appear in English reports.
pmc-13198052:

For preventing a slide in care needs, the cost was about 27,200 euros per case prevented, with better odds. Patients who completed at least fifteen sessions fared better in the value math. Outpatient delivery looked cost-effective against matched controls. The authors call the program more effective but pricier than standard care.
pmc-13198452:

The treated group improved on ten of nineteen face-reading measures. Depression and anxiety scores also eased. The group grew faster at spotting disgusted and neutral faces and misread neutral faces as angry less often. Better fear reading tracked better mood.
pmc-13199852:

Spinal fluid held many white cells, with eosinophils at about six percent. Tests found MOG antibodies in blood and spinal fluid, confirming the diagnosis. The authors speculate that allergy-type signals drew eosinophils into the lesions.
pmc-13202152:

pmc-13202752:

The team ran seven group talks with twenty-one doctors. Three themes stood out. One was what doctors know about drug-proof germs. A second was how they choose to script in real clinics. A third was how they react to a new tool that shows each doctor their own scripting record. Habits varied a lot from doctor to doctor. Patient demand and time pressure both played a part. The authors say feedback tools help, but only if doctors trust the data behind them.
pmc-13207752:

pmc-13210452:

pmc-13210652:

pmc-13212552:

pmc-13212652:

pmc-13213552:

pmc-13214152:

pmc-13214352:

pmc-13215552:

pmc-13216152:

pmc-13219652:

pmc-13221752:

pmc-13222052:

pmc-13222552:

pmc-13222852:

pmc-13222952:

pmc-13223352:

pmc-13223852:

pmc-13224052:

pmc-13227152:

pmc-13229352:

pmc-13230852:

pmc-13230952:

pmc-13231152:

pmc-13232452:

pmc-13232852:

pmc-13232952:

pmc-13233352:

pmc-13233552:

pmc-13233652:

pmc-13234052:

pmc-13234552:

pmc-13235252:

pmc-13236552:

pmc-13236852:

pmc-13237252:

pmc-13237452:

pmc-13238552:

pmc-13238852:

pmc-13238952:

pmc-13239052:

pmc-13239352:

pmc-13239552:

pmc-13239852:

pmc-13240052:

pmc-13240152:

pmc-13240252:

pmc-13242352:

pmc-13242752:

pmc-13242852:

pmc-13244552:

pmc-13245752:

pmc-13250252:

pmc-13251652:
Emanuele Marzetti, Riccardo Calvani, and Hélio Jose Coelho-Junior question a ward habit in geriatric care in their 2026 commentary. Staff often urge older inpatients to eat at least the second plate, usually the protein-rich course, to protect muscle during recovery. The authors ask whether that protein-first push is enough on its own.

They review why intake falls short in hospital: appetite loss, altered taste, swallowing trouble, dry mouth, and chronic illness all play a part. Evidence supports protein above the standard allowance for older adults, and more still during illness or injury. Yet the commentary stresses that total energy matters just as much, because without enough calories the body burns protein for fuel instead of building muscle. Their message is that nutritional care must count energy and protein together, not plates alone.
pmc-13251852:
Elizabeth Tanjong Ghogomu and a large team map the evidence on social prescribing for older adults in a 2026 evidence and gap map. Social prescribing connects patients in primary care with non-medical help, such as exercise groups, benefits advice, or community activities. It targets the social needs that medicine alone cannot fix, from loneliness to money trouble.

The team searched a wide set of databases and sources up to November 2023 with no language limits. Eligible evidence meant systematic reviews and studies with comparison groups that tested whether social prescribing improved wellbeing in older adults. Screening was done independently by two reviewers, with disagreements settled by discussion. The finished map shows where solid effectiveness evidence exists and where it is missing. Decision-makers can use it to fund programs on proven ground and to commission research where the map shows empty space.
pmc-13252752:
Napat Jantaraprasit and a large team build a sharper palm oil forecast for Thailand in this 2026 study. Yield forecasts guide farm choices and climate planning, but coarse weather data and bias in crop models have limited their accuracy.

Their pipeline first shrinks weather and climate data to fine local scale, then feeds a process-based crop simulator whose errors a machine learning model corrects. In Surat Thani province, the crop model alone badly overshot yields, while the hybrid cut the error by nearly two-thirds. Seasonal forecasts reached eight months ahead with useful skill. Long-range climate runs suggest southern Thai palm output is fairly resilient, dipping mid-century before steadying.
pmc-13253152:
Jarrod Ludwig and colleagues read salmon diets in the fats of their eggs in this 2026 study from California. In 2020, several salmon populations were found short of thiamine, vitamin B1, and the team wanted to know whether what mothers ate at sea explained the shortfall.

From 2020 to 2022 they collected unfertilised eggs from Chinook salmon, coho salmon, and steelhead, plus the ocean prey those fish eat, and profiled fats in both. Eggs whose fat pattern matched a herring-rich diet carried more thiamine. Eggs matching anchovy or krill diets ran lower. Fat quality, not quantity, drove egg thiamine, a warning as ocean prey mixes shift.
pmc-13253452:
Luca Carlofrancesco Ammoni and colleagues describe a young woman with lung cancer who could not swallow her targeted therapy in a 2026 case report. She was thirty, with metastatic ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer, a subtype that strikes young non-smokers. Bulky lymph nodes in her neck squeezed her esophagus shut, a problem because lorlatinib, the drug of choice, exists only as tablets.

The team crushed the tablets and gave the standard daily dose through a nasogastric feeding tube. Within days the neck nodes shrank visibly, swallowing returned, and she resumed eating normally. Scans at two weeks showed a partial response, and at six months a PET-CT showed a complete metabolic response, no active tumor signal anywhere. The authors present enteral delivery of crushed lorlatinib as a practical bridge for patients with absolute swallowing failure who need targeted treatment started urgently.
pmc-13253552:
Emily Krauss wrote this 2026 commentary on an updated classification of nerve injuries. Surgeons sorting damaged nerves must judge which injuries will heal alone and which need an operation, and they lean heavily on electrical tests of nerve and muscle.

The paper under discussion expands the classic Sunderland scale at both ends. A new grade zero covers a blood-flow block that silences a nerve while electrical tests stay normal, a pattern long recognised informally. Grade six, added earlier by the senior author, covers mixed injuries. Krauss praises the update's teaching cases and test-reading guidance, calling it essential reading for trainees and a step toward a surgical decision roadmap.
pmc-13253652:
L van der Broeck and colleagues price broken bones that refuse to heal in the Netherlands in this 2026 study. When a long bone fracture never knits, called a non-union, patients face repeated care and long absences from work, and the full societal bill was unmeasured.

Using questionnaires at a specialist clinic, the team counted health care, family, and lost-work costs over the three months before the visit. Health care averaged about 8,900 euros per patient, family costs about 1,400, and lost productivity about 4,300. Quality-of-life scores sat far below population norms. Worse non-union severity and lower quality of life, not the original injury type, drove higher costs.
pmc-13253752:
Juan Sánchez-Mateos and José David Flores-Félix review ways to block bacterial talk in a 2026 paper. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a germ that causes hard, lasting infections, mainly in people with weak immune defenses. It uses quorum sensing, chemical signals between cells, to switch on attack factors and build biofilms, slimy cell layers.

The review covers five ways to jam those signals, from blocking signal making to breaking signals down with enzymes. It also covers blocking the cell parts that receive signals. Gains are real, the authors note, but drug stability and uneven strains still limit use in patients.
pmc-13254252:
Enkui Lian and co-authors describe a simpler lithography set-up in a 2026 methods paper. Lloyd's mirror interference lithography uses overlapping laser beams to print fine patterns into a light-sensitive coating. Their system needs only a fibre-coupled single-frequency laser, a flat mirror, and an optional wave plate.

Using a factory-set fibre laser removes the tricky manual alignment of older set-ups. The system is cheap, robust, and easy to run, the authors say. With a 405-nanometer laser, it made one- and two-dimensional arrays with spacing below 220 nanometers. Full steps for sample prep, exposure, and processing are given.
pmc-13254852:
Yun Hwa Roh and colleagues build an improved prognostic score for breast cancer that has spread to the brain in a 2026 development and validation study. Survival after such spread varies widely, and the standard graded prognostic assessment omits leptomeningeal disease, cancer coating the brain's membranes, along with other modern clinical features. The team assembled 207 radiosurgery patients to build the score and 240 more to validate it.

Median survival in the development group was 13.9 months. Five factors predicted survival: functional status, cancer subtype, number of brain metastases, spread outside the skull, and leptomeningeal disease, while total tumor volume did not. The weighted point score built from these beat the old score on discrimination in its home cohort and matched it in the external one, with a better one-year prediction curve. The authors say the enhanced score can guide treatment choices before radiation begins.
pmc-13255052:
Rahul Singla and colleagues present a 2026 case series on infected knee replacements caused by Achromobacter, an uncommon bacterial culprit. The series covers ten infected knees in six patients treated at a tertiary center in New Delhi starting in 2023. Five patients were women, and four had infections in both knees.

Most patients arrived with draining sinus tracts, and diagnosis relied on culture methods and rapid protein fingerprinting. Two Achromobacter species appeared across the cases, and one patient later relapsed with the other species. Nine knees received two-stage revision surgery, replacing the implant in steps, alongside long tailored antibiotic courses. No patient showed infection at final follow-up. The authors credit accurate diagnosis plus individualized surgery for the clean outcomes.
pmc-13255652:
Zengping Shi and six co-authors present a 2026 interview study on what helps and hinders doctor-patient communication in China's big hospitals. Trust depends on this talk, yet heavy workloads strain it. Seventeen people, eleven physicians and six patient relations coordinators, gave in-depth interviews. Their answers were sorted into patient, physician, and system levels.

On the patient side, low health literacy, emotional distress, and mismatched expectations blocked communication, while trust and readiness helped. Physician barriers included weak style, empathy gaps, and time pressure; listening, warmth, and clear culturally aware explanations helped. System barriers ranged from crowded settings and thin training to media-fed distrust. Supportive institutions, training, smoother processes, and AI-provided background knowledge helped. The authors call for action at all three levels at once.
pmc-13255952:
Sang-Ho Jeong and colleagues present a 2026 nationwide Korean analysis of palliative stomach removal in advanced gastric cancer. Such surgery aims to ease bleeding or blockage rather than cure, and it is offered to patients already in poor shape. Using a large multicenter dataset from the Korean Gastric Cancer Association, the team compared short-term outcomes against curative surgery.

Patients having palliative surgery suffered clearly higher rates of severe complications and death after their operations. Leaks where the gut was rejoined and pancreatic fistulas stood out as more frequent problems. Risk climbed highest when the whole stomach was removed. The authors urge very careful patient selection and honest preoperative conversations weighing likely relief against these substantial dangers.
pmc-13256752:
Charlotte Delrue and co-authors argue in a 2026 review that renal tubular epithelial cells act as central hubs in kidney disease rather than passive victims of it. These cells line the kidney's tubules and constantly sense ischemia, toxins, metabolic stress, and immune signals from their surroundings.

The review gathers new evidence that tubular cells integrate those signals and pass them outward as measurable biomarkers in blood and urine. Advances in multi-omics, extracellular vesicle analysis, and single-cell methods now let researchers pinpoint distinct tubular cell states. Building diagnostics around these cells could improve early detection and patient stratification, although the authors note that translating the approach into personalized treatment remains unfinished work.
pmc-13257652:
Shouchang Jiao and colleagues created plastic films that glow with a twist, literally, after the light goes off. Their 2026 work combines long-lasting room-temperature phosphorescence with circularly polarized light. Such chiral glow is hard to achieve, yet prized for secure displays and labels.

They stirred chiral naphthyl phosphoric acid derivatives into an epoxy resin, then hardened it with heat. The rigid network calmed wasted energy loss and steadied the excited states behind the glow. One blend kept phosphorescing for nearly a second and flipped its emission from fluorescence to phosphorescence on curing. The films were demonstrated in multi-layer anti-counterfeiting designs.
pmc-13258352:
Sijongesonke Peter and co-authors review hybrid molecules built from ferulic and caffeic acids for cancer potential in a 2026 article. These plant phenolic acids carry antioxidant and cell-slowing actions, and chemists have fused them with other active fragments to sharpen anticancer effects. Studies from 2022 to 2025, in cells and in computer models, were synthesized.

Structure patterns that raise potency are charted, along with common synthetic routes to the hybrids. Many hybrids killed cancer cells or slowed their growth more strongly than the parent acids in dish tests. Solubility and targeting weaknesses of the parents motivate the whole hybrid strategy. Medicinal chemists gain a compact design catalog. Animal evidence remains the missing rung before any of these hybrids can be called drug candidates with confidence.
pmc-13258952:
Ziyun Chen and coauthors profile a salt sensitive soybean mutant with combined molecular tools in a 2026 study. Salt harms soybean yield worldwide, yet hormone and metabolism links stay unclear. The mutant was compared with normal plants on ions, metabolites, and gene activity.

Excess sodium buildup and poor potassium retention formed the core defect. A sugar called mannose emerged as a hub linking carbohydrate handling with protein decoration. Two hormone systems, abscisic acid and jasmonic acid, both showed weakened signaling. Metabolic rewiring spread widely across the mutant. Breeders gain a systems map to guide the search for the gene behind salt sensitivity.
pmc-13259452:
Diego Corona Baitelle and coauthors evaluate programmed cycle pruning in Arabica coffee at several stem densities in a 2026 field study. Pruning reshapes canopy light and branch balance across the plant. Four stem densities were crossed with upper and lower canopy sampling, plus a traditional pruning comparison.

Programmed pruning evened out leaf gas exchange between canopy layers. Traditional pruning caused a girdling problem that cut photosynthesis in the upper canopy. Photosynthesis rose with stem density under the programmed system. Growth measures stayed similar between systems, yet grain yield ran higher with programmed pruning. Yield response to density curved rather than rising straight. Growers gain density guidance tied to physiology.
pmc-13259552:
Omar Brijawi, Frank Epitropoulos, and Patrick Chen present a 2026 case report of a delayed complication after an intramural duodenal hematoma. That term means a collection of blood inside the wall of the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. Their patient was a 59-year-old man with coronary artery disease who developed the hematoma after abdominal surgery for a blocked small bowel. He improved with stomach drainage and acid-blocking drugs and went home.

Two weeks later he returned with rectal bleeding and severe anemia, with hemoglobin at 4.9. Scans showed the hematoma had resolved with no active bleeding. A scope exam found diffuse severe erosive duodenitis, meaning raw inflamed duodenum, with shallow ulcers and a red spot blamed for the bleeding. Biopsies confirmed acute inflammatory injury. Transfusion and high-dose acid-blocking treatment stopped further bleeding.
pmc-13259652:
Anna-Mariia Shulhai and coauthors test whether pineal gland imaging features shift at early puberty in girls in a 2026 study. Forty five girls with confirmed early puberty and forty seven matched prepubertal girls had brain scans reviewed. Two readers outlined the small gland and computed texture features independently.

Top predictive features differed between the two readers. Agreement between readers on those features was poor. Validation accuracy stayed near chance for both readers. Cyst based reference models performed no better in the analysis. Hormone levels showed no useful tie to cyst features either. Clinicians learn that pineal texture analysis does not help early puberty workups.
pmc-13260352:
Peter Hsi and co-authors build a lab-grown brain tissue system to study blast-like injury, in a 2026 paper. Blast brain injury is a major concern in military groups. Bubbles forming and collapsing in tissue may drive part of the harm. That process, cavitation, is hard to study in living brains. The team grew three-dimensional tissue with human neurons and support cells. Focused ultrasound then created cavitation inside the tissue.

Injury scaled with dose and time. Cells showed toxic and overexcited responses. They released marker proteins seen in real brain trauma cases. Deeper checks found disturbed force-sensing signals and weakened cell skeletons. Network activity also suffered. The platform lets researchers test protective ideas safely. Candidate drugs can be screened without animal or human risk. The authors see it serving wider cavitation injury questions too. It brings a human cell model to a field that lacked one.
pmc-13260452:
Rodolfo Christiansen leads a 2026 geoscience study of natural hydrogen generation during serpentinization. Serpentinization is a reaction in which water alters mantle rocks and releases hydrogen gas. The team studied two rock types: fertile lherzolites in the Western Pyrenees and depleted harzburgites in Northern California. They combined three-dimensional geophysical imaging, which maps rock properties underground, with numerical models of fluid-rock reactions to estimate production rates.

Estimated rates were low, at about 0.1 to 0.5 tonnes of hydrogen per year per cubic kilometre of reactive rock. Across the full reactive volumes, that totals roughly 300 to 600 tonnes per year. Rates were limited mainly by hydrogen saturation in the fluid and by reaction speed. The authors conclude that large, economically useful accumulations would need thousands to tens of thousands of years to form.
pmc-13260652:
R A Kassab and colleagues compared in 2026 selection indexes for breeding Holstein Friesian cows on a private farm in Egypt. Their data covered 1,863 first-lactation records from German-imported cows managed between 2002 and 2012. Three traits mattered: milk yield over ten months, lactation length, and age at first calving.

Season and year of calving shaped all three traits. Heredity estimates were moderate for milk yield, low for lactation length, and very low for age at first calving. The team built four selection indexes using three different ways to price each trait's economic worth. All three pricing routes predicted the same genetic gain per generation and ranked the indexes alike. They recommend the route based on one phenotypic standard deviation simply because the math is easiest.
pmc-13261052:
Claire M Broderick leads a 2026 human challenge study of how flu infection affects control of mycobacterial infection, the family that includes tuberculosis. People in a flu challenge study gave blood before and after flu infection. A glowing growth test showed how well their blood controlled mycobacteria in the lab. Gene activity, cytokines, and cell tests tracked how flu changed immune reaction to the bacteria.

Flu reduced the immune control of mycobacterial growth in the assay. Innate immune pathways, including type 1 interferon pathways, were switched on by flu, but their later response to mycobacteria was reduced. Many genes' responses to a test microbe were muted after flu. The authors suggest flu may be a risk factor for progression to TB disease, and that flu shots might help protect high-risk groups.
pmc-13261152:
Seamus O'Reilly and co-authors write a 2026 editorial on spreading planetary health research at cancer conferences. Planetary health links human health to the state of the planet. It discusses a study by Delaye and colleagues that scanned a major cancer meeting for work with green benefits.

At the 2025 European Society of Medical Oncology Congress in Berlin, 2,937 abstracts were presented to over 37,000 attendees. Delaye's team found 10 abstracts readable through a planetary health lens. They suggested meaningful cuts in drug use, clinic visits, treatment length, or care load. The topics ranged from preventive care and gentler treatment to marker-guided choices and non-drug measures. None had directly measured green impact. It argues meetings are influential spaces that can spread this message, since health depends on the planet's health.
pmc-13262152:
Md Toasin Hossain Aunkor and colleagues mapped in 2026 a salt-handling gene in Hilsa shad, a fish that migrates between the sea and rivers in Bangladesh. The team gave the first genome-wide identification of Slc12a2 in this species and found it exists as two similar copies. That gene builds a transporter that moves sodium, potassium, and chloride across cell membranes.

Gene activity was measured in gill, kidney, liver, and muscle from fish in the Bay of Bengal and the Surma River. Both gene copies ran markedly quieter in the freshwater fish than in their sea-phase counterparts. The quieting fits a reduced need to expel salt once the fish leave the ocean. The authors say the copies jointly guard the fish's internal balance during migration, and they offer the data as a baseline for this prized food fish.
pmc-13262852:
Qiuling Li and co-authors study support cells in the brain after stroke in rats in a 2026 journal article. After a blocked artery is reopened, a chemical messenger called glutamate builds up and harms brain cells. Astrocytes, star-shaped support cells, clear most of it through a transporter called GLT-1. The team tested how a growth signal pathway affects that transporter.

In their rat model, injury switched the pathway on, stirred up astrocytes, and lowered GLT-1 levels. Blocking the mTOR part of the pathway restored GLT-1, calmed astrocytes, and reduced inflammation, cell death, and movement problems. Blocking the Akt part gave no such protection and lowered GLT-1 further. The authors suggest mTOR blocking as a possible protective route.
pmc-13262952:
Zhijuan Wang and colleagues test a plant compound against liver cancer tied to hepatitis B in a 2026 journal article. The compound is quercetin, a natural substance found in many food and medicinal plants. Using network analysis, docking tests, cell studies, and mouse tumors, the team looked for its main target and how it slows the cancer.

Analysis of the target network pointed to EGFR, a growth signal receptor, as the principal target. In cell tests, quercetin curbed cancer cell growth and movement, with stronger doses weakening EGFR and a chain of signals below it. It also reversed a process that helps cancer cells spread. Mouse studies, checked against a known EGFR blocker, supported the same mechanism, the authors report.
pmc-13263252:
Henna Uosukainen and colleagues follow the long-term health of children who had PFAPA syndrome in a 2026 journal article. PFAPA causes repeating fevers with mouth sores, sore throat, and swollen neck glands, mostly under age five. The Finnish team surveyed former patients treated at three university hospitals from 2008 to 2018, five to sixteen years later, against matched population controls.

Replies came from 98 patients and 490 controls. Allergy-type conditions, called atopy, were the only chronic condition clearly more common in former patients. They also reported more ear infections, ear tube surgery, bronchitis, fungal infections, and hospital stays for infections. Other chronic conditions and childhood exposures matched controls. The authors suggest health care seeking may explain part of the infection gap.
pmc-13263952:
Abdelrahman I Hleeba and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on how well false teeth stick to a 3D printed denture base. They tested sandblasting, which roughens a surface with fine grit, on both standard teeth and milled teeth. Bond strength was the main measure.

The team made 48 samples in three groups: no blasting, blasting with fine grit, and blasting with coarse grit. Both blasting and tooth type changed bond strength, and blasting had the larger effect. Bonds rose as grit size rose, and milled teeth held best in every group. The strongest result came from milled teeth blasted with the coarse grit. Failure patterns also shifted with treatment.
pmc-13264052:
Janak Bahirwani and co-authors pooled the evidence on whether gut endoscopy is safe for patients with very low white blood cell counts. Guidelines warn that infections rise after endoscopy in these neutropenic patients, but hard data were thin. The team searched seven databases and conference abstracts through September 2025. Six cohort studies covering 1,241 patients qualified. Infection-related death within thirty days was zero percent, and infectious complications within a week occurred in about seven percent of patients.

The complications were mostly bloodstream infections, about two percent, and new fever, about five percent. Taking antibiotics before the procedure did not lower infection rates in the pooled data. Rates varied widely between studies, so the averages carry uncertainty. Still, the authors conclude that endoscopy can be performed safely in carefully selected neutropenic patients. The findings give doctors numbers, rather than warnings alone, for weighing the risk.
pmc-13264552:
Helena F Alacha, Daniel A Waschbusch, and Dara E Babinski wrote a 2026 study of strain in caregivers of girls with behavior and attention problems. Most past work focused on boys. The team tracked girls aged 10 to 15 for one year to see how symptoms and strain move together.

The study held 197 girls and their caregivers. Symptoms of ADHD, defiant behavior, and borderline personality traits all rose over the year, while total strain slightly fell. Each symptom type linked to every form of strain, both at one time and later. Defiant behavior grew more tied to strain over time, while the ADHD link to practical strain weakened. The authors say strain is specific to symptom type and shifts as girls grow.
pmc-13264652:
Chenchen Yang and colleagues published a 2026 computer study on Perilla frutescens, a medicinal herb, against atherosclerosis, the fatty buildup that clogs arteries. Herbs act on many targets at once, which makes their action hard to pin down. The team combined network analysis, single-cell data from human plaques, and machine learning to find the herb's key targets.

Their search gave a core set of 10 genes tied to how plaque macrophages, immune cells in the plaque, turn into foam cells stuffed with fat. The gene set sorted patients well in an outside data set. One cell signal route stood out as a hub for inflammatory talk between cells. Computer docking showed the herb's main active compound, luteolin, binds one target strongly, and motion simulations backed that bond. The authors offer the targets for lab testing.
pmc-13264852:
Jennifer Kawi and colleagues describe a trial protocol for self-managed ear acupressure against chronic muscle and joint pain in rural adults in a 2026 paper. Rural patients face more pain, less insurance and fewer non-drug options, which pushes reliance on opioids. The program teaches people to press defined ear points with small seeds or pellets, supported by a phone app, momentary symptom check-ins and tailored motivational messages built to strengthen confidence in self-care.

Earlier pilot work showed the approach was feasible, safe and improved pain and function. The planned pragmatic randomized trial tests real-world effectiveness while tracking implementation at the same time. Stakeholder input shaped the design. If results hold, a low-cost home program could widen pain care access where clinics are distant.
pmc-13264952:
Jihad Bnimoussa and colleagues ask Moroccan youth what drives their mental health and wellbeing, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Young people's own priorities are rarely centred in service planning. The survey covered all twelve regions of Morocco. It asked which factors participants valued most.

A total of 1,182 young people took part, with a mean age near twenty. Family relationships were rated critical by about three-quarters. Fulfilling basic needs, personal safety, and having a sense of purpose also ranked high. Sleep, physical health, and clean air mattered to many. Social media both connected and stressed respondents. The results point to broad, practical targets for future programmes.
pmc-13265252:
Momoko Soda and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a chest wall abscess caused by Gordonia sputi, a rare soil bacterium, in a healthy man. These germs grow slowly and are hard to identify, so diagnosis often drags. Their patient was a 45-year-old man with no immune problems.

After blunt trauma, a painful mass grew on his left chest wall, though he had no fever. Scans showed a contained abscess, and surgeons drained it. First cultures grew nothing, but tissue study hinted at an actinomycete germ. After the wound split open, a second cleaning gave samples that a rapid protein test and gene sequencing named as the rare bacterium. Based on drug tests, he took amoxicillin by mouth for six months. The wound healed fully with no return in a year of follow-up.
pmc-13265652:
Hao Xu and the team pin down a colistin resistance gene found in bacteria from imported beef cattle, in a 2026 genomic study.
