Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic, and genes that defeat it can move between germs. Faecal samples came from 150 cattle imported from Australia to China. Isolates were sequenced and compared with global genomes.

One isolate carried the resistance gene mcr-4.3 on a small plasmid. The plasmid resembled others reported in related bacteria. Global comparison placed the strain within a mixed pool spanning animals, the wild, and humans. One lineage carried most gene-carrying genomes. The findings support joint human and animal watch.
pmc-13266052:
Xiaoyang Li and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on a gentler brain-computer interface that reads brain waves from flicker-free text patterns. Classic systems flash bright blocks, which tire the eyes and confine signals to the back of the head. Their method presents sequences of text characters as the steady stimulus instead.

Sweep tests showed the text method evoked responses at both the back and side-back of the head, unlike plain flicker. It also cared less about stimulus size and brightness. The team built a forty-target speller and tested it live: it transferred about 235 bits per minute, a high speed, and users rated it significantly more comfortable on questionnaires. The authors present text stimulation as a practical direction for fast, comfortable visual interfaces.
pmc-13266852:
Mengnan Li and co-authors critique in 2026 a real-world study suggesting that reusing the drug flumonertinib can help lung cancer patients after targeted therapy stops working. The patients had EGFR-mutant cancer that had progressed on a third-generation inhibitor drug. Li's letter argues that the study's design weakens its hopeful conclusion.

Only forty patients were included, so subgroup claims rested on as few as two to five people per group. Patients treated in earlier lines may simply have had different disease courses, creating bias that mimics a drug benefit. No comparison group received standard chemotherapy, and no molecular testing explained why resistance arose. The critics urge caution before treating rechallenge as proven salvage therapy.
pmc-13267552:
Yuanfang Liu and colleagues map in 2026 how ultrasound settings and liquid ingredients change the output of hydroxyl radicals, the aggressive oxidants behind many cleaning and treatment processes. They estimated radical output with an iodine-based method in a standard salt solution, while varying treatment time, power, on-off cycling, and probe depth. Radical output rose with longer treatment and stronger power.

A sixty percent duty cycle and a probe placed mid-liquid gave the strongest response. Additives shifted results in varied ways: alcohol and alkali generally lowered output, vinegar-like acid rose then fell, and hydrogen peroxide helped at moderate levels but hurt at high ones. A scavenger control cut the signal to about a tenth, confirming radicals drove most of the reading.
pmc-13269952:
Michael A Mastroianni and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Major League Baseball pitchers returning after a second elbow ligament reconstruction, called revision surgery. Results after first-time surgery are well known, but not after revision. Records covered 61 pitchers who had revision surgery from 2014 to 2024.

Only 1.6 percent were back playing at one year, rising to 44.1 percent at two years and 63.2 percent at three years. Average return took 605 days. After first-time surgery, returns were far higher, at 71.9 percent by two years and 82 percent by three. Just 14.3 percent regained their pre-injury value rating within three seasons. The authors call revision outcomes clearly worse.
pmc-13270252:
Cheng-Yi Fan and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 testing a score called SADFUL for spotting blood infection in patients who return to the emergency department unplanned. Records came from two Taiwanese hospitals of different levels, covering March 2019 to December 2022. The score was compared with three simpler tools.

Blood infection was present in 2.2 percent of 5,455 returning patients. The SADFUL score scored 0.64 on an accuracy curve at the academic center, significantly beating the rival tools there. At the rural hospital it scored 0.72 but was not significantly better. Its best cut point also differed, at 2 versus 4. The authors rate all the tools as limited for this job.
pmc-13270552:
Chanelle Galea and Rita Pace Parascandalo report a 2026 cross-sectional study, a one-time survey, on acupressure in care around pregnancy and birth in Malta. Acupressure means firm pressure on set points on the body, and it has been linked to less nausea, pain, and anxiety.

The authors surveyed members of the Malta Midwives Association, inviting all 240 members, and received 94 replies between July and September 2024. Midwives showed strong interest, but only 12 said they used acupressure in practice. Lack of training, lack of schooling on the topic, and lack of clear, evidence-based guides were the main reasons for holding back.
pmc-13271052:
Jiaqi Tong is lead author of a 2026 study protocol, a published plan for a trial not yet reported, comparing two pain drugs after stomach cancer surgery. Patients will have keyhole removal of part of the stomach, plus a nerve block for the upper abdomen, and the question is whether oxycodone controls inner, deep pain better than sufentanil.

The single-centre, double-blind trial will enrol 96 patients and assign them evenly to patient-controlled pain pumps with one drug or the other. The main outcome is a recovery quality score 24 hours after surgery. Other measures include pain scores at rest and in motion, total opioid use, and gut recovery. No results are reported in a protocol.
pmc-13271152:
Keyao Huang is lead author of a 2026 secondary analysis, a new look at earlier interview data, on lung transplant recipients returning to work. Going back to work is a key sign of recovered quality of life after transplant, yet re-employment rates are typically poor, and patients' needs differ widely.

The authors re-analysed deep interviews with 38 recipients from a major hospital in Jiangsu Province, China, and built four user profiles. Rapid Return patients recovered well and rejoined society fast. Meandering Return patients worked but kept balancing health and job demands. Life-Centred patients chose not to work, putting health first. Conflicted and Hesitant patients wanted to work but faced physical, mental, and social barriers.
pmc-13271552:
Lalit Verma and colleagues present in 2026 long-term results for brolucizumab injections in stubborn cases of chronic central serous retinopathy with new vessel growth. These eyes had already failed earlier treatments. The drug blocks a growth signal that drives fluid leakage and abnormal vessels under the retina.

The series covered 30 eyes of 25 patients treated at one center between 2021 and 2025, with injections given as needed. Retinal thickness fell sharply by six months, and vision held steady or improved in most eyes. A smaller group kept those gains at one and two years, and no side effects were recorded during the study.
pmc-13272252:
Ayman El-Menyar is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study comparing mechanical and manual cardiopulmonary resuscitation in traumatic cardiac arrest. Resuscitation means chest compressions to keep blood moving. Heart stoppage after trauma kills most patients despite better trauma systems. Ambulance services increasingly use compression machines during transport.

The review covered 610 patients with blunt trauma arrest treated from 2016 to 2024, average age 34 and mostly male. In total, 220 received mechanical compressions during transport and 390 manual compressions at the scene only. The mechanical group reached hospital alive far more often, at nearly ninety-nine percent against about thirty-nine percent. Yet restored circulation on arrival stayed low in both groups. Overall thirty-day survival for everyone was under one percent.
pmc-13272352:
Attila Szabo and coauthors argue in 2026 that a two-axis model of feeling could sharpen research on how exercise changes mood in older adults. Decades of work confirm exercise benefits aging bodies, yet the emotional machinery behind those benefits lacks a clear frame. The circumplex model sorts feelings by pleasantness and activation, giving that frame.

The authors trace how brain growth factors, oxidative stress control, and hormones may move each axis differently during aging. Exercise dose, type, and timing map onto distinct feeling profiles within the model. Personal traits and health status bend those responses further, which the authors use to propose better study designs.
pmc-13272552:
Tricia Park and co-authors built a labeled dataset of cannabis posts from Reddit in a 2026 data article. Researchers who track public views on cannabis and pain need text where opinion toward specific aspects is marked by hand. The team drew posts from Reddit groups for autoimmune rheumatic diseases.

They filtered posts with a list of cannabis terms, split text into sentences by rules, and labeled each item by hand. The final set holds 479 post and aspect pairs, each marked positive, negative, or neutral both overall and by aspect. Agreement between labelers was moderate. The dataset is public and can train or test language models for health related social media, pain research, and public health tracking.
pmc-13273852:
Pařízek and colleagues test atropine in pigs whose hearts slow during oxygen starvation. Their 2026 journal article is a randomized cross-over trial. The setting mimics emergencies where a patient cannot be intubated or oxygenated.

Eight anesthetized pigs each underwent two apnea episodes. Apnea means breathing was stopped. At the onset of slow heart rate, pigs got atropine or placebo. The order was random. Time to cardiac arrest was the main outcome. Atropine gave 142 seconds, placebo 138 seconds. The difference was not significant, with p equal to 0.803. Four animals arrested faster on atropine, four slower. No gains appeared in oxygen delivery or resuscitation. The authors advise treating the hypoxia itself first.
pmc-13274052:
David Emad Sobhy and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial comparing two surgical routes for broken bones around the eye and cheek. Such fractures can be reached through the eyelid lining, but extra reach may need a cut near the eyebrow. The trial tested a stair-step extension of the eyelid route against the standard route plus that eyebrow cut.

Twenty patients aged eighteen to sixty were split evenly between the two methods. Both gave the same access and exposure time, but the stair-step route took less total operating time. Its patients had less swelling, faster return of feeling below the eye, and only that group had scars described as not noticeable.
pmc-13274552:
Benoît Ferment and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on predicting who responds to a cell therapy for multiple myeloma, a blood cancer of plasma cells. The therapy, idecabtagene vicleucel, re-engineers a patient's own T cells to hunt a marker called BCMA. It is the only such product available in France, and immune factors behind its success were little studied.

The team reviewed every patient treated at Saint-Louis Hospital between October 2021 and December 2024, profiling blood and T cells at collection and tracking the engineered cells' growth over the first month. As the title reports, how strongly the CAR T cells expanded after infusion predicted patient outcomes. Response was judged at six months by international criteria.
pmc-13274852:
Xiang Gao and colleagues present a 2026 journal article sorting Chinese elementary students into profiles of social-emotional competence, skills like managing feelings and getting along with others. The survey covered 11,323 children in grades three to six across forty-two schools in eastern, central, and western China. A statistical grouping method called latent profile analysis did the sorting.

Four profiles emerged: high competence in 25.8 percent of children, medium-to-high in 36.2 percent, low-to-medium in 31.3 percent, and low in just 6.7 percent. Girls, urban students, children with siblings, and those not left behind by migrant parents were more likely to sit in the high group than the small low group. The authors suggest support tailored to each profile.
pmc-13275152:
Ferris Zeitouni and colleagues present a 2026 practical review of AI tools that draft clinical notes from patient conversations. Note-writing burden drives doctor burnout, and AI scribe services have spread fast in response. The article is a primer for doctors weighing these platforms for their own practice.

Across products, core features include live transcripts, note drafting, many languages, custom templates, and health privacy safeguards. Deeply linked systems can summarize old notes and draft referral letters but demand long setup. Simpler tools start fast with weaker record linking. The authors flag real risks alongside the time savings: invented content, privacy exposure, and open legal risk when an AI note is wrong.
pmc-13275252:
Fang Yang and co-authors built a risk tool to predict who benefits from chemotherapy in a rare breast cancer in a 2026 population study. Invasive micropapillary carcinoma spreads early to vessels and nodes, yet whether chemotherapy extends life was unproven. Treating everyone alike may harm low risk patients needlessly.

They analyzed 1,150 patients from a national cancer registry covering 2010 to 2018, plus 199 patients from a Chinese hospital for outside validation. Chemotherapy linked to better overall survival, but not clearly to breast cancer specific survival. A model using marital status, tumor size, subtype, and radiation history split patients into high and low risk. Only the high risk group gained survival from chemotherapy, a pattern the outside cohort confirmed. The authors advise careful, selective decisions.
pmc-13275352:
Kangjie Tang and co-authors tested composite fat and inflammation indices as predictors of heart disease in a 2026 prospective cohort from China. Single measures of belly fat miss the mix of inflammation, blood sugar, and lipids that drives risk. Their index family merges those signals with four different body shape measures.

They followed 5,290 adults aged forty-five and older without heart disease at entry, drawn from a national aging study between 2011 and 2020. A quarter developed cardiovascular disease during follow-up. All four composite indices stayed linked to new disease after wide adjustment, with the highest third carrying clearly greater risk than the lowest. Curves were bent rather than straight, and no firm cutoff emerged. One version, built on waist to height, predicted best and modestly improved standard models.
pmc-13276152:
Jyoti Das and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how faults in a gene for clathrin, a protein that helps cells pull material inside, may cause developmental brain disorders. New mutations in this gene have been linked to learning disability in children. The team recreated two such mutations in fruit flies.

Flies carrying either mutant protein survived less well and learned poorly, whether the change was everywhere or only in nerve cells. Under heat stress, their cells moved internal cargo more slowly and took up fewer signaling molecules. Young nerve junctions looked normal in shape, but markers of synapse maturity, the signals at connection points, were disrupted. The authors offer the fly as a model for tracing how these mutations disturb the developing brain.
pmc-13276252:
Inas Karawia and co-authors report a 2026 preliminary trial on whether alkaline water can cut mouth bacteria in children. Tooth decay is widespread in children, and Streptococcus mutans is a main culprit. The team compared alkaline water with a proven antiseptic mouthwash and plain tap water.

Sixty healthy children aged ten to twelve were assigned by chance to the three rinses for three weeks. Saliva samples were taken before and after. Bacteria counts ended far lower in both the alkaline water and mouthwash groups than in the tap water group. The mouthwash still beat alkaline water head to head. The authors call alkaline water a promising extra hygiene aid, while stressing that longer trials must test whether it truly prevents cavities.
pmc-13276552:
James Bruzzese and Lisa Doan present a 2026 case report on burning back nerves in a patient with a leadless pacemaker. Radiofrequency neurotomy uses heated needles to quiet the small nerves feeding painful spinal facet joints. Its electric current raises fears of disturbing implanted heart devices, and leadless pacemakers, tiny capsules inside the heart, lack specific guidance.

Their patient was an eighty-one-year-old man whose diagnostic blocks had confirmed facet pain. Heart specialists first verified he did not depend on the pacemaker to live. The device was checked but not reprogrammed before the procedure. The team used a bipolar technique, keeping current between two needle tips, under continuous heart monitoring. Everything finished without incident, the device checked out normal afterward, and the patient reported significant pain relief. The authors share their precautions for a growing patient group.
pmc-13276752:
Yael Shapira-Galitz and Evgeni Gershman present a 2026 case report on removing a whole grape from a man's airway. Swallowed foreign bodies are uncommon in adults but dangerous, and soft, slippery objects defeat the usual grasping tools. The patient needed a rescue technique.

The seventy-three-year-old man, who had schizophrenia, arrived with severe oxygen shortage and a collapsed left lung. Scans showed an oval object completely plugging his left main airway. Through a flexible scope, doctors saw a whole grape wedged tight. Forceps slipped off its smooth, fragile skin repeatedly. They cut a narrow channel through the grape and threaded in a balloon catheter. Inflating the balloon behind the grape and pulling gently freed it intact. The authors propose this balloon method as a rescue for large, soft airway blockages.
pmc-13278852:
Joshua B B Garfield leads a 2026 randomized trial of a smartphone training app meant to cut relapse after residential alcohol treatment. The training, called approach bias modification, retrains automatic urges to approach alcohol cues. It works when given during residential care, but few services offer it. Participants leaving treatment were sent a personalized app, with weekly tasks for four weeks.

Only 134 of 171 participants installed the app, leaving the trial underpowered. At three months, past-month abstinence was fifty-five percent in the sham-training control group and fifty-two percent in the training group, a non-significant difference. All secondary outcomes were also non-significant. Longer admissions and session counts may shape any effect, exploratory analyses hinted.
pmc-13279052:
Reed and colleagues ask whether pharmacology degrees build the attitudes the field expects. Their 2026 paper surveys views on the British Pharmacological Society core curriculum, which lists 18 attitudes graduates should hold, from valuing evidence to seeing the subject's social relevance. Knowledge and skills had been assessed before, but attitudes had not.

An online survey reached 118 current undergraduates and 70 graduates through the society's educator network. Both groups mostly agreed their degree had developed each attitude, with agreement strongest for appreciating how pharmacology matters to society. The weakest area in both groups was spotting job opportunities and pursuing career goals. Graduates answered with more spread and stronger views at both ends than students still studying.
pmc-13279152:
Qingcui Wu and colleagues published a 2026 modeling study of Ethiopia's first Marburg virus outbreak, which began in November 2025. By mid-December the country had confirmed 14 cases and 9 deaths, a fatality ratio near 64 percent among confirmed cases. With no licensed vaccine or antiviral drug available, officials relied on non-drug control measures such as isolation and contact tracing. The team built a stochastic epidemic model that adjusts for under-reporting to judge how well those measures worked.

Fitting the model to data from before controls began, they estimated each case generated about 1.13 further cases on average, a modest spread rate. Without interventions they projected roughly 64 cases during the following three weeks, yet only 4 were observed. That gap implies the control measures cut transmission by an estimated 93.7 percent in their analysis. The authors stress timely action and continued surveillance while the outbreak picture remains incomplete.
pmc-13279952:
Lucy R. Boxall and colleagues report a 2026 interview study of what helps or blocks cuts in free sugar intake. Free sugars are sugars added to foods or in juices and honey. Sixty two adults who took more than five percent of their energy from free sugar joined a trial of diet advice. They were interviewed at one, two, four, eight or twelve weeks after advice, while change was live.

Seven linked themes shaped change, from Is it possible to Proof and impact. Themes held know how, personal balance, habits, life realities and broad awareness. By group checks, advice groups held more know how, with practical fixes, than the control group. Early hopes and intent ran high, then met habit and life strain over weeks. Success at twelve weeks split by those forces. Timed interviews catch change as it forms, not just in hindsight.
pmc-13280552:
Muhammad Abdullah Awan and Hammad-ud-din Raza write a 2026 letter on Kawasaki disease with a pustular drug rash, in reply to a case by Li and team. That case held a four year old boy with classic Kawasaki signs: fever, conjunctival congestion, strawberry tongue, cracked lips, extremity edema, neck lymph node swelling and a scarlet like rash. He later developed a pustular eruption that fit acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, or AGEP, a drug rash with many small pustules.

The letter makes one key point: fever that persists after a first IVIG dose should not be taken as IVIG refractory Kawasaki disease at once, when AGEP evolves at the same time. In the case, eye congestion and extremity edema improved after the first dose, while fever persisted. Drug fever from AGEP can mimic persistent inflammation. Telling the two apart can spare extra immune therapy and its risks in children.
pmc-13280752:
Hexia Gan and co-authors build a gene-based test that aims to spot prostate cancer. Their 2026 study joins two drivers of tumor growth: low oxygen inside the tumor and the tumor's escape from immune attack. No test that combines both traits was ready for clinic use.

The team merged gene data from three large public sets and searched for genes tied to both traits. Machine learning tools then narrowed the list to a six-gene signature. The model scored very high on accuracy tests in all check groups. Further analysis linked the score to changes in immune cells inside tumors and to certain cell pathways. The authors present the signature as a step toward a sharper diagnosis tool, one that still needs clinic testing.
pmc-13280852:
Demet Yavuz and colleagues published a 2026 study of how adding polypropylene fibers changes pervious concrete, the porous paving that lets stormwater drain through roads and parking areas into the ground. Such concrete is weak in bending, which limits its working life. The team cast specimens with three fiber dosages, using single-sized limestone aggregate and no mineral additives, and varied cement content. They measured strength, water flow, and porosity, cross-checked pores with CT scans and sliced-sample images.

The highest fiber dose, 0.3 percent by volume, gave the best splitting tensile and bending strength. Fibers came at a hydraulic price: porosity fell as dosage rose, and the most heavily fibered mixes showed the lowest permeability. Imaging-derived porosity matched the measurements well, validating the scanning approach for quality checks. The authors note the strength-permeability trade-off: designers choosing a fiber dose choose where to sit on that curve.
pmc-13280952:
Georgios P D Argyropoulos and colleagues published a 2026 study arguing that memory loss after hippocampal damage is partly explained by shrinkage in the diencephalon, a relay region. The team studied 38 patients whose hippocampus was damaged by autoimmune limbic encephalitis, an immune attack on the brain. Earlier work on this cohort blamed abnormal network activity; here the researchers measured the volumes of diencephalic nuclei and white matter tracts and related them to memory.

Atrophy appeared in the mammillary bodies and in four thalamic nuclei, often as severe as the hippocampal shrinkage itself. Diencephalic volumes predicted memory scores beyond anything hippocampal measurements explained. White matter was compromised inside and beyond the memory network, and the integrity of the fornix, the hippocampal output cable, tracked tissue volumes rather than memory. The authors advise neuroscience to drop the phrase focal hippocampal damage, since the injury and its consequences spread across the circuit.
pmc-13281752:
Hiroyuki Hisada and colleagues published a 2026 scoping review of sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength, in patients having endoscopic resection of digestive tract cancers. The technique removes esophageal, stomach, and colorectal tumors through a scope. Searching four databases to November 2025, the team gathered twenty-eight studies, mostly cohorts from East Asia, and charted how muscle loss related to technical success, complications, and survival.

Prevalence swung wildly, from 13.9 to 72.7 percent, reflecting inconsistent definitions. Nearly all studies measured muscle mass on scans; only one added strength testing. Muscle loss did not impair technical outcomes: complete removal rates and perforation risk were unaffected. The damage showed elsewhere, with pneumonia more often, moderate-to-severe complications more frequent, hospital stays longer in every study, and survival worse, driven by deaths unrelated to the cancer. The authors call it an alarm rather than a reason to withhold the procedure.
pmc-13281952:
Aaron M Brice and colleagues pooled gene studies to find shared virus needs in a 2026 analysis. Viruses must borrow the host cell's machinery to copy themselves. Drugs aimed at host parts could thus work across many viruses and be harder to dodge. Such drugs lag, partly for want of agreed targets. The team merged sixty-two gene-screen studies. They spanned ten virus families flagged for pandemic risk, from flu kin to Ebola kin. Ranking math and protein web maps hunted for common threads.

Four cell systems came up again and again across families. They run cell acid pumps, sugar coating of proteins, shipping through the cell's post office, and protein threading into inner skins. Some top host factors already have blocker drugs on the shelf. The authors say those factors are prime leads for broad antiviral design. Shared needs, they argue, are where pandemic readiness should invest.
pmc-13282052:
Nicholas A Vernice and co-authors wrote a 2026 scoping review on silent rupture of silicone breast implants in older adults. Implants are widely used after cancer surgery and for cosmetic reasons, and rupture risk rises as devices age. Regulators advise scans to check for silent rupture starting five to six years after surgery, then every two to three years. Yet no guidance covers what to do when an older patient feels no symptoms.

The team searched three major databases through January 2025 and found no published guidelines for this group. They note that silent ruptures in older patients rarely cause serious harm with modern implants. Scanning can also bring false alarms, worry, and needless surgery. They advise stopping routine scans after age seventy-five and watching known ruptures unless symptoms appear. Symptomatic cases, they say, need imaging and a shared talk about risks and comfort.
pmc-13282252:
Yi Chen and co-authors published a 2026 study comparing robot-assisted and standard keyhole surgery for belly lymphatic malformations in children. These malformations are fluid-filled lymph vessel growths that can be large and complex. Standard keyhole surgery often pulls the lesion outside the body for removal. The team reviewed one hundred thirty-four children treated at a Chinese children's hospital from 2018 to 2025.

Fifty-seven children had robot-assisted surgery and seventy-seven had standard keyhole surgery. The robot group more often completed cyst removal and bowel repair fully inside the body. The standard group far more often used outside-the-body steps. Complications were few in both groups, four against seven. Hospital costs were much higher for robot surgery, which the authors say limits routine use. For complex lesions, though, they judge the robot approach safe and helpful, especially where delicate inside work is needed.
pmc-13282452:
Louis Mihluedo and co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare spinal birth variant revealed by a serious joint infection in a child. Bertolotti syndrome arises when an enlarged lowest lumbar vertebra forms a false joint with the sacrum or hip bone. It can cause low back pain, usually in adults. Their patient was a thirteen-year-old girl admitted with fever and disabling low back pain.

Magnetic scans showed the false joint, signs of septic arthritis, joint infection, within it, and a neighbouring hip bone abscess. Tests identified Staphylococcus aureus, a common aggressive bacterium. Targeted intravenous antibiotics treated her successfully, and draining the abscess by surgery proved unnecessary. The authors believe she is among the youngest reported with so severe an infectious complication of this variant. They stress early diagnosis and prompt treatment to prevent lasting damage, and remind clinicians that back pain in teenagers can hide structural causes.
pmc-13282552:
Julen Ramón-Rodríguez and co-authors report a 2026 study testing whether a light-based oxygen monitor can judge liver donor graft quality. Donor livers increasingly come from higher-risk donors, where fatty change, called steatosis, matters for transplant success. The team measured regional oxygen saturation on donor skin and directly on the liver surface during transplants at their centre between 2020 and 2022, using a commercial oximeter.

Skin readings succeeded in twenty-seven patients and liver readings in eighteen. Liver surface values linked significantly to the degree of fatty change. Values above fifty-seven percent pointed to mild fat, under thirty percent, with good sensitivity and fair specificity. Donors with lower values of a liver enzyme blood test had higher skin readings. The authors say direct liver oxygen readings track a graft trait that surgeons care about. Such bedside checks could support donor assessment, though this early series is small.
pmc-13282752:
Narges Ghazvini and co-authors present a 2026 study validating a Hungarian version of the Participation Motivation Questionnaire among teenage schoolgirls. The questionnaire asks why young people take part in sport and exercise, and the study frames motives through self-determination theory, which separates inner from external drives. Three hundred twenty-five girls aged thirteen to fifteen, from nine schools around Budapest of varied income levels, completed it.

Statistical analysis produced a twenty-seven-item version with six motive factors, differing partly from the original eight-factor design, with acceptable consistency scores. Motives varied with age, family income, and urban or rural residence. Fitness was the only motive strongly and directly tied to how active the girls actually were. Inner, health, and mastery reasons outweighed ego and external ones. Still, they judge the Hungarian questionnaire fit for school and sport settings, and useful for planning activity programmes.
pmc-13282852:
André Johansson and co-authors present a 2026 paper introducing Triage Effectiveness, a framework for measuring how well emergency department triage actually speeds care for time-critical patients. Triage assigns priority to cut waiting for the sickest, but no method directly measured that core function. The team built the framework from over four hundred sixty-three thousand visits across eight emergency departments.

The scale runs from zero percent, equal to first-come first-served, to one hundred percent, perfect prioritisation. Two measures are offered: one based on actual waiting time saved, one on queue position gained, each calculable in theory from priorities or from observed practice. Queueing models validated the maths, with the rank measure proving more robust. Applying the framework exposed large gaps between theoretical and observed effectiveness everywhere, evidence that patients are often re-prioritised after triage. The authors say the tool can audit triage quality directly.
pmc-13282952:
Music, delivered by video group, is tested as pain support in a 2026 feasibility effort from Andrea McGraw Hunt's team. Many patients with complex health needs cannot attend in-person music therapy. The team asked whether a virtual group could help and what format patients wanted.

Two small cohorts met with support from an osteopathic clinic. Three unique patients took part and gave feedback through surveys and group talks. They reported pain relief, social support, and new insight for daily coping. They liked small groups, song sharing, and guided music imagery. They also used session recordings and shared playlists between meetings. Findings guide a larger future program.
pmc-13283052:
Eight educators describe a story-based tool for finding training gaps in a paper from 2026. Their office supports health science teachers, whose needs shift across a career. After the shift to online work in 2020, the office needed a fast way to assess those needs. Teachers wrote short stories about invented teacher personas, based on their own lived experience.

Seven persona stories were drafted and reviewed by peers. From them, the team drew seventy learning goals and sorted them by career stage. Most goals could be met with resources already on hand. About a third needed new or revised material. The authors present the method as a road map other schools can copy.
pmc-13283352:
Ishbel Orla Whitehead and colleagues described in 2026 how they built staff training on spiritual health for primary care by designing it with the people involved. Spiritual health counts as part of whole-person care, yet primary care staff get little training in it, and the topic can feel taboo. Five workshops brought together doctors, social prescribers, patients, carers, chaplains, and members of the public.

Thirty-eight people took part. Being heard mattered most: participants valued rare space to speak on a sensitive topic, and that openness fed engagement. Rank and outsider status still shaped talk despite careful hosting, and practical choices affected who kept coming. The authors draw lessons for joint design work on touchy, value-laden subjects.
pmc-13283652:
Casey Kuka returned with colleagues in 2026 to test whether kneecap joint shape links two youth knee problems. Osteochondritis dissecans of the kneecap area has no clear cause. Odd joint shape is known in kneecap instability, where the cap slips out of place, so the team asked whether the same shape traits appear in the bone-and-cartilage condition.

Three matched groups of 108 patients each were compared: kneecap-area OCD without instability, repeated kneecap dislocation without OCD, and normal scans. A few measures, including kneecap height index, tilt, and a groove distance, ran higher in the OCD group than in controls, though still inside normal ranges. Every shape measure set the instability group apart from both others. Modelling linked some traits to raised OCD risk.
pmc-13283952:
Paper sensors married to graphene are surveyed by Arya Unnikrishnan and colleagues in a 2026 review of green sensing devices. Paper offers a cheap, flexible, break-down base for tests outside labs. Graphene adds conductivity and sharp sensitivity to that humble base.

Uses span metal and plastic pollutant checks, blood marker tests, and food spoilage sniffing. Wearable strain, pressure, and humidity sensing also feature in the survey. Electrode types include laser-written graphene and graphene blends with other minerals. Reported devices show tiny detection limits and strong bending tolerance. Heat tolerance reached high levels in some cited designs.
pmc-13284052:
Yunjian Huang and a large team compared in 2026 two procedures for cervicogenic headache, head pain referred from the upper neck. Both target the C2 dorsal root ganglion, a nerve cluster near the top of the spine. Radiofrequency ablation burns the target with heat, while endoscopic neurotomy cuts it under direct camera view. Patients entered the study only after a diagnostic block of that nerve eased their pain.

Seventy-six patients were treated, 21 by endoscopy and 55 by ablation. Both groups improved in pain and quality of life at three and twelve months. Results matched at three months, yet the endoscopy group did better at twelve months and reported stronger global improvement. Median pain-free time was 33 months after endoscopy against 8 months after ablation. Numbness in the back of the head was common in both groups.
pmc-13284552:
Myung Sin Kim, Hyun-Ju Kim, and Sang-Hyuk Lee examined in 2026 how early trauma and panic disorder together shape the folding of the brain's surface. Cortical gyrification, the wrinkling of the outer brain layer, forms early in life and has been reported as altered in both panic disorder and trauma survivors. The study scanned 83 panic disorder patients and 83 matched healthy controls, measuring local folding across the surface and recording trauma history with a standard inventory.

One spot, part of the superior parietal lobule, showed a true interaction: patients with early trauma had higher folding values there than patients without trauma. Folding at that spot also rose with panic severity and intolerance of uncertainty scores across everyone. The authors argue trauma history and brain structure must be read together in panic research.
pmc-13284752:
Jelena Filipović Tričković and co-authors report a 2026 cell study of silver nanoparticles made with sage extract for gum disease. Gum disease starts with microbial imbalance and swelling that can destroy tissue and loosen teeth. The particles were made by laser ablation in sage fluid, at two pulse energies, and sized by standard tools.

Particles made at higher energy in sage were small, round, and well spread. At one dose they killed three gum pathogens as well as or better than a common antiseptic rinse in lab tests. That same dose did not harm human gum fibroblasts and boosted their growth and collagen output, while lowering an inflammation marker. The authors see a clear dose window worth further study.
pmc-13284952:
Antonino Maniaci leads a team that translated a 12-item symptom questionnaire for long-term sinus inflammation into Italian and tested whether it still measures well. The work appeared in 2026. Versions of the tool existed in other languages, yet Italian speakers had none, so clinicians lacked a checked way to record how patients felt.

Five Italian ear, nose, and throat centers enrolled 118 adults between January 2024 and August 2025, including healthy controls and patients with or without nasal polyps. Translation followed international guidance for adapting health measures. Repeat testing proved steady, and factor analysis supported two parts, physical and psychological. Patients with polyps reported the heaviest burden.
pmc-13285552:
Root fungi of a rare orchid vary sharply by home ground, Yu Wu and co-authors show in a 2026 field study of Paphiopedilum barbigerum. Knowing which fungi ride with this endangered slipper orchid could aid captive growth and return to the wild. Roots came from twenty-one plants at seven sites: guarded wild ground, unguarded wild ground, and one return site.

Sequencing sorted the fungi into thousands of species, led by two big phyla. Guarded wild roots held the richest fungal mix, laced with dry-hardy kinds. The return site fungal crowd looked much like the unguarded wild crowd, a hopeful sign for replanting. Three shared fungi formed a core set across sites. The authors offer the map for breeders.
pmc-13285752:
D Pesántez and colleagues describe a 2026 test of a smart assistant for early cancer drug trials. Trial teams must answer hard questions from long, tangled protocol files, and hunting through them eats hours. The team built a tool that pairs document search with a large language model to answer queries in plain chat form.

In a two-arm test, staff answered trial questions with or without the assistant, ten people in each arm. Those with the tool replied in about 15 minutes on average, against roughly 27 minutes for the control group. Blinded experts scored answers in both arms as mostly correct, with no real gap in quality. Users also reported high satisfaction, which points to faster trial work at no cost to accuracy.
pmc-13286052:
Anil Pant and co-authors present a new antiviral lead against poxviruses in a 2026 drug discovery study. Mpox keeps spreading, smallpox remains a feared what-if, and the shelf of proven drugs holds only a few entries with shaky human proof. A screen of the team's own compound library hunted for a fresh chemical that could stop these viruses in human cells.

One compound, a hydroxypyridone analog coded ZW-2038, curbed vaccinia, monkeypox, and cowpox viruses at low doses in skin cells. It also cut virus growth in gut tissue models from people and monkeys and in mouse lung tissue kept alive in the lab. Inside infected cells it blocked copying of viral DNA and the gene activity that follows. Mouse tests showed poor uptake by mouth, so the authors frame it as a strong but unfinished lead.
pmc-13286752:
Hua Chu and co-authors test a pressure probe for a pelvic floor problem that makes bowel movements hard to pass. The 2026 study checks the probe against the standard scan test, which uses X-rays or costly magnet scans. All patients in the study came to the clinic with blocked bowel movements.

About four in ten patients had the syndrome on the standard test. The probe gauges how far the pelvic floor drops when a patient strains. That drop, on its own, flagged the syndrome with fair accuracy. Adding other probe signs, such as a pouch in the rectum wall and poor muscle timing, cut false alarms. The team calls the probe a helpful add-on, not a swap for scans.
pmc-13286952:
Jia-Wei Wu and colleagues mine a United States adverse event database for neurological harms linked to tranexamic acid, a clot-preserving drug increasingly used in brain bleeding. Their 2026 study covers reports from 2004 to 2023 and pairs the search with laboratory work on brain cells. Safety worries center on seizures and other nerve complications that worsen outcomes after hemorrhage.

Eight significant neurological signals surfaced, including seizure types. Network analysis nominated three genes as possible mediators of the harm. Computer docking showed the drug binding those targets tightly, and simulations kept the binding stable. Cell experiments supported a neurotoxic effect. The authors urge caution and dedicated safety studies before wider use in brain bleeding.
pmc-13287252:
Yuhei Yamaguchi and co-authors rechecked tumour samples in 2026 from 84 patients with spreading breast cancer. Each HER2 level had first been read with an older test. It was later read with a newer one used to judge eligibility for a targeted drug. Retesting took place between May 2023 and November 2024.

Results disagreed for 60.7% of patients, most often stepping down one grade. Samples taken from spread sites and tumours lacking progesterone receptors were more likely to change. About a quarter of patients whose results changed lost the low-HER2 label that opened access to the drug. The authors urge care when old and new readings are compared in clinic.
pmc-13287452:
Claudia Neubauer and co-authors tested a new photon-counting scanner in 2026 for staging breast cancer through the chest and abdomen, with magnetic resonance imaging as the reference. Seventy-five women with 79 newly found cancers had both scans, with the new scan taken lying face down.

Readers rated cancer visibility and image quality as excellent. Tumour size matched the reference scan closely. Accuracy was good for tumour stage, spread pattern, and armpit nodes, and very high for chest-wall nodes. It was weaker for a non-invasive cancer form. Iodine uptake inside tumours differed by subtype, lowest on average in triple negative cancers. Larger confirmatory work is still needed.
pmc-13287752:
Xu and coauthors find a gene that drives bowel cancer growth and drug proof. Bowel cancer is a top cause of cancer death worldwide. It grows in steps from normal lining to polyp to cancer. Which genes steer those steps has stayed partly unclear.

The gene, called ZNF473, was high in cancer tissue. High levels tracked with poor patient outcomes in the data. Lab tests cut the gene in cancer cells to see effects. Growth and spread fell when the gene was cut. The gene weakens a guard protein that holds cancer back. Loss of that guard lifts a survival protein in cells.
pmc-13287952:
Stanisław Jurk, Andreas Kremer, and Ekkehard Schleussner update guidance on a pregnancy liver disorder in a 2026 review. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is the most common liver problem that occurs only in pregnancy. Bile acids build up in the blood, liver enzyme levels rise, and intense itching is the hallmark symptom. The review gathers current diagnostic criteria and treatment advice in one place.

Ursodeoxycholic acid remains the first treatment choice, easing itching and lowering bile acid levels. Doctors base the timing of delivery mainly on how high the bile acid level climbs, since high levels raise risks around birth. Symptoms usually fade soon after delivery, and blood values return to normal within weeks. The authors stress steady monitoring through the second half of pregnancy. Their summary aims to help clinicians weigh comfort, safety, and delivery timing together.
pmc-13288052:
Yu-Hsu Chen and co-authors mined the Taiwan Biobank in 2026 for signs that flag low bone density. A learning model covered 19,868 adults aged forty and over. All had bone scans between 2020 and 2022. Explanatory plots then ranked which body measures drove each prediction, separately for women and men.

Low density affected 44% of participants. Model accuracy was fair in women and weaker in men. Age, menopause state, and body mass led for women; age, body mass, and waist size led for men. Blood counts, fat share, blood pressure, and kidney and liver markers also carried weight. The authors argue screening should use sex-specific sign sets.
pmc-13288852:
Paul C Toboltoc and co-authors review blood cancer care in the COVID-19 years in 2026. Their piece is a narrative review. Blood cancer needs fast diagnosis. It needs frequent visits and transfusions. Intensive therapy and transplants also feature. The pandemic scrambled all of that.

The authors drew on disruption studies. Registries, remote-care cohorts, and transplant surveys joined in. Harmful delays were split from useful inventions. Protected routes and risk triage helped. Clean infection circuits helped too. Remote review suited stable patients. The advice is to keep the discipline. Crisis limits that only rationed care should go.
pmc-13288952:
Xuanhe Liu and colleagues offer a 2026 trial plan in Anhui, China. The trial tests value-led care for heart risk. Village clinics will take part as whole units. The plan covers 32 clinics in all. Half will get the new care model. Half will keep usual care.

The model ranks care steps by cost value. It guides doctors to pick high-value steps first. Training and feedback will back the model. The trial will enroll 1,920 adults. All will have high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart disease. Cost per good health year is the main result. Checks run at 12 and 24 months.
pmc-13289052: A 2026 correction notice fixes a figure error in a 2015 cancer study. The study dealt with the gene MTA1 and mesothelioma spread. One wound-healing image in Figure 2 was used twice by mistake. An image from one cell line stood in for another. The notice prints the correct figure and its full caption. The caption sums up tests of invasion, migration, and cell growth. No new data or changed claims appear in the notice. It is short and deals with the image swap alone.
pmc-13289252:
Fan Cao and coauthors present a 2026 global analysis of autoimmune disease burden in men over three decades. Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system attacks the body itself. Using Global Burden of Disease estimates for 204 countries from 1990 to 2021, they tracked new cases, total cases, deaths, and years lost to illness or early death.

Overall burden in men fell worldwide across the study years. In wealthy countries, however, new-case rates rose after 2005, and total cases plus years lived with disability rose after 2015 in those settings. Care quality scores in 2021 still varied widely, from 74.97 in low-middle income settings to 90.55 in high income settings as reported. Gaps for young, working-age, and older men point to uneven access that still needs fixing.
pmc-13289352:
Sainan Li and others studied chemical exposure and birth heart defects in 2026. Lasting wastes can reach the womb. Flame retardants and old factory chemicals stood out. No study had tested heart links in a set way. A mother's B vitamins might change risk. That changing role was the key question.

Exposure before birth linked to higher defect risk. Enough B vitamins blunted that link strongly. Shielding showed in the group data. The authors claim first group evidence here. Food may soften harm from surroundings partly. Heart growth is at risk during pregnancy. Vitamin status merits a look in advice sessions. Policy on surroundings also matters greatly.
pmc-13289652:
Marwah I Bin Abdulqader and coauthors offer a 2026 critical review on artificial intelligence in drug discovery. Classic discovery loses most candidates, costs a great deal, and takes many years, while resistance and complex cancers raise the stakes. Machine learning promises faster search of chemical space and smarter molecule design, but real impact needs sober review beyond hype.

The narrative review covers work from 2000 to 2026 across small-molecule drugs, antibodies, anticancer agents, and antibiotics. Methods ranged from classic machine learning to deep learning models of many designs. Selected studies had to report direct drug discovery use, excluding vague or incomplete reports. Strengths in early lab settings are weighed against limits in data, validation, and clinic translation.
pmc-13289752:
Gongze Liu and co-authors build a low-power artificial nose from an ionic thermoelectric device in 2026. Smelling several gases at once usually takes power-hungry detectors. Their device turns tiny heat differences into voltage inside a solid ionic polymer, an effect far stronger than in standard materials. Wafer-scale fabrication packed sensing units smaller than one hundred micrometers across. Each unit pairs the thermoelectric element with a narrow optical filter tuned to one gas.

The combined platform untangled mixed gases species by species. Its responsivity hit a record level near 2,340 volts per watt, about twenty times commercial detectors. Detection limits reached parts per million for carbon dioxide and methane, and parts per billion for carbon monoxide. The authors present the chip as a path to efficient multi-gas monitors. Uses span air quality, industry, and health breath tests.
pmc-13289852:
Shinya Ohno and colleagues report a 2026 case of conversion surgery after strong response to zolbetuximab-based chemotherapy in stomach cancer. Zolbetuximab targets a protein called Claudin 18.2 on tumor cells. A 59-year-old man with stage IV, Claudin-positive cancer and suspected belly spread got the antibody plus capecitabine and oxaliplatin as initial therapy.

After six courses, imaging showed marked tumor shrinkage for the patient. A camera check of the belly found no spread, so surgeons removed part of the stomach with clear margins in a keyhole operation. Tissue grading showed a strong response, final stage fell to IB, and he stayed free of return at twelve months. Heavy bleeding during surgery, likely from treatment scarring, urges caution.
pmc-13289952:
Sohail Agha headed a 2026 quasi-experimental study on social media campaigns to lift HPV vaccination in Bangladesh. Cervical cancer kills many Bangladeshi women, and a single-dose school campaign launched nationally in 2024 across six divisions. Four intervention mixes were tested against a control group, with caregiver surveys before and after involving thousands of respondents online.

Baseline held 3,823 caregivers and follow-up held 7,004 caregivers of girls aged 9 to 17 for comparison. Coverage rose from 10.1 percent to 32.9 percent even in controls, reflecting the national drive everywhere. Targeted social media, alone or with school awareness, added the largest extra gains in adjusted models. School awareness alone added only a small edge.
pmc-13290452:
Genes behind leaf spot resistance and seed dormancy in peanut are hunted by Jie Zhang and colleagues in a 2026 genome-wide association study. Peanut is a major oil and protein crop, and both traits matter to breeders trying to protect yields and seed quality.

The team resequenced 87 accessions from the US peanut mini-core collection, generating 217 Gb of data and 87,726 markers across 20 chromosomes. The accessions fell into three gene pools, and marker density proved sufficient for association mapping. Three candidate genes stood out: one tied to early leaf spot resistance, one to late leaf spot resistance, and one, an ICE1 homolog, influencing both germination and dormancy. Zhang and colleagues propose the markers for selection programs aimed at hardier, better-seeded varieties.
pmc-13290952:
The cell body alone carries a fingerprint of interneuron identity, Maheshwar Panday and colleagues show in an atlas study from 2026. Parvalbumin-positive inhibitory neurons steer cortical plasticity, and while their wiring and genes show rich variety, whether plain soma shape under the microscope holds the same information was unknown.

The team measured 97 shape features in over 14,000 labeled cells from mouse visual and somatosensory cortex. Clustering sorted the cells into 13 shape groups arranged along partly independent size and shape gradients, summarized as four size and five shape categories. Mapped back onto cortical layers, particular shapes concentrated in particular layers, matching the cortex's circuit architecture. Panday and colleagues say standard labeling plus this quantitative lens can extract far more anatomy than size and density counts ever did.
pmc-13291152:
Drug pairs that may raise pancreatitis risk are hunted in a 2026 safety study led by Issei Kazume. Some diabetes drugs based on incretin hormones have been linked to pancreas inflammation. Less clear is how other drugs taken at the same time change that risk.

The team mined a large United States database of reported side effects. Data ran from late 1997 to early 2024. Single drugs were scored for links to acute pancreatitis. Pairs used with the diabetes drugs were then checked for extra risk. Several drugs showed raised reporting rates. Time trends were tracked across six spans. Such signals can guide safer prescribing, though they do not prove cause.
pmc-13291252: Fernando Dias Correia and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to a study on home recovery after knee replacement. The record here consists solely of that correction notice. One flow diagram gave a wrong count of excluded patients. A results table also held wrong spread values for knee bending. Two scores were printed as averages instead of middle values. The fixed diagram and table are reprinted in the note. Judging the study itself requires the full article, not this note.
pmc-13291852:
Guangjun Wang and a large team survey a 2026 review topic: using artificial intelligence to predict biological age rather than counting birthdays. Biological age aims to capture how fast a body is actually aging. The review walks through biomarker choice, feature building, model design, bias correction, and performance checks.

Methods range from classic machine learning to deep networks that fuse several data types at once. The authors highlight asynchronous aging, where organs age at different speeds, as a pattern AI is well placed to detect. Uses include disease risk scoring and population health monitoring. They close with open problems: uneven data, weak general use across groups, hard-to-explain models, and slow movement into clinics.
pmc-13292152:
Tingrun Cui and co-authors test a 2026 diagnostic idea for infected artificial joints: reading neutrophil extracellular traps in joint fluid. These web-like structures spill from neutrophils during infection and are hard to judge with standard tests alone. The retrospective study covered arthroplasty patients from 2018 to 2023, measuring three trap components alongside cell counts and cultures.

Of 153 patients, 64 had confirmed infections. Two trap markers, cell-free DNA and citrullinated histone H3, ran much higher in infected fluid and tracked with white cell counts. A combined index the authors call NETRI reached an area under the curve of 0.922 in their analysis. One-marker positivity suited screening, while two-marker positivity, at 95.5 percent specificity in the data, suited ruling infection in. The authors propose trap testing as a fresh discriminator.
pmc-13292752:
Marwa Bawazir and Sibel A Antonson stage a 2026 reliability contest in adhesive dentistry. Five veteran dentists and five first-year students each bonded six hundred dentin surfaces, split between a universal adhesive and a classic etch-and-rinse system. Surfaces came wet, moist, or dry, and everyone worked both before and after a demonstration of the makers' technique.

The universal adhesive barely noticed who held it: median bond strength was 25.53 megapascals for dentists and 24.96 for students, with tight spreads. The etch-and-rinse lagged and wobbled, at medians of 17.79 for dentists and 13.52 for students. Overall the universal product beat its rival by about 7.38 megapascals across conditions. Dry and moist dentin outbonded wet dentin. The authors conclude operator experience matters for the older system, not the universal one.
pmc-13292852:
Francesco Angelucci and colleagues review, in 2026, what is known about spermidine and Alzheimer disease. Spermidine is a natural compound in cells and food that supports cleanup of worn cell parts, a process that falters as the brain ages.

Animal work links spermidine to better memory, healthier synapses, and less inflammation and cell stress. Human data are thinner: diet studies hint that higher intake goes with better thinking, but they cannot prove cause. The few trials so far were small and mixed, with no steady gain on main memory tests. The authors say firm proof is still lacking and larger trials are needed.
pmc-13293552:
Crowns and bridges must fit teeth snugly, and dentists capture the tooth shape either with putty molds or with digital scanners. Anamika Sinha and co-authors review which method yields the better fit for multi-unit fixed dental prostheses. They searched three major databases and combined results statistically. Fourteen studies qualified: three trials in patients and eleven lab studies on models. Outcomes were the gap at the crown's edge and the space inside it.

Across studies, pieces from digital scans fit better at the edge and inside than putty-mold pieces. The patient trials showed the same trend at the edge and a clear digital advantage inside the crown. Lab studies showed a stronger digital advantage on both measures. One scanner family, Trios, trended toward the best edge fit among the devices. Caution remains: most gaps stayed within limits dentists accept either way.
pmc-13293652:
Tiphaine Douanne and co-authors probe, in a 2026 study, how straight-line ubiquitin chains help drive pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death set off by the NLRP3 sensor. This death guards against infection but must stay tightly controlled to avoid harm.

Chains built by an enzyme team called LUBAC formed in both the priming and killing phases, even without the sensor present. Removing LUBAC parts or blocking them weakened the death, while removing OTULIN, an enzyme that strips these chains, strengthened it. A light-based model that skips priming still needed the chains for the killing phase. Chain control thus gates this death.
pmc-13293852:
Lei Ma and coauthors survey 1,040 university students in China in a 2026 study on artificial intelligence literacy and new ideas. Students reported how well they understand and use AI, plus their anxiety about AI, mental flexibility, and innovative behavior. The authors test whether anxiety and flexibility carry part of the link between literacy and innovation.

Higher literacy went with more flexibility and more innovative behavior, and with less anxiety. Three indirect paths were significant, through anxiety alone, flexibility alone, and both in sequence. Students fell into low, moderate, and high literacy groups, and the pathways differed across groups, which suggests tailored teaching by skill level.
pmc-13294152:
Sam Er Bader and colleagues test brain effects of aortic balloon occlusion during severe bleeding in a 2026 pig study. The REBOA technique blocks the aorta to restore pressure near the heart and brain, but brain metabolism under raised skull pressure was unclear. Bleeding dropped mean arterial pressure to about 40 mmHg, then zone 1 occlusion lasted 90 minutes while brain dialysis tracked lactate and pyruvate.

Shock raised the lactate-pyruvate ratio in both normal and raised pressure groups, signaling starved brain tissue. After occlusion the ratio eased back toward baseline in both groups. Raised pressure slowed only the first 10 minutes of recovery. Acute brain chemistry thus recovered despite high skull pressure.
pmc-13294452:
Samriddhi S Gupte and coauthors propose a stewardship-linked path for reserve antibiotics in India in a 2026 article. India faces too little access for some patients and reckless use for others, both feeding resistance that caused 1.14 million direct deaths globally in 2021 in the cited count. New last-line drugs often never reach poorer countries at all.

Their plan ties facility access tiers to proven stewardship quality, with early planning, targeted oversight, and live use monitoring. Hospitals earn broader access by showing careful prescribing, protecting new drugs while still reaching patients who need them. The model could travel to other countries facing the same access-versus-excess squeeze.
pmc-13294652:
Sadie E Larsen and colleagues describe updating an online decision aid for posttraumatic stress disorder treatment in a 2026 article. Effective treatments exist, yet no method yet shows which option suits which patient best. The National Center for PTSD first released its aid in 2017.

A small team revised the aid with expert and consumer input to match newer guidelines and technology needs. People who screened positive tested core tasks, and Veterans Administration patients and clinicians tried the aid during appointments. Early field testing suggested the aid felt acceptable and balanced, eased decisional conflict, and strengthened confidence in choosing treatment.
pmc-13295052:
Rossella Santonocito and a large team build a formaldehyde sniffer that works with a phone camera, in a 2026 sensor study. The gas seeps from furniture, paints, and glues into indoor air, stings airways, and counts as a human carcinogen, yet lab-grade detectors cost much and stay on benches. Their probe is a carbon nanoparticle dressed with diethanolamine groups set to grab the gas as a team.

In water, the particles sensed the gas down to forty-six parts per billion. Printed on membrane strips and read by a 3D-printed phone platform, the setup sensed one part per billion. That is far under health guide levels, and the strips kept working in damp air where rival carbon sensors fail. Trials on shop paints gave sensible readings. The authors offer the kit as an early warning tool for homes and work sites.
pmc-13295752:
Margaret B Allison and colleagues test a collagen-seeking scan for lung scarring in scleroderma in a 2026 report. Lung disease strikes about half of systemic sclerosis patients at diagnosis and drives most deaths from the illness. A PET probe that binds type 1 collagen had worked in another scarring lung disease but not yet here.

Patients received the probe and underwent combined PET and MRI scanning under a registered trial protocol. Uptake readings were averaged across divided lung regions for whole-lung comparison with healthy volunteers. The work marks the first use of this probe in scleroderma lung disease, opening a path toward earlier spotting of scarring and better timing of treatment.
pmc-13295852:
Sadiq Rehmani and colleagues examine, in 2026, whether side effects from cancer immunotherapy predict longer survival among United States veterans. Earlier reports linked such immune-related events to better outcomes, but type and severity may matter more than presence alone.

Records for 1,707 patients treated between 2010 and 2023 were reviewed, and about a quarter had at least one such event. Overall, having an event did not clearly improve survival once timing bias was handled. Milder events needing no steroids, especially thyroid and skin ones, did link to better survival, while steroid-treated events trended worse. Organ type, the authors argue, shapes the signal.
pmc-13296052:
Nimet Turgut and co-authors measure, in 2026, the small openings in the middle skull base of dogs using cone-beam scans. These holes carry key nerves and vessels, and their size may shift with skull shape, which matters for surgery and diagnosis.

Scans from forty healthy dogs were grouped by skull size using a brain-case length measure. The main openings sat in matching places and shapes on both sides, growing larger as skulls and body weight grew. One small opening was missing in small-skulled dogs. The authors offer the values as a reference for varied dog types.
pmc-13296652:
Taylor S. Hudson, Brianne M. Seagreaves, and Amelia W. Maiga update guidance on disorders of consciousness after traumatic injury in a 2026 review. Patients may sit anywhere from coma to a minimally conscious state, and awareness can fluctuate from hour to hour. Diagnosis and outlook in the first days are therefore genuinely hard.

Repeated examination with a standard bedside scale remains the core of care in intensive care units. The review warns against locking in a grim prognosis too early, when signs are still unstable. Most treatment is supportive, aimed at preventing further brain insults while recovery has time to declare itself. Families and teams both benefit from that measured, humble approach.
pmc-13296952:
Hakan Işıker and colleagues apply, in 2026, a butterfly-inspired optimiser to the problem of running power grids cheaply and cleanly at once. They adapt the method with shrinking populations and self-tuned settings, then test it on standard thirty- and fifty-seven-node networks.

Four goals, cost, loss, emissions and voltage steadiness, were paired into combined problems, including cases with renewable uncertainty. The method found compromise settings balancing cost against emissions and emissions against loss, beating most published rivals on the same tests. The authors claim a first use of this optimiser for such multi-goal power problems.
pmc-13297152:
Onur Bağcı and colleagues study delayed cord clamping in babies born before thirty weeks in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Waiting sixty seconds before clamping lets extra placental blood reach the newborn. Records covered 156 infants in a level-four intensive care unit, seventy of whom received delayed clamping.

The delayed group showed lower rates of brain bleeding, breathing distress, chronic lung disease, and death in raw comparisons. Their early condition scores were also higher, and severe brain bleeding did not occur in that group. After adjusting for birth weight, gestation, and other differences, the gaps lost statistical significance. The authors still favour the practice and want trials including unstable infants.
pmc-13297252:
Krystian Konieczny and colleagues test whether weather sensitivity helps explain why strong body awareness travels with mental symptoms in a 2026 survey study. More than five hundred adults from the general public filled in forms on body awareness, weather sensitivity, and mental symptoms. Maths models then traced direct and indirect links between them.

Body awareness alone explained about a quarter of the spread in symptoms. Adding the two weather measures more than doubled that share. Both weather paths carried a real indirect link, while a direct link stayed as well. The pattern held across many symptom types, from low mood and anxiety to sleep and eating trouble. Weather sensitivity deserves a place in this corner of mental health, the authors say.
pmc-13297352:
Leopold Eckhart, Supawadee Sukseree and Heinz Fischer review, in 2026, holocrine secretion, the self-destructive final step where oil gland cells burst wholesale into sebum. These glands oil hair and skin, and their finishing cells dissolve their own nucleus and parts before the membrane ruptures.

Animal evidence points to a lysosomal enzyme digesting nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, giving the cell's recycling sacs a starring role. The review weighs how tight junctions place the bursting zone, how self-eating tunes the process and what might pop the membrane. Clinical relevance stays an open question.
pmc-13297752:
Your blood type may come with a distinct signature of circulating molecules, indicates a 2026 pilot study by Alessia Di Salvo and co-authors. They measured 73 blood molecules in 56 healthy donors: 24 with group O, 19 with group A, and 13 with group B.

Group A donors carried higher levels of many signals tied to inflammation, vessel growth, and tissue remodeling, including IL-13, IL-23, VEGF family members, and MMP-1. Group B donors stood out for IL-22, P-selectin, and amyloid β1–42, among others. The authors read these profiles as biological differences that might help explain why disease risk varies by blood group, while cautioning that the small exploratory study needs confirmation.
pmc-13298452:
Tests for prostate disease still blur the line between plain swelling and true cancer. Imola Donath-Miklos and her team ask in a 2026 review if fresh blood marks can sharpen that line. They focus on three leads: YKL-40, mannose-binding lectin, and broad marks of DNA methylation in the blood.

Each mark taps a unlike layer of the disease. One tracks immune tone in tissue, one tracks inborn immune range, and one tracks long-set marks left by past immune stress. None is fit to stand alone as a test today. The team place them as add-ons next to PSA, gene tests, and MRI scans. They call for set lab norms and forward-looking trials in prostate care before any clinic use.
pmc-13299452:
Guorui Chen, Bo Zhang, Yicheng Zhang, and Kun Song study how campus environments relate to student health and lifestyle at five Chinese universities, in a 2026 survey analysis. Responses from 909 students passed through two stages: first finding which lifestyle habits connect to health status, then testing which environmental features connect to those habits.

Six lifestyle parameters tied significantly to health, covering exercise frequency and duration, active commuting, nature contact, healthy eating, and self-rated health literacy. Each habit showed its own distinct pattern of environmental links. The authors argue the results support targeted environmental changes in campus design that promote health where students actually live and study.
pmc-13300052:
Viruses hiding in the brain may not match those in blood or spinal fluid, a question Xin Dang and colleagues tackled in a 2026 study. Using matched postmortem samples from the National NeuroAIDS Tissue Consortium, they compared brain, cerebrospinal fluid, and peripheral tissues from people with and without HIV and substance use disorder.

A targeted enrichment method called ViroFind detected material from 27 viruses across the sample sets. Spinal fluid held the narrowest mix, while peripheral samples carried the heaviest load. Hepatitis B and C viruses turned up inside the central nervous system, though neither is classed as nerve-seeking. HIV raised peripheral burden and diversity; substance use disorder did not.
pmc-13300552:
Ahmed Mahmoud Elsoudy and Luciano Candilio review coronary computed tomography angiography as a planning tool before stent procedures, in a 2026 article. The scan once served mainly to rule out blocked arteries, but sharper three-dimensional images, computed flow reserve estimates, and artificial intelligence plaque analysis have widened its role. The authors trace the technology's growth and walk through where a pre-procedure scan now shapes decisions in the catheterization laboratory.

The strongest use case is difficult anatomy, above all chronic total occlusions, where the scan reveals blockage length, stump shape, vessel course, and collateral routes beforehand. Vessel sizing, stent choice, and calcium preparation also benefit. Barriers remain, including calcium blooming that blurs images, radiation dose, contrast risks for kidneys, and the effort of fitting scans into routine workflows. The authors conclude the scan has become a practical roadmap rather than a purely diagnostic test.
pmc-13301352:
Graziella Pompei and co-authors weigh clopidogrel against aspirin as the partner drug for patients who need a blood thinner and a stent, in a 2026 narrative review. People on long term anticoagulation, usually for atrial fibrillation, who then receive a coronary stent face competing risks: clots in the stent and the circulation versus bleeding from stacked therapy. Trials spent two decades trimming triple therapy down to double, an anticoagulant plus one antiplatelet drug.

The review walks through the landmark trials behind double therapy, stratified by anticoagulant type. Head to head evidence for clopidogrel versus aspirin as the single antiplatelet is thin, resting on few recent studies, and no large randomized comparison settles it. The authors flag platelet function and genetic testing as guides for choosing the agent. Their bottom line is a call for the trial the field still lacks, since the wrong default risks avoidable clots or bleeds.
pmc-13301452:
Imen Hammami and co-authors test milk thistle extract against cadmium poisoning in rats in a 2026 study. Twenty-four Wistar rats split into four groups: control, cadmium alone at five milligrams per kilogram, silymarin alone at thirty, and both together, over six weeks. The team tracked weight, blood chemistry, oxidative stress markers across liver, kidney, and testis, plus sperm quality by computer and testis structure under the microscope.

Cadmium cut body weight by about thirty-one percent, raised liver enzymes and creatinine, and crushed sperm concentration from about seventy-five to twenty-two million per milliliter, with severe tubule degeneration. Silymarin clawed it back partway: sperm concentration near thirty-nine million, motility improved, and enzyme and organ markers recovered but incompletely. Computer docking suggested the compound binds the antioxidant enzymes cadmium depletes. The authors call silymarin a partial, promising shield, and propose dose tuning and combinations with chelators.
pmc-13302052:
Hyunsuk Choi, Yong-Suk Moon, and colleagues test in a 2026 animal study whether plasma treatment improves a cattle-bone graft used to rebuild jaw bone. Such grafts fill defects before dental implants, yet they spark new bone slowly. Non-thermal plasma, an energised gas applied at the chairside, was used to activate the graft surface.

Twenty-four rabbits each received two skull defects, one filled with treated graft and one with untreated graft. Animals were examined at two, four, and eight weeks, and treated sites grew significantly more new bone at every point. Treated grafts also broke down faster, with more marrow space, more blood vessels, and more bone-eating cells. The authors see simple plasma activation as a practical way to lift graft performance.
pmc-13302852:
Varvara P. Pavlova and co-authors test, in a 2026 pilot laboratory study, how the hormone estradiol changes antibiotic behaviour inside bacterial biofilms. The model pairs a friendly vaginal Lactobacillus with Cutibacterium acnes, a skin bacterium also found in the vagina. Hormones bathe these communities naturally, yet drug testing usually ignores them.

Estradiol slowed biofilm building by the lactobacilli, while pushing the skin C. acnes strain up and the vaginal isolate down. The hormone also shifted how both species answered the antibiotic clindamycin, sometimes dramatically. In mixed communities the antibiotic's apparent effect flipped direction altogether. Gene activity for bacteria-killing proteins changed without matching the visible behaviour, warning that single-species drug tests can mislead.
pmc-13303252:
Reflection belongs inside competency training, not bolted on afterward, Sara Horton-Deutsch argues in a 2026 commentary on nursing education. Writing solo, she responds to Armstrong and Sherwood's paper on embedding reflective practice across competency development to make feedback learner-centred. Their model follows reflection through three moments: before action, in action, and on action after the fact.

Horton-Deutsch hears a deep harmony with Watson's Theory of Human Caring, where knowing oneself grounds clinical competence. She walks through their practical tools, from Ask-Tell-Ask conversations to mindful pauses, and draws out consequences for faculty development and curriculum design. Reflection, on this reading, builds the habits of mind that sustain a career.
pmc-13303452:
Rosalind T. B. Herrington and co-authors test, in a 2026 mouse study, whether a mother's probiotic supplements reach and alter the placenta and fetal brain. Such supplements are marketed to pregnant women, but their effects on the unborn are rarely examined. Dams on supplements were compared with controls across gut chemicals, placenta, and fetal brain gene activity.

Bacterial fatty acids in the mothers' droppings did not change, yet both organs showed clear gene shifts in the offspring. Female placentas answered more strongly, while male fetal brains reacted more. One placenta gene tied to serotonin uptake rose in females, and a stress-shielding gene fell sharply in males. Brain changes touched forebrain development genes, prompting the authors to warn of possible lifelong effects.
pmc-13303652:
