Lei Luo and co-authors present a 2026 computer modeling study of how pores weaken 3D-printed concrete. Layer-by-layer printing traps air and leaves gaps between layers, which cut the strength of finished parts.

Using a phase-field cohesive zone model, the team varied pore size, shape, tilt, and layout one factor at a time. A single pore hurt most when its flat side faced across the pulling force. In groups, the angle linking pores mattered more than spacing, and rows of pores lined up sideways could trigger sudden brittle breaks. Clusters of small pores proved worse than one large pore alone.
pmc-13304552:
Amanda Cristina Machado Carloto leads a 2026 lab study of curcumin, the turmeric compound, against the parasite that causes leishmaniasis. The spice chemical kills germs in tests but absorbs poorly in the body, limiting real use.

Free curcumin slowed free-swimming parasites and stirred stress inside them, raising reactive chemicals, swelling power units, and packing fat droplets until cell death programs engaged. Packed into beeswax-based nanoparticles, the compound turned gentler on host cells while still clearing infected immune cells. Pairing the particles with a standard drug also cut infection, opening a route toward safer parasite treatment.
pmc-13304652:
Omar Abdelaziz and co-authors review eye surface and cornea problems tied to contact lens wear in a 2026 clinical survey. Lenses correct vision for millions, yet they can disturb the eye surface from mild irritation to blinding infection.

Common troubles such as discomfort, dry eye, and lid bumps are usually mild and settle with simple care. Mid-range inflammation can mimic early infection and confuse first assessment. Germ infection of the cornea is the gravest risk and can advance fast when missed. Risk-based sorting, quick referral, lens hygiene, and patient teaching anchor safe frontline care.
pmc-13304852:
Chen Chen and co-authors warn that ion-beam microscopes can fake the very features they reveal in energy materials in a 2026 perspective. Cutting samples with focused ion beams exposes buried battery layers, but milling, vacuum, and imaging can also reshape them.

Each tool in the chain, from beam cutting to atom probing, may shift shape, chemistry, or phase, especially in light elements and fragile coatings. The authors propose judging every claim against the smallest control that can separate real structure from tool damage. Porous electrodes and reactive interfaces get detailed checklists for trustworthy evidence.
pmc-13304952:
Wei Luo and colleagues tune germanium-silicon quantum dots with high heat in a 2026 study of on-chip light sources. The dots glow at telecom wavelengths and fit silicon chip making, suiting combined electronic and optical circuits.

Fast heating at rising temperatures first deepened then shifted the glow color, while brightness climbed steeply. At the top heat the glow narrowed to a single peak near the key telecom band with about twenty times the starting strength. Microscopy and vibration spectra tie the change to element mixing and a strain flip inside the dots. Heat treatment thus offers a simple tuning knob.
pmc-13306452:
Lokeshwaran Srinivasan and co-authors examine in 2026 how build direction and chamber position affect surface finish in laser-sintered nylon parts. Polyamide 12 pieces were printed in three orientations and placed in inner, middle, and outer chamber zones. Roughness, internal structure, and crystallinity were compared across the set.

Lowest roughness came from Y-oriented parts placed in the inner chamber, while Z-oriented outer parts were roughest. The spread between best and worst reached about ten percent. Microscopy showed smoother, less porous surfaces in inner samples, and heat analysis linked better finish to higher crystallinity. Stable heat in the chamber centre explains much of the pattern, the authors suggest. Their guidance helps operators place and orient parts when surface quality matters most.
pmc-13306552:
Lissethkaren Alvarez Vargas described kidney disease uncovered through swollen glands in a 2026 case report with literature review. Mikulicz disease, an IgG4-related swelling of tear and saliva glands, can mask wider immune disease that also scars the kidneys.

A 49-year-old man reported two years of excess urination and foamy urine, with blood creatinine at 4.2 mg/dL and daily protein loss of 2874 mg in reported tests. Both parotid glands were enlarged on examination. The authors stress separating true Mikulicz disease from look-alike gland swelling, since late kidney diagnosis can leave lasting damage.
pmc-13307152:
João Carlos Ramos compared bending strength of temporary dental materials with and without reinforcement in a 2026 study. Standard bars sized 2 × 2 × 25 mm were made from acrylic resin, a printed resin and a bis-acryl resin for provisional crowns.

Each material split into plain, two glass fibre and one metal reinforced groups in the reported design, then faced three-point bending. Material and reinforcement both shaped strength and stiffness clearly. One fibre product, EverStick C&B, gave the highest values across all bases, strongest in the acrylic resin group. Stronger short term crowns may cut breakage while the final tooth work is still being made.
pmc-13308952:
Liansheng Mai and co-authors report in 2026 three cases of stomach holes blamed on fish bones, where surgery found no bone in two of the three. Each patient came in with sharp upper belly pain after a recent fish meal, and scans showed a thick gut wall plus a line like bright streak.

All three had keyhole surgery at once, and two were switched to open surgery for a fuller search inside. Holes were sewn, washed, and drained in each case, and no snags arose after care for any patient. A fish tale plus scan signs still merit the fish bone call, even when the bone itself hides from the surgeon.
pmc-13309352:
Jaein Cho and co-authors test in 2026 whether a five item frailty score can flag risk in older adults who face lumbar spine surgery. Spine wear drives more such work each year. They drew charts for 967 adults aged 70 years and up at one large Korean hospital from 2020 to 2021, with a year of follow up.

Severe frailty, a score of 3 or more, marked 132 people, or 13.6 percent of the group in the raw count. After weight based tuning for mix ups, severe frailty still tied to in hospital problems, with odds near 1.8 times those of the less frail. High anaesthesia risk grades, need for daily help, and in hospital problems each foresaw harms in the year after.
pmc-13310052:
Xiaoyu Wu and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, the two-sided role that natural killer cells play in the liver during sepsis. Sepsis is organ failure driven by a runaway response to infection, and the liver sits at its center as a filter and immune organ. Killer cells in the liver differ from those in blood and can both guard and injure the organ.

On the guard side, these cells fight microbes, release calming signals, and protect vessel walls by lowering a growth factor. Their killing power also checks viruses inside liver cells. Yet the same killing can damage healthy tissue when control slips. The authors weigh factors that tip the balance and sketch treatment ideas built on that balance.
pmc-13310252:
Yuzhe Pan and co-authors argue for a regional frame to judge healthy eating patterns in China in a 2026 comment. National dietary guidance sets shared principles, summed in the Chinese Food Guide Pagoda. Local food systems, budgets, and habits decide whether those principles can actually reach the table.

Eating advice lands through markets, canteens, cooking habits, and food culture, all of which vary by region. A regional assessment frame could sort when a pattern fits local guidance, when it needs adaptation, and when it can feed back into national advice. The authors lay out the gap between national standards and daily practice. Their aim is guidance that households can afford and accept.
pmc-13310652:
Gui-Long Tanzhu and co-authors review the living neighborhood around brain tumors in a 2026 article. Brain tumors, both those born in the brain and those spread from elsewhere, carry grim outlooks. Their surroundings mix tumor cells, immune cells, neurons, vessels, matrix, and chemical signals in constant cross-talk.

Single-cell and spatial gene methods have newly exposed how varied and arranged those surroundings are. Parts and jobs of each element are summarized, along with the signals they swap and how those swaps steer growth and treatment response. Clinical hopes and hurdles get direct treatment, from immune access to drug delivery. The authors aim the review at researchers designing microenvironment-aware trials.
pmc-13310952:
Go Yoshimichi reports a 2026 case of severe high blood sugar syndrome with lasting higher brain trouble. A woman aged 64 years with type 2 diabetes arrived unconscious and got standard care for hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome. Sugar and body chemistry improved, yet speech loss and failure to recognize objects remained.

A scan method that maps blood flow without dye showed raised flow in the left temporal and parietal brain lobes. Such flow changes may explain why brain signs linger after body chemistry clears. Flow mapping could aid study of brain harm in this acute diabetes crisis.
pmc-13311152:
Yeela Talmor-Barkan leads a 2026 study called RetiMap on retinal vessel measures as windows to body health. Sharp eye photos can show tiny vessels directly, and smart tools can now measure vessel width and density at scale. Past work linked such traits to heart risk, yet often looked at few traits or few risk factors.

Large biobank data have tied vessel traits to blood pressure, smoking, sleep apnea, and blood sugar. Deep tools have also foretold death risk and weight linked ills from photos alone. The new work aims at a wider joint map of vessel traits and body risk to sharpen early warning.
pmc-13311752:
Tsidiso Tolla and co-authors set out a 2026 scoping review protocol on poor mental health in male students and its ties to their sexual violence against women students at African universities.

The review will search six databases plus Google Scholar, open-access listings, and grey sources. A population-concept-context frame will judge which studies fit. Search methods mix phrase and Boolean logic, citation chasing, and filters. Work from rich countries links masculine norms and male distress to such violence, but African evidence is unmapped. The map should show what is known and where research must go next.
pmc-13311952:
Yannan Ding and co-authors give a 2025 bibliometric map of research on information technology in hospital antimicrobial stewardship over twenty years. Software now helps teams curb antibiotic overuse and resistance.

A Web of Science search for 2000 to 2025 yielded 258 English papers. Output rose unevenly to a peak of 49 papers in 2024. The United States led with 131 papers, and hub institutions included Harvard and Imperial College London. Hot terms joined stewardship with machine learning, decision support, records systems, and AI. The field's center of gravity is shifting toward predicting resistance and tailoring treatment.
pmc-13312052:
Giovanni Taverna and colleagues offer a 2026 state-of-the-art review of how several imaging methods together can assess arrhythmic mitral valve prolapse. The valve condition is common and usually harmless, but a minority of patients face dangerous heart rhythms and sudden cardiac death, and telling them apart is the hard part.

The review covers ultrasound of the heart, cardiac magnetic resonance, computed tomography, and PET scanning, weighing what each adds on structure, function, and tissue makeup. The authors tie valve shape and ring mechanics to heart muscle injury and scarring, both diffuse and patchy, as the path toward rhythm risk. Newer magnetic resonance measures that map tissue change may flag early damage, and the review closes by noting where proof is still thin.
pmc-13312152:
Gonzalo Ramírez-Guerrero and co-authors compare two dialysis setups for clearing protein-bound toxins from blood, in a research paper from 2026. These toxins cling to blood proteins, so standard dialysis removes them poorly. They feed heart, nerve, and inflammation problems in kidney failure. One advanced method clears them well but is scarce.

Twenty patients on maintenance dialysis each received one session of a test or standard setup. The test paired a medium-pore membrane with an adsorption cartridge. The standard used high-volume fluid exchange. Toxin drops came out comparable between the two. The paired approach may widen access where the standard is unavailable.
pmc-13312352:
Lucy Findlater and co-authors investigate a cluster of tuberculosis cases in 2026 linked to prisons in England. Prisons are high-risk places for TB spread, since people live close and move often between sites. The team traced cases that shared the same genetic fingerprint of the germ.

Over six years they found twelve cases across London and two other regions. Seven had a prison history, spread across thirteen prisons. Four people had overlapped at one prison, and two at another. Germ family trees showed the cluster likely grew in the community and then entered prisons. Patients with prison history were less likely to finish treatment. The authors blame frequent transfers in part.
pmc-13312452:
Edoardo Simonetti and co-authors report a 2026 spectroscopy study of the electronic structure of the photoactive yellow protein chromophore dissolved in water. This light sensor's core molecule was known to oxidize in sunlight, but no one had measured the energy needed to pull an electron off it in solution.

The team used X-ray, extreme ultraviolet, and multiphoton ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy on a liquid microjet, with high-level quantum chemistry. They pinned the vertical electron detachment energy at 6.8 electron volts, give or take a tenth, and the adiabatic value near 5.9 electron volts. Multiphoton runs also showed a strong two-photon resonance near the detachment threshold that likely drives the known photooxidation, plus a three-photon feature above it. The authors showcase the paired method for weakly soluble light-active compounds.
pmc-13313052:
Luisa F Vazquez Enriquez, Kenia Dominguez Romo, and Jose M Hurtado Cordova present a 2026 case report on how poor treatment adherence can steer a blistering skin disease toward disaster. Their patient, a 73-year-old man, had high blood pressure, diabetes, and chronic heart disease. He developed pemphigus foliaceus, an immune-driven condition producing fragile surface blisters that break into crusted erosions. Initial steroids and topical care failed. He improved only partly after hospital immunoglobulin infusions and a change of immune drug.

Follow-up brought relapses tied to skipped topical therapy and self-stopped steroids. On his final admission, secondary skin and urinary infections with two resistant-prone bacteria advanced to septic shock despite intensive management. The authors stress the combined weight of missed doses, persistent disease activity, immune suppression, a broken skin barrier, and age with multiple illnesses. They argue for education and close monitoring as treatment, not extras.
pmc-13313952:
Mohammed Nabeel Abbas Al-Muhja and Jabbar Abbas Ahmed Al-Saaidi test, in a 2026 rat study, whether packaging curcumin into nanoparticles rescues female reproduction from cadmium damage. Cadmium disrupts the brain-to-ovary hormone axis through endocrine interference and oxidative stress, but curcumin is poorly absorbed. Forty-eight female rats filled six groups. They compared no treatment, cadmium alone, curcumin, cadmium plus curcumin, empty nanoparticle controls, and cadmium plus curcumin nanoparticles, across four weeks.

Cadmium cut body, ovarian, and uterine weights. It suppressed the key hormones from brain signal to estradiol and progesterone, raised prolactin, and switched off hormone receptor and hormone-building genes in ovary and pituitary. Curcumin softened the damage only partly. The nano version restored hormone levels and gene expression to near control values, beating the plain compound. The authors present the polymer-wrapped product as a promising nanotherapy for heavy metal reproductive toxicity.
pmc-13314752:
Maki Yamaguchi and colleagues study how exercise shifts polyamine chemistry in unlike muscles, in a 2026 paper. Polyamines are small molecules that help cells grow, and their handling may set whether a muscle swells with training.

Rats ran freely on wheels, and the team read enzyme patterns in a slow, swelling soleus muscle and a fast plantar muscle that did not swell. Making enzymes rose in the swollen muscle, while breaking enzymes rose in the flat one, in step with more energy proteins, as the authors report. They reason the breaking surge caps growth in fast muscle as its aerobic gear rises. A precursor called putrescine was also fed, yet it barely moved muscle chemistry. The fiber-split result refines how training gains are explained.
pmc-13315452:
Jiaying Hu and a very large team searched blood proteins in 2026 for a marker of calciphylaxis. Lab tests linked it and a TGF-beta binding protein to clotting and wound repair, and blocking related signals weakened serum-driven cell sticking and clotting. Confirmatory tests in a larger combined group supported the marker.
pmc-13315852:
Junting Liu and colleagues review in 2026 brain-computer interface neurofeedback training as rehabilitation for major depressive disorder. The review covers theory, brain mechanisms, and clinical formats, for both non-invasive and invasive feedback tools. Combined plans are discussed, including a paired approach joining wearable brain devices with aerobic exercise at the meeting point of sports neuroscience and psychiatry. Early evidence suggests the training may help, though stronger trials are still needed.
pmc-13315952:
Vaishnavi Hemdev and colleagues review, in a 2026 review, incretin-based therapies for obesity heart failure with kept pumping fraction. The authors support a role for these focused interventions, while noting later effects on mortality and arrhythmia remain unproven.
pmc-13316652:

pmc-13316852:

The recipe of controlled making, light probing, and predictive theory points toward tuning these sheets for future light-based devices.
pmc-13317052:

pmc-13317252:

pmc-13318252:

pmc-13318552:

pmc-13318652:

pmc-13318952:

pmc-13319552:

Combining the two into a prediction chart gave good accuracy in their tests. The authors present both measures as meaningful prognostic tools for this difficult complication.
pmc-13319652:

A total of 168 samples were checked for color shift and surface roughness at the start and after 3, 6, and 12 days at body heat. Red wine stained all types most, with coffee next, while cola and water did least harm. One type faded and roughened most by day 12, and one held its look best. pmc-13319952:

High levels of those forms made inner cell rails more crossed and stiff, and cells with crossed rails grew slower in linked waves. pmc-13320252:

Muscle starter cells on the charged scaffold clung, spread, and matured better, and sound pulses lifted early growth genes further. A small live test over 28 days showed no harm and good hold. The platform may suit wounds where muscle bulk is lost.
pmc-13320352:

A key alarm protein in blood rose in step with that overdrive, and gene reads showed its pathways lit up most in the strongest responders. Lab tests proved the memory effect needs that protein, made by helper immune cells. Blocking it may calm harmful overdrive.
pmc-13320452:

Lasting watch systems, clinician training, and public teaching are set as the top ready steps.
pmc-13320552:

pmc-13321952:

Three measures carried the most weight: the HE4 and CA125 blood markers and the neutrophil count. Results held up across both data sources. pmc-13322052:

The corrected statement also records animal ethics approval, numbered BST-PZ-MICE-20251014-01 in the notice. The original article has been updated, and no results are changed by the correction.
pmc-13322752:

Pressing a strontium oxide and tellurium dioxide mix at 8.8 gigapascals and 900 degrees in a multianvil press gave the new crystal form. The structure closely resembles a barium cousin but adds weak extra contacts between tellurite groups, and that detail breaks its symmetry. Heating brought phase changes near 225 degrees and again at 545 degrees toward the normal high temperature form. Light tests gave direct and indirect band gap values of 4.2 and 4.0 electron volts in the report.
pmc-13323152:
Jin Zhao, Xianguo Liu and Jinhai Liu survey why school sport teachers keep using smart wearables, in a 2026 study of 755 physical education teachers across kindergarten to grade 12 settings. Devices promise data-driven monitoring and feedback in lessons, yet lasting use depends on teacher choice.

Fit between task and technology proved the strongest driver of intent to continue, ahead of expected benefit, social influence and confidence. Task features predicted that fit, while technology features did not, and privacy worries pulled against continued use. Set-based analysis found several distinct paths to high or low intent, rather than one single recipe.
pmc-13323252:
Sha Su and co-authors review engineered extracellular vesicles for ischaemic heart disease, in a 2026 systematic review. Single treatments struggle against the tangled damage of reduced heart blood flow, so vesicles that carry healing signals to set targets draw growing interest.

Engineering routes included loading cargo inside, altering the surface, fusing membranes, pairing with biomaterials and pre-treating source cells. Targeting used guide peptides, antibodies, membrane fusion or direct delivery into heart tissue. Reported benefits ran through less scarring, calmer inflammation and better function across several pathways. Human proof remains ahead, the authors note.
pmc-13324252:
Hossein Khosravi, Marzie Mohammadi Pour, and Mohammad Bahram predict the strength of recycled concrete in a 2026 paper. Its strength forecasts matched the lab values closely. The wrap's stiffness, strength, and thickness mattered most in the model. Reliable forecasts can help engineers design greener columns with fewer costly lab tests.
pmc-13324352:

The paper frames this fusion approach as a route to stronger, more scalable protection for edge devices.
pmc-13324452:
Osamah Badwan and colleagues ask whether frailty predicts outcomes after left atrial appendage occlusion in a 2026 cohort study. The procedure prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation patients who cannot take long-term blood thinners, but many are old and medically complex.

Groups ranged from robust to frail, and matched comparisons followed long-term results. Greater frailty came with stepwise higher death, ischemic stroke, heart events, and geriatric problems. The authors support checking frailty before the procedure so that risk talks and care plans reflect real patient vulnerability.
pmc-13324752:
Junna Ye and team found a double-edged metabolic signal in Still's disease, a chronic self-attacking disorder that can grow into macrophage activation syndrome. Their 2026 study found itaconate, a metabolite made by myeloid cells through the enzyme ACOD1, as a dual regulator of inflammation and tissue injury. Clinical blood-chemistry scans found elevated serum levels of it in patients, traced to blood monocytes and correlated with disease severity.

In laboratory work, it suppressed classic immune signals such as IL-1beta, IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2, yet paradoxically amplified CXCL10, matching high plasma CXCL10 in that syndrome. In a mouse model, deleting Acod1 eased disease and liver damage, lowered CXCL10, and reduced CD8 T cell infiltration of the liver. The authors warn that strategies based on it deserve scrutiny, since the same substance licenses chemokine-driven tissue injury.
pmc-13325452:
Orie Saigo and colleagues test whether pharmacists can ease decisions about cancer genome testing in a 2026 randomized study in Japan. Genome profiling is routine there, yet patients face hard choices with unfamiliar information.

A total of 180 patients were split between standard medication counseling and added structured teaching about genome profiling. The share whose decision conflict fell did not differ, at 49.4 percent against 41.9 percent for the control group. Still, conflict about treatment choice rose far less in the teaching arm, gaining 1.98 points against 3.61 on the conflict scale. Early pharmacist input thus blunted growing doubt even when final choices matched.
pmc-13326252:
Francisco B. Alexandrino and team describe a genetic heart-muscle disease that showed up as acute heart injury in a healthy young man. Their 2026 case paper follows a 46-year-old man with on-and-off chest pain and very high high-sensitivity troponin. Cardiac MRI showed wide ring-like subepicardial late contrast enhancement across ten left ventricular segments without heart-muscle swelling, and genetic testing later found a disease-causing FLNC variant.

Ring-like glow is an uncommon but increasingly recognized pattern tied to genetic cardiomyopathies, particularly desmosomal and nondesmosomal genes such as FLNC, and acute episodes can mimic myocarditis, infarction, or pulmonary embolism. The authors argue that genetic testing earns a central place when acute heart injury shows a nonischemic imaging pattern, since the underlying cause changes counseling and tracking.
pmc-13327352:
Linda S Klavinskis wrote a 2026 personal account of a career spanning viral immunology, vaccines, and brain inflammation. She grew up in a small mill town near the Yorkshire Dales, the daughter of immigrants who reached England after the Second World War. Their stress on learning and hard work shaped her path.

She first aimed at dentistry, then switched to biomedical sciences with microbiology after school dissection work showed her strengths lay elsewhere. Summer jobs in public health laboratories in Leeds gave her cell culture skills and early lab grounding. Her account traces how family history, teachers, and new tools such as recombinant DNA guided a research life, and why she now works to widen access for others.
pmc-13327852:
Liang Chen, Ting Yu, and Yanqing Pan build machine learning forecasts for a lung surgery complication in a 2026 study, working with Guodong Ma. Prolonged air leak, lasting over five days, follows keyhole lung segment removal in many patients and stretches hospital stays. Records covered 610 patients treated between January 2019 and September 2025.

Five learning methods were trained on 70 percent of cases and tested on the rest, using health, lung function, surgery, and tumor details. Air leak occurred in 76 patients, 12.46 percent of the group, and the XGBoost model forecast it best, reaching an AUC of 0.874 on the test set, ahead of standard regression. Explanation tools ranked which factors drove each forecast.
pmc-13327952:
Takahiko Nagamine writes a 2026 letter proposing a brain-heart lens for burning mouth syndrome. The condition brings chronic mouth pain with no clear tissue damage, and standard views treat it as a local nerve problem. Nagamine argues it fits nociplastic pain, where the central nervous system turns pain processing up too high.

Sleep trouble, fatigue, anxiety, and depression often travel with the syndrome. The letter frames them as part of the mechanism, not mere side effects. Low mood can lower pain thresholds while pain deepens low mood. Faulty autonomic control links mouth, brain, and heart in one loop. The framework invites treatments aimed at central calming rather than the mouth alone.
pmc-13328452:
Marcello Silva Neto and team report gate-tunable giant negative magnetoresistance in tellurene, driven by quantum geometry. Their 2026 paper notes that negative magnetoresistance in two-dimensional electron gases is well known, but its roots in complex topological stuff with odd quantum geometry stayed murky. In n-type tellurene films, the team saw magnetoresistance hit minus 90% of zero-field resistance, lasting up to 35 Tesla at freezing temperatures.

The effect faded when the chemical potential moved away from the conduction-band Weyl node, hinting at a quantum geometric root. The team puts forward two workings. One is quantum geometric lift of diffusion. The other is a magnetoelectric spin link that locks the spin of a circling Weyl fermion to its drift in a built-in polar field that breaks inversion. The diffusion lift yields a non-Markovian memory effect in magnetotransport, setting quantum geometry as a driver of giant negative magnetoresistance.
pmc-13328652:
Vania Leandro-Merhi and others put out a hospital nutrition study in 2026. They checked malnutrition in patients in hospital using standard criteria. Body measures are common tools for nutrition checks. Grip strength offers a quick muscle function measure. The GLIM criteria give a shared meaning for malnutrition. The team compared these tools in patients taken in. Arm, calf, and skinfold measures were all noted. Weight loss history was also gathered with care. Tests linked strength and status to body measures.

Weak grip and GLIM malnutrition tracked smaller calves closely. Both also linked to low body weight by BMI. Age added to low weight risk as well. Checks of how well methods agreed were also run. Simple calf and grip measures carried real signal. Busy wards can use them for fast screening. Full nutrition checks can then focus where needed. Early finding supports earlier feeding support.
pmc-13328752:
I Avery Bick and team watched bird diversity and migration across Norway with a national passive sound web. Their 2026 study gathered 37,429 hours of audio from 28 linked sensors in forests over a full spring migration season, April through June. Billions of birds migrate each year, driven by inner cues and climate-linked forces that shift with climate change. The huge time-and-place scale makes timing hard to track with old surveys.

A free detection program sorted bird calls on its own, and expert checks found it sorted 57 species, with fourteen full migrants, at 80% precision or better. Auto detections gave regional arrival curves for Willow Warbler, Common Chiffchaff, and Spotted Flycatcher, and trained sound species maps showing how call odds shift across Norway in spring migration. The team argues that passive sound watching can back up hand surveys to aid policy and conservation planning and action.
pmc-13330452:
Shihan Tian and co-authors use brain wave recordings to separate depressed older adults who also have mild thinking problems, in this 2026 paper. Late-life depression often arrives with such impairment, and that pairing raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease. A cheap brain test that splits the groups could guide care.

The study enrolled one hundred thirteen people: patients with depression alone, patients with both conditions, and healthy peers. Resting brain waves were read for rhythm strength and network links across bands. Machine learning then tried to sort the groups from wave features. A split pattern in the beta band marked the combined group, the authors report, giving a candidate marker.
pmc-13330652:
Giulia Manzi and a large team build a self-care measure for children with complex long-term conditions in a 2026 study. Care at home grows as survival improves, and parents share the work as children mature. Work ran from 2022 to 2023 in four phases, from theory-based drafting to expert review and family interviews.

Eleven tailored versions cover five age groups and three care dimensions: upkeep, watching, and handling change. Eighty-six experts, including clinicians, parents, and patients, judged content in the middle phases. Family interviews with 5 patients and 13 parents checked clarity at the end. Each version holds about 37 items on average in the reported build. Validity scores are detailed for later testing.
pmc-13330852:
Luciana Da Fonseca Da Silva reviews primary tricuspid valve leakage in adults with congenital heart disease in a 2026 article. Causes include Ebstein anomaly and valve dysplasia from birth, plus later damage from infection or other disease. Severe leakage swells the right heart chambers, sparks rhythm trouble, and cuts exercise capacity over time.

Some patients stay nearly symptom-free for decades despite worsening disease. Poor signs include a very large heart, weak ventricles, low oxygen, and rhythm problems. Surgery is advised for symptoms, falling exercise capacity, or growing right chamber size. The Cone repair can restore native valve function with low risk in expert centres. Earlier, tailored repair is backed.
pmc-13332452:
Roshan Giri and co-authors report a 2026 quality improvement project that raised a Nepalese tertiary hospital pharmacy to full good practice standards in five months. Global pharmacy standards are hard to meet in low- and middle-income settings where money and infrastructure run short.

Working in plan-do-study-act cycles, the team decentralized some services, wrote 21 standard operating procedures under the ALCOA+ framework, and trained staff, then audited progress four times against a 125-point national checklist. Median compliance climbed from 57.1 percent to 100.0 percent by the final audit, and the share of high-scoring domains rose from 17.6 to 88.2 percent. Root cause work showed most documentation gaps came from awkward logbook placement rather than staff skill, fixed by moving books to the dispensing counters. The authors offer the project as a repeatable roadmap for similar hospitals.
pmc-13332552:
Mark B Bromberg compiles a 2026 account of flail limb syndrome, a rare lower motor neuron disorder distinct in part from classic ALS. Flail arm syndrome, recognized in 1886, starts in proximal arm muscles, while flail leg syndrome, recognized in 1918, starts in distal leg muscles. Past reports are mostly case series with thin detail on electrical features, thinking, and gene changes. Bromberg gathers those scattered features into one synthesis.

The syndromes make up roughly seven to eight percent of ALS cases and affect men more often than classic ALS does. Each is defined by focal arm or leg weakness lasting about two years before spread to other regions, though mild signs elsewhere may appear early. The course ultimately progresses to respiratory failure. Clinicians gain a clearer portrait for recognizing these focal forms early and for counseling patients about a course that differs from typical ALS.
pmc-13333352:
Junming Xu and co-authors grow liver-like tissue in a 2026 lab study on bile acids. Bile acids help the body handle fats, clear toxins, and balance cholesterol, but lab models rarely copy how the liver makes them. The team grew small organ-like clusters from human stem cells, tuned to act like both liver and bile duct tissue.

A plant compound in the growth recipe boosted bile acid making. The clusters sorted their cells into neat zones and showed strong making and moving skills. Tests found thirty-three kinds of bile acid, mostly in the form the human body favors. A scarred version of the clusters was also built, by adding a growth signal. The system offers a closer model for liver disease studies and drug tests.
pmc-13333752:
Ying Weng, Wanqi Yang, and Yong Lai authored a 2026 review on how gut microbes and their chemical products may shape cognitive problems after stroke through epigenetic routes. The microbiota-gut-brain axis links the intestine to inflammation and repair in the injured brain.

After stroke, gut imbalance changes levels of short-chain fatty acids, B vitamins, tryptophan products, bile acids, and other active compounds. Many of these molecules steer DNA methylation, histone changes, and non-coding RNA activity, switching genes tied to cognition and recovery. The review connects those mechanisms to brain inflammation, oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier damage, and neuron death. It closes by weighing therapies that adjust microbes, supply metabolites, or target epigenetic marks directly.
pmc-13333952:
Qian and five co-authors build a fairer grade for reused water's mark on river health in this twenty twenty-six study. Reused water tops up rivers, yet its long mark on the wild web is hard to call. Past one-mark grades can swing wild on one short breach of a line.

Inside, their grade blends a weight-by-spread step with a rank step in one frame. It treats low-is-bad and band-best marks in their true forms, not as plain lines. A case river fed by a wash plant tests the new grade in full. The grade shows how the boost fades with reach and swings with the year's turns. It dodges the wild swings that lone-mark grades gave on the same data.
pmc-13334852:
Pedro Crepaldi Carlessi and colleagues study 2026 native peoples' rights and the official growth of folk medicine in South America. Since the 1970s, the World Health Organization has pushed folk medicine as a worldwide policy class for culturally rooted health care. In South America, that framework met a distinct political landscape where native peoples emerged as group subjects rallying around rights, land claims, and citizen status. The paper looks at how turning tradition from an identity label into a health rule term remakes how difference can be voiced, claimed, and kept.

Drawing on archive research across ten South American countries plus World Health Organization and United Nations records. The study follows how the global framework has been adopted, reshaped, or displaced across national contexts. Analysis reveals a spectrum of rule arrangements in which official adoption and the political force of group difference are not commensurate.
pmc-13335452:
Shakti P Pattanayak and co-authors found that blocking KDEL receptors can make tumors regress without T cells at first, in a 2026 cancer immunology study. These receptors normally haul escaped proteins back from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum.

Inhibiting one receptor, mainly KDELR2, in even a small fraction of tumor cells triggered heavy infiltration by macrophages and neutrophils. Both immunogenic and non-immunogenic tumors shrank, driven initially by this innate response. During regression, anti-tumor T cells were primed, and animals later resisted a second tumor challenge. Delivering KDELR2-silencing RNA in lipid nanoparticles into tumors reproduced the effect. The authors propose KDEL targeting as a way to ignite immunity in cold tumors that resist T cell therapies.
pmc-13335852:
Wang and coauthors probe fast light tools that make short bursts at high pitch. A thin film of iron and nickel can emit those bursts when hit by laser light. To build better tools, teams must track heat and spin flow at the same time. Past tools could not do both jobs well.

The team used a light pump and probe method on the film. Light hits changed how much signal passed through the film. Those shifts let them track heat in the film over time. They also mapped the burst range in fine steps. The maps show how heat and spin flow shape each burst.
pmc-13336052:
Haoxiang Li and colleagues study 2026 combined reshaping of tumor surroundings via a DNA nano-device combining STING switching on and cell-dump-aimed PD-L1 breakdown. The cGAS-STING pathway is a key part of innate anti-tumor defense; however, its treatment promise is often curbed by poor cell-fluid drop-off of triggers and tumor surroundings that weaken immunity. The authors report a DNA nano-structure-based platform. It at once induces cell-dump breakdown of immune checkpoint protein PD-L1 and switches on the STING pathway.

In murine models of triple-negative breast cancer, the DNA nano-device strongly rewires the tumor surroundings. It boosts branching cell growth and CD8-positive T cell entry. This leads to strong holding back of both primary tumor growth and lung spread.
pmc-13336352:
Xinglin Zhou and colleagues study 2026 machine learning-aided salt mix design for low-heat, top calcium-based liquid metal cells. Calcium-based liquid metal cells are hopeful for large-scale energy storage due to calcium plenty and low cost. Yet real-world uses are curbed by high working heat, self-discharge, low charge power, and charge fading.

The authors develop a machine learning-aided tuning frame. It combines data-driven analysis, ML forecasting, and lab checks to design a ternary molten-salt salt mix. Through multi-trait review of heat hold, melting habits, weight, and cost, KCl was picked as a top third part for CaCl2-LiCl based systems. A many-trait dataset was built to develop a random forest model for exact salt mix tuning. Guided by this model, the salt mix was lab-checked to enable working at 480 degrees Celsius, giving a charge power above 99 percent.
pmc-13336452:
Tengfei Liu and colleagues study 2026 PRMT9 worsening DA nerve loss in PD model by speeding breakdown of DUSP26 and causing mito trouble. Protein Arg taggers add Arg tags and play a key role in disease start. Mito trouble is linked to nerve loss of PD. However, whether PRMT9, found in mito, is part of PD remains unclear.

The authors found that PRMT9 was greatly raised in the brain movement region of PD mice given MPTP and in SH-SY5Y cells given MPP+. In MPP+-exposed SH-SY5Y cells, PRMT9 moved to mito and worsened mito injury, shown as lower mito membrane voltage, lower ATP making, high ROS levels, and mito splitting. Also, PRMT9 lack greatly eased DA nerve loss given MPTP, while extra PRMT9 worsened MPTP nerve loss.
pmc-13336552:
Qiang Yin and co-authors examine in a 2026 chemistry study why phenol breaks apart under light far faster at the surface of water than deep inside it. They look at two controls acting together. One is access to dark energy states in the molecule. The other is how well nearby water can hold the charge that moves during the break.

Large slab models of the surface, unlike small clusters, showed surface states shifted lower by about 0.7 eV compared with bulk water values and spread more widely. Loose, weakly held water settings matched the lowest energies. The findings give modelers fresh inputs for predicting light-driven change where air meets water.
pmc-13336852:
Hao Meng and co-authors use machine learning to lift printable perovskite solar cells in a 2026 study. These cells skip costly hole conductors and precious metals, yet their efficiency had stalled. The team built a clean database of cell recipes and trained a stacked learning model to predict performance.

Across 8 validation experiments, prediction error stayed within 2.16% of measured values in the reported runs. Digging into the model revealed which factors matter most and yielded screening rules for good additives based on molecular fingerprints. Guided by the model, the team built cells reaching an efficiency of 19.36% in hands-on tests, with projections up to 24.32% after fuller tuning. Interpretable models plus targeted tests may speed solar design.
pmc-13337052:
Wenyun Mu and co-authors engineer nanoparticles that attack tumors yet calm nearby tissue in a 2026 study. Heat and radical therapies can harm healthy areas and stir inflammation around tumors. Their gold-ceria hybrids, ACEF, change behavior with their surroundings: folate guides them to tumors, where cell enzymes and calcium trigger clumping.

Clumped particles in tumors convert near-infrared light to heat better and generate harmful radicals for therapy. Scattered particles in normal tissue instead scavenge radicals through cerium chemistry, easing oxidative stress. In animals the particles suppressed main tumors and lung spread, with no obvious body-wide toxicity under the tested conditions. Self-adjusting particles could make aggressive therapy gentler at its edges.
pmc-13337652:
Dragana Milutinović and colleagues surveyed female health workers in Serbia in 2026 about bladder symptoms. Their cross-sectional study covered urinary incontinence and overactive bladder, two parts of lower urinary tract symptoms. It measured how common the problems were, what staff knew, and how they felt about them.

A total of 493 women from primary and tertiary sites in Novi Sad took part using standard symptom and knowledge questionnaires. Incontinence affected 35.5 percent of respondents and overactive bladder affected 53.1 percent, with stress leakage the most common type. Knowledge scores were moderate and attitudes were mostly positive. Findings highlight a care gap even among staff who treat these conditions.
pmc-13338052:
Xiaoji Zhou and colleagues rebuild bladder nerve anatomy in three dimensions in a 2026 cadaver study. Rebuilding bladder function after spinal cord injury requires restoring emptying power while lowering resistance. Sympathetic nerves that tighten the outlet are a key limit.

Bladder tissue from four cadavers, two male and two female, was sliced every 4 mm and stained for a nerve marker. Nerve counts and distance from the inner surface were measured level by level. Density peaked at the bladder neck in women and the prostatic urethra in men. Back regions held far more nerves than front regions in both sexes as reported.
pmc-13338752:
Md Rezwanul Hasan and colleagues tracked early results of combined cataract surgery and silicone oil removal in Bangladesh, in a 2026 prospective study. Silicone oil tamponade helps repair complex retinal detachments but often clouds the lens and raises eye pressure, so removal plus cataract surgery in one sitting could spare patients a second operation. Eligibility required prior retinal surgery with oil in place, a new cataract, and an attached retina. Surgeons performed phacoemulsification with lens implant, then removed the oil through a 23-gauge pars plana route. Early follow-up checked vision, pressure, and retinal status, giving surgeons in similar settings a first read on safety and benefit of the combined approach.
pmc-13338852:
Tan Tian, Yongjie Niu, and Shanjun Bao test boxing-specific sprint training in elite male boxers in a 2026 trial. Repeated sprint work boosts leg power, yet its effect on arm strength and punching was unknown. Sixteen boxers were split into training and control groups of eight.

The training group added three weekly sessions of short all-out heavy-bag punches for four weeks. Upper-body power on a lab Wingate test rose by 16.7 percent for peak power and 20.6 percent for mean power in the reported gains. Bench press power also rose sharply. Post-test gaps versus controls were large, supporting bag sprint work for punch power.
pmc-13339752:
Janitha Iddagoda and colleagues mapped prawn allergy proteins in 2026 to weigh black tiger prawns against white leg prawns, the two main farmed kinds. Prawn allergy is a big global health worry, and prawns are its most common trigger. Protein tests plus computer allergy prediction mapped allergy proteins in raw prawn extracts.

Allergy proteins made up just about 4 percent of proteins found yet 34 to 38 percent of all protein mass, which shows their immune weight. Myosin light chain stood out among the key allergy proteins. The map helps food firms, doctors, and rule makers judge cross reactions and labels for the prawns people eat most.
pmc-13339952:
Dalia Zubidat and colleagues told of two hard kidney cases in 2026 in C3 glomerulonephritis, a rare disease where overactive immune defence harms kidney filters. Both patients had failed several immune drugs with no full remission, so the team tried eculizumab, an antibody that blocks the last steps of immune defence. Kidney function got better for a short while in both cases.

The gain did not last. Protein and blood in urine rose, kidney tests worsened, and both patients reached end stage kidney failure. Repeat kidney samples still showed strong C3 stain in filters, a sign that immune attack went on. The cases warn that blocking late immune steps alone may not halt this disease.
pmc-13342052:
Two routine scans are fused to read marrow immunity in myeloma, in a 2026 study by Minjie Gao and colleagues. Their ImmunoCast-MM system combines stained bone marrow smears with whole-body PET/CT from diagnosis in 243 newly diagnosed patients.

One branch classified cells through learned embeddings; the other built an inflammation fingerprint across tumor, spleen, nodes, and marrow. Contrastive fusion aligned both against flow cytometry, producing an Immune Dysfunction Index. Decoded indices correlated with true cell fractions at ρ values of 0.68 to 0.81, and clustering separated immune-competent from immune-exhausted patients with differing outlooks and drug responses.
pmc-13342852:
Kensington S. Hartman and co-authors report a 2026 plant study on how physical force guides the final cell division that forms stomata, the tiny leaf pores used for gas exchange. Working in the leaf surface layer, the team asked how the last symmetric division lines up so pores end up evenly patterned across plant organs.

The authors found a force-responsive pathway that reads mechanical signals in the tissue and turns the division plane to match broad tissue axes. Without that guidance, the paired guard cells that make a pore fail to form properly. Force, in other words, acts as a patterning cue in leaf growth, alongside the chemical signals long known to shape plant tissues.
pmc-13343352:
Turki Alsaeed, Tracy Washington, and Bo Xia systematically review elderly care in Saudi Arabia in 2026. The kingdom's older population will jump from 5 percent in 2015 to over 20 percent by 2050. Gaps persist in trained geriatric staff, reliance on migrant caregivers, rural access, and cultural reluctance toward institutional care. Technology-led, workforce-focused reform, plus far more aging research, tops their agenda.
pmc-13346852:
Navodika Yaparathna and colleagues analyse outcomes for removable partial dentures in a university clinic study from 2026. Success was tied most clearly to which arch held the denture, what sat opposite it, and how many visits followed fitting, with single-arch cases doing better overall. Lower dentures facing a full upper denture, and cases with dentures in both arches, fared worse, while upper denture success fell as more upper teeth were missing. The findings support judging upper and lower cases apart.
pmc-13347352:
Renata De Carvalho Feitosa and a large team build a wound film. Their study was published in 2026. The film uses chitosan loaded with a plant compound. The compound sits inside sunflower oil droplets. Its name is beta-caryophyllene. Droplets measured near 114 nm wide. The best mix packed in 96 percent of the compound. Films were then cast at skin-friendly acidity.

Each gram of dressing held 13.3 mg of the compound. Films stayed stable under heat checks. Handling checks gave the same result. Cell work showed good tolerance. The film also fought oxidation. It sped fibroblast movement as well. A scratch gap closed fully within 24 hours. That is a hopeful sign for chronic wound care.
pmc-13348252:
Zhi-Ming Yu and Yugui Yao highlight a new infrared instrument. Their commentary appeared in 2026. It also covers a giant chiral light effect. The effect sits in a magnetic crystal. Yuan and collaborators built the instrument. It resolves polarisation under strong magnetic fields. Mode swaps need no warming of the magnet. The team used it on a Weyl semimetal. The result broke that expectation. Giant wide-range circular dichroism appeared. It was seen for the first time in this crystal family. A direct window on chiral states opens up. Light switches may benefit too.
pmc-13348352:
Alice Wickersham and colleagues link school test paths to later offending in a nationwide cohort, in a study from 2026. Among pupils whose standing slid over school years, one in three was cautioned or convicted before leaving school in the reported counts. Pupils who started low yet improved carried only 4 percent higher odds of young adult offending, against 53 percent higher odds for those who stayed low. So watching falls in standing could trigger timely support.
pmc-13348852:
Maryam Maghbool and colleagues report a rare tonsil growth mixing lymph channels, fat, and muscle, in a case report published in 2026. A 28-year-old Iranian man with a sore throat carried a smooth stalked mass on his right tonsil measuring 2 by 1 by 0.3 cm. The tonsil was removed whole without prior scans given the small, benign look of the lump.

Tissue study showed widened lymph channels in a fatty frame with patches of smooth muscle, fully cut out with clean edges in the pathology report. No return appeared over one year of follow-up, supporting full removal as curative while warning that only tissue study can name such rare lumps with certainty.
pmc-13349752:
Ahmed J. Alaraibi and colleagues pool studies on troponin watching during cancer immunotherapy, in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2026. Raised troponin tied strongly to confirmed inflammation, with a pooled log odds value of 4.14 and no clear split among studies in the combined fit. False alarms were common, though, leaving weak rule-in power from a raised value alone, so the authors frame troponin as a watch tool needing partner checks for safe calls.
pmc-13349952:
Xijun Luo and co-authors examined the protein TAZ in gastric cancer tissue in a 2026 clinicopathological study. TAZ helps drive the Hippo pathway, which controls organ size and can fuel cancer when misregulated, but its link with the adhesion protein E-cadherin was unclear.

TAZ message and protein were higher in cancer than in nearby healthy tissue in fresh samples. Staining of stored tissue from 98 patients found TAZ in 67.3 percent of cancers versus 32.0 percent of normal lining, and high TAZ tracked with bigger tumours, lymph node spread, and later stage. Where TAZ rose, E-cadherin tended to fall, hinting TAZ could serve as a warning marker.
pmc-13350252:
Peng Chen and colleagues pooled trial evidence in 2026 on immune checkpoint drugs for advanced nasopharyngeal cancer. This tumour of the upper throat is common in parts of Asia. Seven prospective trials with 1,788 patients were combined.

It is no longer whether these drugs work, but how best to weave them into combined therapy. The synthesis maps those choices.
pmc-13350352:
Tom Heinekamp and colleagues linked grape genes to wine flavour in a 2026 breeding study. Judging wine quality is the slowest step in grape breeding, so finding DNA markers for flavour would speed selection of new vines.
