Statistical models separated vine genetics, growing conditions, and each taster's quirks across eight flavour traits and a total quality score. Gene mapping then tied aroma chemicals to the DNA regions behind them, giving breeders a shortcut toward vines bred for taste as well as hardiness.
pmc-13350552:
Karen D Könings and Subha Ramani wrote a 2026 commentary asking who coaches the coaches in health professions education. Supervisors coach learners toward goals, mixing attention to weaknesses, strengths, and personal meaning, yet coaches themselves rarely get coached.

The authors propose upward coaching, where learners help educators refine their coaching through safe, dialogue-based feedback. Just as learners are expected to build feedback skills and own their action plans, teachers could build their own feedback literacy with learner input. As learners, teaching methods, and AI tools change, such mutual coaching could keep supervision honest and current.
pmc-13351452:
C Lombardo and colleagues published a dataset in 2026 of sound-wave speeds in rock layers beneath the middle and southern Adriatic Sea off Italy. The values come from twelve exploration wells drilled offshore between 1969 and 2000 under a national archive project.

Old paper well logs were digitised into standard files, rock units identified in specialist software, and average wave speeds calculated for each unit. Such velocities let geophysicists convert echo timing from seismic surveys into true depths. Rescuing legacy oil exploration data into reusable form serves geology and hazard research long after the wells themselves are gone.
pmc-13352652:
Eugenia-Corina Budin and co-authors published this survey study in 2026. The team asked lung specialists in Romania what they think of a phone app that uses artificial intelligence to teach medical students. In the app, a virtual patient lets students practice giving brief advice to quit smoking.

The researchers sent a structured survey to respiratory medicine professionals between May and October 2025. Questions covered how useful and workable the app seems, which counseling models teachers prefer, and what design the app should have. The study also weighed expected gains for teaching and public health. Results like these can guide schools that plan to add virtual patients to their courses.
pmc-13352852:
Fengzhi Li and a large team of co-authors wrote this review, published in 2026. It argues that two proteins, a helicase called DDX5 and an enzyme called UbE2T, are prime targets for new cancer drugs. Both help tumors repair DNA damage and keep growing.

The review maps how the two proteins bind and work together, including roles in DNA repair, prostate cancer stem cells, and the immune setting around tumors. It then presents FL118, a small molecule that acts as a dual glue degrader, marking both proteins for destruction at once. In animal tests the drug hit several hard cancers, from bowel and pancreatic tumors to bone cancers and brain tumors. It also worked on cells that resist standard drugs by pumping them out. Animal safety tests in three species looked favorable.
pmc-13352952:
Francesca Lorenzini and Maria Caterina Mione discussed how weakening the nuclear envelope helps melanoma spread, in a 2026 commentary. Cancer cells must squeeze through tight spaces and dense collagen during spread, and fragile nuclei can rupture under that pressure, spilling chromatin and damaging the genome. A recent report by Baird and others points to the Lamin B target as a driver of that fragility.

Overproduction and clustering of the target in parts of the nuclear envelope increase distortion and rupture risk. The commentary highlights the target's sterol reductase action as a hopeful angle for further study. It offers readers a concise explanation of why nuclear workings matter in spread and where new tests might intervene.
pmc-13353052:
Zehra Abay-Nørgaard and a large team showed in 2026 that appetite-regulating neurons and tanycytes can be grown from human pluripotent stem cells. The arcuate nucleus and ventromedial hypothalamus are specialised brain regions that govern appetite and energy use, yet human versions of their cells have been hard to produce in the lab. Reliable lab-grown cells would open new ways to study hunger, obesity, and energy disease.

By tuning the timing and duration of bone morphogenetic protein exposure, the team made ventromedial hypothalamic and arcuate neurons with defined tiny names. The plan also yielded tanycytes, specialised glial cells of the hypothalamus. Teams gain a human cell system for probing appetite circuits and testing steps that animal models cannot fully capture.
pmc-13353152:
Yu Liu leads a 2026 year-long study of how movement skill and physical fitness shape each other in preschoolers. Both traits matter early, but single snapshots cannot show which drives which. A total of 202 children in Chongqing, China, with mean age of 4.65 years, were tested at baseline and after 12 months, and 194 finished, for a retention rate of 96.1 percent.

Eye-hand integration used the Beery VMI-6 short form, and fitness used a five-item national battery. Each trait proved stable over time, with fitness holding a stability value of 0.88. Cross-lagged models, adjusted for age and sex, fitted well. Results clarify direction of influence for planning early movement programmes.
pmc-13353352:
Gutthi Rishitha Reddy and colleagues track oral Candida colonisation during radiotherapy for head and neck cancer in a 2026 prospective study. Mouth soreness from radiation is common and cuts treatment tolerance, while damaged lining invites Candida growth that may worsen soreness. Seventy patients aged 40 to 80 years receiving curative radiotherapy gave swabs from several mouth sites.

Swabs were taken before treatment, in week three, and at the end, then grown to identify Candida species. Soreness was graded weekly on WHO and CTCAE scales. Analysis weighed age, other illnesses, and treatment factors alongside colonisation. Knowing when colonisation peaks may help time preventive mouth care.
pmc-13354952: Beth M Harvey and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of a glial cell path that guides regrowing optic nerve fibers in fish. The note fixes one mutant line name in the methods list of fish lines, swapping a wrong code for the right one. The full corrected list is given next to the first list. The authors state that results and findings do not change.
pmc-13355452:
Austin Clements and others told of a burst belly aortic bulge in a fourteen-year-old girl with tuberous scarring, in 2026. Bulges in children with this multi-organ genetic illness, marked by benign tumours and misshapen lesions in many organs, appear only in rare reports and small series. The link between tuberous scarring and child bulges remains poorly known.

The girl gave to the urgent department with a burst below-kidney bulge, and the report details the op outcome. Only twelve child cases had been told of in the papers surveyed. Surgeons and paediatricians gain a stark reminder that vascular surveillance deserves notice in tuberous scarring, even in childhood.
pmc-13355552:
Takeshi Yamashita and seven co-authors collect eight patients whose brain scans showed cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum, in a two thousand twenty-six neurology case series. These transient MRI lesions accompany infections and other stresses, but the infection-related spectrum was ill-defined.

Cases at one Japanese center spanned two thousand sixteen to two thousand twenty-five; median age was about forty-eight. Five were infection-related, including bacteremia, meningoencephalitis, and COVID-linked myocarditis; one involved Fusobacterium nucleatum bacteremia, a barely documented link. Every lesion sat in the splenium. Follow-up imaging showed complete or near-complete resolution, and seven patients improved clinically. Infections, the authors conclude, dominate this presentation.
pmc-13355852:
Kohei Hashida and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 43-year-old woman who lost taste on both sides after a small bleed in one part of her brain, the left putamen. Taste loss after stroke is common but often missed, and this bleed site had rarely been linked to it. Her sense of smell stayed intact and her other symptoms were mild.

Scans showed the bleed with swelling reaching toward the thalamus, a relay for taste signals. A taste test on day eleven confirmed loss on both sides, worse on one. Other causes were judged unlikely. Her taste slowly returned and was fully back within two months, and the authors urge asking stroke patients about taste.
pmc-13358752:
Yan Ye and co-authors compare drug plans for squamous lung cancer in a 2026 review. This form of non-small cell lung cancer has fewer targeted options than others, so care leans on immune drugs, chemotherapy, or both together. Trials have tested each plan against some rivals but never all at once. The team joined the trials into one network.

They gathered 32 randomized trials with 9,652 patients and compared survival, time without the cancer growing, tumor shrinkage, and severe side effects. A network ranking can show which plan gives the best balance of benefit and harm. Such guidance helps doctors tailor first treatment to each patient's strength and wishes.
pmc-13358852:
Andres Zorrilla-Vaca and co-authors appraise breathing strategies in chest surgery in a 2026 paper. About a third of patients who lose part of a lung suffer lung complications afterward, the leading cause of death in this group. One-lung breathing during surgery adds its own strain. A strategy called open-lung ventilation uses pressure and reopening maneuvers to keep tiny air sacs from collapsing.

The authors weigh the PROTHOR trial, a large randomized test of higher pressure with reopening maneuvers against standard care. Better lung mechanics on the table may not always mean better recovery afterward. Their appraisal helps anesthesia teams set the ventilator with proof, not habit.
pmc-13359752:
Emelia A. M. Hinton and co-authors describe a twist in gut inflammation in a 2026 review. In inflammatory bowel disease, the gut lining tries to repair itself while under immune attack. The signal TNF drives both the attack and, surprisingly, part of the repair, pushing lining stem cells to expand and change. A second signal family, type I interferons, joins the cross-talk.

When both signals stay on for long, the repair program may freeze in place, creating what the authors call regenerative inflammation that keeps the disease going. This framing could explain why some patients never respond to anti-TNF drugs, and it points drug hunters toward the lining itself.
pmc-13359952:
Roberta Carvalho Cesário and co-authors test melatonin against breast cancer cells in a 2026 study. Melatonin, the night hormone, does more than set sleep timing. The team treated two cell types in the lab: a hormone-sensitive luminal type and triple-negative cells, the hardest kind to treat. They tracked growth, movement, and invasion alongside energy production and oxidative balance.

Melatonin slowed growth, migration, and invasion in both cell types and reshaped how the cells make energy and handle oxidation. The strength and shape of the effects differed by subtype. The results support further preclinical work on melatonin as a helper in breast cancer treatment.
pmc-13360652:
Alba Sorroche and others told of a light gold light driver with dual function in two-way H loading of N-rings, in 2026. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers offer a hopeful route to hydrogen storage and spread, and N-rings stand out for high hydrogen room. Light-driven H release under mild problems has drew notice for its green advantages.

A hybrid stuff was built by grafting gold nanoparticles, two to four nanometres in size, into a covalent organic plan matrix, creating a repeat-use light driver. The stuff drives both H release and H loading, letting two-way hydrogen loading and release. Energy teams gain a repeat-use catalyst for hydrogen carrier chemistry.
pmc-13361452:
Hyeonbin Oh and co-authors used machine learning to predict how sound waves change rice flour in a 2026 study. Blasting gelatinized rice flour with ultrasound alters how it dissolves, thickens, and sets, traits that matter for drinks and ready foods. The team processed six rice varieties under nine sound settings and two thicknesses. They asked whether simple flour makeup, like starch, protein, and fiber content, could stand in for variety in the models.

Five model types were trained and compared, from simple regressions to boosted trees. Inputs ranged from process settings alone to settings plus flour makeup. A key test was whether a model trained on known varieties works on one it never saw. Such transfer would let makers predict results for new rice types without fresh trials.
pmc-13361752:
Bello and five co-authors review nine months of admissions for children under five at a hospital in Nguru, north-east Nigeria. Severe acute malnutrition and diphtheria together form a poorly tracked double burden. The team read the records of 1,530 young admissions.

Malnutrition drove over half of all illness cases and nearly three quarters of the 194 deaths. Diphtheria killed the largest share of its own patients, at about 22 percent, with malnutrition close behind. Diarrhea and malaria filled out the main causes of sickness and death. Age, length of stay, and diagnosis shaped each child's outcome. The authors urge policy that treats the two diseases as a linked threat.
pmc-13362452:
Alessia Brossa and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on tiny delivery bubbles that carry cancer drugs to tumors. It compares two kinds: liposomes, made in the lab and already used in clinics, and extracellular vesicles, small bubbles that cells shed on their own. Each kind has clear strengths and clear weak points, from targeting skill to ease of bulk production.

The review then covers hybrids that fuse the two, aiming to pair the natural targeting of cell bubbles with the control and load space of lab-made ones. Early results look good in lab work, yet bulk making and shared standards lag. The authors see hybrids as a strong next step for precise cancer care once those gaps close.
pmc-13363152:
Kohei Mitsui and colleagues present a 2026 study on how a lead-free solder ages at high heat and how that aging affects fatigue life. The solder, a tin alloy with antimony, silver, nickel, and a trace of germanium, is aimed at hot power electronics. The team aged samples, watched a silver-tin phase inside grow coarser over time, and ran repeated bending-style fatigue tests at room heat and at 175 degrees.

Antimony dissolved in the tin slowed the coarsening of the silver-tin grains, since it left less room for silver to move. At room heat both solders tired at the same rate, but at high heat the new alloy resisted the usual fall in hardening. The authors link the stable grains to the steadier hot performance.
pmc-13363252:
Xiaoying Xu and colleagues report a 2026 study on a light-responsive gel for infected bone defects. The gel builds on treated chitosan, a natural polymer, loaded with black phosphorus sheets and a calcium mineral coat formed in place. The phosphorus gives a heat effect under near-infrared light, while the mineral slowly frees calcium and phosphorus ions that bone cells use.

Strong light doses made the gel kill bacteria through heat and reactive oxygen. Gentle light instead nudged bone stem cells to grow and mature into bone-forming cells, with gene reads to match. In rat skull defects, the gel produced better new bone than controls. The dual mode, sterilize hard then heal gently, is the design's core appeal.
pmc-13363752:
Samikhshak Gupta and Vijaya V N Sriram Malladi present a 2026 study on soaking up bending waves in a beam with small passive dampers. Such wave control can quiet machines and structures without power-hungry active systems. They modeled a clamped aluminum beam with dashpot attachments, checked the model against laser vibration scans, and split the wave field into reflected and absorbed parts across a wide frequency band.

Absorption plotted against position, scaled by the local bending wavelength, fell into a repeating pattern with dips at half-wavelength spacing. That rule frees placement from tuning: spring and damping settings have their own best values per frequency, and several dampers placed by the wavelength rule can hold near-peak absorption anywhere. The team offers the pattern as a compact design guide.
pmc-13364252:
Bo Xu, Shuang Wang, and Xiaoyu Tang present a 2026 study on training AI across Internet of Things devices by blending federated and split learning without a single central server. In their semi-decentralized design, devices share the load of big models, split at points that fit each device's power and link, and several edge servers aggregate the shared parts. Since training delay is unknown ahead of time, they treat split and pairing choices as a learning problem in itself.

Their context-aware bandit algorithm reads each site's conditions to guess delays, then improves its choices round by round with provably small long-run regret. Experiments on several networks showed lower training latency and better test accuracy than the rival methods chosen. The work targets privacy-keeping training on weak devices.
pmc-13367552:
Yatin Dholakia reviews in 2026 India's new split tier plan for TB care, built to close gaps in a land that holds more than a fourth of world TB. Plain same care for all misses sick, poor, and high risk folks. The new plan sorts folks by ill weight and life need at first call.

Tiers span town, site, and state aid, with food, mind, and cash checks built in. Case finds turn from wait for signs to risk led hunts. Tech tools join the plan. The aim is care fit to the folk, not the form, as the land drives to end TB.
pmc-13368852:
Carolina Baeza-Velasco leads a team on eating in women with Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with joint and tissue disorders. Past work shows odd eating and weight in such women.

Women with self told EDS filled an online survey. It asked on gut ills, food allergies, mouth pain, and body joy. It also asked on fear and pain when eating, and on food limits. Path tests mapped how those traits link to each other. Gut ills tied to allergies, fear, and pain in eating. Mind traits are part of the web too.
pmc-13369852:
Qinwei An and colleagues watched atoms at a solid and gas boundary in two thousand twenty-six using a microscope chamber that doubles as a tiny reaction vessel. Such boundaries drive the birth of layered materials, yet fleeting steps were never seen live. They filmed a tungsten oxide wire reacting with gas at atomic sharpness.

The surface first rebuilt itself into two layers: a loose, almost liquid top layer and a strained crystal layer beneath. New crystals of a tungsten and sulfur compound started in the rough lower layer and grew upward. Similar filming with a related material suggested the pattern is general. Materials makers gain a step-by-step picture to copy.
pmc-13372852:
Huijin Jeong and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six laboratory study of a citrus-derived bacterium and brain cell protection. The bacterium, Pediococcus pentosaceus TAP041, was tested through the liquid it grows in, without live cells. Stress pathways from oxidation, inflammation, and sugar damage were the targets.

In nerve-like cells, the liquid improved survival and lowered damaging oxygen chemicals under two stress types. It also raised expression of growth and dopamine-related genes. In rat glial cells, it calmed inflammatory signals. Protection was weaker against one sugar-damage chemical. The results suggest a food-derived candidate worth further testing for brain health.
pmc-13374352:
Bimala Dhimal and colleagues compare climate knowledge and diarrhoea prevention in Nepal in a 2026 study. Climate change threatens health, yet how Nepali communities link it to diarrhoeal disease was poorly known. The team surveyed 882 households in four districts of Koshi and Karnali provinces between February and June 2023.

Seventy percent of participants knew about climate change, and among them about two thirds strongly believed it raises diarrhoea risk, with higher agreement in Koshi. About 61 percent linked rising temperatures to more diarrhoea, while only 24 percent linked increased rainfall. Safe water access was reported by about 94 percent, with improved sanitation by about 84 percent. The study points to temperature awareness as a lever for prevention messages.
pmc-13376652:
Camila Hernández-Murillo and six co-authors trace greenstone artifacts in pre-Columbian Costa Rica, from raw material to exchange, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Greenstone's spread shows how ancient societies organized their exchange networks. The team examined objects from the Greater Nicoya and Central Caribbean regions. Non-invasive infrared spectroscopy identified the mineral phases in the artifacts.

The sample covered nine hundred twenty-six objects from fifty-four archaeological sites. Chemometric analysis grouped the objects by what they are made of, and mapped their spread. X-ray diffraction checked five samples that stand for the rest. Each region showed its own pattern of greenstone use. Local minerals like serpentine and quartz moved through short-range procurement. Jadeitite and albitite, by contrast, traveled through long-distance exchange between regions. Jadeite emerges as a key material linking Costa Rica's stone traditions to wider networks.
pmc-13376752:
Mingxi Lin leads an eleven-author team hunting a metabolic weakness in breast cancer that has spread to the brain, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Triple-negative breast cancer brain metastases resist most treatments. The team compared primary tumors with their brain offspring and profiled matched spinal fluid and blood.

Genome-wide CRISPR screens in living animals singled out NDUFB9, a piece of mitochondrial complex I. Knocking it out stalled brain metastasis growth while sparing metastases elsewhere. The mechanism runs through aspartate and asparagine balance. Brain tissue holds little asparagine, forcing cancer cells into a compensatory state that NDUFB9 loss disrupts. The authors nominate complex I as a brain-specific drug target.
pmc-13377552:
Rana and co-authors join gene facts to hone heat hold in rice for farm use. Heat strain is a growth threat to rice yields round the world. Gene and rule webs for heat hold stay dim and split cross works. Past work chased lone paths or lone growth steps in rice. Fresh work now backs a joined view of heat fit in plants. The sweep joins cell facts, rule cues, and gene marks in one frame.

Chief webs span lime and rust cues and heat shock rule nets. Birth growth checks and skin-based strain marks join those webs. Those webs shape breed-step hold and grain grade in hot times. Whole-kin reads and form shift hunts add worth to the frame. They bare heat genes and rule bits past one base stock. Gene hunts, breed picks, and CRISPR tools cap the sweep.
pmc-13377852:
Jun Zhao and co-authors list a key gene set in a cure herb in a 2026 study. The herb, a root used in Chinese care, owes its worth to bitter soap-like parts. A gate enzyme starts the chain that builds those parts, fed by a food path in the plant.

Four gate genes were found and split in two kin sets on two code strands. Their start zones hold stress and hormone cues. Reads in root, stem, and leaf plus spray tests tied gene acts to soap build. The list gives herb farms aims to breed roots with more cure parts.
pmc-13378152:
HuiMin Gao and colleagues published a 2026 study on faster quality checks for Relinqing granule, a product made from the plant Polygonum capitatum. The granule is used for urinary problems, but official checks have rested on just one plant compound. That narrow test cannot capture overall quality.

The researchers isolated twenty compounds from the plant and found that three of them reduced inflammation in tests. They then built a method using near-infrared light, which passes through a sample without destroying it, to predict the amounts of those three compounds. The method matched standard lab tests closely. It could give makers a quick, low-cost way to check each batch.
pmc-13379252:
Ikram Aluahabi and colleagues present a 2026 study on liver biopsy for a rare blood vessel disorder of the liver, shortened to PSVD. Diagnosis rests on biopsy tissue showing no cirrhosis but certain vessel changes, often alongside signs of high pressure in the liver's veins. Guidance calls for a fairly large, intact sample.

The team reviewed nine years of cases at a specialist department and asked whether smaller or broken samples still gave the answer. They gathered clinical, scan, and tissue details for each patient. The study tests whether strict sample rules are always needed, which matters because insisting on them can mean repeat procedures for patients.
pmc-13380452:
Tomohiro Shigematsu and co-authors present a 2026 study on whether a drug for anaemia helps a transplanted kidney work sooner. The drug, daprodustat, mimics low-oxygen signals and has shown kidney-protective effects in earlier lab work. Its value around the time of transplant was unknown.

The study reviewed living-donor kidney transplants at one centre between 2019 and 2023. Patients who received the drug from the day before surgery through the first week were matched with similar patients who did not. The treated group had better kidney function in the first two weeks after surgery. Fewer treated patients had slow-starting grafts, though the study was small and looked back at past records.
pmc-13380752:
Hyungwoo Lee and colleagues describe a 2026 computer method for measuring retinal blood vessels in mice bred to model a hereditary brain vessel disease. The disease, with a very long name shortened to CADASIL, also affects vessels in the eye, which offers a window for study. Precise measures of vessel narrowing are hard to obtain by eye.

The team trained image classifiers to tell normal mice from two mutant lines, using dye-based eye scans. Heat maps from the classifiers marked the vessel areas that drove each decision. A measurement pipeline then traced vessel centres and recorded width, variation, and winding. A further index captured regular bulging along vessels, offering a new way to track the disease.
pmc-13383452:
Ru Jia's team tested whether a school face mask trial is even feasible, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. No trial had tested mask effectiveness in schools, despite masks being a common public health measure. The team first explored barriers with young people, teachers, and parents, then ran a six-week two-arm cluster trial in one school.

Only 93 pupils, or 29 percent of those approached, joined, split 46 to school-rules control and 47 to mask arms. Mask wearing at all times rose from 7 percent at baseline to an average 28 percent across trial weeks, while weekly survey and saliva sample completion varied widely. Recruitment and adherence lagged other settings, suggesting incentives and engagement work must come first.
pmc-13384252:
Abhijith Biji and colleagues fold social and life factors into disease risk models alongside genetic scores in 2026 work. Using the All of Us biobank, with 413,457 people, they compressed over 100 survey measures into a few summary axes. Six chronic diseases were modeled, from asthma and kidney disease to breast and prostate cancer.

Adding the social axes improved prediction for every disease, sometimes more than genetic scores did. Known risks like income and smoking surfaced, along with less expected ones like loneliness and spirituality. Genetic and social risks mostly added up rather than interacting, which supports using both in fairer, sharper risk tools.
pmc-13385652:
Chen and colleagues evaluate a four-level engineering curriculum at a Chinese automotive teaching center, in 2026 education research. The framework blends outcome-based education with the conceive-design-implement-operate model and a teaching-learning-competition loop, progressing students from experiments toward industry-style projects. The team tracked graduate employment, surveyed students' self-assessed competencies, and collected employer feedback to judge whether the structure works at a resource-constrained university rather than an elite school.

During implementation, the graduate employment rate held around 95 percent for four straight years. Job-major alignment, graduates working in their field, ran at about 80.0 percent across the period. The 2023 cohort's starting salary rose 42 percent compared with the 2020 cohort before the framework matured. Students reported high perceived problem-solving ability, and competition results trended positively. Chen argues the competition-driven closed loop gives ordinary universities a workable reform path without budgets.
pmc-13389752:
Efstathios T Detorakis and colleagues report, in 2026, results for a radioactive plaque treatment used after incomplete removal of eye surface cancers. They treated patients with conjunctival melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma whose tumours had not been fully cut out.

Eight patients, four with each cancer type, received ruthenium-106 plaque therapy at a hospital in Heraklion, with no other added treatment to the tumour bed. The plaque delivered a set dose at one millimetre depth, and local control reached three quarters of cases over follow-up ranging from 18 to 75 months. Two patients later needed removal of the eye socket contents after spread. Eye cancer specialists gain small but direct outcome data for a salvage option.
pmc-13390152:
Xu Zhang's team built a two-layer nerve guide that delivers nerve growth factor steadily to injured peripheral nerves, which regenerate poorly on their own. The outer layer, a stiff gelatin-based hydrogel, gives mechanical support, while a softer inner gel carries growth-factor-loaded ZIF-8 nanoparticles.

In lab tests the conduit released its cargo continuously, supported cells, spurred nerve-like outgrowth, and nudged immune cells toward an calming state. In rats with sciatic nerve injury, the guides aided axon regrowth and functional recovery, presenting a versatile platform for peripheral nerve repair.
pmc-13390352:
Tahir and colleagues engineer a cumate-inducible switch for Burkholderia bacteria, in 2026 microbiology research. Such systems let scientists turn a gene on with a chemical signal, key for dissecting how these bacteria, dangerous pathogens, cause disease. Existing switches for Burkholderia are few and leaky. The team mutated the circuit and its regulator protein, CymR, to build a version with minimal background leak and tunable control. They verified it with glowing tags and with the cell's own sugar-tagging machinery.

Proteome-wide comparison showed cumate perturbs the cell differently from the rhamnose system, making the two complementary. Because cumate slips through membranes, the switch worked while they replicated inside eukaryotic cells, using chromosome-integration vectors. Running the glycosylation system inside cells showed that sugar tagging contributes to intracellular replication. Tahir offers the toolkit for virulence studies that switch genes mid-infection, when older systems stay silent.
pmc-13390752:
Julian Aguilar-Rosero and co-authors test, in 2026, whether coffee waste can clean dye from water in a sustainable way. About ninety percent of the coffee fruit's weight goes unused in the commercial cycle, creating a large residue problem for the industry.

Three wastes were tried as absorbents for methylene blue dye: coffee husk, spent coffee, and expired coffee. Tests of crystal structure, heat stability, and chemical groups showed that removing fat aligned the material's structure, while charged carboxyl and hydroxyl groups did the dye binding. Water treatment researchers gain a waste-to-resource option with a stated binding mechanism, plus a comparison across three waste streams from the same industry.
pmc-13391152:
Henry Bair argues that global eye health has undergone a severity transition, not simply a victory over blindness. Among adults over fifty, age-standardised blindness fell substantially between 1990 and 2020, yet moderate and severe damage barely moved and absolute numbers of impaired people rose steeply.

Blindness-centred metrics miss how many years people live in each severity state, so the essay reframes the pattern through morbidity-transition theory: blindness recedes while milder damage persists and grows as groups age. The burden falls hardest where eye-care systems are weakest, demanding metrics and services tuned to moderate damage, not blindness alone.
pmc-13391452:
So-Yeon Jeong's team disentangled species richness from species makeup in germ biofilm growth, building three hundred independent richness gradients of three to twenty species from twenty-four bacterial isolates. Richness often correlates with ecosystem function, but standard manipulations confound how many species are present with which ones.

Richness-biofilm relationships were mostly positive, with hump, U-shaped, null, and negative forms also appearing. Richness alone explained about fifty-four percent of growth variation on average, beating makeup gauges individually, while mid-richness assemblages of ten to fifteen species often outperformed expectations, showing both count and identity matter.
pmc-13392152:
Hannah Merrick and a large team evaluate, in 2026, a primary care health check designed with and for autistic adults. Autistic people face more illness of body and mind than most. They also meet steady barriers when they seek care.

The check ran inside a trial in northern England. That trial tests if the check helps health and if it is worth its cost. Forms and talks with autistic people, carers, and staff judged how the check felt and how it ran in real clinics. Care planners gain proof judged by users. It shows what makes a check truly fit for autistic adults. Just putting the check on a list is not enough.
pmc-13392252:
Songze Chen's team sampled drifting germs and viruses in warm-climate Daya Bay every two hours for three days, catching daily and sub-daily shifts that monthly or weekly sampling misses. Marine germ and viral groups drive nutrient cycling and energy flow, yet their fine-scale time shifts were poorly resolved.

DNA and RNA reading of cellular and viral parts yielded seven hundred genome-built genomes and 118,242 viral units, tracking genomic makeup and reading activity at fine detail. The data set opens study of energy-use-linked promise and germ-virus links in warm-climate bay wild places.
pmc-13392452:
Réka Csáki and a large group of collaborators examined rare changes in KCNA5, the gene for a potassium channel called Kv1.5, in people with pulmonary arterial hypertension. Most such changes sit in a class labelled uncertain, because nobody had tested what they do to the channel. The team drew patients from eight expert centres in Germany and Austria.

Sequencing covered 540 patients and found eleven rare variants, eight of them previously unreported. Six new protein-changing variants went forward for lab testing in frog egg cells, structural work, and cell studies. One variant, noted as G435R in the data, carried far less current than the normal channel. Findings of that kind help clinics judge whether a rare change truly drives disease or is harmless background variation.
pmc-13393252:
Signe Heuckendorff and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol for VIA Family 2.0, a team-based program for families where a parent lives with mental illness. Children of such parents face higher risks of mental health problems and developmental delays, partly because parental symptoms can disrupt care, routines, and stimulation at home.

The planned randomized trial compares the multidisciplinary program with standard treatment. It enrolls 304 children aged 3 to 17 and 128 children aged 0 to 2 whose parent received psychiatric treatment in the past three years. Readers get a clear map of the intervention, the groups studied, and the outcomes the trial will measure.
pmc-13393652:
Maxine Fogarty and six colleagues measured fearfulness and willingness to explore in laying hens across sixty-four flocks on Australian free-range egg farms, then hunted for farm features that track those temperaments. Each flock faced a novel object and an unfamiliar person, indoors and out on the range, at thirty to forty-six weeks of age. Records, manager interviews, and weather data supplied the farm-side variables, modelled together.

Hyline Brown flocks showed less fear of people and of the novel object outdoors than ISA Brown flocks, despite the strains being marketed as near-identical. Aviary housing made hens bolder around people than flat-deck housing did. Tight feeder space per hen strongly predicted fear of the novel object. Unexplained flock-to-flock variation hinted at stockperson culture mattering too. The authors suggest management tweaks that could lift both welfare and productivity.
pmc-13393852:
Resmiye Özdilek and others study AI worry among midwife students in Türkiye in a 2026 survey study. AI is fast reshaping ward work and training, and students must adapt to tech-rich wards, yet little was known about midwife students in particular.

Among 210 students in active ward training, views of the ward learning climate were tied in a negative way to overall AI worry, job-loss worry included. Better ward learning went with less worry. Teachers can see that kind, well-run placements may calm student fears about AI in birth care far more than tech talks alone.
pmc-13393952:
Krishna Nanaware and four colleagues ran a double-blind randomised trial comparing two enzyme-based toothpastes against a control in fifty-four patients wearing fixed braces, whose brackets trap plaque and inflame gums. Both test pastes harness natural salivary enzymes. Plaque, gum inflammation, and bleeding on probing were scored over twenty-four weeks, and saliva was assayed for two biochemical markers of oxidative and inflammatory activity.

pmc-13411252:

pmc-13411352:

pmc-13412252:

pmc-13412552:

pmc-13414052:

pmc-13416152:

pmc-13416752:

pmc-13418052:

pmc-13418152:

pmc-13418852:

pmc-13419952:

Unit leaders get a single map of where the field is moving and what to adopt next.
pmc-13421052:

pmc-13421152:

pmc-13421352:

pmc-13421452:

pmc-13421652:

pmc-13422352:

pmc-13422652:

pmc-13422752:
Sircombe, Pletzer, and Hook run a sentinel survey in this 2026 study of antibiotic-resistant Campylobacter on fresh chicken sold in New Zealand shops. pmc-13423052:

pmc-13423352:

pmc-13424152:

pmc-13424552:

pmc-13424952:

pmc-13425652:

pmc-13425952:

pmc-13426352:

pmc-13426452:

pmc-13427752:

pmc-13428252:

pmc-13428452:

pmc-13429252:

pmc-13430652:

pmc-13430752:

pmc-13430952:

pmc-13431852:

pmc-13432152:

pmc-13432352:

pmc-13432652:

pmc-13432852:

pmc-13433152:

pmc-13433252:

When the rule stretched to new sights, patterns grew still more spare and sight-free. The arc heals the clash, since both views catch true phases of one road. Crowd codes shed bulk as rules firm up, then shed ties to sights as rules go wide.
pmc-13433652:
Giancarlo Di Gennaro and colleagues discuss cenobamate's place in managing drug-resistant epilepsy, where surgery or neuromodulation may follow. One third of people with epilepsy still fail to control seizure frequency and intensity despite modern care, and resistant epilepsy spans many conditions needing a multi-dimensional approach.

Since 2020, cenobamate has joined the antiseizure drug shelf, with an efficacy and safety profile that began improving treatment for resistant cases. The paper positions the drug within the surgery and neuromodulation pathway, helping teams decide when a newer drug should be tried, and when to move toward procedures. Epilepsy clinics get a pathway view rather than a drug-versus-device contest.
pmc-13433952:
Caifeng Liu and co-authors froze a human calcium gate in 2026 in its many poses, with and without its three key guests, to map how the gate's kind-two form bends and clumps. The gate pours calcium from cell stores when a sugar note calls, which shapes signals for life acts from cell death to muscle pull. Kind two had lacked frames while its kin stood mapped.

Frames chart the bend span, pin guest holds, and show shared bones plus kind-only quirks across the clan. Guest-bound gates also stack gate-to-gate at a set face. Live cell films caught gates clumping after guest-driven pours. Snapping that face killed the clumps yet left pours whole. Shape change thus talks to crowd acts past the pour itself.
pmc-13434052:
Zechang Wei and co-authors cast a fluid metal mix in 2026 as a dual-use skin for war gear. It hides heat glow from heat eyes. It also turns heat gaps into power and signals. Stock hide goods do one job, which falls short of mixed field needs. The mix of gallium and indium stays fluid at room heat.

The fluid face throws back room heat rays, which drops its own glow and veils the wearer's mark across a wide heat span. Small heat gaps across the film stir up voltage, since the mix rides the heat-to-charge effect well. That free power feeds live reads of body heat and breath pace. The authors pitch self-fed hide skins that also talk.
pmc-13434152:
Chengwen Li and colleagues report a 2026 route to twisted, spring shaped compounds that carry more than one kind of handedness. Such helix shapes have uses in new materials, yet they are hard to make with the right form. The team designed a flexible ring part that can flip and then settle in one form.

Computer design set a flip barrier that allows change under mild heat. The route gave high control of form, with helix plus axis twists in a single product. Follow up tests traced why each form won. The products can be changed further and show useful light effects for future materials work.
pmc-13434652:
Xing Chen's team rated digital change in an oil and gas production area in China in 2026, using a new national standard with five rated dimensions. They scored three stations and single wells, finding most sites at level two or three, an intermediate stage overall. Emergency handling scored fairly well, but basic capacity and risk prevention lagged, and those gaps were named the main weak points of the shift to digital work.

Five core troubles were listed, from clashes between people and machines to single-worker risks, thin skills, and rules that lag behind the tools. The paper answers with five fixes, covering machine coordination, digital emergency response, worker health, training, and rule reform. Managers get a usable scorecard and a plain list of where digital upgrades must go next.
pmc-13435652:
Cong Zhou's team mapped dual-transmitter neurons across the developing mouse brain in 2026, asking whether cells that use two chemical messengers arise early or only in adults. Older work centered on adults, leaving the developmental origin open. Using genetic labeling that marks glutamate-making and GABA-making cells together, the team screened whole brains from birth to day sixty.

Dual cells were already common during development, appearing at birth in some regions and later in others. Direct RNA checks confirmed both markers in the same cells rather than a switch from one to the other. Neuroscientists get a developmental atlas showing dual identity as a normal, region-timed feature. The map should guide studies of how circuits wire up.
pmc-13436352:
Nestor Biatu and coauthors test a urine strip for tuberculosis in people with HIV in Cameroon in 2026. Stored urine from 798 patients, including 128 with proven TB, was run on the redesigned FujiLAM II strip. Two reference tests and culture grade standards set the truth.

The new strip caught 49 percent of proven cases, ahead of the older strip at 35 percent. False alarms ran lower too, at ninety six percent specificity. Four factory lots gave near alike positive rates, fixing an old flaw. Urine tests reach patients who cannot cough up sputum. Wider rollout could close part of the missed case gap.
pmc-13436552:
Zhao and colleagues tested in 2026 whether four variants in two fat metabolism genes relate to coronary heart disease in a Chinese Han population. Their case-control study genotyped 266 patients with the disease and 112 controls, examining two variants in the ABCA1 gene and two in the LIPG gene, with separate analyses by sex.

Three variants showed no link with disease in the whole group or in either sex. The fourth told a narrower story: in women only, one LIPG variant's T allele appeared more often in patients and carried a nominally higher risk in unadjusted analysis. That signal did not come with the same support in men or overall. The authors urge caution, since the sex-specific result could be a chance finding, and they call for validation in larger independent groups before any clinical meaning is attached.
pmc-13436652:
Melanie F Molina and coauthors chart opioid overdose visits at three California hospitals from 2017 to 2022 in 2026. Monthly counts span 781,488 total visits. Overdose visits numbered 2,536, while medication treatment visits numbered 9,755 in the same window.

All visit types climbed month by month before the pandemic peak. After April 2020 only medication treatment visits jumped at once, by about a third above trend. Overdose visits kept their prior slope without a step jump. Appendicitis visits serve as a control for ward wide swings. Treatment capacity in emergency wards grew steadily through the pandemic years.
pmc-13436952:
Hubert Piwar and co-authors survey what is known about Langer mesomelic dysplasia, a very rare bone disorder tied to complete loss of the SHOX gene. Their 2026 narrative review pulls together reports on its genetics, growth signs, X-ray findings, and detection before birth. Fewer than one hundred cases have been described in print so far.

The ulna and fibula may be small or missing, while learning and lifespan are usually normal. The review explains how SHOX guides bone growth plate cells, and how deletions, enhancer faults, and other variants cut its function. It also compares this disorder with milder SHOX-related conditions, such as Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis and Turner syndrome. Clear gene knowledge, the authors argue, helps families get exact diagnoses, sound advice, and careful checks during pregnancy.
pmc-13437352:
Marta Kasprowicz-Furmańczyk and Agnieszka Owczarczyk-Saczonek propose a new suspect in lichen sclerosus, a chronic skin disease that scars and stiffens tissue. The disease carries an autoimmune pattern, yet what turns lasting inflammation into fibrosis stays unclear. Their 2026 framework points to MAIT cells, a fast-acting class of immune cells that gather in surface tissues and release strong inflammatory signals.

No study has yet measured these cells in lichen sclerosus itself, so the authors build their case from related autoimmune and scarring diseases. They suggest the cells could amplify the dominant immune pattern, injure tissue, and wake fibroblasts through signals tied to the TGF-beta pathway. Because MAIT cells answer to microbe-made molecules as well as inflammation, they might keep the response burning. The authors label the model a hypothesis and call for lab tests to confirm or refute it.
pmc-13439052:
Kun-Chang Wu's team tested a plant diterpenoid in 2026 against non-small cell lung cancer, targeting mitochondrial energy and cancer stemness. Lung cancer remains a leading killer, and new drugs are urgently needed. The compound, isolated from Adenostemma lavenia, was tested on lung cancer cells versus normal fibroblasts, on migration, death, stem markers, mitochondrial function, and mouse grafts.

The compound killed lung cancer cells preferentially, blocked migration, and triggered death. It cut tumorsphere formation and stem markers CD44, CD133, and Notch-1, and crippled oxidative phosphorylation with ATP loss and reactive oxygen buildup that antioxidants blunted. Oral dosing shrank mouse tumors without clear systemic toxicity. Lung teams get a mitochondrial lead with stemness effects, still preclinical.
pmc-13439552:
Bern-Thomas Nyang'wa and colleagues measure drug exposure in patients on short oral regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis, reporting a 2026 analysis from Belarus and South Africa. The regimens pair bedaquiline and pretomanid with linezolid, sometimes adding clofazimine or moxifloxacin. Whether drug levels in blood explained cure speed or side effects was unclear. Exposure levels matched earlier reports, yet higher levels did not mean faster bacterial clearance. The moxifloxacin regimen killed bacteria about a fifth faster than standard care, while the other two ran slightly slower. Severe disease slowed killing regardless of regimen. Higher linezolid exposure tracked with anaemia and low white cell counts. The authors judge the studied doses a fair balance, backing the moxifloxacin version as preferred care.
pmc-13439752:
Jean-Jacques Rouby's team compared discomfort in 2026 across three post-extubation oxygen supports in patients without COPD: high-flow nasal oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, and conventional oxygen. Discomfort shapes tolerance and outcomes, yet comparisons remained contested. For forty-eight hours after tube removal, patients rated interface discomfort while nurses rated support discomfort, at six, twenty-four, and forty-eight hours, split by high versus low risk of breathing failure.

Facial masks caused significant, lasting self-rated discomfort. Nasal prongs and oxygen masks were easier with discomfort easing over time, and high-flow alternating with ventilation caused lasting nurse-rated discomfort while conventional oxygen stayed least uncomfortable regardless of risk. Clinicians get a comfort ranking to weigh against breathing benefit when choosing post-extubation support.
pmc-13440152:
Chandan Kumar Swain and colleagues gather the world literature on illness among handloom weavers, publishing a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Handloom weaving is traditional textile work done in risky, cramped settings, yet pooled health figures were lacking. Searches of three databases yielded 47 eligible studies spanning 1980 to 2024. Publication in the field grew slowly across those decades, and themes shifted from economic history toward muscle, joint, and general health studies.

Pooled risk of musculoskeletal disorders ran about a quarter higher among weavers than comparison groups, though the gap missed statistical significance. Overall disease prevalence likewise matched comparison groups closely. Eye strain, breathing illness, digestive trouble, and poor vision still recurred across individual studies. The authors call for targeted workplace health policies for weavers despite the muted pooled figures.
pmc-13440452:
Beatriz de Souza dos Reis França and colleagues run first validity checks on a Brazilian screening test for early reading trouble, reporting in 2026. The SPRouT test aims to flag young children at risk before reading failure sets in. Twenty-seven children aged four to eight took the Brazilian version alongside standard measures of intelligence and sound-processing skills. Sound skills covered awareness of speech sounds, holding sounds in memory, and fast naming, all known supports of reading.

Scores on the screener moved against the sound measures in the expected direction, with links from moderate to strong once intelligence was set aside. Total scores explained roughly a quarter to a third of the variation in sound skills. The authors read that pattern as early convergent validity, meaning the test aligns with related abilities. Larger, more varied groups and follow-up over time are their stated next steps before clinical use.
pmc-13442852:
Ravi Arukula and coauthors describe a 2026 materials study of coatings that hide barcodes from the eye yet stay clear to near-infrared scanners, a trick useful for secure labels and heat control. The team built a two-layer system, a clear sealer beneath a tinted topcoat, in black, green, and tan. Barcodes were printed on synthetic paper sheets to test how well scanners could still read them.

Black coatings performed best, giving the sharpest edges and the strongest signal. They read reliably at a distance of 15.2 meters, while green and tan lagged slightly when white pigment was added. Particle size proved decisive, with grains near 566 nanometers reading best and broad or coarse mixes scattering more light. The results point to practical hidden labels, though field trials must confirm durability in daily use.
pmc-13443052:
Lee and Pae review screening tools for mental disorders in skin clinics in this 2026 article. Skin diseases and psychiatric conditions frequently coexist. They share roots in immune changes, hormone problems, stress sensitivity, and genetics. Yet dermatologists without psychiatric training struggle to spot mental illness during busy clinics. Unrecognized comorbidity leads to late treatment, poor adherence, and worse outcomes for the skin condition itself, the authors note.

The review assembles simple, validated rating scales that dermatologists can use in routine practice, covering the common psychiatric companions of skin disease and recognized conditions such as dermatological delusions. The authors argue proactive screening can substantially improve both treatment benefit and prognosis. Their aim is practical: give the dermatologist a shortlist of instruments that are quick enough for real clinics and accurate enough to trigger proper psychiatric referral.
pmc-13443152:
Xiaoyi Zhang and coauthors report a 2026 field study of a joint support system for deep pits dug in loess. Loess is the wind-blown silt soil common in parts of China, and site conditions were tricky. The team monitored crest and deep movements at a working excavation and built a two-dimensional numerical model to compare measured and simulated behavior.

The prestressed cables plus soil nails held movement far below alarm levels, with peak crest shift near 3.91 millimeters and deep shift under 1.6 millimeters below a half-meter depth. Shifts grew steadily with dig depth, and the unbraced model failed once digging passed 3.6 meters, confirming the support's value. Field shifts ran below simulated ones, a gap the authors tie to light site loads and simplified grouting in the model.
pmc-13445752:
Limei Xu and coauthors show a 2026 study showing that the enzyme PRMT5 is vital for harm in Toxoplasma gondii, the bug behind toxoplasmosis. The team deleted the prmt5 gene in the fierce RH strain with CRISPR, then tested plaque growth, entry, copying, stage switch, and mouse harm with RNA reading.

The deleted strain lost matching dimethylarginine marks and failed at plaque growth, entry, copying, and switch to dormant cyst stages. All mice given the deleted strain lived ten days, while all wild-type given mice died within the same span. Gene scanning tied the defects to motor and fatty acid pathways, marking PRMT5 as a drug target hope.
pmc-13445852:
Dongyu Song and colleagues quantify a 2026 discrete choice study of what bypass surgery patients want from remote cardiac rehabilitation in China, where uptake runs extremely low. The team surveyed 343 bypass patients, mostly men averaging about 62 years, across six service attributes including provider, personalization, monitoring, format, and cost.

Service provider mattered most, with multidisciplinary teams worth about 93 yuan monthly and doctor-led care about 59 yuan, followed by wearable automatic monitoring and video content. Personalized plans beat fixed protocols, and cost deterred choice. Younger patients favored personalization while older patients favored AI plus team review, guiding patient-centered program design.
pmc-13446352:
Fei Liu and colleagues test oprozomib, a proteasome-blocking drug, against gallbladder cancer in dishes and mouse grafts, in a 2026 study. Gallbladder cancer is the most common bile tract malignancy and carries grim odds. The drug had already shown force against other tumors, which made it a candidate here.

The drug curbed growth in three gallbladder cancer cell lines and slowed grafted tumors in mice without clear toxicity. Treated cells stalled at the gate before division and died in greater numbers. Gene reading and protein checks traced the stall to one branch of the MAPK relay and the death push to two sister branches. The authors present oprozomib as a lead worth carrying toward clinic tests.
pmc-13447152:
Yang Chen and colleagues study male university students in a 2026 cycling trial focused on resilience and stress linked to masculine norms. Pressure to meet traditional male roles can harm mental health, yet few targeted options feel acceptable to young men. Short, intense exercise fits a busy schedule and may appeal where talk-based help does not.

Fifty-four students completed eight weeks of brief all-out cycling sprints, two or three times each week. Peak power rose, resilience scores improved, and both role stress and fatigue ratings fell. A check for whether resilience explained the stress drop found no clear indirect path. With no comparison group and only one group measured before and after, the authors treat the results as early and exploratory rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13447652:
Yi Tang and coauthors construct a 2026 forecasting model for neck-of-womb cancer from lactate tagging-related genes tied to ray therapy-driven gene changes. Using public output data, the team picked key genes, built a Lasso model with cross-checks, and added a chart for living forecast.

Two genes, RFC4 and STMN1, rose in tumors but fell during ray therapy, and the two-gene risk score sorted living in-house. High- and low-risk groups split in immune, vessel, and energy pathways, immune entry, and gene change load, with low-risk patients living longer. The model aids risk sorting and ray therapy biology, pending outside checks.
pmc-13447852:
Joon Kim, Dharshini Ganeshan, David Grattan, and Karl Iremonger study how motherhood changes stress responses in the brain in this 2026 paper. Stress is driven by hormone-releasing neurons in a small brain region that controls the body's stress system. Many had assumed these neurons quiet down while a mother nurses her young, but that idea had never been tested directly.

Using light-based recordings in freely moving mice, the team watched the neurons during stress and pup care. Responses to outside stressors were not lower in nursing mothers than in virgin mice. Still, the stress hormone gene and hormone levels in blood both fell after stress in mothers. Pup cues told a different story: the neurons fell silent when a mother retrieved a pup, and surged when a pup was near but out of reach.
pmc-13448252:
Celso Teixeira-Duarte leads a team revealing how a small molecule switches on a human ion channel to kill cells by sodium overload in 2026 structural work. The channel, TRPM4, opens for sodium when calcium rises and is overproduced in several cancers, making it a tempting drug target. The activator molecule works on the human channel only, not on most animal versions, and that selectivity needed a molecular explanation.

Frozen electron microscopy, electrical recordings and cell death assays together located the binding pocket and the residues that trigger opening. Matching changes explain why the mouse channel ignores the molecule, pinpointing the exact spots that encode human specificity. Since the channel rises in prostate, breast and blood cancers, the map offers a framework for designing necrosis-inducing cancer drugs aimed at this channel.
pmc-13449652:
Sabine Vossler and co-authors compare in 2026 broiler chicks hatched on the farm with those hatched in a commercial hatchery, asking whether skipping transport calms the birds. Their field study ran on a working farm with two houses of roughly 5,700 slow-growing chickens each, followed over seven production rounds. Fear was tested by how chicks reacted to an approaching human and to a novel object on days one and seven, while droppings yielded stress hormone metabolites.

On-farm chicks approached people more readily and behaved less fearfully in the object test, where group differences in approach latency were significant. Their stress metabolite levels ran slightly lower, both groups starting high on day one and settling near 400 nanograms per gram by days four and five. On-farm chicks also weighed more on days one, seven, and forty-two. The authors call the welfare edge real but provisional, pending larger studies.
pmc-13449952:
Mantovani and colleagues make ammonia, a key fertilizer chemical, with light instead of fossil heat. Industry now relies on the Haber-Bosch process, which burns fossil fuels at huge scale. Their 2026 system works in plain water at neutral acidity. A cobalt complex wrapped in pyridine based arms acts as catalyst. A ruthenium dye catches visible light, and vitamin C based ascorbate donates electrons. The starting material is nitrite, found in water.

Under visible light the setup turned nitrite into ammonia with selectivity near total, meaning almost no side products formed. Each catalyst molecule cycled more than two thousand times at best, a durability measure chemists call turnover number. Light flash tests and computer modeling traced the path: nitrite binds the cobalt after it gains one electron, and each later step checks out as energetically feasible. Common metal catalysts, the work suggests, can run solar style ammonia chemistry.
pmc-13450252:
Anas Bin Harun and co-authors survey in 2026 two gut microbes with zoonotic potential in the cats and dogs of Dhaka and Gazipur, Bangladesh. The fungus appeared in 9.1 percent of cats and 11.7 percent of dogs; Blastocystis in 3.6 percent of cats, only kittens, and ten percent of dogs. Female sex and youth were the significant risk markers in dogs and cats respectively. Strain typing turned up four genotypes never described before and several matching those circulating in Bangladeshi children, with most carrying zoonotic potential. Six Blastocystis subtypes appeared, three of them known people-infectors. The authors call for joint human-animal surveillance.
pmc-13450552:
Utpal K Mondal and others heard Nipah virus survivors in Bangladesh in 2026, and wrote up the hardships that last long past the first illness. Themes drawn from the talks traced harm to body, mind, social ties, and money. Survivors told of lives broken across kin, work, and village ties. Health chiefs gain a case, told by survivors, for long-run rehab and social help.
pmc-13452252:
Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 study mapping a rare double-mutant lung cancer at single-cell depth. Two uncommon faults in the EGFR gene combine in about five percent of such cancers. These tumors answer standard targeted drugs far worse than typical cases. The team read single nuclei from stored tumor tissue samples.

One tumor cell group stood out, shaped like cells that spread and invade. That group ran fat-based fuel programs and wore a marker called CD44. Lung immune cells nearby showed stressed, suppressive behavior in the data. A two-protein handshake between tumor and immune cells defined the niche. Blocking that handshake may reopen these tumors to immune attack. Fresh and stored samples agreed, widening the method's future reach.
pmc-13452352:
Jananee Rasiah and co-authors compare in 2026 two frailty gauges inside Alberta's home care assessment system for older adults. Both were run over the same home care group to see how their frailty portraits differ.

The pair agreed only fairly. The acute gauge tied more strongly to hospital use and near-term wobble. The wide index tied more steadily to spread across body, mind, and social deficits. As frailty bands rose, both showed deeper need. The authors call the gauges partners, not rivals, for planning care that lets elders stay home.
pmc-13453652:
Shigeki Matsubara and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on a subtle, dangerous error a leading chatbot made in medical writing. AI tools polish manuscripts well, yet they can invent facts or cite wrong sources. The team fed one chatbot medically correct notes on a severe pregnancy condition and asked for a short review, with a small trap planted in the topic.

The draft cited sound sources and was nearly right, but it claimed the condition could be handled at mid-level hospitals, which is wrong and risky. Asked to double-check, the tool hedged rather than firmly correcting itself. A second test on cholesterol care showed the same blind spot. The authors warn editors to verify, not trust.
pmc-13453752:
Kai Xu and seven co-authors weigh the cost of a new lung cancer drug against standard chemotherapy in China. Their 2026 model runs a ten year horizon in 28 day cycles, fed by a trial where the drug held cancer back for a median of 8.3 months.

The drug added about 28,285 dollars in cost while gaining 0.84 quality adjusted life years, for a ratio near 33,515 dollars per such year. That sits above China's cost effectiveness bar of about 27,906 dollars, and the chance of clearing the bar was only 23.90 percent. A price cut of about 15 percent would flip the verdict, the authors find. The drug's own price swayed the result most of all inputs.
pmc-13454252:
Shikang Liu and four co-authors test whether COVID-19 social controls changed how air pollution tracked respiratory illness in Xi'an, China. Their 2026 study counts 2,052,777 respiratory clinic visits over 2,192 days from January 2020 to December 2025 at one large hospital. The span splits into strict control, transition, and post pandemic phases.

Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide, both combustion gases, showed the strongest links to visits across the whole span. Formal interaction tests fell short of significance, and fine particles plus ozone showed no phase pattern at all. pmc-13454352:
Sakshi Choudhary and others tuned micro-PIV in 2026 to watch shrinking actomyosin gels with no tracer beads. Micro-PIV maps flows in tiny systems, but fast-shrinking gels need tweaks. The team tracked myosin-made actin lumps in place of invasive beads.

True shift scores hinged on tuning the time gap and frame count for group correlation, set against the gel's squash time and shrink stage. Four trust scores were charted, such as shift fields, shift-size maps, radial profiles, and turn scores. With gel spring-back built in, radial strain profiles held firm for odd shapes and off-centre shrinks. Shared radial marks showed inward shrink with a peak shift at mid radii. Biophysicists gain a checked method for live gel motion.
pmc-13454452:
Yachong Liu and twelve colleagues show, in a 2026 materials study, how strain at a crystal boundary can send rare-earth ions traveling far inside nanoparticles. Such layered particles matter for imaging, catalysis, and quantum devices, yet strain inside them is hard to control. The team built three-layer crystals and tuned both their recipe and growth speed to set the strain.

When the size mismatch between layers passed about five percent, ions moved up to 13 nanometers from the core into the shell. They traveled along one preferred crystal direction. Strain also steered where new shell material landed, favoring certain faces, and opened empty sites that eased ion hopping. The authors frame strain as a design dial: set it well, and builders can place active ions exactly where a device needs them.
pmc-13454552:
Barghi and colleagues test whether gases released by bacteria, called volatile compounds, help both plants and the bacteria themselves when lead poisons the soil. Their 2026 study pairs the bacterium Bacillus megaterium with Arabidopsis thaliana, a small plant widely used in lab research. Some groups grew under lead stress, some did not, so the team could trace gases, growth, and lead uptake in each partner.

Gases from stressed bacteria eased lead harm in plants more than gases from unstressed bacteria, lifting plant lead uptake in shoots while cutting markers of cell damage. Plants also turned up genes for protective enzymes, proteins that guard cells from harm. In return, treated plants relieved the lead driven drop in bacterial numbers, so both sides gained.
pmc-13454952:
Sun and colleagues reveal an unexpected way tumors talk to blood platelets in this 2026 study. That cascade, together with a linked RNASEL-ABCE1-PELO axis, destroyed the platelets' messenger RNAs for ribosomal proteins, the machinery that builds new proteins. The work shows tumors can directly rewrite the RNA content of circulating platelets.
pmc-13455352:

The authors applied the attribution rules of a large completed primary care program to beneficiaries in its regions from 2016 to 2021.

Unassigned beneficiaries differed from assigned ones in several ways: 56 percent were men, compared with 43 percent among the assigned group in the study. They were also more often eligible for low-income drug subsidies, dually eligible for Medicaid, and non-White. Testing payment models only on assigned patients is risky, the authors warn. The evidence may not apply to underserved groups. They urge designs that represent the full population.
pmc-13455452:
Concepcion and colleagues survey how transplant centers use cold machine perfusion for donor kidneys in this 2026 study. The team invited surgeons, kidney specialists, and coordinators to describe their practices and concerns.

Respondents came from 88 centers handling 63 percent of 2024 transplant volume, and nearly all were surgeons. Over 90 percent agreed perfusion helps judge kidneys, cuts delayed graft function, and eases scheduling. The commonest barrier was refusal by organ procurement organizations, cited by 58 percent, and three-quarters said those organizations exclusively run the pumps. Acceptable flow and resistance cut-offs varied widely between centers.
pmc-13455552:

The disorder hardens skin and inflames the wrapping around muscles, with eosinophil cells raised in the blood. Their patient was a middle-aged man who arrived with knee pain and swelling.

His skin then thickened and darkened across the thigh and trunk. Blood work showed the expected eosinophil rise plus a weak positive for PM-Scl-100, an antibody tied to overlap syndromes. Scans showed thickened fascial layers with fluid, and a muscle biopsy confirmed the diagnosis while sparing the muscle itself. Strong steroids, a steroid-sparing drug, and protective add-ons brought marked improvement. The authors warn that stray antibodies can mislead, and that biopsy plus clinical matching keeps the diagnosis honest.
pmc-13456052:
Carla Tierney-Hendricks and seven colleagues map, in a 2026 scoping review, the help stroke survivors get while moving between care settings. Forty-nine articles survived, describing 31 transitional care programs built from 23 distinct components. Most programs leaned on person-level pieces such as teaching and self-management coaching. System-level pieces, above all care coordination, appeared less often. Measured outcomes centered on physical function, while thinking and communication outcomes were rarely tracked. People with speech or cognitive problems were often shut out of the studies entirely. The authors call for programs that match their parts to their goals and that include the survivors most often left behind.
pmc-13456452:
Sinan Sousan and colleagues tested whether three store-bought wearable sensors could track heat strain in farmworkers during real field work. Air heat stress stayed near 28 to 29 degrees on the standard wet-bulb globe scale. The team combined the readings into a strain index that estimates how hard the body is working to stay cool.

The temperature sensor returned all of its data. The smartwatch returned 97 percent, and the hydration sensor returned 80 percent of expected readings. A machine learning model using hour-long smoothed averages predicted strain with very high accuracy.
pmc-13456652:
Narmadaa Raman and seven colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, what Malaysian university students know and feel about regenerative medicine, the field that rebuilds tissue with living cells. pmc-13457052:
Jinzhuo Tan and five colleagues trace, in a 2026 mouse study, how aging traps certain bile acids in the gut and starves the rest of the body of their calming effect. pmc-13457152:

pmc-13457352:

pmc-13457552:

pmc-13457952:

pmc-13458352:

pmc-13458552:

pmc-13458652:

pmc-13459452:

pmc-13459652:

pmc-13459952:

pmc-13461052:

pmc-13461252:

pmc-13461352:

pmc-13461552:

pmc-13462852:

pmc-13463152:

pmc-13464352:

pmc-13464752:

pmc-13464852:

pmc-13464952:

pmc-13465652:

pmc-13466752:

pmc-13467352:

pmc-13467452:

pmc-13468652:

pmc-13469052:

pmc-13469252:

pmc-13469652:

pmc-13470052:

pmc-13470552:

pmc-13470752:

pmc-13470952:

pmc-13471552:

pmc-13471652:

pmc-13472952:

pmc-13473052:

pmc-13473152:
