pmc-13473852:
Zihao Liu and colleagues report a qualitative study, published in 2026. It covers bringing AI chatbots into patient education. The team interviewed patients, caregivers, and nurses. The setting was a large hospital in 2025. They explored what each group saw as benefits and risks. Effects on trust between nurses and patients were also explored.

All three groups accepted chatbots as supplementary information tools. Acceptance was conditional, though. Worries about trust differed by role. Chatbots were not seen as a direct threat to trust today. Participants wanted nurse oversight and clear accountability. Older patients' digital skills needed attention too. The authors frame these as conditions for safe, fair use.
pmc-13474552:
Fen Tang and colleagues build a single-cell atlas in 2026 of the human retina in advanced diabetic eye disease. This disease is a top cause of blindness that cannot be reversed, driven by rogue blood vessel growth and scarring. Drugs that block vessel growth do not stop scar tissue, which can pull the retina loose. Tissue from organ donors with and without diabetes was read cell by cell.

One scar-linked cell group stood out, marked by high levels of a gene called SOX15. Tests in mice and cells tied that group to a signal chain that drives fiber growth. Blocking the chain receptor eased scarring in models. The atlas gives drug hunters a named target for the scar side of the disease.
pmc-13474752:
Satya Ranjan Misra and two colleagues surveyed in 2026 how well dental interns across India can spot early mouth cancers and precancerous changes. They questioned 1,220 interns from 23 states and 3 union territories, found online, on knowledge, attitudes, and practices.

Knowledge averaged 5.48 out of 8, attitudes were strongly positive, and most interns reported always checking high-risk sites and counselling on tobacco. Yet only 70.5 percent knew the malignant transformation rate of leukoplakia, and knowledge gaps persisted despite frequent screening. The authors recommend course updates and hands-on training, while cautioning that convenience sampling and self-reports limit the findings.
pmc-13474952:
Liang and colleagues tested dual-energy CT scans in 2026 as a way to judge thyroid cancer stage, spread to neck lymph nodes, and likely outcome. Dual-energy scanning uses two X-ray energy levels, letting doctors measure iodine uptake and other tissue traits as numbers. The study covered 80 patients, 40 with stage III disease and 40 with stage IV disease, whose scans the team compared against pathology and follow-up.

Stage IV tumors showed clearly higher scan enhancement, averaging 185.4 units against 155.7 units for stage III tumors in the comparison. Iodine load also ran higher in stage IV cancer, at 6.8 milligrams per cubic centimeter against 3.2 for the earlier stage group. Patients above a 145-unit enhancement threshold lived longer without disease returning, and two doctors reading the scans agreed almost perfectly, with a consistency score of 0.963 on the study scale.
pmc-13475252:
Shivani Sah and co-authors measure how blur and faint charts degrade vision in 2026 among young adults. Three hundred adults, half with low short-sight and half with normal sight, read eye charts at six meters. Added lenses created graded blur over best correction. Chart contrast stepped down through five levels from full to faint.

Blur cut acuity sharply as lens strength rose, and fainter charts made scores worse at every blur level. The two effects slightly amplified each other at the faintest levels. Short-sighted readers scored a touch worse overall, yet their decline pattern matched normal readers. Chart contrast deserves the same care as lens power in vision testing.
pmc-13477452:
Elisa Gatta and co-authors pool studies on thyroid disease and heart risk in a 2026 review. Low thyroid function, or hypothyroidism, has a disputed link to cardiovascular disease. The team split the question into new heart events versus death from heart causes.

They searched three databases for recent studies and kept nine studies with 9,662 patients. For new cardiovascular events, no clear link appeared across six studies. For cardiovascular death, eight studies showed a much higher risk in hypothyroid patients. The contrast suggests the condition may worsen outlook after disease more than it triggers new events.
pmc-13478052:
Hai Xuan Ho and colleagues report a 2026 case where a bacterial eye infection imitated viral disease for years. A 23-year-old man had five years of recurring redness and high pressure in his left eye, treated as viral inflammation. He arrived with worsening vision loss in that eye.

Examination showed inflammation throughout the eye, iris wasting, and pigment spread. Old scars sat near the optic disc. An active tissue-destroying retinal lesion involved the central vision area, with bleeding and a secondary macular hole. Fluid testing was negative for the usual herpes viruses, yet bacterial testing detected Listeria monocytogenes, a food-borne germ rarely found in the back of the eye. Adding moxifloxacin antibiotic to anti-inflammatory care settled the inflammation within 30 days, and the lesion turned into an inactive scar.
pmc-13478152:
Qiang Li and three colleagues built in 2026 a machine learning early warning system for student academic crises. They combined expert scoring with a ten-indicator system, then trained a radial basis function network that beat recurrent networks and softmax regression on accuracy and convergence.

The web-based system reached 96.32 percent accuracy on large student datasets, with low error, and offers personalised alerts through a friendly interface. The sample was limited to engineering students with male overrepresentation, so wider validation is needed. The authors offer the tool for smart campus management and timely student support.
pmc-13479452:
Tang and colleagues report a 63-year-old man in 2026 whose advanced lung cancer spread through the lung's lymph channels, a pattern called pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis that usually kills within months. His tumor was a cavitary lung adenocarcinoma, a cancer forming a hollow space, and it had also seeded fluid around his heart. Another hospital first mistook the illness for infection and tuberculosis, delaying cancer care.

On arrival he could not tolerate strong chemotherapy, so surgeons first operated to relieve his symptoms and drain the heart fluid. Individualized chemotherapy followed, then immunotherapy, and the sequence held the disease back far beyond the usual course for this complication. He had survived 41 months at last follow-up, an outlier result. The authors set it against a condition found in 6 to 8 percent of metastatic lung cancers and normally tied to rapid decline.
pmc-13479552:
Qingqing Xu and coauthors published a 2026 cross-sectional survey of tooth decay among twelve-year-old children in Shanghai. Decay remains one of the most common chronic diseases of childhood. The school-based survey ran in 2024 and sampled 2,570 children across all sixteen districts using a staged cluster design.

Calibrated dentists examined each child using World Health Organization criteria and recorded decay experience with the standard DMFT index, which counts decayed, missing, and filled teeth. Questionnaires covered family background, diet, brushing habits, dental knowledge and attitudes, and use of dental services. The analysis first compares groups one factor at a time, then builds a multivariable model guided by a theory-based framework. The authors aim to hand Shanghai prevention programs a ranked list of influences worth targeting.
pmc-13480052:
Mesher Ensarioğlu and co-authors report a 2026 study of what predicts hard placement of a double-lumen breathing tube. These wider, stiffer tubes split airflow so one lung can rest during chest surgery, and standard airway checks were built for narrower tubes. The team enrolled 200 adults having planned chest surgery and scored many airway measures before the procedure.

Placement proved hard in 36 patients, or eighteen percent. That group showed higher scores on three standard scales and shorter or narrower airway measures. When all factors were weighed together, only the direct view grade of the airway held as a stand-alone predictor. The team proposes new cut-off values tuned to these tubes for three key measures. Clinics could use the tailored cut-offs to prepare backup plans for patients flagged as high risk.
pmc-13481552:
Mohammed Al Azzawi and eleven colleagues reported in 2026 Ireland's first robotic adrenalectomy program. Robotic removal suits tumours near major vessels, but evidence on launching a new program was thin.

Reviewing the first 50 consecutive patients treated from November 2021 to December 2024, they found a median surgery time of 120 minutes, one conversion to open surgery, and three intraoperative complications. Hospital stay averaged four days with no deaths, reoperations, or readmissions in 30 days, and complete tumour removal in 94 percent. Larger tumours lengthened surgery and stay, while higher body mass did not lengthen surgery, marking the program safe and feasible.
pmc-13481752:
Andreia Gomes-Duarte and co-authors describe a 2026 study blaming damaged fat molecules for part of the harm in ALS. Oxidised forms of a common membrane fat turn up in the spinal fluid of people with the sporadic form of the disease, riding on apoE particles. The team grew human motor nerve cells from stem cells and bathed them in these fats.

Exposure twisted gene activity and drove the clumping of TDP-43, the protein whose clumps mark nearly all ALS cases. The team then built a virus that makes nerve cells secrete a small antibody tuned to the damaged fats. The antibody shielded cells, cut clumps, and in mice given patient spinal fluid it saved nerve cells and behaviour. Shots into pig spinal fluid spread widely, which supports the delivery plan. A first-in-kind target gains a candidate therapy.
pmc-13482552:
Sadeghpour and colleagues teach machine learning models in 2026 to predict lost circulation, the costly accident where drilling mud vanishes into cracks underground instead of returning up the well. They assembled 246,620 data points from 73 wells in one Iranian oil field, mixing rock measurements from well logs with drilling settings and mud properties. Three neural designs competed, two established architectures and a hybrid that chains them together.

The hybrid won clearly, explaining the losses with a fit score of 0.9445 and a small error of 0.0143 on the prediction scale used in the study. Its parents trailed at 0.9054 and 0.9075 on the same fit measure, and importance analysis credited sonic travel time, mud weight, bit size, and calcium content as the strongest signals. The model also mapped three invasion zones in the field, depth bands near 1800 to 2000, 2300 to 2600, and 2800 to 3000 meters.
pmc-13482852:
Wan Jusoh and colleagues built a computer model of a refinery distillation column, the tall tower that boils crude oil and splits it into fuels. Their 2026 study used Aspen HYSYS software and real refinery data for three crude oils. The goal was to predict product yields, meaning how much of each fuel comes out, without waiting for slow laboratory tests.

The model matched measured column temperatures closely, with errors mostly between well under one percent and about one percent of the readings taken. Flow predictions were looser, missing by roughly 2 to 20 percent across the three oils tested. Raising steam flow at the column bottom cut light and medium products by about 2 percent while heavy products rose near 5 percent. Wan Jusoh notes that accuracy depends heavily on how well each crude oil itself is described.
pmc-13483152:
Jinming Xu and co-authors present a 2026 pair of switchable tools for editing a chemical mark on RNA. The mark, a methyl tag on cytosine letters, shapes how messages behave and goes astray in cancers, yet older editors run always-on with no undo. Their systems split the editing enzyme and wake it only when a plant hormone signal arrives, using a tamed CRISPR guide that grips RNA without cutting it.

A light-caged form of the signal adds flash control, so edits can start at a chosen place and moment. In kidney cancer models, targeted edits changed how key transcripts worked and slowed tumour growth in dishes and in animals. Off-target edits stayed low. A reversible, timed editor lets researchers probe what each mark does and hints at RNA drugs that act only where switched on.
pmc-13483552:
Greta Mohr and colleagues test whether computer-altered chest X-rays can teach diagnosis more effectively in medical training. Their 2026 study uses real patient images edited by artificial intelligence so the same chest shows a different yet plausible condition. Forty-two medical students and doctors completed online tasks covering diagnosis, paired image comparison, judging whether images looked real, and planning treatment.

Practice focused on healthy lungs, pneumonia, and fluid around the lung. Learners grew more accurate and better calibrated over time, especially when separating fluid cases from healthy ones, and the paired images exposed weaknesses that ordinary teaching can miss. Real images still gave the highest raw accuracy. Even so, the altered images proved useful for reflection and for aligning confidence with performance.
pmc-13483652:
Chilot Kassa Mekonnen and co-authors estimate how common loneliness is among older adults in Africa and what raises the risk. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathers 18 cross-sectional studies found through major databases and search engines. A random-effects model pools the prevalence figures across countries and study settings.

Pooled prevalence reached 37.86 percent, meaning well over one third of older adults in the included studies reported loneliness. Being married cut the odds substantially compared with being unmarried. Drinking alcohol raised the odds, and depressive symptoms more than tripled them. Variation between studies was extremely high, so the single pooled figure needs care. Even so, the review gives African policymakers a first continent-wide baseline for a neglected problem.
pmc-13483952:
Xiangyu Liu and others build a computer model that predicts, for each patient, which pre-surgery treatment is most likely to erase locally advanced rectal cancer completely. In 2026, the deep-learning plan joins pre-treatment multiparametric MRI scans with medical variables in a multi-site cohort, estimating the chance of disease complete response under several regimens. Current choices are usually population-based, risking too much or too little treatment.

The model performed strongly in testing and in a forward-looking test cohort, with rightness scores above 0.79 in both. It recommended stronger treatment for just over half of merged test patients and lighter treatment for about six percent, while keeping estimated response high. Doctors get probabilistic, patient-specific support for tuning treatment intensity rather than a single rule for everyone.
pmc-13484252:
Dotson and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the many roles of GRK2, a protein that regulates adrenaline-type receptors in the heart. GRK2 is best known for braking beta-adrenergic receptors, the heart's adrenaline sensors, after GPCR signals. The review covers recent work on GRK2's lesser-known jobs in specific cells and compartments.

Beyond receptor braking, GRK2 helps control metabolism, keeps organelles intact, and shapes signalling between cells, especially where immune and vessel cells interact. These noncanonical roles differ sharply by cell type and location. The authors argue the protein's treatment value depends on that context: blocking it everywhere may help one tissue and harm another. They highlight cardio-oncology, where cancer treatment strains the heart, as a field these insights could inform. The review proposes mapping GRK2's roles cell by cell before designing drugs against it.
pmc-13487252:
Gupta and colleagues coordinated a team of small robots that hold formations using sound, cameras, and Bluetooth chatter instead of expensive positioning gear. Their 2026 system runs on cheap ESP32 controllers, splitting attention between audio processing and video while keeping motors synchronized through a time-slotted radio protocol. Each robot senses neighbors directly, so no central computer steers the group.

The robots held line, wedge, and circle formations within about fifteen centimeters of error in the reported trials. Audio packets arrived successfully about 92 percent of the time while control loops ran above fifty cycles per second. Distributed sensing cut energy use by roughly a third, drawing about eight watts per robot against about twelve and a half for the centralized baseline. The formation survived sensor blockages lasting up to two seconds. Gupta targets monitoring and transport tasks.
pmc-13488152:
Sharareh Ebrahimi and co-authors test a multi-strain probiotic for chronic lung disease in a 2026 trial in Iran. The disease, known as COPD, narrows the airways and makes breathing hard over time. In this trial, 120 patients with mild to moderate disease joined for eight weeks. Half took a daily capsule with live helpful germs, and half took a dummy capsule. No one knew who got which until the end.

Lung tests, a standard symptom survey, blood markers, and quality of life scores all improved more in the probiotic group. Breathlessness eased, and one marker of swelling in the body fell. The gains beat those in the dummy group on most checks. The team sees the live germ mix as a helpful add-on, not a swap for standard care.
pmc-13488352:
Lurgio and colleagues measured in 2026 how levels of the illness-causing bacterium Vibrio parahaemolyticus rise and fall through the season in Maine oysters, as the Gulf of Maine warms fast. Eating raw oysters carrying this bacterium can cause stomach illness, and Maine saw its first linked outbreak recently, in 2023, prompting new state rules. The team sampled oysters monthly at three coastal sites.

The bacterium appeared at every site once water reached sixteen degrees. Both illness-linked gene markers rose with sea surface warmth, and one site's marker also tracked saltiness. Pathogenic strains showed up at all three sites, underlining the need to keep harvested oysters cold without breaks. Maine adopted statewide harvest and handling rules in 2024, and the authors offer these baseline numbers to guide harvesters and regulators as summers warm.
pmc-13489152:
Wong and colleagues report a 2026 case in which a balloon ruptured and became trapped during balloon pericardiotomy, a procedure that drains fluid from around the heart. The patient was a 58-year-old woman whose cancer had caused repeated fluid buildup. She had refused surgery, so the team had to free the balloon without opening her chest.

They snared the balloon's near end to secure it, but the far end stayed stuck because the balloon had not fully deflated. Under X-ray guidance, they inserted a needle to decompress the balloon, after which it came out through the skin. The authors describe the rescue as the first of its kind finished without surgery, and they outline snares and forceps as bailout tools.
pmc-13490352:
Fan and team used a surgical robot's readings to watch how cutting the anterior cruciate ligament and replacing the knee change leg alignment in real time. The band stabilizes twist, and a new knee removes it, but the immediate mechanical consequences are rarely quantified inside the operation. Their 2026 study recorded alignment and twist at several bend angles in 110 patients with bow-legged knee arthritis, before band removal, after it, and after the new joint.

Removing the band straightened the maximally extended knee slightly and measurably reduced its bow angle in the in-surgery data. Internal twist of the shin bone increased at bend angles of sixty degrees and above after the cut. The new joint corrected the bowed alignment successfully, yet did not fully restore the original twist pattern in these unloaded readings. Fan notes weight-bearing function may still differ from the passive picture.
pmc-13490752:
Voss and fellow researchers in Austria studied 142 young adults in 2026 to test how creative skill links to white matter, the wiring that joins brain areas. Each person took a drawing based test of figural creativity, meaning idea making shown in pictures. Brain scans then gauged the health of the wiring with two diffusion measures, QA and FA.

Stronger wiring went with higher creativity scores across wide tracts. The strongest links sat in paths that join cortex with deep brain and motor areas. They also sat in the corpus callosum, the bridge between the two brain halves. QA picked up these links more clearly than FA in the same scans. The results point to sense and movement tracts as core routes for creative thought, not mere support.
pmc-13491852:
Mazlum Dursun and six colleagues test in 2026 a new nerve block for pain after gallbladder removal through small incisions. The external oblique intercostal plane block numbs the upper abdominal wall where much of the soreness sits. Sixty-four adults having elective surgery for gallstones were randomized to receive the ultrasound-guided block or standard care, then tracked for a full day.

Pain scores were significantly lower in the block group at every measurement point across the twenty-four hours. Those patients also needed fewer additional painkillers and reported markedly higher satisfaction at the day mark. Heart and blood pressure measures during surgery were part of the recorded outcomes. The authors conclude that the block meaningfully improves comfort after this very common operation.
pmc-13492852:
Tardjibayeva and colleagues report a 2026 study of diet quality in Kazakhstan's kindergartens and schools, . The team surveyed 700 children and adolescents across regions in 2021 to 2023, collecting health and body measures plus food frequency data. They built a Diet Quality Index scored from zero to eighteen, covering meal regularity and key food groups.

The median score sat at about twelve and a half points, roughly seven tenths of the maximum, which the authors call satisfactory overall. But the balance was off: bread, bakery goods, and cereals carried the score, while vegetables, fruits, and nutrient-dense foods were eaten too little. Standard menus keep provision uniform across regions, yet composition needs work. The findings feed directly into the standards revision, pointing at produce gaps rather than meal timing.
pmc-13495252:
Viktoria Koenig, Julian Joestl, Yohannes Mekonen, and Hanano Yamada chart, in a 2026 study, a malaria comeback in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, using routine weekly surveillance data from 2018 to 2024. Reports had flagged renewed malaria across Ethiopia, yet fresh data from Tigray stayed scarce. The team compared weekly case rates against a baseline from 2018 to 2022.

Median weekly incidence in 2023 ran about two and a half times the baseline, and the worst week neared five times it. Rates stayed high through mid-2024. The burden clustered in a small set of districts rather than spreading evenly. The authors say Tigray mirrors the national resurgence and urge steady case and mosquito watching, including checks for an invasive mosquito species, so control teams can aim where the burden truly sits.
pmc-13499052:
Neil Manadan, Burak Celik, Isadora Small, and Shilpa Arora analyse in 2026 which emergency department visits by adults with lupus end in hospital admission. Lupus is an autoimmune disease that flares and settles, often sending patients to emergency care for infections or organ problems. Most prior work looked at outcomes after admission, leaving the front-door decision understudied, so the team used a large national emergency database for 2022.

They counted 376,776 lupus-related visits, of which just under two in five led to admission, a high share that signals heavy acute care needs. Severe infection, heart events such as heart attack and blood pressure emergencies, and kidney failure were the leading reasons, with some diagnoses raising admission odds very sharply. Older age raised admission likelihood, while income did not predict it after adjustment, a pattern the authors link to access gaps.
pmc-13500452:
Byeongho Lee, Jiman Heo, and Chang Han expose water striders to a farm insecticide and watch evolution-relevant traits shift. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, uses clothianidin at a dose too low to kill outright. The drug hits the insects during their final nymph stage. Adults are then followed for lifespan, weight, and activity.

Exposed striders die sooner and weigh about eight percent less. Spread between individuals widens sharply, especially in males. Hidden genetic variety may be surfacing under stress. Selection pressures differ between the sexes as well. Sexual dimorphism could bend under chronic low-dose exposure. Farm runoff reaches many pond insects like these.
pmc-13500652:
Subedi and co-authors build machine learning models to predict how much rubbish countries produce and what it contains. Their 2026 framework covers 217 countries, feeding a neural network and a classic regression with gross domestic product, population, literacy, urbanisation, and household size. The goal is a planning tool aligned with sustainable development targets, able to estimate waste where no measurement programme exists.

The neural network predicted total waste generation well, explaining the large majority of variation between countries and beating both the regression model and the existing global benchmark. Predicting composition proved far harder: the organic, plastic, and paper shares of waste resisted the same variables, with accuracy staying low in the reported scores. The authors blame unmeasured behaviour and regional habits. They caution that composition forecasts need local data before councils should trust them for facility design.
pmc-13501652:
Yuanyuan Chen leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 mouse and cell study of how chronic stress shrinks ovarian reserve. Mice put through chronic unpredictable stress developed the hormonal and tissue signs of diminished reserve. Their brain, blood, and ovary levels of BDNF, a growth factor from neuroscience, all fell. The team then manipulated the pathway: giving recombinant BDNF, blocking its receptor TrkB with ANA-12, and blocking the downstream switch CREB with another compound in cultured granulosa cells.

Added BDNF restored the ovarian index, tissue structure, and estrus cycle, lowered stress hormone levels, and raised pregnancy rates and embryo counts. It also suppressed pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death, in granulosa cells, cutting the NLRP3 inflammasome signals and the interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18 output. The receptor blocker produced the opposite pattern. The authors trace the protection to CREB activation downstream of BDNF and TrkB.
pmc-13503852:
Si Shi leads a team that built a force sensor out of living bacteria, in a 2026 paper. Usual soft sensors tear easily and give skewed readings when stretched. A sensor grown from cells could heal itself and keep working under strain.

The team rewired bacteria so their surfaces carry matching grip pairs, which lets the cells link into a broad net. Sealed in stretchy tubes, the net conducts charge and senses push and pull. Its range can be tuned, and it snaps back within tens of milliseconds after force stops. Stretching it to eight times its length raised resistance by only about a third. The design suits wearables and machines that must endure rough, shifting loads.
pmc-13504252:
Muhammad Shahid Mahmood leads a team building a blood test kit for Babesia infection in cattle, in a 2026 study. The tick-borne parasite causes heavy losses in meat and milk herds in Pakistan and beyond. Fast, cheap herd screening would help vets catch it early.

The kit uses a lab-made copy of a parasite surface protein as bait for antibodies in blood samples. The team checked it against panels of infected and clean samples, plus samples holding sister parasite species. Against a commercial kit on 200 suspect samples, the new test caught about 89 percent of true cases. Its clean-sample accuracy was lower, near 77 percent. The authors say the kit suits wide surveys and clinic screening, where low cost matters most.
pmc-13504752:
Malene Barfod O'Connell leads a team setting out the LiverCare trial protocol, a palliative care program for people with liver cirrhosis, in a 2026 paper. Once cirrhosis worsens, median survival drops from twelve years to two, and hospital visits surge. Yet comfort-focused care is rarely offered to this group.

The study runs in liver units at four Danish hospitals, without random assignment. Trained liver doctors and nurses hold open, exploratory talks with patients and their family caregivers, starting weeks after entry and then twice a year for up to three years. The main measure is hospital use against a past comparison group. Symptom load, quality of life, caregiver strain, and costs are also tracked. The team will judge both effect and how well the program fits daily care.
pmc-13507052:
Pengfei Zhu leads a 2026 team that built a transistor whose electrical polarity can be reset and stored, for flexible logic circuits. Their design stacks three oxide layers that trap charge, paired with layered crystal materials. Trapped charge flips the device between electron and hole flow in a balanced way.

Devices held more than six bits of states for over 1000 seconds and endured hundreds of thousands of cycles. Computer models traced switching to oxygen gaps in the stack. Teams wired the devices into gates that perform eight logic tasks and switch between combined forms. A memory search cell shrank sharply in area. Such parts could support compact computing inside memory.
pmc-13507152:
Sameia Zaman leads a 2026 team that measures kinetic inductance in atom-thin NbSe2, a layered superconductor that still works down to a single layer. Kinetic inductance comes from inertia of paired electrons and grows as films thin, which suits compact quantum devices. The team used microwave waveguides and methods borrowed from quantum circuit labs.

Inductance per square rose as layer count fell, reaching a peak value in the single-layer limit given in the study. Behavior crossed from clean to dirty regimes in the thinnest films, likely from surface scattering and band effects. Nonlinear response stayed modest across films. Such films could serve as small, nearly linear high-inductance parts for quantum detectors and circuits.
pmc-13507352:
Victor Suman, Anton Airinei, and Tamara Potlog synthesize, in 2026 work, assemblies of a sulfur-tagged zinc phthalocyanine dye hitched to silver nanoparticles, then probe how the pairing changes light behavior. Zinc phthalocyanines already serve as light-activated drugs that generate toxic oxygen in tumors. Silver particles concentrate light fields at their surface, which can amplify or drain a dye's glow.

Optical spectra confirmed the joined assemblies and showed size-dependent coupling strength. Depending on particle traits, dye emission was quenched or enhanced, bright-state lifetimes shortened, and dark triplet states lasted longer. Such tuning suits photodynamic therapy, where triplet states drive the therapeutic chemistry. Plasmon pairing offers a dial for photosensitizer design.
pmc-13507752:
Ayodeji Adedeji and seven co-authors pinpoint which part of a helper protein stops other proteins from clumping under heat stress, in 2026 work. The helper, called Grp94, lives in a cell compartment where many proteins are folded. It is known to help folding and also to block clumping, but the basis for the second job was unclear. The team tested it in lab dishes with two model proteins, citrate synthase and luciferase, using light scattering to track clumping.

Grp94 blocked clumping even without using its usual energy source, ATP, and without calcium. The active region turned out to be its front section, the N-terminal domain. A mutant form gripped faulty proteins more tightly and blocked clumping even better at low doses. That tight grip, though, slowed hand-off to the next helper system, a trade-off the authors map in detail.
pmc-13508252:
Parmar, Broders, Nlebedim, and Liu made magnet dust in twenty twenty-six from a mix of two rare earths, iron, and boron, with a wave-heat route. They grew oxide forms with micro-wave heat, then used a cut-and-spread step to form the alloy. The full range from no cerium to all cerium was made in that route.

Scans and heat tests backed the main magnet phase and its fine grain form. Hold strength of the dust ranged wide with the rare earth mix. Extra parts like copper and two kin rare earths raised that hold in the all-cerium dust. Phase shift steps were mapped in full.
pmc-13508352:
Majid Ghodraty leads a thirteen-author review linking gut microbes to the fading of heat-burning brown fat in obesity, in work published in 2026. Brown fat burns energy to make heat, which helps balance body weight. In obesity it often whitens, filling with fat, losing power units, and burning less. Gut microbe imbalance reshapes how the body handles food and signals, the review argues, and those shifts reach the brown fat. Microbe products, bacterial toxins that stir inflammation, and bile acid signals all feed into this cross-talk.

The pathways converge on nerve drive to the fat, power unit growth, and fat flow in and out. The review then weighs fixes aimed at the gut side: fiber and plant compounds, exercise, live or killed microbe supplements, and bile acid targeted drugs. The authors call for proof of cause and for microbe signatures doctors could actually act on.
pmc-13508452:
MohammadJavad Safaie Yazdi and five co-authors compare nerve stimulation through the skin with a standard drug for overactive bladder in women, in 2026 work. The drug class used often causes side effects that make women quit. The trial at a Mashhad hospital in 2023 enrolled 118 women meeting diagnostic rules. Half received stimulation of the tibial nerve near the ankle, in two half-hour sessions weekly for twelve weeks. The other half took a daily five-milligram drug tablet.

Both routes improved symptoms, leakage, and quality of life by clear margins. Stimulation edged ahead on symptom severity and won clearly on leakage reduction. Quality of life gains ended much the same in both groups. Side effects told the sharpest story: nearly nine in ten drug users reported some, while the stimulation group reported none. The authors present stimulation as a strong drug-free option for women who cannot tolerate standard tablets.
pmc-13509752:
Sara Palma Gullì, Rocco Morena, Francesca Serapide, and Alessandro Russo review what it means when intensive care patients carry highly resistant bacteria without yet being ill from them, in 2026 work. Carriage found on screening swabs can stay harmless, or it can mark the first step toward a fast-moving invasive infection. The review covers three resistant groups that trouble intensive care units worldwide.

Risk turns on the germ involved, where it sits, how long it stays, past antibiotic use, illness severity, tubes and lines in place, and how much resistant bacteria circulate in the unit. Gut carriage of one group often seeds later infection, and lung plus multi-site carriage of another flags the highest risk. The authors advise using carriage results to grade risk and guide prevention, not as an automatic trigger to start antibiotics.
pmc-13510052:
Takako Hishiki and eleven co-authors test three drugs, each switching on one member of a fat-control receptor family, in mice with diet-induced fatty liver, in 2026 work. The mouse model used a rich diet plus treated water to build liver fat within four weeks. The team then measured the detailed mix of triglycerides, the main storage fats, in liver tissue with a precise chemical method.

The diet raised total liver triglyceride signal about fivefold and shifted the mix, doubling one mid-size class while shrinking another. None of the three drugs changed the picture in the same way. The first left the total alone yet reshuffled several classes, the second barely moved the mix, and the third cut the total by nearly half while changing which fat types dominated. The authors say each receptor member leaves a distinct fingerprint on liver fat.
pmc-13510952:
Dicks and colleagues argue that bacteria show a basic form of sentience, meaning an awareness of their surroundings, in a 2026 theoretical paper on cell behavior. Their case rests on how particles move inside bacterial cytoplasm, the jelly-like interior of the cell. When metabolism speeds up, that interior shifts from a glass-like state toward a fluid one, and particles inside move in random and chaotic patterns rather than fixed paths.

According to the authors, cells sense these internal movements and answer by switching genes on or off and adjusting proteins after they are made. Surface receptors also monitor chemical changes inside and outside the cell. The paper further discusses liquid-liquid phase separation, where proteins gather into droplets, as a force driving internal turnover. Dicks stresses that any bacterial consciousness would differ greatly from human awareness, and the claim remains debated.
pmc-13511552:
Jingwen Huang, Chang Liu, Laurence S. Sperling, Arshed A. Quyyumi, and Yan V. Sun hunt for blood proteins that carry risk from autoimmune disease to major heart events, using UK Biobank data, in 2026 work. The cohort held more than four hundred thousand people followed for a median of about fourteen years, with autoimmune disease in roughly seven percent. Protein profiles were available for a large subgroup of about forty-four thousand.

Every autoimmune category studied went with higher rates of major heart events, including heart attack, stroke, and heart failure outcomes. Risk of cardiovascular death rose for most categories, though not for gut or nerve autoimmune groups. A high-dimensional pathway analysis flagged dozens of proteins as possible middlemen for the heart event link and a smaller set for death. The authors say these proteins may reveal how immune disease reaches the heart.
pmc-13512552:
Melloni Cook and Kristin Hamre introduce a special issue of the journal Genes, published in 2026. The issue covers genetics of neuropsychiatric disorders. These conditions affect the brain and behaviour. They often begin during development. They can be disabling. Cook and Hamre serve as editors. They explain that treatments remain limited. Treatments often fail. Finding genetic causes offers a route forward. It may bring earlier detection and new drug targets.

The collected studies span many conditions. They include infantile epileptic spasms. Sleep and mood problems are covered. Stress-related disorders, schizophrenia, and autism are included. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders appear too. The studies use human and animal models. One study used whole-exome sequencing. It found a mutation in the SPTBN1 gene in a patient with infantile spasms.
pmc-13514452:
Kılıçarslan and colleagues charted the presentation, complications, and vision outcomes of Fuchs' uveitis syndrome, a chronic eye inflammation usually affecting one eye. Their 2026 retrospective study covers sixty-one patients and sixty-four affected eyes in a Turkish referral population, all given eye examinations, vision measurement, pressure checks, and review.

Kılıçarslan found deposits on the cornea's inner surface in nine of ten eyes. Most often they showed the star-shaped pattern classic for the syndrome. Differing iris color between the eyes appeared in under half, and iris tissue debris in the gel of the eye in about two fifths. Cataract was the commonest complication, affecting about four fifths of eyes, the posterior subcapsular type. Vision barely changed between first and final visits. The authors note the classic picture holds in Türkiye, though iris signs appear less often, likely an ethnic variation.
pmc-13518752:
Irene Peregrin-Alvarez and seven colleagues review in 2026 whether anti-Müllerian hormone, a protein that slows egg follicle growth, could protect the ovary during chemotherapy. Cancer treatment often drains the resting follicle pool, causing infertility and early menopause with wider health effects. No approved medical shield against that damage exists today.

Drawing on lab, tissue, and gene therapy work, the review explains how the hormone signals through its receptor and keeps dormant follicles dormant. Peregrin-Alvarez and co-authors also look beyond chemotherapy to endometriosis, chronic inflammation, and natural aging. They separate proven findings from early hopes, then map what must happen before made-in-lab hormone therapy reaches first human trials.
pmc-13518852:
Braeden Charlton and a large team report a muscle physiology study, published in 2026. It asks whether muscle changes in long COVID and ME/CFS are simply the result of inactivity. ME/CFS is the chronic fatigue condition. The team compared patients' exercise responses and muscle biopsies with those of healthy volunteers. The volunteers had sixty days of strict bed rest. Matched healthy controls were also used.

Bed rest shrank muscle without changing fibre type. Both patient groups carried more fast, sugar-burning fibres. ME/CFS patients showed shrinkage specific to slow fibres. Exercise responses also differed between bed rest and the illnesses. Only bed rest reduced the muscle's energy-producing capacity. These diseases change muscle in their own way, this argues.
pmc-13518952:
Hao Wang and six colleagues examine in 2026 whether the glucose-to-potassium ratio in blood, a simple stress marker, warns of kidney injury after traumatic brain injury. Records for 2,388 patients came from the MIMIC-IV intensive care database, and 56.7 percent developed acute kidney injury during care.

A straight-line link between the ratio and kidney injury vanished after adjustments. Flexible curve modeling instead revealed a J-shaped pattern: risk stayed flat, then climbed steeply once the ratio passed about 30. A random forest model using many clinical variables predicted injury better than classic regression. Wang and co-authors read a high ratio as an early alarm of metabolic decompensation, not a direct cause, urging closer monitoring.
pmc-13520152:
Mahmoud AL Sayed, Ahmed Said, and Mohamed Meselhy review in a systematic way if diet can dial down brain inflammation in Alzheimer's disease, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Neuroinflammation helps drive both Alzheimer's and its precursor, mild cognitive impairment. Food-based steps are attractive here: cheap and low in risk, but the evidence was scattered.

Four major databases were searched for clinical trials and preclinical experiments. The steps that fit the bill were omega-3 fatty acids, ketogenic diets, B-vitamin supplementation, and vitamin-based approaches. Each was judged against neuroinflammatory outcomes in the data. The review weighs how consistent and strong the findings are, across human and animal evidence. A map of what calms brain inflammation guides trials and advice on diet.
pmc-13520252:
Tim Adair, Sergey Timonin, and Vladimir Canudas-Romo decompose in 2026 how Australia's life expectancy swung during the COVID-19 pandemic, using death records from 2017 to 2023 that list every contributing cause. Australia's strict restrictions produced an unusual trajectory among rich countries.

Over half of the 0.6-year life expectancy gain into 2020 came from a drop in deaths involving respiratory infections such as pneumonia, mostly at ages 80 and above. A small dip followed in 2021. Then 2022 brought a 0.7-year fall, driven by surging COVID-19 deaths once restrictions relaxed. Every capital city region echoed the pattern, with Melbourne hit hardest. Multi-cause data reveal how infection control rippled through other diseases.
pmc-13520352:
Konukbay and colleagues surveyed 290 neonatal intensive care nurses in Turkey about continuing breastfeeding while pregnant, and about tandem breastfeeding, nursing a newborn and an older child together. These nurses coach new mothers, so gaps in their knowledge pass to families. Their 2026 cross-sectional study used an online questionnaire covering the nurses' backgrounds alongside what they knew and believed about both practices.

Most nurses were supportive: over three quarters said breastfeeding during pregnancy should continue and mothers should be backed through it. The knowledge lagged the goodwill, since only a little over half knew the concept of tandem breastfeeding, though two thirds accepted that it can be practised after birth. Older, more educated, married nurses with children and longer intensive care experience scored more positively. The authors call for targeted in-service education so support for mothers rests on knowledge, not instinct.
pmc-13520452:
Chayada Chaiyabutr leads a 2026 survey of student views on mixing 3D skin lesion models with standard flat images in dermatology teaching. Skin diagnosis leans heavily on sight, while handling a model adds touch and shape cues that flat photos cannot give.

About nine in ten students preferred the combined approach at learning stations. Flat images scored slightly higher for diagnostic skill and clinical use, while models won praise for hands-on practice, touch skills and interactivity. Results are framed by the VARK model of learning preferences, covering visual, auditory, reading and hands-on styles. Teachers gain support for adding models as a complement, not a replacement.
pmc-13520552:
Diksha Manhas and ten co-authors published a study in 2026 on a saffron compound that may slow metastatic breast cancer. Tumors often overuse an enzyme that turns a common fat into growth signals. Blocking that enzyme could cut the signals, and the plant compound crocetin looked like a candidate blocker.

Computer models showed the compound fitting snugly into the enzyme's active site. In liver preparations it blocked the enzyme in a reversible way and cut formation of the growth signals. In mice it slowed the breakdown of a test drug and, in a breast cancer model, curbed tumor growth while lowering the enzyme in tumors. The work links a kitchen-spice compound to a clear cancer pathway.
pmc-13521552:
Sean Rockwell and colleagues present in 2026 a 59-year-old man whose hormone-excess disorder acromegaly surfaced only after a bicycle crash led to a brain scan. Slow facial, hand and metabolic changes had built for years, including wide tooth spacing, jaw growth, sleep apnoea, hypertension and new diabetes.

Blood tests confirmed excess growth hormone signals, while heart checks before pituitary surgery revealed multi-vessel coronary disease needing four stents. Blood thinners then delayed tumour removal by about seven months. Surgery in March 2025 cleared the tumour with rapid hormone normalisation, although bacterial sinus and meningeal infection complicated recovery. Hormone levels stayed normal at three months.
pmc-13521952:
Li and colleagues describe a hybrid bioelectrochemical system in 2026 that treats wastewater while recovering energy and nutrients from it. The design stacks treatment zones so carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus are each handled in sequence rather than wasted. Such systems aim to turn sewage plants from energy consumers into resource producers.

In their hierarchical process, the treated water's chemical oxygen demand met the Class III surface water standard. Nitrogen removal was complete across the anaerobic, anoxic, and aerobic zones, meaning stages without, with little, and with oxygen. Phosphorus was captured and reused to grow plants hydroponically. The system generated a power density of 0.43 watts per square meter from the waste stream, and its net carbon balance came out negative, at minus 0.413 kilograms of carbon dioxide per cubic meter treated, because recovery offset emissions.
pmc-13522352:
Schrotter and colleagues presented a 2026 model for simulating faulty heart rhythms on a personal computer in near real time. Detailed heart models, called cardiac digital twins, could tailor therapy to each patient, but full physics simulations are too slow for clinic use. Their lightweight model keeps the physics while cutting the computing cost.

The physics informed eikonal model reproduces electrical wave travel through heart tissue and matches clinical electrogram signals. Schrotter tested it against a gold standard model on complex rhythm cases, including a scar driven rapid heartbeat in a whole human heart model. Performance stayed close to real time while accuracy remained high. The authors see the model as core technology for calibrating digital twins in hospitals and industry.
pmc-13522652:
Jesus Serrano-Lomelin leads a 2026 cohort study of newborn health among Métis babies in Alberta, Canada. Composite indicators specific to Métis populations were lacking, so hospital records for nearly eight thousand singleton births to Métis mothers between 2006 and 2016 were analyzed. A standard indicator combining newborn complications and death was used to estimate rates and risk factors.

About one baby in ten experienced an adverse outcome, most often breathing conditions around birth or birth trauma. Death in the newborn period occurred at just under three per thousand live births. Risk rose with illness before or during pregnancy, assisted or surgical delivery, male sex, early birth, and congenital conditions. The authors argue for continued standardized surveillance to guide culturally responsive care improvements.
pmc-13523152:
Jacopo Costantino and colleagues describe an incidental diagnosis of heart amyloidosis during pacemaker implantation in a 2026 case report. An eighty-two-year-old patient fainted in the setting of atrial fibrillation with a slow heart response. Heart ultrasound showed mildly reduced pumping, thickened walls, and a small fluid collection around the heart, leading to a dual-chamber pacemaker using a newer pacing site.

During repositioning of the lead, a small piece of heart muscle stuck to the lead tip was unexpectedly retrieved and sent for analysis. Special staining revealed amyloid deposits, and further testing identified the transthyretin type. A bone scan supported the diagnosis, and targeted therapy was started. The authors highlight awareness among pacing specialists, who often meet conduction problems as an early sign of this disease.
pmc-13523252:
Xue Ming and colleagues model injury risk from carbon-ion radiotherapy for advanced lung cancer in a 2026 retrospective study. One hundred eighty-four patients with locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer received carbon-ion treatment at a high dose per session. Statistical models of normal tissue complication probability were built for inflammation and late injury of the food pipe and for late injury of the central airways.

Risk for several outcomes depended mainly on the highest-dose regions, while late food pipe injury called for limits on both maximum and mean dose. Thresholds derived from the models defined a low-risk group with very low observed injury rates. Combined dose measures in nomograms predicted injury with good accuracy. The authors propose specific maximum dose limits for the food pipe and airways to keep toxicity risk below five percent.
pmc-13523552:
Martin Gilar describes a method for preparing high-performance affinity chromatography columns directly inside the column hardware. Affinity columns capture a chosen target using an attached binding molecule, and preparing them is usually laborious. His 2026 paper builds the column around tiny nonporous polymer particles coated with streptavidin, a protein that grips biotin tags extremely tightly.

The particles were packed into a small steel column rated for high pressure. Biotin-tagged capture molecules were then injected repeatedly until the streptavidin was saturated, watched as a breakthrough signal on an ultraviolet detector. Binding capacity was measured for three ligands, from simple biotin to a tagged antibody. The finished columns quantified messenger RNA and insulin with defined sensitivity and linear ranges. Gilar presents the streptavidin column as a platform for quickly building custom affinity devices.
pmc-13524552:
Hayley M. Pearson and colleagues search, in a 2026 laboratory study, for the specific potassium channels that let bunyamwera virus escape from cell compartments during entry. Bunyamwera virus represents a family of insect-borne viruses that includes agents of serious animal and human disease. These viruses enter cells in sacs called endosomes and must fuse out of late endosomes, a step influenced by potassium levels.

The team screened a silencing library against 342 human ion channels and found nineteen potassium channels whose loss cut viral gene expression by over half, with at least seven acting at entry. Focused drug and genetic tests confirmed three channels controlling escape from late endosomes marked by CD63 and Rab7. The findings name concrete host targets that future drugs might block or repurpose against this virus family.
pmc-13525352:
Elsayed and co-authors published the first meta-analysis in 2026 of factors that predict death in adults with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a rare syndrome where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. Because single studies are small, doctors have lacked a clear picture of which patients face the highest risk. The team pooled results from cohort studies to find consistent warning signs.

The analysis combined eighteen cohorts covering 3,570 adults, and pooled mortality reached 49.5 percent across them, showing how deadly the syndrome is. Disease triggered by cancer carried the worst outlook, with malignancy-associated cases showing an odds ratio of 2.53 for death compared with other causes. Older age, very high ferritin levels, and raised lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme released from damaged cells, each independently predicted death as well. The authors say these markers can help clinicians spot high-risk patients early.
pmc-13525452:
Zaira Rehman and three colleagues published a short neuroscience report in two thousand twenty-six on the Arc gene across sleep and waking. Arc switches on during learning and is essential for lasting memory, much of which consolidates in sleep. Past reports conflicted on whether its baseline levels swing with the sleep-wake cycle.

Forty-four naive Fischer rats were sampled at four time points spanning sleep and wake periods. The density of Arc-marked cells in the hippocampus's dentate gyrus stayed remarkably stable throughout. The authors present the flat baseline as a reference point for resolving earlier contradictions. Future work can now test learning-driven changes against a known steady background.
pmc-13525652:
Qiwen Li and colleagues pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, whether oral frailty is associated with physical frailty in older adults. Oral frailty covers declining chewing, swallowing, and mouth function, while physical frailty reflects multisystem weakening that raises fall and disability risk. A quantitative link between the two had not been firmly established.

Fourteen observational studies, found across three databases through July 2025, entered the synthesis after dual independent screening. Older adults with oral frailty had over three times the odds of physical frailty compared with those without it. Subgroup work pointed to study design, age, region, population type, and assessment method as sources of variation, and sensitivity analysis left results stable. The authors propose early oral screening as a route to delay physical frailty.
pmc-13526052:
Hannah Torlot and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether glucose uptake on PET scans predicts death in non-specific interstitial pneumonitis, a pattern of lung inflammation and scarring with few prognostic markers. Ninety-six patients with team-confirmed diagnoses had baseline scans, and eighty-three completed full lung function testing.

Uptake was measured in diseased lung and in visually normal lung, and a ratio between them was calculated. Sixty-five patients died during long follow-up averaging about eighty-three months. Higher maximum uptake and higher background uptake each predicted mortality, while the ratio did not. One uptake measure stayed independent of the standard risk index in adjusted models, and adding scan data to that index improved survival separation. The authors see scan uptake as a way to refine risk groups.
pmc-13526252:
Khan and colleagues ran STROKESTOP III, a 2026 cluster-randomized trial in Swedish primary care comparing two ways of screening older adults for atrial fibrillation. That is an irregular heart rhythm that raises stroke risk. Sixteen centers in Region Värmland were assigned either to mail invitations to all residents aged 75 to 76, called systematic screening, or to invite patients opportunistically during ordinary visits.

Khan found that people offered screening during visits accepted far more often, with about three fifths of invited eligible patients taking part versus under half in the mailed arm. Yet the opportunistic arm reached less of the total population, because nearly half of attending patients were never assessed for eligibility. Its overall reach fell well below the systematic arm. Those recruited opportunistically also carried heavier cardiovascular risk, including more hypertension and diabetes. The authors recommend combining both strategies to pair wide reach with high uptake.
pmc-13527052:
Md Omar Faruk, Md Abdul Awal, and Kamal Uddin Ahmed Chowdhury validate a Bangla language scale for suicidal thinking in a high risk district of Bangladesh, in work from twenty twenty-six. Jhenaidah district posts suicide rates above national and global averages. No tested local measure of suicidal ideation existed there.

Three hundred residents from six sub districts took the new scale plus well being and symptom measures. Analysis supported a single factor behind the items, explaining over half the score variation. Repeat scores stayed highly stable, and internal consistency and validity checks passed. The authors judge the scale fit for use in the district. They expect it to anchor future suicide research there.
pmc-13527552:
Giovanna Pagani Paccola and colleagues compare, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, tirzepatide against semaglutide for weight loss in adults who are overweight or obese. They restrict the pool to direct head-to-head studies. Both drugs are potent, yet comparative trials were few and earlier syntheses leaned on indirect comparisons.

Ten studies with 41,381 participants and at least twenty-four weeks of follow-up were pooled. Tirzepatide produced greater percentage and absolute weight loss, higher odds of reaching ten, fifteen, and twenty percent loss thresholds, and a larger drop in hemoglobin A1c, a blood sugar marker. Stopping for side effects did not differ, and gut events were similar, while serious side effects occurred more often with tirzepatide. Subgroup checks by design and diabetes status agreed.
pmc-13527952:
Jenna Pride, Geoff Shaw, Marilyn B. Renfree, and Trent A. C. Newman report a 2026 genetics study of MLH1, a DNA repair gene, in marsupials. In koalas and brushtail possums this gene is imprinted, meaning only the copy from one parent is switched on. The team checked the tammar wallaby and searched other marsupial genomes for extra copies.

In wallaby young the gene was marked on the mother's copy and active from the father's, matching the imprinted pattern. The researchers also found retrocopies, extra versions of the gene pasted back into the genome without their usual segments, in wallabies, the bilby, and the marsupial mole. Some retrocopies were switched on and could build a normal-shaped protein, possibly backing up the silenced copy.
pmc-13528052:
Mariana Gonçalves and fourteen colleagues test a gene therapy idea for mucolipidosis type II in a 2026 study. The disease blocks an enzyme that tags proteins for the cell's recycling centers. A common faulty variant sits in the gene GNPTAB. The team tried antisense molecules that make cells skip the faulty section when building the enzyme's message.

In patient skin cells the treatment did nudge enzyme activity up a little. A key marker of disease stayed high, though. Follow-up work in engineered cells explained why. The skipped-section protein formed its first piece but never matured into the working subunit. The skipped section is clearly essential for the enzyme to function. The authors conclude this skipping strategy cannot rescue the enzyme. They say such checks are vital before patient trials.
pmc-13528152:
Ryuhei Sakata and four colleagues describe tricky lung surgery beside a rare vein variant in a 2026 case report. A man in his seventies had a 4.2-centimeter tumor in his left upper lung lobe. A nearby lymph node held cancer too. Scans showed his left brachiocephalic vein ran under the aortic arch, crossing the window where surgeons must work. That path raises the risk of vessel or nerve injury.

The team used keyhole surgery to remove the lobe and clear the node stations. Finding the vagus nerve early let them trace its branch safely. The planned cuts finished with no nerve or vessel harm. A key ligament could not be found, hinting the vein passed behind it. The authors credit three habits: spot the variant on 3D scans first, find nerves early, and free the artery with care.
pmc-13529252:
Leyla Abueid and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-six, whether a modified mitochondrial peptide protects rat kidneys from ischemia-reperfusion injury. That injury follows restored blood flow after a cutoff, and can cause acute kidney failure. The peptide, S14G-humanin, is known for anti-death and anti-inflammatory effects. Forty-eight male rats were split into four groups: sham surgery, injury alone, peptide with sham, and peptide with injury. In injury groups, the kidney artery was clamped for forty-five minutes, then released for a day. The peptide was given minutes before reperfusion.

Injury raised kidney stress markers and cut antioxidant defenses. The peptide restored glutathione and a key enzyme, and lowered two damage markers. It also raised cell energy and mitochondrial function, though two kidney function markers were unchanged.
pmc-13529852:
Marta Plichta and Nanette Stroebele-Benschop study orthorexia risk in Polish students in a 2026 paper. Orthorexia is an unhealthy fixation on eating purely. The survey covered 261 high school and university students from 2022 to 2025. It scored eating fixation, felt social support, body esteem, and diet quality. Groups were split by sex, weight class, and study field.

Women showed higher fixation risk than men. Nutrition students outscored other majors clearly. Body weight itself showed no link with risk. Low support from friends tied with higher risk. So did low esteem about one's weight. Oddly, prouder body attribution and cleaner diets also tied with higher risk. That mix fits a drive for perfect eating. The authors want eating psychology inside school health teaching. Friend support is a lever they highlight.
pmc-13530052:
Matthew J Yan and colleagues describe a 2026 narrative medicine program built to ease mental health stigma in Asian American, Pacific Islander, and Native Hawaiian communities. Silence around distress, the model minority myth, and barriers to care keep many people from seeking help. Their nonprofit program answers with storytelling and reflective writing.

Participants complete the open prompt by choosing a meaningful word that starts with the letter A and reflects their own lived experience. A Los Angeles workshop drew more than 50 teenagers across several community centers. Observers noted freer expression, less shame, and a stronger sense of belonging.
pmc-13530252:
Guillermo Flores leads a large 2026 team hunting genes that drive invasion at the edge of mouth cancers. Cells at the tumor front adopt a half-changed state that resists treatment and spreads, yet its controllers stayed mostly unknown. A lab model holding both steady cell states enabled a genome-wide knockout screen for invasion.

Seventeen invasion modulators surfaced, most never linked to cancer before, clustering around cell skeleton, adhesion, and gene-control themes. One protein stood out as a central driver of change, invasion, and drug resistance. The screen signature matched the front of real human tumors closely.
pmc-13530752:
Fury and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 203, a strength study probing why breaking balls might endanger the elbow ligament. The pitchers at risk are those whose natural delivery leans toward pronation, the inward forearm rotation of a fastball. The flexor-pronator muscles shield that ligament, but their strength may depend on forearm position.

Twenty-eight college and professional pitchers at one off-season facility squeezed a testing device in two forearm positions. Pronated mimicked a fastball, supinated a breaking ball, while they stood in a throwing posture. Overall, fingertip flexion strength ran lower in supination. The deficit concentrated in pronator-biased pitchers, whose strength dropped clearly in the supinated position, while naturally supinating pitchers showed no gap. Injury history made no difference. The authors propose the supination weakness as a mechanism raising ligament risk when pronator types learn breaking pitches.
pmc-13531052:
Rajesh Vijayvergiya and colleagues recount a 2026 emergency during a balloon procedure to open a tight heart valve in a pregnant patient. The 33-year-old woman, at 31 weeks, had critical rheumatic narrowing of the mitral valve. Right after the valve procedure she collapsed with a heart attack pattern and complete heart block.

Urgent imaging found a clot blocking the right coronary artery with no flow. Mechanical clot removal restored full flow without placing a stent, sparing long dual blood-thinner therapy. She later delivered vaginally at 36 weeks, and mother and baby both did well.
pmc-13531752:
Patreeya Kitcharoen and co-authors interview Bangkok cannabis business operators in 2026 about surviving Thailand policy whiplash. The country decriminalized cannabis in 2022, then swung back toward medical-only rules. Thirteen owners, growers, and advocates shared experiences gathered during 2024 and 2025.

Five themes emerged: legal uncertainty, uneven enforcement, market splits, survival tactics, and public health roles. Tourists formed about 60 percent of the market, while local buyers mostly sought therapy. Small Thai operators bore the heaviest burden from missing national law, and many quietly taught customers safe use themselves, filling a gap left by absent public guidance.
pmc-13531852:
Varun Pal and colleagues survey in 2026 how rural women in Uttar Pradesh, India, actually use mobile phones for health. Five villages under a rural training center supplied 374 women for structured interviews on ownership, health use, trust, and barriers. Ownership looked fairly wide at first glance.

Just over half owned a smartphone, while about a third borrowed devices. Over half never used a phone for health at all, and only a tiny share used one regularly. Schooling strongly predicted health use, with unschooled women far behind graduates. Voice calls were preferred, and simple lack of know-how topped the barrier list.
pmc-13531952:
Syed Gohar Hussain Shah and colleagues interview in 2026 Pakistani health students about unpaid clinical placements. Twenty-two students from dentistry, nursing, and allied health programs in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa described their placement experience in Urdu interviews. Placements build skill and identity, yet unpaid rounds strain students daily.

Five themes emerged: daily cost struggles, mental strain, thin guidance, heavy learning settings, and identity growth through exposure. Unmet basic needs like money and safety blocked deeper learning, matching a classic needs hierarchy reading. Clinical exposure still motivated many toward their chosen careers despite the daily hardship.
pmc-13534152:
Jianhua Li and colleagues report in 2026 a new gene change behind a form of inherited diabetes in a Chinese family. The form, called MODY, starts young and runs in families, yet few cases trace to the NEUROD1 gene. Full gene scanning of patients with suspected MODY found a candidate change, confirmed across relatives.

The change swaps one building block in the protein and reshapes its local structure. Lab tests showed the altered protein drove insulin gene activity less well than the normal form. Readers gain a new cause to test for and a hint that GLP-1 drugs may suit such patients.
pmc-13534552:
Ali Mouseli and colleagues assess in 2026 quality of life in patients with psoriasis in southern Iran who qualify for biologic therapy. The chronic skin disease can weigh heavily on daily life, yet real-world data in lower-resource settings are thin. Two standard questionnaires measured general health and skin-specific life quality.

Average scores showed poor quality of life in this group. Pain and discomfort plus anxiety and low mood were the most common problems reported. Worse scores tied to greater disease severity, low schooling, lack of extra insurance, and shorter disease duration, pointing to coverage and literacy reforms.
pmc-13535852:
Ahmed Ehab and six co-authors report two cases of a rare tumor growing in the central airways, one in an adult and one in a child. Their report, with a review of diagnosis and treatment, was published in twenty twenty-six. These tumors, called inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors, sit between harmless and cancerous.

They most often arise in the lung, and airway growth is very rare. Both patients had bad airway blockage, with breathlessness and noisy breathing. Scans, a camera look inside the airways, and tissue tests made the diagnosis. Checking a gene marker called ALK matters, above all in the young, since targeted drugs can treat tumors carrying it. Full surgery is the standard cure, but both cases here were cleared through the airway scope. The report shows scope removal can work for well-chosen patients.
pmc-13536552:
Tian Lei and colleagues study in 2026 whether platelet-rich plasma injections speed recovery after repair of traumatic meniscus tears in the knee. The meniscus cushions the joint, and faster healing could return athletes sooner. Records covered 96 patients treated between January 2023 and August 2024, split evenly between plasma-added and surgery-only care.

At six months the plasma group showed clearly better knee scores, activity levels, pain, and scan healing, with gaps beyond meaningful thresholds. By twelve months most gaps shrank below those thresholds, though return to sport stayed better. Patients with bone bruising seemed to gain most.
pmc-13536752:
Zan Huang leads a 2026 meta-analysis of whether short activity breaks during long sitting help thinking skills. Trials randomly assigned people to keep sitting or to break sitting with brief movement, then tested executive function, which covers working memory, control, and flexible thinking. The synthesis pooled 22 crossover trials with 418 participants and 123 measured effects, with checks for bias and evidence quality.

Activity breaks gave a small gain in executive function overall, clearest for working memory and for speed of response rather than accuracy. Light activity helped, as did walking, while moderate activity showed no clear gain in the pooled checks. Breaks every hour and short breaks of a few minutes looked promising. The authors rate certainty as low and call for stronger trials.
pmc-13536852:
Lena Merten and co-authors combine two X-ray methods to map seed structure across scales, in this 2026 paper. Seeds feed people and industry, and their inner layout shifts with species, breeding, sprouting, and storage. Reading that layout means spanning scales from molecules to cells.

On yellow pea seeds the team paired scanning X-ray scattering, which senses fine structure, with fluorescence, which maps elements. Machine learning then carved the seed into distinct regions without preset models. The fit-free workflow lets samples be compared fairly. The approach promises a fuller picture of how seed architecture is organized and how processing changes it.
pmc-13537452:
Čerlinskaitė-Bajorė and colleagues used clustering to carve emergency patients with acute breathlessness into subtypes that cut across usual diagnoses. Their 2026 study reuses two prospective European cohorts with more than three thousand patients in all. Breathlessness has many causes and the categories predict outcomes poorly, so the team clustered patients on nine admission readings and built a rule tree to reproduce the grouping.

Čerlinskaitė-Bajorė found four subtypes, labeled non-inflammatory, tachycardic, anaemic, and hypoxemic, with inflammation and heart-related blood markers rising stepwise from the first to the last. Belonging to a subtype predicted ninety-day death even with risk factors accounted for. The hypoxemic group faced roughly four to five times the risk of the baseline group in the two cohorts. Adding subtype to a risk model improved its accuracy in both cohorts, backing cluster-based triage for tailored emergency care of breathless patients.
pmc-13538352:
Aleksandra Pięta and co-authors test whether a Paleo diet changes resting energy burn in professional handball players in a 2026 feeding study. Resting metabolic rate guides fueling plans, yet diet effects in elite athletes stay under-studied. Twenty-five players split into a Paleo group of fourteen and a standard diet group of eleven for eight weeks at matched energy intake. pmc-13538652:

pmc-13538952:

pmc-13539952:

pmc-13540952:

pmc-13548252:

pmc-13548552:

pmc-13551852:

pmc-13554252:

pmc-13558052:

pmc-13560652:
