pmc-13563152:
Losing three-quarters of one's wealth late in life scars the mind, in rich lands and poor alike. Ke Peng, Minzhi Xu, Yun Liu, and Yanhong Gong tracked near twenty-four thousand folk over fifty in 2026 across three long studies, in China, the United States, and Mexico. A wealth crash meant a fall of at least three-quarters between the first two survey waves. The team matched the crash to later mood, life joy, and self-rated health.

Folk who crashed showed more low mood and less life joy in all three lands. Self-rated health fell in China and the United States, less clearly in Mexico. In China and Mexico the scar held steady over the years; in the United States it shifted with time. The team urge states to shore up folk hit by such falls.
pmc-13563752:
Kazuma Shinno and seven colleagues give the first nationwide picture of orthostatic dysregulation in Japan, a circulation disorder of the autonomic nerves. It mainly strikes children and often keeps them out of school. Care grew from a psychosomatic tradition, yet real-world practice was never mapped at scale. Their 2026 study drew on a national hospital database and found 7,213 patients first diagnosed between 2016 and 2023, aged six to eighteen. The median age was thirteen, and 55.6 percent were girls.

Mental and behavioural conditions formed the biggest comorbidity group, at 23.6 percent, with sleep disorders at 10.2 percent and school non-attendance at 9.3 percent. Drugs went to 44.0 percent of patients, most often midodrine, which made up 78.3 percent of prescriptions. Blood tests were the commonest procedure. Children given sleep medicines carried heavier loads of developmental disorders and depression. The authors call for care plans fitted to this varied population rather than a single template.
pmc-13563852:
Abdelrahman Saeed and colleagues compared two kinds of replacement aortic valve in people with narrowed aortic valves: stented valves, mounted on a frame, and stentless valves, which promise smoother blood flow. Pooling evidence was overdue, since the choice affects survival, complications, and heart function. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis screened 1,385 records and combined 20 studies covering 3,940 participants.

Death rates, early and long-term, and most complications looked similar for both valve types, as did measures of heart function. One clear difference emerged: patients with stentless valves needed pacemakers significantly more often. The authors conclude that neither valve wins overall, so the choice should weigh that pacemaker risk against any hoped-for flow advantage in each patient.
pmc-13564452:
Mohammadnezamian and eight co-authors tracked immune recovery in HIV care for this study from twenty twenty-six. CD4 cell counts gauge how well treatment is working. The team reviewed records from a counseling center in Kermanshah, Iran, spanning twenty twelve to twenty twenty-three. Complete records existed for seven hundred twenty-eight patients.

Average CD4 counts rose from about three hundred thirty-six at diagnosis to about five hundred twenty-six on treatment. Longer time on therapy linked strongly to better recovery. Higher schooling and older age also helped, as did sexual rather than other transmission routes. Longer infection before care linked to weaker recovery. The authors urge closer support for patients at risk of poor immune rebound.
pmc-13566952:
Ligia Dominguez and seven co-authors review how weight loss surgery affects nutrition and muscle, in this 2026 overview. Bariatric surgery is the strongest treatment for severe obesity, with lasting weight loss and metabolic gains. The same operations, though, shrink protein intake, drain key nutrients, change hormone signals, and unload the muscles, all of which can waste muscle mass.

Muscle loss after surgery is common and rising, and it can coexist with remaining obesity, a mix called sarcopenic obesity. Oddly, strength and metabolic health often improve anyway, which complicates the picture. The authors argue for team based care: careful nutrition planning plus structured exercise to protect muscle. They also call for shared diagnostic standards and targeted prevention research, since long term outcomes hinge on keeping muscle while fat falls.
pmc-13567052:
Haijuan Mei and colleagues test where a titanium nitride layer belongs inside transparent conductive films. Their materials study from twenty twenty-six stacks zinc oxide and silver layers. Such multilayers conduct electricity while passing light. Interface layers can protect or ruin that balance.

Four stacking orders were sputtered onto glass slides. All films kept the same crystal orientation for zinc oxide. Nitride above the silver preserved its crystal feature best. That order raised light transmission and lowered resistance together. Nitride below the silver wrecked both properties instead. A standard figure of merit confirmed the ranking. Solar cells and screens both use such transparent electrodes.
pmc-13567552:
Sun Liya, Lang Zhongmin, and Yu Ying coat copper foam with silica nanofibers to improve boiling in this 2026 paper. Pool boiling moves heat from a hot surface into a liquid. Copper foam already offers many bubble sites. A superhydrophobic fiber layer should lower the barrier to bubble birth and add stable vapor sites.

Electrospinning laid uniform fibers firmly across the foam skeleton. The coated foam kept an open, linked pore structure. Boiling tests showed lower wall overheating and a higher critical heat flux. A fiber loading of 1.8 milligrams gave the best overall performance. Computer fluid simulations matched the measured behavior closely. Better boiling surfaces serve cooling for power electronics and energy systems.
pmc-13568752:
Sunil Kumar and co-authors review AI tools for risk prediction in stable angina in a 2026 paper. Stable angina raises the risk of heart attack, stroke, and death, so sorting patients by risk guides prevention. Older scores rest on straight-line, population-wide assumptions.

Following standard review rules, the team screened 1,250 articles and kept five studies. The models drew on health records, patient questionnaires, and artery imaging measures. Machine and deep learning methods were both represented. The review weighs how well AI can flag coming cardiovascular events in this group and where the evidence stays thin.
pmc-13569452:
Tatiana Barichello and colleagues review, in a 2026 expert article, how infections treated in hospital may feed the brain changes of Alzheimer's disease. Large population studies, brain tissue work, and animal experiments are combined to trace how body-wide and brain infections stir immune alarms that damage the blood-brain barrier and inflame brain tissue.

Activated immune sensors can release particles that seed clumping of amyloid and tau, the hallmark proteins of the disease, while one infection-linked protein boosts the enzyme that makes amyloid. The chain positions infection as an upstream trigger rather than a bystander. Researchers get a mechanistic map for testing whether preventing or treating infections can slow dementia.
pmc-13570252:
Pavel Nefediev, Sergei Golovatch, and Julia Nefedieva described a new millipede genus and species from the Altai Mountains of northeastern Kazakhstan in twenty twenty-six. The animal, named Triramidesmus kazakhstanus, belongs to the family Polydesmidae. It shows a mix of traits not seen before in its whole order.

Its side flanges are notched, its male mating limbs branch three ways, and it carries a distinct inner chamber linked to mating. Most striking, the adult female has almost lost her second pair of legs. The authors suggest this loss eases mating. In females that have already mated, the mating opening is blocked by flattened parts of that leg pair, which hints at rivalry over mates. The paper gives a map and rich images from light and electron microscopes.
pmc-13570352:
Yume Okada and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, skeletons of four Japanese indigenous chicken breeds at seven weeks and as adults. They look for inherited shape differences using specimens and CT scans. The breeds sit on separate family branches, making them promising models for the genetics of body form.

One breed was clearly heavier and longer, while the short-legged Chabo showed a distinctively short neck relative to its body. Birds with eight ribs instead of the usual seven appeared in every breed, common in two of them. Vertebral counts mark this as a new homeotic change, where one body segment takes another's identity. The finding adds a rare within-species example for developmental genetics.
pmc-13570452:
Nikki Adriaens and co-authors check how often three sexually spread bacteria actually cause pelvic inflammatory disease in the Netherlands, in a 2026 study. The disease is a painful infection of the upper genital tract that can scar fertility, and it can also form an abscess on the ovary. Textbooks blame chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and a newer suspect, Mycoplasma genitalium. Dutch doctors wanted fresh numbers from their own clinics.

The study followed women aged eighteen and older diagnosed with the disease or abscess at three hospitals and one sexual health center between 2021 and 2023. Swabs, blood inflammation markers, exams, and symptom diaries were collected at the start and during follow-up. Standard antibiotics were given per national guidance. The authors tracked both clinical recovery and whether the bacteria cleared, testing how much blame each germ truly carries.
pmc-13572352:
Jian Lin and Xiaobin Cheng investigate, in a 2026 study, how PARK2 may restrain colorectal cancer by tagging a partner protein for disposal and thereby quieting the powerful growth driver c-Myc. PARK2 is a gene better known from early-onset Parkinson's disease. Directly blocking c-Myc has proved hard, so indirect brakes matter.

Colorectal cancer worsens sharply once advanced, and c-Myc is abnormally active in most sporadic cases, driving growth and metabolic rewiring after tumor suppressors fail. PARK2 deletions and lowered expression appear in this cancer, and losing even one copy can speed intestinal tumors in models. The study pursues the disposal route as a way to rein in a driver that drugs cannot easily touch.
pmc-13572852:
Juho Laaksonen and five co-authors pool studies of injuries in alpine skiing and snowboarding in a 2026 review. Knowing how often injuries occur, and where on the body, helps resorts and clinicians plan prevention and care. The team searched four databases in early 2025 and combined results with a statistical model.

Eighty two studies were included. At the amateur level, nearly two injuries occurred per thousand skier days, with fractures and sprains most common and falls the leading cause. Limb injuries dominated at all levels, while trunk injuries were also frequent among professionals. Rates varied a lot between studies and sports. The authors provide pooled figures to guide safety work.
pmc-13573352:
Hongyu Lin, with four colleagues, presents a 2026 pooled review of a blood ratio and outcomes after acute ischemic stroke. The ratio sets neutrophils, a white cell tied to swelling, against HDL, the helpful cholesterol form. It thus blends two forces in stroke harm, yet studies of its worth were few and mixed.

Searches of three databases to September 2025 found five studies with 4,138 patients in all. Higher ratios went with worse outcomes overall, but the studies varied so much that the pooled figure is shaky. The link ran stronger in patients who got clot-clearing therapy and at three-month checks. It vanished with standard care and at one month. One study on death found no clear link. The authors rate the ratio a possible flag, in need of firmer trials.
pmc-13574552:
Kocyigit, Mukhamediyarov, Qumar, Fedorchenko, and Zimba analyse retracted social media studies in twenty twenty-six. Social media research has grown fast, and so have retractions. Retractions signal problems with ethics or reliability. The team searched the Scopus database for retracted papers tagged with social media.

They found one hundred forty-one retracted papers through twenty twenty-five. Retraction counts rose significantly over the period, especially in the twenty twenties. Most came from Asia, mainly China and India. The top reason was investigation by the journal or publisher. Unreliable results and referencing problems followed. The authors urge stronger integrity checks and editorial oversight. Transparency, they argue, would improve trust in the field.
pmc-13575152:
Li and colleagues proposed a hybrid intelligence framework in 2026 for managing construction project risk by joining building information modeling, the shared digital model of a project, with predictive analytics. Construction work entangles cost, schedule, resources, and structure, and traditional risk handling leans on expert judgment and periodic checks. The team fused project records, reports, and model data into a single dataset of 1,300 project cases, balancing its risk classes before training.

The framework stacks four engines: a table-learning network, a probabilistic dependency model, a sequence predictor with attention to timing. Monte Carlo simulation for uncertainty, feeding a hybrid optimizer that trades off cost, duration, and risk. Experiments reached accuracy just under 99 percent with near-perfect ranking scores. Dashboards built on the building model present the results visually. The authors offer the system as decision support for earlier, calmer risk control on complex builds.
pmc-13575252:
Li He and three colleagues examine how green finance and new technology together shape growth in China, in a 2026 economics study. Green finance channels money into cleaner projects through tools such as green bonds and green credit. The question was whether pairing that money flow with innovation pays off more than either alone.

The team used data from 30 provinces covering 2013 to 2023, with models that strip out fixed provincial traits and shared yearly shocks. Green finance was scored from bond and credit data, while innovation was tracked through research spending. The two reinforced each other: innovation raised the growth payoff from deeper green finance. The effect ran strongest in the east and weakest in the west. Results held under several methods that guard against reverse causation.
pmc-13575352:
Won Nyeong Kim and co-authors published this crop gene editing study in 2026. Soybean oil quality depends on its fatty acid mix: oleic acid keeps well, while saturated fats are less desired. The team used CRISPR editing to disable several related genes at once. They targeted two gene families, FAD2 and FATB, which push oils toward saturated and polyunsaturated forms. Soybean's duplicated genome meant several near-identical copies had to be hit.

Editing one main gene alone raised oleic acid to about eighty-three percent. Adding edits in two more FAD2 copies and one FATB gene pushed oleic acid past ninety percent. Saturated fat fell by more than forty percent against normal plants. The edited seeds carried more total fat per seed. Gene activity checks pointed to slower fat breakdown rather than faster production. The authors define the edit combinations needed for ultra-high-oleic, low-saturate soybean.
pmc-13575852:
Anette Lohmander, Inghild Riis Kjelsvik, and Christina Persson follow speech growth in Swedish children born with a cleft lip and palate on one side, in two thousand twenty-six. Long-term records of consonant skill in such children are sparse. Their data cover babbling in infancy and speech at ages three, five, and ten.

Thirty-two children with complete records took part, treated with three unlike surgical plans for closing the palate. Average consonant accuracy rose with age but stayed below that of peers at every check. The type of surgery made little group difference, apart from more nose-related symptoms at age three when the hard palate was still open. Making oral stop sounds in infancy predicted later accuracy.
pmc-13575952:
Dilmurod Murodullayev and a large team review in 2026 the chemistry of fungi that live inside plants. These endophytic fungi act like tiny factories, making compounds the plant does not. The review gathers reports from 118 studies published in 2024 and 2025.

Those studies describe 242 compounds not reported before, spanning peptides, alkaloids, polyketides, and more. The fungi Aspergillus and Penicillium were the most productive sources. Many of the new compounds fought inflammation, bacteria, fungi, or algae, or killed cells in lab tests. The authors argue this rich, varied output makes the fungi a strong hunting ground for future drug leads.
pmc-13576352:
Merel E Velu leads a 2026 randomised trial of two trauma therapies for refugee children in the Netherlands. Refugee minors face high rates of post-traumatic stress from war, flight, and ongoing strain. The trial compared EMDR, a therapy using guided eye movements, with KIDNET, a child version of narrative exposure therapy, against a waiting list.

Ninety-six children aged 8 to 18 with full or partial PTSD took part, split evenly across the three arms. Both therapies cut clinician-rated symptom severity clearly against the waiting list after eight weekly sessions. Gains showed in child reports too, though not in caregiver reports. EMDR edged KIDNET on the main clinician measure and needed fewer sessions on average. Dropout ran higher for EMDR at 20.8 percent against 10.9 percent. The authors judge both treatments effective options.
pmc-13576652:
Andreas Fønss Møller and Jesper Grud Skat Madsen present DeepDive, a 2026 deep learning framework for untangling which factors shape single-cell chromatin data. Chromatin accessibility maps show which gene switches are open in each cell. In human cohorts, factors such as obesity and diabetes travel together, so standard tools cannot cleanly separate their effects.

DeepDive rebuilds the accessibility maps while splitting variation into named and hidden sources. It beat leading methods even when some factor labels were missing, and recovered true signals from heavily tangled test data. The split representation also allows what-if experiments: swapping one factor while holding the rest fixed. Applied to pancreatic islet cells, it ranked factors tied to a diabetes-linked beta cell subtype and named candidate gene regulators. The authors pitch it for hard cohort questions.
pmc-13578052:
Anju Maan Ara and co-authors hunt genes that make wheat prone to a leaf blotch disease in a 2026 study. The fungus behind septoria nodorum blotch kills leaf tissue and feeds on the dead cells. It wins when wheat carries genes that sense its toxins and react by dying. The team screened a panel of six hundred nineteen United States hard winter wheat lines.

They challenged the lines with five fungus strains and five toxins, and they read DNA markers across the genome. Between two fifths and two thirds of lines were prone to each strain. Tests for three known sensitivity genes predicted toxin response well. A genome scan confirmed known genes and found new spots, one of which tracked with response to all five strains. The authors built DNA tests to help breeders select against these weak points.
pmc-13578252:
Zhiyuan Wang and colleagues test a targeted drug in a 2026 mouse study of asthma, a lung disease where swollen airways narrow over time. House dust mite exposure drove the model, which showed thick airway muscle, extra mucus, and high levels of immune signals tied to allergy. The drug blocks NLRP3, a protein hub that switches on inflammation.

Treated mice showed calmer airways, less muscle growth, and fewer mucus cells than untreated ones, while the control fluid alone changed nothing. Muscle growth fell alongside weaker signals on a chain running from the IL-6 signal through two switch proteins. The authors say immune cells may share in the gain, and that more work must test whether blocking this hub can slow airway change in children.
pmc-13578552:
Chunyan Deng and colleagues use heart scans to ask whether years lived with HIV leave marks on the heart muscle, in a 2026 study. Modern drug therapy has turned HIV into a long term condition, yet heart injury stays a worry. Eighty three adults with HIV, split into under and over five years of infection, were compared with thirty four matched adults without the virus.

Both HIV groups showed more water held in the heart wall and slower tissue signals than the control group, signs of early change. The longer infection group stood out further, with more scar like tissue, a thicker wall relative to chamber size, and weaker squeeze motion. Scan based models sorted early infection and long infection well. The authors offer the scan markers as a way to catch heart change early.
pmc-13578752:
Marwa Al Hassan and colleagues build a kidney filter on a chip and ask how the support membrane shapes the cells, in a 2026 study. The kidney's filter pairs footed podocyte cells with vessel lining cells across a thin shared wall. Recreating that wall in a dish has stalled kidney research, so the team grew both cell types on facing sides of two membrane materials.

One membrane, a sulfone polymer, held more water in a bound form and had wider, varied pores. Cells stuck, spread, and met in balance far better on that surface, laying down shared matrix where the layers faced. Under gentle flow both membranes held their cells, yet the sulfone one resisted peeling more. The authors back it as the better base for filter models that aim to copy the real organ.
pmc-13579752:
Haodong Yuan and co-authors published a 2026 review on how support cells in the gut wall change identity, and why that matters for disease. Fibroblasts, the gut's scaffolding cells, can convert into contractile myofibroblasts. That switch helps normal repair and keeps the intestine in balance. When it stays switched on, it drives scarring and reshapes the tissue around tumors.

The review stresses that the switch is not a lone decision. Neighboring cells talk the fibroblasts into or out of it, through signals timed and placed with care. Mapping those conversations is the paper's core work. The authors then survey treatments that aim at the conversation network rather than at single molecules. Their targets include inflammatory bowel disease, intestinal fibrosis, and gut tumors. The hope is that re-tuning cell talk could soften the tissue changes that make these diseases hard to treat.
pmc-13579852:
Yu and a large team built a forecast tool in twenty twenty-six for bladder cancer, a common cancer of the urine system. A key drug for it often fails when the cancer learns to resist it. The team sought genes and cell traits that drive that loss.

They joined gene data from single cells with a smart tool that reads stained tissue slides. A cell group with many gene copy shifts had a poor outlook for patients. One gene, RTN3, stood out as a core driver of that group. Lab tests showed RTN3 helps the cancer resist the drug and calms the body's attack on it.
pmc-13580352:
Yanling Li and co-authors map small zones within the main visual area of the brain, in a research paper from 2026. They combine maps of brain wiring and brain activity, since each map alone gives a weaker split. The zone they map first handles sight and is known as V1.

Their grouping method links wiring and activity in one frame. It yields zones that fit biology better than single-map methods. One back zone of V1 showed clear odd patterns in people with autism. Those patterns tracked the weight of social symptoms. The atlas may help sort patients and judge response to care.
pmc-13580452:
Zhang and co-authors review in 2026 a class of fat handling immune cells that grow common in obese fat tissue. These cells carry programs for fat storage, waste clearing, and lysosome work. They gather in ring like clusters around fat cells and in other fat rich spots.

Single cell and spatial studies back their rise in obesity, with like cells seen in humans. Direct proof of what they do, above all in human fat, stays limited. They may buffer fat at first and turn inflammatory later, but that shift is a working model, not settled fact. The review ranks proof by strength and weighs care options that act through these cells.
pmc-13580952:
Children from intact two-parent families tend to do better at school. Tamara Gordeeva, Elena Dvorskaya, and Oleg Sychev ask what carries that advantage. They surveyed 2,402 Russian adolescents in grades 5 to 9. Family types covered intact, single-mother, and stepfather homes. Measures included drive, persistence, homework cheating, grades, and how happy they felt with family life.

Adolescents from single-mother and stepfather homes looked alike. Both groups scored below intact-family peers on family contentment, drive, persistence, and grades. They also reported more homework cheating and weaker attitudes to school. Modeling points to contentment at home as a key middle step. The authors argue warmth, not structure alone, drives much of the gap.
pmc-13581752:
Wenliang Liu and co-authors review how longan fruit extract protects blood vessel linings, in this 2026 paper. Longan is a traditional fruit valued as both food and medicine in China. Its extracts hold sugars, plant acids, and other active compounds that may guard the heart and vessels.

Following standard review rules, the team gathered studies from the past decade. In cell and animal work, longan compounds mopped up harmful free radicals and calmed inflammation signals in vessel walls. They also helped balance nitric oxide, a key vessel-relaxing signal, and blocked an enzyme that tightens vessels. The review maps these paths as a base for future drug work.
pmc-13581852:
Amnah Aldohan and four co-authors study pregnant university students and the gap between what they know and what they do. Their twenty twenty-six study deals with health behavior in pregnancy, where study load, family duties, and health needs collide. Knowing the right habits does not always mean living them.

Five hundred students at nine Saudi universities filled validated surveys, and interviews followed to explain the numbers. Awareness of healthy behavior was very high, yet practice lagged behind it. Quality of life scored better on general health and time use than on emotional and family sides. Students named academic pressure, thin support, and uneven access to services. The authors urge joined-up campus support.
pmc-13582252:
Duc Duong Than and co-authors track a shift in H5N1 bird flu lineages in Laos, in a research paper from 2026. A highly harmful H5N1 group has returned to the region, raising fears of spread and risk to people. The team asks which lineage now sits in poultry markets and how it connects across borders.

Eight viruses from market samples in 2023 and 2024 all fell in a new lineage, distinct from the old local one. The viruses spread across regional branches rather than one local cluster. That pattern points to repeat entries from outside. Gene checks show bird-type traits, with a cutting site linked to high harm.
pmc-13583852:
Satinder Deswal and a team of co-authors studied warning signs for a setback in brain tuberculosis, in two thousand twenty-six. Some patients get worse during treatment even as the germs die off, a response called a paradoxical reaction. The team enrolled more than one hundred fifty new patients and tracked blood and spinal fluid markers.

About three in ten patients had the setback, most within the first two months of treatment. Higher levels of several swelling markers at the start went with higher risk. One marker, ferritin, predicted the setback best, and it stayed a strong sign after other factors were weighed. The authors suggest such markers could flag patients who need early anti-swelling care.
pmc-13583952:
Misa Yanai and co-authors study what drives parenting worries among Japanese parents with cancer who raise young children, in work from twenty twenty-six. A cancer diagnosis strains the whole family, and worries about children run deep. Data came from a web survey of an online patient support network.

One hundred fifty-seven married parents formed the analysis group, most of them women with a median age of forty-five. Higher concern scores tied to uterine or ovarian cancer, chemotherapy, and a past or current mental health history. Wanting hands on parenting support also tracked with higher worry. Wanting practical help stood out across model versions. The authors warn the small, single network sample cannot support firm clinical targeting.
pmc-13584252:
Negin Mirzaei Damabi and colleagues interviewed health workers in South Australia about sexual function care for women who have migrated. Sexual function is a part of health that clinics often skip, and migrant women face added barriers such as stigma, language gaps, and mistrust of services. The 2026 study drew on talks with ten providers, among them nurses, allied health staff, and a gynaecologist.

Providers said routine visits stayed focused on birth control and rarely reached sexual concerns. Cost rules that shut some women out of public cover, weak interpreter support, and split care paths made help harder to reach. The team calls for staff training in safe, culturally aware care, clearer system guidance for patients, and funded therapy shaped to each woman's background.
pmc-13584452:
Sefa Tan and colleagues report on a nerve block for stubborn neck and upper back pain in this 2026 study. The pain pattern, called myofascial pain syndrome, comes from tender muscle and its wrapping tissue and often shrugs off standard care. Under ultrasound guidance, doctors injected numbing medicine into a tissue plane near a back muscle, a block with a long technical name shortened here to the serratus plane block.

Seventy-five patients treated over one year were followed for six months. Pain scores fell fastest in the first hour and kept easing across the follow-up visits. Neck disability scores and quality-of-life scores improved at every check, and no major complications were recorded. Because the study looked back without a comparison group, the authors call for a forward-looking trial to prove the block's worth.
pmc-13584952:
Michelle Prielipp and co-authors measure a repair protein in the spinal fluid of dogs with brain and cord diseases in this 2026 study. The protein, ApoE, is released by support cells after nerve injury. It aids regrowth and calms inflammation. Its links to a known inflammation marker were described in mice, not dogs. The team sampled fluid from well over a hundred dogs in care. Groups covered epilepsy, disc herniation, brain inflammation, and a wasting cord disease, plus healthy controls.

New and sudden lesions made the protein easier to detect. That pattern fits its role as an early response to injury. A fluid marker could help vets sort look-alike diseases faster. It might also track how a lesion heals over time. The study is veterinary neurology with a lab assay at its core. Full group comparisons appear in the article.
pmc-13585552:
Gullapalli and coauthors track a virus shell used to carry genes to the brain. The virus, called AAV2, is a top choice for brain gene care. Teams know little about how long its shell stays in brain tissue. They also know little about how shell stay links to gene output.

The team put AAV2 into a deep brain zone in rats. They checked tissue at five points, from three days to more than a year. Stains marked both whole shells and the new gene product. Shells reached nerve cells fast and spread to linked zones. The maps show how shells clear over time.
pmc-13585952:
Yutaka Miyawaki and colleagues reflect on how long patients with early esophageal cancer can safely wait for surgery. Their cancer type, squamous cell carcinoma of the chest part of the food pipe, was caught at a stage classed cT1bN0M0, early enough for surgery first without prior treatment. Past work on waiting times mostly covered advanced disease, so the safe window for this group was murky.

Their linked study followed 160 patients at seven Japanese hospitals between 2008 and 2021. A wait of about 67 days or more marked the line where three-year freedom from recurrence dropped clearly, though deaths from the cancer itself did not differ firmly. Longer waits, deeper tumor growth, and node spread each predicted return of disease on their own. The authors treat the cutoff as a rough guide that needs testing in a bigger group.
pmc-13586052:
Zuzanna Bechler and Liliana Surmacz trace seventy years of research on a family of long oily molecules called polyisoprenoids. Two branches, polyprenols and dolichols, turn up in every form of life and keep cells alive. Their 2026 review walks through how cells build them in three stages: making five-carbon starter units by two known routes, chaining those units together, and finishing them into working alcohol forms.

These molecules ferry sugars onto proteins, tune how cell membranes flow, and help cells weather stress. Fresh findings have lately redrawn the classic picture of how dolichols are made, a shift the authors call a change of paradigm. Big unknowns remain, above all how the chain-building enzymes are controlled and what these molecules do over long stress. Disease links and test uses round out the survey.
pmc-13586252:
Cuijie Chen and colleagues audited a decade of cell-line authentication in China, checking more than 10,000 samples. Misidentified and contaminated cell lines undermine reproducibility, with an estimated fifth to a third of lines compromised, yet few labs verify routinely. Their 2026 study authenticated 11,087 lines from 6,947 Chinese institutions between 2016 and 2025 using DNA fingerprinting.

Testing volume and accuracy rose steadily each year. HeLa, T24, K-562, HEK293T, and A-549 emerged as the most frequent contaminants, and mutation rates at key fingerprint sites ran far above germline rates. A new weighted algorithm based on site-specific mutation rates beat the classic Tanabe method, cutting false calls. The authors also warn that rising mouse-model use demands fuller reference databases.
pmc-13586452:
Fitness of the heart and lungs is often linked to sharper thinking in later life, but a 2026 comparison across two countries found opposite patterns. Jiangping Ma and four co-authors estimated fitness from everyday measures in about 3,500 Chinese and 6,900 American adults in two long-running aging studies. Both groups sorted into high, middle, and low thinking trajectories over time.

In the American group, fitter adults were a bit less likely to sit in the middle trajectory. In the Chinese group, fitter adults were more likely to sit in the low and middle ones, a surprise that survived extra checks. The authors urge caution and more study of why the link flips.
pmc-13586552:
Dimitrios Papadimopoulos and co-authors report a case where a feared drug side effect masked a dying infection, in work published in 2026. A man aged forty-three came in with acute penile swelling after sex and use of a drug for erection trouble. Lasting erection was the first suspect, but blood gas tests from the organ ruled out the trapped-blood form.

Drugs for germs began at once, yet swelling and redness grew with early dead tissue. A relative then shared a past of poorly treated syphilis, which blood tests confirmed. Surgeons cut away the dead tissue. He healed with function kept, after referral for full syphilis care.
pmc-13586752:
Alessandro Piccirilli and his team set out the traits of a germ strain that can stand up to lots of drugs and bears the NDM-1 shield gene. It was found in Italy. Their 2026 gene study looks at Enterobacter hormaechei, a germ that strikes when it can and drives sick-bay ills.

pmc-13624552:

pmc-13626752:

pmc-13627052:

Stopping the pramipexole ended the behavior. The authors call it the first reported case of its kind and stress the damage hidden, unremembered disorders can do. They urge doctors to warn patients about impulse risks in both waking and sleeping hours before starting these drugs.
pmc-13685052:
Maria Eleni Hatzipanagiotou and co-authors review eight years of care for familial breast cancer at a German center in this 2026 paper. About a third of breast cancer cases involve raised family risk, often tied to inherited gene faults. The team studied hundreds of patients who met the national criteria for high family risk.

Nearly half the patients carried a harmful variant, most often in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes. Tumor types differed by gene: one gene leaned toward a fast-growing form with no hormone response. Drug treatment rates and full response rates also varied by gene, with one group responding best. The study supports care fitted to each patient's genetic profile.
pmc-13687152:
Robert Li, Hong Zhu, and Michael Trush trace how a known carcinogen's breakdown products make toxic oxygen species in mitochondria. Their twenty twenty-six article studies benzo[a]pyrene, a pollutant from smoke and charred food. Its quinone metabolites were known to spawn reactive oxygen, but the route was unclear.

In isolated mitochondria, all four quinones tested drove oxygen use that cyanide could not stop, a sign of redox cycling. Three were strong, and one worked at very low doses, which makes mitochondria potent amplifiers of the stress. Blocking tests point to complexes I and III of the electron transport chain as the main sites. Complexes II and IV played little part.
pmc-13689452:
Zeeshan Sidiq and five co-authors tested a joint PCR assay for tuberculosis and its kin. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, ran in a high burden setting. Fast reads on TB and drug resistance drive control of the disease. A test that spots the TB group, its non TB kin, and first line drug resistance at once could smooth the lab path. They ran two paired assays on three hundred well marked samples.

Half the samples held the TB group; half did not. Set standards from culture and other tests graded the calls. The TB read hit full marks on both catch and rule out in this set. Readers who run TB labs in hard hit lands get a one run path for three asks.
pmc-2798952:
Hilty, Burke, Pedro, and co-authors compare airway microbes in adults with asthma, COPD, and healthy controls. A rich microbial setting in infancy seems to protect against asthma, while infections can trigger asthma attacks. The airways were once thought nearly sterile, making this a fresh question.

The team sampled airway communities at several levels of the bronchial tree. They found disordered microbial communities in asthmatic airways, differing from those of controls. Such differences raise new ideas about asthma care, in which managing airway microbes might join managing inflammation as a treatment goal.
pmc-3138752:
Supek, Bosnjak, Skunca, and co-authors present REVIGO, a tool that summarises long lists of Gene Ontology terms. High-throughput experiments are usually interpreted by testing which gene functions appear more often than chance. The resulting lists can be huge and highly redundant, making them hard to interpret.

REVIGO trims near-duplicate terms and visualises what remains, so the main themes stand out. A shorter, clearer list helps researchers explain an experiment's story to others. The tool became a popular final step in gene function analysis across biology.  Pictures in the tool turn tangled term lists into grouped, readable thematic summaries.
pmc-3665452:
Meier-Kolthoff, Auch, Klenk, and co-authors present genome sequence-based species delimitation with confidence intervals. For twenty-five years, drawing species boundaries among bacteria and archaea rested largely on DNA-DNA hybridization. That slow lab procedure, devised in the early 1970s, served well before genome sequences were available.

Their method, GGDC, estimates the same distances from genome sequences and reports how confident each estimate is. Improved distance functions make digital values track the old lab standard closely. Taxonomists gained a fast, repeatable replacement for a laborious wet-lab ritual.  Improved distance functions reduced the cases where digital and lab values disagreed.
pmc-4455052:
Bao, Kojima, and Kohany updated Repbase in 2015, a database of repetitive elements in eukaryotic genomes. Repetitive sequences make up large parts of many genomes and must be known before a genome can be read well. Repbase began in 1992 as a database of human repeats.

Since then it has served as a well curated reference for almost all eukaryotic genome projects. It holds representative sequences for each repeat family, checked by experts. Genome teams use it to find and mask repeats so gene finding is not confused. Without such a reference, new genome assemblies would be far harder to interpret.
pmc-5661652:
Yiliang Peng and Carlo Croce reviewed the role of microRNAs in human cancer in 2016. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that do not code for proteins but help control how genes are used. Many studies had shown their levels go wrong in tumors.

The review describes how microRNA genes can be copied too often, lost, or silenced by chemical marks. It also covers how single microRNAs can push cancer growth or hold it back. Because these molecules are stable in blood, they may serve as markers for finding cancer early. The authors argue they could also become drug targets in time.
pmc-5891552:
Lidwine Mokkink and colleagues presented the COSMIN Risk of Bias checklist in 2017. Questionnaires that patients fill in about their own health are used in many trials. Reviews of those tools need a way to judge the studies behind them.

The checklist adapts earlier COSMIN standards to the review setting. It asks whether each study of a measurement trait was designed and run well. Ratings are kept separate for each trait, such as reliability or validity. Reviewers use it to avoid trusting scores from weak studies. It supports fair choices among rival questionnaires.
pmc-6844052:
Xinming Jing, Fengming Yang, Chuchu Shao, and coauthors reviewed low oxygen, or hypoxia, in cancer therapy in 2019. Solid tumors often outgrow their blood supply and turn hypoxic inside. That state reshapes gene activity and breeds treatment resistance.

The review explains how low oxygen steadies master switches that favor survival, new vessels, and spread. Radiation and many drugs work worse where oxygen is scarce. Strategies that target the hypoxia program itself are surveyed. Oncologists read it to understand a stubborn root of therapy failure in common cancers. The review also weighs oxygen-sensing drugs now being tested to undo this resistance.
pmc-6853652:
Manoj Kamat, James Blackshaw, Robin Young, and coauthors presented PhenoScanner version 2 in 2019. PhenoScanner stores results from large human genetic association studies. It lets users scan what traits a genetic variant is linked to.

The expanded tool covers many more studies and trait types than the first version. A variant tied to one disease may also affect lipids, behavior, or drug response, and the scan reveals that fast. Such cross-checks help judge whether a gene-based causal claim is believable. The resource serves genetics teams planning follow-up studies. Both batch and single-variant lookups are offered through a simple web form.
pmc-7084952:
Cuiyan Wang, Riyu Pan, Xiaoyang Wan, and coauthors surveyed mental responses in China at the start of the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020. The epidemic was declared an international emergency and strained public resilience. Data were needed to design support for mental health.

Their online survey found high rates of anxiety, depression, and stress in the general public. Women, students, and people with physical symptoms reported worse states. Clear, current health information and protective measures were tied to lower distress. The study was one of the first to size the outbreak's psychological footprint.
pmc-7619452:
Julia Türtscher and two colleagues give the first full account of the skeleton of Myledaphus bipartitus, a freshwater ray from the age of dinosaurs. The species is known from Late Cretaceous rocks in North America, but mostly from teeth and fragments. A remarkably complete specimen from the Dinosaur Park Formation in Alberta, Canada, finally let the team describe the whole skeleton in detail.

The anatomy mixed older, primitive traits with newer derived ones in a combination not seen before. Family-tree analysis placed the ray within Rhinopristiformes, the group that includes today's guitarfishes and sawfishes. Placing a fossil firmly among living relatives sharpens the timeline for when that group's body plans appeared. The detailed description gives future fossil finds a reference skeleton to be measured against.
pmc-9710552:
Pierre-Alain Chaumeil, Aaron Mussig, and Philip Hugenholtz released GTDB-Tk version two in 2022, a memory friendly update of the toolkit that classifies genomes against the Genome Taxonomy Database. The toolkit had been widely adopted across microbiology. But as the database's bacterial reference tree grew, the program's memory demands grew with it, reaching levels many computers could not supply.

The new version restructures how classification works so it needs far less memory while placing genomes the same way. The authors explain the changes and check that accuracy holds. Removing a hardware barrier matters because genome classification is a routine step, and not every lab has a large server on hand.
rosicrucian-manifestos-vaughan-1652:
Thomas Vaughan put the Fama and Confessio into English in 1652, the first English Rosicrucian texts. The two manifestos first came out in German lands in 1614 and 1615. They claimed a hidden brotherhood held deep lore and sought to reform the world.

The Fama tells of Christian Rosenkreuz, his travels, and his vault tomb. The Confessio calls scholars to join the work and share their finds. No proof of the brotherhood ever surfaced, yet the call stirred Europe. Vaughan's version spread the Rosy Cross myth across England in time. Alchemists and seekers mined these pages for secret lore.
self-culture-and-perfection-of-character: O. S. Fowler, editor of a journal of phrenology, wrote this guide to self-culture and the shaping of character, with a section on guiding the young. Its motto declares that a person is self-made or never made. The pages at hand show the title page of a stereotyped printing, sold in New York by Fowlers and Wells at their phrenology rooms on Nassau Street. No chapter text appears in these opening pages, so Fowler's methods and advice cannot be stated beyond the aims his title announces.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Volume VIII of the Slave Narratives holds the Maryland accounts, built from talks with former slaves. The typed records were made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938 for the state of Maryland, and the Library of Congress project put the set together at Washington in 1941. The list of those who spoke begins with Lucy Brooks and Lafayette Brooks, then Charles Coles, James V. Deane, Mrs. M. S. Fayman, and Thomas Foote.
stowe-uncle-toms-cabin-1852:
Harriet Beecher Stowe published Uncle Tom's Cabin in 1852, with the subtitle Life Among the Lowly. The contents alone map a wide cast, from an evening in Tom's cabin to a Quaker settlement. Early chapters show Eliza learning she may lose her child and choosing flight.

Eliza's escape across the ice, little Eva, Topsy, and the cruel Simon Legree became known to millions. Tom's faith under harsh masters forms the moral core of the long tale. The novel sold hundreds of thousands of copies in its first year. It turned broad feeling against slavery and became the best-selling novel of its century.
the-cossacks-a-tale-of-1852: Leo Tolstoy's The Cossacks, a tale of 1852, appears here in the translation by Louise and Aylmer Maude. The contents list runs to more than thirty-nine numbered chapters, with no chapter titles given. The chapters carry no titles of their own. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-intere: Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, so no story text or contents list appears. The header names the work as Most Interesting Stories of All Nations, edited by Julian Hawthorne, and dates the electronic edition December 1998, prepared by Donald Lainson. A companion record under a similar title does show the American contents for the same Hawthorne volume. This record by itself gives no story titles, no authors, and no introduction. Nothing more can be grounded from what is present here.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Volume 19, No. 542, dated April 14, 1832, promotes the Beulah Saline Spa at Norwood. A recent pamphlet by Dr. George Hume Weatherhead drew the magazine's attention. Country people nearby had long used the spring for various diseases, he reported, keeping its healing reputation alive through years of neglect.

Beulah lies seven miles south of London on the Norwood hills, about 390 feet above the sea. Opened to the public late the previous August, the spa already drew several hundred visitors a week through the autumn. Norwood itself, within living memory a forest of oaks and a resort of gipsy families, was filling with new suburban villas along its uneven roads.
the-philosophy-of-phrenology-1852:
An unnamed writer, a member of the phrenological and philosophical societies of Glasgow, wrote The Philosophy of Phrenology, published at Glasgow by W. R. M'Phun. The book is dedicated to the memory of Gall. The scanned title page is rough, but the preface to the first edition can be read. In it the writer says he has kept to principles more than details, aiming at plain, clear style.

Every student, he argues, easily learns the facts of the organs: their place, form, and uses. The philosophic phrenologist looks also to principles, without which his views stay mere trial and error. Facts are only the loose materials of a science; principles bind them into something solid and lasting. The preface sets out a method, not a head reading.
theatrum-chemicum-britannicum-containing: Theatrum chemicum britannicum, 1652. The British chemical theatre. This book preserves that collection. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
theatrvm-chemicvm-britannicum-containing: A battered title page, in rough old spelling, announces the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum. It promises several poetical pieces by famous English philosophers. Those writers treated the hermetic mysteries in their own ancient language. Elias Ashmole collected the pieces into one volume with annotations. The book was printed in London in 1652 for Nathaniel Brooke at the Angel in Cornhill. An address to students of hermetic learning begins. Only these front pages, heavily garbled in transcription, are present here.
tob-0152:
Crowley's Vision and the Voice records his workings of 1909 in Algeria, where he scryed the thirty Aethyrs of the Enochian system. Vision by vision, angels, abysses, and terrible splendors pass before him. The notebooks became one of Thelema's central records of attainment.

Volume four of the notebook edition continues the transcribed series. Crowley crosses the Abyss in the visions and claims the grade of Magister Templi, master of the temple. The text is dense, symbolic, and meant for initiates. The material remains under copyright, with no public-domain text distributed here. Students of Crowley treat the work as his spiritual diary at its most intense.
tob-13152:
A. E. Waite devoted his late work The Holy Grail to the legends of the Grail, the vessel of the Last Supper and the Crucifixion. Waite was both occultist and scholar of Christian mysticism. He had chased the Grail's meaning through years of study.

He traces the tales from early romances onward, asks how they took Christian shape, and argues the Grail hides a secret tradition of the church. The book is dense, learned, and fully Waite's own in its claims. Readers of Arthurian romance and of occult history alike treat it as the mature sum of his Grail research.
turgenev-sportsmans-sketches-1852:
Ivan Turgenev published A Sportsman's Sketches in 1852, his twenty-five sketches of peasant life under serfdom. The sketches exposed serfdom's cruelty so tellingly that the book is credited with helping free the serfs. Turgenev, hunting with his spaniel, listens more than he shoots, and Russia heard its peasants speak.

Khor and Kalinych, the first sketch, pairs a shrewd, practical serf with a dreamy, gentle one in Orel province. Bezhin Meadow gives peasant boys telling ghost tales by a night fire, in pages of famous beauty and dread. Landowners, overseers, and serf actors and singers fill out a survey no statistics could match for truth of life. The sportsman's mild voice let radical matter past the censor into the conscience of the reading class of Russia. Alexander II kept the book by him, it was said, when he signed emancipation.
un-ga-res-1752: West New Guinea passed from Dutch hands toward Indonesia under a deal noted in Resolution 1752, adopted on 21 September 1962. Indonesia and the Netherlands had settled their long fight over the land. The Assembly thanks the Acting Secretary-General for his work in bringing the peace about. It takes note of the deal, accepts the role the deal gives the Secretary-General, and grants him power to carry out the tasks laid on him.
un-ga-res-1952:
Hope and pressure mix in Resolution 1952, adopted by the General Assembly on 11 December 1963, on the question of Northern Rhodesia. The British-run land, soon to become Zambia, stood near the end of colonial rule. The Assembly had read the report of its decolonization team and heard the ruling power report fresh steps toward a new constitution that same month.

The text states again the fixed right of the people of Northern Rhodesia to rule themselves and stand free. It notes with pleasure that votes for a new law-making council will be held in January 1964. Britain is asked to fix, with the new elected rulers, a date for freedom, and as soon as can be. The hope is voiced that no new block will bar the way.
un-ga-res-a-69-52:
United action toward a world free of nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/52, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. All states, it holds, must take fresh, workable steps toward the total end of such arms. The end goal of all arms work is named: full disarmament under strict and sound world check.

Deep worry at the ruinous toll of any use of nuclear arms runs through the text. All states must keep to world law at all times, the law of war among it. Every effort must be made, it holds, to shun the use of such arms at all. The vote stands in a yearly chain that keeps the end goal in sight.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 1752 (XVII) was adopted on 21 September 1962. It welcomed the settlement of the dispute over West New Guinea, also called West Irian. The dispute was between Indonesia and the Netherlands. The Assembly took note of their agreement. It praised the Acting Secretary-General's part in reaching a peaceful deal. It gave the Secretary-General power to carry out the tasks the agreement gave him.

General Assembly Resolution 1952 (XVIII), adopted on 11 December 1963, concerned Northern Rhodesia, the British-ruled territory that soon became Zambia. The Assembly restated the people's firm right to self-rule and independence, in line with the 1960 declaration on ending colonial rule.

The text welcomed word that voting for a new Legislative Council would take place in January 1964. It voiced the hope that independence would come at the nearest possible date. It asked the ruling power to fix that date, working with the newly elected government. It asked that nothing block the territory's move to statehood.

General Assembly resolution 69/52 (2014), 'United action towards the total elimination of nuclear weapons,' strings together the practical agenda of the Non-Proliferation Treaty system. It condemns the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's nuclear tests and missile launches in the strongest terms. It demands it abandon its programmes. It stresses that it can never hold nuclear-weapon state status. For the recognized nuclear powers it urges deeper cuts, test-ban ratification, and a fissile material treaty. It urges security assurances and universal safeguards. This comes ahead of the 2015 treaty review conference.
un-sc-res-1352:
Iraq's oil-for-food program let a sanctioned state sell oil to buy civilian goods, and it needed a short renewal in 2001. The Iraqi people had lived under sanctions for more than a decade. The program was a temporary measure, meant to cover civilian needs until Iraq met the Council's terms. Resolution 1352 was adopted unanimously on 1 June 2001.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the terms of Resolution 1330, the previous oil-for-food decision. Those terms would now run until 3 July 2001. That short span is the whole grant the resolution makes. The Council also stated what it intended next. New arrangements would be considered, to speed the flow of civilian goods into Iraq. At the same time, controls on goods banned under the sanctions had to grow tighter.
un-sc-res-1452:
Sanctions on the Taliban and Al-Qaida froze bank accounts around the world. Some frozen funds covered food, rent, and medicine for listed people. On 20 December 2002 the Security Council carved out a humanitarian exception. It acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The text amended how the asset freeze in resolutions 1267 and 1390 would work. States gained a way to release money for basic needs.

Funds could be freed when a state judged them necessary for basic expenses. Interest and contract payments could still be added to frozen accounts. The sanctions committee had to track which states used the exception. It would keep and update a list of them. The change softened a blunt tool without lifting the freeze.
un-sc-res-1552: In 2005 the Security Council added Resolution 1552 to its record, and the text is kept here through a Wikisource transcription. Formal resolutions like this one often extend or adjust an existing course of action rather than start one. Whatever its subject, the entry's worth lies in the exact official wording, preserved end to end.
un-sc-res-1652:
Côte d'Ivoire's peacekeeping operation was renewed by the Security Council on 24 January 2006. The International Working Group had issued a communiqué on 15 January backing the prime minister's road map to elections. The Secretary-General's report of 3 January 2006 was before the Council. The crisis and the blocks on reconciliation persisted from all sides, the Council said.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the mandates of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and of the French forces supporting it to 15 December 2006. The troop movement provisions of resolution 1609 (2005) ran for the same period. The Council said it would review the mission's tasks and troop levels alongside the coming report on Liberia. The aim was free, fair, open elections no later than 31 October 2006. Progress on the road map would guide any change to the force.
un-sc-res-1752:
Georgia's observer mission was renewed after an attack in the Kodori valley on 13 April 2007. The Secretary-General had reported on 11 January and 3 April. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force shared the work of steadying the zone. Talks on documents covering the non-use of violence and the return of refugees were near completion. Economic recovery in Abkhazia was judged badly needed.

The Council condemned the attack on villages in the upper Kodori valley and called for those behind it to be found. Both sides were told to resume dialogue and to honor the ceasefire and non-violence deals in full. The package of documents on non-violence and refugee return had to be finished without delay. The Council backed the confidence-building proposals put forward by the Group of Friends. It extended UNOMIG's mandate to 15 October 2007. Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity inside its recognized borders were restated.
un-sc-res-1852:
The inquiry into the Beirut bombing that killed former prime minister Rafiq Hariri gained a final extension on 17 December 2008. The International Independent Investigation Commission had sent its latest report. The Special Tribunal for Lebanon was on track to start work on 1 March 2009 at The Hague. The commission asked to run to 28 February 2009 so it could hand over without a break.

The Council welcomed the commission's report and praised the progress made on all the cases in its mandate. It extended the commission's mandate to 28 February 2009. The commission would keep investigating while shifting its operations, staff, and files to The Hague. Lebanon's prime minister had written on 4 December 2008 in support of the request. Once the tribunal opened, its prosecutor would take over the inquiry into the 14 February 2005 attack and any linked cases.
un-sc-res-1952: Adopted in 2010, Resolution 1952 is preserved in this collection as a Security Council act in record form. The transcription is English Wikisource's. Inside, the members state the situation in their shared diplomatic language, then convert it into instructions in numbered paragraphs. The entry keeps the conversion whole, which is where the Council's power lives.
un-sc-res-252:
Jerusalem's status brought Jordan's complaint before the Council in 1968. On 21 May 1968 the Council took up measures Israel had adopted in the city. The General Assembly had already told Israel to cancel such steps. Israel had instead taken more of them. The Council restated that land cannot be gained by military conquest.

It deplored Israel's failure to obey the Assembly resolutions. It held that all Israeli laws and acts meant to change Jerusalem's status are invalid. Taking land and property for that purpose cannot change the city's standing. Israel had to cancel the measures already taken. It also had to stop any further steps of that kind.
un-sc-res-452: For the year 1979, the catalog lists Resolution 452 among the Security Council's formal decisions. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-52: Three years of atomic work went on the record in Security Council Resolution 52, passed on 22 June 1948. The Atomic Energy Commission, set up by the Assembly's first vote in 1946, had sent the Council its first, second, and third reports. The Council rules that the Secretary-General send all three reports to the General Assembly and to all member states. The record of the Council's own talks on the reports goes with them, as a matter of special weight.
un-sc-res-652: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 652, which the catalog dates to 1990. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Iraq's oil-for-food program gained a short bridge in the spring of 2001. On 1 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1352 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The program let Iraq sell oil under UN control to buy civilian goods. Broad sanctions from the 1990 invasion of Kuwait stayed in place.

The text extends the current rules by about a month, to 3 July 2001. It then announces a plan for new rules. A Goods Review List would speed civilian trade. Controls on banned items would grow tighter. Oil cash would be kept inside the UN escrow account. The step led toward the revised sanctions of later months.

Frozen bank accounts can also freeze ordinary life. Resolution 1452, adopted unanimously on 20 December 2002, carved humanitarian room into the Taliban and Al-Qaida sanctions. People on the blacklist could not touch their money at all. That blocked rent, food, medicine, and legal bills, even where no terror link existed.

The text lets states release funds for basic expenses. Food, housing, medical care, taxes, utilities, and lawyers qualify. States must notify the sanctions committee first. Silence for forty-eight hours means consent. Larger extraordinary expenses need the committee's approval. Interest earned on frozen accounts stays frozen. The change kept pressure on listed terrorists while easing pointless hardship around them.

The year 1960 brought a wave of new African states to the UN. Congo won independence from Belgium that summer. Its freedom quickly slid into crisis and foreign meddling. Still, the new republic applied for membership at once. Resolution 152 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960.

Members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of the Congo. The Assembly soon did. A UN seat gave Congo legal standing during its turmoil. It also strengthened the case for the huge UN operation then deploying there. That mission tried to hold the country together. Congo's admission remains a marker of the great decolonization wave that reshaped the UN.

Weapons kept flowing to militias in Ituri and the Kivus, and on 27 July 2004 the arms embargo on armed groups in eastern Congo is renewed. A group of experts had reported on the flow. The parties, the Council found, had failed to meet its demands, and the inflow of arms kept the whole region insecure.

Acting under Chapter VII, the embargo measures are renewed until 31 July 2005. The measures would be reviewed by 1 October 2004 and regularly after that. The group of experts is re-established until 31 January 2005 to track compliance, with a written report due through the sanctions committee before 15 December 2004.

Resolution 1652, adopted on 24 January 2006, extends the UN operation in Côte d'Ivoire through most of that year. The Council had endorsed the international working group's January communiqué and the roadmap for ending the country's division. The Secretary-General's report of 3 January described a peace process still blocked by obstacles from all sides.

Under Chapter VII, the mandates of the UN operation, UNOCI, and the French forces supporting it were extended until 15 December 2006. The special arrangements for reinforcing UNOCI, set the previous June, were extended for the same period. The Council voiced deep worry that the crisis dragged on, a judgment repeated so often in these renewals that it reads as the era's refrain.

Resolution 1752, passed on 13 April 2007, keeps the UN watch team in Georgia for six more months. Two UN reports, in January and April, set out the team's work in Abkhazia. The Council praised the UN chief and his envoy for their steady push. A friends group, Russia as go-between, and a European security body all lent a hand. The team worked hand in glove with a peace force from the post-Soviet bloc, and both held the zone calm.

The team's term ran to October 2007. The Council restated its faith in Georgia's unity and its borders, as the world knows them. A pact could come by calm means alone, it said. Both sides were called back to talks. Trade and jobs in Abkhazia were named a dire need for the folk the war had hurt.

Resolution 1852, adopted on 17 December 2008, covers the final handover in the Hariri murder investigation. The independent commission investigating the 2005 bombing that killed Lebanon's former prime minister had asked for more time. The new Special Tribunal for Lebanon was on track to open at The Hague on 1 March 2009, and Lebanon's prime minister supported the request in a December letter.

The Council extended the commission's mandate until 28 February 2009. The point was continuity: investigators would keep working without a gap while gradually moving operations, staff, and files to The Hague, so the transition finished as the tribunal began. The commission's work on the bombing and other attacks since October 2004 was commended.

Armed groups in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo were still attacking civilians in late 2010. Resolution 1952, adopted on 29 November 2010, renews the sanctions aimed at those groups. The text names the FDLR and the Lord's Resistance Army. Money from illegal mining helped keep such groups armed.

The Council renewed the arms embargo, transport controls, travel bans, and asset freezes until 30 November 2011. It extended the group of experts that monitors the measures. A sixth expert was added to cover natural resources. The text also backed guidelines for companies that buy minerals from Congo. Firms were expected to check their supply chains with care. The aim was to stop the mineral trade from paying for armed groups and abuses.

Resolution 2052, adopted on 27 June 2012, renews the UN Disengagement Observer Force on the Golan Heights. UNDOF watches the area of separation between Israeli and Syrian forces under a 1974 agreement. The Secretary-General reported breaches of that deal, including Syrian troops entering the area in March and shots fired at UN observer teams. Events in Syria's own conflict were starting to spill into UNDOF's zone.

The Council renews UNDOF for six months, until 31 December 2012. It calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338, respect the 1974 agreement in full, show the greatest restraint, and guard UN staff safety and access. It welcomes work to upgrade the force's gear and sites. A report on events and on steps toward Resolution 338 is due at the end of the period.

Jerusalem's status drew a firm Council line in the spring of 1968. On 21 May, it adopted Resolution 252. Thirteen members voted yes and none voted no. Canada and the United States held back. Israel had seized East Jerusalem in the 1967 war. It was now passing laws the Assembly had already called invalid. Jordan brought the matter back to the Council.

The text restates a core rule: land taken by war cannot be kept. It deplores Israel's failure to heed the Assembly. All Israeli steps that tend to change the city's legal status are declared invalid. Land seizures count among them. Israel must undo such steps and take no more. The Council held this line for decades.

Grenada's application for United Nations membership is the subject of Resolution 352, adopted unanimously on 21 June 1974. The Council had examined the Caribbean island's request, filed as document S/11311. Grenada had become independent from Britain in February of that year, under Prime Minister Eric Gairy.

In its only operative line, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Grenada to membership. Admission resolutions follow a fixed pattern because the Charter allows the Assembly to seat a state only after the Council recommends it. The entry in the record is brief, but it documents the small spice-growing island's formal entry into the community of nations in the mid-1970s.

Israeli settlements in the Arab territories occupied since 1967, including Jerusalem, are taken up in Resolution 452. A commission of the Council had examined the settlements and reported with recommendations. Israel had refused to cooperate with the commission. The resolution was adopted in 1979.

The Council praised the commission's work and accepted its proposals. It said that Israel's policy of building settlements in the occupied lands has no legal validity. The policy breaks the Fourth Geneva Convention, the text holds. The government and people of Israel were called on to stop at once. The building and planning of settlements in those lands, Jerusalem included, had to end. The commission was told to keep watching the situation and report back, given the size of the problem.

Early reports of the United Nations Atomic Energy Commission reached the Council in 1948. The commission had been set up after the Second World War to work on control of atomic energy. It sent its first three reports to the Council. Resolution 52, adopted on 22 June 1948, does one thing with them. It tells the Secretary-General to pass the reports to the General Assembly and to all member states. The record of the Council's own talks on the subject went with them, as a matter of special concern.

Namibia won its independence in March 1990, after decades under South African rule, and it applied to join the United Nations within weeks. Resolution 652 was adopted on 17 April 1990, without a vote against it. The Council examined Namibia's application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that the Republic of Namibia be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The recommendation crowned a long campaign, backed by the United Nations for many years, to free the country.
uslaw-usc-t2-s152:
Section 152 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the care and the use of the Smithsonian Library. It sits in Chapter 5, on the Library of Congress. The Smithsonian Institution is to have the use of the library named in a past section. That use is to be in the same way as before the move of the library. All the books, maps, and charts of the Smithsonian Library are to be kept with care.

Those works are to be kept in the same way as the works of the Congressional Library. The Smithsonian Library is not to be moved from that place, save on one of two terms. The first term is a pay-back by the Institution to the Treasury for the costs of binding and of care.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1852:
Section 1852 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the hold-back of state taxes from pay. It sits in Chapter 28, on the Architect of the Capitol, in a part on pay for staff. The rule turns on two marks in the law of a state. The first is that the law of the state calls for a tax on income to be got by a hold-back. That hold-back is a duty put on bosses as a class, to take sums from the pay of their staff.

The sums so held back are to be sent on to the heads of the state. The second mark is that the duty of hold-back is put as a class on the pay of staff who live in that state.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1952:
Section 1952 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with pays from a fund for the kin of two named men. It sits in Chapter 29, on the Capitol Police, in a part on the United States Capitol Police Memorial Fund. The men named are Detective John Michael Gibson and Private First Class Jacob Joseph Chestnut of the Capitol Police. Sums in the fund are to be paid to the kin of those two men, in the shares the text sets.

Half of the sums are to go to the widow and children of Detective Gibson. Half are to go to the widow and children of Private First Class Chestnut. The text shown sets two bars on that rule.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2252:
Section 2252 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers a transfer from the Capitol Guide Service. It sits in Chapter 31 of that title, on the Capitol Visitor Center, in the part on the Office of Congressional Accessibility Services. Part (a) of the section deals with a transfer of powers and staff. The transfer concerns the Congressional Special Services Office of the Capitol Guide Service.

On the transfer date, the items of that office pass as the subchapter directs. The items named are its contracts, debts, records, and property. Its appropriations and other assets and interests pass as well. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
voltaire-micromegas-1752:
Voltaire wrote Micromegas in 1752 as a tale with a sharp point. A giant from a star of Sirius, eight leagues tall, roams the sky. He picks up a small friend from Saturn on his way. The pair come to Earth and at first miss the folk who live here.

With a lens of cut gems they spot a ship full of men of thought. Talk with the small crew shows both pride and true wit in men. The giant laughs at wars fought for specks of mud. The tale is a root work of tales of guests from the stars.
wapping-witch-answer-1652:
Rival prints of the Wapping witch case drew a sharp reply in 1652. A Declaration in Answer to Pamphlets concerning the Witch of Wapping takes the other accounts apart point by point. Such print fights were common, but few over witch cases survive so fully.

The writer charges the first pamphlets with false reports and works to set the record straight. Readers watch two camps argue over what was said, done, and proved. The quarrel shows the witch panic fought out in the press as much as in court. It is a rare, clear look at how trial news was made and unmade.
wapping-witch-relation-1652:
London itself had a witch case in 1652, told in The Witch of Wapping. The pamphlet gives the full relation of the charge and trial in the riverside parish of Wapping. A city case drew eyes that county trials could not.

The text walks readers through the claims, the court work, and the fate of the accused. It brings the hunt for witches to the crowded streets and docks of the capital. Country fears look strange in town dress, and the print knows it. The case shows the panic could touch even the heart of London.
zoist-vol-10-1852:
The Zoist's tenth volume runs from April 1852 to January 1853. A decade of Elliotson's journal now stands in print. Mesmeric practice reports arrive from a loyal band of doctors and amateurs. Trance surgery, once the headline, now shares space with subtler mental cases.

Cerebral physiology still names half the journal's mission on its cover. Somnambulists and their feats draw the curious, as ever. The movement's complete record would fill thirteen volumes by 1856. Volume ten shows a cause grown older, its hopes and habits fixed. What the medical world dismissed, these pages preserved. That preservation is the set's lasting service.
